In Book Two, Chapter Three, George Weasley told Harry Potter that the Burrow was a little way outside the village of Ottery St Catchpole. In Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, the Weasleys drove from Devon to London to catch the Hogwarts Express, with Harry squeezed in among them. Mr Weasley muttered mile after mile about every pothole between Devon and London.

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Harry worked out that the Weasleys' watch over him at school had been planned from home. Somebody in Devon had counted up five children in one castle and allocated them.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, at the end of the summer term of 1994, Hermione and Dracina Malfoy sent two thick letters by a single school owl. They were addressed to Mrs M. Weasley, The Burrow, Ottery St Catchpole, Devon. Mrs Weasley read all twenty pages without saying a word. Then she looked out of the kitchen window, east towards Surrey, and smiled.

pages.title: The broomshed
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The Hogwarts grounds, near the Quidditch pitch
pages.html:
The broomshed is the shed in the Hogwarts grounds where brooms are put away after Quidditch, and where the school's own brooms are kept. Harry Potter was taking his Nimbus Two Thousand back there one evening in his first year when he saw Severus Snape slip off into the Forbidden Forest.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, in 1992, Gryffindor beat Hufflepuff in barely five minutes, with Snape as referee. Some time afterwards Harry left the changing room alone to put his Nimbus away in the broomshed, happier than he could ever remember feeling. On the way he saw a hooded figure come swiftly down the front steps of the castle, making for the Forest. He knew that prowling walk. It was Snape. Harry jumped back on his broom, followed him over the trees and, from the branches of a towering beech, overheard him threatening Professor Quirrell.

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, at Christmas 1992, Ron Weasley told Harry about a way into the broom shed round the back of the pitch, where the lock was broken. Fred and George had been using it for years. With the snow lying thick over the grounds, the two of them had the whole white, empty pitch to themselves.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry had been riding one of the school brooms at practice for a month: an ancient Shooting Star that smelt of the broom shed and pulled to the left.

pages.title: Hufflepuff Quidditch team
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Book One, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Hufflepuff Quidditch team plays for Hufflepuff House in yellow and black. In November 1993, under its new captain, Cedric Diggory, it beat Gryffindor by a hundred points.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, early in 1992, Hufflepuff lost to Gryffindor in barely five minutes, with Snape refereeing. As the match began, Dean Thomas led the Gryffindor stand in songs about them. The Hufflepuff stand, which did not, as a rule, get sung at, looked thoroughly bewildered. At the end the Gryffindors sang 'You lasted five minutes!' As the Hufflepuff team drifted down to the grass, not quite sure what had happened to them, Dean conducted a slower, crueller chant with his scarf, until Professor McGonagall told him that would do. In Chapter Ten the Hufflepuffs were still sore about Dean's singing.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in November 1993, the dementors came onto the pitch in a storm, and Harry Potter fell fifty feet from his broom. Cedric Diggory caught the Snitch right after. He tried to call it off and offered a rematch, but Oliver Wood would not have it. Hufflepuff won by a hundred points. In Chapter Ten, at the end of the month, Ravenclaw flattened Hufflepuff, when Cedric lost the Snitch to a tiny Ravenclaw girl who went past him like a thrown dart.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, on 22 August 1994, Harry Potter met Cedric Diggory at the Portkey on Stoatshead Hill. Cedric was by then both captain and Seeker of the Hufflepuff team, which had beaten Gryffindor the year before when Harry fell from his broom. Fred and George Weasley had never forgiven Hufflepuff for that match, however decent Cedric had been about it.

pages.title: Pomona Sprout
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Pomona Sprout teaches Herbology at Hogwarts and is Head of Hufflepuff House. She is a squat, kindly little witch with earth on her robes and a patched hat over her flyaway hair. It was her Mandrakes that revived the victims of the Basilisk in 1993.

Teaching

Professor Sprout teaches in the greenhouses behind the castle. First-years work in Greenhouse One. Greenhouse Three holds more interesting and more dangerous plants. There her second-years repot Mandrakes, wearing earmuffs against their cries, and prune Abyssinian Shrivelfigs. By the third year they have moved on to Puffapods.

She was one of the teachers who set enchantments to guard the Philosopher's Stone in 1991 to 1992. Hers was the Devil's Snare beneath the trapdoor.

In the saga

On 2 September 1992 she was bandaging the Whomping Willow, which the Weasleys' flying car had battered the night before, and was visibly annoyed when Gilderoy Lockhart interfered. That year her Mandrakes were the cure for the Petrified. She cancelled the last Herbology lesson of the autumn term to put socks and scarves on them herself. In March 1993 she was delighted when they threw a wild party in Greenhouse Three, and she saw them ready in time for the victims to be revived at the end of the year.

When Dracina Malfoy screamed at Goyle over Christmas tea, Sprout half rose from the staff table. While Hagrid was in Azkaban, it was probably she who fed Fang. She also reminded Lockhart of his boast that he knew where the entrance to the Chamber was.

In the autumn of 1993, after Sirius Black's break-in, she somehow kept turning up on the front steps whenever Harry crossed the Entrance Hall. At Christmas dinner, passing the cream, she asked Minerva McGonagall comfortably where her young man with the three rules was now. McGonagall said that she had not had word of him in some years, then changed the subject: 'Eat your pudding, Pomona, it's going cold.'

pages.title: Norbert
infobox: Dragon, Norwegian Ridgeback, Dragon breed, dragon
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Rubeus Hagrid; later Charlie Weasley's colleagues in Romania
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Norbert is a Norwegian Ridgeback dragon, hatched in Rubeus Hagrid's hut in the spring of 1992. Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger helped to smuggle him out of Hogwarts to Romania.

The Norwegian Ridgeback

The Norwegian Ridgeback is a rare breed of dragon. It is black, with a ridge of spines along its back, and it has poisonous fangs, which is unusual in a dragon. Its young learn to breathe fire earlier than those of any other breed, at between one and three months old.

Dragon breeding was banned by the Warlocks' Convention of 1709. It is hard enough to keep Muggles from noticing wizards without people keeping dragons in the back garden, as Ron Weasley pointed out, and in any case dragons cannot be tamed.

In the saga

Hagrid had always wanted a dragon. He won the egg at cards from a hooded stranger in the Hog's Head, who seemed glad to be rid of it. Hagrid had a few drinks that night, and let slip to the stranger how to get past Fluffy. He hatched the egg in his fire, with the help of Dragon Breeding for Pleasure and Profit.

When he hatched, Norbert looked like a crumpled black umbrella. He had huge spiny wings, a jet-black body, stubby horns and bulging orange eyes. He sneezed sparks. Hagrid called himself the dragon's mummy, and let his gamekeeping slide. Norbert trebled his length in a week, eating dead rats by the crate. He bit Ron's hand, which swelled up and turned green. He bit Hagrid's leg as well, and left Fang's tail in a bandage.

At midnight Harry and Hermione carried him to the top of the tallest tower. There Charlie Weasley's friends took him away to Romania, in a harness slung between four broomsticks. Hagrid had packed his crate with rats, brandy and a teddy bear. He sobbed as he sent him off, then cried for a week afterwards. Parting with Norbert is among the memories that queued to sit with Hagrid in Azkaban.

pages.title: The card-playing stranger
aliases: the stranger in the Hog's Head
infobox: Hooded and cloaked; his face never seen
Losing a dragon egg to Hagrid at cards
pages.html:
The card-playing stranger was the hooded man who lost a dragon's egg to Rubeus Hagrid over a game of cards in the Hog's Head, in the spring of 1992, and seemed glad to be rid of it. The egg was the price of finding out how to get past Fluffy. The man under the hood was Quirinus Quirrell.

The game of cards

One night in the spring of 1992 Hagrid was down in Hogsmeade having a few drinks at the Hog's Head, where, as he said, you get all sorts. He fell into a game of cards with a stranger who kept his hood up the whole time and never took his cloak off. The stranger kept buying him drinks. He asked what Hagrid did, and about the creatures he looked after, until Hagrid told him that what he had always really wanted was a dragon.

The stranger said that he happened to have a dragon egg, and would play cards for it. He had to be sure Hagrid could handle it, though, because he did not want it going to any old home. Hagrid told him that after Fluffy a dragon would be easy, and, as he admitted to Harry months afterwards, a good deal more besides: 'So I told him, Fluffy's a piece o' cake if yeh know how ter calm him down. Jus' play him a bit o' music an' he goes straight off ter sleep...'

Hagrid won the egg, which was a Norwegian Ridgeback, and hatched it in his fire. He called the dragon Norbert.

In the saga

Hagrid showed Harry, Ron and Hermione the egg the morning after he won it. He had had it, he said, from a stranger at cards: 'Think he was glad ter be shot of it, ter be honest.' Norbert grew alarmingly fast. In the end he was smuggled up to the top of the castle at midnight, to be sent off to Charlie Weasley in Romania.

Months later, at the end of the exams, it struck Harry how odd it was that a stranger with an illegal dragon egg in his pocket should turn up just when Hagrid wanted one. He went to ask Hagrid what the man had looked like. Hagrid had never seen his face, and admitted that he had told him how to get past Fluffy. Harry concluded that it had been Snape or Voldemort under that cloak.

In the chamber of the Mirror of Erised, face to face with Quirrell, Harry put it together at last. The stranger in the hood at the Hog's Head who had wanted to know all about Fluffy had been Quirrell, who carried Lord Voldemort on the back of his head.

pages.title: Charlie Weasley's friends
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Charlie Weasley, who works with dragons in Romania
Carrying Norbert away from Hogwarts, spring 1992
pages.html:
Charlie Weasley's friends were the four cheerful fliers who came down to the top of the tallest tower at Hogwarts at midnight in the spring of 1992. They carried off Norbert, Hagrid's baby Norwegian Ridgeback, to Charlie in Romania.

The arrangement

Charlie arranged it by letter. Some friends of his were coming to visit, but they could not be seen carrying an illegal dragon about. The handover had to be done in the dark.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, Harry Potter and Hermione Granger hauled Norbert's crate up to the top of the tallest tower. Ten minutes later four broomsticks swooped down out of the darkness. Charlie's friends showed them the harness they had rigged up, so that Norbert could hang between their brooms. Everybody helped to buckle him in. Harry and Hermione shook hands all round, thanking them very much.

pages.title: Fang
infobox: Dog, Hogwarts grounds, dog, boarhound, Hogwarts, Hagrid's pet
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Fang is Rubeus Hagrid's enormous boarhound. He lives with Hagrid in his hut on the edge of the Forbidden Forest. For all his size he is a coward, and much given to slobbering on visitors.

Description

Fang is a huge black boarhound who goes everywhere at Hagrid's heel, even into the Forest on patrol. He is far more frightening to look at than he is in fact, as Hagrid is the first to admit. He shows his affection chiefly by drooling on whoever happens to be nearest, and he likes to lay his great head on a visitor's knee to do it.

In the saga

In the spring of 1992 he sat outside the hut with his tail in a bandage while Norbert was in residence. On the night of the detention he went into the Forest with Hagrid and his crossbow.

In September 1992 he slobbered on Harry in the hut. One Tuesday in December he got his head stuck in a bucket. When Hagrid was taken to Azkaban, Fang howled, and laid his head in Harry's lap. Harry and Ron took him into the Forest to follow the spiders. Silenced with treacle fudge, he cowered in Aragog's hollow, then fled home after the rescue.

In September 1993 he was at Hagrid's heel for the first Care of Magical Creatures lesson. That evening he lay with his head in Hagrid's lap. He moaned under the table while Hagrid wept over the Ministry's letter about Buckbeak. The day after Sirius Black's escape he bounded up to slobber on Ron.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, at the World Cup campsite on 22 August 1994, Harry Potter waved back at Cho Chang, and Hermione Granger clamped her hand on his arm. Ron Weasley calmly prised her fingers off, telling her that Harry was only waving: 'He waves at Hagrid's dog.'

pages.title: Dragons
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The Common Welsh Green; the Hebridean Black
Book One, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Dragons are the great fire-breathing beasts of the wizarding world, and they cannot be tamed. Breeding them was banned by the Warlocks' Convention of 1709. Two breeds live wild in Britain, the Common Welsh Green and the Hebridean Black. The Ministry of Magic keeps them hidden from Muggles by putting memory spells on anybody who spots one.

Breeds and keeping

Abroad there are many more breeds, among them the rare Norwegian Ridgeback and the Hungarian Horntail. Charlie Weasley studies dragons in Romania, and has the burns from the wild ones to show for it. A dragon's egg must be kept in the fire, because its mother would breathe on it. According to Dragon Breeding for Pleasure and Profit, a hatchling should be fed a bucket of brandy mixed with chicken blood every half hour.

Saint George, who slew the most famous dragon in England, was a wizard. Whose strength he slew it with is another matter.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, in the spring of 1992, Hagrid kept an enormous black egg in the heart of his fire. It hatched on his table into a Norwegian Ridgeback, which looked to Harry Potter like a crumpled black umbrella. Hagrid called him Norbert. Ron Weasley pointed out that dragon breeding had been against the law since the Warlocks' Convention of 1709. 'It's hard enough stopping Muggles noticing us without people keeping dragons in the back garden.' Within a week Norbert had grown to three times his length. At midnight on a Saturday, friends of Charlie's collected him from the top of the tallest tower to take him to Romania.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Professor Trelawney told Harry that Saint George had been a wizard, who slew his dragon by magic and let the Muggles believe it was their God. The Fat Friar agreed that George had been a wizard. As for whose strength he had killed his dragon with, said the Friar, Harry was in a rather better position to judge than she was.

Later in the same chapter, watching Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy, Ron looked like a man who has spotted two Hungarian Horntails eyeing each other across a field, only to realise that he is standing between them. Before the Quidditch final Harry dreamt that Slytherin flew out on dragons instead of brooms. Dracina's was the largest, a long, glittering silver-green brute with a face like the statue in the Chamber of Secrets, and she jeered at him from its neck because he had no dragon to ride. Then his Firebolt vanished from under him, leaving him with nothing but a long, bright sword without a single jewel on it.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, at the Burrow on 21 August 1994, Harry Potter noticed what dragons had left on the two eldest Weasley brothers. Charlie, who works with them in Romania, had a large, shiny burn on one arm. Bill's boots were made of dragon hide, not leather.

pages.title: Common Welsh Green
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Common Welsh Green is one of the two breeds of dragon that live wild in Britain, the other being the Hebridean Black. It nests in the high mountains of Wales. As dragons go it is fairly peaceable, preferring sheep to people, and its roar is almost musical. The Ministry of Magic keeps it hidden by putting memory spells on any Muggle who spots one.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, in the spring of 1992, Harry Potter asked whether there were wild dragons in Britain. 'Course there are,' said Ron Weasley. 'Common Welsh Greens and Hebridean Blacks. The Ministry of Magic has a job hushing them up, I can tell you.'

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, while Harry lay in the hospital wing waiting for the bones in his arm to grow back, Ron told him that a Welsh Green had once had a go at his brother Charlie. Madam Pomfrey had grown Charlie a whole new ear. 'You can't even tell which one it was. Well, you can a bit. It's slightly bigger.'

pages.title: Hebridean Black
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland
pages.html:
The Hebridean Black is one of the two breeds of dragon that live wild in Britain, the other being the Common Welsh Green. It lives on the islands of the Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland. It is fiercer than its Welsh cousin, with rough scales, brilliant purple eyes and a row of short, razor-sharp ridges along its back.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, in the spring of 1992, Harry Potter asked whether there were wild dragons in Britain. 'Course there are,' said Ron Weasley. 'Common Welsh Greens and Hebridean Blacks.' The Ministry of Magic, he said, had a job hushing them up. 'Our lot are forever having to put spells on Muggles who've spotted one, so they forget.'

pages.title: Garou
infobox: Homid, lupus and metis; rarely, the biteborn, made by the bite
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Garou are the only werewolves there are. Most of them are born, to human mothers or to wolves. A few are made by the bite: the biteborn, whom the tribes despise as no true Garou although they are Garou in every measure. A Garou can take any of five shapes at will, carries a rage from birth, and counts itself a soldier of Gaia, the living Earth, in her war against the corruption called the Wyrm. They run in packs within thirteen tribes that are older than wands, and they keep their own law. The Delirium, which wipes the sight of them from most minds, hides them from wizards and Muggles alike.

Name and nature

What the Ministry of Magic calls a werewolf is a Garou, and there is no other kind. The Garou do not think of themselves as cursed. They think of themselves as soldiers, born enlisted, and they hold that everything in creation is either sound timber or rot. The rot is the Wyrm. They can smell it in a place, in an object, even in a man. Where they think about wizards at all, they think of them as children playing with matches in a dry wood. Most of the wizarding world, for its part, fears and reviles them.

The Triat and the Wyrm

The Garou say that Gaia, the Earth Mother, made them in the first days to be her warriors and the guardians of everything that lives. They teach that three great powers, together called the Triat, work through creation. The Wyld is raw creation and change. The Weaver is pattern and order. The Wyrm was once the force of ending and balance, which cleared away whatever had served its time. In the Garou telling, the Weaver went mad and bound the Wyrm in its web. The Wyrm went mad in its turn and became the Corruptor.

The being they mean is the one Scripture calls Satan, whom the elder days called Morgoth. He sang out of tune before the world was made, and he has worked against it ever since. Dark magic began with his rebellion. Every vampire descended from Cain belongs to him, through Lilith's trap. That is why a dementor, a Dark Mark and the name of Lord Voldemort all carry the same scent to a Garou: it is the oldest scent there is.

The Impergium and the War of Rage

In the age after the ice, the Garou grew afraid of mankind's numbers and of its growing works. For some three thousand years they held humanity down by culling it, and they call that age the Impergium. Many of them believe that the Delirium is its memory: a hunted creature's fear, still carried at the back of the human skull. The Impergium ended at a great gathering of the tribes called the Concord. The Children of Gaia were foremost in calling for its end, and the Garou agreed to hide among men rather than rule them by fear.

In the same ages the Garou made war on the other shapeshifting peoples, among them the bear-folk, the cat-folk and the raven-folk. Several of those peoples they destroyed outright. The Garou count that War of Rage among their great shames, with the Impergium beside it.

Breeds

The blood runs in families of humans and wolves called Kinfolk, who carry it without ever changing themselves. It can lie quiet for generations, in wizard and Muggle lines alike, until a child is born who has it. Nothing shows until that child is nearly grown and something wakes the blood in the First Change. Homid Garou are born to human mothers and grow up thinking themselves human. Lupus Garou are born to wolves and learn the shape of a man afterwards, as a child learns a foreign tongue. The child of two Garou is a metis, born in the war form, malformed and barren. The first tenet of their law forbids such unions.

A Garou can also be made by the bite, by any Garou, upon anyone, at any hour. It is rare. Their law frowns on it, and most of those who do it regardless serve the Wyrm. They are particular about whom they choose. The Black Spiral Dancers, the fallen tribe, make biteborn on purpose.

Moon signs and forms

The moon is not a Garou's cage but its birth sign. The phase under which a Garou is whelped fixes its role for life. Ragabash, born under the new moon, are tricksters. Theurges, born under the crescent, deal with spirits. Philodox, born under the half moon, are judges. Galliards, born under the gibbous moon, keep their people's histories in song. Ahroun, born under the full moon, are warriors. What the full moon does is raise the tide of rage, so that every Garou is harder to hold on the nights about it.

A Garou can wear any of five shapes at will, moon or no moon. Homid is the human shape. Glabro is a man a hand taller and half again as heavy, whom strangers cross the road to avoid without knowing why. Crinos is the war form, nine feet tall. Hispo is a wolf the size of a pony, and Lupus is an ordinary wolf. Silver burns a Garou in every shape, and silver wounds do not close; most other harm heals while you watch. The wounds a Garou deals, on the other hand, must heal the slow way, without magic, or not at all.

Rage and the Delirium

Every Garou carries a rage from birth. It is a substance rather than a temper, like the fire in a lamp, and a Garou's whole life is the keeping of that lamp. When the rage spills, what is left standing afterwards is a matter of chance. People and animals sense it without understanding it. They keep their distance.

The sight of a Garou in its war form brings on a hot, ancient fear, and the mind will not hold what it has seen. It closes over the place the way water closes over a stone. What grows back is a lie the witness believes for the rest of his life: it was a bear, or a neighbour who went mad and had to be shot. Muggles who see one forget, go mad, or both. Most wizards fare little better. Only the mad, the dying and those with a certain grounding are untouched.

The Litany and the packs

The law of the Garou is the Litany. The Philodox keep it, and it is recited, never written down. Garou shall not mate with Garou. They must combat the Wyrm wherever it dwells and whenever it breeds. They must respect the territory of another, accept an honourable surrender, submit to those of higher station and give the first share of the kill to the greatest in station. They shall never eat the flesh of humans. They must respect those beneath them, for all are of Gaia. They shall never lift the Veil, nor suffer their people to tend their sickness. A leader may be challenged at any time in peace, but never in war. Last of all, they shall take no action that causes a caern to be violated.

Garou live and fight in packs, each bound to a totem spirit. A pack does not leave one of its own to itself for long. Packs gather into septs. Each sept guards a caern, a holy place such as a ring of stones, or a spring in a wood where the trees seem to watch. The Garou can step sideways out of the world into the spirit world, which they call the Umbra. Above the septs stand the thirteen tribes, together called the Garou Nation. A fourteenth tribe, the Black Spiral Dancers, went over whole to the Wyrm.

The war against the Wyrm

The Wyrm works through spirits of corruption, which ride men and beasts alike. It works through poisoned land, through the fallen tribe, through vampires and through dark wizards. Garou can smell its work, and they are compelled to root it out. Many of them believe they are living in the last days of the war, which they call the Apocalypse.

Dark magic is the Wyrm's own craft, so a Garou finds a place like Hogwarts, steeped in dark magic as much as in light, very hard to bear. Animagus magic is a different matter. It is light magic, not touched by the Wyrm at all, and a Garou's war form will tolerate friends who come to it in animal shape.

The biteborn

Garou made by the bite are called the biteborn, and they are rare. In every way the Garou can measure, they are Garou. They wear the five shapes, carry the rage, have a birth sign and learn the Gifts. They walk the spirit world, smell the Wyrm, burn at the touch of silver and raise the Delirium in those who see them. All the same, the tribes despise them as no true Garou. To the tribes they are made things, born of a crime against the Litany and suspected of carrying the taint of whatever bit them. They are treated much as the metis are treated, or worse.

Remus Lupin is biteborn. Fenrir Greyback bit him when he was a very small boy, at a time when there was no cure for it. Before the Wolfsbane Potion was invented, Lupin was liable to change the moment he sensed anything that smelled of the Wyrm. His early changes were agony and a complete surrender to instinct. With nothing else touched by the Wyrm within reach, he tore at himself instead, because he was a wizard.

Lupin later ran with a pack in the hills of mid-Wales, most of them Fianna. They still send for him. They never let him forget that he was bitten, not born, or that he was a wizard, which was worse. He is still himself in his war form, and he remembers everything he does in it. For years he wore a wooden cross, since silver would burn him, until he gave it to Harry Potter in June 1994. His faith is how he keeps the lamp of rage from spilling.

What wizards believe

Almost everything wizards know about werewolves is wrong, because the Delirium takes the memory from nearly everyone who sees the truth. The textbooks are written for a Ministry that classifies only what it can bear to think about. They teach how to tell a werewolf from a true wolf by its snout, its pupils and its tufted tail. They give it two shapes instead of five, and they make the full moon its cage. The Werewolf Registry watches only those three nights a month, which, as Hermione Granger pointed out, are the nights when its precautions matter least.

Gilderoy Lockhart claimed to have faced a werewolf in a telephone box and to have cured one with the Homorphus Charm. No such charm exists, and no spell turns a Garou back into a man. Minerva McGonagall, who has faced Garou, teaches that a werewolf must be Stunned from a distance by at least three casters at once. Silver kills it, she says, not because of any curse but because it simply cannot bear silver. An angry Garou in its war form shrugs off Stunners, however, and the only sound course is to run.

In the saga

In the autumn of 1992, after Lockhart had made Harry Potter play a werewolf in class, McGonagall took Harry aside. She told him about the Garou, Gaia, the Wyrm, the Crinos and the Delirium. She warned him to run faster from one that had black fur and was dancing.

Lupin came to teach at Hogwarts in 1993, with a birth-sign mark scratched into his case. The boggart in the staffroom showed his class a bloodied war form that knew him. In November 1993, with Lupin absent, Severus Snape lectured the third years on the Garou. He set them an essay on recognising and killing them in each of their five shapes. Hermione worked out from it what Lupin was. At Christmas Lupin was away with his pack.

In June 1994 Lupin missed his Wolfsbane Potion and changed on the lawn under the full moon. Harry burned him with a silver Sickle. Sirius Black, untouched by the Delirium, fought him as a dog. Later that night, in the Forbidden Forest, Harry's Shield Charm turned white and forced Lupin back into a man. Lupin resigned after Snape let slip what he was. He told Harry that he could smell the Wyrm everywhere at Hogwarts.

pages.title: Warlocks' Convention of 1709
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Keeping dragons out of Muggle sight
pages.html:
The Warlocks' Convention of 1709 was the wizarding assembly that banned dragon breeding. Dragons are the hardest of all magical creatures to hide from Muggles, and they cannot be tamed.

The ban

The Convention met seventeen years after the International Statute of Secrecy came into force, when the wizarding world had gone into hiding and meant to stay there. Since 1709 nobody may breed dragons. The wild ones are watched over in reserves, such as the one in Romania where Charlie Weasley works.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, in the spring of 1992, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger found that Hagrid had won a dragon's egg. He was keeping it in the fire of his hut. Ron reminded Harry of the law. 'Dragon breeding was banned by the Warlocks' Convention of 1709. Everybody knows that.' It was hard enough, he said, stopping Muggles noticing wizards, without people keeping dragons in the back garden. The egg hatched all the same, into a Norwegian Ridgeback that Hagrid called Norbert. Harry and Hermione smuggled him up the tallest tower one night, where friends of Charlie Weasley collected him for Romania.

pages.title: Ministry of Magic
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
International Magical Cooperation; Magical Games and Sports; Magical Law Enforcement; Magical Transportation; the Regulation and Control of Magical Creatures; Mysteries
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Ministry of Magic is the government of wizarding Britain, led in 1994 by Cornelius Fudge as Minister for Magic. Its first concern is to keep the wizarding world hidden from Muggles. It also registers, licenses, raids and imprisons, sometimes without troubling with a trial. In August 1994 it staged the final of the Quidditch World Cup on a Muggle moor, while its Minister insisted that the Muggles' growing hostility to people with powers was being handled through proper channels.

Secrecy

Its Obliviators put Memory Charms on Muggles who see too much, among them those who spot wild dragons. An under-age witch or wizard who uses magic outside school is warned, and may be expelled.

In 1900, with the other wizarding governments of the world, the Ministry came to an arrangement with the Camarilla, the nearest thing the vampires have to a governing body. It lent the Camarilla its wards and Muggle-Repelling Charms to help keep the Masquerade. In return, no vampire who answers to the Camarilla may hunt, harm or feed on a witch or wizard. It is an old agreement and a fragile one. It has held, more or less, because both sides have more to lose than to gain by breaking it.

Strictly speaking, no magic is allowed when wizards gather in large numbers on Muggle land. The Registry of Proscribed Charmable Objects defines carpets as Muggle artefacts, so flying carpets are banned in Britain.

Registers and Azkaban

The Ministry keeps a register of Animagi, recording each one's animal and markings, because the transformation can go horribly wrong. It keeps a Registry of werewolves too, which watches them only around the full moon. Its prison is Azkaban, which the Dementors guard. The Ministry can send a witch or wizard there without a trial: Sirius Black spent twelve years in it without one.

Abroad

Abroad the Ministry prefers not to look. It declined to recognise the hidden village of Dark wizards in Siberia that Minerva McGonagall raided in the winter of 1966, though its men had been doing something to the people of the valley below for nearly thirty years. It also considers its campaign against the parasite creatures and the Nephilim closed. McGonagall's file at the Ministry is the record of her part in that work.

It looks still less closely at Otherworld, the hidden country beside Britain from which Captain Britain draws his power. It leaves Otherworld strictly alone. It keeps a file on Captain Britain, a Muggle whose powers are an Elvish enchantment and no kind of wizardry, but it has never decided whether the Statute of Secrecy covers him.

Departments

The Ministry works through departments and offices. Barty Crouch heads the Department of International Magical Cooperation, which arranged Portkeys across five continents for the 1994 World Cup. Ludo Bagman heads the Department of Magical Games and Sports. Amos Diggory works for the Department for the Regulation and Control of Magical Creatures, and Arthur Weasley for the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office.

The Department of Magical Transportation licenses Apparition, while a Floo Regulation Panel oversees the Floo Network. Smaller bodies include the Goblin Liaison Office, the Committee on Experimental Charms, the Improper Use of Magic Office and the Muggle Liaison Office. The Obliviators of the Accidental Magic Reversal Squad put mishaps right, chiefly by changing Muggle memories. The Unspeakables of the Department of Mysteries work in such secrecy that nobody knows what they do.

The Muggle crisis

By 1994 many Muggles had turned against anybody born with powers, and some had begun to attack wizards. Barty Crouch, almost alone in the Ministry, reads the Muggle newspapers. He complains that half the Ministry imagines it can all be tidied away with a few Memory Charms. Cornelius Fudge has been to see the Muggle Prime Minister four times since the spring of 1994, coming back from Downing Street grey in the face. He insists that Muggle matters go through the proper office, by confidential channels. Lucius Malfoy has concluded that the Ministry knows a great deal more than it is saying.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, Harry learnt of the Memory Charms put on Muggles who spot wild dragons. In Book Two, Chapter Two, in July 1992, the Ministry warned him over the Hover Charm that Dobby had performed at Privet Drive. That summer it was also raiding wizarding homes. In Chapter Seven, in September 1992, Arthur Weasley faced an inquiry over the flying car. In Chapter Thirteen the Ministry kept Dumbledore overnight in December, while Fudge was in a flap. In Chapter Fourteen it raided Malfoy Manor about a week before Christmas, without finding the hidden room. In Chapter Fifteen, in 1993, it considered closing Hogwarts over the attacks, as it had in 1943. In Chapter Eighteen Harry concluded that it could send a person to prison without a trial.

In Book Three, Chapter Three, Harry remembered the warning that more magic at Privet Drive could mean expulsion. In Chapter Four the Ministry pulled staff off their regular jobs to hunt Sirius Black, then stationed Dementors at Hogwarts. In Chapter Eight Lupin told his class about the arrangement with the Camarilla, made, by his reckoning, about ninety years before, give or take. In Chapter Nine Professor Snape, taking the class in Lupin's place, said that the Ministry had built its werewolf Registry on the one grain of truth in their textbook: that the full moon raises the tide in the Garou.

In Chapter Ten the Ministry ordered Dementor patrols in Hogsmeade after sundown. In the Three Broomsticks that same chapter, Cornelius Fudge assured Professor McGonagall that at least 'those parasite creatures and those Nephilim won't be bothering us again'. In Chapter Eleven, at Christmas dinner, McGonagall told the staff table about Siberia.

In Chapter Twelve, with the Dementor's Kiss now licensed for Sirius Black on sight, Lupin told Harry that of all the things the Ministry had ever licensed, it was the one he would walk to London to stop. In Chapter Eighteen Hermione described the register of Animagi, with each one's animal and markings. It held only seven names this century. In Chapter Twenty, with the Kiss authorised for Black, Hermione explained that Professor McGonagall had had to write all sorts of letters to the Ministry before it would let her have a Time-Turner.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Harry reflected that Sirius, who had spent twelve years in Azkaban without a trial, was on the run for crimes he had never committed because the Ministry was full of idiots.

In Chapter Four Arthur Weasley told Vernon Dursley that he worked for the Ministry. Vernon had never heard of it. At the Burrow Ginny explained that Molly wanted Fred and George to go into the Ministry like their father, while the twins wanted only to open a joke shop. Percy, newly at work in the Department of International Magical Cooperation, was writing a report for Mr Crouch on cauldron thickness. At dinner he complained that Ludo Bagman was making no effort to find Bertha Jorkins, missing in Albania for over a month. He hinted, too, at a top secret event his department was organising for after the World Cup.

In Chapter Five Arthur explained that the whole Ministry had worked for months on the World Cup. At the campsite an Obliviator, worn out from charming the Muggle manager ten times a day, complained that Bagman cared nothing for security. Arthur named the passing officials for Harry, from the Head of the Goblin Liaison Office to two Unspeakables. At lunch Barty Crouch warned that the Muggles were not merely worked up but organised. He would not have the Statute put at risk on British soil. Bagman let slip that something had been agreed and signed for Hogwarts. By dusk the Ministry had given up trying to stop the magic on the campsite.

In Chapter Six Arthur told Harry that a Ministry task force of five hundred had spent a year building the stadium. Harry flattered Cornelius Fudge about the Portkeys, then unsettled him with talk of mutants and Sentinels. Fudge said there were arrangements with the Prime Minister, through channels he called confidential. Lucius Malfoy told Harry afterwards that the Ministry knew far more than it was saying, and that Fudge was frightened. During the match Ministry wizards poured on to the pitch to separate the veela from the leprechauns, without much luck.

pages.title: Dragon Species of Great Britain and Ireland
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Dragon Species of Great Britain and Ireland is a library book on the dragons of these islands, among them the two native British breeds, the Common Welsh Green and the Hebridean Black. Hagrid consulted it in 1992, before he hatched Norbert.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, Ron Weasley went to see which section of the library Hagrid had been in, then came back with an armful of books on dragons. Dragon Species of Great Britain and Ireland was one of them, with From Egg to Inferno: A Dragon Keeper's Guide. Ron pointed out that dragon breeding had been banned by the Warlocks' Convention of 1709. Hagrid hatched Norbert, a Norwegian Ridgeback, all the same.

pages.title: From Egg to Inferno: A Dragon Keeper's Guide
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
From Egg to Inferno: A Dragon Keeper's Guide is a library book on keeping dragons, from the egg onwards. Hagrid consulted it in 1992, when he had a dragon's egg to hatch and no business having one.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, Ron Weasley went to see which section of the library Hagrid had been browsing, then came back with an armful of books about dragons, this one among them. Ron pointed out that dragon breeding had been against the law since the Warlocks' Convention of 1709. Hagrid had always wanted a dragon. Before long he had one, a Norwegian Ridgeback called Norbert.

pages.title: Dragon Breeding for Pleasure and Profit
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Dragon Breeding for Pleasure and Profit is a rather out-of-date library book on hatching and rearing dragons. Hagrid borrowed it in 1992 to hatch the Norwegian Ridgeback egg he had won at cards, and he kept it under his pillow. Dragon breeding has been against the law since the Warlocks' Convention of 1709, which makes the title optimistic.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, Hagrid pulled the book out from under his pillow to show Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger. 'It's a bit out o' date, o' course, but it's all in here,' he said. Keep the egg in the fire, it advised, since dragon mothers breathe on theirs, and once it hatched, feed the baby a bucket of brandy mixed with chicken blood every half hour. It had also shown him how to tell that his egg was a Norwegian Ridgeback. Hermione reminded him that he lived in a wooden house.

pages.title: Dittany
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Dittany is a magical herb with strong healing powers. Madam Pomfrey uses it in the hospital wing at Hogwarts as a green remedy for wounds. A few drops on a fresh cut will close it with a puff of greenish smoke. Its smell hangs about the wing, and about anybody who has lately been there.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, in the spring of 1992, Harry was revising in the library, looking up dittany in One Thousand Magical Herbs and Fungi, when Hagrid turned up there of all places.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, the hospital wing smelt of Dittany on the night Dracina Malfoy lay there after Buckbeak’s attack. In Chapter Seven, on the day Dracina’s brooch went missing, Ron caught the same smell on Hermione as she came up from the dungeons. ‘She smells of the hospital wing,’ he said. ‘Did you notice? That green stuff Pomfrey uses. Dittany.’ As Ron pointed out, the hospital wing was on the first floor, and the dungeons were underground. Harry told himself not to be stupid. Hermione had been with them all day.

pages.title: Astronomy Tower
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The tallest tower in the castle
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Astronomy Tower is the tallest tower at Hogwarts, reached by a long, steep spiral staircase. Astronomy is taught on its top at midnight. Its upper landings are among the quietest places in the castle.

The tower

Students chart the stars from its open top through telescopes, under Professor Sinistra. Few people climb the stairs at any other time, which makes the landings near the top a good place to be alone.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Harry and Hermione climbed to the top of the tallest tower at midnight on a Wednesday with their telescopes under their arms. In Chapter Ten, in the spring of 1992, the baby dragon Norbert was handed over to Charlie Weasley's friends on its top at midnight. In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Harry hid from Dracina's taunts in a window seat on a landing near the top, where hardly anybody ever came; Ron found him there.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, the tower was searched for Sirius Black on Halloween night 1993, along with Trelawney's room and the Owlery. In Chapter Sixteen the third-years sat their Astronomy examination at midnight on top of it, charting the moons of Jupiter. In Chapter Twenty-one Cornelius Fudge saw the Dementors circling it in hysterics. In the Book Three Interlude John Constantine remembered the Slytherins hanging his robes from the tower in the 1960s.

pages.title: The tapestry of trolls in tutus
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
Barnabas the Barmy teaching trolls ballet
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The trolls in tutus are woven into a great old hanging on the fourth floor of Hogwarts. It shows Barnabas the Barmy's foolish attempt to teach trolls ballet, with the trolls, still in their tutus, clubbing him for his trouble. Percy Weasley once found it very interesting indeed.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, in 1992, Dracina Malfoy peered through a gap in Hagrid's curtains and saw the baby dragon, Norbert. Harry Potter chased her halfway up the lawn and brought her down in the grass. She got away from him and ran in through the oak doors. Harry pounded up the marble staircase after her, two steps at a time. The staircase shuddered and swung beneath him. By the time it had finished moving he was on the fourth floor, facing the trolls in tutus, and she was gone.

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, in December 1992, Ambrose Greyhame walked up through the castle. He stopped in front of the trolls in tutus for a whole minute, with his head on one side, then went on, chuckling into his beard.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, once the whole school knew that Sirius Black was after Harry, Percy Weasley took to shadowing him about the castle at a distance of exactly four paces. One day Harry stopped dead in an empty corridor, just to see what would happen. Percy stopped dead too, and examined the trolls in tutus with the frowning attention of a man at a gallery. 'I've no idea what you mean,' he told the trolls, when Harry said he could see him. 'I happen to be patrolling. Head Boy duties. The route is confidential.'

pages.title: The village
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The Three Broomsticks; the Hog's Head
pages.html:
The village is how Hogwarts people speak of Hogsmeade, the all-wizard village below the castle. Hagrid goes down there for a drink. It was there, in 1992, that he won a dragon's egg at cards from a stranger.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, Hagrid told Harry, Ron and Hermione where the egg had come from: 'I was down in the village havin' a few, an' got into a game o' cards with a stranger.' In Chapter Twelve he named the pub as the Hog's Head, 'one o' the pubs in the village', where you get all sorts. The stranger had kept his hood up the whole time. The egg hatched into Norbert. In Chapter Thirteen Harry understood at last that the hooded stranger who had wanted to know all about Fluffy had been Professor Quirrell.

pages.title: Herbology
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Herbology is the study of magical plants, and one of the core subjects at Hogwarts. It is taught by Professor Sprout, the Head of Hufflepuff House, in the greenhouses behind the castle.

Lessons

Lessons are practical, done with trowels, dragon dung and earmuffs. Students learn to handle such plants as the Mandrake, whose cry is fatal once it is fully grown. Devil's Snare, which likes the dark and the damp, is another.

In the saga

By Book One, Chapter Five, Neville Longbottom had already set fire to his own sleeve in an early Herbology lesson. In Book One, Chapter Ten, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger dropped their trowels at the bell, then hurried down to Hagrid's hut, where a dragon was hatching. In Book One, Chapter Twelve, under the trapdoor, Hermione remembered what Professor Sprout had said of Devil's Snare: it likes the dark and the damp. She drove it off with bluebell flames. ‘Lucky you pay attention in Herbology, Hermione,’ said Harry. In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, Neville's Herbology mark made up for his Potions.

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Professor Sprout set the second-years to repotting young Mandrakes, in earmuffs.

pages.title: Romania
infobox: Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Romania is a country in south-eastern Europe, folded round the Carpathian mountains. To wizards it is above all the country of wild dragons, which live in reserves in its mountains, where Charlie Weasley works with them. It has long had a darker name as well, for vampires.

Dragons

Since the Warlocks' Convention of 1709 outlawed dragon breeding, the wild dragons of Europe have been watched over in reserves, and Romania's is among the best known. Charlie Weasley went there to study dragons when he left Hogwarts, and he keeps them still. In the spring of 1992 Norbert, the Norwegian Ridgeback that Hagrid had hatched, was smuggled out of Hogwarts to join him. Arthur and Molly Weasley spent Christmas 1991 in Romania with Charlie.

Vampires

Romania's mountains have sheltered vampires for centuries. Dracula's castle rises in the Carpathians whenever he does, and as Vlad Tepes he ruled Wallachia, which is now part of the country. Angelus of the Aurelian line did terrible things in Romania in the eighteenth century. In 1898, in Romania again, he killed the favourite daughter of the Kalderash, an old Romani clan learned in curse-work, and her people cursed him with his soul in return.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Seamus Finnigan asked Professor Quirrell whether it was true that he had fought a vampire in Romania. Quirrell went white and knocked over his inkwell. His turban, Ron Weasley said afterwards, was stuffed with garlic, so that the vampire could not come for him in the night. In Chapter Eight Mr and Mrs Weasley went to Romania to visit Charlie for Christmas. In Chapter Ten, when Hagrid hatched a dragon, Ron spoke of the burns Charlie had got off the wild ones in Romania. It was Harry who thought of sending Norbert to him.

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry knew that Charlie was in Romania with the dragons. In Chapter Seven Hermione Granger, reading Voyages with Vampires at breakfast, told him that there were thirteen clans of vampires. One of the Ventrue, Angelus of the Aurelian line, had done dreadful things in Romania in the seventeen hundreds. In Chapter Sixteen Harry remembered that Hagrid had cried for a week when Norbert went off to Romania.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Hermione read out the story of 1898, when Angelus killed the favourite daughter of a Romani clan travelling the Carpathians. In Chapter Sixteen Ron said that if Hermione had failed any of her exams, he might as well go off to Romania to keep dragons with Charlie.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, Harry Potter met Charlie Weasley at the Burrow on 21 August 1994, and knew him at once for the brother who worked with the dragons in Romania. Charlie's face was weathered by wind and sun, with one arm bearing a large, shiny burn.

pages.title: Second World War
infobox: Chiefly Britain, the Soviet Union, the United States and China
Against Greta Grindelwald, who was defeated by Albus Dumbledore in 1945
pages.html:
The Second World War was the war of 1939 to 1945 between the Allies and the Axis, the largest war in history. Costumed heroes fought in it on both sides of the Atlantic. Alongside it ran a war in the hidden wizarding world against the Dark witch Greta Grindelwald, which ended when Albus Dumbledore defeated her in 1945.

The war

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Two days later Britain and France declared war. France fell in the summer of 1940, leaving Britain to fight on alone until Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941. That December Japan attacked the American fleet at Pearl Harbor, which brought the United States in.

On 6 June 1944 the Allies landed in Normandy, against a German defence that gave no quarter, and fought their way east across France. Germany surrendered in May 1945. Japan surrendered in August, after atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The war ended formally on 2 September 1945.

Heroes and wizards

Captain America, the one success of the Weapon programme's super-soldier serum, fought through occupied Europe with the Invaders, while Nick Fury led the Howling Commandos. The Justice Society and the rest of the All-Star Squadron fought mostly on the home front.

Greta Grindelwald, a Dark witch who admired Mussolini, fought Captain America, the Invaders and the Justice Society. Dumbledore overcame her in 1945 in the most famous duel of the age. In the last weeks of the war in Europe, Captain America was lost in the North Atlantic, frozen in the ice until 1964. Wolverine, who had fought in the first war, fought in this one too.

In 1944 the vampire painter Brauner raised Dracula's castle with the souls of the war's dead. It stood in Axis lands, beyond the reach of the heroes whom the Spear of Destiny held back. The Church sent Jonathan Morris with the sorceress Charlotte Aulin, who defeated Brauner, then destroyed Dracula.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, before the Easter holidays of 1992, the teachers piled on so much homework that the holidays began to look to Harry Potter like the German defence of Normandy. It was absolutely merciless, and the bodies were piling up.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, in the Top Box at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, Harry Potter explained to Cornelius Fudge what the Muggle word 'mutie' meant. People had been born with powers since the war, Harry said, though nobody minded much until the sixties.

pages.title: Firenze
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
White-blond hair, a palomino body, pale sapphire-blue eyes
The centaurs of the Forbidden Forest, with Bane and Ronan
pages.html:
Firenze is a young centaur of the Forbidden Forest. In the spring of 1992 he saved Harry Potter from Lord Voldemort's servant, and defied his own herd to do it.

Description

Firenze has white-blond hair and a palomino body. His eyes are an astonishing pale blue, like sapphires held up to the light. Like the rest of his herd he reads what is coming in the movements of the planets. He is readier than the others, though, to take a side among humans.

Centaurs keep to themselves in the Forest and have little to do with wizards. The Ministry of Magic classes them as beasts, at their own request. The herd holds that its members have sworn not to set themselves against the heavens, which is why most of them will not meddle in human affairs. His herd includes Ronan and the black-haired, black-bodied Bane.

In the saga

On the night of the Forest detention in 1992 he drove off the hooded figure that was drinking the blood of a slain unicorn. Then he lowered himself on to his front legs so that Harry could scramble on to his back, and carried him away towards safety.

Bane was furious: 'You have a human on your back! Have you no shame? Are you some common mule?' He reminded Firenze that the centaurs had sworn not to set themselves against the heavens. Firenze reared up on his hind legs: 'I set myself against what is lurking in this Forest, Bane. Yes. With humans beside me if I must.'

As they went on through the trees, he told Harry that unicorn blood will keep a man alive when he is an inch from death, but at a terrible price. From the moment it touches his lips he will have only half a life, a cursed life. He hinted that the drinker was Lord Voldemort, keeping himself alive until he could get the Philosopher's Stone.

He left Harry where Hagrid would find him, with a parting word: 'The planets have been read wrongly before now. Even by centaurs. I hope this is one of those times.' Harry told Ron and Hermione afterwards that Bane thought Firenze should have let Voldemort kill him.

In their own words

The planets have been read wrongly before now. Even by centaurs. I hope this is one of those times.Firenze · B1 Ch11

pages.title: Bane
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
That centaurs must not set themselves against the heavens
pages.html:
Bane is a black-haired, black-bodied centaur of the Forbidden Forest, proud and quick to anger. He reads the movements of the planets, and he holds that centaurs must not set themselves against what the heavens foretell. Humans, in his view, are no business of theirs.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, in the spring of 1992, Firenze saved Harry Potter in the Forest from the hooded thing that had just killed a unicorn. Bane burst into the clearing a moment later with a red-haired centaur, and he was furious to see a human on Firenze's back: 'You have a human on your back! Have you no shame? Are you some common mule?'

He reminded Firenze that they had sworn not to set themselves against the heavens. 'Have we not read what is coming in the movements of the planets?' When the other centaur suggested that Firenze had meant it for the best, Bane lashed out with his hind legs. 'For the best! What's that to us? Centaurs concern themselves with what has been foretold!'

Firenze carried Harry away all the same. Harry told Ron and Hermione afterwards that Bane thought Firenze should have let Voldemort kill him.

pages.title: The red-haired centaur
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The red-haired centaur is a mournful centaur of the Forbidden Forest whose name has never been given. In the spring of 1992 he came into a clearing with Bane just after Firenze had saved Harry Potter, and he gloomily suggested that Firenze had meant well.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, he and Bane burst out of the trees, sweating hard, to find Harry on Firenze's back. While Bane raged, the red-haired centaur pawed the ground. 'I'm sure Firenze meant it for the best,' he said gloomily. Bane lashed out with his hind legs at that. When Firenze plunged off into the trees with Harry, the two of them were left behind.

pages.title: The unicorn in the Forbidden Forest
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The unicorn in the Forbidden Forest was a wounded unicorn that came out of the trees to Dracina Malfoy one night in 1992 and let her touch it. A moment later, in front of her and Harry Potter, it was killed. The hooded figure that killed it drank its silver blood.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, Professor Quirrell led Harry, Hermione Granger, Neville Longbottom and Dracina into the Forbidden Forest for their detention, following a trail of silver blood. Then Quirrell screamed and bolted into the trees with his lamp. Harry and Dracina, lost together in the dark, made their way towards a shower of red sparks. They came out into a small clearing.

The unicorn stepped out of the trees. It shimmered, so that small pale flowers opened in the grass round its hooves and glowed. It walked straight to Dracina with its head lowered. Dracina, whom Harry knew only as spoilt and cruel, laid her hand on its white neck as gently as if it might break. Only then did Harry see the wound, low on the far side of its neck. Its blood was silver, the same silver as the trail Quirrell had followed.

Then a hooded shape came out of the trees on the far side and struck the unicorn with a jet of green light. Harry's scar burned. The light went out of the unicorn all at once, and Harry felt a great wave of sadness, as though the whole world were grieving. Dracina screamed and fled. The figure bent over the wound and drank. It was coming for Harry when the centaur Firenze drove it off.

In Chapter Thirteen Quirrell admitted that he had wounded the unicorn earlier that day. He had needed children pure of heart and body: ‘Unicorns don't appear to men like me.’ Lord Voldemort, in the back of Quirrell's head, told Harry that unicorn blood had strengthened him, and that Harry had seen his faithful Quirrell drinking it for him in the Forest.

pages.title: Unicorns
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Pure white when grown; golden as foals
Horn and tail hair in potions; hair in wand cores
The Forbidden Forest, among other places
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Unicorns are pure white horned horses of the northern forests, and the most beautiful creatures in the wizarding world. Their horn and tail hair are used in potions. Their hair makes wand cores, and their blood is silver.

Description

A unicorn foal is pure gold. It turns silver at about two, grows its horn at about four and is pure white by the time it is full grown at seven. Unicorns are so swift that they are seldom caught. They prefer a witch's touch to a wizard's.

Unicorn blood

The blood of a unicorn will keep a dying person alive when they are an inch from death. The price is terrible. To kill something so pure and defenceless is a monstrous act. From the moment the blood touches the drinker's lips, they have only half a life, and a cursed one.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, during a detention in the Forbidden Forest in 1992, Harry Potter saw a unicorn killed and its blood drunk. Harry had only used the horn and the tail hair in Potions. The centaur Firenze told him what the blood is for, and why only somebody with nothing to lose would ever drink it.

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, on his way to Professor Dumbledore's office, Harry remembered that he had once stood in the Forest at midnight a few feet from something drinking unicorn blood.

In Chapter Seventeen, when Ron Weasley asked nervously whether there were werewolves in the Forest, Harry told him there were good things in there too: the centaurs, and the unicorns.

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, on the night of 6 June 1994, a Patronus came across the lake and drove the Dementors off. To the half-conscious Harry it shone like a unicorn, though it was a stag.

pages.title: House-elf
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
One house and one family, for ever
Powerful, but used only with their masters' leave
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
House-elves are small magical servants, each bound to serve one wizarding house and family for ever. Only old, rich families keep them. An elf can leave only if it is set free, and the only way to free one is to give it real clothes.

Service

A house-elf stands about as high as a small child, with huge eyes and long, bat-like ears. It wears whatever rag its family allows, a pillowcase or a tea towel, as the mark of its service. Its family takes good care never to hand it so much as a glove.

House-elves have powerful magic of their own, quite unlike a wizard's. They can come and go with a crack where no witch or wizard can Apparate, but they cannot usually use their magic without their masters' say-so. An elf who speaks ill of its family must punish itself, and most do so without being told.

When Lord Voldemort was at the height of his power, house-elves were kicked like dogs. Hogwarts has more of them than any other dwelling in Britain, over a hundred, who cook and clean unseen in the kitchens beneath the Great Hall.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, Professor Quirrell led Dracina Malfoy into the Forbidden Forest for a detention in 1992. She complained that she had expected to be writing lines. This was work for servants, she said: work for house-elves. She had one herself.

In Book Two, Chapter Two, Dobby told Harry Potter that he was bound to serve one house and one family for ever. He could leave only if he were set free, and his family would never free him.

In Chapter Three Fred Weasley explained that house-elves have powerful magic of their own, although they cannot usually use it without their masters' say-so. Harry remembered Dracina talking about her own elf on the night of that detention. George added that their mother was always wishing for one to do the ironing.

In Chapter Eleven, in the hospital wing, Dobby remembered how it was when He Who Must Not Be Named was strong. House-elves were kicked like dogs, he said, or worse. Only a gift of real clothes can free an elf, which is how Dobby himself was freed at the end of that year.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, Fred had a theory about what Dracina was up to. She was bribing the Hogwarts house-elves, he said, with something dead.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the Top Box at the World Cup final Harry met Winky, Barty Crouch's house-elf, whom he took at first for Dobby. He suspected that she was female, though house-elves are very hard to tell apart. Winky held that house-elves do what they are told and are not paid.

pages.title: The Malfoys' house-elf
pages.html:
The Malfoys' house-elf is the elf Dracina Malfoy calls her own. She mentioned it late in her first year, during a detention in the Forbidden Forest that she thought far beneath her.

The Malfoy elves

The Malfoys keep house-elves at Malfoy Manor, as the old pure-blood families do. The best known of them, Dobby, served the family until the summer of 1993, when Harry Potter tricked Lucius Malfoy into setting him free with a sock. Nothing more is known of Dracina's own elf.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, in 1992, Professor Quirrell took Dracina into the Forbidden Forest for detention, along with Harry Potter, Hermione Granger and Neville Longbottom. She protested that she had understood they would be writing lines. "This is work for servants. For house-elves. I've got one myself, and if you'd simply..." Quirrell shouted her down before she could finish, without a single stutter.

pages.title: The hooded figure
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The hooded figure was the cloaked shape that killed a unicorn in the Forbidden Forest in the spring of 1992, then crawled to drink its blood. It was Professor Quirinus Quirrell, who was carrying Lord Voldemort on the back of his head and drinking the blood on his master's behalf.

Unicorn blood

The blood of a unicorn will keep a creature alive when it is an inch from death, but at a terrible price. To slay something so pure and defenceless to save oneself is monstrous. From the moment the blood touches the lips, the drinker has only half a life, a cursed life. Voldemort, reduced to a shadow, needed only to stay alive long enough to get the Philosopher's Stone.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, Quirrell took four first-years into the Forest that spring: Harry Potter, Hermione Granger, Neville Longbottom and Dracina Malfoy. Then he bolted off the path into the trees and left them there. A wounded unicorn came out of the trees to Dracina. Then a hooded, cloaked shape came out on the far side of the clearing. It moved wrong, too low and too quick. It raised an arm, and a jet of green light hit the unicorn, which fell dead.

Harry's scar burned as though a nail had been driven into it. The shape dropped to all fours and crawled to the body to drink. Then it came towards Harry, silver blood running down the front of its cloak, until the centaur Firenze charged it and drove it off. Firenze told Harry what unicorn blood is used for. He asked whether Harry could think of nobody who had waited years to come back to power.

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, under the school, Quirrell told Harry why he had needed them. 'I had to have children pure of heart and body, you see. Unicorns don't appear to men like me.' Voldemort, speaking from the back of Quirrell's head, put it plainly: 'Unicorn blood has strengthened me these past weeks... you saw my faithful Quirrell drinking it for me in the Forest...'

pages.title: The House points hour-glasses
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The House points hour-glasses are four giant hour-glasses in the Entrance Hall at Hogwarts, which keep each house's points for the House Cup. As points are won or lost, the level of jewels in each glass rises or falls, where the whole school can see it.

The glasses

Gryffindor's glass is filled with rubies, Slytherin's with emeralds, Ravenclaw's with sapphires and Hufflepuff's with yellow diamonds.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, Gryffindor lost a hundred and fifty points in a single night in 1992, which put it last. The next morning the Gryffindors who passed the hour-glasses in the Entrance Hall simply assumed there had been a mistake: the rubies in their glass were much, much lower than they had been. Then the story went round that Harry Potter and a couple of other first-years had lost them.

pages.title: Spotted fire mushrooms
pages.html:
Spotted fire mushrooms are the fungus that Professor Quirrell claimed to be collecting in the Forbidden Forest in 1992, on the night he took a detention of first-years into the Forest. Hermione Granger had never read about any mushroom like them.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, Quirrell told the four first-years in detention that he had special permission to take them into the Forest. He said it without a single stutter, which Harry noticed. Then he explained what he was after. 'Sh-shouldn't be long. Just n-need a f-few things. M-mushrooms. Sp-spotted fire mushrooms. Herbs. Th-things of that n-nature.' 'We need rather more information than that, Professor!' said Dracina Malfoy.

Deep in the trees Quirrell stopped and pointed his lamp at a long, thin, silvery smear on the path. 'The, er, m-mushrooms excrete a l-liquid. Silver. L-like this.' Hermione said that she had not read about any mushroom that did that. 'You're only a f-first-year, M-miss Granger.'

In Chapter Twelve, after Quirrell had run off and left the four of them alone in the Forest in the dark, Harry kept thinking about the mushrooms. Hermione had never read about them, and mushrooms do not bleed silver. In Chapter Thirteen, facing Quirrell under the school, Harry saw it all come horribly clear: the mushrooms, and the two times the stutter had vanished.

pages.title: McGonagall's study
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Professor McGonagall's study is on the first floor of Hogwarts. Pupils caught out of bed at night may be brought there to wait for her.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, in the spring of 1992, Argus Filch caught Harry Potter and Hermione Granger out of bed after they had been up the tallest tower with Norbert the dragon. He left them in the study with the single word 'Wait'. McGonagall came in still in her tartan dressing-gown, with Neville Longbottom trailing behind her.

She had decided that they had lured Dracina Malfoy out of bed with a story about a dragon. 'Honestly, Potter. I've had more convincing lies out of feral mujahideen who were... oh, bother. Never you mind that. You're far too young.' She took fifty points each from all three of them. Then she laid Charlie Weasley's letter on the desk, the one Dracina had taken, and gave Harry the advice she had once given his father: 'I learned the hard way, Potter, that one is only ever punished for what one is caught doing.'

pages.title: Mujahideen
pages.html:
The mujahideen were the Afghan guerrillas who fought the Soviet army in Afghanistan from 1979 until it withdrew in 1989. Professor McGonagall has had dealings with some of them, of a kind she will not explain.

History

They fought in loose bands under their own commanders, many of them armed by the West, from the mountains of a country that invaders have always found hard to hold. When the Russians had gone, they fought on against the Communist government in Kabul until it fell in 1992. Then the victorious factions turned on one another, and in 1994 they are fighting still.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, Professor McGonagall caught Harry out of bed after the business of the dragon. She accused him of luring Dracina Malfoy out with a ridiculous story, and she did not believe a word of his account: 'Honestly, Potter. I've had more convincing lies out of feral mujahideen who were... oh, bother. Never you mind that. You're far too young.' Harry had no idea what a mujahideen was. He put the question away in a drawer in his head marked later.

pages.title: Anti-Dark Force spell
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
An Anti-Dark Force spell is a protective enchantment against Dark magic. In 1992 Harry Potter and Ron Weasley believed that Professor Quirrell had put one round the Philosopher's Stone, which Professor Snape needed to break.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Harry already suspected that there were other things guarding the Stone besides Fluffy. Quirrell, he reckoned, 'must have done some anti-Dark Arts spell that Snape needs to break through'.

In Chapter Eleven, about a week before the examinations of 1992, Harry overheard something that made him think Quirrell had given in to Snape at last. He went back to the library, where Hermione was testing Ron on Astronomy, and told them what he had heard.

'Snape's done it, then!' said Ron. 'If Quirrell's told him how to break his Anti-Dark Force spell...'

Hermione reminded him that there was still Fluffy. They had it the wrong way round all the same: it was Quirrell who wanted the Stone.

pages.title: Confundus Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A mind with no thought left in it
pages.html:
The Confundus Charm, cast with the incantation Confundo, befuddles its victim, who is then said to be Confunded. Because it works on the mind, it can do nothing to a creature with no thought left in its head.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, when Argus Filch caught Harry Potter out of bed in 1992, he told him he had heard every excuse there was.

'I have heard sick owls, lost toads, lucky socks and a boy who swore blind he'd been Confunded by a suit of armour.'

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, in June 1994, Professor Snape told Cornelius Fudge that Sirius Black had bewitched Harry, Ron and Hermione. It was a Confundus Charm, to judge by their behaviour: they seemed to think Black might be innocent. When Harry lost his temper and offered to lend the Minister a knife, since Sirius had one, Snape had his proof. 'Confunded. Thoroughly, deeply confunded. Black has done a very professional job.'

Out in the grounds, in the same chapter, Hermione fired 'Incarcerous!' and 'Confundo!' at the werewolf Lupin had become. The Confundus Charm struck it square between the eyes. It did nothing at all, because there was no thought left in that head to confuse.

pages.title: Hagrid's flute
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Hagrid's flute is the roughly whittled wooden flute that Rubeus Hagrid carved himself and gave Harry Potter for Christmas 1991. It sounds a bit like an owl. It also sends three-headed dogs to sleep, which turned out to matter rather more.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, it was the top parcel on Harry’s first Christmas morning at Hogwarts, wrapped in thick brown paper. Harry blew it, and loved it, because it came from Hagrid.

In Chapter Twelve Hagrid let slip that Fluffy was a piece of cake if you knew how to calm him down: play him a bit of music and he went straight off to sleep. That night, going after the Philosopher’s Stone, Harry pocketed the flute. In the room with the three-headed dog he put it to his lips and blew. It was hardly a tune, but the dog’s eyes began to droop at the first note. Soon he had slumped over on to his side, fast asleep. When Harry went down through the trapdoor, he passed the flute to Hermione to keep the dog under.

pages.title: The harp
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The harp was lying at Fluffy's feet on the night Harry Potter went through the trapdoor in June 1992. Whoever had gone through before him had left it there, having played the three-headed dog to sleep with it. That was Professor Quirrell.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, Hermione whispered to ask what was by the dog's feet. 'Looks like a harp,' said Ron. 'Snape must've left it.' The harp had fallen silent. Harry guessed that the dog must wake the moment the music stopped, and blew on Hagrid's flute until it sank down asleep. Ron was wrong about Snape.

pages.title: Devil's Snare
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Devil's Snare is a magical plant that loves the dark and the damp. It binds whatever struggles in it tighter and tighter. It shrinks from light and warmth, so fire will make it let go.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger dropped through the trapdoor into the dark. Something soft broke their fall, and Ron thought it lucky. It was Professor Sprout's Devil's Snare, the first of the protections round the Philosopher's Stone. Hermione fought her way free to a damp wall, but the harder the boys struggled, the tighter it wound round them. She remembered that it liked the dark and the damp, but could not think how to light a fire without wood. 'HAVE YOU GONE MAD?' Ron bellowed. 'ARE YOU A WITCH OR NOT?' She sent a jet of bluebell flames at it. It cringed away from the light and warmth, unwinding itself from the boys. 'And lucky Harry doesn't lose his head in a crisis,' said Ron afterwards. '"There's no wood." Honestly.'

In Chapter Thirteen, as Quirrell began to unwind his turban, Harry could not move. It was as though the Devil's Snare had come up through the floor and taken him by the ankles.

pages.title: Winged keys
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A chamber beneath the trapdoor, Hogwarts
Big and silver, with bright blue wings
pages.html:
The winged keys were the hundreds of enchanted keys that Professor Flitwick set to guard one of the chambers beneath the trapdoor at Hogwarts, among the defences round the Philosopher's Stone. Only one of them would open the door out of the chamber, and it had to be caught on a broomstick.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, Harry, Ron and Hermione came into a chamber where something glittered high overhead, with a sound like wings. 'They're not birds!' Harry said suddenly. 'They're keys! Winged keys, look!' There were broomsticks waiting, so they took one each and kicked off.

Harry stopped grabbing. He let his broom drift up above the flock, the way he did above a Quidditch match, and watched. One of the keys was flying wrong. It was big and silver, with bright blue wings. The feathers on one wing were crushed and bent. It looked as if somebody had already caught it once, then rammed it roughly into a lock.
