Ron came at it from above while Hermione kept it from going low. Harry went after it flat along the handle, the way he went after the Snitch, and pinned it to the wall with one hand.

pages.title: The giant chessboard
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Living stone chessmen, taller than the students
pages.html:
The giant chessboard was Professor McGonagall's part in the defence of the Philosopher's Stone. It filled a whole chamber under Hogwarts with living stone chessmen, all of them taller than the students. Anybody who wanted to get past had to play their way across.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, Harry, Ron and Hermione reached the chessboard in June 1992. The black pieces stood taller than they did, carved from what looked like black stone, and the towering white pieces across the chamber had no faces. A knight, a bishop and a castle walked off the board for them. Ron took the knight's place, Harry the bishop's and Hermione the castle's.

Ron directed the game. When it came to it, he let the white queen take him. She struck him round the head with her stone arm and dragged him aside, knocked cold. That left Harry free to checkmate the king. The white king took off his crown and threw it down at Harry's feet. Hermione worked out afterwards that McGonagall had transfigured the chessmen to bring them alive.

In Chapter Thirteen, at the end-of-year feast, Dumbledore gave Gryffindor fifty points for Ron's game, 'for the best-played game of chess this school has seen in many years'. Percy could be heard telling the other prefects that his youngest brother had got past McGonagall's giant chess set.

In Book Two, Chapter Six, Ron reminded Harry that he had risked his neck on the giant chessboard for the Stone.

pages.title: The second troll
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Guarding the way to the Philosopher's Stone
pages.html:
The second troll was one of the guardians of the Philosopher's Stone beneath Hogwarts in 1992. It was even bigger than the troll that got into the castle at Hallowe'en. By the time Harry Potter and Hermione Granger reached it, somebody had already knocked it out.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, Harry and Hermione pushed open another door on the way to the Stone. A smell met them so thick that they pulled their robes up over their noses. Flat on the floor in front of them, out cold, lay a troll even bigger than the one they had fought at Hallowe'en, with a bloody lump on its head. 'I'm glad we didn't have to tackle that one,' Harry whispered.

In Chapter Thirteen Professor Quirrell let slip who had done it. 'You saw what I did to the one in the chamber back there, I take it?'

pages.title: Snape's bottle riddle
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Snape's bottle riddle is the rhyming riddle Professor Snape left beside his seven bottles, his part of the defences around the Philosopher's Stone. Its four clues sorted the poisons from the nettle wine and the potions that led onward or back.

The riddle

Seven bottles stood in a row between a purple fire behind and a black fire ahead. Three held poison, two held nettle wine, one led on through the black fire and one led back through the purple. The clues said that poison always stood to the left of nettle wine; that the two end bottles differed, though neither led onward; that neither the smallest nor the tallest held poison; and that the second from each end held the same thing.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, Harry Potter and Hermione Granger were trapped between the two fires the moment they stepped into the chamber. She worked out that the smallest bottle led forward, towards the Stone, while the round bottle at the right-hand end led back. There was only enough in the smallest for one. Harry sent Hermione back through the purple fire to fetch Ron Weasley and send Hedwig to Dumbledore. Then he drank the smallest bottle himself.

pages.title: Body-Bind Curse
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Locks the limbs rigid; only the eyes can move
Burnt off by the heat of a Garou
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Body-Bind Curse, cast with the incantation Petrificus Totalus, snaps the victim's arms to the sides and the legs together. The whole body goes as stiff as a plank, and only the eyes can move. It does no lasting harm. Nor does it hold a Garou in its war form for more than a moment, because the creature's own heat burns the curse away.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, on the night the examinations ended in June 1992, Harry, Ron and Hermione were about to set off after the Philosopher's Stone. Dracina Malfoy was waiting in the Gryffindor common room, having got the password out of Neville. She had come to apologise to Harry for running off and leaving him in the Forest. Hermione thought she was there to stop them for Snape, and her wand came up. 'Petrificus Totalus!' Dracina's arms snapped flat to her sides, and she toppled on to the floor face first, as stiff as a plank, with only her eyes moving.

Harry looked down at her. 'I accept your apology,' he said sadly, 'and I'm sorry for what Hermione did to you. We'll come back for you. All right?' A twinkle came into her silver eyes.

In Book Two, Chapter One, in the summer of 1992, Harry found that he missed that twinkle. In Chapter Three Fred Weasley told him that Dracina had gone round the whole school telling everybody she would get Harry back for the Body-Bind he had put on her. Harry said, automatically, that Hermione had done it.

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, in June 1994, the Garou that Remus Lupin had become rose up on its hind legs over Harry in the grounds. Harry raised his shaking wand. 'Petrificus Totalus!' It was the curse Hermione had used on Malfoy in their first year, the night they went after the Stone. One of the creature's arms snapped in to its side, and its legs jerked together. Then a shudder ran right through it, with a crackling like ice breaking up on a pond in March. The curse flaked away in the moonlight, burnt off by the thing's own heat. Snape's words came back to Harry in a rush: 'Rage as a substance. It sits in them like fire in a lamp.'

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, Harry Potter smiled at Dracina Malfoy in the Top Box, and she smiled back. The twinkle was there again in her silver eyes, as it had been on and off since the Body-Bind in their first year.

pages.title: Anti-Cheating spell
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Anti-Cheating spell is the enchantment put on the special quills that Hogwarts students are given for their written examinations. Examiners have used such charms on their quills for generations.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, it was the sweltering summer of 1992, and it was hottest of all in the big classroom where the first-years sat their written papers. They had been given special new quills for the examinations, bewitched with an Anti-Cheating spell. There were practical examinations too. Professor Flitwick called them one by one into his classroom to see whether they could make a pineapple tap-dance across a desk.

pages.title: Forgetfulness Potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Forgetfulness Potion makes whoever drinks it forget. It is simple enough to be set to first-years.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, the first-years had to brew one in their Potions exam in June 1992. Snape made them all nervous, breathing down their necks while they tried to remember how to make it. More than once Harry wondered whether Snape was slipping a drop of it into their cauldrons, so that they would forget on purpose.

pages.title: The giant squid
infobox: Black Lake, Hogwarts lake, the lake
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Basking in the sun on warm days
pages.html:
The giant squid lives in the lake at Hogwarts, and has done for as long as anybody can remember. It is a placid creature. On warm days it drifts on the surface or basks in the shallows, and it does not seem to mind in the least when pupils tickle its tentacles.

The lake

The squid shares the lake with the merpeople and the grindylows. It has never been known to hurt anybody.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, after the exams of June 1992, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger flopped under a tree by the lake. The Weasley twins and Lee Jordan were tickling the tentacles of the giant squid, which was basking in the warm shallows.

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Ron wondered what Tom Riddle had done to earn his award for special services to the school. Perhaps, he suggested, Riddle had rescued a teacher from the giant squid.

In the Interlude of Book Three, in his third year at Hogwarts in the 1960s, the young John Constantine was dangled by his ankles out of a tower window over the lake by a gang of fifth years. They held him there so long that the giant squid came up to have a look at him.

In Chapter Sixteen, in the cloudless weather as June 1994 drew near, the squid drifted on the flat, glittering lake like an old dog asleep in a bath.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, on the day after Sirius Black's escape, it was basking in the sun in the middle of the lake. A couple of its tentacles waved idly in the air, as though it were too hot to do anything else, while Harry sat in the shade of a beech with Ron and Hermione.

pages.title: The Hog's Head
infobox: Pub, Village near Hogwarts, inn, Hogsmeade, pub
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A severed boar's head, dripping blood
Goats; customers who keep their hoods up
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
The Hog's Head is the smaller, dingier and more doubtful of the two pubs in Hogsmeade. Its sign is a severed boar's head, dripping blood on to the white cloth round it, and the place smells strongly of goats. As Hagrid says, you get all sorts in the Hog's Head.

The pub

It is one small, dirty room, with grimy windows that let in very little daylight. The floor looks like trodden earth, though there is stone under the dirt of centuries. The landlord is Aberforth Dumbledore, the younger brother of Albus, a grumpy old man with long grey hair and a beard, who keeps goats. People who would rather not be seen come there to talk, and nobody asks them questions. There is a back room for private business.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, Hagrid told Harry, Ron and Hermione that he had won Norbert's egg at cards from a stranger, down in the village. In Chapter Twelve they asked him what the stranger had looked like. 'Yeh get all sorts in the Hog's Head. That's one o' the pubs in the village.' The stranger had kept his hood up the whole time, buying Hagrid drink after drink, and had wanted to know all about Fluffy. In Chapter Thirteen Harry worked out that it had been Quirrell.

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, when Hagrid told Harry he could always tell him anything, Harry thought of the stranger in a hood buying Hagrid drinks in the Hog's Head the year before.

In the Interlude of Book Three, John Constantine remembered a day in 1985 when he had stood in the back room of the Hog's Head, with a goat looking in at the window, trying to say sorry to Albus Dumbledore for stealing his Deluminator. He tried to say it out loud, like a schoolboy. Dumbledore let him get about three words out. Then he shouted him down, in language John would not have thought a headmaster knew, and promised to turn his liver into a pair of slippers.

pages.title: Jorvik
pages.html:
Jorvik was the Viking city of York, the chief city of Norse England. It was the home of the völvas, the Norse seeresses who fought a wizarding war against the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London. The war ended in 954, when the Anglo-Saxons took Jorvik.

History

The Danes took York in 866, and for most of the next ninety years it was ruled by Norse kings. Its witches were the völvas, who worked their magic with staff and song. In the south, round London and the old Roman towns, the last Hellenic sorcerers still worked in the classical way. Their incantations were in Latin or Greek, with a great deal of geometry. In Muggle history the end came in 954, when the Northumbrians drove out Eric Bloodaxe, the last king of Jorvik. King Eadred took the kingdom for England.

The magical families of the Viking North-East did not leave when the Saxons came. They simply stopped calling themselves Norse.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, the last of the first-years' examinations in the summer of 1992 was an hour of History of Magic on the war. Harry Potter was rather proud of having got the date, 954, to stay in his head.

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, in November 1992, Hermione Granger explained to Harry that the Viking families had stayed in the North-East after the Saxons took Jorvik. They had just stopped saying they were Norse.

pages.title: Norse völvas
infobox: Völuspá, in the Poetic Edda (Codex Regius, thirteenth century)
The last Hellenic sorcerers of London
pages.html:
The völvas were the seeresses of the Norse world: wise women who travelled with a staff, sang their spells and foretold what was to come. The völvas of Jorvik, the Viking kingdom at York, fought a wizarding war against the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London. Hogwarts first-years are examined on it.

History

A völva worked seiðr, the Norse art of seeing and shaping fate. She was feared as much as she was honoured. Jorvik had been a Viking kingdom since the Danes took York in 866. In 954 the Anglo-Saxons took it, and that ended the völvas' war with the last Hellenic sorcerers as well.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, the last of Harry Potter's first-year examinations, in the summer of 1992, was an hour of History of Magic on the war between the völvas of Jorvik and the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London. Harry was rather proud of having got the date 954 to stay in his head.

pages.title: Hellenic sorcerers
aliases: the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl Who Noticed Him, Chapter Twelve
pages.html:
The Hellenic sorcerers were wizards of the Greek tradition in early medieval England. The last of them, remembered as the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London, fought a wizarding war against the Norse völvas of Jorvik. It ended in 954, when the Anglo-Saxons took Jorvik.

The war

Jorvik was the Norse name for York, which the Vikings had held since 866. In 954 the English drove out Eric Bloodaxe, the last Norse king to reign there, and the wizards' war ended with his kingdom. The völvas were Norse seeresses, who worked their magic with a staff.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, the last exam of Harry Potter's first year, in June 1992, was History of Magic. It was one hour on the war between the Norse völvas of Jorvik and the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London. Harry was rather proud of having got the date to stay in his head.

pages.title: 1637 Werewolf Code of Conduct
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
First-year History of Magic at Hogwarts
pages.html:
The Werewolf Code of Conduct of 1637 is a piece of wizarding law about werewolves. It belongs to the History of Magic course at Hogwarts, and first years revise it for their exams. Hermione Granger learnt it for hers in June 1992, only to find that she need not have bothered.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, the first years came out of History of Magic, their very last exam, into the sunny grounds. Hermione said it had been far easier than she had thought: 'I needn't have bothered learning the 1637 Werewolf Code of Conduct, or the uprising of Elfric the Eager.' Dracina Malfoy, who plainly had not done as well, hissed behind her that nobody needed to know about that, least of all from her.

pages.title: Elfric the Eager
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Elfric the Eager was a figure of wizarding history who led an uprising. His uprising is one of the many topics of History of Magic at Hogwarts.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, Hermione Granger revised his uprising for the first-years' History of Magic examination in the summer of 1992. The paper turned out to be on the war between the völvas of Jorvik and the last Hellenic sorcerers instead. 'That was far easier than I thought,' she said afterwards. 'I needn't have bothered learning the 1637 Werewolf Code of Conduct, or the uprising of Elfric the Eager.'

pages.title: Kosovo
infobox: To Augment forces under Joaquin, summer 1994
pages.html:
Kosovo is a province in the south of Serbia, in what remains of Yugoslavia. Professor McGonagall once spent what she calls a holiday there, during which she learnt a piece of Transfiguration on rather larger targets than her pupils use. In the summer of 1994 it fell to the Augment commander Joaquin.

The holiday

The holiday belonged to McGonagall's secret work as an Unspeakable of the Department of Mysteries, which took her away from Hogwarts on sabbaticals through the 1980s. She has never said what the larger targets were.

The Augment War

In July 1994 Augment forces appeared in the former Yugoslavia, and nobody is sure how they got there. Within five weeks, under Joaquin, they had taken Kosovo, the Montenegrin coast and most of eastern Bosnia.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, McGonagall watched the first-years turn a mouse into a snuffbox for their Transfiguration examination. 'Keep your wrist firm, Potter,' she said, bending over Harry Potter's half-finished snuffbox. 'Firm. That's better. I learned this one on rather larger targets, you know, during a holiday in Kosovo.' When he asked whether it had really been a holiday, she said that it had, then made a note on her parchment. She seemed to have enjoyed her time there, so Harry did not ask any more.

In Book Two, Chapter Five, at the Burrow, Harry filed Kosovo away with Kandahar and Zanzibar Land in the drawer in his head marked later.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on 20 August 1994, the television news at Privet Drive reported that Kosovo had fallen to Augment forces under Joaquin.

pages.title: Kandahar
infobox: A long night Professor McGonagall spent outside it
pages.html:
Kandahar is a city in southern Afghanistan. Professor McGonagall once spent a very long night in the dark outside it, warding a camp against creatures that Hogwarts students learn about in their third year.

McGonagall's night

The night belonged to McGonagall's secret work as an Unspeakable of the Department of Mysteries. Through the 1980s that work took her away from Hogwarts on sabbaticals, and it left her with a great many friends in the Muggle world. She does not talk about it to her pupils, beyond the odd remark that slips out.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, in June 1992, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger tried to warn McGonagall that somebody was going to steal the Philosopher's Stone. She told Harry: 'Potter, I know what I'm talking about. I once spent a very long night in the dark outside Kandahar making certain our camp was properly warded against the... well. You'll learn about those in your third year.' The Stone, she said, was secure.

In Book Two, Chapter Five, at the Burrow in August 1992, Molly Weasley told Harry: 'Professor McGonagall is a sweetheart, Harry. But I know where she's been and who she knows. Pay it no mind, dear.' Harry thought of Kosovo, Kandahar and a place called Zanzibar Land. He put them all away in the drawer in his head marked later.

pages.title: Zanzibar Land
infobox: Central Asia, between the former Soviet Union, China, Afghanistan and Pakistan
pages.html:
Zanzibar Land is a mountainous territory in Central Asia, the place where Minerva McGonagall once met the old friend who taught her to move without a sound. That friend was Big Boss. By 1999 it was a mercenary state under him, and Solid Snake went in to bring him down.

The place

Zanzibar Land lies in the high country of Central Asia, hemmed in by the former Soviet Union, China, Afghanistan and Pakistan. McGonagall knows of it, and she met Big Boss there in the years of their partnership. She also knows, roughly, where he is now. She has not gone to find him.

Uprising and war

In 1997 Zanzibar Land rose against the Commonwealth of Independent States. Mercenaries came to it from all over the world, and the CIS armies were beaten back time after time. In the end it declared itself independent, a fortified military state with Big Boss behind it. It began seizing nuclear weapons from disposal sites round the world.

In 1999, in the middle of a world oil crisis, Zanzibar Land kidnapped the Czech biologist Dr Kio Marv, who had created a micro-organism that refines oil. FOXHOUND, under Colonel Roy Campbell, sent Solid Snake in alone. He destroyed the new Metal Gear D and fought his old comrade Gray Fox hand to hand in a minefield. Then he faced the real Big Boss and defeated him with a lighter held to an aerosol can, for by then he had lost every weapon he carried.

The crisis of 1999 was half hidden at the time by a larger one. That year the Kilaaks, an alien people, set Godzilla on New York, with other monsters on five more of the world's great cities. Snake's mission went almost unreported.

The mission, Operation Intrude F014, began on Christmas Eve 1999. Afterwards the Patriots carried Big Boss's burnt body away, to keep it alive in secret.

In the saga

Book One, Chapter Twelve: Professor McGonagall appeared behind Harry, Ron and Hermione out of nowhere, without a sound. Harry would later learn that she had picked the trick up from an old friend she had once met in a place called Zanzibar Land.

Book Two, Chapter Five: Molly Weasley said that she knew where McGonagall had been, and who she knew. Afterwards Harry thought of Kosovo, Kandahar and a place called Zanzibar Land, then put them all away in the drawer in his head marked 'later'.

pages.title: Big Boss
aliases: McGonagall's old friend from Zanzibar Land
The man with one eye and a cigar
the man I shall not name
infobox: McGonagall's old friend from Zanzibar Land; The man with one eye and a cigar; The man with the knife; Naked Snake; Jack

Minerva McGonagall estranged former partner
Solid Snake son by cloning
Liquid Snake son by cloning
Venom Snake decoy
Solid Snake, Liquid Snake, Solidus Snake
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Big Boss is the most famous soldier of the century: the man who ended Operation Snake Eater in 1964, and the partner with whom Minerva McGonagall went into Siberia in 1966. He is the man with the knife who helped her kill a Goa'uld symbiote, and the old friend from Zanzibar Land who taught her to move without a sound. In 1972 his genome was used, without his knowledge, to make Solid Snake and Liquid Snake. McGonagall has not spoken to him since 1984.

Early life and Snake Eater

Big Boss was born in the mid-1930s, and his friends knew him as Jack. For ten years he was trained by The Boss, the greatest soldier of her generation and the mother of special forces. Together they worked out the close-quarters combat that every special forces soldier now learns.

In August 1964, under the codename Naked Snake, he went into the Soviet Union for the FOX unit, first on the Virtuous Mission and then on Operation Snake Eater. The Boss had apparently defected. A nuclear strike had been made on Soviet soil, and to prove the United States innocent of it he was ordered to kill her. He did. He also destroyed the Shagohod, a nuclear-armed tank, and came out of the jungle of Tselinoyarsk without his right eye. The President gave him the title of Big Boss. Afterwards he learnt that The Boss had been loyal all along, and that she had been ordered to die. He never forgave the men who had used her.

The Boss took him as her pupil in 1950, when he was fifteen. In 1954 he was caught in the fallout of the hydrogen bomb test at Bikini Atoll, which left him unable to father children. She left him in June 1959 for a mission she could not speak of. He did not see her again until the day she turned on him.

The Virtuous Mission was flown on 24 August 1964. It was the first operation of FOX, the CIA unit of Major Zero. The Boss met him on a bridge in Tselinoyarsk, where she threw him into the river. Operation Snake Eater began six days later, on 30 August. He killed her on 2 September, in a field of white flowers beside a lake.

McGonagall and Siberia

In the winter of 1966, some years before she came to teach at Hogwarts, Minerva McGonagall of the Department of Mysteries went into Siberia with Big Boss. He was a young man of roughly her own age, which was to say, as she put it, far too young for the work. Their target was a village of dark wizards forty miles past the last road. Its men had been doing something to the people in the valley below for the better part of thirty years, and the Ministry declined to recognise that the place existed. There were nine of them against the two partners. Two, she said, is the right number. The partners waited four days in the snow, and in the end the wizards came out to them because they were bored.

He taught her three things, and she has found no reason since to amend any of them. You do not announce yourself. Most people are beaten by the weather and their own appetites before anybody fights them at all. The most dangerous moment in any engagement is the moment after you believe you have won. He put it better, she said: the hard part is not learning to carry a weapon, but learning to put it down. She learnt from him, too, how to appear out of nowhere without a sound. She knows of Zanzibar Land because she once met him there.

They did a number of such things together. Once, a very long way from Hogwarts, they came up against a Goa'uld symbiote and its host. No Transfiguration would separate the two. In the end the only thing that answered was a knife, a steady hand and a good deal of help from Big Boss, who was considerably better with the knife than she was. The host died, and so did the creature. McGonagall kept it, and it hangs in a long glass case over the fire in her office.

A soldier without a country

In 1970, on the San Hieronymo Peninsula, Big Boss put down a rebellion of the FOX unit. Out of it he began to build an army of his own, from soldiers who had no other home. In 1972, without his knowledge, Weapon III, Les Enfants Terribles, took his genome to make two more of him: Solid Snake and Liquid Snake, carried by EVA. The following year somebody took the paperwork away to make Khan Noonien Singh and the Augments. When Big Boss learnt what had been done, he broke with the men who had done it.

In 1974 he led Militaires Sans Frontières, a private army based on an offshore platform in the Caribbean, against the Peace Walker nuclear weapon in Costa Rica. In 1975 Skull Face's unit, XOF, destroyed that base while Big Boss was in Cuba rescuing two of his people. The helicopter carrying him home crashed, and he lay in a coma for nine years.

The rebellion of 1970 ended with the founding of the Patriots. Major Zero, who had commanded Big Boss in 1964, used the Philosophers' fortune to build a secret organisation that would make the world one, as he believed The Boss had wanted. Big Boss was a founder, with Ocelot, EVA and two others. In 1971, on Zero's orders, he founded FOXHOUND. It was Zero who had him cloned the next year. When Big Boss walked out, he left his oldest friend as well as his employers.

In Colombia in 1972 he met Kazuhira Miller, with whom he founded Militaires Sans Frontières. The Peace Walker affair of November 1974 ended when a machine that thought with The Boss's mind drowned itself in Lake Nicaragua sooner than start a war. Weeks later a young agent of Zero's, Paz, tried to take his army from him with a stolen Metal Gear. After that he stopped refusing the title of Big Boss.

1984 and the break with McGonagall

When he woke in 1984, Big Boss had another man given his face, memories and life, then sent out into the world as his decoy. Nobody asked the man. He was the medic who had shielded Big Boss in the crash, and he is Venom Snake. Big Boss went his own way in the shadow of his phantom.

McGonagall knows what was done, and it is the cause of their estrangement. It was not politics, nor distance, nor a quarrel. She had watched a man used up by the people who employed him, then watched him do the same thing to somebody else, deliberately, as a tactic. She has not forgiven it. She has not stopped caring, either. Big Boss is alive in 1993, and she knows roughly where he is. She could find him. She does not.

Outer Heaven and after

In 1994 Big Boss commands FOXHOUND, the American special forces unit, while he builds Outer Heaven, a nation for soldiers. In 1995 FOXHOUND sent Solid Snake into Outer Heaven, and the uprising there was put down. In 1999 Snake faced the real Big Boss at Zanzibar Land and defeated him. Big Boss survived that too. He did not die until 2014.

McGonagall knows that David, Solid Snake, is Big Boss's son, from the striking family resemblance. She does not know that he is a clone, nor that Liquid exists. The young man she keeps up with is the son who was to bring down the father she has cut off.

After Zanzibar Land the Patriots took what was left of him. They kept him in an endless sleep for fourteen years, as the emblem of a system he had spent his life fighting. In 2014 EVA, with Revolver Ocelot, brought that system down to set him free. Both died of it.

He woke to find the Patriots gone. He brought Major Zero, by then a helpless man of about a hundred and five, to The Boss's grave at Arlington, where he switched off the oxygen that kept him alive. There he met Solid Snake for the last time. He told his son to find something to live for besides fighting. A virus in Snake's blood, made to kill the founders of the Patriots, killed Big Boss beside the grave.

In the saga

Book One, Chapter Twelve: Professor McGonagall came up behind Harry, Ron and Hermione out of nowhere, without a sound. Harry would later learn that she had picked the trick up from an old friend she had once met in a place called Zanzibar Land. In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry put Zanzibar Land away in his head with Kosovo and Kandahar, as part of her unexplained past.

Book Two, Chapter Eighteen: late in the spring of 1993, shadowing Harry and Ron along a Hogwarts corridor, McGonagall stepped sideways into the shadow of a suit of armour at the exact moment they turned. She had been taught to do it a very long time ago by a man with one eye and a cigar. The man was Big Boss.

Book Three, Chapter Eight: McGonagall told her class about the knife and 'a man I shall not name, who was considerably better with the knife than I was'. Harry spent the rest of the lesson wondering who the man with the knife had been. He wondered, too, whether he had had one eye and a metal arm.

Book Three, Chapter Eleven: at Christmas dinner Professor Flitwick asked about a scar on the back of her hand. McGonagall told the table about Siberia, the nine men, the four days in the snow and the three rules, looking down the table at Harry as she gave them. When Professor Sprout asked where her young man was now, she said: 'I have not had word of him in some years. We did a number of these things together, in the end. He was the better of the two of us, and it did him no good whatever; the people who use men like that use them up.' Then she told Sprout to eat her pudding. Harry knew the look on her face. It belonged to somebody talking about a person who had died, or had gone where they could not be written to.

In their own words

He was the better of the two of us, and it did him no good whatever.Minerva McGonagall · LB

pages.title: Hogwarts examinations
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
At the end of every school year, in early summer
About a week after the last paper
pages.html:
The Hogwarts examinations are the written papers and practical tests that every pupil sits at the end of the school year. Pupils must pass them to go up into the next year. In the fifth year they are the Ordinary Wizarding Levels, or O.W.L.s, and in the seventh the Nastily Exhausting Wizarding Tests, the N.E.W.T.s.

How they are set

The written papers are sat in a big classroom, with special quills bewitched with an Anti-Cheating spell. Each teacher also sets a practical examination in his or her own subject. The results come out about a week after the last paper. In the summer of 1994 Percy Weasley came out of his N.E.W.T.s with the highest grades there were, while Fred and George scraped through with a few O.W.L.s each.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, the first-years sat their examinations in the sweltering summer of 1992. Professor Flitwick called them in one at a time to make a pineapple tap-dance across a desk. Professor McGonagall had them turn a mouse into a snuffbox, giving marks for a handsome snuffbox and taking them away again for whiskers. She had learnt that one, she told Harry Potter, on rather larger targets during a holiday in Kosovo. Snape breathed down their necks while they tried to remember how to make a Forgetfulness Potion.

The last paper was History of Magic: an hour on the war between the Norse völvas of Jorvik and the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London. Then they were free for a whole week, until the results came out. Hermione Granger came out of the hall saying that she needn't have bothered learning the 1637 Werewolf Code of Conduct, or the uprising of Elfric the Eager.

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, the third-years' examinations of June 1994 took a week. Hagrid's Care of Magical Creatures paper was to keep a flobberworm alive for an hour, which made it the easiest examination anyone had ever sat. Professor Lupin's Defence Against the Dark Arts was an obstacle course on the lawn, with a grindylow, Red Caps and a hinkypunk. Harry wrote his History of Magic essay on the witch-burnings. His last examination was Divination, at the end of which Professor Trelawney fell into a trance and made a prophecy.

pages.title: The Potters' old school friends
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Potters' old school friends are the people who were at Hogwarts with James and Lily Potter in the 1970s. In 1992 Hagrid wrote to every one of them asking for photographs of the couple. Their answers filled the album he gave Harry at the end of his first year.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, in June 1992, Hagrid brought Harry a present in the hospital wing: a handsome leather book full of wizard photographs. On every page Harry's parents smiled and waved up at him. They stood by a lake. They stood in a garden, with James's arm round Lily, who was laughing. Lily held a black-haired baby who kept trying to grab her nose.

'Sent owls off ter all yer mum an' dad's old school friends, askin' fer photos,' said Hagrid. 'Knew yeh didn' have any.' Harry could not speak.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, in December 1993, Harry dug the album out from under his books and turned to his parents' wedding photograph. For the first time he looked properly at the third figure in it, laughing, with one hand on James Potter's shoulder. The best man was Sirius Black.

pages.title: The wizened old guard
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Guard at the barrier, platform nine and three-quarters, King's Cross
Letting students through to the Muggle station a few at a time
pages.html:
The wizened old guard stands by the barrier on platform nine and three-quarters at King's Cross. When the Hogwarts Express comes in, he lets the students out in twos and threes. That way they do not all burst out of a solid wall at once, giving the Muggles a fright.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, in June 1992, he was at the barrier when the Hogwarts Express brought Harry Potter back to London at the end of his first year. It took a long time to get everyone off the train. Ron Weasley used the wait to invite Harry and Hermione Granger to stay that summer.

pages.title: Lily Potter's protection
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Lily Potter, dying for her son, 31 October 1981
Old magic, of the Elves and of Númenor
That Harry calls Privet Drive home
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Lily Potter's protection is the old magic Harry Potter's mother left on him when she died for him in 1981. It lives in his blood, and in the blood of her sister, Petunia Dursley. While he can call Petunia's house his home, neither Lord Voldemort nor anything he sends can touch him there.

How it was made

No single spell made it. Several things met that night. There was the power of Lily's dying spell, and there was the evil that keeps Voldemort chained to this world. Above all there was her love. The result is a protection in Harry's very skin, with no scar to show for it. To touch him was agony to Quirrell, who was full of hatred and shared his soul with Voldemort.

An older magic

The protection is older than Lily knew. It is the magic of the Elves and of Númenor. It runs back through her a very long way, through a great many people who never knew what they were passing on, to Aragorn and Arwen, whose line reached her through Susan Pevensie. Harry does not know this.

The condition

The protection holds at Privet Drive only while Harry calls the house his home and Petunia's blood lives under its roof. It is renewed every July that he goes on calling it so. That is why Albus Dumbledore sends him back to the Dursleys every summer, and why neither Tom Riddle nor Tom's true master, the Devil, can touch him there.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, Quirrell could not touch Harry's bare skin without blistering, and Dumbledore afterwards explained why. In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Ambrose Greyhame warned Dumbledore in his study that the protection must hold: Harry had to go back to the Dursleys at the end of each year, for his own sake. In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, Dumbledore told Harry about it himself. ‘The magic of Elves, Harry. And of Númenor.’ In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, Harry thought bitterly of the condition that would always send him back to the cupboard people, however much he wanted to stay at the Burrow.

pages.title: Muggle-born
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A witch or wizard with Muggle parents
Lily Potter; Hermione Granger; Justin Finch-Fletchley; Stephen Strange
Book One, Book Two, Book Four
pages.html:
A Muggle-born is a witch or wizard born to Muggle parents. Muggle-borns are every bit as able as anybody else, but the old pure-blood families despise them, and the cruellest of them call them Mudbloods.

Where the magic comes from

Nobody knows for certain why magic turns up in a family that has never had it. One controversial theory holds that Muggle-borns carry recessive magic from some magical ancestor far back in their line. So little research has ever been done on it that Hermione Granger calls it the magical equivalent of pseudoscience. Lily Potter was Muggle-born, and her own line runs back further than anybody has ever written down.

Stephen Strange, the Sorcerer Supreme, is No-Maj-born, as the Americans say. His parents were No-Majs of Philadelphia. The prejudice of the pure-blood families drove him out of wizarding America when he left Ilvermorny in 1949, and he did not come back to magic until he found Kamar-Taj thirteen years later.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, Albus Dumbledore told Harry Potter of the theory, and of his reason to believe that Lily had descended from a very powerful line of magic indeed. In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, in the autumn of 1992, the Heir of Slytherin seemed to be hunting Muggle-born students. Hermione and Justin Finch-Fletchley were both Muggle-born. Justin was Petrified before Christmas, and Hermione in the spring.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, on 22 August 1994, Arthur Weasley said that some World Cup visitors were arriving by Muggle transport, such as Apache helicopters. Harry Potter knew better: no wizard, not even a Muggle-born, would turn up in an American military helicopter.

pages.title: Hagrid's photograph album
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Moving wizard photographs of James and Lily Potter
pages.html:
Hagrid's photograph album is the leather-bound book of wizard photographs that Rubeus Hagrid gave Harry Potter at the end of his first year at Hogwarts, in June 1992. On every page Harry's parents smile and wave up at him.

The gift

Harry had never owned a single photograph of his parents, as Hagrid knew. So Hagrid sent owls to all of Lily and James Potter's old school friends, asking for photographs, then put what came back into one book.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, as the school year ended in June 1992, Hagrid gave Harry the album. Dumbledore had given him a day off to put it together. It was bound in handsome leather. Its photographs showed Harry's parents by a lake, then in a garden, with his father's arm round his mother while she laughed at something out of the picture. On another page his mother held a baby with black hair who kept trying to grab her nose.

'Sent owls off ter all yer mum an' dad's old school friends, askin' fer photos,' said Hagrid. 'Knew yeh didn' have any. D'yeh like it?' Harry could not speak, and Hagrid understood that well enough.

In Book Three, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1993, Aunt Marge insulted Harry's mother at the table at Privet Drive. Afterwards, sitting on his bed, Harry thought of the album. He thought of one page in particular, where his mother stands laughing in a garden with his father's arm round her.

pages.title: Bertie Bott's Every-Flavour Beans
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
On the Hogwarts Express; at Honeydukes
Every one, earwax and vomit included
pages.html:
Bertie Bott's Every-Flavour Beans are jelly beans that mean exactly what they say. Besides chocolate, peppermint and marmalade, a box may hold spinach, liver or tripe. The unlucky can find vomit, earwax, grass or sprouts.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, they were on the trolley of the Hogwarts Express when Harry bought some of everything. In Chapter Eight Hermione gave Ron a box of them for Christmas 1991.

In Chapter Thirteen, at the end of that school year, Professor Dumbledore told Harry in the hospital wing that he had had the misfortune in his youth to meet one that tasted of vomit, and had never quite trusted them since. He picked out a golden-brown one that he hoped would be toffee all the same. ‘Alas!’ he said. ‘Earwax!’

On the Hogwarts Express going home, Ron got one that was definitely grass. Hermione took a green one, considered it and found that it was sprouts.

pages.title: Honeydukes
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Honeydukes Best chocolate; Pepper Imps; Chocolate Frogs
A passage from Hogwarts comes up in its cellar
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Honeydukes is the sweetshop in Hogsmeade, and it has stood in the village for about five hundred years. It sells everything from Chocolate Frogs to blood lollipops, with a cellar full of stock beneath the shop. A secret passage from Hogwarts comes up through a trapdoor in that cellar.

The shop

The shelves go up to the ceiling. There is nougat in creamy chunks, shimmering pink coconut ice, toffees the colour of honey and hundreds of chocolates in neat ranks. Down one whole wall, under a sign that says Special Effects, are the odd ones. In the far corner a tray under the sign Unusual Tastes holds such things as blood lollipops. Pepper Imps make the eater smoke at the mouth. A slab of Honeydukes Best the size of a roof slate costs eight Sickles. The owners live over the shop.

The passage

Of the seven secret passages out of Hogwarts on the Marauder's Map, one starts in the hump of a statue of a one-eyed witch on the third floor. It runs underground for about an hour's walk, twisting and doubling back on itself. It ends at a trapdoor in the Honeydukes cellar, which sinks so neatly into the dusty floor once it is shut that nobody could say where it was.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, the sweets heaped by Harry's hospital bed in the summer of 1992 looked like the entire stock of Honeydukes. In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, in December 1992, Ambrose Greyhame bought a Chocolate Frog there on his way up to the castle. He laughed so loudly at the card that the witch behind the counter dropped a jar of Pepper Imps.

In Book Three, Chapter Five, Ron Weasley said it was Honeydukes he most wanted to visit; by Hallowe'en he had been talking about it since August. In Chapter Eight, at Hallowe'en 1993, he and Hermione Granger came back from their first visit with as many sweets as they could carry. Hermione had bought Harry the biggest bar of Honeydukes Best they had, the size of a roof slate, and made the man fetch it from the back. It cost eight Sickles.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Harry came up through the trapdoor for the first time. He slipped up the cellar stairs into the shop, where he found Ron and Hermione bent over the Unusual Tastes tray. In Chapter Twelve, after Harry's first Patronus, Lupin put a slab of Honeydukes' best into his hands, the size of a roof tile.

In Chapter Fourteen, in the spring of 1994, Harry came out of the shop again under his Cloak. Later that day he fled back down through the trapdoor. He had to leave the Cloak stuffed in his bag in the dark at the foot of the chute, and after Snape had caught him with the Marauder's Map he did not dare go back for it.

In Book Three, Chapter Seventeen, running down the tunnel under the Whomping Willow, Harry thought it must be even longer than the passage to Honeydukes.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, Ron Weasley took a box of the best chocolates Honeydukes made to the World Cup on 22 August 1994. He kept it rolled up in his spare socks with a borrowed comb and a bottle of Sleekeazy's Hair Potion. All of it was for Plan A, the scheme he had worked out with Pansy Parkinson to bring Harry Potter together with Dracina Malfoy.

pages.title: The tentacled idol
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl Who Noticed Him, Chapter Thirteen
pages.html:
The tentacled idol was a present that Charlie Weasley sent his younger brother Percy in 1991, from Romania, where Charlie works with dragons. Mrs Weasley took it off him, because it had too many tentacles for her liking.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, Harry Potter lay in the hospital wing in June 1992, after going down through the trapdoor. When he told Ron Weasley how wise he thought Dumbledore was, Ron gave him a funny look. It was the look Ron gave Percy when Percy got going about the Ministry. Harry had heard the story of the idol that Charlie had sent Percy the year before, and of how Mrs Weasley had had to take it off him.

pages.title: Platform nine and three-quarters
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Through the barrier between platforms nine and ten
Book One, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Platform nine and three-quarters is the hidden platform at King's Cross station in London, from which the Hogwarts Express leaves for school at eleven o'clock every 1 September. The way onto it is straight through the solid-looking barrier between platforms nine and ten.

The platform

To Muggles the barrier is an ordinary wall of brick. A witch or wizard simply walks at it, or runs at it if nervous, and comes out on the other side. There a scarlet steam engine waits beside a platform packed with families. At the end of term the students come home the same way, back through the barrier into the Muggle station. An old guard lets them out a few at a time, so that the Muggles do not notice whole crowds of children walking out of a wall.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, in June 1992, the Hogwarts Express brought the students home at the end of Harry Potter's first year. A wizened old guard let them out into the Muggle station in twos and threes.

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, Harry ran at the barrier with Ron Weasley. Both their trolleys hit the wall and bounced off it. Harry tried again, leaning on it with all his weight, but the brick stayed brick while the clock ran down to eleven. The two of them flew to Hogwarts in Mr Weasley's car instead. In Chapter Eleven Harry learnt that Dobby the house-elf had sealed the barrier against them.

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on 1 September 1993, Arthur Weasley kept close to Harry's elbow all the way into the station, with Sirius Black on the loose. He strolled up to the barrier, apparently very interested in an InterCity 125 that had just come in at platform nine, and leant casually against it. Harry did the same. Together they fell sideways through the solid metal on to platform nine and three-quarters.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, on 22 August 1994, Arthur Weasley explained why the World Cup had been set on a deserted moor. There were places Muggles could not penetrate, he said, such as Diagon Alley or platform nine and three-quarters, but they were far too small for a hundred thousand wizards.

pages.title: King's Cross
infobox: The magical barrier between platforms nine and ten
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
King's Cross is the London railway station from which the Hogwarts Express leaves for school every year on 1 September, from platform nine and three-quarters. Wizarding families reach the platform by walking straight at the magical barrier between platforms nine and ten. To Muggles it is solid brick.

The station

To Muggles King's Cross is an ordinary mainline terminus, with a great concourse and a great many pigeons. At the end of every term families wait there for the train, wizarding families on the platform and Muggle ones on the other side of the barrier. The barrier can be sealed, which is how two second-years came to miss the train in 1992.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, in the summer of 1992, the Dursleys collected Harry Potter from King's Cross at the end of his first year. Dracina Malfoy warned him there to watch out the next year.

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, the barrier sealed itself against Harry and Ron Weasley. They crashed into solid brick and missed the Hogwarts Express. In Chapter Eleven Harry learnt that Dobby had sealed the gateway to keep him away from school.

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, inside Tom Riddle's diary, Harry watched the young Riddle's disappointment at having to leave Hogwarts. He remembered wearing the same face on the platform the summer before, as he watched Uncle Vernon's car pull up. In Chapter Nineteen, in June 1993, he stopped in the middle of the concourse with his trunk and his owl, then made the sign of the Cross. He did it clumsily, feeling very silly, and he did it all the same. In Book Three, Chapter One, he remembered it. On 1 September 1993 he left for school from here.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, in June 1994, Molly Weasley flung her arms round Harry on the Muggle side of the barrier. Over his shoulder she gave Vernon Dursley a long, thoughtful, measuring look. Vernon did not know why, but he took a step backwards and trod on a pigeon.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: Harry remembered that the Ministry of Magic had lent the Weasleys two cars to get to King's Cross in 1993. In Chapter Five Mrs Weasley planned to take the children there in the week after the World Cup, and worried about what to wear on the Muggle side of the barrier.

pages.title: Ravenclaw Quidditch team
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A flat formation of three Chasers
pages.html:
The Ravenclaw Quidditch team plays in blue for Ravenclaw house at Hogwarts. In 1993 to 1994 its captain was Roger Davies, a big fifth-year Chaser built like a rower, and its Seeker was Cho Chang, a fourth-year who flew a Comet Two Sixty.

Style of play

Under Davies the team flew a formation Harry Potter had never seen a school side use. All three Chasers flew level, passing the Quaffle sideways in short, quick bursts, so that there was never anybody out in front to mark. It had one weakness, which Harry spotted in the end. The Chasers always turned the same way, into Davies, because he was the big one and they were all watching him.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, Ravenclaw steamrollered Gryffindor in the last match of the season, in the summer of 1992, while Harry lay unconscious in the hospital wing. In Book Three, Chapter Ten, at the end of November 1993, Ravenclaw flattened Hufflepuff. Harry watched Cedric Diggory lose the Snitch to a tiny Ravenclaw girl who went past him like a thrown dart.

In Chapter Thirteen Ravenclaw met Gryffindor with their flat formation and went three goals clear. One of their Beaters struck Alicia Spinnet across the forearm with a fair shot. Harry told the Weasley twins to stop defending and put both Bludgers on the Ravenclaw Chasers' turn. Soon afterwards a Bludger came at him from his blind side, and only the Firebolt got him out of its way. Gryffindor won by two hundred and thirty points to seventy.

pages.title: The Hogwarts Express driver
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The driver of the Hogwarts Express drives the scarlet steam engine that carries Hogwarts students north from King's Cross to Hogsmeade station, and brings them home again. Between her rounds, the trolley witch is to be found up front with him.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on 1 September 1991, Hermione Granger went up to the front of the train to ask the driver how far they still had to go. He told her they were almost there. She came back along the corridor to tell Harry Potter and Ron Weasley to get their robes on.

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on 1 September 1993, the trolley witch found Professor Lupin asleep in Harry's compartment. If he was hungry when he woke, she told them, she would be up front with the driver.

That evening the train stopped with a jolt in the dark, still short of Hogwarts. All the lamps went out. Hermione set off to ask the driver what was going on, but she collided with Ginny Weasley in the doorway and never got there. When the dementor that had come aboard was gone, Lupin handed round chocolate. Then he went to speak to the driver himself.

pages.title: Dudley's gang
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
St Grogory's Primary School, Little Whinging
pages.html:
Dudley's gang is the band of boys who follow Harry Potter's cousin, Dudley Dursley, about Little Whinging. All through Harry's years at primary school they bullied him. Everybody at school knew that the gang hated Harry, and nobody wanted to disagree with them, so Harry never had a friend there.

Members

Its best-known member is Dudley's best friend, Piers Polkiss, a thin, rat-faced boy whose job, as a rule, is to hold the victim still while Dudley does the hitting.

Harry Hunting

The gang's favourite game was Harry Hunting, which they played every summer behind the shops. At school they went for him in the playground whenever the teachers were not looking. Dudley used to hang Harry off the school roof by his ankles while his friends made a game of kicking his head, hard enough to make it ache for days. When Harry was nine they gave him a beating he has never forgotten, nor how alone he felt afterwards.

Harry carries a cruel voice at the back of his head, one that has been there for as long as he can remember. It sounds a bit like Uncle Vernon, a bit like Aunt Petunia and a bit like Dudley's gang in the playground.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, when Dracina Malfoy taunted him, Harry shouted the worst of it in her face: 'My cousin Dudley used to hang me off the school roof by my ankles, and his mates made a game of kicking my head!'

In Book One, Chapter Nine, seeing Neville Longbottom left miserable on his own, Harry remembered himself at nine, after Dudley and his gang had finished with him. He gave Neville his last Chocolate Frog.

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, the gang's voices were among those that made up the cruel voice in Harry's head. In Chapter Eighteen, in the Chamber of Secrets, Tom Riddle told Harry that he had seen the playground in Harry's memories, along with what the boys did there when the teachers were not looking.

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, talking with Sirius Black, Harry thought of the gang playing Harry Hunting every summer behind the shops, and he wanted to tell his godfather everything.

pages.title: Divination
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Optional subject, from the third year
Tea leaves, palms, fire omens, the crystal ball
The Inner Eye, or the Sight
Book One, Book Two, Book Three
pages.html:
Divination is the art of seeing what is to come, and an optional subject at Hogwarts from the third year. Its teachers hold that it needs the Inner Eye, which is rare. Professor McGonagall holds that it is among the least exact of the magical disciplines.

The subject

Third-years begin with the leaves of the teacup and move on to the lines of the hand. After fire omens they come to the crystal ball. Like a great deal of magic, Divination is said to be affected by the phase of the moon. Professor Trelawney teaches it at the top of the North Tower, up a silver ladder through a trapdoor, in a hot, dim room lit red, where the fire gives off a thick, sweet smell.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Hermione Granger reported Professor Sinistra's view that the phase of the moon affects almost everything, Divination obviously. In Book One, Chapter Eleven, she said the centaurs' warnings sounded like fortune-telling, which Professor McGonagall called a very imprecise branch of magic. In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, Percy Weasley recommended Divination to Harry Potter as a third-year subject.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, Trelawney set out the year's work and foretold that one of the class would leave it for good around Easter. Harry's death was read in his tea leaves the same morning. McGonagall told the class that Divination was among the least exact of the magical disciplines. In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Trelawney began the crystal ball by having her class relax the conscious mind, so as to clear the Inner Eye. When Harry asked about the prophets of the Bible, she dismissed them as desert folk tales. When he asked about Christmas, she told him that names were merely labels, and that the Inner Eye looks beneath them. Later in the lesson she saw the Grim again, this time in Harry's crystal ball. Hermione called it ridiculous, was told that her mind was hopelessly mundane, and walked out of Divination for good. Lavender Brown at once remembered the prophecy about Easter.

pages.title: The Hogwarts kitchens
infobox: Low in the castle, directly beneath the Great Hall
Tickle the pear in the painting of a bowl of fruit
pages.html:
The Hogwarts kitchens lie low down in the castle, directly beneath the Great Hall, and every meal the school eats is cooked there. About a hundred house-elves work in them, more than in any other dwelling in Britain. Four long tables stand in the kitchens exactly below the four house tables upstairs, and the food laid on them rises through the ceiling to the golden plates.

The kitchens

A corridor from the ground floor leads down to them, with a tall window looking out over the lawns to the lake. A suit of armour stands near them. The way in is through a painting of a bowl of fruit: tickle the pear, which giggles, turning into a large green door handle. Students who find their way there are made very welcome, since the elves will press food on anybody at any hour.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, at Christmas 1991, Harry Potter, lost in the dark under the Invisibility Cloak, knew there was a suit of armour near the kitchens. He reckoned he must be five floors above it. In Chapter Nine, after Gryffindor beat Hufflepuff in 1992, Fred and George Weasley nicked cakes from the kitchens for the party in Gryffindor Tower. In Chapter Thirteen Albus Dumbledore told Harry that his father had used the Cloak 'mainly for sneaking down to the kitchens for food, as I recall.'

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, Harry found the Fat Friar floating at the tall window of the corridor to the kitchens, watching the lake turn gold as the sun went down. Later that term George Weasley told Harry he had seen Dracina Malfoy coming up out of the kitchens at night, on her own, carrying a parcel. 'Smelt worse than Ron's socks,' said Fred. 'The parcel, not her.' His theory was that she was bribing the house-elves with something dead.

pages.title: Muggle
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Book One, Book Two, Book Four
pages.html:
A Muggle is a person with no magic, and the word wizards use for everybody who is not one of them. Most Muggles have no idea that the wizarding world exists, and the Ministry of Magic works hard to keep it that way.

Muggles and wizards

Under the Statute of Secrecy, wizards hide themselves from Muggles. When a Muggle sees something he should not, such as a wild dragon, the Ministry puts a memory spell on him. Often it hardly needs to, since Muggles will go to great lengths not to notice magic.

Wizarding feeling about Muggles runs from Arthur Weasley's delight to the contempt of the old pure-blood families. Harry Potter was brought up by Muggles. Hermione Granger comes from a Muggle family, and Seamus Finnigan's father is a Muggle.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the Hogwarts Express, Ron Weasley asked Harry what the Muggles who had brought him up were like. In Book One, Chapter Ten, Ron observed that it was hard enough stopping Muggles noticing wizards without people keeping dragons in the back garden.

In Book Two, Chapter One, after another summer with the Dursleys, Harry understood at last why so many witches and wizards walled themselves off from Muggles, though Hermione's parents sounded perfectly nice. In Book Two, Chapter Four, Arthur Weasley explained why it was so hard to get a conviction for Muggle-baiting. ‘Bless them, they’ll go to any lengths to ignore magic, even with it staring them in the face...’ In Book Two, Chapter Five, he called it ingenious how many ways Muggles had found of getting along without magic. In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Harry argued that there were enough dreadful Muggles about for wizards not to fight each other over blood.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, at supper at the Burrow on 21 August 1994, Molly Weasley could not think what had got into the Muggles. They always used to be such nice, unobservant people, she said, and Arthur added sadly that you could once have Apparated into the middle of a bus queue unnoticed. By then Muggles were turning on anybody they suspected of having powers: a witch in Godalming had had her windows put in twice, and HUMANS FIRST had been painted on the front door of Mrs Fenwick, who keeps bees.

pages.title: Wizarding money
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Seventeen Sickles to a Galleon; twenty-nine Knuts to a Sickle
pages.html:
Wizards pay in three coins: gold Galleons, silver Sickles and bronze Knuts. There are seventeen Sickles to the Galleon and twenty-nine Knuts to the Sickle. The goblins of Gringotts keep the wizarding world's gold in their vaults deep under London.

Reckoning

Witches and wizards brought up among Muggles do not always get the hang of it. John Constantine, a wizard for thirty years near enough, still thinks it is like something a mad uncle made up at Christmas to keep the children quiet.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter One, Harry Potter stood outside Madam Malkin's with a bag of Galleons in his pocket. The girl beside him, Dracina Malfoy, had eyes the colour of a new Sickle. In Chapter Two, on his first journey to Hogwarts, he bought some of everything on the trolley, handing over eleven silver Sickles and seven bronze Knuts. The Dursleys had never once given him money for sweets.

In Chapter Eight his aunt and uncle sent him a fifty-pence piece for Christmas, Sellotaped to a note. 'That's friendly,' said Harry. Ron Weasley, though, was fascinated by the coin. 'Weird!' he said. 'Look at the shape of it! This is money?' At Christmas dinner Percy nearly broke a tooth on a silver Sickle buried in his slice of pudding.

In Book Two, Chapter Five, the Weasleys' vault at Gringotts held a very small pile of Sickles and one gold Galleon. Mrs Weasley felt right into the corners before she swept the lot into her bag.

In the Book Three Interlude, in the summer of 1993, the Knight Bus charged John Constantine eleven Sickles to Hogsmeade, or thirteen with hot chocolate. He found them mostly in the lining of his coat. Later that night Harry paid his own fare with a fistful of gold Galleons, far more than it came to, in the hope that it might buy him a little quiet as well as a bed.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Five: at the World Cup campsite on 22 August 1994 the twins bet Ludo Bagman every coin they had on the final: thirty-seven Galleons, fifteen Sickles and three Knuts. The Muggle manager, Mr Roberts, had already had two campers try to pay him with great gold coins the size of hubcaps.

pages.title: Dobby
infobox:
Harry Potter the wizard he tried to protect, the wizard he tries to protect, liberator
Dracina Malfoy implied 'Mistress', mistress, as Harry understood it, former young mistress
Lucius Malfoy master, former master
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
Lucius Malfoy, through a trick of Harry Potter's
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Dobby is a house-elf who served the Malfoy family until the summer of 1993, when Harry Potter tricked Lucius Malfoy into freeing him with a sock. All through the year before, with great devotion and very little sense, he tried to keep Harry away from Hogwarts, where he knew a plot was waiting for him.

Bondage

A house-elf is bound to serve one wizarding family for ever, and can leave only if his masters give him real clothes. The Malfoys took care never to hand Dobby so much as a glove. He went about in an old pillowcase with holes torn in it for his arms and legs, which was the mark of his bondage. He is no taller than a bedside table, with huge, bulging green eyes the size of tennis balls, long ears like a bat's and a thin, pointed nose. Like all his kind he has a strong magic of his own, which needs no wand.

An elf must punish himself for speaking ill of his family. Dobby did so constantly. He shut his ears in the oven door. He banged his head against walls and window frames. Once he even broke a water jug over his own skull. His family sometimes reminded him to do extra punishments. He was threatened with death most days: 'Five times, on a good day.' He remembers that when He Who Must Not Be Named was strong, house-elves were kicked like dogs. Harry's survival, he says, was like the sun rising for the bound ones.

In the saga: the warning of 1992

Dobby had been watching Number Four, Privet Drive since before the summer of 1992. What he saw there, the cupboard, the bread and the bars on the window, he reported to the young Dracina Malfoy. Dracina ordered him to warn Harry of danger at Hogwarts. Dobby had overheard enough of his master's plans to be frightened, so he took the order as a command to stop him.

On 31 July 1992 he watched Harry from the hedge. That evening he appeared on Harry's bed during the Dursleys' dinner for Mr and Mrs Mason. He burst into loud tears at being asked to sit down like an equal, hailed Harry as a champion of the light, and warned him that terrible things would happen at Hogwarts that year. Asked whether He Who Must Not Be Named was behind it, he shook his head, and spoke of powers that no decent wizard would use.

He admitted that he had been stealing the letters Ron, Hermione and Hagrid wrote to Harry. He had hoped that Harry would think himself friendless, and would stay away. When Harry refused to promise not to go back, Dobby levitated Aunt Petunia's pudding of cream and sugared violets. He dropped it on the floor, then vanished with a crack, and the Ministry's warning about the Hover Charm landed on Harry instead.

On 1 September he sealed the barrier at King's Cross. When his young mistress found out, she ordered him to iron his hands, and he showed Harry ten bandaged fingers. When he heard that Harry had reached the castle anyway, he let his master's supper catch fire. He was beaten so hard for it that he could not sit down for a week.

In November he bewitched a Bludger to hurt Harry badly enough to be sent home, insisting all the while that he wanted him alive. That night, in the hospital wing, he let slip that the Chamber of Secrets had been opened before. He stopped himself on the very edge of naming 'the Di...'. His master had told him to tell nobody, not even the mistress, though he had told her a little. Dracina complained afterwards that he had misread her order completely: she had told him to warn Harry, not to stop him.

In the saga: freedom

At the end of the school year in 1993 Dobby came into Professor McGonagall's office at Lucius Malfoy's heels, bandaged from head to foot. While punishing himself, he managed to signal to Harry that his master was behind the diary. Lucius kicked him out through the door. Harry hid his own sock inside the ruined diary and handed it to Lucius, who threw the sock away. Dobby caught it.

'Master has given Dobby a sock,' he said, in a trembling voice. 'Master threw it, and Dobby caught it, and Dobby... Dobby is free.'

Dobby flung his arms round Harry's middle. Harry had wanted to kill him for most of the year, but now that he had the chance he found that he could not bring himself to do it. Instead he made Dobby promise never to mess him about again, with no more barriers, Bludgers or puddings. In future he was to ask first. Dobby swore to serve Harry Potter of his own will for ever and ever. He would be a champion of the light, he said, as Harry Potter was. Then he vanished with a crack.

In the saga: afterwards

In the autumn of 1993 Dracina compared Professor Lupin's darned robes to the dress of 'our old house-elf'. Where Dobby has gone since he was freed is not generally known.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the Top Box at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, Harry briefly took Barty Crouch's house-elf Winky for Dobby, whom Ron and Hermione had heard all about but never seen. Winky said that Dobby talked of Harry all the time, but that freedom had gone to his head: he wanted paying, could not get another position and was getting up to high jinks unbecoming to a house-elf. Harry admitted that he had freed Dobby mainly to mess Lucius Malfoy about, though Dobby had seemed happy to be free.

In their own words

Mistress was very clear on Dobby telling Harry Potter this...Dobby · B2 Ch2
Dobby is threatened with death most days, sir. Five times, on a good day.Dobby · B2 Ch11
Harry Potter would die for his friends!Dobby · B2 Ch11
Master has given Dobby a sock. Master threw it, and Dobby caught it, and Dobby... Dobby is free.Dobby · B2 Ch19

pages.title: Gilderoy Lockhart
infobox:
Harry Potter student he courts for publicity, student who exposed him
Molly Weasley admirer
Hermione Granger admirer, former admirer
Minerva McGonagall colleague who exposes him
Severus Snape Duelling Club assistant
The Armenian warlock took credit for his deeds
The witch who saw off the Bandon Banshee took credit for her deeds
Hogwarts staff, Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher, author, Defence Against the Dark Arts, fraud, former Hogwarts staff
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Order of Merlin, Third Class; Honorary Member of the Dark Force Defence League; five times winner of Witch Weekly's Most Charming Smile Award
Magical Me; Voyages with Vampires; Gadding with Ghouls; Travels with Trolls; Year with the Yeti
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Gilderoy Lockhart is a celebrated writer of adventure memoirs who taught Defence Against the Dark Arts at Hogwarts from 1992 to 1993. He was handsome, vain and the only applicant for the post. He turned out to have done none of the deeds in his books: he had stolen them from other people, then wiped their memories. In the end he lost his own memory in the tunnels of the Chamber of Secrets.

Early life and career

Gilderoy Lockhart was born on 26 January 1964. He was sorted into Ravenclaw, and he was at Hogwarts from 1975 to 1982. He was gifted at exactly one thing, the Memory Charm, and he built his whole fame on it.

He sought out people who had done remarkable things, among them an Armenian warlock who rid a village of werewolves and a witch who saw off the Bandon Banshee. He found out how they had done it, took the credit, then wiped their memories. His books, illustrated with winking photographs of himself, made up seven of the eight set texts for the second year in 1992 to 1993.

He holds the Order of Merlin, Third Class. He is an Honorary Member of the Dark Force Defence League, and he has five times won Witch Weekly's Most Charming Smile Award, which he likes people to know he does not talk about. He quotes Joseph Campbell on the hero's journey. His favourite colour is lilac.

At Hogwarts

In August 1992, signing copies of his autobiography Magical Me at Flourish and Blotts, he pulled Harry Potter into a photograph for the Daily Prophet and announced that he would be teaching Defence at Hogwarts that year.

His first lesson was a quiz about himself. Then he let loose a cage of Cornish pixies, failed to stop them with 'Peskipiksi Pesternomi' and hid under his desk. Professor McGonagall forbade him to bring any creature into a classroom again without her written permission, on pain of leaving by the window the pixies had used. He spent the rest of the year reading his books aloud and acting out his exploits, with Harry as his prop.

His claims were endless, and McGonagall exposed several of them. He said Mrs Norris had suffered the Transmogrifian Torture. He claimed to have wrestled a vocal-cord parasite out of a man's throat in Africa. He boasted of foiling a Transylvanian cult of three hundred red-robed Dracula worshippers, led by a fourth-generation Tzimisce, with the help of 'old Julius Carrow'. He mispronounced Tzimisce. As for Julius, he was a real friend of Professor McGonagall's, but he was no Carrow: Lockhart had made the surname up.

He claimed, too, to have fought beside the Master, grandsire of Angelus, after a fortnight's training from the Slayer. When Hermione pointed out that the Master had been sealed away since 1937, he called it a psychic projection and gave her five points. He was right, for once, that there is only ever one Slayer at a time, and that the Master is Angelus's grandsire. He also claimed to have cured the Wagga Wagga werewolf with a Homorphus Charm, which does not exist.

Trying to mend Harry's broken arm on the Quidditch pitch, he removed all its bones. At his Duelling Club Snape blasted him off the stage with a Disarming Charm. Watching Harry duel Dracina Malfoy, he seemed suddenly older, as if he had understood something he had once read or written about, and he loosened his collar.

On Valentine's Day 1993 he covered the Great Hall in pink flowers and thanked the forty-six people who had sent him cards. He had hired a dozen dwarfs to act as cupids. Catching sight of Harry with Dracina, he mouthed 'Young love!' at them.

Exposure and fall

After Hagrid's arrest he insisted that the danger had passed. By late May his hair had lost its gloss and his robes their sleekness. Pupils had begun to look at him with a cold, measuring contempt.

When Ginny Weasley was taken, the other teachers goaded him into facing the monster alone. Harry and Ron found him packing to flee. He confessed his frauds and tried to wipe their memories. Instead he was disarmed, then forced down the pipe into the Chamber's tunnels. There he seized Ron's broken wand and cast Obliviate. The spell backfired, wiping his own memory and bringing down the roof.

Fawkes carried him back up the pipe. Lockhart hummed placidly to himself all the way, and remarked that it was just like magic. Afterwards he asked whether he had been a hopeless professor. Dumbledore announced that Professor Lockhart would not be returning, since he needed to go away and find his memory. The staff cheered, Snape included.

In their own words

That's Joseph Campbell, by the way. A Muggle, but a very smart man.Gilderoy Lockhart · B2 Ch5
I could whip up a Mandrake Restorative Draught in my sleep!Gilderoy Lockhart · B2 Ch10
Your faith in me is most gratifying, Harry.Gilderoy Lockhart · B2 Ch10
A psychic projection. Of course! Well spotted, Miss Granger, take five points.Gilderoy Lockhart · B2 Ch11

pages.title: Colin Creevey
infobox:
Harry Potter hero, idol
Colin Creevey's father father
Ginny Weasley friend, best friend
Gryffindor, Hogwarts student, Muggle-born, first-year, Basilisk victim
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Colin Creevey is a Muggle-born Gryffindor, a year below Harry Potter, who worships Harry and follows him everywhere with a camera. In November 1992 the Basilisk from the Chamber of Secrets Petrified him. In 1993 he founded Harry's fan club.

Background

Colin is very small, with mousy hair. His father is a Muggle milkman, and he has a younger brother, Dennis. He never knew that the odd things he could do were magic until his Hogwarts letter came. He was sorted into Gryffindor in 1992. He photographs everything with a Muggle camera to send home, and develops the pictures in a potion so that they move.

First year, 1992 to 1993

In his first week Colin asked Harry for a signed photograph, which gave Dracina Malfoy something to jeer at. The upshot was a double portrait of Harry and Gilderoy Lockhart, in which Lockhart kept trying to drag Harry back into view. Colin learnt Harry's timetable by heart. He said hello to him six or seven times a day, followed him down to Quidditch practice and asked whether he could photograph Ron being sick with slugs. Harry found him a nuisance, but he always made time for him, as though Colin were a little brother who thought Harry had hung the moon. In Charms Colin sat next to Ginny Weasley, and promised to teach her how to make photographs move.

When Harry was hurt in the Slytherin match, Colin photographed him lying on the pitch. That night he was found Petrified on the stairs, with his camera held up to his face. He had a bunch of grapes with him, which he seemed to have been bringing to Harry. The inside of the camera had melted. He had seen the Basilisk only through his lens, and that had saved his life. Dracina sneered to Crabbe and Goyle that he should never have been let through the gates. He lay in the hospital wing through the winter and spring of 1993, until he was revived with Mandrake juice.

Second year, 1993 to 1994
