After the Chamber, Colin and Ginny became best friends. In 1993 he ran a Harry Potter fan club of eight or nine younger pupils, who wore red HP badges. When Harry fell from his broom in the Hufflepuff match, Colin brought him a get-well card signed by the whole club. Harry treats him like a little brother, helping him with his homework and teasing him about Ginny.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: by August 1994 Colin and Ginny Weasley had been as thick as thieves ever since they came out of the hospital wing together after the Chamber. Harry had heard that they were closer still now, with their fan club and its round red badges.

pages.title: Errol
infobox:
Ron Weasley family owl
Molly Weasley owner
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Errol is the Weasley family's owl, an ancient great grey who is devoted, exhausted and given to collapsing on arrival. He has carried the family's post to Harry Potter since 1992.

Description

Errol is old and feeble; Harry reckons him about a hundred years old. He cannot fly in a straight line, and he has never in his life arrived anywhere without crashing into it. He is not really up to long journeys, so the younger Weasleys are not supposed to use him for them. He is a family owl, not Ron's own, as Ron once had to point out to Hermione: all Ron had of his own was Scabbers. Ron once joked that his mother would set Errol on the Ministry.

In the saga

In August 1992 Errol brought Hermione's letter to the Burrow, and then could not stand on his perch. On 2 September 1992 he crashed into Hermione's milk jug at breakfast, carrying Mrs Weasley's Howler for Ron.

In the summer of 1993 Ron sent him to Privet Drive with Harry's birthday Sneakoscope. He went straight into the lampshade, fell in a heap of grey feathers on Harry's essay and slept in Hedwig's cage. For Aunt Marge's visit Harry sent Hedwig back to Egypt with him for a week. Hedwig flew slowly, with a great many backward glances, so that Errol could keep up.

In the summer of 1994 he carried an enormous fruitcake and a heap of meat pies from Mrs Weasley to Privet Drive. He needed five whole days in the airing cupboard to get over the trip. After that Percy's owl, Hermes, brought the parcels.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, on 21 August 1994, Ron Weasley explained that he kept Pigwidgeon up in his attic bedroom because the tiny owl annoyed Errol and Hermes. Pig annoyed Ron too, he added.

pages.title: Hermes
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Hermes is Percy Weasley's screech owl. Percy's parents bought him when Percy was made a prefect in 1991, and he is named after the messenger of the Greek gods.

Percy's owl

Hermes is a handsome, well-kept screech owl. He is much the more reliable of the two owls at the Burrow. The other is Errol, the elderly family owl, who has been known to collapse in the middle of a delivery.

Arthur and Molly Weasley bought Hermes as Percy's reward for becoming a prefect. On the same occasion Percy's old rat, Scabbers, was handed down to Ron. On the Hogwarts Express in 1991 Ron explained it to Harry Potter: 'Dad bought Percy an owl for being made Prefect, but they couldn't aff... I mean, I got Scabbers.'

Percy treats Hermes as a mark of his position. He does not share him.

In the saga

In the summer of 1992 Percy kept Hermes busy with a great many letters, written in secret to his girlfriend, Penelope Clearwater. Ron tried to borrow Hermes to write to Harry, but Percy would not lend him. He said he needed him. Ron had to rely on Errol instead.

On 1 September 1993 Hermes travelled to Hogwarts with the family's luggage. That morning he sat in his cage beside Hedwig, on top of the heap of trunks by the Leaky Cauldron's door.

By August 1994 Percy had begun work at the Ministry of Magic. That summer Molly Weasley sent Harry food parcels at Privet Drive. Errol carried the first, and needed five whole days in the airing cupboard to get over it. After that Hermes delivered the rest, with an air of great self-importance very like his owner's.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, on 21 August 1994, Ron Weasley told Harry Potter that he had to keep Pigwidgeon up in his attic bedroom, because the tiny owl annoyed Hermes and Errol. Pig annoyed Ron too, he added.

pages.title: The Weasleys' ghoul
infobox: The Burrow ghoul; The Weasley ghoul
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The attic of the Burrow, above Ron Weasley's room
Flesh; fed garden gnomes by Molly Weasley
Banging on the pipes; howling for sacrifices at night
To be a high-level servant of a Prince
pages.html:
The Weasleys' ghoul lives in the attic of the Burrow, directly above Ron Weasley's bedroom. It bangs on the pipes, groans and howls down them for sacrifices at night. It eats flesh. Since having it removed would need a professional the family cannot afford, Molly Weasley keeps it fed on garden gnomes. It never comes out of the attic. It claims to be a high-level servant of a Prince.

The ghoul in the attic

Getting rid of a ghoul is a job for a specialist. As Ron has explained: 'We tried to get him out, but we need a proper professional, and for a ghoul it's too bloody expensive.' The family are saving up. In the meantime Molly feeds it gnomes from the garden. The only thing that quietens it is Molly going up with the poker.

The ghoul keeps saying that it is a high-level servant of a Prince. Ron reckons it is talking nonsense. It has its uses all the same. Molly has threatened to set it on reporters from the Daily Prophet, while Ron has promised to set it on anybody who comes for Harry Potter.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, flying Harry to the Burrow in August 1992, George told him that instead of a house-elf the family had only a lousy old ghoul in the attic. Harry was horrified. Ron explained that it never came out of the attic, which he seemed to think settled it.

In Book Two, Chapters Four and Five, Harry learnt what it was to sleep below it. Ron's room was right under the ghoul, which banged on the pipes and groaned. Its howling for sacrifices down the pipes was all very well at breakfast, Harry found, and much less so at three in the morning.

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, the Daily Prophet reported that Mrs Weasley had told its reporters to get off her doorstep, or she would set the family ghoul on them. In Chapter Fifteen, Ron promised Harry that if the Dursleys wanted him back, his mother would set the ghoul on them. In Chapter Seventeen he made the same promise against the Ministry: 'And if they try, we've got a ghoul. He keeps going on about being some high level servant of a Prince. But I reckon he's talking nonsense.'

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, Ron offered Harry the whole family as his own, ghoul and all. 'It's got too many redheads in it, the ghoul bangs the pipes all night, but it's yours if you want it.'

pages.title: Mr Mason
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Dursleys' dinner party of 31 July 1992
pages.html:
Mr Mason is a rich Muggle builder with a very big nose. On 31 July 1992 he came to dinner at Number Four, Privet Drive, with his wife, and Vernon Dursley hoped to sell him an enormous order of drills.

Life

He is married to Mrs Mason, who has been terrified of birds of every size since she was a girl. He is said to be a marvellous golfer, and he tells a very funny story about some American plumbers.

Before the dinner the Dursleys spoke of him and his wife as 'those people', with a prejudice they never put into plain words.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter One, Uncle Vernon talked of nothing else for a fortnight. He meant to have the deal signed before the News at Ten, and to be looking at villas in Majorca the next day. Aunt Petunia began to remind him of something about the Masons. He told the family to put their personal feelings aside for the sake of the business, Harry especially, because he knew how Harry could be about 'those people'. Harry had not the faintest idea what he meant. It was Vernon and Petunia who had warned him about 'those people' in the first place.

In Chapter Two, Dobby the house-elf brought Aunt Petunia's pudding crashing down on the kitchen floor, but Uncle Vernon very nearly carried it off. It was the owl that finished it. A Ministry owl swooped in to drop a letter on Mrs Mason's head, and she fled the house screaming about lunatics. Mr Mason stayed only long enough to explain that his wife was terrified of birds, and to ask whether this was the Dursleys' idea of a joke. Uncle Vernon, trying to be diplomatic, asked whether 'their people' were always nervous of birds. Mr Mason went purple, shouted 'Why, I never...!' and left, slamming the front door behind him.

pages.title: Mrs Mason
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Birds of every size and description
The Dursleys' dinner party of 31 July 1992
pages.html:
Mrs Mason is the wife of Mr Mason, a rich Muggle builder. She has been terrified of birds of every size and description since she was a girl. In July 1992, at dinner with the Dursleys, an owl dropped a letter on her head.

The dinner party

The Masons came to Number Four, Privet Drive, on 31 July 1992, so that Vernon Dursley could sell Mr Mason a great many drills. Dudley had rehearsed taking her coat and leading her through to the dining room. Aunt Petunia had practised asking where she had found her dress.

Aunt Petunia was passing round the after-dinner mints when an enormous barn owl came in through the open dining-room window. It dropped a letter squarely on Mrs Mason's head and sailed out again. The letter was from the Ministry of Magic, and it was for Harry. Mrs Mason screamed like a banshee and ran out of the house shouting about lunatics.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, the evening ended with the owl. Earlier, Dobby the house-elf had brought Aunt Petunia's great pudding of cream and sugared violets crashing down on the kitchen floor, but Uncle Vernon had very nearly carried that off. After Mrs Mason fled, her husband stayed only long enough to explain about the birds.

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, lying in the hospital wing with the taste of Skele-Gro in his mouth, Harry ate a sweet that tasted exactly like the sugared violets on that pudding. In his memory of the night, Dobby had dropped the whole thing on Mrs Mason's head.

pages.title: Mafalda Hopkirk
infobox: Ministry of Magic, Improper Use of Magic Office
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Improper Use of Magic Office, Ministry of Magic
The warning sent to Harry Potter on 31 July 1992
A Hover Charm at number four, Privet Drive
pages.html:
Mafalda Hopkirk works in the Improper Use of Magic Office at the Ministry of Magic, which deals with magic done by underage wizards and with magic that risks being noticed by Muggles. Her name was on the official warning Harry Potter received on his twelfth birthday, 31 July 1992.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, a barn owl delivered the letter to number four, Privet Drive, dropping it on Mrs Mason's head in the middle of Uncle Vernon's dinner party. It said that a Hover Charm had been used at Harry's place of residence that evening at twelve minutes past nine. Underage wizards were not permitted to do spells outside school, under the Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery of 1875. Magic that risked notice by Muggles was a serious offence under the Statute of Secrecy. Just above her signature it said, ‘Enjoy your holidays!’

The charm had been Dobby's, who had floated Aunt Petunia's pudding up to the ceiling and dropped it. The Ministry did not know that. Uncle Vernon learnt from the letter that Harry was not allowed to do magic out of school, and locked him in his bedroom.

pages.title: Mr Borgin
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Borgin and Burkes, Knockturn Alley, London
Stooped, with greasy hair and an oily voice
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Mr Borgin is the proprietor of Borgin and Burkes, the largest shop in Knockturn Alley, which buys and sells Dark artefacts. He is a stooped man with greasy hair and a voice as oily as his hair. He fawns on his grander customers, Lucius Malfoy above all, and is plainly afraid of him.

The shop

Borgin and Burkes stocks skulls, cursed jewellery, glass eyes, poisons and Hands of Glory, among a great deal else. The Hands of Glory Borgin sells are the cheap sort, with a candle stuck in the palm. He calls them the best friend of thieves and plunderers.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, Harry Potter came out of the wrong grate into the shop by Floo, and hid in a big black cabinet when Lucius Malfoy came in with Dracina. Borgin greeted them with delight and began to show Lucius something just in today, very reasonably priced. Lucius raised one black-gloved hand, and Borgin stopped as if he had been switched off. The smile stayed where it was. The man beneath it was plainly frightened.

Lucius was selling, not buying. With the Ministry carrying out more raids, he had a few items at home that needed to be discreetly moved along. Borgin put on a pince-nez to read the list. When Dracina pointed at the withered hand on its cushion, he left the list to scurry over and explain the Hand of Glory. With a candle in it, he said, it gave light only to the holder. Later he sighed that wizard blood was counting for less everywhere. When Lucius said it was not so with him, Borgin agreed, with a bow so deep that Uncle Vernon would have admired it.

In a glass case lay an opal necklace whose card warned that it had claimed the lives of nineteen Muggle owners to date. When the haggling was done, Lucius told Borgin to come to Malfoy Manor the next day to collect the goods. The moment the door shut, Borgin dropped the oil. If the stories were true, he muttered, Lucius had not sold him half of what was hidden in his manor.

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine's Hand of Glory, with each of its fingers made into a candle, was not the cheap sort that Borgin sold. In Book Four, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1994, Dracina wrote to Harry that Mr Borgin still had the opal necklace in his shop, with its card saying it had killed nineteen Muggle owners. She had always thought twenty a rounder number, she added, and Harry had only to say the word.

pages.title: Mundungus Fletcher
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Order of the Phoenix, in the first war
pages.html:
Mundungus Fletcher is a wizard of the shadier sort, well known to the Ministry of Magic. He played a great many tricks on Arthur Weasley when Arthur was younger, and in August 1992 he tried to put a hex on him behind his back during a Ministry raid.

Character

Mundungus is a petty crook who knows every other crook in the country, which makes him useful. He belonged to the Order of the Phoenix in the first war against Lord Voldemort. He is loyal to Albus Dumbledore, who once got him out of a tight spot.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in August 1992, Arthur Weasley came home to the Burrow after a night of nine raids. 'And old Mundungus Fletcher tried to put a hex on me when I had my back turned.'

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, Ron Weasley was proud of having punched Sirius Black in the dormitory. His dad always said, Ron explained, that you should never sneak up on a man while he was asleep. His dad would know, after all the tricks old Mundungus Fletcher used to pull on him when he was younger.

pages.title: Mortlake
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Mortlake is a wizard whom the Ministry of Magic took in for questioning in August 1992, over some extremely odd ferrets. The case belonged to the Committee on Experimental Charms. What the ferrets did, or what Mortlake had done to them, is not recorded.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in August 1992, Arthur Weasley came home to the Burrow after a night of nine raids. Over a pot of tea he told his family about it. There had been some pretty nasty stuff that was not his department, he said: 'Mortlake was taken in for questioning about some extremely odd ferrets, but that's the Committee on Experimental Charms, thank goodness...'

pages.title: Perkins
infobox: Ministry of Magic, Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office, Ministry of Magic
pages.html:
Perkins is an old warlock who works in the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office at the Ministry of Magic. He and Arthur Weasley make up its entire staff. Between them they deal with bewitched objects made by Muggles that might end up back in a Muggle shop or house.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, as the Weasley boys flew Harry Potter to the Burrow in their father's car, Ron told Harry about the office. The year before, an old witch had died. She had owned a tea set given to her by a Muggle French nobleman, once under a curse, and his peasant wife. The set was sold to an antiques shop, where a little old Muggle lady bought it. When she tried to serve her friends tea in it, the pieces came alive. They started dancing and speaking to one another. The teapot sang, apparently. The old lady died of shock, and the other people there went mad. There were only the two of them in the office, so Perkins and Mr Weasley had to cover it all up with Memory Charms. Mr Weasley worked overtime for weeks.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Five: Arthur Weasley borrowed Perkins's tent for the 1994 World Cup, since Perkins no longer camps much, poor fellow, because of his lumbago. Inside it was done out exactly like Mrs Figg's front room, smelling powerfully of cats, with an old copy of Which Broomstick that Perkins had left behind.

pages.title: Celestina Warbeck
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Celestina Warbeck is a popular witch who sings on the wizarding wireless, where she is billed as the singing sorceress. She sings on the programme Witching Hour, and she is a great favourite in the Weasleys' kitchen at the Burrow.

Career

Celestina Warbeck has been singing on the wizarding wireless for many years. Her songs are loud, sentimental affairs with a great deal of love in them, and she sings them with tremendous feeling. Molly Weasley has loved them since she was a girl. She and Arthur Weasley danced to one of them when they were eighteen.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1992, Harry Potter saw the kitchen at the Burrow for the first time. Unless his ears were playing tricks on him, the old wireless by the sink had just announced that Witching Hour was coming up next, with the popular singing sorceress herself. The whole place was so cosy that it made his throat ache.

pages.title: Mr Granger
infobox:
Hermione Granger daughter
Mrs Granger wife
Muggle, Granger family, dentist, Friends of Humanity
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Mr Granger is a Muggle dentist, the husband of Mrs Granger and the father of Hermione Granger. He and his wife run a dentist's surgery together. In 1994 he bought the family computer on which Hermione played Myst. By August 1994 he and his wife were going to the Thursday meetings of Friends of Humanity. His car carries a sticker reading KEEP BRITAIN HUMAN.

Life

The Grangers are respectable, mild and thoroughly middle class. Both are dentists, both are atheists, and both always say that nobody flosses properly. Mr Granger owns a copy of In Search of Schrödinger's Cat, which is where Hermione first read about the Many Worlds interpretation. He plays Beethoven on compact disc.

To Harry Potter, Hermione's parents are people who have never done him any harm. In the summer of 1993, while Aunt Marge held forth about foreigners, Harry counted them among the people he knew who were not bad people at all.

In the saga

In Diagon Alley in August 1992 Mr Granger was changing ten-pound notes at Gringotts when Arthur Weasley greeted him with delight. Arthur towed him off for a drink at the Leaky Cauldron. He and his wife were left shaking after Arthur's brawl with Lucius Malfoy in Flourish and Blotts. On 31 August 1993 they dropped Hermione at the Leaky Cauldron, with early birthday money.

In 1994 he bought a computer with a CD-ROM drive, to do the surgery's accounts at home. He pays Demon Internet ten pounds a month for a modem connection. He gave up on the game Myst after one evening. Hermione finished all four of its endings, then used his connection to read the Myst newsgroups.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, before dawn on 22 August 1994, Hermione told Harry Potter that her parents go to the Friends of Humanity meetings in the church hall on Thursday nights, though not on the marches. Her father has a sticker on the back of his car reading KEEP BRITAIN HUMAN. Her parents think magic is different because it comes in a book with rules, Hermione said, and she was sure they would keep the Statute of Secrecy for her sake.

pages.title: Mrs Granger
infobox:
Hermione Granger daughter
Mr Granger husband
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Mrs Granger is a Muggle dentist, the wife of Mr Granger and the mother of Hermione Granger. She shares her husband's surgery and his atheism. By 1994 she may have been quietly helping Hermione and Dracina Malfoy. By August 1994 she and her husband were going to the Thursday meetings of Friends of Humanity in their church hall.

Life

Like her husband, Mrs Granger is a dentist. Like him and their daughter, she is an atheist. The family keeps a Christmas tree at home all the same. She and her husband write to Hermione every week during term. Nobody else in the family has any magic at all. The Grangers learnt that their daughter was a witch only when her Hogwarts letter came, and it was a great surprise to them all.

In the saga

Mrs Granger went with her family to Diagon Alley in August 1992. She was alarmed by Lucius Malfoy's insults, and by the brawl that followed in Flourish and Blotts. On 31 August 1993 she and her husband dropped Hermione at the Leaky Cauldron with early birthday money.

In 1994 she was at King's Cross to meet Hermione at the end of term. She lent her the camera with which Hermione photographed the island in Myst off the computer screen. She rationed the modem, because of the phone bill. Harry wondered whether she was the unnamed helper in the understanding between Dracina and Hermione.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, on 21 August 1994, Hermione murmured that 'she' would never believe Mrs Weasley's account of house gnomes, then said quickly that she meant her mother, though the haste of the answer suggested somebody else. In Chapter Five Hermione told Harry Potter that both her parents go to the Friends of Humanity meetings in the church hall on Thursday nights, though not on the marches. She was sure that they loved her all the same, and that they would keep the Statute of Secrecy for her sake.

pages.title: Justin Finch-Fletchley's mother
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Justin Finch-Fletchley's mother is a Muggle. Her son's name was down for Eton, and she was slightly disappointed when he went to Hogwarts instead.

A wizard in the family

Justin is Muggle-born, the first wizard in his family. His mother came round once he had made her read Gilderoy Lockhart's books. After those, Justin said, she began to see how useful it would be to have a fully trained wizard in the family.

Lockhart's books were full of his adventures with banshees, werewolves and vampires, none of which, it turned out, had happened to him.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, filling flowerpots with dragon-dung compost in Herbology, Justin told Harry Potter that his name had been down for Eton. He was very glad he had come to Hogwarts instead. His mother, he admitted, had been slightly disappointed.

pages.title: Moaning Myrtle
infobox:
Peeves tormentor
Olive Hornby tormentor she haunted
Harry Potter fancies
ghost, Hogwarts ghost, Hogwarts, Basilisk victim
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The out-of-order girls' bathroom on the second floor
pages.html:
Moaning Myrtle is the ghost of a Muggle-born Ravenclaw girl, killed by the Basilisk when Tom Riddle opened the Chamber of Secrets in 1943. She haunts the girls' bathroom where she died, whose sink hides the entrance to the Chamber. In 1993 her account of her own death led Harry Potter there.

Life and death

Myrtle Elizabeth Warren was a Muggle-born witch in Ravenclaw at Hogwarts in the early 1940s. She was a plain, unhappy girl with thick glasses, and the others teased her without mercy. In June 1943 Olive Hornby made fun of her glasses. Myrtle locked herself in a cubicle of the second-floor girls' bathroom to cry.

While she was there she heard a boy come in, speaking a strange language. She unlocked the door to tell him to go and use his own toilet. She saw a pair of great yellow eyes by the sinks, and died. The boy was Tom Riddle, speaking Parseltongue to the Basilisk he had loosed from the Chamber of Secrets. Riddle framed Rubeus Hagrid for her death, and Hagrid was expelled.

She came back as a ghost, determined to haunt Olive Hornby, and did so until the Ministry of Magic made her stop. Then she went back to the bathroom where she had died.

Character

Myrtle is the squat ghost of a girl with lank hair and thick, pearly spectacles. She lives up to her name. She sulks on top of a cistern, picking at the spots on her chin. Her tantrums flood the bathroom and the corridor outside, which is why the bathroom has been out of order for years. She keeps a list of everything people call her. 'I do have feelings, you know,' she has said. 'Even if I am dead.'

Peeves torments her constantly. By 1993 she had been dead fifty years, and she complained that in all that time she had not received a single card. She brightens whenever Harry Potter is kind to her. She has plainly taken a fancy to him.

In the saga

Harry, Ron and Hermione met her at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party on Hallowe'en 1992. Goaded by Peeves, she accused Hermione of mocking her, listed the names people called her and fled in tears. A few days later she told them that she had noticed nothing on Hallowe'en night. Peeves had upset her so much, she said, that she had tried to kill herself, before remembering that she was already dead, and had dived into a toilet.

Since nobody ever went into her bathroom, the three of them brewed their Polyjuice Potion in one of her cubicles. Afterwards Myrtle was delighted by Hermione's cat's face, and predicted that she would be teased for ever.

In the new year she told Harry about a posh girl with long, straight, shiny hair, who had searched her bathroom on hands and knees in the night, whispering at the sinks. The girl had then thrown her bag at Myrtle and run away crying. She had left the taps running, so that the corridor flooded.

In the summer term of 1993 Harry and Ron came to her with Lockhart. She described her death to them. Harry found the tiny snake on the copper tap of one sink, then opened the Chamber with Parseltongue. Afterwards Myrtle told him that if he had died, he would have been very welcome to share her toilet.

In their own words

I do have feelings, you know. Even if I am dead.Moaning Myrtle · B2 Ch10
I've been dead fifty years and not one card!Moaning Myrtle · B2 Ch15
If you had died, you'd have been very welcome to share my toilet.Moaning Myrtle · B2 Ch19

pages.title: Sir Patrick Delaney-Podmore
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Sir Patrick Delaney-Podmore is the bearded ghost who leads the Headless Hunt, a company of headless huntsmen on ghost horses. He has blackballed Nearly Headless Nick from the Hunt more than once, because Nick's head is not fully severed. In 1992 he burst into Nick's five hundredth Deathday Party to mock him.

The Headless Hunt

The Hunt rides out on ghost horses, each rider carrying his own head. Its pastimes, Head Juggling, Head Polo and Horseback Head Juggling among them, call for a head that comes off properly. Nick's head, after forty-five blows of a blunt axe in 1492, still hangs on by an inch of skin and sinew. On account of that one inch, Sir Patrick will not have him.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, the Hunt rejected Nick's application yet again in October 1992. On 31 October a dozen ghost horses burst out of the dungeon wall into his Deathday Party, every rider headless. Sir Patrick was at the front, blowing a horn, with his bearded head under his arm. He crammed it back on his neck and roared at Nick, 'Still hanging on by a thread, eh?' Then he pretended to jump at the sight of three living guests, so that his head fell off again, to the crowd's delight.

Harry Potter shouted at him: 'Oi. You're not invited. Get out!' Sir Patrick's head, from the flagstones, gave Harry a look of the most aristocratic contempt. 'We go where we please, boy!' it said. During Nick's speech the Hunt started a game of Head Hockey, and Sir Patrick's head went sailing past Nick's nose to loud cheers.

pages.title: The Grey Lady
infobox: The Baron, later the Bloody Baron
A window on a tower landing
pages.html:
The Grey Lady is the ghost of Ravenclaw house: a tall, pale, beautiful figure in a high-collared gown, who speaks to almost nobody. In life she was Helena, the daughter of the founder Rowena Ravenclaw. She is one of the very few beings at Hogwarts old enough to remember Gandalf from the castle's beginnings.

Life

Helena was the daughter of Rowena Ravenclaw, and she grew up in the first years of Hogwarts. When she was very small Gandalf came to her mother's house, and the two of them argued all night by the fire. In the morning her mother said that he was the only man in the world who had ever won an argument with her.

As a young woman Helena longed to be cleverer than her mother, and more important. She stole Rowena's diadem, which was said to make its wearer wiser, and fled with it to Albania. Rowena never told the other founders that it was gone, and pretended to the end that she still had it.

When Rowena fell mortally ill, she sent the Baron, who had long loved Helena, to bring her home. Helena refused him, and in his rage he killed her in an Albanian forest. Before she died she hid the diadem in a hollow tree. She came back to Hogwarts as a ghost.

Character

The Grey Lady has the look of somebody who has been waiting a very long time for something, and has stopped expecting it to come. In October 1992 Nearly Headless Nick complained that she would not speak to anyone. Hermione Granger, for her part, talked about her at length over lunch on Hallowe'en 1992.

Her favourite window is on a quiet landing near the top of a tower, where the moonlight lies across the floor.

In the saga

On the night of the Duelling Club in December 1992, Ambrose Greyhame met her at her window on his way through the castle. She went perfectly still. Then she whispered, 'You came to my mother. When I was very small.' She remembered the argument he had won. Her eyes filled with something that would have been tears, if ghosts could cry. He put a finger to his lips. She bowed her head and stepped back into the shadows. He touched his hat to her as he went past.

In the spring of 1994 Harry Potter came looking for the Fat Friar at her favourite window. She gave him an odd, searching look, and drifted away without a word.

In their own words

You came to my mother. When I was very small.The Grey Lady · LB

pages.title: The Wailing Widow
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A crusader, who came home a week too late
pages.html:
The Wailing Widow is a ghost from Kent. In 1392 her husband went off to the Crusades and did not come back, so she drowned herself in a well. He came back a week later, and she has been wailing about it ever since.

Life and death

Her husband was one of the Englishmen still taking the cross at the end of the fourteenth century, when crusades were fought in Barbary and the Baltic as well as in the East. When the time for his return came and went without him, she gave him up for dead. She threw herself into a well. A week later he came home.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Ron Weasley asked Hermione Granger who the Wailing Widow was, since he had heard of her. Hermione told him her story in a torrent, along with a great many others. The Widow came all the way up from Kent for Nearly Headless Nick's five hundredth Deathday Party on 31 October 1992. Nick mentioned it with pride.

pages.title: The Wailing Widow's husband
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter Nine
pages.html:
The Wailing Widow's husband was a man of Kent who went off to the Crusades in the fourteenth century. His wife believed he was never coming back, and in 1392 she drowned herself in a well. He came home a week later.

Life

English knights were still going on crusade in the 1390s, to the Barbary coast of Africa or to the pagan lands of Lithuania. Which crusade he went on is not recorded. His wife has been wailing about it ever since, as a ghost. She came all the way up from Kent for Nearly Headless Nick's five hundredth deathday party.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, at Nearly Headless Nick's deathday party at Hallowe'en 1992, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter the Widow's story. Her husband had gone off to the Crusades and not come back, or so she thought. In fact he came back a week after she drowned herself.

pages.title: Brother Aldric
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 9
Hanged, drawn and quartered by Henry VIII's men
In four pieces; holds his left arm on with his right
Hiding the abbey's books from the King's commissioners
pages.html:
Brother Aldric is the ghost of a monk of Glastonbury Abbey who was hanged, drawn and quartered by Henry the Eighth's men. He comes in four pieces, which do not always agree on where to go. He holds his left arm on with his right. Before he died he hid the abbey's books from the King's commissioners in a cave on Glastonbury Tor. They were never found.

Life and death

Glastonbury was one of the oldest abbeys in England, and one of the richest, with one of the finest libraries in the country. When Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries, the King's commissioners came for it in 1539. Its aged abbot, Richard Whiting, was hanged, drawn and quartered on the Tor, together with two of his monks. Brother Aldric died the same way. Before he did, he hid the abbey's books in a cave on the Tor, where the King's men never found them.

He is a tall, mournful ghost with a voice like a cellar door. For about four hundred and fifty years nobody asked him about anything but his quartering.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Hermione Granger counted him among the famous ghosts who might be at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party. At the party, on 31 October 1992, she found him: a tall monk, not quite assembled. Was it true, she asked, that he had hidden the abbey's books in a cave on the Tor, and that they were never found? 'Young lady,' he said, 'it is entirely true. Would you care to know where?' She would. It took her about thirty seconds to write down the answer. Then she came running after Harry and Ron, glowing. 'He told me!' she said.

pages.title: The Welsh knight killed at Crécy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 9
26 August 1346, at the Battle of Crécy
A crossbow bolt through his visor
pages.html:
The Welsh knight killed at Crécy is the ghost of a knight from Wales who died at the Battle of Crécy in 1346, when a crossbow bolt went straight through the visor of his helmet. He is one of the ghosts Hermione Granger has read about.

Crécy

Crécy was Edward III's great victory over the French, won chiefly by his English and Welsh archers. The crossbowmen that day fought for France. They were Genoese mercenaries, and they opened the battle before the English longbows cut them down. Few Englishmen or Welshmen died at Crécy. This knight was one of them.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Hermione listed him for Harry Potter among the famous ghosts who might be at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party in October 1992.

pages.title: The Yorkshire lady bricked up in a chimney
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 9
pages.html:
The Yorkshire lady bricked up in a chimney is the ghost of a lady from Yorkshire whose own steward walled her up inside a chimney. She was found in 1812, when the chimney was swept.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter about her in October 1992, as one of the famous ghosts who might be at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party. How long she had been in the chimney before the sweep found her, and what became of the steward, Hermione did not say.

pages.title: The Yorkshire lady's steward
infobox: Bricking his mistress up inside a chimney
A lady from Yorkshire, now a ghost
pages.html:
The Yorkshire lady's steward was the servant who bricked his own mistress up inside a chimney. Nobody found her until the chimney was swept, in 1812.

The lady

The lady walks as a ghost now. Her steward's name has not come down, nor his reason, nor what became of him afterwards.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Hermione Granger reeled off the ghosts Harry Potter could expect to meet at Nearly Headless Nick's five hundredth deathday party, on Hallowe'en 1992. Between a Welsh knight shot through the visor at Crécy and a Glastonbury monk who comes in four pieces, she named a lady from Yorkshire who had been bricked up inside a chimney by her own steward.

pages.title: The gloomy nuns at the Deathday Party
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The gloomy nuns were a huddle of ghost nuns among the guests at Nearly Headless Nick's five hundredth Deathday Party, on 31 October 1992. Who they were in life, and how they came to die, is not recorded. One of them, at least, has a sense of humour.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger passed them on their way round the edge of the dungeon. Later Harry shouted at Sir Patrick Delaney-Podmore to get out, and told the Headless Hunt that Nick would plaster the walls with them if they did not keep running away on their horses. There was a short, astonished silence. Then, somewhere at the back of the room, one of the gloomy nuns gave a single scandalised giggle.

pages.title: The ragged ghost in chains
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A ragged man wrapped in chains
pages.html:
The ragged ghost in chains was one of the guests at Nearly Headless Nick's five hundredth Deathday Party, on 31 October 1992: a ragged man wrapped in chains. His name and his story are not recorded. He is not the Bloody Baron, the ghost of Slytherin, who was also at the party and who, according to Nick, will not stop talking about his own chains.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger passed him as they made their way round the edge of the crowded dungeon, just after a huddle of gloomy nuns.

pages.title: The knight with an arrow in his forehead
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
An arrow sticking out of his forehead
pages.html:
The knight with an arrow in his forehead is a ghost who goes about with an arrow still sticking out of the middle of his brow. He was among the guests at Nearly Headless Nick's five hundredth Deathday Party in 1992. How he came by the arrow is not recorded.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger passed him at the party, deep in conversation with the Fat Friar, the cheerful ghost of Hufflepuff.

pages.title: The portly ghost at the banquet table
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Trying to taste a rotten salmon
pages.html:
The portly ghost at the banquet table was a guest at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party who tried to taste the food. Ghosts cannot eat. Hermione Granger supposed that the banquet had been left to rot so that its flavour would be strong enough for them to taste.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry Potter watched him come up to the long black table, crouch and walk slowly through it with his mouth held wide, so that one of the stinking salmon passed straight through his face. 'You'll get there eventually, mate,' Harry told him. 'Almost,' said the ghost sadly, and drifted off.

pages.title: The cold voice in the walls
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Basilisk of the Chamber of Secrets
pages.html:
The cold voice in the walls was the voice Harry Potter heard moving through the stones of Hogwarts in the autumn of 1992, speaking of hunger and of killing. Nobody else could hear it. It was the Basilisk of the Chamber of Secrets, travelling through the pipes inside the walls, and Harry heard it because he is a Parselmouth.

The Basilisk

A Basilisk is a giant serpent, the King of Serpents, hatched from a chicken's egg beneath a toad. It can live for many hundreds of years, and its stare kills. Salazar Slytherin's Basilisk lived in the Chamber beneath the school. In 1992 the memory of Tom Riddle, working through Dracina Malfoy, set it loose on the castle once more.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, on 5 September 1992, Harry was serving a detention in Gilderoy Lockhart's office, addressing envelopes to his fans by candlelight, when he heard a voice so cold and venomous that it went into the bone: 'Come... come to me... let me rip you... let me tear you... let me kill you...' Lockhart had heard nothing. He thought Harry must be getting drowsy.

In Chapter Nine, on Hallowe'en, Harry heard it again in the dungeon passage as he left Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party. It was hungry. It had been hungry for so long. It was time to kill. The voice moved upwards through the castle, and Harry ran after it until it cried out, '... I smell blood... I SMELL BLOOD!' Ron and Hermione could hear nothing at all. The voice led them to Filch's cat, Mrs Norris, Petrified and hanging from a torch bracket.

In Chapter Sixteen, in 1993, Harry heard it once more at the foot of the marble staircase, on his way to fetch his Quidditch things: '...hungry... so long... so long in the dark... let me out... let me taste... kill this time... kill...' He yelled out loud.

In Chapter Eighteen Harry worked out at last what it was: 'That's why I've been hearing that voice all over the place, and nobody else has heard it. It's because I understand Parseltongue...'

pages.title: Gladys Gudgeon
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Being a huge fan of Gilderoy Lockhart
The first Harry Potter addressed in his detention, autumn 1992
pages.html:
Gladys Gudgeon is a witch who is, in Gilderoy Lockhart's own words, a huge fan of his. She writes to him, and he answers her with signed photographs of himself.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1992, Harry Potter served a detention in Lockhart's office, addressing the envelopes for his fan mail by candlelight under dozens of framed Lockharts. Lockhart handed him the first. ‘This first one's to Gladys Gudgeon, bless her. Huge fan of mine.’

pages.title: Veronica Smethley
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Being a fan of Gilderoy Lockhart
pages.html:
Veronica Smethley is one of Gilderoy Lockhart's many admirers. Hers was the envelope Harry Potter was addressing, in lilac ink, when he first heard the cold voice in the walls of Hogwarts.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Harry was nearly four hours into his detention in Lockhart's office, writing out Veronica Smethley's address for what felt like the thousandth time, when he heard a voice of ice-cold venom: ‘Come... come to me... let me rip you... let me tear you... let me kill you...’ He jumped so hard that a great lilac blot spread across her street. Lockhart, who had heard nothing, thought Harry was talking about his six months at the top of the bestseller list.

pages.title: Hetty Bayliss
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The flying Ford Anglia, at noon on 1 September 1992
pages.html:
Hetty Bayliss is a Muggle from Norfolk. At noon on 1 September 1992, while she was hanging out her washing, she saw an old car flying through the sky.

The flying car

The car was Arthur Weasley's turquoise Ford Anglia, enchanted to fly. Harry Potter and Ron Weasley were flying it north to Hogwarts after the barrier at King's Cross had sealed itself against them. Its Invisibility Booster was faulty, so it kept popping back into sight.

Mrs Bayliss was one of six or seven Muggles who saw it that day.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, Professor Snape read the report of her sighting aloud to Harry and Ron from the Prophet, under the headline FLYING FORD ANGLIA MYSTIFIES MUGGLES. She was named in it as Mrs Hetty Bayliss of Norfolk, who had seen the car at noon while hanging out her washing.

pages.title: Angus Fleet
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Reporting the flying Ford Anglia to the police
pages.html:
Angus Fleet is a Muggle from Peebles, a small town in the Scottish Borders. On 1 September 1992 he saw an old car flying through the sky, and he reported it to the police.

The flying car

The car was Arthur Weasley's turquoise Ford Anglia, which he had enchanted to fly. Harry Potter and Ron Weasley were flying it north to Hogwarts, because the barrier at King's Cross had sealed itself against them that morning. The car's Invisibility Booster was faulty, so it kept flickering back into sight.

Six or seven Muggles saw it that day, in places as far apart as London, Norfolk and Peebles. Mr Fleet is the only one of them known to have gone to the police.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, Professor Snape caught Harry and Ron after they had crashed the car into the Whomping Willow. He unrolled that evening's Prophet, which carried the headline FLYING FORD ANGLIA MYSTIFIES MUGGLES, and read the report aloud. Mr Angus Fleet of Peebles, who had reported the car to the police, was among the witnesses it named.

pages.title: The two Muggles in London who saw the flying car
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
London, over the Post Office Tower
pages.html:
The two Muggles in London were convinced that they had seen an old car flying over the Post Office Tower on 1 September 1992. They were quite right.

The flying car

The car was Arthur Weasley's turquoise Ford Anglia. His son Ron was flying it north to Hogwarts with Harry Potter, after the barrier at King's Cross had sealed itself against them. Its Invisibility Booster was faulty. Six or seven Muggles reported the car that day, among them Mrs Hetty Bayliss of Norfolk and Mr Angus Fleet of Peebles.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, Professor Snape read the report aloud to Harry and Ron from that evening's Prophet, under the headline FLYING FORD ANGLIA MYSTIFIES MUGGLES.

pages.title: P. Hoskins
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Kwikspell, a correspondence course in beginners' magic
Could not warm a teapot without setting light to the cosy
Scouring Charms that are the talk of the street
pages.html:
Mrs P. Hoskins of Wolverhampton is a witch whose testimonial appears in the advertising for Kwikspell, a correspondence course in beginners' magic. For years she could not so much as warm a teapot without setting light to the tea cosy. Since the course, she says, her Scouring Charms have been the talk of the street.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in the autumn of 1992, Harry Potter read her testimonial in the Kwikspell envelope that Argus Filch had left lying on his desk. Hers came first, just above Mr L. Ashby's.

pages.title: L. Ashby
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Kwikspell, a correspondence course in beginners' magic
His brother-in-law became a hatstand after Lesson Four
pages.html:
Mr L. Ashby of Kendal is a wizard whose testimonial appears in the advertising for Kwikspell, a correspondence course in beginners' magic. His brother-in-law always used to laugh at his wandwork. Since Lesson Four, Mr Ashby reports, the brother-in-law has not laughed once, chiefly because he is presently a hatstand.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in the autumn of 1992, Harry Potter found a Kwikspell envelope on the desk in Argus Filch's office, and read the testimonials on the sheaf of parchment inside. Mr Ashby's ended with ‘Thank you, Kwikspell!’ Harry could not think why Filch should want a course in beginners' magic. Filch, it turned out, is a Squib.

pages.title: L. Ashby's brother-in-law
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Brother-in-law of Mr L. Ashby of Kendal
pages.html:
Mr L. Ashby's brother-in-law always used to laugh at Ashby's wandwork. Then Ashby took Kwikspell, the correspondence course in beginners' magic. After Lesson Four the brother-in-law stopped laughing, chiefly because Ashby had turned him into a hatstand. When Ashby wrote his testimonial for the course, he was a hatstand still.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry Potter read Ashby's testimonial among the Kwikspell papers on Argus Filch's desk.

pages.title: Colin Creevey's father
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Colin Creevey's father is a Muggle milkman. He could hardly believe it when his son turned out to be a wizard, and Colin has been sending him photographs from Hogwarts ever since.

Family

Colin is Muggle-born. He never knew that the odd things he could do were magic until his Hogwarts letter came in 1992, and his father was as astonished as he was. Mr Creevey also has a younger son, Dennis.

Colin takes pictures of almost everything with his Muggle camera, to send home to his father. A boy in his dormitory told him that if he developed the film in the right potion, the pictures would move.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Colin explained all this to Harry Potter in the courtyard, while working up the courage to ask for a photograph. 'My dad's a milkman, he couldn't believe it either.' He wanted a picture of himself standing next to Harry to send home.

pages.title: Oliver Wood's father
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 9
pages.html:
Oliver Wood's father served in the Royal Air Force. His son Oliver, the Keeper and captain of the Gryffindor Quidditch team, is almost as keen on Muggle jet planes as he is on Quidditch.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, late in October 1992, Fred and George Weasley came back from spying on the Slytherins at practice. 'Seven green blurs,' Fred reported. 'That's all you can see. Seven green blurs, going past like something the Muggle air force would have.' This made Oliver perk up. He had told Harry Potter before that his dad was in the RAF. He had even shown Harry a big magazine full of Muggle jet planes, explaining at length their payloads and the damage they could do. He did it as enthusiastically as he or Ron explained the Quidditch results, which was very enthusiastically indeed.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, at the World Cup campsite on 22 August 1994, Oliver Wood dragged Harry Potter off to meet his parents. Oliver was about to start his Basic Recruit Training Course with the RAF, following his father into the service.

pages.title: The lady from the council
pages.html:
The lady from the council came once to Number Four, Privet Drive. She had a cup of tea with the Dursleys and went away again. Like Harry Potter's teachers and the dinner lady at St Grogory's, she believed the Dursleys rather than Harry.

Why they believed the Dursleys

Uncle Vernon would explain that the boy was very disturbed, that he told stories, and that they did their best. The Dursleys had a nice house and a clean car. Harry was a scrawny boy with broken glasses, who said things that could not be true.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, at the Burrow, Mrs Weasley asked Harry whether what Ron had told her about the Dursleys was true. Harry's first thought was to lie. The lady from the council had believed them in the end, like all the others. Mrs Weasley looked at him with such plain, ordinary kindness that the lie would not come.

pages.title: The Scottish Muggle gentleman
infobox: A desk at a very dull-sounding office near the river
pages.html:
The Scottish Muggle gentleman is the man Minerva McGonagall worked alongside long ago, who needed a great deal of gold to go missing in a hurry. She turned a vault's worth of it into beetles for him. He was James Bond, agent 007 of MI6.

McGonagall

He had a way of asking, McGonagall said, that one found hard to refuse. He also had a desk at a very dull-sounding office near the river, though he was seldom at it. From 1960 to 1962 she had a romance with him. It ended when she found out how brazenly he had lied to her.

She has not heard from him in a good many years. She expects he has retired somewhere warm and is lying about it. In fact he has been held since the mid-1980s at Wolfburg Penitentiary, in isolation and without trial, a long way from anywhere warm.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, while Harry Potter was trying to turn a beetle into a button, McGonagall told the class about the vault of gold. 'A Muggle. Scottish. He had a desk at a very dull-sounding office near the river, though he was seldom at it.' Something that might have been fondness crossed her face.

In Chapter Fifteen, listening to Gilderoy Lockhart boast, she thought of what she had done to 'that charming MI6 agent who so brazenly lied to her face for the last and very final time'.

pages.title: The old witch who owned the enchanted tea set
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A gift from a French nobleman, once cursed, and his peasant wife
pages.html:
The old witch who owned the enchanted tea set died in 1991. Her tea set had been given to her by a French nobleman, a Muggle who had once been cursed, together with his peasant wife. After her death it was sold to an antiques shop, with dreadful results.

The tea set

A little old Muggle lady bought it, took it home and tried to serve her friends tea in it. The whole set came alive. The pieces danced and talked to one another, while the teapot sang. The old lady died of shock, and her friends went mad. Arthur Weasley worked overtime for weeks. The Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office has only two wizards in it, Arthur and an old warlock called Perkins. Between them they had to do Memory Charms and all sorts to cover it up.

The nobleman's story is the old French tale of Beauty and the Beast.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1992, Ron Weasley told Harry Potter the story in the flying car, to explain what his father did at the Ministry. 'Dancing,' said Harry. Ron added: 'The teapot sang, apparently.'

pages.title: The formerly cursed French nobleman and his peasant wife
infobox: A nobleman, once under a curse
A peasant girl, later his wife
An enchanted tea set, to an old witch
pages.html:
They are a French Muggle couple: a nobleman who once lived under a curse, and the peasant girl he married. They gave an old witch a tea set that could come alive, dance, talk and sing.

The curse

The curse that lay on him made a beast of him. It was broken when the peasant girl came to love him as he was. They married afterwards.

The tea set

The old witch kept the tea set until she died in 1991. It was sold to a Muggle antiques shop, and the old Muggle lady who bought it died of shock when it came alive as she served her friends tea. The Ministry of Magic had to use Memory Charms on her guests, who had gone mad.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, Ron Weasley told Harry Potter the story on the way to the Burrow, to explain what his father did at the Ministry.

pages.title: The old Muggle lady who bought the tea set
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
An enchanted tea set, from an antiques shop
pages.html:
The old Muggle lady who bought the tea set died of shock in 1991, when the enchanted tea set she had bought from an antiques shop came alive as she poured for her friends.

The tea set

The set had belonged to an old witch, who was given it by a formerly cursed French nobleman and his peasant wife. When the witch died, it was sold to a Muggle antiques shop, where the old lady found it. She tried to serve her friends tea in it. The pieces came alive, started dancing and spoke to one another. The teapot sang.

The old lady died of shock. Her guests went mad, and the Ministry of Magic had to put Memory Charms on them. Arthur Weasley, who with an old warlock called Perkins made up the whole of the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office, worked overtime for weeks.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, Ron Weasley told the story to Harry Potter, to explain what his father did at the Ministry.

pages.title: The Daily Prophet photographer
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Big and black; lets off purple smoke with every flash
Gilderoy Lockhart's signing at Flourish and Blotts, August 1992
pages.html:
The Daily Prophet photographer was a short, bad-tempered man who covered Gilderoy Lockhart's book signing at Flourish and Blotts in August 1992. His big black camera let off a puff of purple smoke with every blinding flash.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, he danced round Lockhart's table taking pictures, and trod on Ron Weasley's foot. ‘Out of the way, there,’ he snarled at Ron, backing up for a better shot. ‘This is for the Daily Prophet.’ Ron told him that his fist would be for the Daily Prophet if he did not get some space.

When Lockhart spotted Harry Potter in the queue and hauled him to the front, the photographer clicked away like mad, wafting thick purple smoke over the Weasleys. Lockhart told Harry that together they were worth the front page.

After the brawl between Arthur Weasley and Lucius Malfoy, Fred Weasley heard Lockhart asking him whether he could work the fight into his report. It was all publicity, Lockhart said.

pages.title: The Flourish and Blotts assistant
aliases: the harassed wizard at the door
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Failing to stop a brawl in August 1992
pages.html:
The Flourish and Blotts assistant is a harassed wizard on the staff of the Diagon Alley bookshop. He was on duty on the August day in 1992 when Gilderoy Lockhart signed books there. He could do nothing whatever to stop Arthur Weasley and Lucius Malfoy fighting among the shelves.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, the crowd for Lockhart's signing was made up mostly of witches of about Mrs Weasley's age. The harassed wizard at the door was saying, 'Calmly, please, ladies... don't push, there... mind the books, now...'

When Arthur threw himself at Lucius and sent him backwards into a bookcase, a dozen heavy spellbooks came thundering down on everybody's heads. 'Gentlemen, please... please!' cried the assistant. It was Hagrid who broke it up. The assistant looked as though he would have liked to stop them leaving, but he barely came up to Hagrid's waist, and he thought better of it.

pages.title: The old witch with the tray of fingernails
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A tray of what looked like human fingernails
pages.html:
The old witch with the tray of fingernails is a witch of Knockturn Alley who trades in what look horribly like whole human fingernails. She has a mouthful of mossy teeth, which she shows when she leers.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, Harry Potter came out of Borgin and Burkes lost and jumpy. The old witch stepped into his path with her tray, leering at him, and Harry backed away. Then Hagrid came striding up the alley, shouting Harry's name. The witch jumped, and a cascade of fingernails went over her feet. Hagrid hauled Harry away by the scruff of his neck, knocking the tray clean out of her hands. Her shrieks followed them all the way out into Diagon Alley. Harry later called her the woman selling toenails.

pages.title: The two shabby wizards in Knockturn Alley
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The two shabby wizards in Knockturn Alley were a pair who stood in the shadow of a doorway in the summer of 1992, watching Harry Potter and muttering to each other.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry came out of Borgin and Burkes, the biggest shop in an alley given over to the Dark Arts. Across the way was a window full of shrunken heads. Two doors down, a large cage seethed with enormous black spiders. The two wizards watched him from their doorway and muttered, which made Harry very jumpy. He set off, holding his broken glasses straight, hoping against hope for a way out.

pages.title: The guard at King's Cross
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The guard at King's Cross is a Muggle railway guard at the London station. On 1 September 1992 he yelled at Harry Potter and Ron Weasley when their trolleys crashed into the magical barrier to the Hogwarts platform, which had sealed itself against them.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, the two boys walked at the barrier, broke into a run a few feet from it and hit solid wall. Both trolleys bounced off. Ron's trunk came off with a bang, Harry went over backwards, and Hedwig's cage rolled away across the concourse with Hedwig shrieking inside it.

People stopped to stare. The guard demanded to know what in blazes they thought they were doing. Harry gasped that he had lost control of the trolley.

Dobby the house-elf had sealed the barrier, to stop Harry going back to school. Harry and Ron flew to Hogwarts in Mr Weasley's car instead.

pages.title: The Gringotts goblins
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Keeping the gold; guarding the vaults; driving the carts
Carts that hurtle along miniature railway tracks
pages.html:
The Gringotts goblins run Gringotts, the wizarding bank in Diagon Alley. They keep its gold, guard its vaults far beneath London and drive customers down to them in small carts that hurtle along miniature railway tracks through the tunnels.

The bank

Goblins are a short, clever, proud people, with long fingers and feet. They have run the bank for centuries, and wizards trust them with their gold, if not with much else. Gringotts is held to be the safest place in the world for anything a wizard wants to keep safe, except perhaps Hogwarts. The two peoples have a bloody history behind them in the goblin rebellions. Their dealings at the bank are correct rather than warm.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, a bowing goblin showed the Weasleys and Harry Potter into the bank. Goblins drove them down to the vaults in small carts that hurtled along miniature railway tracks through the tunnels. Harry enjoyed every second of the ride. He felt dreadful when the Weasleys' vault swung open on a very small pile of Sickles and one gold Galleon, which Mrs Weasley swept into her bag after feeling right into the corners.

pages.title: The Gryffindor fifth-year
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Gryffindor fifth-year is an older student who congratulated Harry Potter on arriving at Hogwarts in a flying car, on 1 September 1992. Harry had never spoken to the fifth-year in his life.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, Harry and Ron Weasley missed the Hogwarts Express in 1992. They flew Arthur Weasley's enchanted Ford Anglia to school instead, crashing into the Whomping Willow. When they reached Gryffindor Tower, the whole house was still up, waiting for them. 'Good on you,' said the fifth-year, and somebody thumped Harry on the back as though he had just won a marathon.

pages.title: The Slytherin fifth-years in the courtyard
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter Seven
pages.html:
The Slytherin fifth-years in the courtyard were a knot of older Slytherins who laughed loudly when Dracina Malfoy mimicked Molly Weasley's Howler on 2 September 1992.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Mrs Weasley's Howler had exploded over Ron at breakfast that morning, in front of the whole Great Hall. Later, in the courtyard, Dracina caught Colin Creevey asking Harry for a signed photograph and announced it to everybody. When Ron told her to eat slugs, she warned him not to start any trouble, or his mummy would have to come and take him away from school. Then she put on a high, mocking voice. 'If you put another toe out of line...' A knot of Slytherin fifth-years nearby laughed loudly.

pages.title: Gandalf
aliases: the old man at the lych-gate
infobox: Ambrose; Ambrose Greyhame; Merlin; Mithrandir; Olórin; Gandalf the Grey; Gandalf the White

Albus Dumbledore former pupil and dear friend
Greta Grindelwald former pupil
God the Lord who sent him, sent by
Aragorn old friend (implied), old friend
Godric Gryffindor guided him to found Hogwarts
Helga Hufflepuff guided her to found Hogwarts
Rowena Ravenclaw guided her to found Hogwarts
Salazar Slytherin guided him to found Hogwarts
King Arthur Pendragon adviser (implied)
The Fat Friar implied visitor to his school
Zordon fellow Istar
Harry Potter parishioner
wizard, Middle-earth, legendary wizard, Little Whinging, Istari, St Michael's Church, wizarding history
Maia; one of the five Istari
Vicar of St Michael's Church, Little Whinging
Narya: a plain ring with a single red stone
Knotted grey wood, taller than himself
The first wizards of men; the four founders of Hogwarts; Albus Dumbledore; Greta Grindelwald
Roma of Otherworld, an Elf-lady of the Grey Havens
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Gandalf is a Maia, one of the spirits who were before the world was made, and one of the five Istari, the wizards sent out on commission in the elder days. In the Third Age he was Gandalf the Grey, who sent Bilbo Baggins to Erebor, fell with the Balrog in Moria and came back as Gandalf the White. After the Flood, God charged him with teaching men light magic as a counterweight to Morgoth. Britain remembers him as Merlin, adviser to King Arthur. He brought the four founders of Hogwarts to one table and taught Albus Dumbledore the magic of the staff. In the 1990s he is the vicar of St Michael's Church in Little Whinging, under the name of Ambrose Greyhame.

Names

He has had a great many names in a great many languages, some of which nobody speaks any more, and one or two of which nobody but he has ever spoken. In the West he was Olórin. The Elves called him Mithrandir, the Grey Pilgrim, and the Rohirrim called him Greyhame. To witches and wizards he is Merlin, the name he bore as adviser to a young king in the West Country. It is still printed on Chocolate Frog cards and sworn by in oaths such as 'Merlin's beard'. The old chronicles of Britain called Merlin Ambrosius, and the name he goes by at present is Ambrose Greyhame.

In his letters Albus Dumbledore calls him simply Ambrose.

To Brian Braddock, Captain Britain, he is Merlin too: the name he gave when he chose him in 1976.

Olórin

Before the world was made, Gandalf was Olórin, one of the Maiar, the spirits who served the Valar in the Undying Lands. He dwelt in Lórien, the gardens of Irmo, the master of dreams. He went often to the house of Nienna, from whom he learnt pity and patience. He was the wisest of the Maiar.

He loved the Elves. He walked among them unseen, or in their likeness, and they never knew where the fair visions in their hearts had come from.

The Istari

About the year 1000 of the Third Age the Valar sent five of the Maiar into Middle-earth to unite all who would resist Sauron. They came in the likeness of old men, and they were forbidden to match Sauron's power with power or to rule by fear. Olórin did not want to go. He said that he feared Sauron, and he was told that this was the best reason of all for sending him.

He came last of the five, and seemed the least of them. Círdan, at the Grey Havens, saw further than the rest and gave him Narya, the Ring of Fire, which is set with a red stone. For two thousand years he wandered without a home, a friend to Elves, Men and hobbits. The Elves called him Mithrandir, the Grey Pilgrim.

In 2063 he went into the fortress of Dol Guldur, and the Necromancer who hid there fled before him. In 2850 he went in again and found that the Necromancer was Sauron. In 2941 he sent Bilbo Baggins to Erebor with Thorin Oakenshield and twelve dwarves. That same year the White Council drove Sauron out of Dol Guldur.

He found out the truth about the ring Bilbo brought home, and in 3018 he told Frodo Baggins what it was. Saruman, the head of his order, had gone over to the enemy. He held Gandalf prisoner at the top of Orthanc until the eagle Gwaihir carried him away.

He led the Fellowship of the Ring south. In Moria he stood on the Bridge of Khazâd-dûm against a Balrog of Morgoth and broke the bridge beneath it, but it dragged him down into the abyss. He fought it from the deepest water to the peak of Zirakzigil, threw it down and died there himself. He was sent back as Gandalf the White.

As the White Rider he healed Théoden of Rohan, broke Saruman's staff and held the gate of Minas Tirith against the Lord of the Nazgûl. When the War of the Ring was won he set the crown on Aragorn's head before Minas Tirith. At the end of the Third Age he sailed from the Grey Havens into the West, wearing Narya openly at last.

He learnt much of the art of not being noticed from the hobbits, small, quiet folk who were better at it than any wizard he had ever met. He remembers Aragorn hooded in a dark corner of a crowded inn in the rain, looking like a vagabond until he pushed back his hood. He remembers, too, Legolas, a prince of the forest folk with an infuriating habit of keeping score.

The commission after the Flood

When the ice that had lain a mile thick on the mountains drew back at last, its meltwater came down out of the north in a flood that lasted a hundred years. It drowned whole countries: the black towers by the warm seas; the temples where men had worshipped a great serpent, and fed it; the sorcerers who had learnt their craft from the thing in those temples. Afterwards a few frightened families huddled round small fires on the cold new shores, with nothing at all.

Gandalf was sent to them by God, the One beyond the golden gates, who did not often send anybody and who had never once quite given up on Man. He sat by their fires among the skins and the smoke, teaching them the first words. He taught them how to call a flame, how to ask the rain to wait and how to heal a cut. Above all he taught them how to tell, when a voice came out of the dark offering power, that it was never the voice of a friend.

This was light magic, given expressly to counteract Morgoth, and the Patronus Charm was among the first spells. Over thousands of years men went off in a hundred directions with what he gave them. They quarrelled over it, forgot half of it and made up the rest. In the end they forgot whose hands had passed it down. He also made sure that the knowledge of making a thing like the One Ring was lost. Some of it survived all the same, carried through forgotten ages by dark hands such as those of 'that damn Stygian', the man history calls Herpo the Foul.

Merlin of the chronicles

Long afterwards, when he had been sent back to teach men, the Britons knew him as Merlin. The old chronicles of Britain tell a great many stories about him. Most of them are half true, and Gandalf has corrected very few of them.

They say that he was a boy without a father, the son of a princess of Demetia, and that some said his father was a spirit of the air. Gandalf was never born at all, which is the simplest reason why nobody could find his father.

They tell how the British king Vortigern could not make the walls of his tower stand, and how his wise men told him to wet the foundations with the blood of a fatherless boy. The boy they brought was Merlin. He showed the king a pool beneath the foundations, where two dragons lay, one red and one white. When they woke they fought, and Merlin told the king what their fighting meant: the long war of the Britons against the Saxons.

They say that he brought the stones of the Giants' Dance over from Ireland by his art, to stand on Salisbury Plain as a monument to the British dead. The stones had in fact been standing there for thousands of years.

They say that by his art Uther Pendragon came to Igraine at Tintagel in her husband's shape, and that Merlin took the child of that night, Arthur, to be brought up in secret. They say that he set the sword in the stone, took Arthur to the Lady of the Lake for Excalibur, and guided the first years of his reign.

The Welsh remember another Merlin as well, Myrddin Wyllt, who went mad after a battle in the north and lived as a wild man in the Caledonian forest, prophesying to the beasts. Gandalf says that was somebody else.

Last of all, the chronicles say that the Lady of the Lake learnt his secrets from him and shut him away for ever, in a cave, under a stone or inside an oak. Legend could not believe that Merlin would leave of his own accord, so it found a woman to lock him up. He simply left, when his work at Camelot was done.

King Arthur

For one long, strange stretch of years he advised a young king in the West Country, a boy with a sword, a round table and a great deal more courage than sense: Arthur Pendragon. Buying a Chocolate Frog in Hogsmeade in December 1992, he looked at his own card for some time. He thought the nose quite wrong and the beard far too tidy. Then he laughed so loudly that the witch at Honeydukes dropped a jar of Pepper Imps.

The founders of Hogwarts

After Arthur's time the magic Gandalf had given men was still scattered across the isle, among peoples who did not trust one another and taught it in their own ways, or not at all. In the tenth century he set out to give it a home of its own: one school, where the young of every people could learn it properly, out of sight of those who feared them.

In 979 he gathered the four most quarrelsome young wizards of the isle and stood them in the mud on a crag above a lake. There was the tall, proud girl from the glens, Rowena Ravenclaw, and the red-headed firebrand from the moors, Godric Gryffindor. There was the round, warm-hearted farm girl from the valleys, Helga Hufflepuff, who was in his private opinion the cleverest of the four. Last came the watchful young man from the fens who spoke to adders, Salazar Slytherin. He taught all four of them while the school took shape. It took him eleven years to get them to sit down at the same table, and he broke two staffs banging on it for order.

He mentored each of them in a different way. He gave Godric something to fight for besides the fight. He made Rowena admit that not everything worth knowing could be written in a book, which took most of a decade. He let Helga feed them all, and listened when she told them to sit down. He watched Salazar the most closely, and trusted him more than Salazar ever trusted anybody.

Under his eye they chose the crag Rowena had seen in a dream, raised the castle stone by stone and wove round it the enchantments that hide it from Muggle eyes. He taught them the old light magic at its roots, and how to teach it in their turn. They took their first pupils before the building was finished.

The Fat Friar remembered him coming up out of the valley in the snow, when the hall had only half a roof. The door opened before anyone touched it. He told the muddy first-years by the kitchen fire that magic was a gift from Somebody who had never given up on them: 'Don't let anybody tell you it's yours to do as you like with.'

In the years after Hogwarts opened in 990, when the four could teach without quarrelling more than was reasonable, Gandalf judged that his work there was done. He left as he had come, on foot, down the valley. He came back from time to time, and once argued all night with Rowena by her fire, but he no longer stayed.

He was gone before the quarrel over the Basilisk, and before Salazar Slytherin left the castle. Whether he saw it coming, he has never said. Long afterwards, walking the road to the castle alone in the snow, he said to nobody: 'You did well, all of you. Better than I ever told you.'

The sword he had placed in Godric Gryffindor's hands was Andúril, which belonged to Godric by blood as one of Aragorn's heirs. Millennia had worn the blade down, so Godric took it to the goblin smith Ragnuk the First to be mended. That repair is what let the goblins lay claim to it afterwards. After Godric died, the goblins named it the Sword of Gryffindor and claimed to have forged it, meaning to take it for themselves. Gandalf stole it back before they could and kept it hidden for a later heir. The histories say only that the sword vanished. It stayed with Gandalf until he carried it back to Hogwarts in December 1992.

Albus Dumbledore and the staff

In the summer of 1892, when Albus Dumbledore was eleven, Gandalf found him skimming stones in the river at the bottom of the lane near his home, where he had been sent out of the house for setting fire to the curtains. Gandalf asked him what he could do with a good stick. He spent six summers teaching him the magic of the staff, an art that Dumbledore believes fewer than five living wizards still command. 'A wand's a staff that's gone to town and learned manners.'

He taught him the way a staff is held, leant on and listened to, which is most of the art. He taught him to make a light without a word, to keep a fire burning in the rain and to put out another man's fire across a field. Above all he taught him that power is a gift, given for others, and that the voice in the dark offering more of it is never a friend.

Albus was a gifted pupil, and a proud one, which Gandalf knew how to manage. They have been friends ever since. Dumbledore still writes to him across the sea, and Gandalf still calls him 'my dear boy'.

Greta Grindelwald

In the last of those summers, in 1899, he also taught Greta Grindelwald, who took to it faster than Albus did.

He was charmed by her from the first. She was the quickest wit he had met in centuries, and she argued with him the way Rowena Ravenclaw once had, for the joy of it. He could see at once how Albus had fallen in love with her.

He saw the other thing in her too: the certainty that her own cleverness gave her the right to rule. He has never said whether he could have stopped what came of it.

He was there at her very beginning, and at the end as well, in the ruins with the smoke going up. His regrets about her are not small ones.

He still speaks of her wit with something like fondness, which Albus, who never stopped loving her, understands better than anyone.

Merlin and Captain Britain
