He hauled Harry to the front for the photographer, announced to the crowd that he would be teaching at Hogwarts and presented Harry with his entire works. Then Lucius Malfoy sneered at Ginny Weasley's second-hand books. Arthur Weasley threw himself at him, and the two fathers came to blows on the floor among the collapsing shelves. While they fought, Dracina mocked Ginny's spilt books as low-class, second-hand rubbish, until Ginny threw books at her head. When Hagrid pulled the fathers apart, Arthur had a cut lip. Lucius had been caught in the eye by an Encyclopaedia of Toadstools.

In Chapter Eighteen the truth came out. Lucius had slipped the diary inside Ginny's battered old Transfiguration book. He had told Dracina to pick up the Weasley girl's book, and Ginny had screamed at her. In a temper Dracina swept up every book in sight, the diary among them. 'One pure-blood girl is very much like another, from where I was sitting,' said Riddle. In Chapter Nineteen Harry told Lucius to his face that he had slipped the diary into Ginny's book.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the shop's window held an iron cage of about a hundred copies of The Monster Book of Monsters, fighting one another. The manager had been bitten five times that morning and swore he would never stock them again. Inside, Harry saw Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the Worst Is Coming, with a black dog as large as a bear on its cover. In Chapter Nine Dracina, her arm in a sling, turned herself into every wounded maiden on every book cover in Flourish and Blotts as she passed Harry on the path. In Chapter Sixteen Harry remembered Lucius in the shop the summer before last, sneering at Ginny's books.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, Arthur Weasley and Lucius Malfoy came face to face in the Top Box at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994. Harry Potter remembered all too clearly the last time they had met, in Flourish and Blotts, where they had come to blows.

pages.title: Quality Quidditch Supplies
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Quality Quidditch Supplies is the Quidditch shop in Diagon Alley, and Harry Potter's favourite shop in the world. It sells broomsticks, team robes, balls and everything else a player could want.

The Firebolt

In August 1993, a week after Harry came to stay at the Leaky Cauldron, the shop put the new Firebolt on show on a newly erected podium. It was a state-of-the-art racing broom with a handle of ash, able to accelerate to 150 miles an hour in ten seconds, and its price was given only on request. The proprietor told the crowd that the Irish International Side had just put in an order for seven. Harry never asked how much it cost. He went back almost every day all the same, just to look at it. Seamus Finnigan and Dean Thomas came in to ogle it too.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, Ron Weasley stood for a long time in front of a full set of Chudley Cannons robes in the window. In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the shop was showing the Firebolt.

In Chapter Twelve, after a Firebolt had come for Harry with no card, Oliver Wood argued that it could not possibly have been sent by Sirius Black. Black was on the run, said Wood. He could hardly have walked into Quality Quidditch Supplies to buy one.

pages.title: Gambol and Japes
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Gambol and Japes is a wizarding joke shop in Diagon Alley. It is a favourite with Fred and George Weasley.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger found the twins in Gambol and Japes with their friend Lee Jordan. They were stocking up on Dr Filibuster's Fabulous Wet-Start, No-Heat Fireworks.

Filibuster fireworks turned up all through the year that followed. In Chapter Six the twins set some off in the Burrow's kitchen on the last evening of the holidays, filling it with red and blue stars. In Chapter Nine they fed one to a Salamander in the Gryffindor common room to see what would happen. In Chapter Twelve Harry lobbed one of Fred's fireworks into Goyle's cauldron in Potions as a diversion. In Chapter Nineteen the very last of them went off on the Hogwarts Express on the way home.

pages.title: The Diagon Alley junk shop
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Broken wands; wonky brass scales; potion-stained cloaks
pages.html:
The Diagon Alley junk shop is a tiny shop full of other people's cast-offs: broken wands, wonky brass scales and potion-stained cloaks. Nobody goes in for anything new.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, while the Weasleys were doing their school shopping in Diagon Alley, Percy Weasley was found in the junk shop. He was deep in a small and very dull book called Prefects Who Gained Power.

pages.title: The second-hand robe shop
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The second-hand robe shop in Diagon Alley sells wizarding robes that somebody else has worn first, for a good deal less than new ones cost. It does steady trade with families who have more children than Galleons.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, the Weasleys split up on the steps after their visit to Gringotts. Mrs Weasley took Ginny to the second-hand robe shop, to fit her out for her first year at Hogwarts. Ginny was the youngest of seven, and the Weasleys' vault had turned out to hold only a very small pile of Sickles, with one gold Galleon.

pages.title: The marble staircase
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Hogwarts, rising from the Entrance Hall
The first floor and the floors above
pages.html:
The marble staircase is the splendid staircase that sweeps up from the Entrance Hall at Hogwarts to the floors above. Anybody going upstairs from the Great Hall goes by it.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, after the start-of-term feast in 1991, Percy Weasley led the new Gryffindor first-years out of the Great Hall and up the marble staircase on the long climb to their tower. Harry was too full of treacle tart by then to be surprised by anything.

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, on Hallowe'en 1992, Harry glanced back from the top of the dungeon stairs and saw a flicker of silver-blonde hair on the marble staircase. Dracina Malfoy was going up it alone, away from the feast, at a quick light run, with one hand pressed flat to the front of her robes as though she were holding something against her. Then the stairs turned and she was gone.

Soon afterwards Harry tore up the same staircase himself, following a voice nobody else could hear, with Ron and Hermione clattering after him.

pages.title: The Hogwarts lake
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Below Hogwarts, at the foot of its cliff
pages.html:
The Hogwarts lake is the great lake below the castle, which stands on a cliff above it. It is better known as the Black Lake.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on the night of 1 September 1992, Ron Weasley flew his father's Ford Anglia out over the lake towards the castle, with Harry Potter beside him. The water lay a mile below them, smooth and black as glass. Over the lake the engine gave a loud clunk, spluttered and died. The nose dropped. The car fell towards the castle wall, swung away from it by inches, and came down into the Whomping Willow. In Chapter Nine, that October, the rain came down for days and the lake rose.

pages.title: The London Underground
pages.html:
The London Underground, which Londoners call the Tube, is the Muggle railway that runs through tunnels beneath London. Its first line opened in 1863, and it is the oldest underground railway in the world. Hagrid took Harry Potter on it to Diagon Alley in the summer of 1991.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, Harry told Mr Weasley that he had gone on the Underground with Hagrid, who had barely fitted through the barriers. Mr Weasley lit up at once. He wanted to know whether there had been 'escapators', and exactly how they worked. A few minutes later Fred vanished into green fire by Floo powder, making it look, Harry thought, as easy as feeding a ticket into the barrier on the Tube.

pages.title: Snape's office
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The dungeons of Hogwarts, along a cold passage
pages.html:
Snape's office lies along a cold passage in the dungeons of Hogwarts. It belongs to Severus Snape, the Potions master, and it is about as welcoming as he is. Its walls are lined with shelves of jars, each with something slimy floating in it, glistening in the firelight.

The office

In March 1994 a small cauldron was simmering over a low blue flame in one corner, sending up a thin thread of grey smoke that smelt faintly bitter, like burnt grass. The fireplace is connected to the Floo Network, so Snape can summon other members of staff through it, and he keeps a jar of Floo powder on the mantelpiece.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on the night of 1 September 1992, Snape took Harry Potter and Ron Weasley there after they flew the Weasleys' car into the Whomping Willow. The fireplace was black and empty. Snape unrolled that evening's Prophet and read them the reports of the Muggles who had seen them, Mr Angus Fleet of Peebles among them.

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, in March 1994, Dracina Malfoy came to the office with mud caked across her expensive cloak. 'Potter is in Hogsmeade,' she told Snape. He fetched Harry down to the dungeons. Harry had been inside only once before, in his second year, and Snape seemed to have collected a good many more slimy things in jars since then. There were little smears of dried mud on the flagstones in front of the desk.

When the Marauder's Map insulted him, Snape flung a handful of Floo powder into the fire. 'Lupin!' he called into the flames. 'I want a word!' A few seconds later Professor Lupin climbed out of the grate, beating ash from his shabby robes.

pages.title: Greenhouse Three
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Hogwarts greenhouses, behind the castle
Mandrakes; a Venomous Tentacula; hanging flowers the size of umbrellas
pages.html:
Greenhouse Three is the Hogwarts greenhouse where Professor Sprout keeps the more interesting and more dangerous plants. Students first work in it in their second year.

The greenhouse

Inside it smells of damp earth and fertiliser, with the heavy scent of the enormous flowers, each the size of an umbrella, that hang from the roof. Its plants include the Mandrakes, whose cry is fatal when they are fully grown. There is also a Venomous Tentacula, which was teething in September 1992.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on 2 September 1992, Harry Potter's year had their first lesson there, repotting Mandrakes. Until then they had only ever worked in Greenhouse One. Professor Sprout warned them to be careful of the Venomous Tentacula, because it was teething. Justin Finch-Fletchley introduced himself to Harry over the dragon-dung compost. In Chapter Sixteen, in March 1993, several of the Mandrakes threw a loud, wild party in the greenhouse that kept half of Hufflepuff awake and made Professor Sprout very happy indeed.

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, in March 1994, a Puffapod went off in Ron Weasley's face during Herbology. Dracina Malfoy was waiting for Harry outside Greenhouse Three when the lesson ended, standing quite alone on the gravel path.

pages.title: Lockhart's office
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Framed photographs of Lockhart, several of them signed
pages.html:
Lockhart's office was where Gilderoy Lockhart worked while he taught Defence Against the Dark Arts at Hogwarts, in the school year of 1992 to 1993. It was on the second floor, lit by a great many candles. Its walls were covered with countless framed photographs of Lockhart himself, several of which he had signed.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, on a Saturday evening in the autumn of 1992, Harry Potter dragged his feet along the second-floor corridor to serve a detention in Lockhart's office. It was there that he first heard the cold, murderous voice that nobody else could hear.

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, at Hallowe'en 1992, Mrs Norris was found Petrified. Lockhart offered his office, which was the nearest, just upstairs from the corridor. Dumbledore laid the cat on the desk there. The photographs of Lockhart all round the walls ducked out of sight, some of them in hair curlers.

pages.title: Filch's office
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Punishment records; polished chains and manacles; confiscated goods
pages.html:
Filch's office is the room at Hogwarts from which Argus Filch, the caretaker, carries on his long war with the students. Most of them go to a good deal of trouble never to see the inside of it.

The office

It is a dingy room with no window. A single oil lamp hangs from the low ceiling over the desk, and a smell of fried fish has soaked into the walls. Wooden filing cabinets line the room, holding the particulars of every pupil Filch has ever punished. Fred and George Weasley have a drawer to themselves.

On the wall behind the desk hangs a collection of chains and manacles, very lovingly polished. Everybody knows that Filch is forever begging Dumbledore to let him hang students up by their ankles. One drawer of a filing cabinet is labelled Confiscated and Highly Dangerous.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, Filch caught Harry Potter dripping mud from Quidditch practice and marched him down to the office. Harry had never been inside before. Filch was halfway through writing out his crime when something crashed on the ceiling overhead, and he ran off to catch Peeves. Left alone, Harry found a purple envelope from Kwikspell, a correspondence course in beginners' magic, lying on the desk. When Filch came back, he saw that it had moved. He went the colour of brick, flung it into a drawer and sent Harry away without a punishment. The crash had been Nearly Headless Nick's doing: he had persuaded Peeves to drop a cabinet over the office.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Fred and George told Harry how they had been dragged into the office in their first year for letting off a Dungbomb in a corridor. While Filch was going on at them, they noticed the drawer marked Confiscated and Highly Dangerous. George dropped another Dungbomb as a diversion. Fred had the drawer open in a second, and out came the Marauder's Map, which they were now handing on to Harry.

pages.title: The girls' toilet on the first floor
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Hogwarts, off the corridor of the Hallowe'en attack
The entrance to the Chamber of Secrets
pages.html:
The girls' toilet on the first floor, as Hermione Granger called it, is the out-of-order girls' toilet at Hogwarts that Moaning Myrtle haunts. Myrtle keeps having tantrums and flooding it, so nobody goes in if they can help it, which made it the perfect place to brew Polyjuice Potion. Under one of its sinks lies the entrance to the Chamber of Secrets.

The toilet

It opens off the corridor on the second floor where Mrs Norris was found Petrified on Hallowe'en 1992. It is the most dismal, depressing bathroom Harry Potter has ever set foot in. Under a big, cracked, speckled mirror stands a row of chipped stone basins. The floor is always damp. The wooden doors of the cubicles are scratched and flaking. One hangs off its hinges. Myrtle sits in the end cubicle, on top of the cistern or down in the U-bend.

One of the copper taps has a tiny snake scratched on its side. When the tap is spoken to in Parseltongue, the whole basin sinks out of sight, leaving a pipe wide enough for a man to slide into. It leads down to the Chamber of Secrets. Myrtle died in the end cubicle in 1943, the last time the Chamber was opened. She had been hiding there, crying, because Olive Hornby had teased her about her glasses. When she unlocked the door to tell a boy talking in a strange language to go and use his own toilet, she saw a pair of great yellow eyes by the sink in front of her cubicle.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party on Hallowe'en 1992, Hermione steered Harry Potter and Ron Weasley away from Myrtle. 'She haunts the girls' toilet on the first floor,' she said. It had been out of order all year, she explained, because Myrtle kept having tantrums and flooding it. She herself never went in there if she could help it.

In Chapter Ten the three of them went in, ignoring the large OUT OF ORDER sign, to ask Myrtle whether she had seen anything on Hallowe'en night. Later that term they brewed their Polyjuice Potion in one of its cubicles, since nobody else ever came in. In Chapter Fifteen, in the new year, Myrtle told Harry about a posh girl with long, straight, shiny hair who had come crashing in one night to search the place on her hands and knees. The girl had whispered at the sinks, thrown her bag at Myrtle, then run away crying. In Chapter Eighteen Myrtle told Harry how she had died. Harry found the little snake scratched on the tap and opened the Chamber of Secrets.

pages.title: The second-floor corridor
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Heir of Slytherin's message, Hallowe'en 1992
pages.html:
The second-floor corridor at Hogwarts is a long, dim passage of tall windows, near Moaning Myrtle's bathroom. On Hallowe'en 1992 the Heir of Slytherin announced there that the Chamber of Secrets had been opened.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry followed a voice nobody else could hear up from the Entrance Hall to a corridor awash with water, with Ron and Hermione behind him. Between two of the tall windows, in letters a foot high, something had been daubed across the stone in red: THE CHAMBER OF SECRETS HAS BEEN OPENED. ENEMIES OF THE HEIR, BEWARE. Beneath it Mrs Norris hung by her tail from a torch bracket, as stiff as a board.

In Chapter Eighteen, on 29 May 1993, Professor McGonagall told the staff that the Heir had left a second message, directly under the first: Her skeleton will lie in the Chamber for ever. The student taken was Ginny Weasley.

pages.title: The Deathday Party dungeon
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Nearly Headless Nick's five hundredth deathday, Hallowe'en 1992
pages.html:
The Deathday Party dungeon is the roomy dungeon at Hogwarts where Nearly Headless Nick held the party for his five hundredth deathday on Hallowe'en 1992. For that one night it was given over entirely to ghosts.

The dungeon

It is reached by a passage that was lit, for the party, with long, thin black candles burning a cold, bright blue, and its doorway was hung with black velvet. Inside, a chandelier blazed midnight blue over hundreds of pearly-white ghosts, most of them waltzing. An orchestra of thirty musical saws played on a platform draped in black. Walking into it was like walking into a cold store.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger went to the party at Nick's invitation instead of to the Hallowe'en feast. Peeves called Moaning Myrtle over to them, and she fled the dungeon in tears. Later that night the three of them were found beside Filch's Petrified cat. They had to explain to the teachers why they had missed the feast.

pages.title: Dungeon five
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Frog brains on the ceiling, October 1992
pages.html:
Dungeon five is one of the dungeon rooms beneath Hogwarts Castle. In October 1992 some third-years splattered frog brains all over its ceiling. Argus Filch, the caretaker, spent a whole morning cleaning them off.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Nearly Headless Nick warned Harry Potter to make a brave retreat, because Filch was in a foul temper. He had a cold, and he had been cleaning dungeon five all morning. Harry, dripping mud from Quidditch practice, did not get away in time. Filch marched him off to his office, muttering about dung, frog brains and rat innards.

pages.title: Chamber of Secrets
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Deep beneath Hogwarts, under the lake
A sink in the second-floor girls' bathroom
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Chamber of Secrets is the hidden hall Salazar Slytherin built deep beneath Hogwarts before he left the school. He sealed it so that only his heir could open it, and loose the Basilisk inside. For centuries it was dismissed as a legend. Tom Riddle opened it in 1943, when a Muggle-born girl died. It was opened again in 1992 to 1993, through Riddle's diary and the possessed Dracina Malfoy, until Harry Potter killed the Basilisk down there with the sword from the Sorting Hat.

Legend

According to the legend, Salazar Slytherin built a chamber inside the castle without the knowledge of the other three founders. Before he left he sealed it, so that nobody could open it until his own true heir came to the school. The heir alone would be able to break the seal. He would release the horror waiting inside, and with it purge the school of everyone unworthy to study magic.

Many times over the centuries the most learned witches and wizards have searched the castle for it. So has a long line of headmasters and headmistresses. In 1992 Professor Binns told his class that the whole thing was perfect nonsense, a story to frighten the credulous. There was not one scrap of evidence, he said, that Slytherin had ever built so much as a secret broom cupboard.

In truth Slytherin had kept the Basilisk to defend Hogwarts from Muggles. It was his use of it for that, not any wish to purge the school, that parted him from Godric Gryffindor.

The way in

The entrance is a sink in the out-of-order girls' bathroom on the second floor, which is haunted by Moaning Myrtle. It is marked by a tiny snake scratched on the side of one copper tap. When it is spoken to in Parseltongue, the sink sinks out of sight. Beneath it is a pipe wide enough for a man to slide down.

The pipe drops far below the dungeons into a slimy stone tunnel, which seems to run under the lake. Its floor is littered with the small bones of animals. The tunnel ends at a solid wall carved with two entwined serpents, with emeralds for eyes. It parts when commanded in Parseltongue.

The Chamber

Beyond the wall lies a long, dimly lit hall. Towering stone pillars, carved with more entwining serpents, rise into the darkness through a greenish gloom. At the far end stands a colossal statue of Salazar Slytherin, ancient and monkeyish, with a long, thin stone beard that reaches almost to the hem of his robes. The Basilisk lived inside the statue, and came out through its mouth.

The opening of 1943

Tom Riddle, Slytherin's last living descendant, found the Chamber in his fifth year and opened it. In June 1943 a Muggle-born Ravenclaw girl called Myrtle was killed in the bathroom above it, after which the school was to be closed. Riddle framed the third-year Rubeus Hagrid for the attacks, along with his pet Acromantula, Aragog, and Hagrid was expelled. Riddle kept the memory of that year in a diary. He meant it to lead somebody else, one day, to finish Slytherin's work.

The opening of 1992 to 1993

In the summer of 1992 a pile of books was spilt across the floor of Flourish and Blotts. Dracina Malfoy kept a small black book from among them, and began to write in it. It was Riddle's diary. It had been set loose as part of a plot of Lucius Malfoy's, who later admitted that he had been 'instructed'. The memory inside the diary fed on her confidences, and little by little it took control of her.

On Hallowe'en 1992 a message appeared on a wall of the second floor, daubed a foot high in glimmering red: 'The Chamber of Secrets has been opened. Enemies of the heir, beware'. Beneath it hung Filch's cat, Mrs Norris, Petrified. Colin Creevey was Petrified in November. In December it was Justin Finch-Fletchley, together with Nearly Headless Nick. In the spring it was Hermione Granger, with the Ravenclaw prefect Penelope Clearwater. The two girls were saved from death by a mirror, Justin because he saw the creature through Nick, Colin because he saw it through his camera.

Dracina lost hours at a time. She woke in corridors with red on her hands, and she fell ill when the diary was taken from her. The rest of the school, having heard Harry speak Parseltongue at the Duelling Club, decided that he was the heir.

In the summer term of 1993, with Dumbledore suspended and Hagrid in Azkaban, Dracina was drawn down into the Chamber wearing Harry's stolen Quidditch scarf. Ginny Weasley had followed her, and was taken too. From a page clutched in Hermione's fist Harry worked out that the monster was a Basilisk, moving about the castle through the pipes. He opened the entrance with Parseltongue. Ron and Gilderoy Lockhart went down with him. Lockhart's Memory Charm backfired through Ron's broken wand and brought the roof of the tunnel down. Harry went on alone.

Harry in the Chamber

Harry found Dracina collapsing, Ginny bleeding and the memory of Tom Riddle taking solid shape beside the open diary. Riddle explained how he had possessed Dracina, and how Lucius Malfoy's plot had worked. He spoke of a union between the Potter bloodline and the Malfoy one. He spoke, too, of Lily Potter's ancient lineage. Then he revealed that he was Lord Voldemort. Harry refused his offer of revenge on the Dursleys, and called him a fraud.

Riddle set the Basilisk on him. One of its fangs caught Harry's arm, but a warm presence and a fatherly voice held him up. Fawkes brought him the Sorting Hat, and out of it Harry drew a sword. It was Andúril, though it was not until the following winter that Harry worked that out. When the Basilisk's stare struck him, it met a golden heat like an opened furnace, and went no further. Its thrashing brought down several of the pillars. Harry stood astride Dracina on the cold stone, with a strength that was not his own pouring into his arms. He cut off the Basilisk's head with a single stroke. Then he drove the sword through the diary, and Riddle was destroyed.

As the venom came back into him Harry collapsed in Dracina's arms. A man in a white robe was standing by a fallen pillar, watching him with pride. Harry and Dracina both saw him. Harry, looking up from the floor, saw the kind, grave face of Christ from the window of St Michael's Church in Little Whinging. The Fat Friar told him afterwards that Christ had been there all along.

Harry woke unharmed, with his head in Dracina's lap. She healed Ginny's cut, then Fawkes carried them all back up the pipe. The doors of the Chamber were shut again, with the Basilisk's carcass still inside.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: Ginny Weasley and Colin Creevey had been as thick as thieves since they came out of the hospital wing together after the Chamber. In Chapter Six Narcissa Malfoy told Harry that Lucius had been trying not to like him ever since that business with the Chamber.

pages.title: Surrey
infobox: The Dursleys, of number four, Privet Drive
pages.html:
Surrey is the English county south-west of London where the Dursleys live, at number four, Privet Drive, in the town of Little Whinging. Harry Potter grew up there, in the cupboard under their stairs.

The county

It is a county of tidy commuter towns, where nothing in the least unusual is supposed to happen. Mrs Arabella Figg lives in Little Whinging too, a couple of streets from the Dursleys, and Ambrose Greyhame is the vicar of St Michael's Church there.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, at the Burrow in the summer of 1992, Molly Weasley held Harry in a long hug. Over the top of his head she turned a look towards the window, the south and Surrey that would have frightened Uncle Vernon very badly indeed. In Chapter Six she turned the same look on the window, in the general direction of Surrey, more than once that summer, after Harry had gone out to the paddock.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: at dinner in the Burrow garden on 21 August 1994 Molly Weasley's gaze kept drifting over the hedge towards the east, where Surrey lay. Each time there was nothing kind in her face, only fury and a grim, patient relish.

pages.title: London
infobox: Diagon Alley; Knockturn Alley; platform nine and three-quarters at King's Cross
The Master's court; Drusilla (about 1860); William the Bloody (1880)
pages.html:
London is the capital of Britain, Muggle and wizarding alike. Diagon Alley is there, together with the Ministry of Magic, and the Hogwarts Express leaves from King's Cross.

History

In the tenth century the last Hellenic sorcerers worked out of London, fighting a wizarding war against the Norse völvas of Jorvik until the Saxons took that city in 954.

The city has a long, dark history among vampires. In 1760 Darla brought Angelus there to be presented to the Master, who kept his court in a lair beneath the streets. About 1860 Angelus found the devout young witch Drusilla in London. He killed her family one by one and drove her into a convent. On the day she took her holy orders he came through its chapel and sired her. In 1880 she sired William the Bloody there.

Long afterwards Professor McGonagall tangled with William the Bloody himself in a cellar in Whitechapel, in the East End. She came out of it with her life and very little else.

From the end of 1987 the Excalibur team kept watch over London. In 1988 it caught Mojo's Warwolves, creatures that wear the skins of the people they kill, and they were put on show at London Zoo, in Regent's Park. In 1989 the team's Nazi doubles from another world attacked the Tower of London, where the Weird Happenings Organisation has its headquarters.

In the summer of 1996 London burned. Black Air, a secret government unit, had joined a captive being to a demon that lay beneath the city, with the help of the London Inner Circle of the Hellfire Club. The streets broke out in fires and riots. Then the Excalibur team stormed Blackwall, Black Air's headquarters, and the demon was bound.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, two Muggles in London became convinced that they had seen an old car flying over the Post Office tower. They were right: Ron Weasley and Harry Potter were in it.

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, in September 1992, Hermione Granger told Harry of the atrocities Angelus had committed in London. She told him too that William the Bloody had been sired there.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, at breakfast at the Burrow on 22 August 1994, Arthur Weasley complained that the Muggles had been letting all kinds of people into Britain. Harry Potter decided that one day he would tell Mr Weasley about the people who really were coming to Britain, and about what he had seen on the streets of London with Hagrid, the summer he was eleven. It was one of the only things he had ever agreed with Uncle Vernon about.

pages.title: The Post Office tower
infobox: The Post Office's microwave telephone links
pages.html:
The Post Office tower is the tall, round tower in central London that was built to carry the Post Office's telephone and television links by microwave. It opened in 1965, and was the tallest building in London until 1980.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, Professor Snape took Harry and Ron down to his office. There he unrolled that evening's Prophet and read it aloud. Two Muggles in London were convinced they had seen an old car flying over the Post Office tower. It was Mr Weasley's Ford Anglia, in which Harry and Ron had flown north after the barrier at King's Cross refused to let them through. Six or seven Muggles had seen it in all, among them Mrs Hetty Bayliss of Norfolk, who had been hanging out her washing at the time.

pages.title: Norfolk
pages.html:
Norfolk is a flat county of wide skies on the east coast of England. At noon on 1 September 1992 Mrs Hetty Bayliss saw a flying car there while she was hanging out her washing.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, Severus Snape held up that evening's Prophet under the headline FLYING FORD ANGLIA MYSTIFIES MUGGLES. He read it aloud to Harry Potter and Ron Weasley. Six or seven Muggles had seen the car. Among them were Mrs Bayliss in Norfolk, two people in London who had seen it over the Post Office tower and Mr Angus Fleet of Peebles, who had reported it to the police.

pages.title: Peebles
infobox: Mr Angus Fleet, who saw a flying car
pages.html:
Peebles is a small Scottish town in the Borders, on the River Tweed, south of Edinburgh. On 1 September 1992 one of its Muggles, Mr Angus Fleet, reported to the police that he had seen a flying car.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, the car was Arthur Weasley's Ford Anglia, which Ron Weasley and Harry Potter flew north to Hogwarts after the barrier at King's Cross sealed itself against them. Six or seven Muggles in all saw it on the way. That evening Severus Snape unrolled the Prophet in his office, under the headline FLYING FORD ANGLIA MYSTIFIES MUGGLES, and read the reports aloud to the two boys. Mr Angus Fleet, of Peebles, was among them.

pages.title: Kent
pages.html:
Kent is the county in the south-east corner of England, often called the Garden of England. It is the home county of the Wailing Widow, a ghost who drowned herself in a well in 1392, believing that her husband would never come back from the Crusades. He came home a week later.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, at Nearly Headless Nick's five hundredth deathday party at Hallowe'en 1992, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter the Widow's story. Nick himself was proud to tell Harry that she had come all the way up from Kent.

pages.title: Glastonbury
pages.html:
Glastonbury is a small town in Somerset, below the Tor, a steep green hill with a lonely church tower on its top. Its abbey was once one of the richest in England. When the King's commissioners came for it, a monk named Brother Aldric hid the abbey's books in a cave on the Tor, where they never found them.

The abbey

The monks of Glastonbury claimed in 1191 to have found the grave of King Arthur in their grounds. They also claimed that Glastonbury was Avalon. It was not; Avalon was the Grey Havens of the Elves, a long way from Somerset. In 1539 Henry the Eighth's men closed the abbey and took its riches. Brother Aldric was hanged, drawn and quartered. His ghost comes in four pieces, which do not always agree on where to go, and he holds his left arm on with his right.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in the Gryffindor common room, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter and Ron Weasley about the ghosts who would be at Nearly Headless Nick's deathday party. Among them was a monk from Glastonbury who had been hanged, drawn and quartered by Henry the Eighth's men.

At the party itself, on 31 October 1992, she found Brother Aldric among the guests, a tall, mournful monk who was not quite assembled. She asked him whether it was true about the books. Nobody had asked him about anything but his quartering for about four hundred and fifty years. 'Young lady,' he said, in a voice like a cellar door, 'it is entirely true. Would you care to know where?' He told her, and she wrote it all down.

pages.title: Wolverhampton
pages.html:
Wolverhampton is a large industrial town in the West Midlands of England, on the edge of the Black Country. It was made a city in 2000.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in the autumn of 1992, Harry was left waiting in Filch's office and picked up a glossy purple envelope from the desk. It held a leaflet for Kwikspell, a correspondence course in beginners' magic, with a testimonial from Mrs P. Hoskins of Wolverhampton: 'For years I couldn't so much as warm a teapot without setting light to the cosy. Since Kwikspell, my Scouring Charms are the talk of the street!'

pages.title: Kendal
infobox: Mr L. Ashby, a Kwikspell customer
pages.html:
Kendal is a market town in Cumbria, on the edge of the Lake District, famous among Muggles for its mint cake. It is the home of Mr L. Ashby, whose testimonial appears in the advertising for Kwikspell, a correspondence course in beginners' magic.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in the autumn of 1992, Harry Potter found a Kwikspell envelope on Argus Filch's desk. He read the testimonials inside, among them Mr Ashby's: 'My brother-in-law always laughed at my wandwork. He has not laughed since Lesson Four, chiefly because he is presently a hatstand. Thank you, Kwikspell!'

pages.title: Egypt
infobox: Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Egypt is the country of the Nile, in the north-east of Africa, and the heir of Stygia. Every dark art that Europe knows came there by way of Egypt. It is also the place where the dead are weighed. Ra once ruled it as its sun god. Bill Weasley works there for Gringotts, breaking curses in the tombs.

Stygia's heir

Stygia was the old kingdom of sorcerers in the south, before the Ice Age ended and the Flood washed that world away. Egypt rose after it and inherited its craft. From Egypt the dark arts passed to Greece, then to Rome, then to England and the rest of Europe. A wizard who goes looking for the beginnings of his own magic finds Egypt, then Stygia, then nothing, because that is where the written record drowns.

The weighing of the dead

The dead are weighed in Egypt, and something still stands guard over the weighing. The tombs hold more than gold. Some of them hold things that sit up on their slabs and ask an intruder questions.

The Goa'uld Anubis took the name of the jackal-headed god of the dead, but it is not he who keeps watch over the weighing.

Ra

Ra, the greatest of the Goa'uld, once ruled Egypt as its sun god. Through the gate at Giza he carried Egyptians away to other worlds as slaves. Some five thousand years ago the people rose against him, with Thor, the son of Odin, fighting at their side, and Ra fled. The Egyptians buried his gate in the sand, where it lay until 1928.

Thor, the son of Odin, fought beside them in that rising. He came in a storm, a rare thing in Egypt, and broke Ra's guards while the people stormed the gate. Ra forbade the Goa'uld ever to speak of Earth again.

Apocalypse, the first of the mutants, was born at Akkaba in the years after the rising.

The Black Pharaoh

Egypt did not stay free of false gods for long. Some centuries after the rising, about 2600 BC by the later accounts, a king called Nephren-Ka served Nyarlathotep from the throne of Egypt. He built a temple with a windowless crypt about the stone called the Shining Trapezohedron. Later ages called him the Black Pharaoh. What he did there caused his name to be struck from every monument and record, so that the histories of Egypt do not know he lived.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, Bill Weasley was away in Egypt, working for Gringotts. In Chapter Fourteen Arthur and Molly Weasley went out to visit him there for Christmas 1992.

In Book Three, Chapter One, Arthur Weasley won seven hundred Galleons in the Daily Prophet Grand Prize Galleon Draw. The family spent it on a month in Egypt with Bill, in the summer of 1993, among the cursed tombs. Ron wrote to Harry that he should see what the Egyptian wizards put in the tombs. One had a curse on the door that turned you inside out if you said the password wrong.

In Chapter Four Fred and George told Harry that they had tried to shut Percy in a pyramid. Something all in bandages had sat up on its slab. It asked Percy whether he had lived with a true heart, and whether he was ready to have his heart weighed. 'And Percy answered,' said George. 'For about ten minutes. With examples.'

In Chapter Fourteen, in the spring of 1994, Ron spent ages in the Hogsmeade post office pretending to ask what it would cost to owl Bill in Egypt. In Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Sirius Black showed Harry and the others the crumpled cutting he had kept: the Daily Prophet photograph of the Weasleys in Egypt, with Scabbers on Ron's shoulder. It was how he had found out where Peter Pettigrew was hiding.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on 20 August 1994, the Muggle news reported that the American Egyptologist Dr Daniel Jackson had been declared dead after an accident at an excavation near Giza.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, Ludo Bagman introduced the referee, Hassan Mostafa, Chairwizard of the International Association of Quidditch, who had come all the way from Egypt.

pages.title: Eton College
infobox: Eton, across the Thames from Windsor
pages.html:
Eton College is the most famous Muggle boarding school in England, at Eton, across the river Thames from Windsor. King Henry VI founded it in 1440. Justin Finch-Fletchley's name had been down for it before his Hogwarts letter came.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on 2 September 1992, Justin introduced himself to Harry Potter over the dragon-dung compost in Greenhouse Three. 'My name was down for Eton, you know.' Ron Weasley looked at Harry with his eyebrows up, waiting to be told what an Eton was.

In Chapter Ten Harry, remembering how Justin had turned on his heel at the sight of him in a corridor, thought bitterly: Eton boy, indeed. In Chapter Twelve Ernie Macmillan told his friends in the library that Justin had let slip to Harry that he was Muggle-born. Justin had even told Harry that he had had a place at Eton.

pages.title: Timbuktu
infobox: The southern edge of the Sahara, near the River Niger
pages.html:
Timbuktu is an ancient city in Mali, in West Africa, on the southern edge of the Sahara near the River Niger. In the Middle Ages it was a great centre of trade and learning. To the British it has long stood for the most remote place anyone can think of.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1992, Ron showed Harry his Chudley Cannons bedspread and boasted that all the Chudleys were from England. 'What are those Muggles playing at, letting blokes from bloody Timbuktu play for English teams?' he said.

In Book Four, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1994, Dracina wrote to Harry that Pansy Parkinson, who had never cared about Quidditch in her life, had suddenly taken up the Chudley Cannons. 'I just appreciate that they're all English,' Pansy had said. Harry knew exactly where she had got that from.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, at the World Cup campsite on 22 August 1994, the Muggle site manager, Mr Roberts, asked whether the Weasley party were foreign. 'Yeah,' said Harry Potter sarcastically. 'We're from bloody Timbuktu.'

pages.title: Improper Use of Magic Office
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery; the Statute of Secrecy
pages.html:
The Improper Use of Magic Office is the office of the Ministry of Magic that detects magic done where it should not be, and warns or punishes whoever is to blame.

Work

It watches above all for underage witches and wizards doing magic outside school. It can tell where a spell has been cast, but not who cast it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, on the evening of 31 July 1992, the Office detected a Hover Charm at number four, Privet Drive, at twelve minutes past nine. The spell was Dobby's, but the letter went to Harry Potter. Signed by Mafalda Hopkirk, it reminded him that underage wizards are not permitted to perform spells outside school. It cited the Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery of 1875 and Section 13 of the Statute of Secrecy. It ended: 'Enjoy your holidays!'

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, on 21 August 1994, Molly Weasley complained at the Burrow that Fred and George were wasting their brains on joke inventions. If they carried on the way they were going, she said, they would end up in front of the Improper Use of Magic Office.

pages.title: Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office is the small office at the Ministry of Magic that deals with bewitched Muggle-made objects. Arthur Weasley heads it, with one colleague, an old warlock called Perkins. Ron Weasley calls it the most boring department there is.

The work

Its business is to stop bewitched Muggle-made things from ending up back in Muggle shops and houses. Ron's favourite example is a tea set that an old witch had been given by a formerly cursed French nobleman and his peasant wife. After her death it was sold to an antiques shop. When a little old Muggle lady served her friends tea from it, the whole set came alive and danced. The teapot sang. The old lady died of shock, and the office spent weeks on Memory Charms covering it up.

There are raids as well. One night's raids in the summer of 1992 turned up a few shrinking door-keys and a biting kettle, the work of Muggle-baiters. Lucius Malfoy thinks Arthur a disgrace to the name of wizards, and an ill-paid one. Arthur, who is mad about everything to do with Muggles, does not mind. It was awkward all the same when the head of the office was fined fifty Galleons in 1992 for enchanting a Muggle motor car.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, in the flying car, Ron told Harry where his father worked, and why it was boring. In Chapter Four Mr Weasley came home from nine raids with a few shrinking door-keys and a biting kettle to show for them. In Chapter Five Lucius Malfoy asked him in Diagon Alley whether they were paying him overtime. In Chapter Fourteen the Daily Prophet reported that Arthur Weasley, who heads the office, had been fined fifty Galleons over the car.

In Book Three, Chapter One, the Prophet named him again, as 'Arthur Weasley, 43, of the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office', when he won its Grand Prize Galleon Draw and took his family to Egypt to visit Bill.

pages.title: Committee on Experimental Charms
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Committee on Experimental Charms is the office of the Ministry of Magic that deals with new, untried charms and the trouble they cause. Arthur Weasley, who has trouble enough of his own, is thankful that its cases are not his.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in August 1992, Arthur Weasley came home to the Burrow after a night of raids for the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office. He had found a few shrinking door-keys and a biting kettle. There had been some pretty nasty stuff that was not his department, he said. 'Mortlake was taken in for questioning about some extremely odd ferrets, but that's the Committee on Experimental Charms, thank goodness...'

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, at the World Cup campsite on 22 August 1994, Arthur Weasley pointed out Gilbert Wimple of the Committee on Experimental Charms among the Ministry people passing by. Wimple, said Mr Weasley, had had his horns for a while now.

pages.title: International Confederation of Warlocks
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The International Confederation of Warlocks is the name under which the Statute of Secrecy is cited in the official letters of the Ministry of Magic. It is another name for the International Confederation of Wizards, which signed the Statute in 1689.

Section 13

Section 13 of the Statute makes any magic that risks the notice of Muggles a serious offence. The Ministry quotes it to any young witch or wizard caught doing magic in the holidays.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, the Ministry's warning letter to Harry Potter in July 1992 reminded him 'that any magical activity which risks notice by members of the non-magical community (Muggles) is a serious offence under Section 13 of the International Confederation of Warlocks' Statute of Secrecy'.

pages.title: Witch Weekly
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Witch Weekly is a popular wizarding magazine, read by witches all over Britain. It gives a Most Charming Smile Award, which Gilderoy Lockhart has won five times in a row.

The magazine

It runs to fashion, household charms and the doings of famous wizards. Pansy Parkinson reads it. Lockhart likes people to know that he does not talk about his awards.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Lockhart told Harry: 'I know, I know, it's not quite as good as winning Witch Weekly's Most Charming Smile Award five times in a row, as I have.' Minutes later, at the start of the lesson, he introduced himself to the class as five times winner of the award: 'But I don't talk about that.' In Chapter Fifteen he was still signing himself five-times winner, on a card wishing Hermione Granger a swift recovery. In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express on 1 September 1993, Pansy was reading Witch Weekly, and did not look up.

pages.title: Dark Force Defence League
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Dark Force Defence League is a wizarding society which, as its name says, stands against the Dark Arts. Its best-known member is Gilderoy Lockhart, who belongs to it as an Honorary Member, and who mentions it whenever he gives his name in full.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Lockhart introduced himself to his first Defence Against the Dark Arts class in September 1992 by pointing at his own portrait on the cover of Travels with Trolls. 'Gilderoy Lockhart, Order of Merlin, Third Class, Honorary Member of the Dark Force Defence League, and five times winner of Witch Weekly's Most Charming Smile Award. But I don't talk about that.'

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Lockhart sent Hermione Granger a get-well card in the hospital wing, signed with the same titles. Ron Weasley snatched it out of the wastepaper basket by her bed and read it out in a high, gushing voice. Hermione said, in a huff, that she had decided she did not like Lockhart any more. She thought he was lying about a great many things.

pages.title: Headless Hunt
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A head that is properly off
Head Juggling, Head Polo, Horseback Head Juggling, Head Hockey
pages.html:
The Headless Hunt is a band of headless ghosts who ride ghost horses, led by Sir Patrick Delaney-Podmore. It admits only those whose heads came properly off. That is why it has turned Nearly Headless Nick away again and again.

The Hunt

Its members hack about the countryside on horseback with their heads under their arms. Their games include Head Juggling, Head Polo, Horseback Head Juggling and Head Hockey, none of which Nick could play. Nick's execution took forty-five blows with a blunt axe. At the end of it an inch of skin and sinew still held his head on.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, the Hunt turned Nick down again. 'Not that I wanted to join, you understand,' he told Harry Potter, with Sir Patrick's letter still in his hand. On Hallowe'en a hunting horn rang out at Nick's Deathday Party, and a dozen ghost horses burst out of the dungeon wall. On every one sat a rider with no head on his shoulders. Sir Patrick held his bearded head up high so that it could see the crowd, then mocked Nick in front of everyone.

Harry stood up for Nick, loud and clear: 'Nick's a great ghost.' Soon afterwards the Hunt began a game of Head Hockey. Nick tried gallantly to win his audience back, and gave up when Sir Patrick's head went sailing past his nose to loud cheers.

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, after the Duelling Club, Harry tried a joke. By stopping a snake from biting Justin Finch-Fletchley's head off, he said, he had saved Justin a job with the Headless Hunt. The joke did not land.

pages.title: Kwikspell
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Kwikspell is a correspondence course in beginners' magic, for witches and wizards whose spells fizzle. Argus Filch, the Hogwarts caretaker, who is a Squib, takes it in secret.

The course

Its brochure comes in a large, glossy purple envelope with silver writing on it, and promises an all-new, never-fail, rapid-result, simple-to-learn method. One satisfied pupil, Mr L. Ashby of Kendal, writes: 'My brother-in-law always laughed at my wandwork. He has not laughed since Lesson Four, chiefly because he is presently a hatstand.'

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, Harry Potter read the envelope while he waited in Filch's office. When Filch came back he saw that it had moved, went the colour of brick and flung it into a drawer. 'If I thought you'd read my private... not that it's mine... for a friend...' he spluttered. Harry lied that he had not, and Filch let him go unpunished.

pages.title: Malfoy family
aliases: the noble and ancient house of Malfoy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
William the Conqueror, to Armand Malfoy
pages.html:
The Malfoys are an old, rich pure-blood family of Dark wizards, who style themselves the noble and ancient house of Malfoy. They came over from Normandy with William the Conqueror, who gave Armand Malfoy his land in Wiltshire, and Malfoy Manor stands on it still. In 1994 the family is Lucius Malfoy, his wife Narcissa and their only child, Dracina, who is its heir.

History

The histories say that the big Norman wizarding families won William the Conquest with Dark magic, mostly, and that the old Anglo-Saxon families, who were light wizards, lost. The Malfoys have been Dark wizards from that day to this. They like to claim more than Normandy, all the same. Dracina was brought up to say that the Malfoys were in Britain before there was a Britain, and the family tree in the drawing room at the Manor takes up the whole wall.

The family counts its pride in centuries. Tom Riddle held that Malfoy blood was older even than the Potters', which is very old indeed. The Manor has forty bedrooms, peacocks on the lawn and portraits of the family's ancestors on every wall. Under the drawing-room floor there is a hidden room for the more precious Dark artefacts. Until 1993 the Malfoys also kept a house-elf, Dobby, whom Harry Potter tricked Lucius into freeing with a sock.

Other families think less of the Malfoys than the Malfoys think of themselves. Hagrid thinks less of them than most.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Hermione Granger explained that the Norman wizarding families had won William the Conquest with Dark magic. Dracina, overhearing, said that the Malfoys were in Britain before there was a Britain. When Hermione corrected her, citing Armand Malfoy and his land in Wiltshire, two spots of pink appeared on Dracina's cheeks.

In Book Two, Chapter Three, Fred Weasley told Harry from the driving seat of the flying car that the Malfoys had been Dark wizards all the way back to the Norman conquest. Harry had heard that before, from Hermione, with Dracina's cheeks going pink. Then he remembered Dracina talking of having a house-elf, during their detention in the Forbidden Forest. In Chapter Five, after Arthur Weasley's fight with Lucius in Diagon Alley, Hagrid told Arthur he should have ignored him: 'Rotten ter the core, the whole family, everyone knows that.'

In Chapter Fourteen Dracina, who had no idea that she was talking to Harry and Ron under Polyjuice Potion, boasted that the Ministry had raided the Manor the week before. Its men had walked right over the hidden room without finding it. In Chapter Eighteen Tom Riddle told Harry: 'The Potters are very old blood, Harry. Older than you know. And the Malfoys are older still.'

In Book Three, Chapter One, Dracina wrote to Harry that her father had forbidden them to correspond, because a Malfoy does not have friends among the Potters. In Chapter Seven her boggart, in her father's shape, sighed over her: 'There has not been a Malfoy who came second in eleven hundred years, and I had rather hoped that the first one would not be my only child.'

In Chapter Twenty-one, on the dock at Myst, Hermione called her spoilt. Dracina answered with the Manor: forty bedrooms, a wing of her own, a pony, peacocks on the lawn. Then she summed it up: 'It is the biggest, most beautiful cage in all Wiltshire, and I have lived in it all my life.'

In the Book Three Interlude John Constantine remembered his first day at Hogwarts in 1964. A small, stammering boy shook his hand very formally and gave his name as 'L-Lucius Malfoy'. Then he drew himself up: 'Of the n-noble and ancient house of M-Malfoy.'

pages.title: Weasley family
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The Burrow, near Ottery St Catchpole, Devon
Bill, Charlie, Percy, Fred, George, Ron, Ginny
pages.html:
The Weasleys are a large, red-haired pure-blood family who live at the Burrow, outside Ottery St Catchpole in Devon. Arthur Weasley has seven children with his wife, Molly: Bill, Charlie, Percy, Fred, George, Ron and Ginny. They are poor, every one of them has been in Gryffindor, and they have taken Harry Potter in as one of their own.

The family

Arthur is the son of Septimus Weasley and Cedrella Black. Molly was born a Prewett, and they married in 1969. Arthur heads the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office at the Ministry, which pays badly; most of the children's robes, books and wands are second-hand.

Bill, the eldest, is a curse-breaker for Gringotts in Egypt. Charlie works with dragons in Romania. Percy was a prefect, then Head Boy in 1993 to 1994. The twins, Fred and George, are the family's jokers. Ron is Harry's best friend. Ginny, the youngest and the only girl, came to Hogwarts in 1992.

Standing

For all their poverty, the Weasleys are one of the most prominent pure-blood families in Britain, which made Arthur, and his Muggle Protection Act, worth ruining. In 1992 Lucius Malfoy meant Tom Riddle's diary to end up with Ginny, so that Arthur's own daughter would be found attacking Muggle-borns. It ended up with Lucius's own daughter, Dracina, instead.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry saw how little money the family had: Mrs Weasley hoped to pick up a lot of Ginny's things second-hand. He learnt, too, that every one of them had been in Gryffindor. In Chapter Nineteen, in Lucius Malfoy's hearing, Dumbledore called the Weasleys one of the most prominent pure-blood families. He asked Lucius to imagine the effect on Arthur Weasley if his own daughter had been found attacking and killing Muggle-borns. It was very fortunate for the Weasleys, he observed, that the diary had ended up with Dracina.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994 all nine Weasleys sat down to dinner in the Burrow garden with Harry and Hermione, though not one of them had heard of the Augment War, mutants or metahumans. In Chapter Five their pitch at the World Cup campsite, at the top of the field by the wood, was marked with a little sign reading WEEZLY. With Harry and Hermione the party numbered ten.

pages.title: Lestrange family
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Rodolphus Lestrange; Rabastan Lestrange; Bellatrix Lestrange, born Black
pages.html:
The Lestranges are an old pure-blood wizarding family, joined by marriage to the Blacks. The brothers Rodolphus and Rabastan Lestrange served Lord Voldemort as Death Eaters. Both are in Azkaban.

The family

Rodolphus Lestrange married Bellatrix Black, the twin sister of Narcissa Malfoy. She became as devoted a Death Eater as her husband or his brother Rabastan. After Voldemort's fall in 1981 the brothers joined Bellatrix and Barty Crouch the younger in torturing two Aurors, the Longbottoms, with the Cruciatus Curse. They hoped to learn where their master had gone. All four were sentenced to life in Azkaban.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Ron Weasley named the Lestranges, with the Blacks, as families who would rather marry their own sisters than a Muggle-born.

pages.title: Black family
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Orion and Walburga Black; their sons Sirius and Regulus; Cygnus Black and Druella Rosier; their daughters Bellatrix, Andromeda and Narcissa
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Blacks are one of the oldest and proudest pure-blood families in wizarding Britain, whose motto is Toujours pur. Sirius Black is its most notorious son. His cousins, the Black sisters, married into the Lestrange and Malfoy families: Dracina Malfoy's mother, Narcissa, is one of them.

The family

Sirius was the elder son of Orion and Walburga Black. His younger brother, Regulus, followed the family into Lord Voldemort's service. Sirius went the other way, into Gryffindor, and became the best friend of James Potter.

The Black sisters

Cygnus Black and Druella Rosier had three daughters. Bellatrix and Narcissa were twins, alike in everything but their hair. They were very close. They started at Hogwarts together in 1971, in the same year as James Potter, Lily Evans and their cousin Sirius. At school both decided that James was theirs, and they feuded over him for years, until Lily won him. It was the only real quarrel the twins ever had.

Bellatrix married Rodolphus Lestrange and became one of Voldemort's most devoted Death Eaters. She has been in Azkaban since the end of the first war. Narcissa married Lucius Malfoy, and their daughter Dracina was born in 1980. The third sister, Andromeda, married the Muggle-born Ted Tonks, and the family struck her off.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Ron Weasley named the Blacks, with the Lestranges, as families who would rather marry their own sisters than a Muggle-born.

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, Remus Lupin asked Harry Potter to remind him, when all this was over, to tell him about James and the Black sisters. Harry asked whether they were related to Sirius Black. 'Oh, yes,' said Lupin.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, Harry told Dracina Malfoy that Sirius was innocent. 'Sirius Black,' she said at last. 'My mother's cousin. The mass murderer. Is innocent.'

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, Narcissa Malfoy told Harry Potter that Bellatrix was her twin sister, and that both of them had loved his father. She spoke too of 'my cousin Sirius', who could not bear to be in the same room as Lily for a month after whatever Lily had done to Bellatrix in their last spring at school.

pages.title: The Belmonts
infobox: Eastern Europe, near Wallachia and Transylvania
Leon, Sonia, Trevor, Christopher, Soleiyu, Simon, Juste, Richter, Julius
The Morris family, the Belnades, Alucard
pages.html:
The Belmonts are a family of vampire hunters who have been at war with Dracula since 1094, when Leon Belmont swore that his line would hunt the night for ever. Roughly once a century Dracula comes back. Each time he does, a Belmont takes down the whip called the Vampire Killer and goes up the mountain to his castle. In 1993 and 1994 the whip belonged to Julius Belmont. The blood of the Belnades witches has run in the family since Trevor Belmont married Sypha Belnades in the fifteenth century. For much of the nineteenth century the Belmonts themselves were missing, and their Morris kin carried the whip in their place.

Leon's oath

The family begins with Leon Belmont, a baron and knight of the late eleventh century. In 1094 he gave up his title to rescue his betrothed, Sara Trantoul, from the vampire Walter Bernhard. In the course of the rescue the alchemist Rinaldo Gandolfi's whip became the Vampire Killer. Then Leon's friend Mathias Cronqvist took Walter's soul for himself and rose as the vampire who would one day be called Dracula. Leon swore that his descendants would hunt him, and all his kind, for ever. Every Belmont since has been brought up to that oath.

The family's strength has not always made it welcome. Some time before 1476 the people of Wallachia grew frightened of the Belmonts' powers and drove them out. They took them back only when Dracula's armies came and there was nobody else who could stand against them.

The line of succession

The war has passed from parent to child for nine centuries. These are the Belmonts who carried it, in order.

Leon Belmont, 1094. The founder, a baron who had fought in the Church's wars. He gave up his title to rescue his betrothed, Sara Trantoul, from the vampire Walter Bernhard, and destroyed Walter with the newly made Vampire Killer. When his friend Mathias Cronqvist rose as a vampire, Leon swore the oath the family has kept ever since. For three and a half centuries after him the Belmonts hunted the night as he had sworn. Few of their names are recorded.

Sonia Belmont, 1450. Leon's descendant, and the first of the family to face Mathias under his new name of Dracula. His own son, Alucard, fought beside her. The Belmont chronicles hold that Alucard was the father of her son Trevor. Whatever the truth of it, Trevor was a mortal man, and so has been every Belmont since.

Trevor Belmont, 1476 to 1479. Sonia's son. When Dracula's armies came, the Church called him back to the Wallachia that had driven his family out. He destroyed Dracula in 1476 with Alucard, the pirate Grant DaNasty and the sorceress Sypha Belnades, whom he later married. He was still in the field in 1479, when he crossed paths with Hector, who had once been one of Dracula's Devil Forgemasters. Every Belmont after him descends from Trevor and Sypha together.

Christopher Belmont, 1576 and 1591. He destroyed Dracula in 1576, but the vampire survived as mist. Fifteen years later he came back and seized Christopher's son.

Soleiyu Belmont, 1591. Christopher's son and heir. Dracula carried him off at his coming-of-age feast and turned him into a demon to guard the newly risen castle. Christopher went after him, set him free and destroyed Dracula a second time. The line ran on from Christopher's house to Simon.

Simon Belmont, 1691 and 1698. In 1691 he fought his way through the castle and destroyed Dracula, but he took a curse from him in the battle. Seven years later, with the curse still on him, Simon gathered the scattered parts of Dracula's body and burned them in the ruins of the castle. When Dracula rose from the fire, Simon destroyed him too, and the curse lifted.

Juste Belmont, 1748. Simon's grandson, in whom Sypha's Belnades blood ran strongly enough for him to work magic. In 1748 he fought a revenant raised from Dracula's relics. The relics had possessed his friend Maxim Kischine, and the castle they raised held their friend Lydie Erlanger prisoner. Juste rescued them both.

Richter Belmont, 1792 and 1797. In 1792 the dark priest Shaft raised Dracula, and Richter destroyed him. He rescued the captives from the castle, among them the girl Maria Renard and Annette, whom he married. He vanished in 1796. In 1797 Alucard found him in the castle under Shaft's control and set him free.

The missing years. For much of the nineteenth century the Belmonts were missing, and others fought in their place. Nathan Graves fought in 1830. Shanoa of the Order of Ecclesia fought in the same century, and Cornell in 1844. In 1852 it was Reinhardt Schneider and Carrie Fernandez, a girl of Sypha's Belnades blood. The whip itself went to the Morris family, distant kin of the Belmonts. Quincy Morris died destroying Dracula in 1897. His son John carried the whip in 1917, and John's son Jonathan in 1944.

Julius Belmont, from the 1980s to 1999, and 2035 to 2036. Then the whip came back to the Belmonts. In 1993 and 1994 it was held by Julius Belmont, a man of about thirty who was actively hunting. In 1999, with Alucard beside him, Julius destroyed Dracula for good in the Demon Castle War. The war took his memory. He came back to the fight in 2035 and 2036 as the nameless hunter called J.

The war is therefore more than nine hundred years old, and more than five hundred under the name Dracula. The figure of about four hundred years that Hermione Granger gave in 1992 is wrong. She had it from Gilderoy Lockhart's Voyages with Vampires, which was mistaken, as Lockhart's books so often are.

Kin

The Morris family descends from the Belmonts by a distant line; Quincy Morris was a Texan. The Morrises held the Vampire Killer while the Belmonts were missing, and they paid for it. Quincy died of his wounds in 1897. John Morris carried the whip in 1917, with Eric Lecarde beside him, and died of it some years later. Without Belmont blood, anyone who calls on the whip's full power pays for it with his life, unless he has first mastered the whip. Jonathan Morris carried it in 1944 with the sorceress Charlotte Aulin. He won its full power by overcoming the spirit held in the whip itself, which met him in the shape of Richter Belmont, and so escaped his father's fate. After him the whip went back to the Belmonts.

The Belnades are the family of Sypha Belnades, the sorceress who fought beside Trevor in 1476 and married him. Through her, every Belmont since Trevor has Belnades blood. In Juste it came out strongly enough for him to work spells. Sypha's own family went on as the Belnades, and kept producing witches who fought beside the Belmonts. Carrie Fernandez was one, in 1852. Another was Yoko Belnades, a witch in the Church's service, who worked with Julius in 2035 and 2036.

Alucard, Dracula's dhampir son, has fought beside the family more often than anyone outside it: with Sonia in 1450, with Trevor in 1476, for Richter in 1797 and with Julius in 1999.

The Schneiders, like the Morrises, are kin of the Belmonts by a distant line; Reinhardt Schneider fought in 1852. So are the Renards, the family of Maria Renard, who fought beside Richter in 1792. In the nineteenth century, while the Belmonts themselves were missing, a village called Wygol was peopled by their descendants. Albus of the Order of Ecclesia sought those villagers out for their blood, hoping it would let him master a weapon forged from Dracula's power.

How they fight

The Belmonts fight with the Vampire Killer, holy water, crosses, axes and daggers. They learn how from their parents, who learnt it from theirs. The whip gives its full strength freely only to Belmont blood. The family has few dealings with the wizarding world, but it is not unknown there: Professor McGonagall counts Julius among her old friends.

Among the Kindred

To the Kindred the Belmonts are the most dangerous kind of mortal hunter: a family with a holy relic in its keeping. The best of them also have what the Kindred call True Faith: a faith strong enough to burn and repel the undead. A Belmont with the Vampire Killer in hand and that faith behind him can stand against vampires that no other mortal could face.

Dracula ignored the Masquerade at every return, raising his castle, his monsters and his armies of the dead in plain sight of mortals. The Camarilla, which has never been keen to fight him itself, has been content since its founding in 1435 to let the Belmonts deal with him. The Society of Leopold, the Catholic hunters who carry on the work of the Inquisition, honours the family but has never commanded it. The Belmonts answer to Leon's oath, and to God.

In the saga

In September 1992 Hermione Granger told Harry Potter about a family who had been hunting Dracula for about four hundred years. They were called the Belmonts, they had a whip, and every hundred years or so, when he came back, one of them had to go up the mountain. The true figure is longer: more than five hundred years under the name Dracula, and nine hundred since Leon.

On Halloween 1992 Professor McGonagall mentioned her old friend Julius, who had been in Transylvania for some years and always carried a whip. Gilderoy Lockhart's claim to know him as 'Julius Carrow' was false. By December 1993 Hermione had read the Belmont chronicles.

pages.title: Clan Ventrue
infobox: Can feed on only one kind of mortal
Hardestadt; Mithras; Jürgen the Sword-Bearer; the Master and the Aurelian line (Darla, Angelus, Drusilla, William the Bloody)
pages.html:
The Ventrue are the clan of kings, with old money and old manners. They think of themselves as royalty, and they run things, or believe they do. Besides leading the Camarilla, they sit on the boards of Muggle banks and in Muggle parliaments. On the rare occasions when the Kindred have dealings with the Ministry of Magic, it is a Ventrue who does the talking. The Aurelian line of the Master and Angelus is a Ventrue line, although it has never answered to the clan.

The founder

The clan descends from the Ventrue Antediluvian, one of the thirteen of the Third Generation. He was Embraced about 9300 BC by one of Cain's three childer in Enoch, the First City. He was among those who rose against the Second Generation and slew it, about 8990 BC. When Cain cursed the clans for that slaying, about 8980 BC, the curse he laid on the Ventrue was a narrowed hunger, bound for ever to one kind of prey.

What became of the founder afterwards is not known. No Ventrue will say whether he sleeps somewhere or was destroyed long ago, and it is likely that none of them knows. The Master, the fourth-generation Ventrue who founded the Aurelian line, claims that the Antediluvian sired him, which would make the Master one of the oldest Kindred walking. He will never reveal his sire's name. The clan has never been able to prove the claim, or to disprove it, which it finds very trying.

Gifts and curse

The Ventrue command with Dominate, which bends a mortal's will with a look and a word. They win loyalty and awe with Presence. They endure with Fortitude, shrugging off wounds that would destroy other Kindred, and bearing even fire a little longer than most. Like every power over the mind, their Dominate fails against a vampire of an earlier generation than their own, which is one reason the clan cares so much about lineage.

Their curse is a refined palate. Each Ventrue can feed from only one kind of mortal, and would starve sooner than drink from anybody else. One was known who could take blood only from priests; another, only from left-handed men with red hair. Others are bound to soldiers, to the rich, to virgins or to the people of a single nation. A new Ventrue learns the limit in the first nights after the Embrace, when other blood will not stay down.

The restriction governs only the blood of mortals. Animal blood will keep a Ventrue alive, though it gives little strength, and the blood of other vampires lies outside the curse altogether.

The clan of kings

The Ventrue choose their childer from among the powerful and the successful. In older centuries they took aristocrats and officers; in the modern nights, bankers, industrialists, lawyers or politicians. They prize breeding, manners and achievement, expecting a childe to have earned something before the Embrace. Inside the clan, rank follows age and lineage. Elders are owed deference, and favours are kept on account. The clan judges its own members in its own councils, and would never dream of letting an outsider do it.

They hold more princedoms in the Camarilla than any other clan, and they think of the sect as theirs to run. No Kindred work through mortals as much as they do. They own companies, sit on the boards of Muggle banks, have seats in Muggle parliaments and pull strings that few mortals ever see. The other clans call them the Blue Bloods, not always kindly.

Remus Lupin put it more simply. They think of themselves as the kings, he said: old money, old manners. They run things, or think they do.

From the Second City to Rome

After Cain departed into Nod, the Third Generation built the Second City and ruled it together. The Ventrue were among its lords until it fell to the wars of the founders and their childer. Then the clan's childer went west. In the ancient world they lived among the Greeks, and above all in Rome, which they claim to have guided from its early days. The Ventrue regard the Roman order of law, roads and Senate as their own design.

Rome's long war with Carthage was also a war between Kindred. Carthage was the city of the Brujah, where Kindred and mortals were said to live openly side by side. The Ventrue accused it of harbouring worshippers of the Devil among its vampires. Rome, guided by the Ventrue, destroyed the city in 146 BC, and the Brujah have never forgiven them. Under the Empire the Ventrue followed the legions across Europe. Mithras, a Ventrue whom Roman soldiers worshipped as a god, ruled the Kindred of London for centuries afterwards.

The Dark Ages

When Rome fell, the Ventrue did not. In the Middle Ages they were the lords of Europe's Kindred, ruling as feudal princes over cities and countryside. They held their domains from one another as vassals, with mortal kings and bishops for their creatures. In the east they fought the Tzimisce for the lands beyond the Elbe and the Carpathians. Jürgen the Sword-Bearer carried that war into the Baltic with the crusading knights of Germany.

The late Middle Ages went hard with them. The Inquisition burned vampires across Europe. The elders, the Ventrue foremost among them, saved themselves by giving their own childer to the fires. The young answered with the Anarch Revolt, striking at the elders in their havens. The Ventrue Hardestadt called the convocation of elders of 1435, from which the Camarilla grew and at which the Masquerade was proclaimed. At the Convention of Thorns, at Thornbury in England in 1493, the Ventrue made the peace on the elders' side.

They have led the Camarilla ever since. A minority of the clan went over to the Sabbat instead. These Ventrue antitribu think of themselves as the Sabbat's knights.

The modern nights and the Ministry

The Ventrue moved from land into trade, from trade into banking and from banking into industry. They have kept pace with every change in the mortal world's money since. In Europe and the Americas the princes of most great cities are Ventrue. On the Camarilla's Inner Circle the clan is the most powerful voice.

That position makes the Ventrue the clan that deals with the wizards. In 1900 the Camarilla came to an arrangement with the wizarding governments of the world, which came to the table through the International Confederation of Wizards. The British Ministry of Magic was one of the parties. The wizards would lend their wards and Muggle-Repelling Charms to help keep the Masquerade. These are the enchantments that hide Diagon Alley, Hogwarts and every wizarding house. In return, no vampire who answers to the Camarilla would ever hunt, harm or feed on a witch or wizard.

It is the Ventrue who very occasionally sit across a table from somebody at the Ministry, being polite about the agreement. The arrangement is old and fragile. It has held, more or less, because both sides have more to lose than to gain by breaking it. The Sabbat, which never signed it, has tried more than once to break it.

The Aurelian line

The Aurelian line is the clan's most famous bloodline, and the one it least likes to discuss. Its founder, the Master, is a fourth-generation Ventrue who claims the Antediluvian as his sire. He is too powerful to be bound to either the Camarilla or the Sabbat. He gathered a priesthood of vampires, the Order of Aurelius. From his blood came Darla, sired in the Virginia colony in 1609; Angelus, sired by Darla in Galway in 1753; Drusilla, sired by Angelus in London about 1860; and William the Bloody, sired by Drusilla in London in 1880.
