Each of them carries the clan's curse in a form of its own. The Master can feed only on the devout. Darla can feed only on fair-skinned, dark-haired young men of confidence and drive, which describes Angelus exactly; her blood has been bound to that kind since 1609. Angelus can feed only on blonde, fair-skinned women of strength and beauty. That describes Darla, and it describes Buffy Summers, who became the Slayer in 1996, just as well. Drusilla feeds only on the frightened. William feeds only on those who fight back.

By the clan's standards the line is a scandal. The Master sired his favourite from a dying prostitute, not from among the powerful. His descendants, answering to no sect, ignored the Masquerade quite blatantly through the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Angelus cut crosses into his victims' cheeks, and it was in all the broadsheets.

The Camarilla, the sect the Ventrue lead, often secretly supported or manipulated mortal hunters to bring Angelus down. The Society of Leopold was one of them, with hunters such as Daniel Holtz. None of the hunters knew whose money they were spending. The line's great days ended in 1898, when the Kalderash cursed Angelus with a soul. In 1937 the Master was sealed beneath a town in California, after a ritual went wrong.

Later nights

In 1997 the Master broke free of his prison beneath Sunnydale, California, when the Slayer Buffy Summers briefly died at his hands. She destroyed him the same night. Angel staked Darla that year. Drusilla sired her again in December 2000, and because of the particular manner of her siring she remained of the fifth generation.

In the saga

On 2 September 1992 Hermione Granger read in Voyages with Vampires that there were thirteen clans. At breakfast she told Harry Potter that the Ventrue were the ones who thought they were royalty. Later that autumn Gilderoy Lockhart told his class that he had fought an elder of the Clan Ventrue, a creature so old he had forgotten his own name and called himself only the Master. The fight was Lockhart's invention. The Master's lineage, by the Master's own claim, was not.

Remus Lupin described the Ventrue to Harry's class in October 1993, with their particular tastes in blood. Lavender Brown thought it ever so snobbish. 'It's a family failing,' said Lupin. Dracina Malfoy laughed, and looked to see whether Harry had laughed too.

pages.title: Aurelian bloodline
infobox: Darla, Angelus, Drusilla, William the Bloody
pages.html:
The Aurelian bloodline, the Aurelians for short, is the line of vampires from which Angelus came. It is the Ventrue line founded by the Master, and it takes its name from the Order of Aurelius, the priesthood of vampires that served him.

The line

The Master, a Ventrue of the fourth generation, sired Darla in 1609, in the Virginia colony. Darla sired Angelus in Galway in 1753. Angelus sired Drusilla in London about 1860, and Drusilla sired William the Bloody in London in 1880.

Like every Ventrue, each of them can feed from only one kind of mortal.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, at breakfast on the first morning of term in September 1992, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter that there were thirteen clans of vampires. Among the Ventrue, the ones who think they are royalty, there had been one called Angelus, from the Aurelian bloodline, who went right across Europe in the seventeen hundreds.

pages.title: Royal Air Force
pages.html:
The Royal Air Force is Britain's Muggle air force, and the oldest independent air force in the world. It was formed on 1 April 1918, near the end of the Great War, and won the Battle of Britain in 1940. Oliver Wood's father served in it.

The Woods

Oliver Wood's father was in the RAF. Oliver once showed Harry a big magazine full of Muggle jet planes, then explained their payloads at length, with all the enthusiasm he gives to Quidditch results.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Fred Weasley, dripping in the changing room, described the Slytherins on their new brooms: 'Seven green blurs. That's all you can see. Seven green blurs, going past like something the Muggle air force would have.' This made Oliver perk up, since his dad had been in the RAF. George added that their own dad had a picture of a jump-jet in the shed, and that they go straight up.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, at the World Cup campsite on 22 August 1994, Oliver Wood introduced Harry Potter to his parents. Oliver told him breathlessly that he was about to start his Basic Recruit Training Course with the RAF, just like his dad.

pages.title: WWF
pages.html:
WWF, the World Wrestling Federation, is the American company that stages professional wrestling for Muggle television. Its shows reach Britain by satellite, and Dudley Dursley is devoted to them.

The wrestling

Its stars have included Hulk Hogan, the Undertaker, Bret Hart and the British Bulldog. The results are settled in advance, which its fans prefer not to dwell on. In August 1992 more than eighty thousand people filled Wembley Stadium to watch the British Bulldog beat Bret Hart.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter One, Harry remembered that Dudley had read nothing at all since the Dursleys had the Sky satellite dish put up and he discovered WWF.

pages.title: Nimbus Two Thousand and One
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Nimbus Two Thousand and One is a racing broom made by the Nimbus Racing Broom Company. It came out in August 1992 and left the old Two Thousand series standing. A month later Lucius Malfoy bought seven of them for the Slytherin Quidditch team, which has flown them ever since.

The broom

It is sleeker than the Nimbus Two Thousand, which had only come out the year before, and a great deal faster. It was the fastest broom on the market until the Firebolt came out the following year.

Every player on the Slytherin team has ridden one since the autumn of 1992, at Lucius Malfoy's expense. His daughter Dracina owns two of them.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, the Slytherin team turned out on seven brand-new Nimbus Two Thousand and Ones, a gift from Lucius Malfoy a month after the broom came out.

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, the Slytherins flew them in the November match against Gryffindor, much faster than Harry Potter's Nimbus Two Thousand. When Dracina threw her broom across a Bludger's path in front of Harry, the Bludger cracked its tail.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, the whole Slytherin team was still riding them, paid for by Lucius, as it had since the previous year.

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, with Harry reduced to an old school Shooting Star, Dracina stepped into his path in the Entrance Hall. 'Potter, I've got a Nimbus. The Two Thousand and One.' She had two of them, she told him; he was to take the spare one for Saturday. 'It's entirely selfish. I've every intention of beating you in the spring, and I shan't enjoy it if people can say afterwards that you were on a broom out of a shed.' The broom reached him in the Owlery, roped in brown paper, with a note in small spiky handwriting: 'Mind the left-hand foot-rest, it goes if you kick it. D.'

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, once he had the Firebolt back, Harry returned the Nimbus to the Owlery in its brown paper, with a note that had taken him four drafts. Dracina rode the other one in the Quidditch final against Gryffindor in Chapter Fifteen.

pages.title: Cleansweep Five
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Cleansweep Five is an old racing broom from the Cleansweep Broom Company, long since overtaken by newer models. Fred and George Weasley, the Gryffindor Beaters, fly one each.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, the Slytherin team came on to the pitch with seven brand-new Nimbus Two Thousand and Ones, bought by Lucius Malfoy. Their captain, Marcus Flint, smiled nastily at the twins’ Cleansweep Fives. Dracina Malfoy suggested that Gryffindor might raise some gold for new brooms themselves. ‘You could raffle off those Cleansweep Fives. I expect a museum would bid for them.’

pages.title: The Weasleys' Ford Anglia
infobox: Arthur Weasley's Ford Anglia; Ford Anglia; Mr Weasley's car; The Ford Anglia
enchanted Muggle artefact, enchanted car, Weasley family
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Flight; cushioned seats; tyres that never go flat; an engine that runs on vegetable oil; a stretched boot and back seat; an Invisibility Booster (faulty)
pages.html:
The Weasleys' Ford Anglia is an old turquoise Muggle car, which Arthur Weasley bought rusty and enchanted in secret to fly. In September 1992 his son Ron flew it to Hogwarts with Harry Potter and crashed it into the Whomping Willow. It has lived wild in the Forbidden Forest ever since.

Enchantments

Mr Weasley is enormously proud of the car. On the morning of 1 September 1992 he kept Harry standing in the yard at the Burrow for twenty minutes, with a trunk in each hand, while he explained every charm he had ever put on it. Its seats carry a Cushioning Charm. Its tyres never go flat. Its engine runs on straight vegetable oil instead of petrol, with a further charm to stop Muggles noticing that it never needs filling up. The boot and the back seat have been stretched inside to hold far more than they should. 'Not a word to Molly,' Mr Weasley whispered, as he showed Harry the boot. On the dashboard is a large red button labelled Invisibility Booster, which is faulty.

Mrs Weasley would not hear of flying it. 'We aren't flying a Muggle car through broad daylight,' she told her husband. 'Think of the Statute of Secrecy, for Merlin's sake.'

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, in August 1992, Fred, George and Ron flew the car to Privet Drive to rescue Harry Potter from the Dursleys, who had put bars on his window. They tied a rope round the bars and pulled them clean off the wall. In Chapter Nineteen Harry told Dracina Malfoy that Ron had come in a flying car and ripped them off.

In Book Two, Chapter Six, the barrier at King's Cross sealed itself against Ron and Harry on 1 September 1992. They flew the car north to Hogwarts instead. Over London the Invisibility Booster turned out to be faulty, and the car kept flickering back into sight. Six or seven Muggles saw it, as Severus Snape read out to them afterwards: two in London who were convinced they had seen an old car flying over the Post Office Tower, Mrs Hetty Bayliss of Norfolk, at her washing line, and Mr Angus Fleet of Peebles, who told the police.

Over the Hogwarts lake the engine died. The car came down into the Whomping Willow, which beat in the roof, and Ron's wand snapped in the crash. Then the car came to life by itself. It threw out their trunks and Hedwig's cage, then roared away into the Forbidden Forest with its one remaining door flapping.

In Book Two, Chapter Seventeen, late in the spring of 1993, Harry and Ron followed a trail of spiders into the Forest with Fang. In a clearing they found the car with its headlamps blazing. It had been roaming the Forest on its own for months. Its wings were scratched and plastered with mud. Where the door on Ron's side had been there was only a gap with a bit of bramble caught in it. It rolled forward to meet Ron like a big turquoise dog that had found its owner. 'The Forest's turned it feral...' said Ron.

Later that night it came thundering down into Aragog's hollow and scattered the spiders. It drove Harry, Ron and Fang out of the Forest on its own, losing a wing mirror to an oak on the way. At the edge of the trees it stopped to let them out. Then it reversed slowly back into the Forest and was gone. Arthur Weasley was never told.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: by August 1994 the car was still living wild among the trees of the Forbidden Forest, where it was presumably still frightening the centaurs. The Weasleys, who no longer had a car, came to fetch Harry from Privet Drive by Floo instead.

pages.title: Floo powder
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Thrown on a fire, it turns the flames emerald green
The Floo Network, run by the Ministry of Magic
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Floo powder is the glittering powder that witches and wizards use to travel by fire. A handful thrown into a fireplace turns the flames emerald green. The traveller steps into them, says the name of the destination clearly and is whirled away past a great many other grates until the right one comes.

Fires and grates

The fireplaces of wizarding Britain are joined together in the Floo Network, which the Ministry of Magic keeps in order. Speaking clearly matters. A traveller who mumbles, or coughs on the ash, may come out of a stranger's grate a long way from where he meant to be. A fire on the Network can also be used to call somebody, who may then climb out of it in person.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry travelled by Floo for the first time, from the Burrow, where the Weasleys keep their powder in a flowerpot on the mantelpiece. Mrs Weasley told him to speak clearly and to mind he got out at the right grate. He swallowed a lungful of hot ash, coughed out something like Diagon Alley and came out of the wrong grate altogether. He landed in a dim shop in Knockturn Alley, black with soot, with his glasses broken. Going home from the Leaky Cauldron that evening, he took his glasses off first and put them in his pocket.

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, Snape took a handful of glittering powder from a jar on his own mantelpiece and flung it on the fire. ‘Lupin!’ he called into the flames. ‘I want a word!’ A few seconds later Lupin climbed out of the grate, beating the ash from his shabby robes.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994 Arthur Weasley carried Floo powder in a little drawstring bag to fetch Harry from Privet Drive, where the Dursleys had boarded up the fireplace. A pinch thrown on the fire turned the flames emerald green, and each traveller cried 'The Burrow!' on stepping in. To Harry the green flames felt pleasantly warm, like breath on his skin.

pages.title: Hand of Glory
infobox: Dark artefact, Borgin and Burkes, occult
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (1998)
The hand of a hanged man, pickled and dried
Light for its holder alone; with the proper words, enchanted sleep on a household
pages.html:
A Hand of Glory is the withered, pickled hand of a hanged man, made to hold a candle or to be one. Wizards know it as a burglar's curiosity, sold in Knockturn Alley, that gives light only to the person holding it. The old thieves of Europe knew better. Lit in a house at night with the proper words, it keeps everybody in the house asleep until it is put out.

The artefact

A Hand of Glory is made from the hand of a man hanged on the gallows. It is cut from the body, then pickled and dried. The common sort, of the kind Borgin and Burkes sells, has a candle set in its palm. Finer and older examples have each finger made into a candle itself. Whatever the kind, its flame gives light to the holder alone, which is why Mr Borgin calls it the best friend of thieves and plunderers.

Wizards have decided that it is no more than that. They have forgotten what the old thieves of Europe always knew. Lit in a house at night, with the proper words, a Hand of Glory keeps everyone in the house asleep until the flame is put out. If one finger will not light, somebody in the house is still awake.

Constantine's Hand

John Constantine owns a Hand of Glory cut from a hanged man on the gallows of Prague two hundred years ago. It is not the cheap sort that Borgin sells. Each of its brown, shrivelled fingers has been made into a candle. He bought it years ago from a dealer in Prague's Old Town, for more money than he cared to think about, and he swore at the time that he would never use it. Before August 1993 he had already used it four times.

In August 1993 he lit it in the dark hall of Shacklewell House in New Mexico. ‘Let those who rest more deeply sleep,’ he whispered. ‘Let those awake their senses keep...’ One by one the dead fingers caught, burning with a thin, greasy, yellow flame that gave light to nobody but him. The thumb would not light. The owner of the house, Ephraim Shacklewell, had never been able to sleep, and he was indeed awake.

In the saga

In the summer of 1992, in Borgin and Burkes, a Hand of Glory lay on a cushion in a glass case while Harry hid in a cabinet nearby. Dracina pointed at the withered thing. ‘Ewwww, what is that disgusting thing, Father?’ she asked.

Mr Borgin hurried over to explain, sounding deferential and defensive at once. With a candle inserted, he said, it gave light only to the holder; it was the best friend of thieves and plunderers. He tailed off at Dracina's look of disgust. Lucius Malfoy laid a hand on his daughter's shoulder, quite gently. ‘I hope my daughter will amount to more than a thief or a plunderer, Borgin,’ he said. Then he added that if her school marks did not pick up, that might indeed be all she was fit for.

In August 1993 John Constantine used his own Hand of Glory to rob Shacklewell House.

pages.title: The cursed opal necklace
infobox: cursed object, Borgin and Burkes, Dark object
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Cursed; has claimed the lives of nineteen Muggle owners to date
pages.html:
The cursed opal necklace is a necklace of opals laid out on black velvet in Borgin and Burkes. A small card beside it gives fair warning. The necklace is cursed, and has so far claimed the lives of nineteen Muggle owners.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, Dracina Malfoy darted to the glass case in Mr Borgin's shop and stood over the necklace with her hands pressed together. Harry, watching from inside a black cabinet, had never seen her look so plainly delighted by anything. She had drawn breath to call her father over when she read the card beside it. Caution: Do Not Touch. Cursed. Has Claimed the Lives of Nineteen Muggle Owners to Date. She pouted.

In Book Four, Chapter Two, writing to Harry Potter in August 1994 about his relatives, she brought it up again. 'Besides all that, Mr Borgin still has an opal necklace in his shop with a card on it that says it has killed nineteen Muggle owners. I have always thought twenty a rounder number.' Harry laughed at that, until it occurred to him that she was probably not joking.

pages.title: The black cabinet in Borgin and Burkes
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The black cabinet in Borgin and Burkes is a big black cabinet, deep in dust, which stands in the shop on Knockturn Alley. Harry Potter hid in it in the summer of 1992.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry's first journey by Floo powder went wrong, and he came out of the fireplace in Borgin and Burkes. Just before the Malfoys came in, he shot into the cabinet and pulled the doors to, leaving a crack to see through. It was a hundred years deep in dust, and he had to give his whole attention to not sneezing.

Through the crack he watched Lucius Malfoy do his business with Mr Borgin. Dracina wandered about the shop, looking at things, until she found herself looking straight at the cabinet. She walked up to it and put out her hand for the handle. 'Come, Dracina!' said her father at the counter, and she turned away.

pages.title: The vanishing cabinet
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Hogwarts, the floor above Filch's office
pages.html:
The vanishing cabinet was a large black-and-gold cabinet at Hogwarts, which Argus Filch held to be extremely valuable. In October 1992 Peeves dropped it onto the floor above Filch's office, at Nearly Headless Nick's urging, and it was wrecked.

Vanishing cabinets

Vanishing cabinets are made in pairs. Whatever is shut inside one comes out of the other, however far apart the two may stand.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, Argus Filch caught Harry Potter dripping mud from his Quidditch robes and marched him down to his office to be punished. Before Filch could finish writing him up, Nearly Headless Nick persuaded Peeves to crash the cabinet right over the office. Filch hurried off to see, leaving Harry alone with a Kwikspell envelope on the desk.

Filch came back triumphant. 'That vanishing cabinet was extremely valuable!' he was saying to Mrs Norris, with relish. 'We'll have Peeves out this time, my sweet.' Harry got away without so much as a detention. He owed Nick for it, so he agreed to go to Nick's Deathday Party on Hallowe'en.

pages.title: Tom Riddle's diary
infobox: Dracina's diary; Riddle's diary; The small black book
Dracina Malfoy, Dark object, dark artefact, dark magic
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
A newsagent's on Vauxhall Road, London
1993, by Harry Potter with the sword, in the Chamber of Secrets
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Tom Riddle's diary was a cheap black notebook into which the sixteen-year-old Tom Riddle poured a piece of himself. Lucius Malfoy planted it in 1992, and it was his own daughter who picked it up. It possessed Dracina Malfoy for months and opened the Chamber of Secrets through her, until Harry Potter destroyed it in the Chamber.

Description and making

The diary is small and thin, with a shabby black cover worn pale at the corners, like something bought for a few pence in a junk shop. The name T. M. Riddle is stamped on the back in worn gold. Printed inside the back cover is the name of a newsagent's on Vauxhall Road, London. Its pages look blank, and neither Aparecium nor a Revealer will show anything on them. It stays spotless even when a bottle of ink is smashed over it.

Riddle made it in 1943, the year he opened the Chamber of Secrets and a girl died in a bathroom, so that his sixteen-year-old self would be preserved inside it. It is a Horcrux: a piece of a soul poured into a vessel, to wait, whisper and be carried. It was made so that whoever carried it would love it and hold it ever tighter, until they could not let go. In this it is a crude copy of the One Ring. Ambrose Greyhame recognised it at once as made in the same way as the gold ring he had once known.

Powers

Ink written in the diary sinks into the page, and the memory inside writes back in a neat, sloping hand. It can draw a reader through a page into Riddle's memory, as it drew Harry into 13 June 1943.

It breeds a craving in anyone who writes in it, leaving them sick while they have it and desperate without it. It feeds on what they pour into it, until it can move their hands and walk them about while they believe themselves asleep.

1992 to 1993

Lord Voldemort instructed Lucius Malfoy to plant the diary on Ginny Weasley. At Flourish and Blotts in August 1992 Lucius slipped it into Ginny's old Transfiguration book. When the brawl there was over, Dracina Malfoy gathered up the spilled books in one sweep. She pressed one into Ginny's hands and stuffed the rest into her own bag. The small black book was among them, and it went home with her.

From the first days of term she was seen writing in it, then stopping, waiting and reading, with her lips moving. She called its voice Tom, her understanding friend. That autumn she grew pale, sleepless and withdrawn. She lost hours. She could not eat, and she woke in places she did not remember, with red marks on her hands. Through her the memory opened the Chamber, set the Basilisk on the school and wrote on the walls.

On Christmas night 1992 Harry, disguised as Gregory Goyle, took the diary from the Slytherin common room. It felt cold against his chest. He felt a strong urge to write in it, and resisted, locking it in his trunk wrapped in his Invisibility Cloak. Deprived of it, Dracina ransacked the dungeon and raved in the Great Hall about a thief who had taken her 'precious'.

Harry later wrote in it himself. It answered him by name, told him that Dracina wrote about him constantly, and asked whether he had noticed 'what's underneath'. In the spring his dormitory was ransacked and the diary taken back to Dracina. The next morning she appeared radiant, and perfectly well.

In the Chamber at the end of the year the memory took solid form, revealed itself as Lord Voldemort and insisted that the diary could not be destroyed. Harry drove the sword through it. Black ink gushed out like blood, and Riddle dissolved, screaming.

Afterwards

Lucius learned only in McGonagall's office that his own daughter had carried the diary, and he went white. Harry hid his sock inside the ruined book and handed it back to him. Lucius tossed the sock carelessly aside, and in doing so freed his house-elf, Dobby. The pierced diary went home with Lucius.

Dracina was possessed by it for months, which in public passed as her being 'unwell'. It wrote itself into her head until there was hardly any of her left. Harry suspects that the Garou who attacked them in June 1994 could still smell it on her. She has wanted to tell Harry something about it since June 1993.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, Narcissa Malfoy thanked Harry Potter for saving her daughter's life three times: 'A troll, a diary and a werewolf, once a year, every year she has been at that school.' The diary was the second of the three.

pages.title: Ginny Weasley's diary
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Ginny Weasley's diary is a pink diary with a lock, a present from her mother, which Ginny has kept for years. It is a perfectly ordinary diary, which is more than could be said for the other diary at large at Hogwarts in Ginny's first year.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, the Weasleys’ car had already gone back twice, for George’s fireworks and Fred’s broom, when Ginny shrieked that she had left her diary on her bed. It had to turn back a third time.

In Chapter Sixteen, after Riddle’s diary vanished from Harry’s dormitory, Ron mentioned that Ginny was always writing in a diary of her own, every night, under the covers. ‘Had it for years. Mum gave it her. Pink thing, with a lock.’ He laughed at the idea that his sister could have turned out Harry’s trunk, but the laugh came out a little uncertain.

pages.title: Ron Weasley's wand
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Fourteen inches, willow, one unicorn tail-hair (1993)
pages.html:
Ron Weasley's first wand was a hand-me-down from his brother Charlie, chipped along its length, with the unicorn hair at its core nearly coming out of the tip. It snapped nearly in two when Ron crashed his father's flying car into the Whomping Willow on 1 September 1992. Mended with Spellotape, it spent the rest of that year doing almost anything except what Ron asked of it.

After the Willow

Patched up, the wand crackled, sparked and smoked. Later it took to blowing great purple bubbles, then to whistling like a kettle. Its spells went wrong, or nowhere, or on to Ron.

In the tunnels beneath the school in 1993, Gilderoy Lockhart used it to cast a Memory Charm. The charm backfired and brought the tunnel roof down. After that Ron had no wand at all.

In the summer of 1993 he got a new one: fourteen inches, willow, with a single unicorn tail-hair.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the Hogwarts Express, Ron dug the wand out of his trunk to show Harry. It had seen better days. It was chipped along its length, and something white gleamed at the tip. 'The unicorn hair's nearly coming out.'

In Book Two, Chapter Six, the wand snapped nearly in two in the crash on 1 September 1992, with the tip hanging off by a few splinters. In Chapter Seven Ron patched it with borrowed Spellotape. It crackled and sparked at odd moments all the same.

In Chapter Eight it leapt out of his hand in Charms and hit tiny Professor Flitwick squarely between the eyes. On Saturday 5 September, on the Quidditch pitch, Ron pointed it at Dracina Malfoy after she had called Hermione a Mudblood. A jet of green light shot out of the wrong end and hit Ron himself in the stomach. He spent the rest of the morning belching up slugs.

In Chapter Fifteen it blew great purple bubbles that floated off round the classroom. In Chapter Eighteen it had started to whistle like a kettle. 'Can you imagine me sitting exams with this?' Down in the tunnels under the school, Gilderoy Lockhart got hold of it to cast a Memory Charm, without noticing that it was held together with Spellotape. The charm backfired and brought the tunnel down. After that Ron had no wand.

In Chapter Nineteen, at one in the morning in the hospital wing, Harry sat on the end of Dracina Malfoy's bed and argued with her. He told her that one of her claims was like saying Ron's wand was brilliant because it kept blowing up. Dracina took him at his word. 'Weasley's wand is brilliant. It's the most dangerous object in this castle. It took out a whole tunnel.'

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Ron showed Harry its replacement. 'Brand-new wand. Fourteen inches, willow, containing one unicorn tail-hair.'

pages.title: Hagrid's pink umbrella
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The pieces of Hagrid's snapped school wand
pages.html:
Hagrid's pink umbrella is the flowery pink umbrella that Rubeus Hagrid keeps about him. Hagrid is not supposed to do magic, since he was expelled from Hogwarts in his third year and his wand was snapped in two. The umbrella does a fair amount of it all the same.

What it can do

On the night of Harry Potter's eleventh birthday in 1991, when Hagrid came for him at the hut on the rock in the sea, he used the umbrella to give Dudley Dursley a curly pig's tail. In Diagon Alley he tapped the bricks in the wall behind the Leaky Cauldron with its tip to open the archway.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1992, Harry noticed the umbrella leaning against the back wall of Hagrid's hut, while Hagrid was owning up to giving his enormous pumpkins a bit of help. Harry had a strong suspicion that Hagrid's old school wand lived inside it, since Hagrid was not meant to do magic. He had been expelled in his third year, and Harry had never found out why. Any mention of it made Hagrid clear his throat and go mysteriously deaf.

In Book Three, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1993, Harry sat on a wall in Magnolia Crescent, certain that he would be expelled himself for blowing up Aunt Marge. He thought of what had been done to Hagrid fifty years before. Hagrid had been innocent, but his wand had been snapped all the same. All he had left of it, Harry reckoned, were the pieces hidden inside that pink umbrella.

In Chapter Eleven, in December 1993, Harry could not bring himself to ask Hagrid why he had never once mentioned Sirius Black. Hagrid was the only person who had ever come for him, on an island in the sea, with a pink umbrella and a squashed birthday cake in his coat.

pages.title: Harry's photograph album
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
June 1992, at the end of Harry's first year
Under his pillow at Privet Drive; in his bedside cabinet at Hogwarts
James and Lily Potter's wedding, with Sirius Black as best man
Book One, Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Harry's photograph album is the leather-bound album of wizard photographs of his parents that Rubeus Hagrid made for Harry Potter at the end of his first year. Hagrid filled it by writing to everybody who had ever known Lily and James Potter. Harry can recite every photograph in it, in order, page by page.

The photographs

The photographs move, as wizard photographs do. James and Lily stand together by a lake. In a garden, James has his arm round Lily while she laughs at something out of the picture. Lily holds a baby with black hair who keeps trying to grab her nose. Later in the album comes the wedding photograph, with a third figure laughing beside the couple, one hand on James's shoulder: the best man, Sirius Black.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, Hagrid gave Harry the album in June 1992. It was bound in handsome leather. Its wizard photographs showed his parents by a lake, in a garden, and his mother holding a black-haired baby who kept trying to grab her nose.

In Book Two, Chapter Three, locked in his bedroom at Privet Drive in the summer of 1992, Harry kept the album under his pillow. When Ron, Fred and George Weasley came for him in their father's flying car, it was among the first things he passed out through the window.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, in December 1993, Harry dug the album out of his bedside cabinet at Hogwarts, looking for one picture. He had just learnt that Sirius Black had been his father's best friend. In the wedding photograph he found him: the best man, young, handsome and laughing, with the same laugh as James. Harry had only ever seen that face in the Daily Prophet, as a waxy ruin.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on 20 August 1994, Harry watched a Muggle news report from a protest outside the United Nations in New York. A woman of about forty spoke to the camera. She had long dark red hair and green eyes. Harry's heart gave an odd lurch, because she looked the way the girl in his album might have looked if she had lived to be forty and had a hard time of it.

pages.title: The Weasley kitchen clock
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The clock on the wall of the Burrow's kitchen has one hand and no numbers. Round its rim, where the numbers ought to be, are written such things as Time to make tea, Time to feed the chickens and You're late.

Description

It hangs on the wall of a small, rather cramped kitchen, with a scrubbed wooden table and chairs in the middle. It does not so much tell the time as tell the household what ought to be done about it. Books stand three deep along the mantelpiece, with titles such as Charm Your Own Cheese, and an old wireless sits by the sink.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in August 1992, Harry Potter sat on the very edge of a kitchen chair at the Burrow and looked about him. He had never been inside a wizard's house before. The clock with one hand was one of the first things he saw.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, at Christmas 1993, Ron told Harry by the fire that he was on Mrs Weasley's list. For a moment Harry could see the whole Burrow waiting for him: the ghoul, Mrs Weasley's mince pies and the one-handed clock that told you when it was time to feed the chickens.

pages.title: The Burrow's kitchen mirror
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Over the kitchen mantelpiece, the Burrow
Telling Harry to tuck his shirt in
pages.html:
The mirror over the kitchen mantelpiece at the Burrow is a talking mirror with firm views on dress. In the summer of 1992 it told Harry Potter to tuck his shirt in every time he went past it.

Talking mirrors

Talking mirrors are common in wizarding houses, and few of them keep their opinions to themselves. The one over the basin in room eleven at the Leaky Cauldron took a similar interest in Harry's hair a year later.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, the mirror told Harry, 'Tuck your shirt in, young man, honestly, the state of you,' every single time he passed it. The Weasleys, who had lived with it all their lives, thought nothing of it.

pages.title: Self-Shuffling playing cards
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Ron Weasley's bedroom at the Burrow
pages.html:
Self-Shuffling playing cards are a wizarding pack that shuffles itself, which saves the dealer the trouble. A pack is the sort of thing found lying about in any wizarding household with children in it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1992, a pack of Self-Shuffling playing cards lay on the floor of Ron Weasley's bedroom at the Burrow. Ron's room is a small one at the top of the house, and very orange, since nearly everything in it is in the colours of the Chudley Cannons.

pages.title: Howler
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Shouts its message in the sender's voice, magnified a hundred times
pages.html:
A Howler is a scarlet envelope that delivers a telling-off in the sender's own voice, magnified until it fills a room. Left unopened, it begins to smoke at the corners. Opened, it shouts its message at enormous volume and then bursts into flames.

Receiving one

A Howler is the wizarding way of being furious with somebody at a distance, in front of everybody. The wisest course is to open it at once and get it over with. Neville Longbottom once ignored one from his grandmother, and it was horrible.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on 2 September 1992, the Weasleys' owl Errol brought Ron a Howler from his mother at breakfast in the Great Hall. Ron and Harry had flown his father's car to school the day before. Mrs Weasley's voice, a hundred times louder than it ever was in the kitchen at the Burrow, rattled the plates on the table and shook dust out of the rafters. Ron slid so far down in his chair that only his crimson forehead showed above the table.

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, two days after Sirius Black got into Gryffindor Tower with Neville's list of passwords, Neville's grandmother sent him one. A huge barn owl brought it down the Gryffindor table at breakfast, and Neville ran for the doors holding it out at arm's length. It went off in the Entrance Hall. His grandmother's voice, magnified until it rattled the suits of armour, told him that he had disgraced the entire family. Everybody else within half a mile heard it too.

pages.title: Dr Filibuster's Fabulous Wet-Start, No-Heat Fireworks
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Light when wet; give off no heat
pages.html:
Dr Filibuster's Fabulous Wet-Start, No-Heat Fireworks are wizarding fireworks that will light even when they are wet. They give off no heat at all. Fred and George Weasley are seldom without some.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry came across the twins in Gambol and Japes, in Diagon Alley. They were stocking up on Filibuster fireworks with Lee Jordan.

In Chapter Six, on the last night of the summer of 1992, they filled the Burrow’s kitchen for half an hour with red and blue stars that bounced from the ceiling to the walls, while Mrs Weasley pretended to be cross. The next morning the car had to turn back because George had forgotten his.

In Chapter Nine they found out what happens when you feed one to a Salamander. It shot into the air and whirled round the Gryffindor common room like a Catherine wheel, spitting tangerine stars, until it dived into the fire.

In Chapter Twelve Harry lit one of Fred’s with his wand and lobbed it into Goyle’s cauldron in Potions. Swelling Solution went up in a fizzing green fountain over half the class. Dracina Malfoy got a faceful, and her nose blew up like a balloon. In the uproar Hermione slipped out of the dungeon, coming back with the front of her robes bulging.

In Chapter Nineteen, on the Hogwarts Express home in June 1993, Harry and his friends set off the very last of the twins’ stock.

pages.title: Ogden's Old Firewhisky
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Ogden's Old Firewhisky is the best-known brand of firewhisky in wizarding Britain. Firewhisky is a strong spirit that burns all the way down, which is rather the point of it. It is sold by the bottle or by the glass, and it is not for children.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Gilderoy Lockhart went through the answers to the quiz about himself that he had set his class. He reminded them that in chapter twelve of Wanderings with Werewolves he named his ideal birthday gift as harmony between all magic and non-magic peoples. 'Though I wouldn't say no to a large bottle of Ogden's Old Firewhisky!' Of all the things he said about himself that year, it was one of the few that nobody had any reason to doubt.

pages.title: Spellotape
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Spellotape is the wizarding answer to sticky tape. It will hold almost anything together, though, as Ron Weasley found, it cannot make a broken wand behave.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Ron patched his broken wand with borrowed Spellotape. It had snapped nearly in two in the Whomping Willow on 1 September 1992. The tape held the two halves together. It did nothing at all for the wand's behaviour, which for the rest of the year was sparking, smoking and backfiring.

pages.title: Colin Creevey's camera
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Melted inside, in the autumn of 1992
pages.html:
Colin Creevey's camera is the ordinary Muggle camera that Colin, a Muggle-born Gryffindor, brought with him to Hogwarts in 1992. He took it everywhere, and he took a great many pictures of Harry Potter with it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Colin came up to Harry with the camera clutched in both hands, went bright red and asked whether he might have a picture. He wanted to prove that he had met him. He was taking loads of pictures to send home to his father, who was a milkman. A boy in his dormitory had told him that if he developed the film in the right potion, the pictures would move.

In Chapter Eight he sat high in the empty stands at an early-morning Quidditch practice, taking picture after picture of Harry.

In Chapter Eleven Professor McGonagall found Colin Petrified on the stairs, with a bunch of grapes beside him; he had been on his way to visit Harry in the hospital wing. The camera was still held up in front of his face. Professor Dumbledore worked it gently out of his stiff fingers and opened the back. Steam hissed out, with a sharp smell of burnt plastic. The whole inside of the camera had melted.

In Chapter Twelve Ginny Weasley told Harry, into her sleeve, that Colin had been going to show her how his camera worked. He had promised to teach her to make the pictures move. In Chapter Fourteen, in the Slytherin common room, Dracina Malfoy did a cruel impression of Colin snapping away with an imaginary camera.

In Chapter Eighteen Harry worked out why the camera had melted. Colin had seen the Basilisk through it. The Basilisk had burnt up all the film inside, but Colin had only been Petrified.

pages.title: Quidditch Cup
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Won in 1994, for the first time in seven years
pages.html:
The Quidditch Cup is the silver trophy for which the four Hogwarts houses play every school year. Whichever house ends the season with the most points wins it. In 1994 Gryffindor won it for the first time in seven years.

The competition

Each house plays each of the other three once a season. The Cup goes on points, not on wins alone, so the margin of a victory can matter as much as the victory itself.

Before 1994 Gryffindor had gone seven years without it, ever since the days when Ron Weasley's brother Charlie was Seeker. In 1992 the team should have won it, but lost the last match while its Seeker lay unconscious in the hospital wing.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, Ron Weasley looked into the Mirror of Erised and saw himself as Quidditch captain, holding the Quidditch Cup. He was holding the House Cup as well.

In Chapter Thirteen, while Harry lay in the hospital wing after facing Quirrell, Ravenclaw steamrollered Gryffindor in the last match of the season.

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Oliver Wood told his team that they should have won the Cup the year before. 'We're easily the best team.' That evening, in detention, Filch made Ron buff up the Cup fourteen times before he was satisfied.

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, Gryffindor had not won the Cup for seven years. Oliver Wood, in his last season, was desperate to win it. 'This is our last chance. My last chance. To win the Quidditch Cup. I leave in June.'

In Chapter Fifteen, before the final, somebody stuck a paper lion in the empty space in the trophy cabinet, where everybody could see it. Gryffindor beat Slytherin, and Dumbledore was waiting in the stands with the great silver Cup.

pages.title: Special Award for Services to the School
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Tom Riddle (1943); Harry Potter and Ron Weasley (1993)
pages.html:
The Special Award for Services to the School is a Hogwarts honour, given only rarely. The trophy room holds a gold shield awarded to Tom Riddle fifty years ago, which does not say what it was for. Harry Potter and Ron Weasley each received the award in 1993, after the Chamber of Secrets.

Riddle's shield

Headmaster Dippet gave Riddle his award in 1943, after Riddle had framed the young Rubeus Hagrid for the attacks of that year. A girl had died. Dippet hushed it up, and the shield gives no reason at all.

Fifty years later the same Chamber gave Harry and Ron theirs. Each award was worth two hundred points to Gryffindor, which won the House Cup on the strength of them.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, on 5 September 1992, Ron did his detention in the trophy room with Filch. He had another slug attack all over a Special Award for Services to the School. 'Took ages to shift the slime...'

In Chapter Fifteen Ron remembered where he had seen the name Riddle: on the fifty-year-old award he had polished in detention. 'It was the one I chucked up slugs all over. You spend an hour scrubbing slug slime out of somebody's name, mate, you don't forget it in a hurry.' In the trophy room Harry found Riddle's gold shield tucked away at the back of a corner cabinet. It did not say why it had been given to him.

In Chapter Nineteen, Dumbledore gave Harry and Ron each a Special Award for Services to the School, with two hundred points apiece for Gryffindor. Their four hundred points won Gryffindor the House Cup for the second year running.

pages.title: Percy's statue from Charlie
pages.html:
Percy's statue was a present to Percy Weasley from his brother Charlie. Their mother took it away from him. Nobody has said what was wrong with it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, flying Harry Potter to the Burrow in their father's car in the summer of 1992, George Weasley told him that Percy had been acting very oddly. Ever since their mother had taken away the statue Charlie gave him, George said, Percy had been sending a lot of letters and spending hours shut up in his room. 'I mean, there's only so many times you can polish a prefect badge...'

pages.title: The enchanted tea set
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A formerly cursed Muggle French nobleman
Arthur Weasley and Perkins, of the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office
pages.html:
The enchanted tea set came from a Muggle French nobleman who had once been under a curse. In 1991 it was sold to a Muggle, came alive in her house and killed her with shock. Arthur Weasley worked overtime for weeks to tidy up after it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, Ron Weasley explained his father's job to Harry Potter by way of the tea set. It had belonged to an old witch, a gift from the nobleman and his peasant wife. When she died, it went to an antiques shop, where a little old Muggle lady bought it and took it home.

When she tried to serve her friends tea in it, it came alive. The pieces danced about and talked to one another. The old lady died of shock, while her friends went mad. Arthur and an old warlock called Perkins, who between them make up the whole office, had to use Memory Charms to cover it up.

pages.title: Shrinking door-keys
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Shrinking door-keys are ordinary Muggle keys, jinxed to go on shrinking until they are too small to find. Wizards with a nasty sense of humour sell them to Muggles, as a form of Muggle-baiting. Arthur Weasley's office at the Ministry of Magic deals with them.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, Arthur Weasley came home to the Burrow after a night of nine raids. He had found a few shrinking door-keys and a biting kettle, he told the family. George asked why anybody would bother making door-keys shrink. 'Muggle-baiting,' sighed Mr Weasley. Convictions were very hard to get, he explained, because no Muggle will admit his key keeps shrinking. 'He'll swear blind he just keeps losing it.'

pages.title: Galleon
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Galleon is the gold coin of wizarding Britain, the most valuable of its three coins. Seventeen silver Sickles make a Galleon, and twenty-nine bronze Knuts make a Sickle. None of them is any use in a Muggle shop.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, Harry rode down to the Weasleys’ vault at Gringotts with them. It held a single Galleon and a small pile of Sickles. Harry felt worse than he had in Knockturn Alley. At his own vault he shovelled coins into a bag as fast as he could. He tried once more to press a handful on Mrs Weasley, who refused him kindly but firmly. In Chapter Fourteen Mr Weasley was fined fifty Galleons for enchanting a Muggle car.

In the Book Three Interlude, in the summer of 1993, Harry paid his Knight Bus fare with a fistful of gold Galleons, far more than the fare. By the look of him he hoped it would buy him some peace as well as a bed. Stan Shunpike pocketed it without a word. John Constantine, on the same bus, thought him an amateur: you never paid more than you needed to, not in front of anybody. John had been a wizard for thirty years, near enough, and had never got the hang of wizards’ money himself. It seemed to him like something a mad uncle had made up at Christmas to keep the children quiet.

pages.title: Hover Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Lifts an object and holds it in the air
4 Privet Drive, 31 July 1992, at twelve minutes past nine
pages.html:
The Hover Charm lifts an object into the air and holds it there. It is a simple, everyday piece of magic. On 31 July 1992 it earned Harry Potter his first official warning from the Ministry of Magic, for a spell he had not cast.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, Dobby the house-elf came to 4 Privet Drive on Harry's twelfth birthday to stop him going back to Hogwarts. While Uncle Vernon entertained the Masons to dinner, Dobby lifted Aunt Petunia's pudding off the top of the fridge with a Hover Charm. Then he let it fall.

The Ministry could tell that magic had been done in the house, but not who had done it. So Harry got the letter. It informed him that a Hover Charm had been used at his place of residence that evening at twelve minutes past nine. The Dursleys locked him in his room.

pages.title: Memory Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Wipes memories from a mind, or alters them
The Ministry of Magic, to keep the Statute of Secrecy
pages.html:
The Memory Charm, cast with the word Obliviate, wipes memories from a mind or changes them. The Ministry of Magic uses it all the time to make Muggles forget magic they were never meant to see. In the wrong hands it is one of the cruellest spells there is, because the victim never knows what he has lost.

At the Ministry

Most of the clearing up after careless magic among Muggles ends with a Memory Charm. The Ministry keeps Obliviators for the purpose, though smaller offices do their own. Arthur Weasley's Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office, which in 1992 was only Arthur and an old warlock called Perkins, spent weeks of overtime on it after the business of the enchanted tea set.

Gilderoy Lockhart

Gilderoy Lockhart built his whole career on the charm. He tracked down people who had done remarkable things. He got them to tell him exactly how they had done it, then put a Memory Charm on each of them and wrote the book himself. 'If there's one thing I pride myself on, it's my Memory Charms,' he said.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1992, Ron Weasley told Harry Potter about the tea set. An old witch had died the year before. Her tea set, a gift from a formerly cursed Muggle French nobleman and his peasant wife, was sold to an antiques shop. The little old Muggle lady who bought it tried to serve her friends tea in it. The pieces came alive, dancing and speaking to one another. The old lady died of shock. The others went mad. Arthur and Perkins had to use Memory Charms to cover it all up.

In Chapter Eighteen Lockhart confessed it all to Harry and Ron in his office, then drew his wand to put a Memory Charm on both of them. Harry disarmed him first. Down in the tunnel to the Chamber of Secrets, Lockhart knocked Ron flat and seized his wand, not noticing that it was held together with Spellotape. 'Obliviate!' The broken wand went off like a small bomb. The charm bounced off the ceiling and hit Lockhart in the face. When he came round, he had no idea who he was.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Five: at the World Cup campsite on 22 August 1994 a Ministry wizard in plus fours put the Memory Charm on the Muggle manager, Mr Roberts, leaving him dreamy and untroubled. Roberts needed it about ten times a day. To Harry, Obliviating Muggles like this was like putting a plaster on a werewolf bite.

pages.title: Cushioning Charm
infobox: An invisible cushion over a seat
pages.html:
The Cushioning Charm puts an invisible cushion between a seat and whoever is sitting on it. Elliot Smethwyck invented it in 1820 for broomsticks, which until then had been very hard to sit on for long.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, the Weasleys' luggage lay in the yard of the Burrow like the baggage of a small army. Mr Weasley explained to Harry Potter, with enormous pride, every charm he had ever put on his Ford Anglia. There was a Cushioning Charm on the seats. Another charm kept the tyres from going flat, and another let the engine run on vegetable oil instead of petrol.

pages.title: Engorgement Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Engorgement Charm makes a thing swell to many times its proper size. It works on living things as well as on objects.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, Hagrid was growing pumpkins for Hallowe'en 1992. They had already reached the size of boulders. Hagrid admitted he had been giving them a bit of help. Harry Potter noticed his flowery pink umbrella leaning against the back wall of the hut, and suspected that Hagrid's old school wand lived inside it. Hagrid was not supposed to do magic.

'An Engorgement Charm, I suppose?' said Hermione, halfway between disapproval and amusement. 'Well, you've done a good job on them.'

In Chapter Nine, through the wet October that followed, the pumpkins went on swelling until they were the size of garden sheds. By the Hallowe'en feast they had been carved into lanterns big enough for three men to sit in.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, on 21 August 1994, Dudley Dursley ate one of Fred Weasley's Ton-Tongue Toffees at Privet Drive, and his tongue swelled to a foot long. Arthur Weasley tried to reassure the Dursleys that it was only an Engorgement Charm, which he could correct, though he admitted that he was not entirely sure. His words did nothing to calm them.

pages.title: Freezing Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Stops a creature or object dead where it is
pages.html:
The Freezing Charm stops its target dead, holding a creature motionless where it is until somebody lifts the charm or puts the creature somewhere safe. It is the obvious answer to anything small, quick and troublesome, such as a Cornish pixie.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on 2 September 1992, Gilderoy Lockhart let a cage of Cornish pixies loose on his second-year class. They wrecked the room. Lockhart's own spell did nothing whatever. When the bell went, he left Harry, Ron and Hermione to put the rest back in their cage. Hermione stopped two of them dead with a neat Freezing Charm and stuffed them back behind the bars. 'He just wants to give us some hands-on experience,' she said.

pages.title: Peskipiksi Pesternomi
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Peskipiksi Pesternomi is the spell Gilderoy Lockhart bellowed at a classroom full of Cornish pixies. Whether it was ever meant to do anything is not known. On that occasion it did nothing whatever.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on 2 September 1992, Lockhart opened a cage of Cornish pixies in front of his second-years. The pixies went off in every direction like fireworks. They lifted Neville Longbottom into the air by his ears, shot through the window and wrecked the classroom.

Lockhart rolled up his sleeves and brandished his wand. Then he bellowed, 'Peskipiksi Pesternomi!' at the top of his voice. It did nothing whatever. One of the pixies took the wand off him and threw it out of the window. Lockhart dived under his own desk. When the bell rang, he left Harry, Ron and Hermione to round up the rest. Hermione did it with a Freezing Charm.

pages.title: Slug-vomiting curse
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Makes the victim belch up slugs for hours
None; it has to wear off
pages.html:
The slug-vomiting curse makes its victim belch up large, glistening slugs for hours. It is a difficult curse even with a sound wand, and with a broken one it may go off at the wrong end.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, on 5 September 1992, Dracina Malfoy called Hermione Granger a Mudblood on the Quidditch pitch. The two girls went for each other's hair. Harry pulled Dracina off, and she shoved him away. 'Get away from him!' cried Ron Weasley, and his wand came up to curse her. There was a bang. A jet of green light shot out of the wrong end of his broken wand and hit him in the stomach. He opened his mouth, gave an almighty belch, and several slugs slid out into his lap.

Harry and Hermione hauled him off to Hagrid's hut, which was nearest. Hagrid set a big copper basin in front of him. 'That's a difficult curse to work at the best of times, but with a broken wand...' said Hermione. There was nothing to do except wait for it to stop. That evening, in detention, Ron brought up more slugs all over a Special Award for Services to the School.

pages.title: Scouring Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Cleans away dirt, ink, slime or stains
pages.html:
The Scouring Charm, Scourgify, cleans whatever it is pointed at, lifting off dirt, spilt ink, slime or stains in one pass. It is ordinary household magic. Cast with too much feeling, it takes the colour out of the cloth along with the stain.

Household magic

Scouring Charms are everyday magic, which is why it is so embarrassing not to manage them. Kwikspell, a correspondence course in beginners' magic, boasted of them in its leaflets. One testimonial, from a Mrs P. Hoskins of Wolverhampton, said that for years she could not so much as warm a teapot without setting light to the cosy. Since Kwikspell, her Scouring Charms had become the talk of the street.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, Harry Potter read that testimonial in a glossy purple Kwikspell envelope on Argus Filch's desk, while he waited to be punished for dripping mud on the floor.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in November 1993, Dracina Malfoy's inkwell cracked in Charms and bled blue all over her notes. Hermione Granger's hand went up before anyone else's with a neat Scourgify. She passed Dracina her own spare quill as well. In Chapter Ten, in Potions, Ron Weasley threw a crocodile heart that hit Dracina full in the face. Hermione came down the aisle with her wand out. 'Hold still, Malfoy. Let me. Scourgify.' The mess came off Dracina's robes, her cheek and her crown of plaits in one neat pass.

In Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, a rusty smear of Dracina's blood had dried on the front of Harry's robes. Hermione looked at it, and her lips went very thin. 'Scourgify,' she said, with a flick of her wand. The smear vanished, and so did most of the colour from Harry's robes, in a patch the size of a dinner plate.

pages.title: Pepperup Potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Smoke from the ears for several hours
pages.html:
Pepperup Potion cures a cold at once, but leaves whoever drinks it smoking at the ears for several hours afterwards. It is the hospital wing's standby every winter at Hogwarts.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, half the school seemed to be sneezing, and the staff were not much better. Madam Pomfrey's Pepperup Potion went out of the hospital wing by the gallon, so that the corridors between lessons looked like a railway station.

Ginny Weasley had been looking peaky for a week, so Percy stood over her at breakfast with a bottle until she drank it. Within seconds steam was pouring out from under her red hair, which made her look like a small girl whose head had caught fire.

pages.title: Photograph developing potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Wizarding photographs move because the film is developed in the right potion. Once the film has been developed, the people in the picture go on with their own small lives inside its border, waving, wandering out of shot or refusing point-blank to do as they are told.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Colin Creevey told Harry that a boy in his dormitory had said the pictures would move if he developed the film in the right potion. In Chapter Eight he ran up to Harry with the result. In it Lockhart was tugging with both hands at Harry's arm, while the photographic Harry put up a stiff fight and refused to be dragged into view. Lockhart gave up in the end and slumped against the white border, panting.

pages.title: Ghoul
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Weasleys' ghoul, at the Burrow
pages.html:
A ghoul is a flesh-eating creature that makes its home in the attics and barns of wizarding houses. It moans, bangs on the pipes and howls in the night, but it seldom leaves its attic. Getting rid of one takes a professional, and costs a great deal.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1992, George Weasley told Harry Potter that all the family had was a lousy old ghoul in the attic. Harry was horrified. They had tried to get it out, Ron explained, but for a ghoul you needed a proper professional, which was far too expensive. They were saving up. In the meantime Mrs Weasley fed it the gnomes sometimes, and it never came out of the attic.

In Chapter Four Ron admitted that his bedroom was right under the ghoul, which was always banging on the pipes and groaning. In Chapter Five Harry found its howling for sacrifices down the pipes all very well at breakfast, but rather less so at three in the morning, with his pillow over his head. In Chapter Fourteen Mrs Weasley told the Daily Prophet's reporters that she would set the family ghoul on them if they did not get off her doorstep. In Chapter Seventeen Ron said that the ghoul kept going on about being some high-level servant of a Prince, though he reckoned it was talking nonsense.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, Ron told Harry that the family was his if he wanted it. 'It's got too many redheads in it, the ghoul bangs the pipes all night, but it's yours if you want it.' Harry said he would take it tomorrow, ghoul and all, but he did not believe he could ever really belong to it.

pages.title: Garden gnome
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Small, brown and leathery, with a head like a potato
pages.html:
Garden gnomes are small, brown and leathery. They have bald, knobbly heads exactly like potatoes, hard little horny feet and teeth like needles. They infest wizarding gardens, and they are nothing like the fat little Father Christmases with fishing rods that Muggles put on their lawns.

De-gnoming

The cure is a de-gnoming. Each gnome is caught by the ankles, swung round until it is too dizzy to find its way back to the gnome-holes, then thrown over the hedge. It does not hurt them. They always come back all the same. They are not very bright: the moment they hear that a de-gnoming has begun, they come storming up to have a look.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in August 1992, Mrs Weasley sent Harry Potter, Ron and the twins out to de-gnome the garden of the Burrow. Ron hauled the first one, squealing 'Gerroff me!', out of a peony bush and slung it twenty feet. Harry meant to drop his first gnome gently over the hedge. Sensing a soft touch, it sank a row of teeth like needles into his finger, and he flung it so hard that Ron reckoned it had gone fifty feet. Before long a crowd of gnomes was trudging off across the field with their little shoulders hunched. 'They'll be back,' said Ron. 'They love it here.' Mr Weasley, he added, was too soft with them, because he thought they were funny. Later that day a straggle of gnomes was creeping back through the hedge one by one. Mrs Weasley sometimes feeds them to the family ghoul.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994 Crookshanks chased a gnome across the flagstones of the Burrow, a thing like a potato with legs, caked in mud, no higher than Harry's knee. It flung itself headfirst into an old Wellington boot, where it giggled madly. The Burrow's gnomes sprint through the rosebushes laughing like maniacs.

pages.title: Cornish pixie
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Cornish pixies are electric blue, about eight inches tall, with pointed faces. Their voices are so shrill that a cageful of them sounds like budgies having a row. Let loose, they go off in every direction like fireworks and wreck whatever they can reach.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, at his first lesson on 2 September 1992, Gilderoy Lockhart released a cage of freshly caught Cornish pixies on his second years. They went off in every direction like fireworks. Two of them seized Neville Longbottom by the ears and lifted him clean into the air, so that he ended up swinging from the candelabra. Others smashed the window, sprayed the class with ink and shredded the books. Four of them got into Dracina Malfoy's hair. 'Potter, do something!' she screamed, and Harry Potter beat them off her with a copy of Gadding with Ghouls.

Lockhart's spell, 'Peskipiksi Pesternomi!', did nothing whatever. A pixie threw his wand out of the window, and he dived under his desk. When the bell rang, he left Harry, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger to put the rest back in their cage. Hermione stopped two of them with a neat Freezing Charm.

In Chapter Eleven, on the steps outside the Great Hall, Professor McGonagall told Lockhart in front of half the school exactly what he had done. 'You released a cage of Cornish pixies into a room full of twelve-year-olds and then hid under your desk. Mr Longbottom spent a quarter of an hour hanging from a chandelier by his ears.' There were no more pixies after that. In Chapter Sixteen Ron said that all he had learnt from Lockhart was never to let pixies out of a cage. In Book Three, Chapter Seven, the pixies were still the only practical lesson in Defence Against the Dark Arts the class had ever had.

pages.title: Mandrake
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A powerful restorative; the cure for Petrification
The cry of a mature Mandrake is fatal
pages.html:
The Mandrake, or Mandragora, is a magical plant and one of the most powerful restoratives known, used in most antidotes. Its root is an ugly, mottled baby. Once the plant is fully grown, its cry is fatal to anybody who hears it.

Growing Mandrakes

A seedling's cry will not kill, but it can knock a listener out for hours. That is why young Mandrakes are repotted by people wearing earmuffs.

As they leave childhood Mandrakes grow sulky and secretive. They throw parties. They are mature once they start trying to climb into each other's pots. Then they are cut up and stewed into a draught that cures Petrification.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on the first day of lessons in September 1992, Harry Potter's year repotted Mandrake seedlings in Professor Sprout's greenhouses, wearing earmuffs. Hermione Granger told the class that the Mandrake was a powerful restorative. Its cry, she said, was fatal to anyone who heard it.

In Chapter Ten, over the Petrified Mrs Norris at Hallowe'en, Professor Dumbledore told Filch that Professor Sprout had recently managed to procure some Mandrakes. As soon as they were fully grown, a potion made from them would revive his cat. Gilderoy Lockhart said he could whip up a Mandrake Restorative Draught in his sleep.

In Chapter Twelve, in December, a blizzard cancelled the last Herbology lesson of term. Professor Sprout wanted to put socks and scarves on the Mandrakes, a fiddly job she would trust to nobody else, now that it mattered so much for them to grow quickly. They had Mrs Norris and Colin Creevey to bring back.

In Chapter Fifteen, early in 1993, Madam Pomfrey reported that the Mandrakes were growing sulky and secretive, which meant that they were leaving their childhood behind them. In Chapter Sixteen, in March, several of them threw a loud, wild party in Greenhouse Three. It kept half of Hufflepuff awake, and made Professor Sprout very happy indeed. Once they started trying to climb into each other's pots, she told Harry, she would know they were grown.

In Chapter Eighteen Professor McGonagall announced that the Mandrakes were at last ready for cutting. That night, in Chapter Nineteen, Madam Pomfrey was handing out Mandrake juice to the Basilisk's victims.

pages.title: Venomous Tentacula
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Spiky and dark red, with long feelers
pages.html:
The Venomous Tentacula is a spiky, dark red magical plant with long feelers that creep out towards anybody standing too close. Its bite is poisonous. Its seeds are a Class C Non-Tradeable Substance, which may not be bought or sold.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on the first day of lessons in September 1992, Professor Sprout warned Harry Potter's class to be careful of the Venomous Tentacula in Greenhouse Three, because it was teething. As she said it, the plant's long feelers came inching over her shoulder. She gave it a sharp slap, and it drew them in.

pages.title: Whomping Willow
infobox: magical plant, Hogwarts grounds, Hogwarts, tree
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
1971, the year Remus Lupin came to Hogwarts
The tunnel to the Shrieking Shack
Press the knot on its trunk
pages.html:
The Whomping Willow is a very old, very valuable tree in the grounds of Hogwarts, which attacks anything that comes within reach of its branches. It was planted in 1971, the year Remus Lupin came to the school, on top of the entrance to a secret tunnel. Pressing a knot on its trunk freezes it.

The tree and the tunnel

The Willow was planted because Lupin came to Hogwarts. He was a Garou, and once a month, on the full moon, he was smuggled out of the castle through the tunnel to transform in the Shrieking Shack. The tree was put at the tunnel mouth to stop anyone coming across him while he was dangerous.

In their schooldays Peter Pettigrew, the smallest of Lupin's friends, used to slip under the branches as a rat to touch the knot that freezes it, so that the others could follow him down the tunnel. Sirius Black once told Severus Snape, as a joke, that he could get in after Lupin by prodding the knot with a long stick. Snape tried it. James Potter went after him and pulled him back, at great risk to his own life.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, Harry and Ron crashed Mr Weasley's flying Ford Anglia into the Willow, which very nearly killed them. Harry thought it was probably guarding something. Snape, that evening, spoke of considerable damage to a very valuable tree. In Chapter Seven Harry saw it in the distance with several of its branches in slings. In Chapter Fourteen he thought guiltily of the car, which nobody had seen since it crashed into the Willow and roared off into the Forest.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in November 1993, Harry fell from his broom in a storm, and the wind carried his Nimbus Two Thousand down on to the Willow. Ron put what was left of it into his hands in a small drawstring bag. In Chapter Ten Lupin told Harry that the tree had gone in the same year he did, in his own first year at Hogwarts. The Weasley twins showed Harry the tunnel on the Marauder's Map, though they reckoned nobody had ever used it, with the Willow planted smack on top of the entrance.

In Chapter Twelve Lupin promised Harry a story: 'I shall tell you about your father and the Whomping Willow, which is a story you will like, plus one or two about your mother which you had better not repeat.' In Chapter Thirteen Cedric Diggory said he was sorry about the Nimbus: 'That tree's a menace.'

In Chapter Seventeen, chasing Scabbers in the dark, Harry, Ron and Hermione ran right under it. The Willow slashed Hermione's shoulder and struck Harry's face, while the great black dog dragged Ron backwards into a wide gap between its roots. Then Crookshanks wove in among the flailing branches to press his front paws to a knot on the trunk, and the tree froze as if it had been turned to stone. In Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Lupin told them the rest: 'The truth is that it was planted because I came to Hogwarts.'

In Chapter Twenty, back in time by the Time-Turner, Harry and Hermione watched it all again from the edge of the Forest. They saw Lupin snatch up a broken branch from the grass to jab the knot, and a couple of minutes later Snape picked up the same branch to do the same.

pages.title: Salamander
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
As long as its fire burns
pages.html:
The Salamander is a small, bright orange lizard that lives in fire. It is born from the flames, it feeds on them, and it lives for as long as its fire burns. Taken out of the fire, it can survive for up to six hours if it is regularly fed pepper.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in the autumn of 1992, Fred and George Weasley fed a Filibuster firework to a Salamander in the Gryffindor common room, to see what would happen. Fred had liberated it from a Care of Magical Creatures class. It shot into the air, whirled round the room like a Catherine wheel spitting tangerine stars, and dived at last into the fire.

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, on a raw January morning in 1994, Hagrid kept nine bright orange salamanders, each about a forearm long, running up and down the logs of a white-hot bonfire. His class spent the lesson fetching dry wood to keep it going. It was the only warm thing anybody did all week.

pages.title: Kelpie
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Water of every kind, from lochs to wells
A horse with bulrushes for a mane
A Placement Charm and a bridle
pages.html:
The kelpie is a shape-shifting water demon of Britain and Ireland. It most often takes the form of a horse with bulrushes for a mane. It lures the unwary on to its back, then dives with them to the bottom of its loch or river and eats them.

Habits

The largest kelpie in the world lives in Loch Ness, where it prefers to show itself as a sea serpent. The proper way to deal with one is to put a Placement Charm on it, then a bridle over its head, which makes it quite docile.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1992, Gilderoy Lockhart gave Hagrid a great deal of advice about getting kelpies out of a well. Hagrid had not asked for it. ‘Like I don' know,’ he growled afterwards, over the teapot.

pages.title: Vampire
infobox: Cain, through the blood magic of Lilith
pages.html:
Vampires, who call themselves the Kindred, are the walking dead who live on human blood. Every one of them descends from Cain. A vampire's soul is destroyed when it is sired, and a hunger called the Beast takes its place. Since 1435 they have hidden under their own law of secrecy, the Masquerade.

Origins

God cursed Cain for the murder of his brother Abel: he was to be deathless, soulless, and burned by the sun. Shortly after Noah's Flood, Lilith, a servant of the Devil, tricked him into blood magic. From it Cain rose as the first vampire.

Vampirism therefore comes from Morgoth, the Devil, through Cain and Lilith. That is why a believer's cross repels a vampire. It is also why fire and the sun are what they all fear.

Cain sired three childer, Enoch, Irad and Zillah, who in their turn sired the thirteen Antediluvians in the First City. From those thirteen come the thirteen clans.

Clans and sects

Each vampire stands one generation further from Cain than its sire, and the older the blood, the stronger it is. By the old count there are thirteen clans, among them the Ventrue, the Nosferatu, the Toreador and the Tzimisce. Most Kindred in the West answer to the Camarilla, which keeps the Masquerade; the Sabbat despises it.

Since 1900 the Camarilla has had an agreement with the wizarding world. Wizards lend their own concealment spells to help keep the Masquerade, and no Camarilla vampire may hunt or feed on a witch or wizard.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on the first morning of term in September 1992, Hermione Granger read Gilderoy Lockhart's Voyages with Vampires at breakfast. There were thirteen clans of vampires, she told Harry Potter, the Ventrue among them. The book covered the Nosferatu too, with Angelus, William the Bloody and Dracula.

In Chapter Ten, with History of Magic sunk into its usual stupor, Harry wished they could learn about vampires instead. Lockhart's tales had told him a good deal about their clans, generations and lineages. So had Hermione's books.

In Book Three, Chapter Three, Harry had still never met a vampire, although Lockhart claimed to have fought several, including something he called a Tzi-mi-see. Professor McGonagall had since told Harry, quite deliberately, that a Tzimisce did not fall down when you hit it, but came apart and walked off in several directions. Hermione's books went into great detail about Angelus.

In Chapter Eight, in the second week of October 1993, Professor Lupin taught the class about vampires. A stake through the heart does not kill most of them, he said; it only pins them. What kills them is fire, and the sun. They hide under their own law, the Masquerade, which came into force in 1435. About ninety years before, he said, the Ministry had come to an arrangement with the Camarilla, the nearest thing they have to a governing body. The Sabbat never signed anything at all.

There were thirteen clans by the old count, he said, descended from a progenitor so old that vampires no longer agree who the first was. They must be invited in: Lupin made the class say it back to him three times, ‘Never ask one in. Never, ever ask one in.’ Some can take hold of a mind through the eyes, and some bind with a blood bond. Vampirism destroys the soul, Lupin said, and leaves a hunger called the Beast. He had never met one he would turn his back on.

In Chapter Twelve Lupin told Harry that a body emptied by the Dementor's Kiss has to be filled by something, perhaps a beast of the sort a vampire carries.
