In Chapter Thirteen Harry reflected that Hermione followed real vampires the way Lavender Brown and Parvati Patil followed Take That.

pages.title: Ghost
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Cold, like plunging into icy water
Barely, and only very strong, rotten food
pages.html:
A ghost is the imprint left behind by a witch or wizard who was afraid to go on. Ghosts are pearly-white and see-through. They give off cold, and walking through one is like plunging into icy water.

Nature

Ghosts cannot eat. They can barely taste anything except very strong, rotten food, which is why the food at a Deathday Party is left to go off. A ghost keeps its Deathday on the anniversary of its death. Nearly Headless Nick says that ghosts are dreadful gossips who go on endlessly about how they died.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, Nearly Headless Nick told Harry Potter that he had been turned down for the Headless Hunt yet again. Dracina Malfoy had already stopped him on the stairs to offer her condolences, having had the news from the Bloody Baron. 'They're dreadful gossips, ghosts,' said Nick. When Harry agreed, Nick turned to him with the deepest gratitude. All of them, he said, went on and on about how they died.

On Hallowe'en Harry, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger went to Nick's five hundredth Deathday Party in the dungeons, instead of the feast. Hundreds of pearly, see-through people were waltzing to thirty musical saws, and it was like walking into a cold store. On the table lay great rotten fish, cakes burned to charcoal and a haggis crawling with maggots. The grey cake, shaped like a tombstone, read Sir Nicholas de Mimsy-Porpington, died 31st October, 1492. Hermione supposed that the food had been left to go off so that the ghosts could just about taste it. A portly ghost walked slowly through the table with his mouth held wide open, so that a stinking salmon passed straight through his face. 'Almost,' he said sadly, and drifted off.

pages.title: Ent
pages.html:
The Ents were the shepherds of the trees in Middle-earth, tall as trees themselves and very like them. They were slow to anger and terrible when roused. The eldest of them, Treebeard, was the oldest living thing that still walked beneath the Sun in the Third Age. They had lost the Entwives long before. In 3019 of that age the Ents marched on Isengard and broke it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter One, on his twelfth birthday in July 1992, Harry Potter was staring at the hedge at Privet Drive, where a moment before a pair of enormous eyes had blinked at him. Dudley wanted to know what he was looking at. Harry asked him whether he had read The Lord of the Rings, then remembered that Dudley never read anything at all. 'Never mind, Dudley. I'm trying to turn this bush into an Ent. It'll help Aunt Petunia with the gardening.' Dudley went backwards so fast he nearly sat down. His father, he stammered, had said Harry was not to do magic.

pages.title: Flesh-Eating Slug
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Flesh-Eating Slugs are a garden pest that can strip a vegetable patch bare. Wizards keep them off with Flesh-Eating Slug Repellent, which can be bought in Knockturn Alley.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, Harry Potter came out of the wrong grate by Floo powder and found himself lost in Knockturn Alley. Hagrid found him there. 'I was lookin' fer a Flesh-Eatin' Slug Repellent,' he growled. 'They're ruinin' the school cabbages.' In Chapter Sixteen, after Hagrid had been taken away, Ron Weasley asked a little hesitantly about that meeting in Knockturn Alley. 'He was buying Flesh-Eating Slug Repellent,' said Harry at once. 'For the cabbages. He said.'

pages.title: Squib
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A person born to wizard parents with no magic
pages.html:
A Squib is somebody born to wizard parents who has no magic at all. Squibs are rare, and in the old families they are often a source of shame. Argus Filch, the caretaker at Hogwarts, is one, and keeps it as quiet as he can.

Causes

Why they happen is argued over. Arthur Weasley's view is that inbreeding among the same few families is to blame, since the families most anxious about their blood are the ones that marry their cousins.

Squibs of the tribes

A Squib can be born to one magical parent as well as to two, and to the witches of the Romani tribes as well as to the old families. Pietro Maximoff, the mutant called Quicksilver, is the son of a Romani witch, and he has no magic at all, though his twin sister, the Scarlet Witch, has plenty. His speed is a mutant's power, not a wizard's.

The Braddocks

One of the oldest Squib lines in Britain began in King Arthur's house, in the generations after Arthur, when a child born without magic was sent out to live among Muggles. Its descendants, the Braddocks of Essex, have been Muggles ever since and have never known where they came from. One of them is Captain Britain, whose powers are an Elvish enchantment, not magic of his own.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, in Hagrid's hut, Ron Weasley explained to Harry Potter, between slugs, what a Squib was: somebody born to wizard parents who had no magic. ‘Dad reckons it’s what you get when the same five families keep marrying each other for three hundred years. Doesn’t stop them doing it.’

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, after Mrs Norris was Petrified, Filch accused Harry of knowing that he was a Squib. Harry protested that he did not even know what a Squib was. Then he remembered Ron's words, and before he could stop himself he asked Filch, ‘Oh. Are your mum and dad siblings or something? That would explain a lot.’ In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, Neville Longbottom, whose gran was always saying he was practically a Squib, feared the monster would come for him next.

pages.title: Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery
aliases: Decree for the Restriction of Underage Wizardry
infobox: Decree for the Restriction of Underage Wizardry
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery is the wizarding law of 1875 that forbids underage witches and wizards to do magic outside school. Under Paragraph C, the penalty for further spellwork is expulsion.

In practice

The Improper Use of Magic Office at the Ministry of Magic watches for magic in places where underage wizards live, and a first offence usually brings a warning letter. The Ministry can tell where magic has been done, but not always who did it. Accidents are treated more kindly, at least when the Minister has reasons of his own.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1992, a Hover Charm was worked in the Dursleys' kitchen at twelve minutes past nine, while Uncle Vernon was entertaining the Masons to dinner. Dobby the house-elf had done it, but the warning came to Harry Potter. Signed by Mafalda Hopkirk, it cited the 1875 Decree, Paragraph C, and Section 13 of the Statute of Secrecy.

In Book Two, Chapter Six, stranded at King's Cross, Ron Weasley argued that underage wizards were allowed to use magic in a real emergency, under ‘section nineteen or something of the Restriction of Thingy’. In Book Three, Chapter Three, after he had blown up Aunt Marge, Harry was sure he would be expelled under the Decree. Cornelius Fudge told him it had been an accident.

pages.title: International Statute of Wizarding Secrecy
infobox: International Statute of Secrecy; Statute of Secrecy
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Each wizarding government: in Britain the Ministry of Magic, in the United States MACUSA
Section 13 (magic that risks Muggle notice); Clause 73 (concealment of magical beasts)
By some accounts, the Masquerade of the Kindred (1435)
The agreement of 1900 with the Camarilla
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The International Statute of Wizarding Secrecy is the law by which the witches and wizards of the world keep themselves hidden from Muggles. The International Confederation of Wizards signed it in 1689, and it came into force in 1692. Above all it hid the wizarding world from the Church, after centuries of burnings. Some wizards say it was inspired by the Masquerade, the far older law by which the vampires hide. Since 1900 the wizarding governments of the world have also lent their own concealment magic to the Camarilla to help keep that Masquerade. In return, no Camarilla vampire may hunt, harm or feed on a witch or wizard.

Before the Statute

The wizarding world and the Church were at each other's throats for some fifteen hundred years. The old magic of Britain was bound up with the old religion, with druids and standing stones. When the missionaries came, it was all right for a while. Many of the early monks were wizards. Half the healing charms in use today began in their infirmaries, and some monasteries were all but schools of magic with a cross on the roof. The Fat Friar of Hufflepuff, who was a boy at Hogwarts when the school was new, became a Benedictine monk at a priory of exactly that kind.

Then the Church took fright, as Muggles do, and decided that magic was the Devil's work. The monks gave way to Inquisitors and witch-finders. Then the burnings began. Plenty of witches and wizards could protect themselves. The Flame-Freezing Charm made the fire no more than a tickle for anybody who knew it. But not everybody had a wand on them when the mob came, and Muggles with magical children suffered worst of all.

Wizards remember. They live to be a hundred and fifty. They keep portraits that talk, and ghosts who were there. There are people at Hogwarts today who personally watched their friends burn.

The Statute of 1689

In 1689 the International Confederation of Wizards signed the Statute of Secrecy, and in 1692 it came into force. From then on the witches and wizards of every nation withdrew from the Muggle world into hiding. Each wizarding government took on the work of concealing its own people, places and beasts. Wizarding streets and villages vanished behind charms. Hogwarts was made to look, to any Muggle, like a ruin with a sign warning DANGER, DO NOT ENTER, UNSAFE. Muggles who saw what they should not were made to forget it.

In hiding from the Church, the wizarding world also turned its back on Christianity, and it has kept it at arm's length ever since. That is why Hogwarts has no chapel and nobody says grace there. It is also why the castle laughs at talk of angels. As Hermione Granger put it in 1993, it is not that wizards do not care about Christianity: they hate it, right down in the bone.

What the Statute requires

The Statute forbids any magic that risks being noticed by Muggles. Section 13 makes such magic a serious offence. It is under the Statute that the Improper Use of Magic Office of the Ministry of Magic warns and punishes those who break it. Clause 73 makes every wizarding government responsible for hiding the magical beasts within its borders. That is why dragons are kept on reserves, and why the Muggle-Repelling Charm guards so many of their haunts.

The Statute is kept by the wizards' own concealment magic: wards, Muggle-Repelling Charms, Unplottable places, the Fidelius Charm and the Memory Charms of the Obliviators. Young witches and wizards are bound besides by the Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery of 1875. A single Hover Charm at the wrong window can bring a letter from the Ministry citing both.

In America

In North America the Statute is enforced by MACUSA, the Magical Congress of the United States of America, which was founded in 1693 in the aftermath of the Salem witch trials. From 1790 to 1965 Rappaport's Law went further than the Statute did anywhere else. It forbade American witches and wizards even to befriend No-Majs, let alone marry them.

The Masquerade

The vampires were in hiding long before the wizards. The Masquerade, the first law of the Kindred, came into force in 1435 at the convocation of elders from which the Camarilla grew. Any vampire who lets a mortal see what it is will be hunted down and destroyed by its own kind, a good deal less gently than any Obliviator would manage. Some wizards say the Statute of Secrecy was inspired by it.

The agreement of 1900

In 1900 the wizarding governments of the world, meeting through the International Confederation of Wizards, came to terms with the Camarilla. The wizards would lend the Kindred their own concealment magic to help keep the Masquerade: the wards, the Muggle-Repelling Charms, the enchantments that hide Diagon Alley, Hogwarts and every wizarding house from Muggle eyes under the Statute. In return, no vampire who answers to the Camarilla would ever hunt, harm or feed on a witch or wizard. The British Ministry of Magic was one of the parties. Its dealings with the Kindred are mostly with the Ventrue.

The agreement is old and fragile. It has held, more or less, for most of the century, because both sides have more to lose than to gain by breaking it. It binds only the Camarilla. The Sabbat, which never signed it, thinks the Masquerade cowardice and the agreement worse. It has tried more than once to break it. The independent clans, the Assamites, the Followers of Set, the Giovanni and the Ravnos, are no party to it either.

Other secrets

The wizards are not the only ones in hiding. The Garou are hidden by the Delirium, which wipes the sight of them from human minds. The Watchers' Council keeps the secret of the Slayer among Muggle occultists. Since the coming of the costumed heroes in 1938, the age of heroes has also given the wizarding world a cover it never looked for. Muggles who see magic now put it down to some metahuman's powers, or to a conjuring trick, just as for fifty years they put the act of the American wizard Zatara down to stage illusion.

Witches and wizards who live in public keep the Statute by being disbelieved. Zatanna Zatara does real magic on stage, and her audiences take every spell for a trick. The Scarlet Witch of the Avengers and Amanda Sefton of the Excalibur team are taken for mutants. Stephen Strange is taken for a showman with a stage name. The ministries have learnt to let them be.

Enemies of the Statute

Not every wizard accepts it. Greta Grindelwald meant to tear it up and rule the Muggles openly, in a fascist empire of wizards, under the banner of the greater good. Many of Lord Voldemort's followers have shared her contempt for it.

In the saga

Book Two: in the summer of 1992 the Ministry wrote to Harry Potter after Dobby's Hover Charm at Privet Drive, citing the Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery and Section 13 of the Statute of Secrecy. Molly Weasley cited the Statute when she refused to fly the family car in daylight.

Book Three: in September 1993 Hermione Granger told Harry that the Statute of 1692 had hidden the wizarding world from the Church in particular, and she explained why wizards hate Christianity. She put the Fat Friar in the fourteenth century, which was some way out: he had been a boy at Hogwarts when the school was new. In October 1993 Remus Lupin told his third years that the Statute was recognised in 1692, and that some say it was inspired by the vampires' Masquerade of 1435. The Ministry and the Camarilla, he added, had come to their arrangement about ninety years before. Later that year he said that versions of the Patronus Charm were carved into things older than the Statute.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Five: on 22 August 1994 Harry feared that a single Muggle parent ringing the number on a Friends of Humanity leaflet would be enough to break the Statute, with a riot on top. At lunch at the World Cup campsite Barty Crouch said that he would not have the Statute put at risk on British soil because half the world's wizards could not be trusted to keep their tents plain.

pages.title: Muggle Protection Act
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Muggle Protection Act is Arthur Weasley's measure at the Ministry of Magic, meant to protect Muggles from wizards who would torment them. Lucius Malfoy has wanted it thrown out from the start.

Background

Arthur works in the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office, which spends its days on biting kettles, shrinking door-keys and worse. After his enchanted car crashed into the grounds of Hogwarts in 1992, Lucius, a governor of the school, demanded that he step down.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, Harry Potter overheard Lucius Malfoy at Borgin and Burkes: ‘There are rumours of a new Muggle Protection Act, and no doubt that flea-bitten, Muggle-loving fool Arthur Weasley is behind it...’ In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, the Daily Prophet quoted Lucius demanding that the Act be thrown out at once. In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, Dumbledore suggested to Lucius that the Act would have been wrecked if Ginny Weasley had been found attacking Muggle-borns.

pages.title: Muggle-baiting
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Muggle-baiting is the sport of selling Muggles enchanted objects to torment them. A favourite is a door-key that keeps shrinking to nothing, so that its owner can never find it when he wants it.

Convictions

It is very hard to get a conviction for it, because no Muggle will admit that his key keeps shrinking. He will swear blind that he just keeps losing it. Arthur Weasley's office at the Ministry of Magic deals with it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, Arthur came home tired after a long night, yawning about a few shrinking door-keys and a biting kettle. When George asked why anybody would bother making door-keys shrink, his father sighed: ‘Muggle-baiting.’

pages.title: Ordinary Wizarding Levels
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Twelve each, Bill and Percy Weasley
pages.html:
Ordinary Wizarding Levels, or O.W.L.s, are the examinations Hogwarts students sit at the end of their fifth year, one in each subject they study. The grades they earn decide which subjects they may go on to take to N.E.W.T. level.

Grades

The pass grades are Outstanding, Exceeds Expectations and Acceptable. The fail grades are Poor, Dreadful and Troll. Twelve O.W.L.s is a great many.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, Fred Weasley told Harry Potter that Percy's results had come the day before Harry arrived at the Burrow: twelve O.W.L.s, and he had hardly gloated at all. George explained them to Harry. Bill, he added, had got twelve too.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: Ron told Harry in August 1994 that Fred and George had got fewer O.W.L.s than their mother expected. In Chapter Five, Summoning the twins' hidden Ton-Tongue Toffees, Mrs Weasley shrieked that it was no wonder, when they had spent six months developing them.

pages.title: Head Boy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Tom Riddle; Bill Weasley; Percy Weasley (1993 to 1994)
pages.html:
The Head Boy is the senior boy at Hogwarts, chosen from the seventh year to lead the prefects alongside the Head Girl. He wears a silver badge, and expects to be listened to.

Holders

Tom Riddle was Head Boy half a century ago, before he became Lord Voldemort. The Weasleys have produced two: Bill in his day, and Percy in 1993, whom his mother greeted as the second Head Boy in the family.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, Ron Weasley told Harry Potter that Bill had been Head Boy. In Book One, Chapter Eight, the Mirror of Erised showed Ron himself as Head Boy, older than he was and on his own. In Book Two, Chapter Five, Ron's brother George took fright at Percy's twelve O.W.L.s: ‘If we’re not careful we’ll have another Head Boy in the family. I don’t think I could stand the shame.’ In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Harry and Ron found Tom Riddle's name on a list of former Head Boys.

In Book Three, Chapter One, Ron wrote to Harry that Percy was Head Boy, and that he had not stopped polishing the badge since. In Book Three, Chapter Four, Mrs Weasley showed off the brand-new silver badge in the Leaky Cauldron. It was soon altered to read Bighead Boy.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, Harry Potter met Bill Weasley for the first time at the Burrow on 21 August 1994. Knowing that Bill had once been Head Boy, Harry had always pictured him as an older Percy, fussy about the rules. Instead Bill turned out to be cool, with his long hair in a ponytail and a fang hanging from one ear.

pages.title: Order of Merlin
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Albus Dumbledore (First Class); Gilderoy Lockhart (Third Class); Peter Pettigrew (First Class, after his supposed death)
pages.html:
The Order of Merlin is the best-known honour in the wizarding world. It is given in three classes, and the Ministry of Magic decides who receives it. Albus Dumbledore holds the Order of Merlin, First Class, while Gilderoy Lockhart holds it Third Class. Peter Pettigrew was given it First Class for dying, which he had not done.

The three classes

First Class is given for outstanding bravery or distinction in magic. Second Class is for achievement beyond the ordinary, and Third Class for contributions to magical knowledge or entertainment. Lockhart's is Third Class.

Pettigrew and Snape

In 1981, after the Potters died, Sirius Black was believed to have blown Peter Pettigrew to pieces in a Muggle street. The Ministry awarded Pettigrew the Order of Merlin, First Class, after his death. He had not died. He had spent the next twelve years as a rat.

In June 1994 Cornelius Fudge talked of giving Severus Snape the Order of Merlin, Second Class, for his part in the capture of Black, or First Class if he could manage it. Black escaped that same night. Fudge withdrew the award.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Gilderoy Lockhart introduced himself to Harry's class at their first lesson as 'Gilderoy Lockhart, Order of Merlin, Third Class, Honorary Member of the Dark Force Defence League, and five times winner of Witch Weekly's Most Charming Smile Award.'

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Cornelius Fudge told Madam Rosmerta at the Three Broomsticks that Peter Pettigrew had got the Order of Merlin, First Class, 'which was something, I hope, for his poor mother.' In Chapter Eleven Ron told Harry what Pettigrew's mother had got back: 'The Order of Merlin, First Class, and Pettigrew's finger in a box.' In Chapter Twelve the award was on the list of facts about Black's crime that Harry went over at night instead of sleeping.

In Chapter Twenty, Fudge talked of rewarding Snape for the capture of Black. 'Order of Merlin, Second Class, I'd say. First Class, if I can wangle it!' Hermione told Dumbledore that Pettigrew had cut off his own finger so that everybody would think he was dead. The Ministry, she said, had given him the Order of Merlin for it.

In Chapter Twenty-One, with Black gone, Fudge told Snape that he would have to reconsider the award. 'Next time, perhaps!' In Chapter Twenty-Two, Lupin told Harry that this had been the final straw for Snape. 'I think the loss of the Order of Merlin hit him hard.'

pages.title: The Hero's Journey
pages.html:
The Hero's Journey is the pattern that the Muggle scholar Joseph Campbell found beneath the hero stories of every age and people. The hero is called away from ordinary life into a world of wonders. There he meets a guide, passes through trials, wins a great victory and comes home changed, with something to give the people he left behind.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, at Flourish and Blotts in August 1992, Gilderoy Lockhart hauled Harry Potter to the front of the crowd for the Daily Prophet's photographer. He announced that Harry had come in to buy his autobiography, which Harry flatly denied. Lockhart laughed it off and gave him the book free of charge. 'In the hopes this helps his Hero's Journey. That's Joseph Campbell, by the way. A Muggle, but a very smart man.' Then he announced that he would be teaching Defence Against the Dark Arts at Hogwarts that September, and presented Harry with his entire works. Harry tipped the lot into Ginny Weasley's cauldron.

pages.title: Deathday
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The anniversary of a ghost's death
pages.html:
A deathday is the anniversary of a ghost's death. Ghosts may celebrate one with a Deathday Party, especially a round-numbered one, and hardly any living people are ever invited.

Deathday parties

They are held at night by the light of black candles. The food is left to go rotten, since that is the only way a ghost can come close to tasting it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Nearly Headless Nick invited Harry Potter to his five hundredth deathday party, on Hallowe'en 1992, in one of the roomier dungeons. Harry accepted, though it meant missing the school feast. Hermione Granger was thrilled: hardly anybody living, she said, ever got invited to one. At breakfast she reminded him bossily that a promise was a promise, and she did not give him the smallest chance to wriggle out of it.

The dungeon was full of hundreds of ghosts, waltzing to thirty musical saws under a chandelier of a thousand black candles. The living guests could see their breath. On the tables lay great rotten fish, cakes burned to charcoal and a haggis crawling with maggots, with a grey cake shaped like a tombstone in pride of place. Hermione supposed that the food was left to go off so that the ghosts could just about taste it.

pages.title: Heir of Slytherin
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Opening the Chamber of Secrets and commanding its monster
Tom Riddle, blamed on Rubeus Hagrid
Riddle's diary, through the possessed Dracina Malfoy
Dracina Malfoy, Harry Potter, Rubeus Hagrid
pages.html:
The Heir of Slytherin is the descendant of Salazar Slytherin who, according to legend, alone can open the Chamber of Secrets and command the monster inside it, to purge Hogwarts of the Muggle-born. The true heir is Tom Riddle, Lord Voldemort, Slytherin's last living descendant. In 1992 to 1993 the heir's work was done by the memory in Riddle's diary, through the possessed Dracina Malfoy, while the whole school took Harry Potter for the heir.

The legend

The legend, as Professor Binns told it to his class in 1992, says that Salazar Slytherin sealed his Chamber so that none might open it until his own true heir came to the school. The heir alone would be able to break the seal and release the horror within, to cleanse the school of all those unworthy to learn magic. The heir was said to be sworn to purge the school of the Muggle-born. Parseltongue, Slytherin's famous gift, is the mark of the line and the key to the Chamber.

The legend has the founder's purpose wrong. Slytherin kept his Basilisk to defend Hogwarts from Muggles. It was his use of it for that purpose, not any wish to purge the school, that parted him from Godric Gryffindor. The Sorting Hat, which knew him, insists that he was never evil.

Slytherin's line

Slytherin's blood came down through the Gaunt family to Tom Marvolo Riddle, the son of Merope Gaunt and a Muggle, Tom Riddle. His mother lived just long enough to name him: Tom after his father, Marvolo after her own father, Marvolo Gaunt.

Riddle discovered his ancestry at Hogwarts. He opened the Chamber in his fifth year, in 1943, and when a Muggle-born girl called Myrtle died, he framed the third-year Rubeus Hagrid for it. As Lord Voldemort, Riddle is the last living descendant of Slytherin.

In the saga

On Hallowe'en 1992 a message on the second-floor wall warned the enemies of the heir to beware. Dracina Malfoy pushed to the front of the crowd with a red stain on her finger, and repeated the warning at Hermione Granger: 'You'll be next, Mudblood!'

Harry, Ron and Hermione were convinced that Dracina was the heir. Hermione brewed Polyjuice Potion so that the boys could question her in the Slytherin common room.

In December Harry spoke Parseltongue to a conjured snake at the Duelling Club, and the school decided that he was the heir. Ernie Macmillan said so to half of Hufflepuff in the library. Justin Finch-Fletchley ran from him, while Fred and George mocked the whole idea. Dracina herself gazed at Harry in rapture after the duel, and whispered that it was him, that it always had been. Then she told the school, Harry included, that she knew he was the heir and was on his side.

At Christmas, disguised as Goyle, with Ron as Crabbe, Harry heard her describe her lost hours, the red on her hands and the comfort of Tom in her diary. Harry took the diary away with him. In February 1993 it showed him a memory of 13 June 1943, in which Riddle caught Hagrid with a monster in a box, and for a while Harry concluded that Hagrid had opened the Chamber.

In the spring Ernie asked Harry whether Dracina was the heir, and Harry could only answer 'Maybe'. In the Chamber, Riddle's memory, grown solid, told him the truth. The heir's acts of that year had been his own, carried out through Dracina. With Harry's own wand he wrote his name in the air in letters of thin fire, TOM MARVOLO RIDDLE, then rearranged them to read I AM LORD VOLDEMORT. Harry told him to his face: 'You're a half-blood, Tom. Just like me.'

Afterwards Dumbledore told Harry that his Parseltongue had come from Voldemort on the night he was marked. It was his choices, Dumbledore said, not his abilities, that showed what he truly was.

pages.title: Harry's inner voice
infobox: Only once, before the Mirror of Erised
pages.html:
Harry Potter's inner voice is the small, mean voice in the back of his head that tells him he is useless and unwanted. The Dursleys spent ten years training it, and it sounds like all three of them at once.

How it works

The voice is quiet at Hogwarts, where people are kind to him, and it grows fainter with every kind word. It is loudest at Privet Drive. It laughs at most of his hopes, and it comes back whenever he is frightened or blames himself. Only once has it ever fallen silent: in front of the Mirror of Erised, and then not for long.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, the voice grew fainter with every kind word the Quidditch team said to Harry. In Book One, Chapter Eight, on Christmas Day 1991, it told him that he did not deserve his presents. Over Christmas dinner it laughed at him, reminding him that he would be on the train back to the Dursleys in the summer, and by the end of the meal it was louder than it had been all day. In front of the Mirror of Erised it fell silent for the first time in his life. When his fingers met the cold glass, it began to laugh again.

It came back in the chamber of flying keys in Book One, Chapter Twelve: ‘You’ll never do it. You’ve never been good at anything.’ In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, as Quirrell closed in on him, it was there again: ‘Useless. Failure. Of course you’re going to die, you’ve never done one thing right in your life.’

In Book Two, Chapter One, in the summer of 1992, it rang at Privet Drive like a bell, telling him that his friends had only ever pretended to like him. In Book Two, Chapter Three, at the Burrow, it called him ungrateful and asked why anybody would let him stay anywhere. In Book Two, Chapter Six, when the Whomping Willow came crashing down where Ron Weasley had been lying, it told Harry that Ron was dead and that it was his fault. It had never been so loud.

pages.title: Gilderoy Lockhart's Guide to Household Pests
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Gold lettering; a winking photograph of the author
pages.html:
Gilderoy Lockhart's Guide to Household Pests is a book of advice on ridding a house or garden of gnomes and other nuisances. Its cover has the author's name in swirling gold letters, with a large photograph of him underneath, winking. Molly Weasley keeps it on her kitchen mantelpiece and thinks it wonderful.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1992, Mrs Weasley pulled it down from the mantelpiece at the Burrow to see what Lockhart had to say about de-gnoming. George groaned that they knew how to de-gnome a garden. Harry Potter looked at the cover, where a very good-looking wizard with wavy blond hair kept winking up at them in a way Harry found hard to warm to. 'Oh, he is marvellous,' said Mrs Weasley. 'So dishy, and he knows his household pests, all right, it's a wonderful book...' Fred whispered that Mum fancied him.

pages.title: Magical Me
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Flourish and Blotts, 12.30 to 4.30 p.m., August 1992
pages.html:
Magical Me is the autobiography of Gilderoy Lockhart. It spent six solid months at the top of the bestseller list, a fact Lockhart was always happy to mention.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, a banner across the upper windows of Flourish and Blotts announced that Lockhart would be signing copies of his autobiography that day, from 12.30 to 4.30. It was the August day in 1992 that ended in a brawl in the shop. The crowd was mostly witches of Mrs Weasley's age. Lockhart spotted Harry Potter in it and gave him a free copy. Then he announced that Harry and his schoolfellows would shortly be getting the real thing: he was to be their new Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher. 'God help us all,' Harry said, before he could stop himself. Luckily the cheering drowned him out.

In Chapter Eight, Harry was addressing envelopes for him in detention when he heard a voice that nobody else could hear, and cried out. Lockhart took it for admiration. 'Six solid months at the top of the bestseller list!' he said. 'Broke all records!'

In Chapter Eleven, after Harry had played the Wagga Wagga werewolf for a whole lesson, Lockhart set the class an ode for Thursday, twelve lines at the very least, on his triumph at Wagga Wagga. The finest was to be rewarded with a signed copy of Magical Me.

pages.title: Break with a Banshee
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Break with a Banshee is one of the memoirs of Gilderoy Lockhart, in which he tells how he banished the Bandon Banshee. It was on the Hogwarts second-year booklist for 1992 to 1993, together with six more of his books.

Description

Like every book Lockhart wrote, it tells of a deed somebody else did. The Bandon Banshee was really seen off by a witch with a hairy chin, who lost all memory of it to his Memory Charm. Lockhart put his own name on the cover instead.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, the book appeared on Harry Potter's list for his second year, the first of seven titles by Lockhart. Fred Weasley guessed that the new Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher must be a fan. At Flourish and Blotts, Harry, Ron and Hermione each grabbed a copy before creeping up the long queue towards the table where Lockhart sat signing.

In Chapter Eighteen, in May 1993, Lockhart owned up to Harry and Ron in his office, while he packed to run away. His books would not have sold a quarter as well, he said, if people had not believed he had done it all himself. Besides, the witch who saw off the Bandon Banshee had a hairy chin.

pages.title: Gadding with Ghouls
infobox: Gilderoy Lockhart, Hogwarts set text, book, Lockhart
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Lockhart catching a ghoul with a tea-strainer
pages.html:
Gadding with Ghouls is one of the memoirs of Gilderoy Lockhart, and the one he thinks his best. It was a set text for second years at Hogwarts in 1992 to 1993. It ends with Lockhart catching the last ghoul with nothing but a tea-strainer. Like all his books, it describes deeds that other people did, before he wiped their memories.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Lockhart let a cage of Cornish pixies loose on his class. Four of them got into Dracina Malfoy's hair. 'Potter, do something!' she screamed. Harry waded in with his copy of the book, beat them off her, then knocked the last one out of her hair with the spine. She sat perfectly still, with her hands over her face.

In Chapter Eleven Hermione Granger kept three pictures of Angelus folded inside the cover of her copy. One was an engraving, while two had been cut out of a book on vampire history; in all three he was brooding. That autumn she needed a teacher's signature for a book in the Restricted Section. She told Lockhart that it might help her understand a part of Gadding with Ghouls. Lockhart beamed at her. 'Between ourselves, I think it might be the best thing I've ever written.' The tea-strainer, she told him, had made her put the book down to walk round the room. He signed the note with a gigantic peacock quill. Afterwards she held the book to her chest with both arms, the way a small girl holds a doll.

In Chapter Seventeen, listening to Lockhart hint that he had always known Hagrid was a bad lot, Harry wanted to throw the book straight into his gleaming face. In Book Three, Chapter Three, in August 1993, Harry remembered how Hermione had charmed that signature out of Lockhart, hugging the book afterwards. He put on the same face himself to charm Cornelius Fudge.

pages.title: Holidays with Hags
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Holidays with Hags is one of the memoirs of Gilderoy Lockhart, an account of time spent among hags. It was on the Hogwarts second-year booklist for 1992 to 1993, together with six more of his books. Like all of them, it tells of deeds that other people did, before he wiped their memories.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1992, the Hogwarts letters came to the Burrow at breakfast. Harry Potter's list for his second year had seven of Lockhart's books on it, from Break with a Banshee to Year with the Yeti, Holidays with Hags among them. Fred Weasley, who had been told to get the same books, decided the new Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher must be a fan. George warned that Lockhart's books were really expensive, and Mrs Weasley, looking worried, said they would manage.

pages.title: Travels with Trolls
infobox: Gilderoy Lockhart, Hogwarts set text, book
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Second-year Defence Against the Dark Arts, Hogwarts, 1992 to 1993
A winking portrait of the author
pages.html:
Travels with Trolls is one of Gilderoy Lockhart's books of his own adventures, in this case among trolls. It was one of the seven Lockhart titles set for second-year Defence Against the Dark Arts at Hogwarts in the school year 1992 to 1993, when Lockhart himself taught the subject. Like the rest of his books, it tells of deeds that other people had really done, before Lockhart wiped their memories and took the credit.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, the book was on Harry Potter's second-year list. In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Lockhart began his first lesson by picking up Neville Longbottom's copy and holding it up, so that the class could see his own portrait winking on the cover. He winked too. Then he set them a quiz about himself.

In Book Two, Chapter Sixteen, Harry found his dormitory ransacked. The contents of his trunk had been flung all over the room, and he trod on loose pages of his Travels with Trolls on his way across to his bed. Somebody had been looking for something.

pages.title: Voyages with Vampires
infobox: Gilderoy Lockhart, Hogwarts set text, book
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Vampires, and Lockhart's adventures among them
Second-year Defence Against the Dark Arts, Hogwarts, 1992 to 1993
pages.html:
Voyages with Vampires is Gilderoy Lockhart's book on vampires, written up as the story of his own travels among them. It was a set text for second-year Defence Against the Dark Arts at Hogwarts in the school year 1992 to 1993. Most of what Hermione Granger knew about vampires in her second year came out of it.

Contents

Whatever the truth of Lockhart's own part in it, the book is a fair general guide to the Kindred. It describes the thirteen vampire clans, among them the Ventrue, who think themselves royalty, and the Nosferatu. It tells of Angelus, of the Aurelian bloodline, who went right across Europe in the eighteenth century. There is William the Bloody, sired in London, whose name came from his poetry. Chapter nine is given to Dracula, together with the Belmont family, who have hunted him down the centuries with a whip.

Not all of it is right. Hermione took from it that the Belmonts had been hunting Dracula for about four hundred years, when in fact they have hunted him since 1094.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, the book was on Harry Potter's second-year list, among seven titles by Lockhart.

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, on the first morning of term, Hermione had it propped open against the milk jug at breakfast. She told Harry, with shining enthusiasm, about the clans, the Ventrue, Angelus and a whole convent in London. She told him about William the Bloody. Dracula was real, she said; he was in chapter nine. A family called the Belmonts had been hunting him for about four hundred years, with a whip. Every hundred years or so he came back, and one of them had to go up the mountain.

Ron Weasley told her he was eating. She shut the book when his Howler had finished. After lunch she had her nose in it again on a step in the courtyard, somewhere round the Nosferatu, Harry supposed. When Ron pulled out his wand on Dracina Malfoy there, Hermione shut the book with a snap and warned him that Lockhart was coming.

pages.title: Wanderings with Werewolves
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Werewolves, and Lockhart's adventures among them
Second-year Defence Against the Dark Arts, Hogwarts, 1992 to 1993
pages.html:
Wanderings with Werewolves is Gilderoy Lockhart's book of his adventures among werewolves, and one of the seven Lockhart titles set for second years at Hogwarts in the school year 1992 to 1993. The village it tells of was really saved from its werewolves by an old Armenian warlock. Lockhart found out how he had done it, wiped his memory and put the story in a book of his own.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Lockhart set his first class a quiz about himself. Afterwards he told them that a few of them needed to read Wanderings with Werewolves more carefully. In chapter twelve, he said, he clearly stated that his ideal birthday present would be harmony between all magic and non-magic peoples, though he would not say no to a large bottle of Ogden's Old Firewhisky. Ron Weasley stared at him in open disbelief.

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, packing to run away, Lockhart admitted the truth to Harry and Ron. Nobody, he said, wanted to read about some ugly old Armenian warlock, even if he did rid a village of werewolves. The warlock would have looked dreadful on a cover.

pages.title: Year with the Yeti
infobox: Gilderoy Lockhart, Hogwarts set text, book
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A year Lockhart claims to have spent with a yeti
Second-year Defence Against the Dark Arts, Hogwarts, 1992 to 1993
pages.html:
Year with the Yeti is Gilderoy Lockhart's account of a year he claims to have spent with a yeti, and one of the seven Lockhart titles set for second years at Hogwarts in the school year 1992 to 1993. In it Lockhart reveals that his favourite colour is lilac. That part, at least, is true. The deeds were somebody else's.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, after the quiz at his first lesson, Lockhart told the class that hardly any of them had remembered his favourite colour was lilac, though he said so in Year with the Yeti.

In Book Two, Chapter Fifteen, Hermione Granger announced from her bed in the hospital wing that she did not like Lockhart any more. She thought he was lying about a great many things. She was drawing breath to explain exactly what, starting with the Master, when Madam Pomfrey shooed Harry and Ron out. She had meant to work her way through the whole of Year with the Yeti.

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, when Lockhart packed to flee, his lilac robes were bundled into a trunk with the jade green and the midnight blue.

pages.title: The Standard Book of Spells, Grade 2
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Standard Book of Spells, one grade for each year at school
pages.html:
The Standard Book of Spells, Grade 2 is the Charms textbook for second years at Hogwarts. It is the second volume of Miranda Goshawk's graded series, with one grade for each year at the school. In 1992 it was the only book on the second-year list that Gilderoy Lockhart had not written.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, the book headed the list that came with Harry Potter's Hogwarts letter in the summer of 1992, above seven titles by Lockhart.

Harry was apt to forget it. In Book Two, Chapter Nine, he had to go back up to the dormitory for it, and Hermione Granger was waiting at the foot of the stairs when he came down. He always forgot it on Thursdays, she told him. He had not known that himself.

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Ron Weasley sat in the common room in a foul temper, blotting his Charms homework. When he reached absent-mindedly for his wand to clear the smudges, it set the parchment on fire. Ron slammed the book shut, fuming nearly as much as his homework.

pages.title: Miranda Goshawk
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
The Standard Book of Spells, Grades 1 to 7
pages.html:
Miranda Goshawk is the witch who wrote The Standard Book of Spells, the series of Charms textbooks from which Hogwarts pupils learn their spells. There is one grade for each year of school, from Grade 1 for first-years to Grade 7 for the seventh year, so every pupil needs a new one each September.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, The Standard Book of Spells, Grade 2 by Miranda Goshawk headed the list of books Harry Potter needed for his second year. The other seven books on the list were all by Gilderoy Lockhart.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, The Standard Book of Spells, Grade Three was one of the last books on Harry's list at Flourish and Blotts.

pages.title: A Beginner's Guide to Transfiguration
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
A Beginner's Guide to Transfiguration, by Emeric Switch, is the Transfiguration set book for first years at Hogwarts. Copies last for years, which is as well in a family with seven children. Ginny Weasley began school in 1992 with a very old, very battered second-hand one.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, Lucius Malfoy drew Ginny's copy out of her cauldron in Flourish and Blotts, from among the glossy new Lockharts, to mock the Weasleys' poverty. When the fight that followed was over, he thrust it back at her: 'Here, girl. Take your book. It's the best your father can give you.' Dracina, beside her, knocked it straight out of her hands on to the floor. Ginny slapped Dracina's own book out of her grip in return.

Lucius then told his daughter to pick the book up for her, since they were dignified pure-bloods. Dracina crouched to sweep up the whole heap at her feet, Ginny's books and her own. She pressed one into Ginny's hands without looking at it, then stuffed the rest into her own bag. Among them was a small black book that Harry had not noticed before.

pages.title: Encyclopaedia of Toadstools
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Hitting Lucius Malfoy in the eye, August 1992
pages.html:
The Encyclopaedia of Toadstools is a heavy reference book on fungi. In August 1992 a copy caught Lucius Malfoy in the eye during his fight with Arthur Weasley in Flourish and Blotts.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Lucius Malfoy sneered at the Weasleys in the middle of a crowded bookshop, and Arthur Weasley went for him. The two of them rolled across the floor in a tangle of robes and Lockharts. Hagrid had to wade through the sea of books to pull them apart by their collars. Arthur had a cut lip. Lucius had been caught in the eye by an Encyclopaedia of Toadstools, and he was still holding Ginny's old Transfiguration book.

pages.title: Prefects Who Gained Power
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Hogwarts prefects and their later careers
A junk shop in Diagon Alley
pages.html:
Prefects Who Gained Power is a small, deeply boring book. Its back cover calls it a study of Hogwarts prefects and their later careers. Percy Weasley, a prefect with his eye on the Ministry, found it absorbing.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, in August 1992, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger came upon Percy in a tiny junk shop in Diagon Alley. Among the broken wands, the wonky brass scales and the old cloaks stiff with potion stains, he was deep in Prefects Who Gained Power. Ron read the back aloud and said it sounded fascinating. Percy told him to go away. As they left, Ron told the others in an undertone that Percy wanted to be Minister for Magic, with ideas that would make Grindelwald tell him to steady on.

pages.title: Charm Your Own Cheese
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
On the kitchen mantelpiece at the Burrow
pages.html:
Charm Your Own Cheese is a wizarding cookery book on making cheese by magic. A copy stands on the kitchen mantelpiece at the Burrow, the Weasleys' house, with Enchantment in Baking and One Minute Feasts: It's Magic!

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1992, Harry Potter sat down in the Burrow's kitchen, the first wizard's house he had ever been inside. Books stood three deep along the mantelpiece, with titles like Charm Your Own Cheese. On the wall opposite hung a clock with one hand and no numbers, marked with things like Time to make tea. It was so cosy it made his throat ache.

pages.title: Enchantment in Baking
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
On the kitchen mantelpiece at the Burrow
pages.html:
Enchantment in Baking is a wizarding cookery book on baking with magic. Molly Weasley, who cooks for a large family, mostly by magic, keeps it on the kitchen mantelpiece at the Burrow. It stands there three deep with the others, among them Charm Your Own Cheese and One Minute Feasts: It's Magic!

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1992, Harry Potter saw it on the mantelpiece the first time he sat down in the Burrow's kitchen. It was the first wizard's house he had ever been inside, and it was so cosy it made his throat ache.

pages.title: One Minute Feasts: It's Magic!
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
On the kitchen mantelpiece at the Burrow
pages.html:
One Minute Feasts: It's Magic! is a wizarding cookery book that promises whole meals in a minute. Molly Weasley keeps a copy on the kitchen mantelpiece at the Burrow, where the books stand three deep.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, in the summer of 1992, Harry Potter sat at the Weasleys' kitchen table for the first time. It was the first wizard's house he had ever been inside. Books stood three deep along the mantelpiece, with titles like Charm Your Own Cheese, Enchantment in Baking and One Minute Feasts: It's Magic! on their spines. The clock on the wall had one hand and no numbers. The wireless by the sink was about to play Celestina Warbeck. The cosiness of it all made Harry's throat ache.

pages.title: The Adventures of Martin Miggs, the Mad Muggle
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Adventures of Martin Miggs, the Mad Muggle is a wizarding comic about a Muggle called Martin Miggs. Ron Weasley collects it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, Ron showed Harry Potter his bedroom at the top of the Burrow in the summer of 1992. His schoolbooks were heaped in a corner beside a pile of comics, every one of them about Martin Miggs. His wand lay on a fish tank full of frogspawn on the windowsill, next to Scabbers, asleep in a patch of sun. Ron watched Harry almost nervously, as though waiting to hear a verdict on the room.

pages.title: Witching Hour
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
On the Weasleys' wireless at the Burrow, August 1992
pages.html:
Witching Hour is a wizarding wireless programme that features the popular singing sorceress Celestina Warbeck. Molly Weasley is fond of her songs.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, on his first morning at the Burrow in the summer of 1992, Harry Potter heard the old wireless by the kitchen sink announce that Witching Hour was coming up next, with Celestina Warbeck. The kitchen had a clock that told the time in jobs, such as feeding the chickens, and the mantelpiece was stacked three deep with books of household magic. It was so cosy that it made his throat ache.

pages.title: Mafalda Hopkirk's warning letter
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Mafalda Hopkirk, Improper Use of Magic Office
A Hover Charm, at twelve minutes past nine
The Decree for the Reasonable Restriction of Underage Sorcery, 1875
pages.html:
Mafalda Hopkirk's warning letter was the official warning the Ministry of Magic sent Harry Potter on his twelfth birthday, 31 July 1992, for a Hover Charm he had not performed. It told him that further spellwork could get him expelled. It ended by wishing him a happy holiday.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, the house-elf Dobby made Aunt Petunia's pudding float during the Dursleys' dinner for the Masons, then dropped it on the kitchen floor. Uncle Vernon might still have saved his deal, but the owl finished it: an enormous barn owl flew in through the dining-room window and dropped the letter on Mrs Mason's head. When the Masons had gone, Uncle Vernon thrust the letter into Harry's face and made him read it. It began: 'We have received intelligence that a Hover Charm was used at your place of residence this evening at twelve minutes past nine.' It reminded him that underage wizards were not permitted to perform spells outside school, and that any magic which risked notice by Muggles was a serious offence under the Statute of Secrecy. It closed: 'Enjoy your holidays!'

Uncle Vernon had not known until then that Harry was forbidden magic at home. He locked him in his bedroom that night. The next morning he paid a man to put bars on the window.

pages.title: Molly Weasley's letter to Dumbledore
infobox: Where Harry Potter would live from now on
pages.html:
Molly Weasley's letter to Dumbledore was written at the Burrow in August 1992, after Harry Potter had told her what life with the Dursleys was like. It informed the Headmaster, in terms that left no room for discussion, where Harry would be living from now on.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, Harry was staying at the Burrow. He had told Mrs Weasley about the Dursleys on the sofa on his first morning there. She put some of what she felt into the letter. Besides settling where Harry would live, it informed Dumbledore of several other things, chief among them her opinion of a Headmaster who had let it go on for eleven years. Ron knew that opinion well. His mother had given it at the kitchen table, in a voice that made the crockery hum. What she did not put in the letter she kept, and fed, while she waited.

pages.title: Flying Ford Anglia Mystifies Muggles
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
FLYING FORD ANGLIA MYSTIFIES MUGGLES was the headline in the Daily Prophet on the evening of 1 September 1992. The story reported six or seven Muggle sightings of the flying car in which Harry Potter and Ron Weasley had gone to Hogwarts.

The story

The car was Arthur Weasley's old Ford Anglia, which he had enchanted to fly. Two Muggles in London were convinced they had seen it over the Post Office Tower. At noon in Norfolk Mrs Hetty Bayliss saw it while hanging out her washing. Mr Angus Fleet, of Peebles, reported it to the police.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Six, Professor Snape took the two boys down to his office, unrolled that evening's Prophet and held it up. 'You were seen,' he hissed. Harry read the headline. 'Bugger,' he said. Snape read the story aloud.

pages.title: Lockhart's quiz
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Lockhart's quiz opened Gilderoy Lockhart's very first Defence Against the Dark Arts lesson at Hogwarts, in September 1992. It ran to three sides, the class had thirty minutes to do it, and every question was about Lockhart. Only Hermione Granger got full marks.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Lockhart went through the papers in front of the second-years. Hardly any of them had remembered that his favourite colour was lilac, though he said so in Year with the Yeti. A few needed to read Wanderings with Werewolves more carefully, since he clearly stated in its twelfth chapter that his ideal birthday present would be harmony between all magic and non-magic peoples. Ron Weasley stared at him in open disbelief. Hermione, however, had known his secret ambition: to rid the world of evil and market his own range of hair-care potions. Lockhart turned her paper over, cried 'Full marks!' and gave Gryffindor ten points. Then he lifted a large covered cage on to his desk.

pages.title: Snape's note to the Slytherin team
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
To train the new Seeker, Dracina Malfoy
pages.html:
Snape's note to the Slytherin team was a signed note from Professor Snape giving the Slytherin Quidditch team the pitch on Saturday 5 September 1992, so that they could train their new Seeker. Oliver Wood had booked the pitch for Gryffindor that morning. The note overrode him.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eight, the Gryffindors had been out since dawn when the Slytherins walked on to the pitch. Wood bellowed that it was their practice time. Marcus Flint produced the note and read it out: 'I, Professor S. Snape, give the Slytherin team permission to practise today on the Quidditch pitch, owing to the need to train their new Seeker.' The new Seeker pushed her way out from behind six large teammates. It was Dracina Malfoy, looking enormously pleased with herself. Her father had just bought the whole team new brooms.

pages.title: The message on the wall
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Between two windows on the second floor at Hogwarts
'THE CHAMBER OF SECRETS HAS BEEN OPENED. ENEMIES OF THE HEIR, BEWARE.'
Tom Riddle, with Dracina Malfoy's hands
pages.html:
The message on the wall is the warning that appeared on the second floor at Hogwarts on Hallowe'en 1992, daubed between two tall windows in letters a foot high that glimmered red in the torchlight: 'THE CHAMBER OF SECRETS HAS BEEN OPENED. ENEMIES OF THE HEIR, BEWARE.' Mrs Norris hung stiff from a torch bracket beneath it.

Who wrote it

The hand was Dracina Malfoy's, though she did not know it. Tom Riddle's diary had slipped so far into her that it could use her hands and walk her about the castle. 'I wrote on the wall with her hands,' Riddle told Harry Potter in the Chamber in May 1993. On the night itself, nobody noticed the red stain down the side of the finger she pointed with.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger were the first to find it, after following the voice only Harry could hear. Hermione screamed and flung her arms round Harry. Then the feast ended, and the corridor filled with students from both ends. Dracina pushed to the front, dishevelled, so pale that she was almost grey. Pointing straight at Hermione, she shouted: 'Enemies of the heir, beware! You'll be next, Mudblood!' Harry shouted at her to leave Hermione alone. She turned on her heel and pushed back into the crowd.

In Chapter Ten the letters were still wet as the crowd broke up. For days afterwards Argus Filch scrubbed at them with Mrs Skower's All-Purpose Magical Mess Remover, which did no good whatever. They went on gleaming as brightly as on the night they were written.

pages.title: Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The five hundredth anniversary of Nick's death
Hundreds of ghosts; three living students
pages.html:
Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party was held in one of the dungeons at Hogwarts on 31 October 1992, five hundred years to the day after Sir Nicholas de Mimsy-Porpington's botched beheading. Hundreds of ghosts came to it from all over Britain. So did three living guests, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, who missed the Hallowe'en feast to be there.

Deathdays

A deathday is the anniversary of a ghost's death, which some ghosts keep as the living keep their birthdays. Ghosts cannot eat, though many of them miss it badly, so the food at a deathday party is left to rot until its smell is strong enough for them almost to taste.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, the Headless Hunt turned Nick down yet again in October 1992. Still smarting, he saved Harry from a punishment in Filch's office, and in gratitude Harry promised to come to his party. Ron was appalled at missing the feast. Hermione held them both to the promise.

The dungeon was lit by black candles under a chandelier blazing midnight blue. It was like walking into a cold store. Thirty musical saws played on a platform draped in black while hundreds of pearly ghosts waltzed: a huddle of gloomy nuns, a ragged man in chains, the Bloody Baron and Moaning Myrtle among them. The Fat Friar was deep in conversation with a knight who had an arrow sticking out of his forehead. The Wailing Widow had come all the way up from Kent. Hermione got out of Brother Aldric of Glastonbury where he had hidden his abbey's books.

On the banquet table lay rotten fish, cakes burnt to charcoal, a maggoty haggis and a slab of furry green cheese. In pride of place stood a grey cake shaped like a tombstone, inscribed in tarry icing: Sir Nicholas de Mimsy-Porpington, died 31st October, 1492. A portly ghost walked slowly through the table with his mouth open, trying to taste a stinking salmon. 'Almost,' he said sadly.

Nick was about to make his speech when a dozen ghost horses burst out of the wall, every rider headless, with Sir Patrick Delaney-Podmore at their head. Sir Patrick mocked Nick in front of everybody. Harry shouted at him to get out, and got a sneer of aristocratic contempt: 'We go where we please, boy!' Harry told the room that Nick was a great ghost. 'And he'd plaster the walls with all of you lot if you didn't keep running away from him on your horses.' One of the nuns gave a single scandalised giggle. Nick looked at Harry as though he had waited five hundred years for somebody to take his side. Nobody heard much of his speech, though, because the Hunt had started a game of Head Hockey.

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, after they had been found that night beside Filch's Petrified cat, the three of them had to explain to the teachers why they had missed the feast. There had been hundreds of ghosts, they said, and Nick had invited them. 'We had to listen to the musical saws, Professor.'

pages.title: Hallowe'en feast
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Live bats; Hagrid's pumpkins, carved into lanterns
pages.html:
The Hallowe'en feast is held in the Great Hall at Hogwarts every year on 31 October, and it is one of the great occasions of the school year. In each of Harry Potter's first three years at the school, something went badly wrong on the night of it.

The feast

From the morning of Hallowe'en the corridors smell of baking pumpkin. The Great Hall is hung with live bats. Hagrid grows the pumpkins in the patch behind his hut, swelling them through the autumn until they are the size of garden sheds, before they are carved into lanterns. After the pudding there is sometimes entertainment. In 1993 the Hogwarts ghosts did formation flying, and Nearly Headless Nick had a great success with a re-enactment of his own bungled beheading.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Six, at the feast of 1991, Professor Quirrell came sprinting into the Hall with his turban askew. He gasped out that there was a troll in the dungeons, then fainted. He had let it in himself.

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, the Hall in 1992 had the usual live bats, and Hagrid's monstrous pumpkins had been carved into lanterns big enough for three men to sit in. There was a rumour that Dumbledore had booked a troupe of dancing skeletons for after the pudding. Harry, Ron and Hermione missed all of it, because they had promised to go to Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party in the dungeons. On their way up from the party they found the first message of the heir of Slytherin on a wall of the second floor, with Filch's cat hanging Petrified beneath it.

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, after the ghosts' entertainment at the feast of 1993, the Gryffindors went up to their tower and found the Fat Lady's portrait slashed to ribbons. Sirius Black had tried to get in.

pages.title: The 1992 Ministry raids
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Dark objects, and Muggle artefacts bewitched against the law
Arthur Weasley, nine raids in one night
Lucius Malfoy's sale of his Dark objects
Searched in December 1992; the Ministry missed the hidden room under the drawing-room floor
pages.html:
The Ministry raids of 1992 were a wave of searches of wizarding homes that the Ministry of Magic carried out in the summer of 1992. Arthur Weasley took part in nine of them in a single night. Lucius Malfoy, expecting a visit, quietly sold off some of the things at home that might have incriminated him. When the Ministry did search Malfoy Manor, that December, it found very little.

The raids

The raiders were looking for Dark objects, and for Muggle things bewitched against the law, which is the business of Arthur's own Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office. They were not popular with the people raided. Mundungus Fletcher tried to put a hex on Arthur while his back was turned. There were rumours, too, of a new Muggle Protection Act, which Lucius Malfoy blamed on Arthur.

Arthur's own shed is full of Muggle things that he takes apart, bewitches and puts back together. As his son Fred pointed out, if he ever raided his own house he would have to put himself straight under arrest.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, flying Harry Potter to the Burrow in August 1992, Fred told him about the shed. 'If he raided our house he'd have to put himself straight under arrest.'

In Book Two, Chapter Four, Arthur came home at breakfast after a long night at work. 'What a night,' he mumbled, groping for the teapot. 'Nine raids. Nine!'

In Book Two, Chapter Five, Harry came out of the Floo network in the wrong grate, in Borgin and Burkes, and overheard Lucius Malfoy. He unrolled a list for Mr Borgin of a few items at home that needed to be discreetly moved along, if the Ministry were to call. He had not been visited yet, he said, since the name Malfoy still commanded a certain respect. Later that day, in Flourish and Blotts, Lucius needled Arthur in front of everybody. 'Busy time at the Ministry, I hear,' he said. 'All those raids... I do hope they're paying you overtime?'

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, at Christmas 1992, Dracina told the two boys she took for Crabbe and Goyle that the Ministry had raided Malfoy Manor the week before. 'Not that they found much,' she said. Her father's precious Dark artefacts were kept in a room under the drawing-room floor that nobody knew about. The Ministry's men had walked right over the top of it, twice.

pages.title: Battle of Crécy
pages.html:
The Battle of Crécy was fought on 26 August 1346 in northern France, early in the Hundred Years' War. Edward III of England beat a far larger French army under Philip VI there, chiefly with his English and Welsh archers. Among the dead was a Welsh knight who still walks as a ghost, killed by a crossbow bolt that went straight through his visor.

The battle

Edward had landed in Normandy that July and marched north, burning as he went. Philip caught up with him near the village of Crécy. The English took up a position on a slope, with the men-at-arms on foot and the longbowmen on the flanks.

The French opened the attack late in the afternoon with their Genoese crossbowmen, who had marched all day and whose bowstrings had been soaked by a thunderstorm. The longbowmen shot them down. Then the archers cut to pieces one charge of French knights after another, until it was dark. The blind King John of Bohemia had himself led into the fighting with his horse tied to his knights' horses, and died there. Edward's sixteen-year-old son, the Black Prince, fought in the front line.

It was one of the worst defeats the French nobility ever suffered. It left Edward free to besiege Calais, which fell to him the following year.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, Ron Weasley asked Hermione Granger who all the ghosts at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party would be. Out came a torrent of famous deaths. Among them was a knight from Wales who had a crossbow bolt go straight through his visor at the Battle of Crécy.

pages.title: The Crusades
infobox: 1095, at the call of Pope Urban II
The recovery of Jerusalem and the Holy Land
1291, the end of the crusader kingdoms in the East
Into the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries
pages.html:
The Crusades were the holy wars that the Christian kingdoms of Europe fought from 1095 onwards, above all to win back Jerusalem and the Holy Land. Long after the last crusader city in the East had fallen, knights were still taking the cross. One of them was the husband of the Wailing Widow, who came home from the Crusades a week after she had drowned herself, in 1392.

The holy wars

Pope Urban II preached the first crusade at Clermont in 1095. In 1099 the crusaders took Jerusalem, and the kingdoms they founded in the East lasted for nearly two hundred years. Saladin retook the city in 1187. Richard the Lionheart fought him in the Third Crusade but never won it back. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade sacked Christian Constantinople instead, and in 1291 Acre, the last great crusader city, fell.

Crusading went on long after that, against the Moors, the pagans of the Baltic and the Turks. In 1390 English knights sailed against Mahdia in Barbary. In 1392 Henry Bolingbroke, the future King Henry IV, set out to fight beside the Teutonic Knights in Prussia.

The Kindred and the Crusades

The vampires of Europe went east with the Frankish armies, and the Assamites of Alamut fought them there. In 1141 a French crusader knight, Christof Romuald, was Embraced into Clan Brujah at Prague. Michael the Patriarch, the Toreador elder who ruled the Kindred of Constantinople and called the city his work of art, perished when the Fourth Crusade sacked the city in 1204.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, in October 1992, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter and Ron Weasley about the Wailing Widow, a ghost from Kent. She had drowned herself in a well in 1392 after her husband went off to the Crusades without coming back. He came back a week later. She has been wailing about it ever since.

pages.title: The Hufflepuff match
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Gryffindor won, Harry Potter catching the Snitch in about five minutes
Neville Longbottom against Crabbe and Goyle; Ron Weasley against Dracina Malfoy
pages.html:
The Hufflepuff match was the Quidditch match between Gryffindor and Hufflepuff in Harry Potter's first year at Hogwarts, refereed, to everyone's alarm, by Professor Snape. Harry caught the Snitch in about five minutes. The fight in the stands is better remembered. Neville Longbottom got the better of Crabbe and Goyle single-handed, while Dracina Malfoy screamed for help that never came. The pair have kept out of Neville's way ever since.

The referee

Snape had never refereed a Quidditch match before. Harry, Ron and Hermione took it as proof that he meant Harry harm. In fact, as Quirrell admitted at the end of the year, Snape had offered so that he could keep watch over Harry, whose broom had been jinxed at his first match.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, Dracina sat just behind Ron Weasley and Neville in the stands, needling them both. Crabbe sat on one side of her, Goyle on the other. When Harry went into a spectacular dive she leant forward to Ron's ear. 'You're in luck, Weasley! Potter's obviously spotted some money on the ground!' Ron launched himself at her, and the two of them went backwards over the bench.

'Crabbe! Goyle! Now!' she shrieked. Nothing happened. Neville had climbed over the seat to pull Ron off her before he was expelled for hitting a girl, and the two Slytherins found him in their way. To the astonishment of everybody, Neville included, he hit Goyle in the stomach. Then he took on both of them single-handed, making a surprisingly good job of it. When nobody came, Dracina stopped screaming and fought Ron herself. She raked four lines down his cheek, pulled out a handful of his hair and bit his ear.

Up in the air, Harry shot past Snape and pulled out of the dive with the Snitch in his fist. Nobody could remember it ever being caught so fast. Ron gave Dracina a black eye, by accident, he said. Neville was knocked out cold, but Madam Pomfrey said he would be fine. 'Mate, he battered them!' Ron told Harry.

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, Harry noticed in the autumn of 1992 that Crabbe and Goyle still made themselves scarce whenever Neville was about, as they had done ever since the Hufflepuff match.

pages.title: Ernie Macmillan
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (July 1998)
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Ernest Macmillan, known as Ernie, is a pure-blood wizard of Hufflepuff House in Harry Potter's year. Stout and pompous, he was the loudest of those who believed Harry to be the Heir of Slytherin during the attacks of 1992 to 1993, until he made a formal apology.

Life

Ernie is proud of his family, which he says can be traced back through nine generations of witches and wizards. He speaks with a self-important formality, as though he were addressing a meeting. His closest friends are his fellow Hufflepuffs Hannah Abbott and Justin Finch-Fletchley. Hufflepuff shares Herbology with Gryffindor, so Ernie has spent a good deal of his school life in the greenhouses alongside Harry's year.

In the saga

After Harry was revealed as a Parselmouth at the Duelling Club in December 1992, Ernie told Justin to stay in the dormitory. He was convinced that Harry was the Heir of Slytherin, a dark wizard powerful enough to have survived You-Know-Who's curse, since talking to snakes is what dark wizards do. He insisted that he had seen Harry set the snake on Justin. When Justin was found Petrified, he shouted that he had caught Harry red-handed. Professor McGonagall had him waft the Petrified Nearly Headless Nick up the stairs with a conjured fan. He went on saying it until Harry called him a complete plonker outside Herbology.

After Hermione's Petrification in 1993 Ernie formally apologised to Harry, and shook his hand. He then suggested that Dracina Malfoy might be the Heir instead. In early 1994 he told Ron that Hermione had never missed a Muggle Studies class, though many of them clashed with Divination.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, Ernie shouted hello to Harry Potter across the World Cup campsite on the morning of 22 August 1994. He was one of several Hogwarts students there with their families.

In their own words

He talks to snakes. Everyone knows that's what dark wizards do.Ernie Macmillan · B2 Ch12

pages.title: Warrington
infobox: Slytherin, Slytherin Quidditch team, Hogwarts student, Chaser
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Warrington is a Chaser on the Slytherin Quidditch team. He played against Gryffindor in November 1992, and again in the final of 1994, when the Weasley twins' Bludgers twice knocked the Quaffle out of his hands.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, in the match of November 1992, Warrington and Adrian Pucey sandwiched Alicia Spinnet between them. Madam Hooch blew her whistle at the pair of them.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, early in the final, Warrington intercepted the Quaffle from Alicia and went tearing up the field. Then a Bludger from George Weasley hit him, and he dropped it. Later Fred Weasley smashed another Bludger into him. Warrington dropped the Quaffle again, and Alicia snatched it out of the air to score, making it seventy points to ten.

pages.title: Millicent Bulstrode's cat
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Millicent Bulstrode's cat is the pet of the Slytherin girl Millicent Bulstrode. One of its hairs, caught on Hermione Granger's robes, turned Hermione part-cat when she put it into a Polyjuice Potion at Christmas 1992.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, Hermione kept a single dark hair that she had found on her robes after Millicent held her in a headlock at the Duelling Club. On Christmas Day 1992 she put it into her Polyjuice Potion, meaning to pass as Millicent in the Slytherin common room. Polyjuice Potion is not meant for animals. When she came out of her cubicle, her face was covered in black fur. Her eyes had gone yellow, and two long, pointed, furry ears were poking up out of her bushy hair. 'It was a c-cat hair!' she howled. 'It must have been off M-Millicent's cat!' Madam Pomfrey, who asked no questions, took one look at her and put her to bed in the hospital wing.

pages.title: Tracey Davis
pages.html:
Tracey Davis is a thin, dark Slytherin girl in Harry Potter's year, and a friend of Pansy Parkinson's. She was laughing with Pansy in the Slytherin common room on Christmas night 1992 when Dracina Malfoy flew at them.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, on Christmas night 1992, Harry was sitting by the fire in the Slytherin common room, disguised as Gregory Goyle with Polyjuice Potion. Pansy came through from the dormitories with a thin, dark girl he thought was called Tracey Davis. Pansy was laughing at the idea that Potter could be the Heir of Slytherin. Tracey sniggered. Then Dracina came out of her chair like a cork out of a bottle, screaming at Pansy to shut up, and Tracey squealed.

In Chapter Fifteen, on Boxing Day, it was all over the castle by lunchtime that Dracina had turned the Slytherin dungeon upside down looking for something she had lost. She had screamed at Pansy, at Tracey, at Crabbe and at Goyle. In Chapter Sixteen, on the morning of the Hufflepuff match, Harry looked across at the Slytherin table and stared. Dracina was sitting in the middle of it, radiant, laughing at something Pansy had said, with Pansy on one side of her and Tracey Davis on the other.

pages.title: Crabbe's older cousin
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter Eleven
pages.html:
Crabbe's older cousin is a Slytherin, a cousin of Vincent Crabbe's and older than him. At the Slytherin match against Gryffindor in November 1992 he took his jacket off, ready to fight.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, Dean Thomas led the Gryffindor stand in a song he had spent three weeks teaching the house. It went to a tune he had learnt on the terraces at West Ham, and it was very rude about Slytherins. By the third chorus it was coming from three sides of the stadium.
