The Aurelian line is a Ventrue bloodline founded by the vampire called the Master. Its most famous members are Darla, Angelus, Drusilla and William the Bloody. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries they terrorised Europe, in open defiance of the Masquerade.

Lineage

The line begins with the Master, a Ventrue of the fourth generation who claims to have been sired by the clan's Antediluvian. It takes its name from the Order of Aurelius, the priesthood of vampires that served him. As a Ventrue line, it counts itself among the nobility of the Kindred.

The line runs straight down, a generation at a time. The Master sired Darla in the Virginia colony in 1609. Darla sired Angelus in Galway in 1753, Angelus sired Drusilla in London about 1860, and Drusilla sired William the Bloody in London in 1880.

Angelus sired two others of the seventh generation, the Puritan Penn in the eighteenth century and the sailor Sam Lawson in 1943.

One kind of blood each

Like every Ventrue, each of the Aurelians can feed from only one kind of mortal. The Master drinks only from the devout. Darla drinks only from young men with fair skin and dark hair. They must be men of confidence and drive, which describes Angelus exactly.

In his years as the Scourge of Europe, Angelus fed only on blonde, fair-skinned women of strength and beauty, which describes Darla. It describes Buffy Summers just as well. Since 1898 he has not fed on people at all. Drusilla drinks only from the frightened. William drinks only from those who fight back.

History

Angelus, Darla and the rest were unaligned like the Master, answering neither to the Camarilla nor to the Sabbat. During their reign of terror they blatantly ignored the Masquerade. Angelus cut crosses into the cheeks of his victims, and it was in all the broadsheets of the day.

For exactly that reason the Camarilla often secretly supported or manipulated vampire-hunting organisations to pursue Angelus. Among them was the Society of Leopold, whose hunters, such as Daniel Holtz, never knew whose money they spent. All of this came before the Camarilla's agreement of 1900 with the wizarding world.

The line's great days ended twice: in 1898, when the Kalderash cursed Angelus with a soul, and in 1937, when the Master was sealed beneath a town in California. In 1997 its surviving members came together again in that town, Sunnydale.

In the saga

Hermione Granger first mentioned the Aurelian bloodline in September 1992, as Angelus's line. Later that autumn she told Gilderoy Lockhart's class that she had read three books on the Aurelian line. All three said that the Master had been trapped under a town in California since 1937. In the autumn of 1993 she read the history of its most famous member from Blood Nobility: The Great Kindred Lineages.

pages.title: The Transylvanian Dracula cult
infobox: A fourth-generation Tzimisce, by his account
pages.html:
The Transylvanian Dracula cult is a band of Dracula worshippers that Gilderoy Lockhart claimed to have foiled. By his account there were three hundred of them, all in red, with a cat on their altar. Their leader, he said, was a Tzimisce of the fourth generation. Professor McGonagall, who had been in Transylvania herself, showed the story up for what it was.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, on Halloween night 1992, Lockhart told the story over the Petrified Mrs Norris. McGonagall asked pleasantly whether he knew her old friend 'dear Julius', who had been in Transylvania for some years. He always carried a whip. Lockhart said that old Julius Carrow had helped him foil the cult. Julius was Julius Belmont, and no Carrow.

Lockhart went on. The leader was a Methuselah of 'Clan Tzi-mi-see', a shapeshifter who had come at him in the shape of a great wolf made out of men. McGonagall murmured to Harry that it was Tzimisce: three syllables, not four. One does not kill one of the fourth generation with a wand held so, she added, nor with a wand at all, if one has any sense.

In Chapter Eleven Lockhart told the rest of it to his class, with Harry standing in as the vampire. His Tzimisce, he revealed, had been in league with an elder of Clan Ventrue who called himself the Master. Afterwards McGonagall told Harry that a Tzimisce does not fall down when you hit it: 'It comes apart and walks off in several directions.'

pages.title: Channel 4
pages.html:
Channel 4 is a British television channel. At number four, Privet Drive, it is chiefly known as the channel that shows documentaries about serial killers.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, Hermione Granger kept three pictures of the brooding vampire Angelus folded inside her copy of Gadding with Ghouls. The way she looked at them under the table in Charms reminded Harry Potter uncomfortably of Aunt Petunia. Petunia watched every documentary about serial killers that Channel 4 put on, with her mouth slightly open and her tea going cold, while Uncle Vernon glared at her from the other armchair.

In Book Three, Chapter One, the rational part of Harry's mind had been raised in Little Whinging on Uncle Vernon's opinions and Aunt Petunia's Channel 4 documentaries. It had a perfectly good explanation for the man in the plain white robe whom Harry had seen by a fallen pillar in the Chamber of Secrets. Harry had been dying, with Basilisk venom in his blood, and dying people saw things.

pages.title: Andúril
aliases: The sword from the Sorting Hat
the sword from the Sorting Hat

Aragorn wielder
Harry Potter drew it from the Sorting Hat
Godric Gryffindor, sword, ancient weapon, Chamber of Secrets
The Fellowship of the Ring (1954), as the shards of Narsil; reforged as Andúril
First Age, by Telchar of Nogrod, as Narsil
At the foot of Orodruin, at the end of the Second Age
At Rivendell, as Andúril, for Aragorn
Elendil, Aragorn, Godric Gryffindor, Harry Potter
pages.html:
Andúril, the Flame of the West, is the sword of Elendil, reforged for his heir Aragorn. Hogwarts has long known it as the Sword of Gryffindor. It belongs to the ancient and noble line that comes down from Aragorn's marriage to Arwen, through Godric Gryffindor, to Harry Potter. In 1993 Harry drew it from the Sorting Hat in the Chamber of Secrets and killed the Basilisk with it.

Narsil and Andúril

The sword was forged in the First Age by Telchar, the Dwarf smith of Nogrod, and named Narsil. It came to Elendil, the first High King of Arnor and Gondor. At the end of the Second Age, Elves and Men made their Last Alliance against Sauron. Elendil fell fighting him on the slopes of Orodruin, and the sword broke beneath him. His son Isildur took up the hilt-shard, and with it cut the Ruling Ring from Sauron's hand. For three thousand years afterwards the shards were kept by Isildur's heirs at Rivendell.

Before the Fellowship of the Ring set out from Rivendell, Elven smiths reforged the blade for Aragorn, the heir of Isildur. He named it Andúril, Flame of the West. On its blade were traced seven stars between a crescent moon and a rayed sun, with many runes besides. Aragorn bore it through the War of the Ring, in Moria, at Helm's Deep, on the Paths of the Dead and on the Pelennor Fields. He bore it afterwards as King Elessar.

It passed down the line of Aragorn and Arwen. That line survived the Flood, and the forgetting of the old ages. Ambrose Greyhame, who knows the sword's whole history, has said that things which have been broken and made again are often the strongest of all. This one, he says, does not mind being broken.

Godric Gryffindor and the goblins

The sword came to Godric Gryffindor from Gandalf, who put it into his hands when he gathered the four founders. It was Godric's by right of blood. He was one of Aragorn's descendants, of the ancient and noble line to which the sword belongs. He was also one of the series of brave men who have carried it, and Dumbledore has said that only men of his calibre can wield it. It was never Gryffindor's by origin.

By then millennia had worn the blade down: tens of thousands of years of wars, floods and forgotten hands since it was reforged at Rivendell. Godric took it to the goblins, the finest smiths of the isle, to be repaired. The goblin smith Ragnuk the First did the work.

That repair was the root of the goblins' claim. After Godric died they put about the name "the Sword of Gryffindor", and said they had forged it for him: there was a story of a ruby-set blade made by Ragnuk the First. The claim was a trick, the pretext on which they meant to take the sword for themselves. It had just enough truth in it to be believed, because goblin hands had worked the blade. Before they could take it, Gandalf stole it back. He kept it hidden, holding it for the day when another of Aragorn's heirs would need it. The histories record only that the Sword of Gryffindor vanished.

The real blade bears no rubies, no lion and no name. Dumbledore called the name by which Hogwarts knew it a trick of the goblins, and said that it had borne several names before that one.

Description

The sword is long, much longer than the Sorting Hat is deep. Its blade is bright as water and seems to hold its own light even in darkness. A line of strange letters runs down its whole length. The guard sweeps out in two long curves, and the grip is bound in dark leather worn smooth by hands. The pommel is plain pale metal, with the same letters cut round it.

It bears no jewels, no lion and no name. It looks like something out of a much older story than any wizard's castle. When it is raised against evil it bursts into white flame, almost blue, and its letters kindle along the blade like a fuse. In Harry Potter's hand it felt as though it had been made for him.

Return to Hogwarts

On the night of the Duelling Club in December 1992, Ambrose Greyhame walked up from Hogsmeade in the first snow with the sword under his left arm. It was wrapped in old oilcloth and tied with string. When he looked in at Harry duelling in the Great Hall, the package stirred against him with a hearthstone warmth, like a dog that has heard its master's step. He told it to be patient. It was not yet time.

The next morning he gave it to Dumbledore. He said that it had slept a long time since Godric used it, and had earned its rest. He asked whether it was truly needed now. Dumbledore said it would be, soon. When Greyhame had gone he hid it inside the brim of the Sorting Hat, which swallowed it with a sigh, like something recognising an old friend.

In the saga

In the Chamber of Secrets in 1993, wounded and alone before the Basilisk, Harry pulled the sword out of the Sorting Hat that Fawkes had brought him. He had the strange feeling that he had read about it as a child, hiding from Dudley in a corner of a library. The blade burst into white flame as he struck the Basilisk's jaw. Standing astride Dracina Malfoy, with a strength poured into his arms from outside himself, he cut off its head in one stroke. Then he drove the sword through Riddle's diary and destroyed it. Riddle called it a borrowed sword from a long-forgotten ancestor.

Afterwards, in Professor McGonagall's office, Dumbledore put it back into Harry's hands. He told Harry of its bloodline and its names. It had chosen him in his moment of need, he said, and Harry would need it again one day, soon. Harry left it on the desk.

Over the following year Harry read Dudley's copy of The Lord of the Rings. When he reached Narsil reforged, and Aragorn coming up the river with Andúril drawn, he became certain, though he told nobody, that the Sorting Hat had given him Andúril. He could not remember any stars on the blade, but he had been busy with a Basilisk at the time. By August 1994 he was sure that the Elves, his mother's blood and the sword were knotted together somehow, though he could not see how. The sword is the heirloom of his mother's line, which descends from Aragorn and Arwen.

pages.title: The One Ring

The Black Speech in elvish letters, seen only when heated
To rule the other Rings of Power and their bearers
The Ruling Ring; the first Horcrux
Sauron; Isildur; Déagol; Sméagol, called Gollum; Bilbo Baggins; Frodo Baggins; Samwise Gamgee, for a short time

pages.html:
The One Ring was the Ruling Ring, which Sauron forged in the fire of Orodruin about the year 1600 of the Second Age to rule the other Rings of Power. Into it he put a great part of his own native power, so that while it lasted he could not be wholly ended. It was the first Horcrux, and every Horcrux since is an imitation of it.

The Lord of Gifts

In the Second Age the greatest smiths among the Elves lived in Eregion, which Noldor under Celebrimbor, grandson of Fëanor, founded about the year 750. Their brotherhood was called the Gwaith-i-Mírdain, the People of the Jewel-smiths. About the year 1200 Sauron came among the Elves in a fair form, calling himself Annatar, the Lord of Gifts. Gil-galad and Elrond would not treat with him, but the smiths of Eregion took him in.

Sauron had been a Maia of Aulë the smith before the world was made, so it was the Elves who learnt from him, not he from them. Under his teaching the smiths of Eregion reached the height of their skill about the year 1500, when they began to forge the Rings of Power. First they made many lesser rings, essays in the craft. With his help they then made the Seven and the Nine.

About the year 1590 Celebrimbor finished the Three Rings of the Elves, Narya, Nenya and Vilya, working alone. Sauron never touched them. They were made by the craft he had taught all the same, so they too were bound to whatever ruled the rest.

The forging

About the year 1600 Sauron forged the One Ring in secret in the Sammath Naur, the Chambers of Fire in the mountain Orodruin, in his own land of Mordor. It was made to rule the other rings. Through it he meant to see all that was done with them, even to read the thoughts of those who wore them and bend their wills. In the same years he finished the Dark Tower of Barad-dûr.

The Elven rings were very great, so the ring that governed them had to be greater still. Sauron let a great part of his own native power pass into it. While he wore it he was mightier than he had ever been. But his fate was bound to it now. While it lasted he could not be wholly ended, and if it were unmade his power would go with it.

It was a plain ring of gold, with no stone, and only the fire in which it had been made could unmake it. On its band, inside and out, ran an inscription in the Black Speech of Mordor, written in elvish letters. The letters could be seen only when the ring had been heated, and they faded as it cooled. They were two lines of a longer verse, which begins 'One Ring to rule them all'.

When Sauron first put it on, the Elves were aware of him at once. Celebrimbor saw what he meant to do. The Elves took off their rings, and they would not use them while Sauron wore the One.

What it did

The Ring had a will of its own, and it always sought to go back to its master. It could grow larger or smaller on a hand, so it could slip from a finger to betray its bearer. A mortal who wore it could not be seen by the living, though he grew plainer to the eyes of wraiths. It gave him no more life, but it kept him going until every minute was a weariness. It made its bearers love it, need it and hold it tighter, until they could not let go. Any mortal who kept it long enough would fade into a wraith himself.

The War of the Elves and Sauron

Celebrimbor gave Nenya to Galadriel. He sent Narya and Vilya to Gil-galad in Lindon, so the Three were hidden before Sauron came for them. In 1693 Sauron made war on the Elves to take all the rings for himself. In 1697 he laid Eregion waste and seized the Nine from the house of the smiths. Under torment Celebrimbor told him where the Seven were kept, but never where the Three had gone. He died of his torment, and Sauron's Orcs carried his body on a pole as a banner.

Númenor sent a great fleet to Gil-galad's aid in 1700, and in 1701 Sauron was driven out of Eriador. Afterwards he dealt out the rings he had taken. He gave the Nine to great kings of Men, three of them lords of Númenor, who became the Nazgûl, his Ringwraiths. The Seven went to the lords of the Dwarves. The Dwarves could not be made into shadows, but their rings filled them with greed for gold. In time dragons consumed four of the Seven, and Sauron took back the other three.

Númenor and the Last Alliance

In 3262 Ar-Pharazôn, King of Númenor, carried Sauron off a prisoner to the island, where Sauron corrupted him. When Númenor was drowned in 3319, Sauron's fair body perished with it. His spirit fled back to Mordor, where he took up the Ring again. He could never again take a shape that seemed fair to anyone.

At the end of the long siege of Barad-dûr, in 3441, Sauron came down to fight on the slopes of Orodruin. He slew Gil-galad and Elendil. Elendil's sword Narsil broke beneath him as he fell. With the hilt-shard Isildur cut the Ring from Sauron's hand. Sauron was overthrown, and his spirit fled into hiding.

Elrond and Círdan counselled Isildur to cast it into the fire close at hand. He would not. He kept it as weregild for his father and his brother. He wrote down what he knew of it before he left Gondor: it had been 'hot as a glede' when he took it, and the letters had faded as it cooled. It was precious to him, he wrote, though he bought it with great pain.

Isildur's Bane

In October of the year 2 of the Third Age Orcs fell on Isildur and his three elder sons at the Gladden Fields, beside the Anduin. Isildur put on the Ring and fled into the river. It slipped from his finger in the water. The Orcs saw him as he came out, and they shot him dead. In Gondor's lore the Ring was called Isildur's Bane ever after.

It lay in the river for nearly two thousand five hundred years. About the year 2463 a river-hobbit called Déagol found it while he was fishing. His friend Sméagol asked for it as a birthday present. When Déagol refused, Sméagol strangled him and took it. The Ring made Sméagol a thief and a sneak, so his family turned him out. About 2470 he crept into the roots of the Misty Mountains, where he lived in the dark beside an underground lake. He called the Ring his precious. It lengthened his life and wore it thin, until he was the creature called Gollum.

Bilbo and Frodo

In July 2941 the Ring left Gollum. Bilbo Baggins of the Shire, lost in the goblin tunnels, found it lying on the floor. He won a game of riddles with Gollum, then slipped past him invisible to escape. Gandalf believed that Bilbo was meant to find the Ring, and not by its maker.

Bilbo kept it for sixty years. It hid him when he wore it, and it kept him from growing old, but it left him feeling 'thin, sort of stretched'. At his farewell party on 22 September 3001 he left the Shire, and Gandalf persuaded him to leave the Ring to his heir, Frodo Baggins. Bilbo was the first bearer ever to give it up of his own will. Gandalf began to suspect what it was.

Gollum, meanwhile, had left the mountains in 2944 to hunt for the thief. He was caught in Mordor. Under torment he gave Sauron two words, Shire and Baggins. In 3017 Gandalf read the scroll of Isildur at Minas Tirith. In April 3018 he came back to Bag End. In a little round room with a fire in the grate, he threw Frodo's ring into the flames, then let him take it out. It was not even warm. Fine letters of fire came up on it, and Gandalf knew it for the One.

The Quest

On 23 September 3018, at nightfall, Frodo left Bag End with the Ring, on the day the Black Riders entered the Shire. Their chief wounded him on Weathertop on 6 October. On 25 October the Council of Elrond at Rivendell resolved that the Ring must be unmade in the fire where it was made, and Frodo took the task on himself. The Fellowship of the Ring set out from Rivendell on 25 December. When it broke on 26 February 3019, Frodo went on towards Mordor with Samwise Gamgee. Gollum, who had been following them, became their guide.

At Cirith Ungol Frodo was stung by Shelob and carried off by Orcs. For a short time Sam bore the Ring, then gave it back to him.

The end of the Ring

On 25 March 3019 Frodo stood at last in the Sammath Naur, at the brink of the Crack of Doom. There the Ring was too strong for him, and he claimed it for his own. Gollum fell on him in the dark, biting off the finger that wore it. Dancing for joy at the edge, Gollum fell into the fire with his precious. So the Ring was unmade where it was made.

Barad-dûr fell, and the Nazgûl perished. Sauron's power ended for ever. The Three lost their power. In 3021 their bearers sailed into the West with Frodo and Bilbo.

The first Horcrux

A Horcrux is a made thing into which its maker has put part of himself, so that he cannot be ended while it lasts. The Ring was the first. It can never be made again in quite the same way. Its maker was a Maia, a spirit who was there before the world was made, and what he put into it was his own native power. No mortal wizard has such power to give. The only others who ever learnt Sauron's ring-lore were the Elven-smiths of Eregion, and they have gone out of the earth.

Gandalf made sure the knowledge was lost. Some of it survived all the same, carried forward by dark hands. After the Flood a Stygian, the man history calls Herpo the Foul, filled the gaps by guesswork. He invented the modern Horcrux. A mortal has no native power of that kind to give, so it costs its maker the tearing of his own soul. Every Horcrux since is a cruder instrument than the Ring. Lord Voldemort's are the work of a man rebuilding a lost art from a damaged manual. He believes he stands at the summit of the discipline, when in fact he is standing in its ruins.

The diary

In December 1992 Gandalf felt on Dracina Malfoy, who was carrying Tom Riddle's diary, the same coldness he had felt from the Ring long ago: the gold thing that whispered and wanted. The diary was nothing like so great, and it had been made by other hands for another purpose. But it was made in the same way: a piece of someone poured into a vessel to wait, to whisper and to be carried.

When the diary was taken from her early in 1993, Dracina went along the tables of the Great Hall hunting for it, screaming that it was 'mine, mine, my precious'. Harry Potter destroyed the diary in June 1993 with Andúril, the sword whose shard had once cut the Ring from Sauron's hand.

pages.title: Narya
aliases: the ring with a red stone
the ring with the red stone
infobox: One of the Three Rings of the Elves
Celebrimbor of Eregion, in the Second Age
pages.html:
Narya, the Ring of Fire, is one of the Three Rings of the Elves. It is set with a single red stone. Gandalf has worn it since the Third Age, and he wears it still as Ambrose Greyhame: a plain ring whose stone sometimes seems to light his pipe for him.

The Ring of Fire

Celebrimbor of Eregion, the greatest of the elven smiths, made the Three Rings alone about the year 1590 of the Second Age. Sauron never touched them, though they were made by the craft he had taught, so they too were bound to the One. Once Sauron's purpose was known, Celebrimbor sent Narya to Gil-galad in Lindon. Gil-galad gave it to Círdan the Shipwright at the Grey Havens. When the Istari came over the sea in the Third Age, Círdan saw more deeply than anyone else into what Gandalf was. He gave him the ring, telling him it would support him in his labours and help him rekindle hearts in a world grown cold.

It gives its bearer strength against weariness, and it stirs the hearts of others to courage. Gandalf kept it hidden through the long struggle against Sauron. At the end of the Third Age he wore it openly on his hand when he sailed from the Grey Havens into the West with the other Ring-bearers. It came back with him when he was sent again, after the Flood.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, on a snowy night in December 1992, Ambrose Greyhame let himself into Albus Dumbledore's empty office to wait for him. He sat down in the chintz armchair by the fire, laid a long package across his knees and took out his pipe. He lit it with a touch of one finger to the bowl. On that finger he wore a plain ring with a single red stone. As the tobacco caught, the stone glowed for a moment like an ember, as though it were the ring that had done the lighting and not the finger. He sat by the fire all night, blowing smoke rings that turned into little ships, little trees and a little mountain with a red light at the top.

pages.title: The sugared violets
infobox: Small and white, tied with a creased green ribbon
'Drink all of your Skele-Gro. Don't you ever, ever be so stupid again.'
pages.html:
The sugared violets were a dozen sugared violets in a small white box, left at Harry Potter's bedside in the hospital wing in November 1992, after the rogue Bludger broke his arm. There was a card with them but no name. They were from Dracina Malfoy. Harry thought they were from Ginny Weasley, and ate every one.

The box

The box was tied with a thin green ribbon that was creased, as though it had been tied in something else first and untied in a hurry. Inside, in tissue paper, lay twelve violets, purple and frosted. The card was written in small, neat, spiky handwriting. The last word had been pressed so hard that the nib had gone through the card: 'Drink all of your Skele-Gro. Don't you ever, ever be so stupid again.'

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, Harry woke in the hospital wing to a faint, sweet smell and found the box on his bedside cabinet. When he asked who had brought it, Madam Pomfrey's face went oddly soft. 'A young lady,' she said. 'Wouldn't give her name. Stood at the end of your bed for about ten minutes while you were sleeping and cried fit to flood the place.' The girl had made her promise faithfully not to tell him who she was.

Harry decided they must be from Ginny Weasley. He ate one, and it tasted exactly like the sugared violets on top of Aunt Petunia's pudding on the night of the Masons' dinner, before Dobby dropped the whole thing on Mrs Mason's head. He put the card under his pillow without quite knowing why.

In Chapter Twelve, sure that whatever had attacked Colin Creevey was under Dracina's control, he was so angry that he ate the last of the violets without tasting them. They had probably come from Ginny, he thought.

In Chapter Sixteen, turning over what Tom Riddle's diary had told him about Dracina, Harry thought again of the box of sugared violets he had decided were from Ginny. He thought of the card, too, in spiky handwriting he had seen somewhere before.

In Chapter Eighteen, as he lay dying in the Chamber of Secrets, one of Harry's last thoughts was that he had never told her the violets were nice. Then somebody lifted him up and held him. Somebody was crying, saying his first name over and over. His face was pressed against something soft that smelled faintly of sugared violets. It was Dracina.

pages.title: The rogue Bludger
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The rogue Bludger was the Bludger that Dobby the house-elf bewitched in November 1992 to chase Harry Potter, and nobody else, for a whole Quidditch match. Dobby meant to hurt Harry badly enough that he would be sent home from Hogwarts, out of danger.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, the Bludger hunted Harry alone from one end of the match to the other. Dracina Malfoy threw her broom across its path in front of him, and it clipped the tail of her Nimbus with a crack like a breaking branch. Then it came back for Harry and broke his right elbow. When it was finally caught, it fought like a cat in a sack while Fred and George Weasley wrestled it into its box.

Afterwards Gilderoy Lockhart tried to mend the arm, and took the bones out of it instead. Madam Pomfrey had to grow all thirty-three of them back overnight. That night Dobby came to Harry's bed in the hospital wing and owned up. He had wanted Harry hurt, not killed. 'Dobby only meant Harry Potter hurt enough to be packed off home!'

pages.title: Hermione's eagle-feather quill
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A little box lined with green velvet
pages.html:
Hermione's eagle-feather quill is the long, dark, glossy quill that Hermione Granger gave Harry Potter for Christmas 1992. It came in a little box lined with green velvet. It was also the quill Harry used to write in Tom Riddle's diary.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, the quill was among Harry's presents on Christmas morning 1992, with treacle fudge from Hagrid and Flying with the Cannons from Ron. Hermione watched his face anxiously while he opened it. She had wanted, she said, to give him something he would use every day. 'Something you'd keep.'

That night, sitting by the dying fire with Riddle's diary open on his knees, Harry found that his hand had drifted all on its own towards the quill, which lay on the table beside his chair. He wanted very badly to dip it in ink and write something on the clean, blank page. He snatched his hand away as though the quill had bitten him.

In Chapter Fifteen, still in the Christmas holidays, he took the diary out of his trunk, picked up the quill and wrote Hello at the top of the first page. The ink shone for a moment, then sank into the paper and was gone. A moment later ink began to ooze back out of the page.

pages.title: Chocolate Frog cards
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Chocolate Frog cards are the collectable cards found one to a packet in Chocolate Frogs. Each shows a famous witch or wizard, with a short account of them on the back. The figures in the pictures move, and they often wander out of the frame, coming back when it suits them.

Famous faces

Some cards are hard to come by. Ron Weasley has five hundred or so, but he has never managed to get Agrippa or Ptolemy. Others turn up in packet after packet. Ron has six of Morgana, whose followers once hunted the descendants of King Arthur so hard that the family changed its name to Potter to escape them.

The pictures are not always faithful, either. When Ambrose Greyhame advised a young king in the West Country, he went by the name of Merlin. That name is still printed on the cards. Greyhame thinks the picture has the nose quite wrong, and the beard far too tidy.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the Hogwarts Express, Ron told Harry how many cards he had and which ones he still could not get. Harry’s first card was Albus Dumbledore. Ron, who had just got Morgana again, offered her to Harry to start a collection.

In Chapter Nine Harry gave Neville Longbottom the last Chocolate Frog from Hermione’s Christmas box, and Neville gave him the card. It was Dumbledore again. On the back Harry read of Dumbledore’s alchemical work with his partner, Nicolas Flamel, the name he had been trying to place for weeks.

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Ambrose Greyhame bought a Chocolate Frog in Hogsmeade on his way through, out of curiosity, and looked at the card for some time. He laughed so loudly that the witch behind the counter at Honeydukes dropped a jar of Pepper Imps.

pages.title: Mrs Skower's All-Purpose Magical Mess Remover
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The message on the wall, autumn 1992
pages.html:
Mrs Skower's All-Purpose Magical Mess Remover is a wizarding cleaning fluid, sold by the bottle, which promises to shift any mess at all. At Hogwarts in the autumn of 1992 it met one it could not shift.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, after his cat, Mrs Norris, was found Petrified on Hallowe'en, Argus Filch paced up and down the spot where she had been found. Harry saw him scrubbing at the message on the wall with a bottle of Mrs Skower's. It did no good whatever. The letters went on gleaming as brightly as on the night they were written: THE CHAMBER OF SECRETS HAS BEEN OPENED. ENEMIES OF THE HEIR, BEWARE.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, before the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, advertisements in gold raced across the gigantic blackboard that faced the Top Box across the stadium. One was for Mrs Skower's All-Purpose Magical Mess Remover, under the slogan 'No Pain, No Stain!'

pages.title: Arthur Weasley's flying car
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Going back into the Forbidden Forest
pages.html:
Arthur Weasley's flying car is an old turquoise Ford Anglia that Mr Weasley enchanted to fly. It can also turn invisible, and it holds a great deal more luggage than any Muggle car should. Since 1992 it has been living wild in the Forbidden Forest.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, Ron, Fred and George borrowed the car from their father. They flew it to Privet Drive in the middle of the night, tore the bars off Harry’s bedroom window and carried him off to the Burrow. In Chapter Four Mrs Weasley found out. Mr Weasley explained that there was a loophole in the law, so long as he had never meant to fly the car. His wife told him that he had made sure of the loophole when he wrote the law.

In Chapter Six, on 1 September 1992, the barrier to the platform at King’s Cross would not let Ron and Harry through, so they flew the car to Hogwarts. Over the lake it began to shudder and lose speed. It crashed into the Whomping Willow, threw out their trunks and Hedwig’s cage, then roared off into the Forbidden Forest with its one remaining door flapping.

By Chapter Fourteen nobody had seen it since. Dracina Malfoy showed Ron, who had drunk Polyjuice Potion and was wearing Crabbe’s face, a cutting from the Daily Prophet. Mr Weasley had been fined fifty Galleons for enchanting a Muggle motor car. Lucius Malfoy, into whose school grounds it had crashed, was demanding that he step down.

In Chapter Seventeen the car turned up again in the Forest, running wild, its wings plastered with mud. It came just in time to rescue Ron and Harry from the spiders. It drove them out to the edge of the trees, then reversed back into the Forest and was gone.

pages.title: House-point hourglasses
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Rubies, emeralds, sapphires and yellow diamonds
Keeping count of house points for the House Cup
pages.html:
The house-point hourglasses are four giant hourglasses against the wall of the Entrance Hall at Hogwarts, one for each house. Instead of sand they hold jewels: rubies for Gryffindor, emeralds for Slytherin, sapphires for Ravenclaw and yellow diamonds for Hufflepuff. They keep count of the house points through the year, for the House Cup.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Ambrose Greyhame came up to the castle through the snow one night in December 1992. Standing in the Entrance Hall, he looked up at the hourglasses full of jewels against the far wall and laughed out loud.

'Hourglasses!' he said, delighted. 'Points! Oh, that's very good. Whose idea was that? That'll have been Rowena's. That's exactly the sort of thing she'd have done. Make a competition of it, and then make sure everybody wins something.'

He was in a position to know. Long ago he had rounded up four of the most quarrelsome young wizards in the land, the founders of Hogwarts, and stood them in the mud on a crag above a lake to make them build something together.

pages.title: Expelliarmus
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Takes the wand out of an opponent's hand; cast hard, it throws the opponent off his feet
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Expelliarmus, the Disarming Charm, takes the wand out of an opponent's hand. Cast with force, it throws the opponent off his feet as well. It shows as a jet of scarlet light. It is simple to learn, and it is the first spell most young duellists are taught. Harry Potter learnt it by watching Severus Snape use it, and it has been the spell his hand knows best ever since.

How it works

The charm is aimed at the person, not the wand. The wand simply leaves the hand that was holding it and goes spinning up into the air, where anybody quick enough can catch it. A strong Expelliarmus knocks the opponent backwards too, into whatever happens to be behind him. Several wizards casting it at the same target at once can knock him out cold. Against a creature with no wand, it does nothing at all.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, Gilderoy Lockhart opened his Duelling Club in the Great Hall in December 1992, with Professor Snape as his assistant. On the count of three Snape cried 'Expelliarmus!' There was a dazzling flash of scarlet light, and Lockhart was blasted clean off the end of the stage into the wall. He tottered back up on to the stage and told everyone that he could have blocked it if he had wanted to.

In Chapter Eighteen, when Lockhart drew his wand to put a Memory Charm on Harry and Ron, Harry got in first. Lockhart flew backwards over his own trunk into the wall, and Ron threw his wand out of the window. 'Watched Snape do that one in the Duelling Club,' said Harry. On the Hogwarts Express home, in Chapter Nineteen, the friends practised disarming each other the length of the compartment. Ron, who had no wand left to be disarmed of, kept score. Harry was getting very good at it, which Ron said was not fair, since Harry had had Snape to copy.

In Book Three, Chapter Seventeen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Sirius Black used Ron's wand to disarm Harry and Hermione. A few minutes later Remus Lupin burst in and disarmed Harry all over again. In Chapter Eighteen, when Snape would not get out of the way, Harry cast it at him. Ron and Hermione cast it at the very same instant. The bang shook the door in its frame. Snape flew backwards into the wall, out cold, and his wand dropped on to the bed beside Crookshanks. 'Did you see how far he went?' Hermione whispered. 'Mine was the strongest. I could feel it.'

In Chapter Nineteen, out on the moonlit grounds, Harry cast it at the Garou that Lupin had become, simply because it was the spell his hand knew best. The scarlet light splashed harmlessly off the creature's chest, like water thrown on a bonfire. There was no wand to take. Later the same night, when Peter Pettigrew snatched up Lupin's fallen wand, Harry's Expelliarmus sent it spinning out of his hand into the dark.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, before dawn on 22 August 1994, Harry Potter went through the wand movements he had practised all summer with a pencil in front of his wardrobe mirror. The Disarming Charm came first: a flick, then a sharp jab. He went through them to steady himself, after Mrs Weasley had told him how much he deserved some peace.

pages.title: Everte Statum
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Everte Statum is a jinx that flings its target backwards off their feet. It hits like a swinging door.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, Professor Lockhart's Duelling Club met in the Great Hall in 1992. Snape paired Harry Potter with Dracina Malfoy. Lockhart told them to cast their charms to disarm on the count of three, but Dracina started on two. 'Everte Statum!' The spell hit Harry square in the chest like a swinging door. He went backwards off his feet, head over heels, and landed hard on his back with all the breath knocked out of him. Dracina laughed, a high, wild, delighted laugh. Harry was up again before he had properly thought about it.

pages.title: Rictusempra
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Doubles the target up with helpless laughter
pages.html:
Rictusempra, the Tickling Charm, doubles its target up with helpless laughter, as though somebody were tickling them all over at once. It is a jet of silver light. It looks harmless, but a person who cannot stop laughing cannot easily fight back.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, at the Duelling Club in December 1992, Dracina Malfoy knocked Harry Potter flat with Everte Statum before Lockhart had finished counting. Harry got up and pointed his wand straight at her. 'Rictusempra!' A jet of silver light caught her in the stomach. She doubled up, wheezing, laughing helplessly with tears springing from her eyes. Even so, she kept her wand up and gasped out a Tarantallegra through the laughter.

Later, when Snape came down to stop them, Harry's Rictusempra crossed Dracina's Tarantallegra in the air, so that Snape had to jerk aside to avoid them both.

pages.title: Tarantallegra
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Makes the victim's legs dance uncontrollably
pages.html:
Tarantallegra sets its victim's legs dancing: a frantic, kicking, high-stepping dance that cannot be stopped by will alone. The rest of the victim has to go wherever the legs take it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, at the Duelling Club in December 1992, Dracina Malfoy gasped it out at Harry Potter while she was still doubled up by his Rictusempra. Harry's legs jerked out from under him and began a frantic quickstep all by themselves. He went jigging sideways into a knot of Ravenclaws, who scattered. 'Dance, Potter! Go on!' Dracina shouted after him. A Finite only half undid it.

Later, when Snape came down to stop them, her Tarantallegra crossed Harry's Rictusempra in the air, so that Snape had to jerk aside to avoid them both.

pages.title: Finite
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Ends whatever spell is at work on its target
pages.html:
Finite is the general counter-charm. It ends whatever spell is at work on its target, and it is the short form of Finite Incantatem. Said in a hurry, under pressure, it does not always finish the job.

Use

Because it is meant for any spell at all, Finite is less sure than a counter-jinx made for one particular jinx. Even so, it is often the only counter-charm a young witch or wizard knows, which is why it is the one they reach for when something goes wrong.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, at the Duelling Club in December 1992, Dracina Malfoy's Tarantallegra set Harry Potter's legs dancing a frantic quickstep. 'Finite!' Harry gasped, jabbing his wand at his own knees. It was the one counter-charm he knew. It half worked: his legs slowed to a wobbly shuffle, enough for him to catch himself on a pillar and fire back.

pages.title: Flipendo
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (video game, 2001)
pages.html:
Flipendo is a knockback jinx. It strikes its target like a hard shove and sends it reeling, or tumbling right over. It is one of the simpler jinxes, the sort a second-year might fire off in a hurry, and a quick enough wand can turn it aside.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, at the Duelling Club in December 1992, Harry Potter had just half undone Dracina Malfoy's Tarantallegra when he fired back the first thing that came into his head. It was Flipendo. Dracina flicked her wand sideways. The jinx glanced off it in a spray of blue sparks and hit a suit of armour behind her, which fell over with a noise like a cutlery drawer being emptied down a flight of stairs.

pages.title: Furnunculus
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Brings the victim out in boils
pages.html:
Furnunculus is a jinx that brings its victim out in boils. The result is ugly, painful and quite harmless in the long run, which makes it exactly the sort of jinx schoolchildren throw at one another. Like most jinxes, it hits whoever is in its way, which is not always the person it was meant for.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, at the Duelling Club in December 1992, Harry Potter shouted 'Furnunculus!' at Dracina Malfoy. She ducked. The jinx went over her head and hit Vincent Crabbe, who howled as his face erupted in boils. Dracina was not impressed. She wanted to know whether boils were really the best that the Boy Who Lived could do.

pages.title: Densaugeo
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
Densaugeo is a jinx that makes teeth grow, fast and long. It works on whatever it hits, which need not be a person.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, at Professor Lockhart's Duelling Club in 1992, Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy were duelling far beyond the disarming they had been told to practise. Dracina kept saying that somebody had told her Harry was special. Harry demanded to know who she was talking about.

'Nobody!' Her voice cracked. 'Densaugeo!'

Harry threw himself sideways. The jinx skimmed past his ear. It hit a flagstone instead, which sprouted a row of long, yellowish teeth. A girl near the front screamed.

pages.title: Serpensortia
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Conjures a snake from the end of the wand
pages.html:
Serpensortia conjures a snake, which shoots out of the end of the caster's wand and lands ready to strike. It is a showy spell, and a dangerous one, since the snake is a real snake.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, at the Duelling Club in December 1992, Dracina Malfoy was swaying on her feet at the end of her duel with Harry Potter. She lifted her wand one last time. 'Fine,' she whispered. 'Fine. If you won't see... I'll show you.' Then she cried 'Serpensortia!' A long black snake shot out of her wand, fell to the floor between them and reared up, ready to strike.

Lockhart tried to get rid of it, but his spell only flung it ten feet into the air. It came down furious and went straight for Justin Finch-Fletchley. Harry heard himself shouting at it to leave Justin alone. The snake stopped. Dracina stared at Harry with her face lit up from the inside like a lamp. Snape waved his wand, and the snake vanished in a little puff of black smoke.

pages.title: Stunning Spell
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Three at once, from three directions, at the very least
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
The Stunning Spell, Stupefy, knocks its target senseless. A Stunner is the standard way to stop a dangerous person or beast without killing it. Against something big enough one Stunner is not enough, and against an angry Garou no number of them will do.

Against werewolves

Professor McGonagall's advice for a werewolf in its wolf shape is to Stun it from as far away as you can manage, and never alone. 'Three Stunners at once, from three different directions, is the very least. One is a waste of breath.'

A Garou in its war shape is another matter altogether. 'Three Stunners won't trouble it any more than a cat's sneeze would,' she said. 'You run, and you hope that whatever it's angry with isn't you.'

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, in the autumn of 1992, McGonagall gave Harry Potter this lesson in an alcove outside the Great Hall, after Lockhart had told his class about the Homorphus Charm. Harry went over it under his breath until he was sure he would remember it: silver, three Stunners, run, black fur, run faster.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, in the Forbidden Forest in June 1994, Hermione Granger cast two Stunners and an Impediment Jinx at the werewolf that Remus Lupin had become. The spells hit it in the chest, the throat and the face. It did not even blink. 'Those Stunners of yours were extremely well cast,' Dracina Malfoy told her afterwards. 'For all the good they did.'

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, in the summer of 1994, Harry Potter practised the Stunning Spell with a pencil in front of his wardrobe mirror, from notes in the back of Dudley's old exercise book. Before dawn on 22 August he went through it in his head, after the Disarming Charm and the Shield Charm.

pages.title: Homorphus Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Turns a werewolf back into a man
pages.html:
The Homorphus Charm is supposed to turn a werewolf back into a man. It does not exist. Gilderoy Lockhart claimed to have cast it on a werewolf outside Wagga Wagga, and Professor McGonagall, who knew a great deal more about werewolves than he did, said flatly that there is no such charm.

Lockhart's story

According to Lockhart, a great slavering brute had come at him across a moonlit pasture outside Wagga Wagga. He caught it by the scruff, knelt on its back, pressed his wand to the great vein of its neck and, with the very last of his strength, performed the Homorphus Charm. The fur fell away before his eyes, he said. There knelt a man, weeping in the moonlight, with his whole life given back to him. The charm itself, he said, was 'Fiendishly difficult. Fiendishly.'

The truth

'There is no spell that turns a werewolf back into a man, not on the full moon or on any other night,' McGonagall told Harry Potter. 'If there were, I can think of several people who'd be very glad of it.' A werewolf in its wolf shape does not stop to be knelt on. Whoever really dealt with the werewolf of Wagga Wagga, it was not done with a Homorphus Charm.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, in the autumn of 1992, Lockhart acted the story out in class with Harry playing the werewolf, growling, howling and whimpering on cue. He set the class an ode of twelve lines at the very least on his triumph. Afterwards McGonagall took Harry aside. She told him there was no such charm, then taught him what he would really need: three Stunners from three directions, silver, or running.

pages.title: Transmogrifian Torture
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Transmogrifian Torture is a curse that Gilderoy Lockhart claimed to have seen many times. He said so over the stiff body of Mrs Norris on Hallowe'en 1992. Mrs Norris had in fact been Petrified, which was something else entirely.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Albus Dumbledore laid Mrs Norris on the desk in Lockhart's office, which was nearest, and bent to examine her. Lockhart circled round them all like a moth, making suggestions. 'Definitely a curse,' he said. 'Probably the Transmogrifian Torture. I've seen it many times. So unlucky I wasn't there, I know the very counter-curse that would have...'

Then Professor McGonagall, without lifting her eyes from the cat, asked whether he had considered a parasite of the vocal cords. It was a strain that spread by language, she said, through Russian soldiers in Afghanistan and conscripts in Africa. Lockhart lit up at once. He remembered the language parasites well, he said; he had been there himself, in Africa, and had wrestled the thing out of a fellow's throat with his bare hands. McGonagall said nothing. She only smiled, very slightly. Harry understood that she had been standing exactly where Lockhart claimed to have been, and that Lockhart had never been within a thousand miles of it.

pages.title: Polyjuice Potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Turns the drinker into another person for exactly one hour
Book Two, Book Three, Book Four
pages.html:
Polyjuice Potion turns whoever drinks it into somebody else for exactly one hour. It is among the most difficult potions there are, harder than anything at the back of the sixth-year book, and it takes about a month to brew. Hermione Granger brewed it in a girls' toilet in her second year.

Brewing

The recipe is given in Moste Potente Potions, a book kept in the Restricted Section of the Hogwarts library. It calls for lacewing flies stewed for three weeks, leeches, fluxweed gathered at the full moon, knotgrass, powdered Bicorn horn, shredded Boomslang skin and, last of all, a piece of the person to be imitated, usually a hair.

The finished potion looks like thick, dark mud, bubbling sluggishly. When the hair goes in, it hisses like a kettle, froths up wildly and changes colour, seldom to anything pleasant.

Drinking it

It tastes of boiled socks, with something much worse underneath. The change begins at once. It hurts: the drinker feels as though somebody had got hold of him at both ends and was rolling him out like pastry. An hour later, to the minute, he turns back into himself.

The potion is not meant for animal transformations, as the book makes plain. A dose made with a cat's hair turns the drinker partly into a cat, and the fur does not go when the hour is up.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, in the autumn of 1992, Hermione Granger proposed the potion as a way into the Slytherin common room, to find out whether Dracina Malfoy was the Heir of Slytherin. In Chapter Eleven she got the teacher's signature she needed out of Gilderoy Lockhart by telling him the book was about slow-acting venoms.

They brewed it in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, where nobody ever came except Myrtle. The Bicorn horn and the Boomslang skin could only be had from Snape's private store-cupboard. In Chapter Twelve Harry threw a firework into Goyle's cauldron, and in the uproar Hermione slipped out to steal them.

In Chapter Fourteen Hermione added the last of the lacewings early on Christmas morning 1992, and the potion was ready. That evening Harry drank it as Goyle, with Ron as Crabbe; both Slytherins had been knocked out by Hermione's Sleeping Draught. Hermione's own hair, taken from Millicent Bulstrode's robes, turned out to be a cat's. Madam Pomfrey took one look at her. 'Polyjuice gone wrong, is it? Animal hair? Hm.'

In Chapter Fifteen Ron told Hermione that making Polyjuice Potion in a toilet in her second year was N.E.W.T. work, which nobody else in their year could have managed. 'You got one hair wrong. One. That's not stupid.' In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, she quoted a footnote from Moste Potente Potions, the book she had got out of the Restricted Section for the Polyjuice.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, on 22 August 1994, Harry Potter reminded Hermione Granger that she had brewed Polyjuice Potion in their second year, when hardly anybody in the school could have done it. It was one of his reasons for telling her that he could not do any of it without her.

pages.title: Skele-Gro
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Burns all the way down, like a lit candle
pages.html:
Skele-Gro is a potion that regrows bones overnight, every one of them if need be. It works, but growing bones is a horrible business. The potion burns all the way down, like swallowing a lit candle, and the night that follows is spent in pain.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, a rogue Bludger broke Harry Potter's arm in the Slytherin match of November 1992. Gilderoy Lockhart tried to mend it with a spell and took all the bones out instead, leaving something that looked like a long, pink, wobbly sock full of custard. Madam Pomfrey brought a large bottle of Skele-Gro. Harry coughed and choked on it. She went off still tutting about dangerous sports and incompetent teachers. He had thirty-three bones to grow back before morning, and he grew them all.

A small white box of sugared violets was left by his bed, with a card in small, neat, spiky handwriting: 'Drink all of your Skele-Gro. Don't you ever, ever be so stupid again.' Madam Pomfrey said only that a young lady had left them. 'Eat one if you like, Potter, they'll take the taste of the Skele-Gro away.' They did.

In Chapter Fifteen, on Valentine's Day 1993, Lockhart filled the Great Hall with pink decorations. Snape looked at them as though somebody had just made him drink a pint of Skele-Gro.

pages.title: Mandrake Restorative Draught
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Night of 29 to 30 May 1993, on the Basilisk's victims
pages.html:
The Mandrake Restorative Draught is the cure for Petrification, brewed from fully grown Mandrakes. It also returns people who have been Transfigured or cursed to their proper selves.

Brewing

The Mandrakes must reach their full size first, which takes most of a school year. As they leave their childhood behind them they grow sulky and secretive. They are ready for cutting once they start trying to move into each other's pots.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Seven, at the second-years' first Herbology lesson of the year, Hermione told Professor Sprout that Mandrake is a powerful restorative, used to return people who have been Transfigured or cursed to their original state. The class spent the rest of the lesson repotting young Mandrakes, with earmuffs on.

In Chapter Ten, on Hallowe'en 1992, Dumbledore promised Filch that Mrs Norris would be cured: Professor Sprout had recently got hold of some Mandrakes, and as soon as they were fully grown he would have the potion made. Gilderoy Lockhart broke in: 'I could whip up a Mandrake Restorative Draught in my sleep!'

In Chapter Twelve, in a December blizzard, Professor Sprout put socks and scarves on the Mandrakes, a fiddly job she would trust to nobody else. In Chapter Fifteen Madam Pomfrey reported that they were becoming sulky and secretive. In Chapter Sixteen, in March 1993, several of them threw a loud, wild party in Greenhouse Three, which kept half of Hufflepuff awake. In Chapter Eighteen Professor McGonagall announced that they were ready for cutting at last.

In Chapter Nineteen, on the night of 29 to 30 May 1993, Harry stood in the hospital wing doorway while the sharp green smell of Mandrake juice came out from under the curtains round Hermione's bed. That night the juice was given to the Basilisk's victims, and it revived them.

pages.title: Swelling Solution
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Seven times anticlockwise, then once the other way
pages.html:
Swelling Solution makes whatever it touches swell up. A splash of it on the skin will blow up an ear, a lip or a nose in a matter of seconds. Second-years at Hogwarts brew it in Potions. A Deflating Draught brings the swelling down again.

Brewing

According to Dracina Malfoy, who is very good at Potions, it must be stirred seven times anticlockwise, then once the other way.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, in December 1992, Harry's Swelling Solution came out like gravy. Dracina took his stirring rod and put it right. 'Anticlockwise, Potter, anticlockwise, seven times, then once the other way, I told you that in October...'

Then Harry threw a firework into Goyle's cauldron. Goyle's potion went off like a bomb, coming down over half the class. Ears, lips and noses swelled up all round the dungeon. Dracina's nose blew up like a balloon. Goyle's eyes swelled to the size of dinner plates. In the confusion Hermione Granger slipped out to raid Snape's stores for the Polyjuice Potion, while Snape handed out Deflating Draught all round.

pages.title: Deflating Draught
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Deflating Draught is the antidote to the Swelling Solution. A single dose brings the swelling down.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, Harry lobbed one of Fred's Filibuster fireworks into Goyle's cauldron, and the Swelling Solution erupted over half the class. Seamus's ear inflated like a pink cushion, Pansy Parkinson's lip swelled up over her chin, and Dracina Malfoy's nose blew up like a balloon. In the confusion Hermione slipped out of the dungeon. Snape ordered everyone who had been splashed to come to his desk at once for a Deflating Draught. When everybody had swallowed a dose, the swellings all went down, and Snape fished the blackened remains of the firework out of the cauldron.

pages.title: Sleeping Draught
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Puts the drinker straight to sleep
pages.html:
A Sleeping Draught sends whoever takes it into a deep sleep. A simple one is well within the reach of a clever second-year, and it can be hidden in food without anybody noticing until it is too late.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, on Christmas Day 1992, Hermione Granger needed hairs from Crabbe and Goyle for the Polyjuice Potion. She held up two plump little chocolate cakes, beautifully iced. 'These have got a Sleeping Draught in them. Only a simple one.'

After Christmas tea Harry balanced the cakes on the end of the banisters in the Entrance Hall. The two Slytherins came out from their fourth helpings of trifle, ate them at once and were out cold. Harry and Ron pulled out some of their hair, then shut them in a broom cupboard. Later that evening a muffled hammering from the cupboard showed that they had woken up.

pages.title: Methuselah
pages.html:
A Methuselah is a vampire of the Fourth or Fifth Generation, a thousand years old or more, standing just below the Antediluvians in power. There are very few of them.

The elders

Most Methuselahs have withdrawn from the affairs of younger vampires. Many sleep for centuries in torpor, and those who wake tend to work through others. Dracula, a Tzimisce, is of the Fourth Generation. So is the Master, the Ventrue at the head of the Aurelian line.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, in his office on the night Mrs Norris was found Petrified, Gilderoy Lockhart told of a cult of Dracula worshippers he claimed to have foiled in Transylvania. Its leader, he said, was a Methuselah: ‘Fourth generation, if you can credit it. Clan Tzi-mi-see.’ Professor McGonagall murmured that he was saying it wrong: it was Tzimisce, three syllables, not four. Nor, she added, was that how one killed one of the fourth generation, not with a wand at all, if one had any sense. In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, in front of his class, Lockhart added a second Methuselah, an elder of Clan Ventrue who called himself the Master.

pages.title: Phoenix
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Bursts into flame on its Burning Day; rises again from the ashes
Healing tears; great strength in flight
pages.html:
The phoenix is a magnificent scarlet and gold bird that never truly dies. When its time comes, on what is called its Burning Day, it bursts into flame and rises again from its own ashes as a chick.

Powers

A phoenix can lift enormous weights. Its tears heal almost any wound, and its song gives courage to the pure of heart. It is one of the last remnants of an age long gone.

The Phoenix Force

The phoenix has nothing to do with the cosmic power that Muggles also call the Phoenix, which wore Jean Grey's form in 1980 and died on the Moon that year. Since the middle of the 1980s the same power has been bound to Rachel Summers, Jean's daughter from another future, who took the name Phoenix in 1985. The two share a name, a liking for fire and a habit of coming back. Otherwise they have nothing in common.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Fourteen, in December 1992, Harry Potter was sent to Professor Dumbledore's office for the first time. He watched Fawkes burst into flames there on his Burning Day. Dumbledore told him that phoenixes can lift enormous weights, that their tears will heal almost any wound and that there is no friend more faithful in the world. ‘They're some of the very last remnants of a long gone age, Harry.’

pages.title: Chameleon Ghoul
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Ordinary objects, such as a suit of armour
pages.html:
A Chameleon Ghoul is a shape-changing creature that can pass itself off as an ordinary object, such as a suit of armour or a hanging on a wall, and so lie in wait in plain sight.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, in the winter of 1992, Ron Weasley wondered how the monster of the Chamber was getting round the castle without anybody seeing it. Hermione Granger, prodding leeches down to the bottom of the Polyjuice Potion with a stick, said it might be invisible. Or it might be able to change its shape and look like a suit of armour. 'There's a thing called a Chameleon Ghoul that can...' 'You've read too many books, Hermione,' said Ron. The monster was a Basilisk, and it was in the pipes.

pages.title: Blood-Sucking Bugbear
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Blood-Sucking Bugbear is a dark creature with a taste for blood, the sort of thing a gamekeeper suspects when something gets into his hen-coop at night.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, in the winter of 1992, Hagrid met Harry Potter in a corridor, with snow in his eyebrows and a dead rooster swinging from his fist. 'Tha's the second one this term,' he said. 'Foxes, maybe. Or a Blood-Suckin' Bugbear.' He meant to ask the Headmaster for leave to put a charm round the hen-coop. In Chapter Fourteen, walking Harry back to Gryffindor Tower, he talked the whole way about the rooster and the Bugbear he would have a word with if he ever caught it. Harry knew he was doing it to stop him thinking. In truth the heir of Slytherin had killed the roosters, because the crowing of a rooster is fatal to a Basilisk.

pages.title: Flobberworm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The flobberworm is a thick brown worm up to ten inches long, and it does very little at either end. It eats lettuce, though not too much of it. It does best when left entirely alone. Most people hold it to be the dullest creature in the wizarding world.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, at the Quidditch match, a Ravenclaw sixth year said he had had more excitement watching Flobberworms breed than watching football. In Chapter Fourteen Dracina Malfoy told Harry Potter and Ron Weasley, who were disguised by Polyjuice Potion as her friends, that the Weasleys bred like Flobberworms. In Chapter Fifteen she told Ron that he had the brains of one.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, after Buckbeak hurt Dracina in September 1993, the school governors said that Hagrid should have started small, with Flobberworms. He lost his nerve and did. In Chapter Eight the class had been poking lettuce down flobberworms for three weeks running. 'What is the point of them?' Ron demanded. 'It doesn't do anything,' said Harry. 'That's why they're safe.' In Chapter Eleven Hagrid admitted that he had lost the lot. 'Over-fed 'em on the lettuce, see.'

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, Hagrid's exam was to keep a flobberworm alive for an hour. Flobberworms do best when nobody touches them, so nobody had ever sat an easier exam. Dracina paid no attention to hers at all, which was why it was in better health than anybody else's.

pages.title: Dementors
infobox: Azkaban guards; Dementor; Dementors of Azkaban
Azkaban, Azkaban guards, Dark creature, Azkaban guard
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The Ministry of Magic, as the guards of Azkaban
Hope, happiness and, through the Kiss, the soul
Blind; they feel their way by feeding on emotion
Harry Potter's stag Patronus; a Garou's war form
pages.html:
Dementors are tall, hooded, blind things that feed on human happiness, and on the soul itself through the Dementor's Kiss. They were made, and their maker is the enemy the Garou call the Wyrm. The Ministry of Magic employs them to guard the prison of Azkaban. In the school year of 1993 to 1994 it posted them round Hogwarts to catch Sirius Black.

Description

A dementor towers to the ceiling in a hooded cloak of black rags. The hand that comes out of the cloak is greyish, glistening and scabbed, like something dead that has rotted in water. It draws long, rattling breaths. The air goes cold round it, and lamps go out. Under the hood there are no eyes, only grey skin stretched over hollows and a slack, gurgling mouth.

Dementors are blind. They feel their way towards people by feeding on their emotions, which is why the simpler feelings of an animal are harder for them to find. Lupin calls them among the foulest things that move upon the earth. They infest the darkest, filthiest places, glorying in decay and despair.

Effect

A dementor brings a deep cold inside the chest. It drains away hope and every happy memory, leaving a person alone with the worst of himself. After one came into his compartment, Ron Weasley felt that he would never be cheerful again. Muggles cannot see dementors, but they feel them as a chill.

Arthur Weasley says that Azkaban feels as if all the light had been sucked out of the world, and that the dementors drive half the prisoners mad. Cornelius Fudge says they never tire. Dumbledore warned the school in 1993 that they cannot be fooled by disguises or Invisibility Cloaks, and that they do not understand pleading. Near them Harry Potter hears his mother's last moments. Since January 1994 he has heard his father's too.

The Kiss

A dementor lowers its hood only to use its last and worst weapon. It clamps its mouth on the victim's and sucks out the soul. The body can go on living as long as brain and heart still work. But the place where the soul was has to be filled with something, and what fills it is never the victim's own: a beast, of the kind a vampire carries, or one or two other things Lupin would not describe. Otherwise there is no self and no memory, only an empty shell.

The soul is not sleeping, or waiting to be fetched. It has been eaten. It will not be given back at the end of all things, when everything else is, because the Kiss denies its victim Heaven. Lupin called it the one thing the Ministry has ever licensed that he would walk to London to stop. In early 1994 the Ministry licensed the dementors to perform it on Sirius Black if they found him.

Origin

Dementors are made things. Teaching Harry the Patronus Charm in January 1994, Lupin spoke of 'a foul, evil thing like a dementor, and whatever it was that first thought of making dementors'. They exist, he said, 'to find, to open, to empty'. He would not say what had made them until Harry had finished his training.

Their maker is Morgoth, whom the Garou call the Wyrm and Scripture calls Satan. Lupin smells him on them, and his voice tears into a growl whenever they are near.

Azkaban is a fortress on an island in the North Sea. A dark sorcerer called Ekrizdis built it in the fifteenth century, and the dementors were already haunting it when the Ministry made it a prison in the eighteenth century. They have been its guards ever since.

Defences

The Patronus Charm drives them back. It stands between the caster and the dementor as a lamp holds off the dark. True faith repels them too. Sirius Black, twelve years a prisoner in Azkaban, found that once he truly believed in God the dementors stopped coming to him. His Animagus form, a dog, was also hard for them to feel.

Until June 1994 dementors had now and then been torn apart by creatures such as a Garou in its war form, but no wizard's spell had ever killed one.

At Hogwarts, 1993 to 1994

After Black's escape in the summer of 1993 the dementors were angrier than ever. On 1 September 1993 they searched the Hogwarts Express. One came into Harry's compartment and he collapsed; Remus Lupin drove it off with a silver defence. They guarded every entrance to the grounds, two of them at the gates, but Dumbledore would not let them into the castle.

In November 1993 more than a hundred of them came on to the pitch during the Hufflepuff match, drawn by hunger for the crowd's feeling. Harry fell fifty feet from his broom before Dumbledore drove them off with an enormous silver Patronus. From December they patrolled Hogsmeade every night after sundown by order of the Ministry, and searched every house in the village twice. In 1994 they guarded the roads out of it. At the Ravenclaw match in March 1994 Dracina Malfoy, Crabbe, Goyle and Marcus Flint stood on the grass at the edge of the pitch, directly below Harry, disguised as dementors.

In June 1994 about a hundred dementors closed on Sirius Black, Harry and Hermione Granger by the lake. One of them was lowering its hood to Kiss Harry when a silver stag drove them back. The stag was Harry's own. He had cast it from the far shore after going back three hours in time, and where it struck them the dementors came apart into smoke. A white arrow falling from the stars destroyed the last of them. Lupin, in his war form, destroyed several more in the Forest.

The survivors, frightened and starving now that Black had been taken out of their reach, tore round the grounds in a howling frenzy for the rest of the night. They kept well away from the boy who had killed them, until the teachers drove them off before dawn. For the first time, they were afraid.

pages.title: Bicorn
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Its horn, powdered, in Polyjuice Potion
pages.html:
The Bicorn is a magical beast with two horns. Its horn, ground to powder, is one of the ingredients of Polyjuice Potion. It is not kept in the student cupboard at Hogwarts.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, Hermione Granger read out the recipe for Polyjuice Potion. Most of it could be taken from the student cupboard, but she had no idea where they would get powdered Bicorn horn. Harry Potter, as he always did when he was worried, tried to drown it in sarcasm. 'And the Bicorn. Where's a Bicorn, Hermione? Is there a Bicorn shop? Is it in Diagon Alley next to the ice-cream place?' In Chapter Twelve, during double Potions, Harry lobbed one of Fred's Filibuster fireworks into Goyle's cauldron. In the uproar that followed, Hermione slipped into Snape's private stores. She came back with the Bicorn horn and the Boomslang skin hidden in her robes.

pages.title: Boomslang
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Its shredded skin, in Polyjuice Potion
pages.html:
The boomslang is a slender green tree snake of southern Africa, whose venom stops the blood from clotting. Its skin, shredded, is one of the ingredients of Polyjuice Potion, and one of the hardest to come by.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, Hermione Granger read out the recipe for Polyjuice Potion and warned that the shredded Boomslang skin was going to be awful to get. Harry Potter pictured knocking on the door of Snape's private stores. 'Excuse me, sir, sorry to bother you, have you got any Boomslang skin going spare? Shredded, if it's no trouble. He'll probably throw in a biscuit.' In Chapter Twelve Hermione stole some from those very stores, while Harry's firework in Goyle's cauldron kept Snape busy.

pages.title: Spider
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Common in the castle; giant ones in the Forbidden Forest
pages.html:
Spiders are common in Hogwarts castle, and much less common in Ron Weasley's company if he can help it. Their mortal enemy is the Basilisk, the king of serpents. Wherever one goes, they flee from it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, on the Wednesday after Hallowe'en 1992, Hermione Granger noticed some twenty spiders at the window by the message on the second-floor wall. They were scuttling and shoving to get out through a small crack in the glass, as though they were all fleeing something. What they were fleeing was the monster of the Chamber of Secrets.

Ron told her then that he did not like spiders. When he was three, Fred had turned his teddy bear into a dirty great spider, because Ron had broken Fred's toy broomstick.

In Chapter Sixteen, as he was led away to Azkaban, Hagrid said very slowly and carefully that anybody looking for answers had only to follow the spiders. Harry and Ron heard him from under the Invisibility Cloak.

In Chapter Seventeen there seemed to be no spiders left in the castle to follow. At last Harry saw a line of them hurrying across the vegetable patch. Later, at night, he and Ron followed the trickle of spiders deep into the Forbidden Forest, to a hollow full of spiders the size of carthorses. Aragog told them there that the thing in the castle was an ancient creature which spiders fear above all others.

In Chapter Eighteen the page in Hermione's fist gave Harry the reason: spiders flee before the Basilisk.

pages.title: Language parasite
infobox: Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain (1 September 2015)
The vocal cords of its host
Russian soldiers in Afghanistan; conscripts in Africa
pages.html:
The language parasite is a parasite of the vocal cords, bred in the 1980s as a weapon. Each strain was tuned to a single language. It lay quiet in anybody who spoke another tongue, but in those who spoke its own it woke, and it killed them.

Outbreaks

The first outbreaks came in 1984. The few who knew the truth kept very quiet about it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, after Mrs Norris was found Petrified at Hallowe'en 1992, Professor McGonagall asked Gilderoy Lockhart whether he had considered a parasite of the vocal cords. She had seen something rather like it before: a strain that spreads by language, which had gone through Russian soldiers in Afghanistan and conscripts in Africa. Lockhart lit up at once. He remembered the language parasites well, he said. He had been there himself, in Africa, and had been the one who identified the thing; he had wrestled it out of a man's throat with his bare hands.

Professor McGonagall straightened up and said nothing. She only smiled, very slightly. Harry understood that she had stood exactly where Lockhart claimed to have been, and that Lockhart had never been within a thousand miles of it.

pages.title: Hobbits
pages.html:
Hobbits are a small, unobtrusive people of Middle-earth, half the height of Men or less, who lived quietly in the green country of the Shire in the Third Age. They never studied magic of any kind. All the same, they could vanish without a sound when big folk they would rather not meet came blundering by, and no wizard has ever quite matched them at it.

The Shire

Hobbits were a merry people with curly brown hair, which grew thick on the tops of their feet as well, so that they seldom bothered with shoes. They liked peace, well-tilled earth, six meals a day when they could get them and a pipe of good leaf afterwards.

Two of them, Bilbo Baggins and his heir Frodo, were drawn into the affairs of the great. The history of the One Ring turned on what they did. Gandalf was long their friend, and learnt a good deal from them.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, at the Duelling Club in December 1992, Ambrose Greyhame stood by a pillar in the Great Hall, and nobody noticed him. He had learnt a great deal about not being noticed over the years. Some of it he had learnt from ‘small, quiet folk who'd been better at it than any wizard he'd ever met’. The folk he meant were, by every sign, the hobbits.

pages.title: Monster of the Chamber of Secrets
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The Chamber of Secrets, beneath Hogwarts
Mrs Norris, Colin Creevey, Justin Finch-Fletchley, Nearly Headless Nick, Hermione Granger, Penelope Clearwater (1992 to 1993)
pages.html:
The monster of the Chamber of Secrets, called in the old legend the horror within the Chamber, was the creature Salazar Slytherin left sealed beneath Hogwarts. Legend held that only the Heir of Slytherin could command it. It was a Basilisk.

Legend and truth

According to the legend, only Slytherin's true heir could open the Chamber. He would release the horror inside and purge the school of all who were unworthy to study magic. The purge was only a story. In truth Slytherin kept the Basilisk, the king of serpents, to defend Hogwarts from Muggles.

A Basilisk's stare kills. Seen indirectly, through a camera, a mirror or a ghost, it only Petrifies, which is why nobody died of it in the school year of 1992 to 1993.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, after the Chamber was opened at Hallowe'en 1992, Professor Binns told Harry Potter's class the legend. ‘It is generally held to be some sort of monster,’ he said, ‘which the heir of Slytherin alone can command.’ He thought the whole thing perfect nonsense.
