pages.html:
The Avengers are a team of superhumans founded in New York in 1963. With the Justice League they are one of the two largest superhuman organisations in the world. They work under an accord with the United Nations, which kept them out of the Augment War in 1993, and in August 1994 an Avengers delegation stood with Superman before the Security Council. Of the famous early Avengers, only Captain America, who first fought the Nazis in 1940, is still on active service.

The war years

No team called the Avengers existed before 1963, but its oldest member had fought in one very like it twenty years before. Steve Rogers was born in New York on 4 July 1920. Weapon I made him a super-soldier in 1940, and in December of that year he came to public notice as Captain America, with a teenage partner called Bucky. Once America was in the war he fought beside the Sub-Mariner, Namor, who had been born the same year. He fought beside the Human Torch as well, the android that Phineas Horton had built, and beside the Torch's young partner, Toro.

The four of them, with Bucky, saved Winston Churchill from the Nazi superman called Master Man. Churchill suggested afterwards that they ought to be a team, and they fought the rest of the war as the Invaders. Later they were joined by two British heroes, Union Jack and Spitfire. Miss America and the Whizzer followed.

The Invaders went where the strongest heroes of the All-Star Squadron could not: into occupied Europe, against the Red Skull, Baron Heinrich Zemo and the armies of the Axis. Captain America and Bucky also fought beside Sergeant Nick Fury's Howling Commandos.

In the last weeks of the war in Europe in 1945, Rogers and Bucky tried to stop an explosive-laden drone that Zemo had launched. It blew up in the air. Bucky was lost. Rogers fell into the North Atlantic, where the serum kept him alive, frozen in a block of ice, for nineteen years.

After the war

The public was not told that Captain America was gone. At the government's request, other men wore the costume to keep the symbol alive. The first, William Naslund, who had fought in the war as the Spirit of '76, led a new team in 1946, the All-Winners Squad. With him were the Human Torch, Toro, the Sub-Mariner, the Whizzer, Miss America and a new Bucky, Fred Davis. Naslund was killed in 1946. Jeff Mace, the Patriot, wore the costume after him until 1949.

In 1953 and 1954 yet another Captain America appeared, hunting communist agents in the McCarthy years. He called himself a commie-smasher. He was William Burnside, a young scholar obsessed with Rogers, who had taken a version of the super-soldier serum without the Vita-Rays that made it safe. It drove both him and his partner mad. They were put into suspended animation. When Burnside was revived in 1972 he fought the real Captain America, and lost.

In 1959 Nick Fury, then of the Central Intelligence Agency, led a covert team that hunted surviving Nazis under the name of the Avengers. Its members included Dum Dum Dugan, Namora, Dominic Fortune, Ulysses Bloodstone, Kraven the Hunter and the man later called Sabretooth. It was never made public, so the name was free when the Avengers of 1963 took it.

The founding, 1963

The Avengers came together in the summer of 1963, almost by accident. Loki, Thor's adopted brother, cast an illusion that made the Hulk seem to have wrecked a train, in the hope of tricking Thor into fighting him. Rick Jones, the teenager whose life Bruce Banner had saved at the gamma bomb test in 1962, sent out a radio call to the Fantastic Four for help. It was answered instead by Thor, Iron Man, Ant-Man and the Wasp.

They found that the Hulk was not the real enemy. They beat Loki together, and they stayed together. The Wasp gave them their name. Tony Stark, who was then presented to the public as Iron Man's employer, gave the team his family's mansion on Fifth Avenue for its headquarters, with the Stark butler, Edwin Jarvis, to run it. He paid its bills through a foundation named after his mother. The Hulk left within weeks, distrusted by the others and distrusting them.

Thor is an Asgardian, and does not age as men do. Stark had come to public notice in his armour only at the end of 1962, and Pym earlier the same year. Janet van Dyne, a young heiress, had become the Wasp in 1963 after her father's murder.

The 1960s

Early in 1964 the Avengers found Captain America frozen in a block of ice in the North Atlantic, where the Sub-Mariner had thrown it in a temper. By the calendar Rogers was forty-three, but in body he was still the young man of 1945. He joined at once and soon led the team. The same year Baron Heinrich Zemo, the man who had launched the drone of 1945, gathered the first Masters of Evil against the Avengers. In 1965 he was killed in a rockslide in South America during a fight with Rogers.

In 1965 the founders stepped down. They left Captain America in charge of three newcomers with criminal records. One was Hawkeye, the circus archer Clint Barton. The other two were mutant twins, Pietro and Wanda Maximoff, who had been members of Magneto's Brotherhood of Evil Mutants. They called themselves Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch. The team survived, and from then on it was always a shifting roster rather than a fixed band.

Pym was soon back as Goliath, and later as Yellowjacket, with Van Dyne beside him. They married in 1968. Hercules of Olympus joined in 1967. In 1968 the Black Panther joined: T'Challa, king of the African nation of Wakanda, and the team's first Black member. The Vision joined the same year. He was an android built to destroy the team by Ultron, the robot Pym had made and lost control of. The Black Knight, Dane Whitman, joined in 1969. Kang the Conqueror, a warlord from the far future, became one of the team's most persistent enemies.

The Scarlet Witch was the first witch ever to serve with the Avengers, thirteen years before Zatanna joined the Justice League, though neither the team nor the public knew it. Everybody took her magic for part of her mutant power, and they still do. Her brother, Quicksilver, is a Squib.

The 1970s

In 1971 the Avengers were drawn into the war between the Kree and Skrull empires, which is described below. For a time they were disbanded by Skrull impostors. The Black Widow, Natasha Romanoff, a Soviet agent who had defected in the 1960s, joined in 1973. That year Loki and the demon Dormammu tricked the Avengers into a war with the Defenders. In 1975 the Vision married the Scarlet Witch. In 1976 the Beast, Hank McCoy, formerly of the X-Men, joined.

In 1974 Captain America was hounded by the Secret Empire, and for a time he gave up his name. From 1977 the team was put under the scrutiny of Henry Peter Gyrich, the National Security Council's liaison. Both stories are told below. In 1979 Ms Marvel, Carol Danvers, joined, while the Falcon, Sam Wilson, was made a member under Gyrich's rules.

In 1973, while the Avengers and Captain Mar-Vell fought Thanos for the Cosmic Cube, the Justice League was holding off Darkseid's Parademons over the Pacific coast. In 1977 the Avengers brought Thanos down with Adam Warlock's help, on information Darkseid had sent to the League for his own ends.

In 1974 Agatha Harkness, the witch who was governess to the Richardses' son, Franklin, took the Scarlet Witch as her pupil and taught her true witchcraft.

The 1980s

Wonder Man joined in 1980, Tigra in 1981, She-Hulk in 1982 and Captain Marvel, the New Orleans harbour patrol officer Monica Rambeau, in 1983. The Wasp chaired the team for much of the decade. Captain Marvel succeeded her in 1987. In 1984, under the Vision's chairmanship, a second branch opened on the west coast. Hawkeye chaired it from a compound at Palos Verdes, California. With him were Mockingbird, Wonder Man, Tigra and Iron Man, who was then James Rhodes inside the armour, though the public did not know it.

In 1984 most of the Avengers were among the heroes the Beyonder carried off to Battleworld in the Secret Wars. Captain America led the heroes' side there. That summer the demon Nightmare broke the Hulk's mind. The Hulk smashed his way across America to New York, where he fought the city's heroes, Thor among them, through the streets and across Central Park. A family's picnic was one of the things in his way. Namor joined the team in 1985.

In 1986 Baron Helmut Zemo, Heinrich's son, led a new Masters of Evil in a siege of Avengers Mansion. They seized the mansion, wrecked it, beat Jarvis nearly to death and left Hercules in a coma. That winter, when President Reagan grounded every costumed hero in America, the order applied to the Avengers as much as to the League. In 1987 the team moved to Hydrobase, an artificial island off the coast, while the mansion was rebuilt.

In 1987 Rogers gave up the name and costume of Captain America rather than serve as the agent of the government's Commission on Superhuman Activities. The Commission gave them to John Walker. Rogers took them back in 1989, when Walker became the U.S. Agent. At the end of 1989 Hydrobase sank, and the team went back to the rebuilt mansion.

1990 to 1992

Sersi, one of the immortal Eternals, joined at the turn of 1990. Early that year Spider-Man, then a man of about forty-three, joined too, as a reserve member. In late 1991, when Odin banished Thor, the architect Eric Masterson served in his place among the Avengers, as Thor. In 1992 the team was caught up in Operation Galactic Storm, the war between the Kree and the Shi'ar that spilt over into Earth's part of space. It split over Iron Man's decision to execute the Kree Supreme Intelligence. Captain America opposed it, but it went ahead without him. The same year the Black Widow, then a woman in her early fifties, became the team's chairwoman, an office she still holds.

Crystal of the Inhumans joined in 1991.

When the Shi'ar took over the broken Kree Empire, they found Goa'uld ships on the Kree frontier and drove them off. The Avengers never saw them.

As the Cold War ended, the American charter under which the Avengers had worked was given up under a treaty between Washington and Moscow. The team took a charter from the United Nations instead. It is the accord under which the Avengers still operate. In 1992 Tony Stark, whose nervous system was failing, faked his own death. He left Rhodes a heavier suit of armour, War Machine.

In 1991 the Avengers went into space with the Justice League, under Captain America, against Thanos and the Infinity Gauntlet, on a day that was afterwards undone.

In the spring of 1991 the West Coast Avengers answered a call from the Lady of the Lake, Roma of Otherworld, and went into Limbo beside the Excalibur team against Victor von Doom.

1993 and 1994

Thor came back at the end of 1992, and Odin gave Masterson an enchanted mace of his own, Thunderstrike. Thor has since been called away from Earth to command Asgard's fleet in its war with the Replicators. Masterson, as Thunderstrike, stands among the Avengers in his place. Stark returned early in 1993 but has since retired. Rhodes has kept the War Machine armour, and with it his old friend's place. Spider-Man announced his retirement at the start of the summer of 1993, at about forty-six. The west coast branch was wound up at the end of 1993.

On 30 July 1993, with Khan Noonien Singh's forces in New Delhi, the Avengers and the Justice League issued a joint statement from New York. The United Nations accord under which they operated, it said, expressly prohibited unilateral action in any ongoing conflict between sovereign states. They would act only at the request of the Security Council, and under its authority. The Council made no such request. When the coalition offensive went into India in the spring of 1994, it went without them.

On 19 August 1994 an Avengers delegation stood at the Security Council, a little apart from the League, behind Superman as he asked for leave to act in the Balkans. Captain America was there, seventy-four by the calendar, looking no more than thirty. Thunderstrike and War Machine stood beside him. He was not the team's chairman; since 1992 that office had been held by the Black Widow. By then none of the others who had made the team famous in the 1960s was on its active roster. Thor was at war among the stars. Stark had retired. The Hulk had been a fugitive for thirty years. Pym, Van Dyne, Hawkeye, Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch were no longer on active service with it.

The Council adjourned without a vote. Russia had said that it would veto any resolution sending superhumans into Serbia without Belgrade's consent. China had said that it would oppose any resolution allowing superhumans to act on a nation's soil without its government's consent.

Onslaught, 1996 to 1997

By the summer of 1996 Eric Masterson, Thunderstrike, had died, and the Black Knight was far away with Sersi of the Eternals. The Black Widow still chaired the team.

That summer Onslaught, the being born in Charles Xavier's mind, came into the open, and his Sentinels came down on Manhattan. The Avengers sent word to everyone who had ever served. The old ones came out of retirement: Tony Stark in his old armour one last time, Hank Pym as Giant-Man, Janet van Dyne as the Wasp, Clint Barton as Hawkeye, Wanda Maximoff as the Scarlet Witch, the Vision, Pietro Maximoff as Quicksilver and Sam Wilson as the Falcon. Most of them were in their fifties or sixties, and looked thirty. Spider-Man, who had a little daughter to raise, would not come. Thor came home from Asgard's fleet to fight beside them.

In August 1996, in Central Park, Onslaught became a thing of pure force that could not be struck. Thor flew into him first. Captain America followed with most of the team, among them Iron Man, Hawkeye, the Scarlet Witch, the Vision, Giant-Man, the Wasp and Crystal. Their bodies gave Onslaught substance, so that the X-Men could destroy him. The world believed that they had been destroyed with him.

Of those who fought, the Black Widow, Hercules, Quicksilver and the Falcon were left, with James Rhodes, whose War Machine armour had died in Onslaught's pulse. Quicksilver had lost his sister and his wife on the same day. The Black Widow tried to gather a new team, but nobody she asked would serve. Late in 1996 she stood the Avengers down.

In fact Franklin Richards had caught the fallen as they fell and carried them into a world of his own making. He brought them home late in 1997, exactly as old as they had been when they fell. Thor went back to Asgard's fleet, while Tony Stark went back to his retirement. That winter the Avengers came together again.

The quarrel over Atlantis

The Sub-Mariner's feud with Aquaman has drawn the Avengers in again and again. In 1965 Captain America took Hawkeye, Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch down to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge to hold Namor back, while the Justice League held back Aquaman.

In 1981 the team helped the League clear up after the two kings' bodyguards fought in the lobby of the United Nations. When Namor joined the Avengers in 1985, the team had to keep him away from any business that touched the League. In 1987 and again in 1990 the Avengers stood beside the League between the two kings at sea. At Superman's funeral in 1992 the Black Widow, the team's chairwoman, took Namor by the arm and walked him to the far end of the procession.

The story is told in full on the page The feud of Aquaman and the Sub-Mariner.

Godzilla

In January 1965 three monsters were loose in Japan at once: Godzilla, the great reptile of that country, the flying monster Rodan, with King Ghidorah, a three-headed golden dragon from the stars. Japan asked for help for the first time. The Avengers were then Captain America, Iron Man, Thor, the Wasp and Henry Pym, who had begun as Ant-Man but was calling himself Giant-Man. They went, beside the whole Justice League.

Thor met King Ghidorah's lightning with his own, which was the first thing that had made the dragon give ground. Iron Man drew its fire away from a crowded town until his armour ran dry. Giant-Man held a broken bridge together while the Flash took the townspeople across it. Captain America ran the ground with Batman. It was the Wasp who saw the larva of Mothra crawl out between Godzilla and Rodan, who had been fighting each other all day. She told Superman that the three seemed to be talking. Both teams stood back, for the first time in their histories, to let the monsters drive King Ghidorah away themselves.

By 19 December 1965 the founders had stepped down. When the Xiliens of Planet X loosed the same three monsters on Japan, Captain America took Hawkeye, Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch. He was the only Avenger who had been there in January. He told the other three what he had learnt: keep out of Godzilla's breath, get the people away, do not expect to win. Quicksilver cleared the towns with the Flash, who was a great deal faster, which Quicksilver did not enjoy. Hawkeye spent the night quarrelling with the League's own archer. The Scarlet Witch did best of all: her hexes tripped Godzilla twice, which nobody on either team had managed in January. When the Xiliens' control broke, both teams stood back again.

In the summer of 1979 Godzilla appeared in Times Square. Captain America, Iron Man, Thor, the Vision, the Scarlet Witch, Yellowjacket and the Wasp went against him beside the Fantastic Four. All but the Vision had met him in Japan in 1965. Thor wrestled him on the side of the Empire State Building until the building began to crack. They could not stop him, which did not surprise them. He left when a boy called Rob Takiguchi asked him to.

The Avengers and the world

The Avengers were born into the Cold War, and the first of them to wear armour was made in Vietnam. At the end of 1962 Tony Stark was demonstrating his weapons to the American forces there when a booby trap wounded him. A local warlord took him prisoner, and he built the first armour to escape. James Rhodes, the Marine helicopter pilot who flew him out, became his closest friend and in time his successor. Through the 1960s the team fought communist agents and Soviet armoured men. Two of its own members, Hawkeye and the Black Widow, began on the wrong side of that struggle.

The team also reflected the struggle for civil rights. The Black Panther joined in 1968. The Falcon, a Harlem social worker who had fought beside Captain America since 1969, was made a member in 1979 by government order, when Gyrich insisted that the reduced roster must include a Black member. He served for some months and then resigned, because he would not be a token.

The Kree-Skrull War of 1971 to 1972 began as a political scandal. The Avengers had sheltered the Kree officer Captain Marvel. Senator H. Warren Craddock opened hearings of an Alien Activities Commission into the alien presence on Earth, in the manner of the investigating committees of the 1950s. When the Avengers refused to hand Captain Marvel over, Craddock turned public anger against them. Pickets gathered at the mansion. Three men who looked like Captain America, Thor and Iron Man announced that the team was disbanded; they were Skrulls. S.H.I.E.L.D., under Nick Fury, hunted Captain Marvel. The real Avengers re-formed and followed the war into space. It was ended by Rick Jones, who called up out of himself a power that the Kree Supreme Intelligence had woken in him. Craddock was revealed as a Skrull, and a mob killed him.

The Skrull impostors were three of the cows of 1961; Craddock's double was the fourth.

In 1974, the year of Watergate, Captain America was the target of the Secret Empire, a subversive organisation that planned to seize the government. It smeared him through a front called the Committee to Regain America's Principles, then framed him for murder. Rogers followed its leader, Number One, into the White House, where Number One, a man high in the American government, shot himself. Disillusioned, Rogers gave up the name for a time. He fought as Nomad, the man without a country, before taking up the shield again at the turn of 1975.

From 1977 the Avengers answered to the government through Henry Peter Gyrich, the National Security Council's liaison. Gyrich disliked superhumans. He held the team's priority clearance: its right to fly its Quinjets through American airspace, and to act with official sanction. At the turn of 1979 he cut the active roster to seven: Captain America, Iron Man, the Vision, the Scarlet Witch, the Beast, the Wasp and the Falcon. Gyrich later served on the Commission on Superhuman Activities, which in 1987 took Captain America's name away from Rogers. In the winter of 1986 to 1987 the Avengers, like every other costumed hero in America, were grounded by President Reagan's executive order.

At the end of the Cold War the team exchanged its American charter for one from the United Nations, and with it took on the limits that kept it out of the Augment War in 1993. The anger at superhumans that filled the streets outside the United Nations on the night of 19 August 1994 had older roots than Khan. One bedsheet there read HULK KILLED MY DAD, painted under a big green fist. The Hulk, a founding Avenger for a few weeks in 1963, had killed two people at a picnic in Central Park in the summer of 1984. One of them was a boy of six.

Hank Pym's work on the living cell is one of the roots of longevity medicine, together with Reed Richards's research and the Wayne Foundation's money. Thanks to it, many of the heroes who first came to public notice in the 1960s were still in their prime thirty years later.

Line-ups

Founding line-up, 1963: Thor, Iron Man, the Hulk (who left within weeks), Ant-Man and the Wasp. Rick Jones and his Teen Brigade helped them.

1964 to 1965: Captain America (from early 1964). After the founders stepped down in 1965: Captain America, Hawkeye, Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch.

The later 1960s: Goliath (Pym), the Wasp, Hercules (1967), the Black Panther and the Vision (1968), the Black Knight (1969).

The 1970s: the Black Widow (1973); Mantis, the Beast and Moondragon (1976). In 1979, Gyrich's seven: Captain America, Iron Man, the Vision, the Scarlet Witch, the Beast, the Wasp and the Falcon. Ms Marvel served beside them.

The 1980s: Wonder Man, Tigra, She-Hulk, Captain Marvel (Monica Rambeau), Starfox, Namor and Doctor Druid. The west coast branch, from 1984: Hawkeye, Mockingbird, Wonder Man, Tigra and Iron Man (James Rhodes).

1990 to 1992: Sersi, Spider-Man (reserve), Rage, Quasar, Crystal and Thor (Eric Masterson), with the Black Widow as chairwoman from 1992.

1994: the Black Widow (chairwoman, in her mid-fifties), Captain America (seventy-four, looking thirty), Thunderstrike (Eric Masterson, in his thirties), War Machine (James Rhodes, in his forties), the Black Knight (Dane Whitman, in his fifties), Crystal (in her forties), Hercules (immortal) and others.

Deaths, retirements and successors: Bucky was lost in 1945. In Captain America's absence his costume was worn by William Naslund, who was killed in 1946, by Jeff Mace until 1949 and by William Burnside from 1953 to 1954. From 1987 to 1989 John Walker wore it. Pym gave up the name of Ant-Man, which passed to Scott Lang in 1979. James Rhodes wore the Iron Man armour from 1983 to 1985, and has worn War Machine since 1992; Stark has retired. Eric Masterson served as Thor from 1991 to 1992, and has carried the mace Thunderstrike since; Thor is away at war. Spider-Man retired in the summer of 1993. The Hulk left in 1963, and he has been hunted ever since.

1996, against Onslaught: the Black Widow (chairwoman), Captain America, Crystal, Hercules and War Machine, with Thor home from the stars. Out of retirement came Iron Man (Tony Stark, for the last time), Giant-Man (Hank Pym), the Wasp, Hawkeye, the Scarlet Witch, the Vision, Quicksilver and the Falcon.

Those who fell into Onslaught in August 1996, to come home late in 1997, were Captain America, Thor, Iron Man, Hawkeye, the Scarlet Witch, the Vision, Giant-Man, the Wasp and Crystal.

In the saga

Book Three, Chapter Two: the Muggle news of 31 July 1993 reports a joint statement issued in New York late the night before by the Avengers and the Justice League. The statement says that the United Nations accord under which they operate expressly prohibits unilateral action in any ongoing conflict between sovereign states. They will act in India only at the request of the Security Council, and under its authority. The statement is greeted with anger in Delhi.

Book Four, Chapter Three: on the news of Saturday 20 August 1994 the Avengers stand a little apart from the Justice League at the United Nations, behind Superman, as he asks the Security Council for leave to act against Khan's forces in the Balkans. Harry notices that they look nothing like the Avengers on Dudley's old lunchbox. The man with the hammer has been replaced by a big blond man with a mace. The red and gold armour has given way to a heavier gunmetal suit bristling with guns, with a different man inside it. Only Captain America, in his blue mask with the white A, with the round shield on his back, is the same as ever. Everybody knows, Harry reflects, that they gave him something that stopped him getting any older, and he does not look a day over thirty. Spider-Man is not there; he retired the summer before, which Dudley still has not forgiven him for. Outside the United Nations that night, a protester carries a sheet reading HULK KILLED MY DAD.

pages.html:
The Justice League is the world's foremost association of superhuman heroes, founded by seven of them at the turn of 1960. With the Avengers, it is one of the two largest such organisations on Earth. It worked under a United Nations charter from 1987 until July 1994, when the charter was suspended a month after the League's New York embassy was destroyed. Led by Superman, it now works from the Watchtower, a half-built station on the Moon. On 19 August 1994 it asked the Security Council for leave to defend Belgrade against Khan's forces. The Council adjourned without a vote, with Russia and China opposed.

Founding, 1959 to 1960

The League's seven founders were the most powerful heroes of the day, and most of them had long worked alone. Superman had been in the public eye since 1938. Batman, in the person of Bruce Wayne, had followed in 1939. Wonder Woman had come to America in 1941 and had served through the war with the Justice Society. She had not aged a day since.

Aquaman, Arthur Curry, the son of a lighthouse keeper and a woman of Atlantis, had come out of the sea in 1941. The Martian Manhunter, J'onn J'onzz, had been stranded on Earth since 1955, and he had kept his true nature almost secret. Barry Allen had been the Flash since 1956. Hal Jordan had been Green Lantern only since 1959.

His mother's people say that their kingdom is the true Atlantis, a claim the Sub-Mariner disputes. Aquaman had been quarrelling with the Sub-Mariner about it since 1942. The League would spend a good part of the next thirty years keeping them apart.

They first fought together against seven alien invaders, the Appellaxians, who came down in different parts of the world to compete for the right to rule it. A different hero answered each one. When it was over the seven found one another and agreed to stay together.

Their first case as a League, at the turn of 1960, was against Starro, a giant alien starfish that had made slaves of the people of Happy Harbor, Rhode Island. A local teenager, Snapper Carr, helped them beat it. They made him a member as a mark of honour, although he had no powers of any kind. They set up their headquarters in a hollowed-out mountain outside the town, the Secret Sanctuary.

The League had no fixed leader at first; its chairmanship went round the members in turn. Unlike the Justice Society, which had been founded at the President's request, it answered to nobody but itself.

The 1960s

The League grew through the decade. Green Arrow, Oliver Queen, an archer who had fought crime since 1941, joined in 1961. The Atom, the physicist Ray Palmer, who could shrink himself to any size, followed in 1962. In 1964 came Hawkman, Katar Hol, a police officer of the planet Thanagar.

In 1961 Barry Allen sought out Jay Garrick, the first Flash, and two years later the old Justice Society re-formed. From 1963 the League and the Society joined forces nearly every summer, a custom that lasted until the Crisis.

In 1964 the League's young partners, Robin, Kid Flash and Aqualad, founded a team of their own, the Teen Titans. Kid Flash was Wally West, who had gained Barry Allen's powers in 1959 at about the age of ten.

The decade ended badly. In 1968 Wonder Woman gave up her powers for a time and left the League. In 1969 Snapper Carr, tricked by the Joker, gave away the location of the Secret Sanctuary, and the League abandoned it. Black Canary, the daughter of the Justice Society's Dinah Drake, joined the same year. She became one of the League's mainstays.

The 1970s

From 1970 the League worked from a satellite in orbit 22,300 miles above the Earth, reached by teleporter. Its members took turns at monitor duty on board, watching the world's emergencies from above.

In the same year Green Lantern and Green Arrow set out together by road to see America for themselves. They found poverty, racism and polluted towns. They found drugs, too, which in 1971 turned out to have caught Green Arrow's own ward, Roy Harper, Speedy. That year the Guardians of the Universe chose John Stewart, a Black architect from Detroit, as Hal Jordan's reserve. The travellers came home changed men, and the League changed with them.

New members came in steadily. The Elongated Man, Ralph Dibny, joined in 1973, as did the android Red Tornado. Hawkgirl followed in 1977. Zatanna, a stage magician whose real magic the public takes for tricks, joined in 1978, as did the young Firestorm at the end of the decade.

Wonder Woman had regained her powers. In 1976 she proved herself again in a series of trials watched by the League, and she rejoined it. In 1979 Mister Terrific of the Justice Society was murdered during one of the summer cases the two teams shared.

In 1973 the League fought Darkseid's Parademons over the Pacific coast of America, while the Avengers went after Thanos and the Cosmic Cube. In 1977 Darkseid's servant DeSaad brought the League word of Thanos's ship; it was a trick, and the League was waiting when the Parademons came for the Soul Gems.

The 1980s

In 1984 an alien attack left the satellite unusable. Aquaman, then chairman, was angry that so few members had answered the alarm. He dissolved the League and re-formed it in Detroit with those willing to give it their whole time. The veterans who stayed were the Martian Manhunter, Zatanna and the Elongated Man. With them came four newcomers: Vixen, Gypsy, Vibe and Steel. The new League worked from a bunker in the city. Aquaman himself left in 1985.

In 1984, too, several of the League's members were among the heroes the Beyonder carried off to Battleworld in the Secret Wars.

The Crisis of 1985 to 1986 took Barry Allen, who had been the Flash for twenty-nine years. Wally West, then about thirty-six, took up his name. Supergirl died in the same catastrophe. The world came out of it unsure of what it had lived through.

Within a year Darkseid's campaign to turn America against its heroes reached its height. In the winter of 1986 to 1987 President Reagan grounded every costumed hero in the country. The Detroit League did not survive it. At the turn of 1987 Professor Ivo's androids killed Vibe and Steel. The League came to an end with them.

A new League came out of the struggle at the start of 1987. Its members were Batman, the Martian Manhunter, Black Canary, Blue Beetle (Ted Kord), Mister Miracle, Guy Gardner of the Green Lantern Corps, Doctor Fate, Captain Marvel and Doctor Light (Kimiyo Hoshi). The businessman Maxwell Lord stood behind it. Booster Gold joined within weeks, and Captain Atom soon after. Doctor Fate's service was short, for that year Kent Nelson's long career came to an end.

Later in 1987 the League accepted a charter from the United Nations. It gave the League diplomatic standing, with embassies in New York, Paris and Moscow. For some years it called itself Justice League International.

In 1988 the League fought beside the world's armies against the Alien Alliance of the Dominators. As the invaders left they set off a gene bomb, which struck down the League with nearly every other hero on Earth. In 1989 a European branch, Justice League Europe, opened in Paris. Its members were Captain Atom, Power Girl, the Elongated Man, Animal Man, Metamorpho, Rocket Red and the Flash, Wally West, by then a man of about forty.

1990 to 1992

In 1991 and 1992 a run of disasters shook the League badly. Maxwell Lord fell into a coma. The old enemy Despero rampaged through New York. Members were killed, and others walked out. The United Nations, losing patience, withdrew its support for a time, and the League broke into pieces. It was rebuilt in 1992 with its charter intact. Its American and European branches carried on under new leadership.

In the autumn of 1992 the League was the first to meet the grey creature later called Doomsday, as it smashed its way across the Midwest. Its members at the time included Blue Beetle, Booster Gold, Guy Gardner, Fire, Ice, Maxima and Bloodwynd. They were beaten in a single fight, and Blue Beetle was left in a coma.

Superman took up the battle and followed Doomsday to Metropolis. On 18 November 1992 the two of them killed each other in front of the Daily Planet. The League attended his funeral as a body.

In 1991 the League fought beside the Avengers against Thanos and the Infinity Gauntlet, on a day that was afterwards undone.

1993 and 1994

At the turn of 1993 Wonder Woman called the League together again. She led it through the months of mourning, with new members including the Ray, Black Condor and Agent Liberty. The Martian Manhunter led a smaller task force of his own the same year.

In the summer of 1993 Mongul's forces destroyed Coast City and its seven million people. They were acting for the Cyborg Superman, who wore Superman's symbol and claimed to be him. The real Superman came back from the dead later that year, rejuvenated, as young as in the photographs of 1938 and with his hair grown long. He has led the League since his return.

On 30 July 1993, with Khan Noonien Singh's forces in New Delhi, the League and the Avengers issued a joint statement from New York. The United Nations accord under which they operated, it said, expressly prohibited unilateral action in any ongoing conflict between sovereign states. They would act only at the request of the Security Council and under its authority. The statement was greeted with anger in Delhi. The Security Council, fearing the precedent, kept the League out of India.

At the turn of 1994 Hal Jordan, broken by the loss of Coast City, destroyed the Green Lantern Corps and all but one of its masters. Then he vanished, after thirty-four years as Green Lantern. Since January 1994 the last ring has been worn by a young Los Angeles artist, Kyle Rayner, who serves in the League under Superman.

That spring Superman went after Doomsday again. In May Lex Luthor's aide fired sonic torpedoes under downtown Metropolis, flattening it for the second time in two years.

In June 1994 the League's embassy in New York was destroyed in an attack. In July the United Nations suspended the charter under which the League had worked since 1987. The League withdrew to the Watchtower, a station it had begun to build on the Moon and had not finished. From July into early August it fought through Zero Hour, when time itself broke down and was begun again. The power behind that catastrophe was Hal Jordan, one of the League's own founders, now calling himself Parallax.

On Friday 19 August 1994, with Khan's forces under Joaquin within forty miles of Belgrade, Superman went before the Security Council in New York. The League stood behind him, and so did a delegation of the Avengers. He spoke without notes. He said he understood that the Council feared it could never make the League leave once it was let in. He asked to be given orders in writing, and to be held to them. 'People are dying while we wait to be asked,' he said. 'The Justice League is ready. The Watchtower is ready. We can be in Belgrade within the hour.'

The Council adjourned without a vote. Belgrade had not asked for help. Russia said it would veto any resolution sending superhumans into Serbia without Belgrade's consent. China said it would oppose any resolution allowing superhumans to act on a nation's soil without its government's consent. Washington was 'studying the request', and Britain's position was understood to be similar. The Council was to meet again on Tuesday 23 August.

That night more than twenty thousand people protested outside the United Nations, chanting 'No more capes!' There were smaller crowds in Los Angeles, Chicago and what remains of Metropolis.

Early in October 1994 the League fought beside the Power Rangers for the first time. Lord Zedd had made a bargain with Brainiac, an alien machine mind who collects cities, and Brainiac shrank Angel Grove into a bottle. The League and the Rangers won it back together, in full view of the world. The story is told on the page The bottling of Angel Grove.

The quarrel over Atlantis

Aquaman's feud with the Sub-Mariner has dragged the League under the sea more often than any enemy. In 1965 it went down to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge to restrain its own founding member, while the Avengers restrained Namor, and Superman stood between the two armies for three days. In 1981 it helped the Avengers clear up after the two kings' bodyguards fought in the lobby of the United Nations.

In 1987 the new Justice League International sent the Martian Manhunter to the drowned ruins that an earthquake had lifted out of the Atlantic, where both kings fought for nine days until the ruins sank under them. In 1990 the League spent a fortnight at sea between Namor's salvage fleet and Aquaman's whales. At Superman's funeral in November 1992 it was the Martian Manhunter who took Aquaman by the arm and walked him away from Namor.

The story is told in full on the page The feud of Aquaman and the Sub-Mariner.

Godzilla

Godzilla, the great reptile of Japan, struck Superman out of the sky over Tokyo Bay in 1954, six years before there was a League. Its members never forgot it. Two of them met him singly: Green Lantern in the Bering Sea in June 1962, then the Flash at Nagoya in April 1964. Neither tried to fight him.

In January 1965 three monsters were loose in Japan at once: Godzilla, Rodan and King Ghidorah, a three-headed dragon from the stars. Japan asked for help for the first time. All ten members of the League went: Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, the Flash, Green Lantern, Aquaman, the Martian Manhunter, Green Arrow, the Atom and Hawkman. The Avengers went too, who were then Captain America, Iron Man, Thor, Giant-Man and the Wasp. The two teams had never worked together before.

Superman would let nobody into Godzilla's breath. He fought King Ghidorah beside Wonder Woman, Iron Man and Thor, whose lightning was the one thing that made the dragon give ground. Green Lantern, whose ring had no power over a golden dragon, tried to part Godzilla from Rodan. The Martian Manhunter read Godzilla's mind, where he found nothing but temper. The Flash cleared the towns. Batman directed the ground with Captain America. When the larva of Mothra talked the two monsters round, the heroes stood back to let all three drive King Ghidorah away. Neither team had done such a thing before.

On 19 December 1965 the Xiliens of Planet X loosed the same three monsters on Japan under their own control. The same ten went. The Avengers had changed: Captain America now led Hawkeye, Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch, with whom he had stood beside Superman on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that year. Green Arrow took an instant dislike to Hawkeye, which was returned. This time the League did not try to win. The Martian Manhunter found only the Xiliens' machines in Godzilla's mind, so the League held the monsters out of Tokyo for one night, waiting for the control to be broken. When it was, the League stood back a second time.

In March 1972 the Atom, on monitor duty in the satellite, saw Gigan approaching the Earth with King Ghidorah. Superman met them above the atmosphere with Green Lantern but could not turn them. The League followed them down to Tokyo, where it kept the crowds clear while Godzilla fought the pair off, with Anguirus. Its log records that the Earth was defended that day by Godzilla, the League assisting.

In February 1988, under the new charter, Japan asked the United Nations for the League when Godzilla came up off its coast. Batman went with the Martian Manhunter, Blue Beetle, Booster Gold, Guy Gardner and Doctor Light, Kimiyo Hoshi, who is Japanese. Guy Gardner attacked against orders, for which he was knocked into the sea. Doctor Light led Godzilla away with a great light over the water, as flares had drawn him at Osaka in 1955. Nobody was hurt, which Batman thought the best result the League had had all year.

The League and the world

The League was founded as a private association. For its first quarter of a century it answered to nobody but its members. It had no government sponsor, as the Justice Society had had, and it kept its distance from Washington. That independence did not survive the 1980s.

It ended in two steps. The first came in the winter of 1986 to 1987, when President Reagan issued an executive order grounding every costumed hero in America. He did so after a campaign of fear on television, which was afterwards found to have been the work of Darkseid's agent Glorious Godfrey. The Detroit League did not outlive the order. The order itself was lifted after the march on Washington early in 1987. The second step came later that year, when the new League, through the efforts of Maxwell Lord, accepted a charter from the United Nations.

The charter of 1987 made the League something like a small nation, with embassies and diplomatic rights, in return for a measure of international control. It was signed in the last years of the Cold War. The League kept an embassy in Moscow, and the Soviet Union lent it one of its armoured Rocket Reds, Dmitri Pushkin, who served in it through the Soviet state's last years. The charter bound the League not to take sides in wars between states without the Security Council's authority. It was that clause the League invoked in 1993.

The cause of civil rights reached the League through Green Lantern. Hal Jordan's journey across America with Green Arrow at the start of the 1970s brought questions of race and poverty to the League's own table. So did the choice of John Stewart as Earth's second Green Lantern in 1971.

In 1993 and 1994 the Augment War brought the League's position to a crisis. Its refusal to act in India in July 1993 was the charter working as intended. The Council's refusal to let it act was the Council's fear of setting a precedent. A year later, after the loss of the embassy and the charter, a good many of the Council's members simply did not trust it.

Russia and China set themselves against any superhuman action on a nation's soil without its government's consent. Public opinion in America and Europe turned the same way. Coast City, destroyed by a killer wearing Superman's symbol, is one of the protesters' two great grievances. Metropolis, wrecked twice in two years, is the other. The pollsters' word for people with powers, metahumans, has become a word of suspicion.

The newsreaders of August 1994 set the League's troubles in a longer line: the Justice Society's refusal to unmask before Congress in 1951, Reagan's grounding of 1986 and the suspension of the charter in July 1994.

Line-ups

Founding line-up, turn of 1960: Superman, Batman (Bruce Wayne), Wonder Woman, the Flash (Barry Allen), Green Lantern (Hal Jordan), Aquaman and the Martian Manhunter. Snapper Carr, who had no powers, was made a member as a mark of honour.

Joined in the 1960s: Green Arrow (1961), the Atom (Ray Palmer, 1962), Hawkman (Katar Hol, 1964) and Black Canary (1969). Joined in the 1970s: the Elongated Man (1973), Red Tornado (1973), Hawkgirl (1977), Zatanna (1978) and Firestorm (at the end of the decade). Wonder Woman was away from 1968 to 1976.

The Detroit League, 1984 to 1987: Aquaman (until 1985), the Martian Manhunter, Zatanna, the Elongated Man, Vixen, Gypsy, Vibe and Steel.

The International League, from 1987: Batman, the Martian Manhunter, Black Canary, Blue Beetle, Mister Miracle, Guy Gardner, Doctor Fate, Captain Marvel and Doctor Light. Booster Gold and Captain Atom joined soon after. Justice League Europe, from 1989: Captain Atom, Power Girl, the Elongated Man, Animal Man, Metamorpho, Rocket Red and the Flash (Wally West).

Autumn 1992: Blue Beetle, Booster Gold, Guy Gardner, Fire, Ice, Maxima and Bloodwynd, with Superman.

1993: Wonder Woman's League, with the Ray, Black Condor, Agent Liberty and the survivors of 1992.

1994: Superman (leader), Wonder Woman, the Flash (Wally West, about forty-five), Green Lantern (Kyle Rayner, since January), the Martian Manhunter, Blue Beetle and others. Batman, the third man to wear the cowl, works with the League but is never seen with it in daylight. He did not stand with it at the United Nations.

Deaths, retirements and successors: Barry Allen died in the Crisis of 1985. Wally West has been the Flash since. Hal Jordan fell and vanished at the turn of 1994. Kyle Rayner wears the last ring. Bruce Wayne gave up the cowl to Dick Grayson in 1980. Dick put it away in the summer of 1990, and Terry McGinnis took it up in the summer of 1991. The public knows only that Batman has been more than one man. Vibe and Steel were killed in 1987. Kent Nelson's service as Doctor Fate ended the same year. Superman died in November 1992 and came back to life in 1993. Aquaman left the League in 1985. The Martian Manhunter, who has served in more of its line-ups than anyone, remains.

In the saga

On the morning of 31 July 1993 the breakfast news at the Dursleys' reported that pressure was mounting on the world's two largest superhuman organisations to intervene against Khan. Late the night before, in New York, the Avengers and the Justice League had issued a joint statement, read from a podium by a man in a very good suit. The terms of the United Nations accord under which they operated, it said, expressly prohibited unilateral action in any ongoing conflict between sovereign states. They would act only at the request of the Security Council and under its authority. The statement was greeted with anger in Delhi.

On the news of Saturday 20 August 1994 Harry Potter saw Superman at the Security Council. Along the wall behind him were the people he had brought. One was a tall woman in red and gold with a gold tiara, who looked no older than she did in Dudley's old annuals. Another was the Flash: not the one of the annuals, who had died in 1985, but the boy who used to run beside him, grown into a man of forty-five or so. There was a young Green Lantern in a mask Harry had never seen, who had turned up out of nowhere in January after the old one vanished. Last of all there was a huge green-skinned man with a heavy brow, standing so still that he might have been carved. Batman was not there.

The newsreader explained that a year before, the Council had kept the League out of India for fear of setting a precedent. In June its New York embassy had been destroyed, and in July the charter under which it had worked since 1987 had been suspended. Since then it had been operating from a half-built station on the Moon, which it called the Watchtower. Harry waited for her to smile, and she did not.

pages.title: United Nations Security Council
infobox: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States
The Avengers and the Justice League, under the UN accord
pages.html:
The United Nations Security Council is the body of the United Nations charged with keeping the peace between nations. Under the accord by which the world's superhuman organisations work, the Avengers and the Justice League may act in a conflict between sovereign states only at its request, under its authority.

The Council

The Council has fifteen members. Five of them hold permanent seats with a veto: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. It meets at the headquarters of the United Nations in New York, round a long curved table. In 1993 it kept the Justice League out of India, for fear of setting a precedent. In July 1994 the United Nations suspended the charter under which the League had worked since 1987.

After Superman's appeal to the Council on 19 August 1994, protesters against the superhumans gathered outside the United Nations in New York. There were twenty thousand of them that night. By 22 August there were three hundred thousand, arriving by coach from all over America.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1993, the Avengers and the Justice League issued a joint statement from New York. The terms of the accord, they said, 'expressly prohibit unilateral action in any ongoing conflict between sovereign states'. They would act only 'at the request of the Security Council, and under its authority'. Delhi was angry.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Three, the news of 20 August 1994 reported that the Council had heard Superman the day before. He stood at the end of the long table, with the Justice League behind him and the Avengers a little apart, Captain America among them. He offered to put the League under written orders: 'People are dying while we wait to be asked.' The Council adjourned without a vote, to meet again on the Tuesday. Russia said it would veto any resolution sending superhumans into Serbia without Belgrade's consent. China would oppose any resolution letting superhumans act on a nation's soil without its government's consent. Outside the United Nations more than twenty thousand people had gathered to protest against the superhumans.

In Chapter Four, at dinner at the Burrow on 21 August, Harry told the Weasleys that Superman had spoken to the Security Council on the Friday, while twenty thousand people outside shouted 'No more capes'. Arthur had never heard of the Council. Percy dismissed it as a Muggle committee of no consequence.

In Chapter Five Hermione told Harry, from Arthur's old transistor radio, that there were now three hundred thousand protesters outside the United Nations. Harry reflected that the crowd in New York was three times the size of the whole World Cup. At lunch Percy, who had called the Council a Muggle committee of no consequence the night before, nodded hard at Barty Crouch's warnings about the Muggles.

In Chapter Six, at the stadium, Harry wondered whether Arthur would want to bless the protesters outside the United Nations, who were screaming for people like Harry to be punished. He told Cornelius Fudge that the Muggles shouted mutie at the protests in New York.

pages.title: Power Rangers
infobox: Mighty Morphin Power Rangers, 'Day of the Dumpster' (28 August 1993)
The Power Coins, made by Ninjor
Red, blue, black, yellow, pink; green from late 1993
pages.html:
The Power Rangers are a team of young Californians in coloured suits and helmets, based in Angel Grove, who fight monsters with their giant robot. They came to public notice in the summer of 1993, when five of them fought a giant starfish at the Bull Ring in Birmingham. By August 1994 there are six of them, on the news nearly every morning. Zordon made them.

Origin

Zordon of Eltar chooses who carries the Power Coins, which Ninjor made in his Temple of Power. He raised a first team of Rangers with them in the 1960s. It never came to public notice, and it was a disaster. In 1993 Rita Repulsa was set free on the Moon and turned on Earth. Zordon tried again with five teenagers of Angel Grove, and the second attempt worked.

Zordon's first team fought Psycho Green on the Moon in July 1969; three of the five died. In the autumn of 1994 Lord Zedd took Rita's place on the Moon. In November 1998 Zordon gave up his form. His light took the evil out of Rita, Zedd and Divatox.

The team

Each Ranger carries a Power Coin in a morpher. At the call of 'It's Morphin Time', each is transformed into an armoured Ranger with a helmet and weapons. The Red Ranger, Jason Lee Scott, draws on the Tyrannosaurus; the Blue, Billy Cranston, on the Triceratops; the Black, Zack Taylor, on the Mastodon; the Yellow, Trini Kwan, on the Sabre-toothed Tiger; and the Pink, Kimberly Hart, on the Pterodactyl. Each coin also calls a giant fighting machine, a Zord. The five Zords combine into the Megazord, the robot the size of a cathedral that the news calls their combat vehicle.

Later in 1993 a sixth joined them: Tommy Oliver, the Green Ranger. He carried the Green Power Coin that Rita had stolen, and he came to them first as her servant. Their identities are secret. Their base is Zordon's Command Center outside Angel Grove, where Alpha 5 keeps the machines running.

Fear and trust

At the end of October 1993 Rita Repulsa turned the Rangers' own Zords on the cities of the world, in full view of everybody. The world's armies could do nothing against them. The Rangers won their Zords back, but a great many people have been afraid of them ever since.

Grace Sterling, the head of Promethea, sent her relief crews into the cities that had been hit. Then she went on television to defend the Rangers, at a time when few others would. In the summer of 1994 opinion about them is divided, as the news from Angel Grove shows.

The winter of 1994 to 1995

The world had been unmade once already, in September 1994, by Lord Drakkon, the Tommy Oliver of another world. The Rangers mended it. Afterwards nobody on Earth remembered.

Early in October 1994 the Rangers fought beside the Justice League for the first time, when Lord Zedd made a bargain with Brainiac, an alien who collects cities. Brainiac shrank Angel Grove into a bottle. The two teams won the city back together, in full view of the world. The story is told on the page The bottling of Angel Grove.

In November 1994 Jason Lee Scott, Zack Taylor and Trini Kwan left for a peace conference in Geneva, as everybody believed. They had gone into space instead, as the Omega Rangers, an order far older than Zordon's. Their friends learnt the truth in December. The rest of the world never did.

In December 1994 Grace Sterling made a second Green Ranger with the mended Dragon Coin: Matt Cook, a schoolboy of Angel Grove. Over Christmas, under a dome that Lord Zedd had raised over the city, he took off his helmet on every screen in it. For a few weeks he was the only Ranger whose name the public knew.

The weeks that followed were the worst the Rangers had known. Zartus of Eltar invaded the Earth, and his ships held the sky for a matter of days. In February 1995 Rita Repulsa, as Mistress Vile, let Dark Specter into the world. His corruption got into the Morphin Grid itself, so that any Ranger who morphed was turned against the rest.

When the Rangers cleansed the Grid, the world was mended for the second time. Everything broken since Zedd's dome stood whole again. The world kept no memory of those weeks: not the dome, not the Green Ranger's face, not the Eltarian ships. Only the Rangers of both teams remembered them, with Zordon, Alpha 5 and a very few others.

Methods

The Rangers fight on foot first. When Rita's monsters are made to grow to giant size, they fight with the Zords. They always get everybody out first. All the same, their battles are hard on buildings, and some insurance policies in Angel Grove carry a clause that excludes superhuman combat.

The Beetleborgs

There was one company of armoured heroes whom the Rangers met again and again. From September 1996 the town of Charterville had three heroes of its own, the Beetleborgs, whose powers came from a wish granted by a phasm named Flabber. All three were children: Drew McCormick, his sister, Jo, and their friend Roland Williams. Five times between 1996 and 1998 the Rangers' enemies took an interest in Charterville, so the two teams fought side by side.

On 19 October 1996 Prince Sprocket of the Machine Empire sent Klank to Charterville with Orbus and a company of Cogs. The Zeo Rangers went after them. Jason Lee Scott arrived first, as the Gold Ranger, with Tommy Oliver bringing the Zeo Megazord behind him. On 3 May 1997 the space pirate Divatox had Flabber carried off to grant her a wish. Tommy's Turbo Rangers helped to get him back. Their youngest, the Blue Ranger, Justin Stewart, was twelve years old, the Beetleborgs' own age. He became their friend.

On 20 September 1997 Divatox joined forces with the Beetleborgs' enemy Nukus. Their changelings wrecked the park at Angel Grove as false Beetleborgs, while others wrecked Charterville as false Rangers. The two teams came to blows before Justin stopped them. T.J. Johnson's Rangers then joined their Turbozords to the Beetleborgs' Battle Vehicles to finish the changelings. On 25 October the Beetleborgs came to Angel Grove, where Nukus was fetching back an artist whom Divatox had stolen from him.

The last meeting was on 21 February 1998, in the Charterville cemetery. Astronema's warrior Ecliptor seized the Astral Axe, which commanded a giant named Boron. Andros, the Red Space Ranger, pulled it out of his hand with the help of Drew McCormick. Neither team ever gave away the other's names.

Other teams in California

The Rangers are not the only young Californians to fight in armour in these years. From September 1994 the VR Troopers of Crossworld City fought the creatures of Grimlord, for the most part in another world where no camera could follow them. The two teams are not known ever to have met.

Godzilla

In the spring of 1994 Rita Repulsa stole a gem called the Multiversal Focus, which can carry its holder anywhere. She asked it for a land with no Power Rangers. It took her to Japan, where she joined the Xiliens of Planet X, an alien people whom Godzilla had been keeping off the Earth since 1965. The Green Ranger was carried there with her, so Zordon sent the other five after him.

The Rangers fought Godzilla before they understood him. He wrecked the Dragonzord, then fought the Megazord until both went down. After that the Megazord fought beside him against Rita's monsters, with those of the Xiliens. When King Ghidorah was called down, the Megazord joined the mended Dragonzord as the Mega Dragonzord, which helped Godzilla to beat it. Rita fled through the gem, which had cracked. Godzilla promptly turned on the Rangers, who went home.

In the saga

Book Three, Chapter Two: on 31 July 1993 the Dursleys' news showed helicopter film of the previous afternoon in Birmingham. Five people in red, blue, black, yellow and pink ran in a line across a rooftop towards an enormous pink thing with far too many arms. Behind them a robot the size of a cathedral stood up out of the canal. The city centre had been evacuated for six hours, and there were no fatalities. Dudley, sausage halfway to his mouth, looked as though he would like to be one of them. It was the first time Harry had seen him want to be anything. Harry thought the suits silly, the robot sillier and the group pose embarrassing.

Book Three, Chapter Four: Harry was trying to explain the Muggle world to Lucius Malfoy, who had never heard of the Rangers. 'They've got no magic, Mr Malfoy. Not a drop. They've got suits, and a sort of robot, and they go and stand in front of a thing like that, in a shopping centre, with people screaming, because somebody's got to and they can.' They save people, he said, because it is the right thing to do.

Book Four, Chapter Three: by August 1994 there were six Rangers on the news every morning. The newest was green, with a gold shield across his chest, and Dudley adored him. The same bulletin showed a young man in Angel Grove whose shop had been flattened by their robot on its way to a ten-storey monster. Dudley could not understand why anybody would be against people who saved people's lives.

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994 Harry remembered how Dudley had watched the Power Rangers the morning before, with his mouth slightly open, as though they were the most wonderful thing that had ever happened.

pages.title: The Birmingham starfish creature
infobox: A pink starfish with far too many arms, about the size of a double-decker bus
Gas Street canal basin and the Bull Ring, Birmingham
pages.html:
The Birmingham starfish creature was a pink monster with far too many arms, about the size of a double-decker bus. On 30 July 1993 it came out of the canal basin near Gas Street in Birmingham and attacked the Bull Ring shopping centre. The Power Rangers fought it there, in the summer they first came to public notice.

The attack

On the afternoon of 30 July 1993 the creature came out of the canal basin near Gas Street and began attacking the Bull Ring shopping centre. Eyewitnesses described it as a starfish roughly the size of a double-decker bus: pink, enormous, with far too many arms. Birmingham city centre was evacuated for six hours.

The Californian team came straight over. They engaged the creature with their combat vehicle shortly after four o'clock. Film taken from a helicopter showed a round tower block at the heart of the city, with smoke coming off the shopping centre beside it. Five figures in red, blue, black, yellow and pink were running in a line across a rooftop towards the thing. Behind them, over the office blocks, a robot the size of a cathedral was standing up out of the canal, with lights where its eyes should be. Nobody was killed, though a number of shoppers were treated for shock. West Midlands Police asked anyone with information about the creature's origin to come forward.

In the saga

Book Three, Chapter Two: the attack was on the Dursleys' news on the morning of Harry's thirteenth birthday. Dudley stopped with a sausage halfway to his mouth. He watched the five Rangers leap off the roof as though he would like to be one of them, and Harry thought it was the first time he had ever seen Dudley want to be anything. Harry had seen the Rangers before, in bits, on the news and on the backs of cereal packets.

Book Three, Chapter Four: Harry described it to Lucius Malfoy as 'a starfish the size of a bus. It wouldn't have looked out of place in the Forbidden Forest.'

pages.title: Spider-Man
aliases: the man in a mask who climbed walls
infobox: Peter Parker; Peter Benjamin Parker; Spidey
Human, changed by a spider's bite
A spider's strength in proportion to his size, with its agility; clings to walls; a sixth sense for danger; mechanical web-shooters of his own design
The Fantastic Four; the Avengers; the Black Cat; Daredevil; Superman; the Justice League
The Green Goblin; Doctor Octopus; the Vulture; Kraven the Hunter; the Kingpin; the Hobgoblin; Venom; Carnage
Late June or early July 1993; his identity was never made public
Forensic scientist in the crime laboratory of the New York police; father of Spider-Girl
pages.html:
Spider-Man is the masked New York hero in a red and blue suit who climbs walls, swinging from one building to the next on lines of web. He came to public notice in 1962, as a teenager, and was for thirty years one of the most famous people in the world. He fought beside the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, the Justice League and, twice, Superman. At the start of the summer of 1993, in his mid-forties, he announced his retirement, without ever having let anybody see who he was. Under the mask was Peter Parker of Forest Hills, Queens, a photographer and scientist, who gave it up when his wife, Mary Jane, gave birth to their first child. The world never learnt his name. In 2008 their daughter, May, who had inherited his powers, took up his old work herself as Spider-Girl.

The bite, 1962

Peter Parker was an orphan, brought up in Forest Hills, Queens, by his Uncle Ben and Aunt May. His parents, Richard and Mary Parker, had died when he was very small. In 1962, when he was a shy, clever schoolboy at Midtown High, he was bitten at a science exhibition by a spider that had been exposed to radiation. He found that he had the strength of a spider in proportion to his size, and its agility. He could cling to walls, and a sixth sense warned him of danger. He built the mechanical web-shooters himself.

He used his powers first for money. In a mask he took on a wrestler called Crusher Hogan for a cash prize, and won. He then made himself a costume and went on television. When a burglar came running past him at the studio, he let the man go, because it was none of his business. Days later the same man shot and killed his Uncle Ben. Spider-Man ran the killer to ground in an empty warehouse, and Parker learnt from it that great power brings great responsibility. He has lived by that ever since.

The menace, 1963 to 1965

In 1963 Spider-Man tried to join the Fantastic Four, expecting to be paid for it. He lost interest when he heard that they paid nobody. The same year he saved the astronaut John Jameson, whose space capsule had gone out of control. The astronaut's father, J. Jonah Jameson, the publisher of the Daily Bugle, called Spider-Man a menace all the same. He went on calling him one for thirty years, while buying photographs of him from Peter Parker, who took them himself.

Within two years he had met most of the enemies he was to fight for the rest of his career: the Vulture, Doctor Octopus, the Sandman, the Lizard, Electro, Mysterio, the Green Goblin and Kraven the Hunter. Doctor Octopus was Otto Octavius, an atomic scientist whose four mechanical arms had been fused to his body in an accident. The Lizard was Dr Curt Connors, a surgeon who had lost an arm, whose experiment to grow it back had turned him into a reptile. In 1964 six of them banded together as the Sinister Six. They took Betty Brant hostage with Aunt May.

Betty Brant, Jameson's secretary, was Peter's first love. At Midtown High the school's star athlete, Flash Thompson, bullied Peter Parker while worshipping Spider-Man. Peter finished at Midtown High in 1965.

Empire State University, 1965 to 1968

At the end of 1965 Peter went up to Empire State University in Manhattan, where he met Gwen Stacy and Harry Osborn. That winter Aunt May fell gravely ill. The only cure, a serum called ISO-36, was stolen by Doctor Octopus, who was calling himself the Master Planner. In the Master Planner's underwater hideout Spider-Man was pinned under tons of fallen machinery, with the serum just out of his reach. He lifted it off himself by will alone, and he got the serum to Aunt May in time.

In 1966 the Green Goblin learnt who Spider-Man was, captured him and unmasked himself in turn. He was Norman Osborn, the father of Harry Osborn, a rich industrialist. In the fight that followed he fell into a tangle of live electrical wires, and the shock wiped out every memory of his life as the Goblin. Peter kept the secret for Harry's sake.

For months Aunt May had been trying to introduce Peter to the niece of her neighbour, Anna Watson. He had dreaded it. When at last they met, late in 1966, the niece turned out to be a beautiful red-haired girl, Mary Jane Watson, whose first words to him were: 'Face it, Tiger... you just hit the jackpot!'

In 1967, worn out by the strain of it all, Peter threw his costume into a dustbin and gave up. A new crime boss, the Kingpin, began at once to take over the city's gangs. Remembering Uncle Ben, Peter took the costume back from Jameson's office, where it had ended up, and went after the Kingpin.

Captain Stacy, 1968 to 1972

Gwen's father, Captain George Stacy, a retired police officer, became a friend of Peter's and a quiet admirer of Spider-Man. In 1970 Doctor Octopus's runaway arms brought a chimney down into the street during a fight with Spider-Man. Captain Stacy threw himself over a small boy to shield him from the falling bricks. Dying, he called Spider-Man by his real name, Peter, and asked him to look after Gwen. Gwen, who never knew what her father had known, blamed Spider-Man for his death.

In 1971 Harry Osborn, who had lost Mary Jane, began taking pills, and nearly died of them. The strain of it brought back Norman's memory, and the Green Goblin with it. Spider-Man took him to see his son in hospital, and the sight wiped the memory out again. The same year Peter brewed a formula to take his powers away. It gave him four extra arms instead. He was rid of them only with the help of Dr Curt Connors.

The death of Gwen Stacy, 1973

By 1973 Gwen Stacy was the love of Peter's life. That year Norman Osborn's memory came back for good. As the Green Goblin he seized Gwen and carried her to the top of a bridge, then threw her off. Spider-Man caught her by the leg with a line of web, but when he drew her up she was dead.

Spider-Man hunted the Goblin down, beside himself with grief. In their last fight the Goblin sent his glider at Spider-Man's back. Spider-Man's sixth sense warned him, he jumped aside, and the glider ran Norman Osborn through. He died where he fell.

In the days afterwards Peter, half out of his mind, told Mary Jane to go away. She went to the door, closed it and stayed. From that day they were close.

The Punisher and the Jackal, 1974 to 1975

Some people blamed Spider-Man for Norman Osborn's death. In 1974 a man calling himself the Jackal used that to set a hired gunman, the Punisher, on him. The Punisher, a former Marine who made war on criminals and killed them, soon found that he had been lied to. That year Harry Osborn found his father's Goblin costumes, put one on, and came after Spider-Man, whom he blamed for his father's death. He was beaten, and spent a long time afterwards under the care of doctors. Aunt May, meanwhile, very nearly married Doctor Octopus, who wanted something she had inherited.

The Jackal was Professor Miles Warren, who had taught Peter and Gwen biology at Empire State University. He had been in love with Gwen, and blamed Spider-Man for her death. In 1975 he showed Peter a young woman who was Gwen to the life, grown from cells he had taken from her. He had grown a copy of Peter as well.

The two Spider-Men fought at Shea Stadium, where Warren had tied a bomb to the reporter Ned Leeds that only the real Spider-Man could disarm. In the fight one of them was struck down by falling debris. Warren, sane again for a moment, saved Ned Leeds and died in the blast. The copy of Gwen left New York to make her own life. Peter, who knew he was himself because he loved Mary Jane rather than Gwen, dropped the dead man's body down the chimney of an incinerator. Nothing more ever came of it.

Graduation, 1976 to 1979

In 1976 Spider-Man met Superman for the first time, as told below. In 1977 he went into space with the Avengers, Captain Mar-Vell, the Thing and Adam Warlock against Thanos, the Mad Titan, who meant to put out the stars. Warlock turned Thanos to stone.

Aunt May had a heart attack at the start of 1978. That summer Peter hid a diamond ring in a box of Cracker Jack for Mary Jane. She gave it back, saying she was too free a spirit to be tied to one man. In the autumn he took his degree at last, after a missing credit in physical education had nearly kept him from it.

In June 1979 Peter and Mary Jane parted. The same month Jameson sacked him from the Bugle. That summer he began graduate studies at Empire State University. A cat burglar called the Black Cat came into his life too. She was Felicia Hardy, who was trying to free her father from prison. She fell for Spider-Man rather than for the man under the mask. For years afterwards she drifted in and out of his life.

In the autumn of 1979 Mysterio tricked Peter into believing that Aunt May had died, and for a while he took away Spider-Man's powers. At the turn of 1980, with Peter still powerless, the burglar who had killed Uncle Ben came back. He seized Peter and Aunt May, hunting for a gangster's loot that he believed was hidden in the Parker house. Peter took off his mask in front of him. The burglar fled, and died of a heart attack. The loot, when it was found, had been eaten by silverfish.

In the autumn of 1977 Peter shared rooms for a while with Brian Braddock, an English physicist who had come to Empire State University for a year. Peter guessed that Brian was Captain Britain. Brian never guessed Peter's secret. When the Maggia hired the assassin Arcade to get rid of Captain Britain, Arcade carried Spider-Man off with him by mistake, and Spider-Man got them both out of Arcade's Murderworld.

The Globe and the Juggernaut, 1980 to 1983

In 1980 Peter took photographs for a rival paper, the Daily Globe, until a scheme against it forced it to stop printing for a time. Mary Jane left New York for Florida the same year, and was gone for more than three years. Aunt May, recovering from heart surgery at a nursing home, met Nathan Lubensky there, a lively old man in a wheelchair with a weakness for a bet. They were engaged by the end of 1980. In 1982 she turned her house in Forest Hills into a boarding house.

In 1982 the Juggernaut came to New York to seize Madame Web, a blind old woman with the gift of second sight. Spider-Man threw everything he could find at him: electricity, a wrecking ball and a petrol tanker, which blew up. None of it slowed him. At last Spider-Man led him into the wet concrete of a building's foundations, where he sank and was sealed in. Madame Web lived, but she had lost her memory and her powers.

In 1983 a new goblin appeared, the Hobgoblin, who had found one of Norman Osborn's hidden stores of weapons. Nobody knew who he was, and he was to trouble Spider-Man for years. The Black Cat, meanwhile, had become Spider-Man's partner, and more than his partner. Mary Jane came back to New York that summer. The same summer Peter gave up his graduate studies, which broke Aunt May's heart when she found out.

The black costume, 1984 to 1986

At the start of 1984 Spider-Man paid a visit to a boy called Tim Harrison, whose room was full of everything he had been able to collect about him. Spider-Man took off his mask for the boy and told him about Uncle Ben. Tim had leukaemia, and only weeks to live. That year Peter also told the Black Cat who he was, and found that she much preferred Spider-Man to Peter Parker.

Early in 1984 he was among the heroes taken to Battleworld in the Secret Wars. There he found what he took to be a new costume, black with a white spider, which answered his thoughts and made its own webbing. He brought it home. In the autumn Mary Jane told him that she had known for years that he was Spider-Man, and she told him at last about her own unhappy family.

The same autumn Reed Richards of the Fantastic Four found that the black costume was alive, and meant to join itself to Peter for good. Reed got it off him with sound, which it could not bear. It got loose. In the spring of 1985 it came back in the shape of his old red and blue suit. Peter fought it in a church bell tower, where the din of the bells drove it off him. After that he wore a copy of the black costume in plain cloth, which the Black Cat had made for him.

At the end of 1985 a killer called the Sin-Eater shot Captain Jean DeWolff of the New York police, a friend of Spider-Man's, in her sleep. He went on to kill a judge and a priest. The Sin-Eater was a police sergeant, Stan Carter. When Spider-Man caught him, he beat him so savagely that Daredevil had to pull him off. Daredevil learnt Peter's name in the course of the case, and at the end of it the two men told each other who they were. In the winter of 1986 to 1987 President Reagan grounded every costumed hero in America, Spider-Man among them, until the march on Washington early in 1987.

Marriage, 1987

In the summer of 1987 Peter asked Mary Jane to marry him, and at first she said no. At Pittsburgh airport, after she had tricked her father, Phillip Watson, into confessing that he had led her sister Gayle into a theft, she changed her mind. They were married in 1987. She took his name alongside her own, as Mary Jane Watson-Parker.

That autumn Kraven the Hunter, who had spent more than twenty years trying to prove himself Spider-Man's better, shot him with a tranquilliser rifle and buried him. For two weeks Kraven went out as Spider-Man in a copy of the black costume, beating criminals savagely, until he caught the killer called Vermin. Then Peter dug his way out of the grave. Kraven let him beat Vermin, then shot himself, leaving a confession that cleared Spider-Man of everything done in his name.

Venom, 1988 to 1989

Eddie Brock had been a reporter on the Daily Globe until the Sin-Eater case ruined him: he had believed a false confession, and named the wrong man as the killer. He blamed Spider-Man. In the church where Peter had fought it off, the living costume found Brock at prayer, full of hatred for the same man, and joined itself to him. In the spring of 1988 they came out as Venom.

Venom knew everything the costume knew, including who Spider-Man was, and Peter's sixth sense gave no warning of him. He came to the Parkers' home and terrified Mary Jane. Spider-Man fought him in the same church tower. He saw that the costume's supply of webbing was running low, and he made Venom waste the last of it. Venom fell from the roof with nothing to hold him, and was taken away to prison.

Mary Jane could not bear the sight of the black costume after that, so Peter went back to red and blue. The Parkers moved into a smart flat in Bedford Towers on the Upper West Side. Their landlord, Jonathan Caesar, was obsessed with Mary Jane. In the autumn of 1988 he kidnapped her and held her in a hidden room in the building. She knocked him out with a lamp, and he was arrested.

From prison he had the Parkers evicted, and saw to it that no agency would hire Mary Jane as a model. In the spring of 1989 they moved in with Aunt May in Forest Hills. Peter had gone back to Empire State University at the end of 1988, as a graduate student and research assistant. At the end of 1989 the Parkers took a loft in SoHo, above Harry Osborn and his wife, Liz.

The Avengers, 1989 to 1991

In the winter of 1989 to 1990 an accident with a scientific device filled Spider-Man with a cosmic power far beyond his own. For a few weeks he was one of the strongest beings on Earth. He beat Titania, Magneto and Goliath. He once punched the Hulk into orbit. The power, it turned out, was that of Captain Universe, which comes to a chosen few in time of need. With the last of it he stopped a giant robot, the Tri-Sentinel, from causing a nuclear disaster in New York, and then it left him.

He had never been a regular Avenger, though he had often worked with them. Early in 1990, at about forty-three, he joined as a reserve member. That summer Doctor Octopus gathered a new Sinister Six: Electro, the Hobgoblin, Mysterio, the Vulture and himself. The Sandman, who had gone straight, refused to join, so Octopus turned him to glass. The scheme turned on a chemical that would cure addiction to cocaine, but would also eat away the ozone layer. Spider-Man brought the Sandman back to himself, beat the Six and recovered burundite, the one mineral that could stop it, which Thor carried into orbit.
