In August 1990 the Vulture seized Aunt May at a yacht's christening on the docks. Nathan Lubensky, her companion of ten years, caught hold of the Vulture to free her, and was carried into the air. He let go. Spider-Man caught him with a line of web, but Nathan's heart gave out, and he died in May's arms.

The next month Jonathan Caesar, out of prison and still obsessed with Mary Jane, was shot dead at her television studio. She was acting by then in a soap opera, Secret Hospital, which she did not much like. The man who shot Caesar was a police clerk called Goldman, who was secretly obsessed with her too. Mary Jane knocked him out with a can of hairspray and her handbag.

In the spring of 1991 Venom broke out of prison. When he escaped, a drop of the living costume was left behind in his cell, on the hand of his cellmate, a murderer called Cletus Kasady. Venom then took Spider-Man to a deserted island in the tropics to fight him to the death. Spider-Man set off an old mine full of gas, and left a charred skeleton behind in a Spider-Man suit. Venom believed that he was dead, and stayed on the island. Later that year Spider-Man was among the heroes who went into space under Captain America against Thanos and the Infinity Gauntlet, on a day that was afterwards undone.

Harry and Carnage, 1991 to 1992

In the autumn of 1991 Harry Osborn remembered that he had once been the Green Goblin, and put on the mask again. In the last of their fights Peter knelt in front of him and offered Harry his life. Harry turned aside at the last moment, and crashed. He was locked up in the Vault, the prison for superhuman criminals.

In the spring of 1992 Cletus Kasady broke out of prison as Carnage, in a red living costume of his own, grown from that drop. He killed people across New York for the pleasure of it. Spider-Man could not beat him alone. He flew to Venom's island to fetch him, and Venom agreed to help in return for his freedom.

The fight ran from a heavy metal concert at Madison Square Garden into the subway, and back again. Spider-Man rigged the Garden's loudspeakers to blast out a sound the creatures cannot bear, and Carnage went down. Venom then turned on Spider-Man. The Human Torch and Mister Fantastic were waiting with a sonic gun. Venom went back to prison, in the Vault, and Carnage was locked up in Ravencroft, an asylum for the criminally insane.

The last year, 1992 to 1993

In the autumn of 1992 Mary Jane found that she was expecting a baby. It was the beginning of the end of Spider-Man. At the turn of 1993 Venom broke out of the Vault again. In March, at a derelict amusement park, he was talked down by Ann Weying, the wife he had divorced. Silver Sable's mercenaries, hired by Jameson, attacked him there, and a Ferris wheel broke loose. Spider-Man and Venom held it up between them. Afterwards they agreed to leave each other alone, and Venom went west to San Francisco.

In the spring Harry Osborn, out of custody for lack of evidence, was dying of the Goblin formula. He planned to blow up the new Norman Osborn Foundation building at its opening, with Peter inside. He drugged Peter and started the timer. Mary Jane, holding Harry's small son, Normie, brought him back to himself. Harry got Mary Jane and Normie out of the building, then went back in for Peter. He brought Peter out too, then collapsed. He died in the ambulance, holding Peter's hand.

Soon after Harry's funeral Carnage escaped from Ravencroft. He freed another inmate, Shriek, and gathered a band of killers. Among them were Doppelganger, a six-armed creature in Spider-Man's likeness, and the Demogoblin. For days they rampaged across New York, while Shriek's power over minds turned ordinary people into a violent mob. Spider-Man fought them beside Venom, who came back from San Francisco for it. Captain America, the Black Cat, Firestar, Iron Fist, Deathlok and Nightwatch joined them. So did the young pair called Cloak and Dagger.

In the end a device of the Rand Corporation flooded the killers with feelings of love and hope, which took the fight out of most of them. Carnage fought on until he and Venom crashed into a bank of generators. Spider-Man and the Black Cat pulled him out of the flames alive. On Captain America's advice he was put into stasis. Spider-Man had refused, all through, to kill. All the while Mary Jane was very near her time.

In June 1993 Mary Jane gave birth to a healthy daughter. They named her May, after Peter's aunt, and she came to be called Mayday. Peter had been an orphan himself. He had spent thirty years risking his life as Spider-Man, and he would not make his daughter an orphan. In late June or early July 1993, at about forty-six, he announced that he was giving it up. Nobody knew then who had been under the mask, and nobody knows now.

Later life, 1993 to 2008

Peter Parker went to work as a forensic scientist in the crime laboratory of the New York police. One of his colleagues there was Phil Urich, a nephew of the Bugle reporter Ben Urich, whom May grew up calling Uncle Phil. In time the family settled in a house in Forest Hills, where Peter had grown up. Aunt May, very old by then, lived to see the great-niece who was named after her.

Peter and Mary Jane never told May about Spider-Man. They hoped she would never need to know, and that whatever the spider had done to his blood had not been passed on to her. The costumes and the web-shooters were packed away in the attic. For fifteen years Spider-Man stayed there.

In the summer of 1996, when Onslaught's Sentinels came down on Manhattan, the Avengers sent word to everyone who had ever served with them. The call reached Spider-Man on the old Avengers card he had kept from his reserve days. Peter said no. He had a little daughter to raise, and he would not make her an orphan. The Avengers never learnt who had refused them.

Superman

In 1976 Lex Luthor and Doctor Octopus found themselves in the same federal prison in New Mexico, said to be escape-proof. Luthor had tools hidden under false skin on his arm. With them he put the guards out of action, then gave Octopus back the use of his mechanical arms. Within hours Octopus was carrying him over the wall on his back.

Their scheme turned on Comlab, the world's first orbiting communications laboratory. With a circuit Luthor had stolen from S.T.A.R. Labs they took control of it. Its laser stirred up storms across the world: a hurricane tore through the Midwest, and a tidal wave rose towards the East Coast. Luthor demanded ten billion dollars from the American government.

Peter Parker was at a world news conference in New York to take photographs for the Bugle, with Mary Jane beside him. Clark Kent and Lois Lane were there for the Daily Planet. When Lois slipped from a scaffold, Peter caught her. Then a figure in Superman's costume made Lois and Mary Jane vanish. It was Luthor in disguise.

Each hero took the other for the culprit, and they fought above the city. Luthor struck Spider-Man in secret with red sun radiation, which made him strong enough to knock Superman about. Superman pulled a punch that would have killed him, and the wind of it still sent Spider-Man flying across the city. When the radiation wore off, Spider-Man found that he was only hurting his own fists. The two of them compared notes, and saw that they had been tricked.

The trail led them to Mount Kilimanjaro, where Masai tribesmen guided them to a hidden base of Luthor's. There they fought a warrior from the tribesmen's own country, who had vanished months before and come back charged with red sun radiation, with a glowing sword in his hand. From a launch silo in the base they went up after the villains into space.

On board the satellite Luthor cut off the gravity. Spider-Man played on Octopus's greed until he saw that Luthor's plan would leave him nothing to rule. Octopus smashed the controls, and the storms began to die away. Superman flew down to break the tidal wave, while Spider-Man webbed up Luthor and Octopus. The two heroes shook hands in New York, and handed their prisoners over to the police.

Afterwards the two couples, Clark Kent with Lois Lane and Peter with Mary Jane, went out to dinner together. Neither man knew the other's secret. Each, it turned out, had left an automatic camera running during the battle, and each had a scoop for his paper.

In 1981 Doctor Doom drew the Hulk to Metropolis with a tiny transmitter. The Hulk's rampage broke open the underground cell of the Parasite, a creature who drains the powers of anyone he touches. Doom took him into his service. Superman found the transmitter, destroyed it and calmed the Hulk. Bruce Banner was taken to S.T.A.R. Labs for a cure, though the Hulk broke out and wandered off before it was finished.

The Bugle sent Peter Parker to Metropolis to photograph the Hulk. Perry White of the Daily Planet paid him three times what Jameson did. Clark Kent, meanwhile, took leave from the Planet to work for a while at the Bugle in New York. For a time each man was doing the other's job.

Doom's plan, which he called Project Omega, was a chain of underground stations that would make the world's coal, oil and atomic fuel useless. His own reactor would then be the only power left on Earth, and the world would have to take him as its master. Superman went to the Latverian Embassy in New York, where Doom admitted everything, safe behind his diplomatic immunity.

Doom laid false evidence to draw in Wonder Woman. She clashed with Spider-Man before they saw that they were on the same side. Doom's men caught her, meaning to feed her powers to the Parasite. Spider-Man followed her captors, and learnt the whole of the plan.

In the final battle Doom turned Kryptonite on Superman. The Parasite, swollen with the powers of Superman, Wonder Woman and the Hulk, knocked Spider-Man senseless. Spider-Man cleared the Kryptonite dust off Superman with his webbing. Superman then took Doom's gauntlet, which was built to resist the Parasite, and knocked the creature out with it. He held the damaged reactor back from inside while Spider-Man's sixth sense found the lever that shut it down. The Parasite went back to his cell. Doom reached his embassy seconds ahead of Superman, and his immunity saved him once again.

The Justice League and its heroes

Spider-Man never joined the Justice League, but he met most of its famous members over the years, in New York more often than not. Five of those meetings were long remembered by the people who took part in them. The first was with Batman, in the last years of the first man to wear the cowl.

Early in 1979 the Scarecrow, Jonathan Crane, escaped from Arkham Asylum with a store of his fear gas, and came to New York to sell it. His buyer was Mysterio, Quentin Beck, the special-effects man turned criminal whose illusions had been troubling Spider-Man for fifteen years. They planned to fill a Broadway theatre with the gas on the night of a charity gala. Mysterio's illusions would turn the audience's fear to panic, and in the panic they would rob the guests.

Peter Parker was there to take photographs for the Bugle, with Mary Jane on his arm, though she had turned down his proposal the summer before. Among the guests was the Gotham millionaire Bruce Wayne. Nobody in the theatre knew that he was Batman, or that he had followed Crane's trail to New York. When the gas came, both men slipped away.

On the theatre roof Batman took Spider-Man for one of the thieves, and Spider-Man took Batman for one of Mysterio's illusions. They sorted it out quickly. Spider-Man's sixth sense, which no illusion can fool, showed them where the real thieves were. Batman had long since made himself an antidote to Crane's gas, and he gave Spider-Man a dose of it.

They caught Mysterio among the scenery high above the stage, and Crane in the street outside. Batman took Crane back to Arkham himself, while Spider-Man left Mysterio for the police. The Bugle's photographs of the fight were Peter Parker's. Batman noticed that, and kept the thought to himself.

In the spring of 1982 Barry Allen, the police scientist of Central City, came to New York to speak at a meeting of forensic scientists at Empire State University. Peter Parker, then a graduate student there, sat in on his lecture. He had no idea that the careful, unhurried man at the lectern was the Flash. Mary Jane was still away in Florida.

That week Captain Cold, one of the Flash's oldest enemies, came to New York to rob the diamond dealers of West 47th Street. He had hired Speed Demon, a New York criminal who could outrun anything on the roads, to carry the stones away. Spider-Man could not catch Speed Demon, and the Flash could not get near Cold, whose gun turned the street to ice under his feet. So they changed partners. The Flash ran Speed Demon round Manhattan until he dropped, while Spider-Man came at Cold from above, out of reach of the ice. A thick wad of web sealed the barrel of the cold gun, and it froze solid in Cold's hands.

Both men were in custody by evening, and Barry Allen gave the rest of his lectures on time. Peter kept his notes. Eleven years later he was doing the same work himself.

In the early summer of 1986 Sinestro, the renegade Green Lantern who had been Hal Jordan's greatest enemy for a quarter of a century, came to New York. He meant to shame Hal in front of the world by bringing down the Statue of Liberty on the eve of the celebrations for its hundredth birthday. For the work he hired the Shocker, Herman Schultz, a New York safecracker who had built himself gauntlets that shook things to pieces. The Shocker wore a quilted yellow suit, and Green Lantern's ring had no power over anything yellow.

Peter Parker had gone out to Liberty Island to photograph the restored statue. Spider-Man, in the black costume he wore in those years, fought the Shocker over the statue's crown and torch, while Hal fought Sinestro above the harbour. Spider-Man webbed the Shocker's gauntlets shut, and Hal drove Sinestro off. The celebrations went ahead in July as planned. Hardly anybody watching them on television knew how close they had come to being called off. That evening Peter told Mary Jane all about it, which a few years earlier he could not have done.

In the summer of 1988 the Beetle, Abner Jenkins, a New York mechanic who had built himself a flying suit of armour, made a bargain with the Royal Flush Gang. The Gang were robbers dressed as playing cards, who had troubled the League since the 1960s. Together they meant to steal the Bug, Blue Beetle's flying craft, from the League's embassy in New York. Spider-Man, newly back in red and blue, had been following the Beetle for a week.

On the night of the raid he followed the Beetle over the embassy wall, and Guy Gardner of the Green Lantern Corps tried to arrest him as an intruder. Blue Beetle and Booster Gold sorted out who was who. The thieves got the Bug into the air over the Hudson with the Beetle at the controls. Spider-Man clung to the outside of it while Blue Beetle took control of it from the ground, and brought it back to the embassy roof. There the League's Batman, who said very little, was waiting for the Royal Flush Gang.

The Batman of those years was Dick Grayson, though hardly anybody knew it. He did not ask Spider-Man's name, and gave the impression that he did not need to. Maxwell Lord offered Spider-Man a place in the League. He turned it down, having a wife, the rent on an expensive flat and no wish to be on television.

In the summer of 1989 Wonder Woman came to the United Nations to speak for Themyscira, as she often did. The Cheetah, Barbara Minerva, an English archaeologist with a cat's speed and claws, followed her to New York for the golden lasso, which she had tried to steal before. She found an ally in the Kingpin, Wilson Fisk, who had a use of his own for a rope that made men tell the truth. With it he could have found every traitor in his organisation.

Peter Parker was at the United Nations to photograph Wonder Woman for the Bugle. The Parkers were living with Aunt May again by then, since Caesar had cost them their flat as well as Mary Jane's modelling work. The Cheetah came at Wonder Woman in the gardens by the East River, while the Kingpin's men kept the police busy elsewhere.

Spider-Man swung down to help, and found the golden lasso round his own waist. Wonder Woman, not sure of him, asked him one question only: whether he meant anybody harm. He said that he did not, and she let him go without asking his name. Together they ran the Cheetah to ground in a warehouse on the West Side, where the Kingpin's men were waiting for her with a boat. The Cheetah got away over the rooftops. The Kingpin's men went to prison, and nothing could be proved against the Kingpin. Wonder Woman kept her lasso.

Mayday and Spider-Girl

May Parker grew up in Forest Hills knowing nothing of her father's past. At Midtown High School, Peter's old school, she was a popular girl, the star of the girls' basketball team. In 2008, when she was fifteen, her powers showed themselves in the middle of a game. She felt a tingle at the back of her skull, leapt for the basket and shattered the backboard.

The same year Harry Osborn's son, Normie, by then a grown man, put on the Green Goblin's mask to avenge his father and grandfather on Spider-Man. He stopped May on her way home with a message for her Uncle Pete: the Goblin was back, and Peter was to meet him at the Brooklyn Bridge. Peter knew who it was. Mary Jane took May up to the attic, and told her who her father had been.

Peter went to the bridge as himself. May followed him in an old Spider-Man costume from the attic. In the fight she saved Normie from an oncoming lorry, and Normie was put into an institution. The Parkers burnt everything that had belonged to Spider-Man, not knowing that May was already designing a costume and web-shooters of her own.

Soon afterwards she went out as Spider-Girl against a teleporting gunman called Mr Nobody. Her parents learnt of it from the Bugle. They were against it at first, then helped her. That year the living costume that had become Venom broke loose, and took hold of Peter again. Phil Urich freed him, then helped to train May.

Her enemies included Killerwatt, Mr Abnormal, Funny Face and the Dragon King, who turned out to be the school caretaker. Raptor, Brenda Drago, the daughter of a man who had once been the Vulture, began as an enemy and became a friend. The Black Tarantula, Fabian LaMuerto, a crime lord, was by turns her enemy and her ally. Her closest friends at school were Davida Kirby, Moose Mansfield, Jimmy Yama and Courtney Duran. Felicity Hardy, the Black Cat's daughter, found out her secret.

Late in 2008 a band of her enemies, the Savage Six, kidnapped two of her friends, and a jolt from Killerwatt took away her powers. Normie Osborn broke out and seized her while she was helpless. He cut her free instead of killing her, and from that day the feud between the two families was over. Normie became her friend, and in time he married Brenda Drago. Her powers came back the next year.

By then Mary Jane was past sixty. Medicine had moved on a long way in her lifetime. Decades of longevity medicine, the work of Reed Richards, Hank Pym and the Wayne Foundation, meant that a woman in her sixties could have the body of a woman of thirty, so she could carry a second child. The pregnancy was still a hard one. Benjamin Richard Parker, called Benjy, was born in 2009 at Midtown Medical Hospital, named after Uncle Ben and his grandfather Richard Parker. That night May was alone in Central Park, fighting the most dangerous enemy she had yet met, with no help to be had. Mary Jane, already in labour, sent Peter to her. When May reached the hospital at last, she found her father in tears.

Peter put the costume on again only a handful of times. In 2009 he knocked out Mr Nobody. Later that year the Hobgoblin, Roderick Kingsley, came after May's friends, so Peter took the costume out of storage to fight him. He gave May his own web-shooters. May, badly hurt, beat the Hobgoblin, though he got away.

Later in 2009, at her mother's wish, May gave up the mask for a while. She ran for the student council, and lost to Davida. She went out with Gene Thompson, the son of Peter's old school rival Flash Thompson. When the Hobgoblin threatened her friends again, Mary Jane let her go back to it.

In 2010 a fragment of the Carnage creature, kept in a laboratory, took hold of Moose Mansfield, who hoped it might save his dying father. It carried off Peter with Benjy, and turned the baby into a small Carnage of his own. Peter fought it in a suit of sonic armour, and May destroyed the creature with a sonic blaster. The sound left Benjy partly deaf, until Normie Osborn found a way to restore his hearing. Benjy, it turned out, had spider powers too.

During a war between the city's gangs in 2010 Peter went out at night as a masked vigilante called Wild Card, in a costume Normie supplied. That year Wes Westin, a young artist who had worked out that May was Spider-Girl, told her so on her own porch, and kissed her. She was seventeen, and she went on as Spider-Girl.

In the saga

Book Three, Chapter Four: in Diagon Alley in August 1993, Harry asks Lucius Malfoy whether he has heard of Spider-Man: a man in New York, in a red and blue suit, who climbs walls. He has been in the papers for years, Harry says, and announced his retirement about a month before. Harry thinks he must be a nightmare for the Statute of Secrecy. Mr Malfoy has never heard of him. If such a man existed, he says, the Wizengamot would have heard of him: 'We have Obliviators for a great deal less than climbing walls.' He dismisses Spider-Man as a Muggle entertainment. It is on their news, he says, and it is their business. Harry realises that the wizarding world genuinely does not know.

Book Four, Chapter Three: Spider-Man is not among the Avengers at the United Nations in August 1994. He retired the summer before, which Dudley still has not forgiven him for.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the Top Box at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, Lucius Malfoy reminds Harry that he asked in Diagon Alley the summer before about a man in a mask who climbed walls. Mr Malfoy had thought at the time that Harry had been out in the sun too long. He has since made enquiries, very quietly, and now understands why Harry asked.

pages.title: John Major
infobox: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, from November 1990
pages.html:
John Major has been the Muggle Prime Minister since November 1990, when he followed Margaret Thatcher into Downing Street. In 1993 Cornelius Fudge took the step, unprecedented in peacetime, of briefing him on the escape of Sirius Black from Azkaban.

Prime Minister

Major grew up in south London and left school at sixteen. He worked in banking before he entered Parliament in 1979, and rose quickly, becoming Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1989. He won the general election of April 1992.

In September 1992 the pound was forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. Uncle Vernon Dursley has loathed him for it ever since. Major has a grey, careful, reasonable face, which always seems to be apologising for something before anyone has asked.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, in August 1993, the Daily Prophet reported that Fudge had briefed the Muggle Prime Minister on Black's escape. The International Confederation of Wizards criticised him for it. 'The Prime Minister has given me his word that he will say nothing of what Black truly is,' said Fudge. 'And frankly, who would believe him?'

Uncle Vernon had loathed Major for about a year, since something had happened to the pound and something called the ERM. He had once tried to explain it over dinner with the salt cellar and the pepper pot. Harry had never been able to see anything wrong with Major's face. Meeting Fudge at the Leaky Cauldron, he decided that Fudge was the Muggle Prime Minister, only with a bowler hat. He tried to imagine John Major outside a pub at five in the morning, waiting for a thirteen-year-old who had been rude to his aunt, and could not.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, the news on 20 August 1994 reported that the Prime Minister had come back early from his holiday on the Thursday, as the Augments swept through the Balkans. Labour and the Liberal Democrats were calling for Parliament to be recalled.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, in the Top Box at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, Harry Potter pressed Cornelius Fudge about the troubles in the Muggle world. Fudge began to speak of arrangements between 'the Prime Minister and I', then stopped himself. Lucius Malfoy afterwards told Harry that Fudge had been to see the Muggle Prime Minister four times since the spring, coming back from Downing Street grey in the face.

pages.title: Stan Shunpike
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (July 1999)
pages.html:
Stan Shunpike is the conductor of the Knight Bus, the purple triple-decker that carries stranded witches and wizards through the night. One night in August 1993 he picked up a boy in Magnolia Crescent who called himself Neville Longbottom. The man in the raincoat was already aboard.

The Knight Bus

Stan is eighteen or nineteen, with large, protruding ears like trophy handles and quite a few spots on his chin. He works the bus with its elderly driver, Ernie Prang, whom he calls Ern. He greets every passenger with the same patter: 'Welcome to the Knight Bus, emergency transport for the stranded witch or wizard.'

The fare is eleven Sickles, wherever the passenger is going. Thirteen buys hot chocolate as well. Fifteen buys a hot-water bottle as well, and a toothbrush in any colour the passenger likes. The bus will go anywhere at all, as long as it is on land. It is also a non-smoking bus, as Stan never tires of telling people: 'Non-smokin' bus, this is, mate! Says so on the door!'

August 1993

On the night Harry Potter ran away from Privet Drive in August 1993, the Knight Bus nearly ran him over in Magnolia Crescent. Stan laughed at him for falling into the gutter. He asked about Harry's scar, then his name, and he accepted 'Neville Longbottom'. Harry paid him in Galleons, far more than the fare, and Stan pocketed them without a word.

On the way to London he told Harry the story of Sirius Black's massacre. Black, he said, had been a close supporter of You-Know-Who, and had expected to be his second-in-command. Stan was sure the Muggles had been told it was a gas explosion, though Ern remembered it as a mutant attack.

One other passenger was awake that night: a dishevelled Liverpudlian in a slept-in suit and raincoat, who was John Constantine. Stan made him put out his cigarette three times. The last time he threw it out of the window himself. He helped old Madam Marsh off the bus with great care, and he sent his birthday wishes to her grandson. That made Harry decide he liked him, and it made Stan harder for Constantine to hate.

When Cornelius Fudge named Harry outside the Leaky Cauldron, Stan shouted that he had seen the scar and known it all along. Then he ran back to the bus, sure he could smell smoke.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, on 22 August 1994, Harry Potter found a cigarette end still smoking in the grass at the World Cup campsite. He had hardly ever seen a wizard smoke. The only one he could think of was the dodgy bloke on the Knight Bus the summer before, and Stan had not let him light up.

In their own words

Non-smokin' bus, this is, mate! Says so on the door!Stan Shunpike · B3 Interlude

pages.title: Ernie Prang
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (July 1999)
pages.html:
Ernie Prang is the elderly driver of the Knight Bus. He is a man of very few words, with very thick glasses, who drives the bus at terrifying speed through the night.

Description

Ernie wears glasses as thick as the bottoms of milk bottles, and has an owlish face to go with them. He steers from an armchair. He holds the wheel the way Aunt Petunia would hold a spider, at arm's length and with distaste. He turns it very little and very late, so that the bus spends as much of its time on the pavement as off it. It never hits anything. The things it is about to hit get out of the way, lamp posts, letter boxes and whole farmhouses among them.

For the most part Ernie says 'Ar', and leaves the talking to Stan Shunpike, his conductor. Stan sets him off with 'Take 'er away, Ern', and every so often calls on him to agree with a story.

The Knight Bus is a violently purple triple-decker. It comes for any stranded witch or wizard who sticks out a wand hand at the side of the road. At night its decks are full of brass bedsteads instead of seats, and it travels in leaps so sudden that the beds slide about. Muggles never seem to notice it.

August 1993

Ernie was at the wheel in August 1993, on the night the bus picked up Harry Potter in Magnolia Crescent. Harry gave his name as Neville Longbottom. The bus carried him through Wales, where it set down a Madam Marsh at Abergavenny, and on to the Leaky Cauldron in London. John Constantine was on board as well.

When Stan told the story of Sirius Black, he asked Ernie how the Ministry had covered up the massacre. Ernie remembered: 'Mutant attack, Stan.' Of Black's madness he said, in his slow voice, 'If he weren't when he went to Azkaban, he will be now.' He would blow himself up, he said, before he set foot in the place. When Stan wondered how Black would fare against the Azkaban guards, Ernie shivered: 'Talk about summat else, Stan, there's a good lad. Them Azkaban guards give me the collywobbles.'

At the Leaky Cauldron, when Stan found out who 'Neville' really was, Ernie's owlish face peered over his shoulder with great interest.

pages.title: Madam Marsh
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Very old, very small and faintly green
On the Knight Bus to Abergavenny, August 1993
Seven on the Sunday; has a bicycle; can do his tables
pages.html:
Madam Marsh is a very old, very small witch who suffers badly from travel sickness on the Knight Bus. One night in August 1993 she rode it to Abergavenny, faintly green, to visit her grandson. He was turning seven on the Sunday, he had a bicycle, and he could do his tables.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, Harry Potter was on board, calling himself Neville Longbottom. The bus was somewhere in Wales when Ern told Stan Shunpike to go and wake Madam Marsh, because they would be in Abergavenny in a minute. Stan brought her down the narrow stairs with his arms held out on either side of her, not touching, ready to catch her. She held the banister with both hands.

When the bus braked she clamped a handkerchief to her mouth and tottered down the steps. Thanking Stan into the handkerchief, she told him all about her grandson. Stan told her to wish the boy happy birthday from Stan, straightened her cloak where it had slipped, then threw her bag out after her on to the verge. ‘Sweet old lady, that,’ he told Ern.

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine, who was on the same bus, heard Ern send Stan upstairs to wake her.

pages.title: Madam Marsh's grandson
pages.html:
Madam Marsh's grandson is a little boy who lives near Abergavenny, in Wales. He turned seven on a Sunday in August 1993, and his grandmother went by the Knight Bus to see him for his birthday. He has a bicycle, and he can do his tables.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, Stan Shunpike saw the very old, very small witch off the Knight Bus at Abergavenny. She told him, into her handkerchief: 'I'm going to see my grandson, you know. He's seven on Sunday. He's got a bicycle.' A moment later she added: 'He's a very clever boy. He can do his tables.' Stan told her to tell him that Stan said happy birthday. It was one of the things that made Harry Potter decide, somewhere around Aberdeen, that he liked Stan.

In the Book Three Interlude John Constantine watched the same scene from his seat on the bus. It made Stan a good deal harder to hate, which John found very annoying. He decided to hate him anyway, on principle.

pages.title: The wizard in the nightcap
aliases: The tiny wizard in the nightcap
infobox: The tiny wizard in the nightcap
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The back of the Knight Bus, August 1993
pages.html:
The wizard in the nightcap is a tiny wizard who slept at the back of the Knight Bus one night in August 1993, all the way from Liverpool to the Leaky Cauldron in London. He snored for most of it, with his mouth open.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, when Harry Potter climbed aboard, the little wizard muttered in his sleep, ‘Not now, thanks, I'm pickling some slugs,’ and rolled over.

In the Book Three Interlude, he was already snoring at the back when John Constantine got on in Liverpool. At the Leaky Cauldron, Harry went into the pub. Stan Shunpike and Ern followed him in with his trunk. The bus was empty apart from the wizard in the nightcap, who was still snoring and, as far as John was concerned, did not count. John lit a cigarette at once.

pages.title: Tom the barman
infobox: Tom; Tom the innkeeper; Tom the landlord
Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Kept an eye on Harry Potter for Cornelius Fudge
pages.html:
Tom is the landlord of the Leaky Cauldron, the small, grubby pub on Charing Cross Road that leads from Muggle London into Diagon Alley. He is old, bald, wizened and toothless. He is usually to be found behind his bar, wiping a glass. In August 1993 he kept an eye on Harry Potter for the Minister for Magic, Cornelius Fudge.

The landlord

Muggles walking past the Leaky Cauldron do not see it. Upstairs Tom lets rooms. Downstairs he serves breakfast to a mixed company of witches, wizards, warlocks, dwarfs and the occasional hag. He was behind his bar in July 1991, when Rubeus Hagrid first brought the eleven-year-old Harry Potter through the pub, and strangers queued up to shake the boy's hand.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, Fudge was waiting at the Leaky Cauldron for Harry when he ran away from Privet Drive in August 1993. Tom appeared through the door behind the bar with a lantern. ‘You've got him, Minister!’ he said, and offered beer or brandy. Harry heard the words got him, and his stomach turned over. Tom brought tea and crumpets to the private parlour in an apron over his nightshirt. Afterwards Fudge told Harry that Tom would be keeping an eye on him, and Tom showed him up to room eleven, where Hedwig was already waiting on top of the wardrobe.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry once read straight through his lunch, so that Tom had to come and take the plate away from under the book. On the second morning a dwarf threw a kipper at a party of warlocks. The two parties had been feuding since the year nine hundred and something, over a ritual that was meant to turn the dwarfs' beards to gold but had only made them itch. Eleven hundred years, said Tom, if you asked the dwarfs; nine-fifty if you asked the warlocks. They could not agree on that either.

Nobody remembered what the ritual had been for. Tom held his glass up to the light. ‘That's the thing about carrying a grudge, Mr Potter. You carry it. Not the other fellow.’ Grudges, he said, were heavy things. Harry found that he could not shake the words off.

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the morning of 1 September 1993, Tom woke Harry with his usual toothless grin and a cup of tea.

In Book Four, Chapter One, in a dream Harry had in the summer of 1994, the Leaky Cauldron stood halfway up a hill street, where the post office ought to have been. Tom stood in its doorway, old, bald and toothless, exactly as Harry remembered him, wiping a glass with a dirty cloth. He nodded as Harry went past. ‘Evening, Tom,’ he said. Harry supposed he must be talking to himself, since that was his name. He did not stop.

In their own words

That's the thing about carrying a grudge, Mr Potter. You carry it. Not the other fellow.Tom · B3 Ch4

pages.title: Florean Fortescue
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (July 1999)
Proprietor of Florean Fortescue's Ice Cream Parlour
pages.html:
Florean Fortescue keeps the ice cream parlour in Diagon Alley, and he knows a great deal about the medieval witch-burnings. In August 1993 he fed Harry Potter free sundaes, helped him with his homework and gave him a piece of wisdom that held firm when Lucius Malfoy tried to talk him round.

The parlour

Florean Fortescue's Ice Cream Parlour stands in Diagon Alley, with tables set out in the sun where customers may sit over a sundae for as long as they like. Its owner is a scholarly sort of wizard. He has a particular knowledge of the witch-hunts of the Middle Ages, which he shares freely with any student who sits down at his tables with a History of Magic essay.

Harry's summer in Diagon Alley

In August 1993, while Harry was staying at the Leaky Cauldron, he did his holiday homework at the tables outside the parlour. Florean gave him a free sundae every half an hour. On the second afternoon he leant over Harry's shoulder with a knickerbocker glory in one hand, reading his essay on witch-burning upside down, and told him what people get wrong about it.

Most of the people the Muggles burnt were not wicked at all, he said. But the Muggles who burnt them were not monsters either. They had only been frightened. Most of them went home afterwards and cried. As Florean put it, 'Frightened people do the most dreadful things in the world, and they're still only frightened people.' That did not excuse what they had done, but if Harry wanted to understand it, it was the place to start: 'Nobody was ever wicked for its own sake. Not even the ones you'd think.'

Harry looked at the knickerbocker glory for some time before he picked up the spoon. Then he wrote they were frightened in the margin of his essay in biro, and underlined it, without quite knowing why.

Lucius Malfoy, and after

Later that month Lucius Malfoy walked Harry down Diagon Alley, urging him to stop living like a Muggle. For several seconds Harry found himself nodding. Then something in the back of his head said they were frightened, in Florean's voice, with a knickerbocker glory in its hand. Harry stopped nodding. It was Florean's words that kept him from agreeing.

For the rest of the summer Harry read The Lord of the Rings at Florean's tables, with a sundae going soft at his elbow. Florean read over his shoulder and pointed out the good bits. When Mr Weasley heard that Florean kept giving Harry sundaes, he said, 'Good. Good man, Florean.'

Harry did not forget the lesson. In his History of Magic examination in June 1994 he put in every scrap of what Florean had taught him about the witch-hunts, and covered both sides of four rolls of parchment.

In their own words

Frightened people do the most dreadful things in the world, and they're still only frightened people.Florean Fortescue · B3 Ch4
Nobody was ever wicked for its own sake. Not even the ones you'd think.Florean Fortescue · B3 Ch4

pages.title: The proprietor of Quality Quidditch Supplies
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The proprietor of Quality Quidditch Supplies runs the shop in Diagon Alley that Harry Potter likes best of all. In the summer of 1993 he had the new Firebolt on show on a podium in the middle of the shop, and crowds gathered to stare at it.

The Firebolt

The broom had a streamlined handle of ash with a diamond-hard polish. Every birch twig in its tail had been chosen by hand. It could reach a hundred and fifty miles an hour in ten seconds. The sign beside it gave the price as available on request.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the proprietor told the crowd round the podium that the Irish International Side had just put in an order for seven Firebolts. They were favourites for the World Cup, he said. Harry did not ask the price. He went back almost every day after that, just to look at the broom.

pages.title: The square-jawed wizard and his son
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The square-jawed wizard was one of the crowd that came to stare at the new Firebolt in Quality Quidditch Supplies in August 1993. With him was his son, a boy younger than Harry Potter.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, the wizard was telling his companion that the broom had just come out. It was a prototype, he said. His son, swinging off his father's arm, squeaked, ‘It's the fastest broom in the world, isn't it, Dad?’ Harry, squeezed into the same crowd, thought it the most magnificent broom he had ever seen in his life.

pages.title: The manager of Flourish and Blotts
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Two hundred copies of the Invisible Book of Invisibility
pages.html:
The manager of Flourish and Blotts is the long-suffering wizard who runs the bookshop in Diagon Alley. In August 1993 he was at the end of his tether over The Monster Book of Monsters, which had to be kept in a cage.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, the manager hurried over as Harry Potter came in. He drew on a pair of very thick gloves, took up a large, knobbly walking stick and headed for the cage of Monster Books. When Harry said he already had one, the manager was enormously relieved. He had been bitten five times already that morning.

Poking the stick through the bars to knock the fighting books apart, he vowed never to stock them again. He had thought the shop had seen the worst when it bought two hundred copies of the Invisible Book of Invisibility. They had cost a fortune, and nobody ever found them.

He found Harry a copy of Unfogging the Future for Divination. When he saw Harry staring at Death Omens, he warned him lightly not to read it. It would only make him see death omens everywhere, he said, and it was enough to frighten anyone to death.

pages.title: The mirror in room eleven
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Over the basin in room eleven, the Leaky Cauldron
pages.html:
The mirror in room eleven hangs over the basin in the room at the Leaky Cauldron where Harry Potter stayed in August 1993. Like a good many wizarding mirrors, it talks, and it has opinions about his hair.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry tried to make his hair lie flat in front of it. 'You're fighting a losing battle there, dear,' said the mirror, in a wheezy voice. Harry snapped at it to shut up.

Later Harry told his reflection out loud that he was not going to be murdered. 'That's the spirit, dear,' said his mirror sleepily.

pages.title: The hag in the balaclava
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The hag in the balaclava was a breakfast guest at the Leaky Cauldron in August 1993. She looked very suspiciously like a hag, and she wore a thick woollen balaclava. She sat down in a corner, ordered a plate of raw liver, ate it and left a tip.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry Potter was staying at the Leaky Cauldron, where he liked watching the other guests at breakfast. She came in on his fourth morning there, in the same weeks that a party of dwarfs and a party of warlocks were throwing kippers at each other across the room.

pages.title: The wizard who turned his toast into a hedgehog
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The wizard who turned his toast into a hedgehog was one of a group of venerable-looking wizards at breakfast in the Leaky Cauldron in August 1993. They were arguing over the latest article in Transfiguration Today. He became so cross about it that he turned his toast into a hedgehog, and had to be helped.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry Potter watched it happen. He was staying at the Leaky Cauldron for the last weeks of the summer holidays, and he ate his breakfast there every morning, watching the other guests.

pages.title: The beard-gold feud
aliases: the feud of the warlocks and the dwarfs
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 4
A ritual that was meant to turn the dwarfs' ancestors' beards to gold
pages.html:
The beard-gold feud is a quarrel between warlocks and dwarfs that has been going on since the tenth century. It began with a ritual that the dwarfs' ancestors had been promised would turn their beards to gold. It merely made them itch. Nobody now remembers what the ritual was for, and the two sides cannot even agree on how long it has lasted.

The quarrel

The dwarfs say that the feud is eleven hundred years old. The warlocks say nine hundred and fifty. Nobody has ever settled the difference. The feud is carried on wherever the two parties meet, which in the summer of 1993 meant the breakfast room of the Leaky Cauldron, where kippers were the weapon of choice.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry Potter, staying at the Leaky Cauldron in August 1993, watched a party of wild-looking warlocks in bearskins and a party of raucous dwarfs eat their breakfast at neighbouring tables. On the second morning a dwarf threw a kipper. Harry said to Tom, the innkeeper, that it had been going on for a thousand years.

'Eleven hundred, young sir, if you ask the dwarfs,' said Tom, wiping a glass. 'Nine-fifty if you ask the warlocks. They can't agree on that either.' Harry asked whether anyone remembered what the ritual had been for. 'Not a soul.' Tom held the glass up to the light. 'That's the thing about carrying a grudge, Mr Potter. You carry it. Not the other fellow. He's gone home and put his feet up. Heavy things, grudges.' The warlocks threw the kipper back. The sentence stuck to Harry, and would not come off.

pages.title: The witch at the Magical Menagerie
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A rat tonic to Ron Weasley; Crookshanks to Hermione Granger
pages.html:
The witch at the Magical Menagerie keeps the cramped, noisy pet shop in Diagon Alley where every inch of wall is hidden by cages. In August 1993 she examined Ron Weasley's rat, Scabbers. She also sold Hermione Granger a huge ginger cat that had been in the shop for ages, because nobody wanted him.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Ron brought Scabbers to her counter because the rat had been off colour since Egypt. She told him to bang the rat on the counter, pulled a pair of heavy black spectacles out of her pocket and looked him over. ‘He's been through the mill, this one,’ she said. An ordinary common or garden rat, she explained, could not be expected to live longer than three years or so. She sold Ron a small red bottle of rat tonic.

At that moment Crookshanks sprang from the top of the highest cage on to Ron's head and went for Scabbers. ‘NO, CROOKSHANKS, NO!’ cried the witch, but Scabbers shot out of her hands like a bar of soap and fled from the shop.

In Chapter Eight, quarrelling with Ron about Crookshanks, Hermione reminded him that Scabbers had been ill before the cat ever went near him: ‘you heard what that witch said, he's old’. In Chapter Eleven Harry remembered that the witch had given rats about three years, no more. Scabbers had in fact been with the Weasleys for twelve, which no ordinary rat could manage. He was Peter Pettigrew.

pages.title: The Ministry drivers
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Two old-fashioned dark green Ministry cars
The Weasleys, Harry Potter and Hermione Granger to King's Cross, 1 September 1993
pages.html:
The Ministry drivers were two furtive-looking wizards in suits of emerald velvet who drove the Ministry of Magic's cars. On 1 September 1993 they took the Weasleys, Harry Potter and Hermione Granger from the Leaky Cauldron to King's Cross. The cars were the Ministry's precaution, with Sirius Black at large.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, Mr Weasley marched Harry across the pavement to the first car. The Ministry cars seemed almost ordinary, though Harry noticed they could slide through gaps that Uncle Vernon's company car could never have managed. At King's Cross, with twenty minutes to spare, the drivers found them trolleys and unloaded their trunks. Then they touched their hats in salute to Mr Weasley and drove away, somehow jumping to the head of an unmoving queue at the traffic lights.

pages.title: Remus Lupin
infobox: Lupin; Moony; Professor Lupin; Professor R. J. Lupin; R. J. Lupin; Remus; Remus John Lupin

Harry Potter pupil, student, former pupil
James Potter friend from school, school friend, friend
Severus Snape colleague and enemy, colleague and old enemy, school rival
Albus Dumbledore employer
Lily Potter friend, introduced him to his faith, friend, brought him to faith
Sirius Black former friend, friend
Jesus Christ implied source of his Patronus memory
Peter Pettigrew former friend
Hogwarts staff, Defence Against the Dark Arts, Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher, Garou (implied), Christian, Marauders, Garou, werewolf
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Garou, biteborn: made by the bite as a very small boy
A pack of mostly Fianna Garou in the hills of mid-Wales
Cypress, ten and a quarter inches, unicorn hair
pages.html:
Remus Lupin taught Defence Against the Dark Arts at Hogwarts in 1993 to 1994, and he was the best teacher of the subject Harry Potter had known. He is a Garou, one of the warrior people sworn to Gaia against the Wyrm. He is biteborn, however, made by the bite rather than born. The tribes hold that against him, though he is Garou in every measure. He was a friend of James Potter and one of the four makers of the Marauder's Map. He holds his rage in check with the Wolfsbane Potion, the faith Lily Potter gave him and a great deal of prayer.

Early life

Remus John Lupin was born on 10 March 1960 to Lyall Lupin, a wizard, and Hope Howell, a Muggle. As a very small boy he was bitten by Fenrir Greyback of the Black Spiral Dancers, in revenge on his father. Garou are normally born, not bitten, and their law frowns on making others by the bite; those who do it regardless mostly serve the Wyrm. His parents tried everything, but there was no cure. Before the Wolfsbane Potion was discovered, he was liable to transform whenever he sensed anything that smelled of the Wyrm, and it seemed impossible that he could ever go to school.

Hogwarts and the Marauders

When Albus Dumbledore became Headmaster, he admitted Lupin to Hogwarts. The Whomping Willow was planted in Lupin's first year. The Shrieking Shack and its tunnel were built so that Madam Pomfrey could take him out of the castle at each full moon. With nothing Wyrm-touched to attack, he tore at himself. His screams gave the Shack its name as the most haunted building in Britain, a rumour Dumbledore encouraged.

He was sorted into Gryffindor. For the first time in his life he had friends: James Potter, Sirius Black and Peter Pettigrew. He told them his mother was ill. Sirius decided for two months that it was a girl. It was James who worked out the truth. In their fifth year the three of them became Animagi, because Animagus magic is light magic and his war form would tolerate them in animal shape. Together they roamed the grounds and Hogsmeade at night. As Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot and Prongs they made the Marauder's Map.

Lupin watched James caught between three girls. Two of them, the sisters Bellatrix and Narcissa Black, had each decided he was theirs; the third had decided he was nobody's. Later he stood at James's wedding to Lily Evans. After Sirius sent Severus Snape down the tunnel at the full moon, it was Lupin who apologised to Snape for the stupidity of his friends.

Faith

Through all the Hogwarts years Lily was the only believer among them, and she was tutted at for it. After the Potters married she brought Lupin to Christ, the first of the three men to go. His faith is how he carries being Garou, and how he keeps the lamp of his rage from spilling.

From James and Lily's wedding until June 1994 he wore a plain wooden cross on a knotted leather cord. His crosses have to be wooden, because silver burns him; he keeps a box of them at home and can easily carve another. When the war form rises, he prays: the Lord's Prayer, 'Deliver us from evil', 'Lighten our darkness'. He told Harry the teaching about forgiving seventy times seven, and admitted that he finds forgiving Snape difficult every day. Some days he fails at it altogether.

After 1981

Within days of the Potters' deaths, every friend who had known what he was and stayed with him was gone. Believing Sirius a murderer, Lupin left the wizarding world and went where wizards do not go. In the hills of mid-Wales he found a pack, mostly of the Fianna, the tribe of the Celtic lands. He helped them deal with a quarry that had poisoned a valley for thirty years, and with the things that crawled out of its slag heaps.

They never fully accepted him. He was biteborn, bitten rather than born, which the tribes count as no true Garou. He was also a wizard, and the Garou think wizards play with the Wyrm's fire. They still send for him, as they did on Christmas Day 1993. Among wizards he was shunned, unable to find paid work, until Dumbledore gave him a job.

Nature

The mark knife-scratched into his battered case, a crescent lying on its back above three short strokes, is his birth sign. It is the crescent moon of the Garou who deal with spirits, the Theurges. Like all Garou he has five shapes: the Homid man, the heavier Glabro, the nine-foot Crinos war form, the pony-sized Hispo wolf and the Lupus wolf. He carries Rage like fire in a lamp.

He smells dark magic as the reek of the Wyrm: on dementors, on Pettigrew, on Snape's left arm, at Voldemort's name. He finds Hogwarts hard to bear, because it is steeped in dark magic as well as light. The signs show through his manners: a deep organ note in his chest, almost too low to hear, flaring nostrils, amber eyes that catch the light, nails longer than nails ought to be, a shadow too large for him. He can smell tears round a corner. His boggart is his own war form. The Wolfsbane Potion, which Snape brews for him, suppresses the compulsion to transform and root out the Wyrm, though the compulsion never truly goes away.

Teaching

He took the Defence post after two teachers had lasted a year each, and taught it with practical good sense. He began with Riddikulus, against a boggart in the staffroom wardrobe. Then came Red Caps, which cowered from him because they keep away from anything that has carried a great deal of blood, followed by kappas, grindylows and hinkypunks.

In October 1993 he taught vampires. Garlic, he said, is mostly folklore; invitations are real; stakes only pin them; fire and the sun kill them. 'A cross in a coward's hand is a stick of wood', he told the class, but in the hand of somebody who believes in Jesus Christ it is a different thing altogether. He explained the Masquerade of 1435. He explained, too, the agreement that the Camarilla had made in 1900, some ninety years earlier, with the wizarding governments of the world, the Ministry among them. He also covered the Sabbat, the clans and the Beast. He said he had never met a vampire he would turn his back on, because vampirism destroys the soul.

His examination was an obstacle course. He gave full marks to Harry and to Dracina Malfoy.

The Patronus

From January 1994 he taught Harry the Patronus Charm, at eight on Thursday evenings in the History of Magic classroom, with a boggart from Filch's filing cabinet. He taught that the charm is older than the Statute and older than wands, found rather than invented. There is no dark version, and there cannot be. It runs on light magic, on something derived from God meeting the caster's own soul, with a happy memory as the meeting place. Only a good soul can cast it, and 'the caster does not make the light; he agrees to it.' His own memory is of something done for him that he could never have earned, given by somebody a good deal older than Dumbledore, to whom Lily introduced him.

He told Harry that the Dementor's Kiss eats the soul, so that it is not given back at the end of all things, and that he would walk to London to stop it. No one, he said, is above forgiveness if they seek it earnestly. Denying a man his final judgement draws the attention of very nasty people. After the first lesson, once Harry had gone, he collapsed on the floor with his hands over his face. When Harry's first corporeal Patronus struck at the Ravenclaw match, Lupin would say only that it had looked 'bright'.

In the saga: 1993 to 1994

Harry first saw him asleep in the last compartment of the Hogwarts Express: shabby, ill, smelling of the Forest at night. When a dementor boarded, he growled like a large dog warning something off, drove it away with something silver and handed out chocolate. All year he watched Harry constantly, from windows, from stairs and from the stands. When Harry described a dream of a watching man who smelt of old blood, Lupin went grey and fought for control. Such a dreamer, he said, should seek God, or at least a priest. When Harry asked whether he was religious, he nodded once.

At Christmas, when Dumbledore said he was unwell, he was in fact away with his pack on a Wyrm matter. In March he confiscated the Marauder's Map in Snape's office, keeping downwind of Snape and praying silently. Afterwards he rebuked Harry for gambling his parents' sacrifice for a bag of tricks.

On the night of the escape he saw Pettigrew's name on the map and followed it to the Shrieking Shack. There he disarmed the children and embraced Sirius. Sirius steadied him by quoting 'Be ye angry, and sin not', so that he pulled back from transforming. On the lawn, having missed his potion, he began the Lord's Prayer as the full moon came out, and became a nine-foot Garou. His cross snapped off. He called Harry 'Wyrm' and hunted him, until a silver Sickle burned a black mark on his nose that never healed.

He fled into the Forest as a wolf the size of a pony, and destroyed several dementors there. When the creature found Harry again among the trees, it spoke his name in what was left of Lupin's voice. Harry's white shield forced it back into Lupin's human shape. He remembered all of it: 'all instincts, rage and compulsion. But still me.'

When Snape let his nature slip, Lupin resigned the next morning, saying that parents would not want a werewolf teaching their children. He gave back the Cloak and the map. He told Harry that Christianity was a gift given to everyone, and urged him to go to church. He gave Harry the wooden cross, telling him to keep it with him at the Dursleys'. He left by carriage with his suitcase and the empty grindylow tank, saying, 'God keep you, Harry.'

On the night of the escape the claws of his war form had raked Harry's left arm above the elbow. Madam Pomfrey did her best, but the wounds had to heal without magic, and by the summer they were four long pale lines.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: by August 1994 Lupin's wooden cross always hung round Harry's neck, and Lupin was one of the very few who knew that Sirius Black was innocent. In Chapter Six Lucius and Narcissa Malfoy both thanked Harry for saving Dracina in June from the werewolf, which had been Lupin in his war form.

In their own words

They're... unnatural.Remus Lupin · B3 Ch5
Is there a problem with that girl?Remus Lupin · B3 Ch5
A cross in a coward's hand is a stick of wood.Remus Lupin · B3 Ch8
When a man dreams of a visitor like that... he would have gone to seek God. Or at least a priest.Remus Lupin · B3 Ch10

pages.title: Silvanus Kettleburn
infobox: Hogwarts staff, Care of Magical Creatures
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
From the time of Armando Dippet's headship until 1993
pages.html:
Silvanus Kettleburn taught Care of Magical Creatures at Hogwarts for many decades. In the summer of 1993 he retired, in Dumbledore's words, to enjoy more time with his remaining limbs.

Career

For decades Kettleburn's enthusiasm for his subject ran well ahead of his caution, and it cost him a good deal of himself. By the time he retired he had lost several limbs to the creatures he taught.

He was already teaching when Albus Dumbledore was a young member of staff. That was when the school put on a Christmas pantomime of the tale of the Fountain of Fair Fortune, and Kettleburn supplied the Worm. It was an Ashwinder swollen with an Engorgement Charm. It exploded during the performance, and set the Great Hall alight. Kettleburn was put on probation, and pantomimes were never staged at the school again.

He was still teaching through Harry Potter's first two years at Hogwarts, before the subject was open to Harry's year.

Retirement

Kettleburn retired at the end of the 1992 to 1993 school year, saying he had had enough. Albus Dumbledore went straight down to Rubeus Hagrid's hut to offer him the post. Hagrid took the class from September 1993. He began with a dozen hippogriffs in a paddock, and he set The Monster Book of Monsters as the textbook.

pages.title: Sir Cadogan
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
An empty field, on a landing at the top of the seventh staircase
Short and stout, in full armour
A fat grey pony, dappled on the rump
Guardian of Gryffindor Tower, November 1993 to March 1994
pages.html:
Sir Cadogan is a short, stout knight in a painting at Hogwarts, who challenges almost everybody he meets to a duel. His portrait shows an empty field, with a fat grey pony grazing in it, and hangs on a bare landing at the top of the seventh staircase. From November 1993 to March 1994 he guarded Gryffindor Tower in the Fat Lady's place, until he was sacked for letting Sirius Black in.

The knight

He wears full armour and carries a sword a great deal too long for him. His pony, which he calls a coward and a glutton, will not let itself be caught, so he mostly goes about on foot. Drawn up to his full height, he comes roughly level with the pony's knee.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, on 2 September 1993, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger came off the seventh staircase in search of the North Tower. A fat grey pony wandered into the empty painting, followed on foot by its rider, who had very evidently just come off. He called them rogues and whirled his sword about his head. One sweep carried him round in a full circle and dumped him on his face. When he leant on the sword to get up, the blade went into the turf like a spade into wet sand, and stuck. "A blade of this quality, villain, does not stick. It bides."

When Harry offered to carry him in his pocket as his midget knight, Sir Cadogan went a deep, painted purple. Then he roared with laughter and hailed Harry as a wit. "I had rather a wit at my side than ten dull swords." He led them to the North Tower from frame to frame, shouting challenges at the furniture. In the next painting along, two startled ladies on a swing dropped their fans. At the top he stuck his head into a picture of some gloomy-looking monks, who recoiled, and bellowed his farewells.

Harry kept thinking about the stuck sword all the way up the stairs: a man so angry that his own blade had gone into the ground, so that he was no use to anybody, least of all himself.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, after Black slashed the Fat Lady at Hallowe'en, Sir Cadogan was the only painting in the school willing to take her place. "That's because he's a nutter," said Seamus Finnigan, as Sir Cadogan challenged the entire queue for the common room to single combat. He fell over his own sword, then came up through the grass of his painting shouting that it was a flesh wound. He spent half his time challenging people to duels and the rest inventing passwords of fiendish complexity, which he changed at least twice a day. "Scurvy braggart" got you in on Monday morning but not by Monday lunchtime. By Wednesday the whole of Gryffindor House was going about with lists; "Oddsbodikins" was on Hermione's.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, early in the Christmas holidays of 1993, Harry, Ron and Hermione went out through the portrait hole to visit Hagrid. "Stand and fight, you yellow-bellied mongrels!" Sir Cadogan shouted after them. On Christmas Day, when Harry and Ron came back from lunch, he was holding a Christmas party of his own. His guests were a pair of monks from a nearby landscape, three previous headmasters of Hogwarts and his pony, which had been given something out of a bucket. Sir Cadogan, hiccuping, wished the two boys a merry Christmas. The password was "Scurvy cur".

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Neville Longbottom made Sir Cadogan tell him the week's passwords in advance, wrote them down and lost the list. Harry gave the password, "Oddsbodikins", and Sir Cadogan swung forward with extreme reluctance, like a man opening a door to the tax collector.

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, in March 1994, Sirius Black read the whole week's passwords off a little piece of paper, and Sir Cadogan let him in. "He had 'em!" he told Professor McGonagall proudly. "Had the whole week's, my lady!" Neville owned up to having written them down. In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, Sir Cadogan was sacked. His portrait was hauled back up to the empty landing on the seventh floor, with the little knight bellowing challenges at Filch the whole way, and the Fat Lady came home.

In their own words

A blade of this quality, villain, does not stick. It bides.Sir Cadogan · B3 Ch6
I had rather a wit at my side than ten dull swords.Sir Cadogan · B3 Ch6
Stand and fight, you yellow-bellied mongrels!Sir Cadogan · B3 Ch11

pages.title: Sir Cadogan's pony
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Sir Cadogan's pony is the fat grey pony, dappled on the rump, that grazes in the painted field of his portrait at Hogwarts. Sir Cadogan calls it a coward and a glutton. It will not let itself be caught, so the knight generally goes about on foot.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, on 2 September 1993, the pony wandered into the empty field from the edge of the frame and put its head down to graze. Its rider followed on foot, clanking, with grass stains all over his knees; he had very evidently just come off. Sir Cadogan told Harry Potter and his friends that he would have carried them to the North Tower himself, if only the beast would let itself be caught. Drawn up to his full height, the knight came roughly level with the pony's knee.

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, on Christmas Day 1993, the pony was a guest at Sir Cadogan's Christmas party, along with a pair of monks and three former headmasters of Hogwarts. It had been given something out of a bucket, and was swaying gently.

pages.title: The ladies on the swing
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The painting beside Sir Cadogan's, at the top of the seventh staircase, Hogwarts
pages.html:
The ladies on the swing are two painted ladies who sit on a swing in the picture next to Sir Cadogan's portrait at Hogwarts. They carry fans, which they dropped in alarm when Sir Cadogan burst in on them in 1993.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, on 2 September 1993, Sir Cadogan set off to guide Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger to the North Tower. He went out of the side of his own frame and straight into the next painting along, where the two startled ladies on the swing dropped their fans. Then he clanked on ahead of the three of them from frame to frame, shouting challenges at the furniture.

pages.title: The gloomy monks
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A painting near the top of the North Tower stair, Hogwarts
pages.html:
The gloomy monks are the painted monks in a picture near the top of the twisting stair to the North Tower at Hogwarts. They recoiled when Sir Cadogan put his head into their picture.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, on 2 September 1993, Sir Cadogan led Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger from frame to frame to the North Tower, for their first Divination lesson. At the top of a stair so tight and twisting that they were dizzy by the end of it, the knight stuck his head into the monks' picture to bellow his farewells. The monks recoiled. "Fare you well, brothers-in-arms! Should you ever have need of a stout heart and a strong arm, you have only to call upon Sir Cadogan!" "Right you are," said Ron under his breath, as the knight vanished. "Next time we need a lunatic."

pages.title: Sybill Trelawney
infobox: Professor S. Trelawney; Professor Trelawney; Sibyll; Sibyll Trelawney; Trelawney; Sybill Patricia Trelawney
Hogwarts staff, Divination, Divination teacher, Seer
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Great-great-granddaughter of the Seer Cassandra Trelawney
Top of the North Tower, reached by trapdoor and silver ladder
pages.html:
Sybill Trelawney teaches Divination at Hogwarts from a stifling, perfumed room at the top of the North Tower. Most of her predictions are theatre, gloom and guesswork. Twice in her life, though, she has fallen into a true prophetic trance, the second time during Harry Potter's exam in June 1994.

Background

Sybill Patricia Trelawney is the great-great-granddaughter of Cassandra Trelawney, a celebrated Seer. She was sorted into Ravenclaw. In 1980 she applied for the Divination post. At her interview with Albus Dumbledore, at the Hog's Head in Hogsmeade, she made the first of her two real predictions, and afterwards she remembered nothing of it. Part of that prophecy was overheard by a young Death Eater, Severus Snape, who carried it to his master.

She rarely comes down from her tower, saying that the bustle of the school clouds her Inner Eye.

Teaching

Her classroom is reached by a trapdoor and a silver ladder. It is a hot attic lit red, like a tea room, full of chintz armchairs and poufs. She teaches tea leaves, palmistry and the crystal ball. She is very thin, with huge spectacles that magnify her eyes. Over her sequinned shawl she wears so many beads and bangles that she jingles. Harry thought she looked like a glittering insect. Every year she predicts the death of a pupil, and none has ever obliged her.

In September 1993 she told Neville Longbottom not to count on his grandmother's health, and she warned Parvati Patil against a red-haired man. She told Lavender Brown that the thing she dreaded would come on 16 October. She predicted that one of the class would leave the circle around Easter. In Harry's cup she found a falcon, a club, a skull and finally the Grim. When he asked her about signs, she mocked the question as Muggle superstition about angels. She dismissed a shaft of light upon a trunk as weather, though Harry was almost sure he had never mentioned a trunk.

She took against Hermione Granger for her lack of aura. When she called Hermione's mind hopelessly mundane, Hermione walked out for good. She has dismissed the prophets of the Bible as desert folk tales, and she claims that Muggles borrowed Christmas from wizards. Saint George, she says, was a wizard who let Muggles believe God had slain the dragon: 'A true Seer does not require a burning bush.' She told Harry that his life line was the shortest she had ever seen.

In the saga

At Christmas dinner in 1993 she refused to make the table up to thirteen, warning that the first of thirteen to rise is the first to die. She claimed to have Seen that Professor Lupin would not be with them for long, adding that he had fled when she offered to gaze for him.

In June 1994 she gave Harry the highest marks she had ever awarded, for visions he had invented to mock her subject. At the end of his exam her voice went harsh and deep. Her eyes rolled as she foretold that the Dark Lord's servant would break free that night and set out to rejoin his master before midnight. Afterwards she remembered nothing, and denied it. Dumbledore judged the prediction real, which brought her total to two.

In their own words

My dear boy, that is not Fate. That is weather.Sybill Trelawney · B3 Ch6
My dear, it is the Grim.Sybill Trelawney · B3 Ch6
Never forget, when thirteen dine together, the first to rise is the first to die!Sibyll Trelawney · B3 Ch11
A true Seer does not require a burning bush.Sybill Trelawney · B3 Ch15

pages.title: Padma Patil
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Padma Patil is a Ravenclaw witch in Harry Potter's year at Hogwarts, and the twin sister of Parvati Patil of Gryffindor. She shares her sister's passion for India, which neither of them has ever visited.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, on 1 September 1991, the twins were sorted one after the other, among the last few of the year, just before Sally-Anne Perks and Harry.

In Book Three, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1993, Aunt Marge held forth in the Dursleys' kitchen about foreigners. Harry thought of the people he knew, among them Dean Thomas, Angelina Johnson and the Patil twins. None of them was a bad person at all, he thought, as long as you did not get the twins started on India, which they had never visited but felt very passionate about.

pages.title: The strange Ravenclaw girl
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 2
Talking about crime statistics to Angelina Johnson
pages.html:
The strange Ravenclaw girl is a Hogwarts student in the year below Harry Potter. She once started going on about crime statistics to Angelina Johnson, and found out how sensitive Angelina was about that sort of thing. Dean Thomas was the same.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1993, Harry sat through Aunt Marge's visit to Privet Drive, thinking about his friends at school. They were not bad people at all, he thought, as long as you didn't get Dean started on football, or the Patil twins on India. The same went for Angelina on crime statistics, as the strange Ravenclaw girl had found out. Aunt Marge was a dreadful woman, Harry decided, and that had nothing to do with race.

pages.title: Bilius
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Ron Weasley, whose middle name is Bilius
The day after he saw a Grim
pages.html:
Bilius was Ron Weasley's uncle. He saw a Grim, and he was dead the next day. Ron, whose middle name is Bilius, takes the Grim very seriously indeed because of it.

The Grim

The Grim is a giant spectral dog that haunts churchyards, and wizards hold it to be the worst omen of death there is. Most of them are terrified of it. The Weasleys had Uncle Bilius to show them why.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, at Harry Potter's first Divination lesson on 2 September 1993, Professor Trelawney saw the Grim in Harry's teacup. At lunch that day Harry admitted that he had seen a big black dog on the night he left the Dursleys', in Magnolia Crescent. Ron's fork hit his plate. When Hermione Granger said it was probably a stray, he stared at her as if she had lost her mind. 'Hermione, if Harry's seen a Grim, that's... that's really bad. My uncle Bilius saw one and... and he was dead the next day!'

Hermione called it a coincidence. In her view, wizards who saw a Grim were simply so frightened that they dropped dead: the Grim was not a warning but a cause.

In Chapter Ten, after the dog had appeared a second time, in the top row of an empty stand during the Hufflepuff match, Harry remembered how white Ron had gone over Magnolia Crescent, with his uncle Bilius in mind. He kept the second sighting to himself.

pages.title: Molly Weasley's mother
pages.html:
Molly Weasley's mother is the witch who brought up Molly Prewett and her two brothers. Her sons, Fabian and Gideon, were both killed fighting Death Eaters in the first war against Lord Voldemort. When the young Molly dosed a boy with love potion, her mother wanted to know what she had done to him.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, at breakfast in the Leaky Cauldron on 1 September 1993, Mrs Weasley told Hermione Granger and Ginny about a love potion she had made as a girl. The boy followed her round for the whole of the Easter holidays with a look on his face like a spaniel. Her mother asked, as Molly told it, Molly, what have you done to that boy, and Molly said nothing, Mum. She had to keep topping him up with three drops in his pumpkin juice every morning for a fortnight, or he would have come round.

pages.title: Wendelin the Weird
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Being burnt at the stake forty-seven times
A variety of names and hats
A History of Magic, by Bathilda Bagshot
pages.html:
Wendelin the Weird was a medieval witch who enjoyed being burnt at the stake. A simple Flame-Freezing Charm turned the flames into a mild, tickly warmth. She liked the feeling so much that she got herself burnt forty-seven times, under a variety of names and hats.

The burnings

Between 1300 and 1400 many thousands of people were burnt as witches across Europe. The Muggles of the time lived in terror of witchcraft, but they had almost no way of detecting it, so nearly all of those they burnt had no magic whatever. On the rare occasions when they caught a real witch or wizard, the Flame-Freezing Charm saw to the rest, and the condemned had only to shriek convincingly for the crowd. Wendelin is remembered chiefly because she kept coming back.

Not every witch fared so well. The Fat Friar, who watched the Church's view of witchcraft harden over the centuries that followed, saw friends of his burn.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, late on the night before his thirteenth birthday in July 1993, Harry Potter sat at his desk at Privet Drive writing an essay for History of Magic: Witch Burning in the Fourteenth Century Was Completely Pointless. Discuss. He copied down the passage about Wendelin from Bathilda Bagshot's A History of Magic, which records her forty-seven burnings. Then he bent over the parchment and wrote about her. He had got as far as forty-seven times in various disguises when his hand began to ache.

In Chapter Sixteen, in June 1994, Harry told Hermione Granger outside the History of Magic examination that he meant to do the burnings properly. He would not stop at the Flame-Freezing Charm, he said, or at Wendelin the Weird letting them burn her forty-seven times because she liked the tickly feeling. He would put in what Florean Fortescue had told him about why the Muggles were so frightened. He would put in, too, what the Fat Friar had said about the long years when wizards had got on well enough with the Church. Hermione thought it brilliant.

pages.title: Cassandra Vablatsky
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Cassandra Vablatsky is a celebrated Seer, born in 1894, and the author of Unfogging the Future, the Divination textbook set for third years at Hogwarts.

Unfogging the Future

Her book is a thick, black-bound guide to the basic methods of fortune-telling, palmistry, crystal balls and bird entrails among them. The symbols for reading tea leaves are on pages five and six.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry Potter found her book on his list when he went to Flourish and Blotts. The manager climbed a set of steps to take down a copy, and called it a very good guide to all the basic methods. Harry was not listening. On a table nearby he had seen a black dog the size of a bear on the cover of Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the Worst Is Coming.
