In Chapter Six, at Harry's first Divination lesson on 2 September 1993, Professor Trelawney sent the class to pages five and six of the book for the meanings of the tea leaves. Ron Weasley used it to read Harry's cup. A bent cross meant trials and suffering; a sun meant great happiness. In Chapter Fifteen Hermione Granger crammed her copy into her bag as she walked out of Divination for good. In Chapter Sixteen, waiting for the Divination examination in June 1994, Neville Longbottom had it open across his knees at the chapter on crystal-gazing.

pages.title: The teacher at St Grogory's
aliases: Harry's teacher in the last year at primary school
infobox: Harry's teacher in the last year at primary school
St Grogory's Primary School, Little Whinging
Harry Potter's last year at primary school
pages.html:
The teacher at St Grogory's taught Harry Potter in his last year at primary school in Little Whinging. This teacher always believed Dudley Dursley over Harry, and once held up Harry's school jumper in front of the class to show them what neglect looked like.

The jumper and the glasses

The same teacher let Dudley off for breaking Harry's glasses with his fist in the playground, because boys would be boys.

The voice

The cruel voice at the back of Harry's head sounds like Uncle Vernon, Aunt Petunia and Dudley all at once. Lately it has begun to sound like Professor Snape as well, and like this teacher, who always believed Dudley over him.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in Diagon Alley in August 1993, Harry's anger kept coming up out of nowhere, bringing old memories with it. One of them was this teacher, holding up his jumper to show the class what neglect looked like, then letting Dudley off because boys will be boys.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, on the dock at Myst Island in June 1994, Harry opened his mouth to tell Dracina Malfoy and Hermione Granger how he felt. The old voice stopped him. It sounded like this teacher, among others: Don't be so stupid, boy. Look at you. Who do you think you are?

pages.title: The woman at Harry's primary school
infobox: St Grogory's Primary School, Little Whinging
pages.html:
The woman at Harry's primary school, St Grogory's in Little Whinging, always believed Dudley Dursley over Harry Potter. Harry counts her among the Muggles who were able to hurt him whenever they liked.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1993, after Aunt Marge's visit, Harry found that he was angry with Muggles. He did not mean Hermione's parents. He meant the Dursleys, Aunt Marge, the man who had put the bars on his window, the woman at the primary school who had always believed Dudley, and the whole long row of them going back as far as he could remember. Every one of them had been able to hurt him whenever they liked, and he had never once been able to hurt them back.

In Chapter Four, walking down Diagon Alley beside Lucius Malfoy, Harry caught himself nodding along. Mr Malfoy had the facts exactly right, he thought: the cupboard, the bars, the dog biscuits and the woman at the primary school.

pages.title: The man who barred Harry's window
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Fitting bars to Harry Potter's bedroom window
The morning after the Masons' dinner, summer 1992
pages.html:
The man who barred Harry's window is a Muggle tradesman whom Uncle Vernon paid, in the summer of 1992, to fit bars on Harry Potter's bedroom window at Number Four, Privet Drive. He did the job on the morning after the Masons' dinner party, while Uncle Vernon whistled.

The bars

After that Harry was locked in his room, with a slice of cold bread pushed through a cat flap in the door three times a day, when the Dursleys remembered. Three days later Ron Weasley came for him with Fred and George, in their father's flying car. They fixed a rope to the bars and pulled them clean off the wall.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Two, on the morning after the Masons' dinner, Uncle Vernon paid a man to put bars on Harry's window, though he fitted the cat flap in the bedroom door himself.

In Book Three, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1993, Harry counted the man among the Muggles who had been able to hurt him whenever they liked.

pages.title: The old woman crossing herself
infobox: In church at Christmas, when Harry Potter was seven
pages.html:
The old woman crossing herself is the woman Harry Potter once saw making the sign of the cross in church when he was a small boy. It was the only time he had seen it done until he made the sign himself, in June 1993.

In church

Harry was seven. It was Christmas, and Aunt Petunia had taken the family to church because the Polkisses had started going. Through a gap in the carols, the old woman touched her forehead, her chest and each shoulder in turn.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in Diagon Alley in August 1993, Harry listened to Lucius Malfoy talk about Muggles. By Mr Malfoy's measure, Hermione's parents, who had never done a thing to Harry, were exactly the same as Aunt Marge. Harry thought of them, and of Dean's family. He thought, too, of the old woman in the church, with her hand going forehead, chest, shoulder, shoulder.

pages.title: The churchwarden
infobox: Being a man Vernon Dursley wanted to sell drills to
pages.html:
The churchwarden is a Muggle whom Vernon Dursley once wanted to sell drills to. For his sake the Dursleys once went to church.

The Dursleys and the Church

The Dursleys are not churchgoers. They think about God precisely as much as most of Little Whinging does, which is not at all, except to feel rather superior to anybody who does.

They have been to church perhaps twice that Harry Potter can remember. The first time was one Christmas, because the Polkisses had started going and Aunt Petunia was not going to be outdone. The second time was for the churchwarden. They left Harry at Mrs Figg's for that one.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, in the summer of 1993, Harry walked to St Michael's three times in a month. Each time he stood on the pavement looking at the door, then turned round and walked home again. He had only been inside a church once in his life. The Dursleys had been perhaps twice. One of those visits had been for the churchwarden.

pages.title: Arabella Figg
infobox: Her cats; minding Harry Potter as a child
pages.html:
Arabella Figg is an elderly neighbour of the Dursleys in Little Whinging, and she is quite mad about cats. Whenever the Dursleys went out without Harry Potter, which was as often as they could manage, they left him with her. She is a Squib, born into a wizarding family without any magic of her own. She lives near Privet Drive because Albus Dumbledore asked her to keep an eye on Harry.

Harry's childminder

All through Harry's childhood the Dursleys dumped him at Mrs Figg's house whenever they had somewhere to go that did not include him. Harry remembered how the Dursleys weighed it up: take the boy to the zoo, or leave him with Mrs Figg. They left him with her, for instance, on one of the few occasions they went to church, because a man Uncle Vernon wanted to sell drills to was a churchwarden.

Her house smells of cabbage and is full of cats, as well as photographs of cats. She made Harry look at pictures of every one she had ever owned, Tibbles, Snowy, Mr Paws and Tufty among them. Harry never suspected that she knew anything about magic. She took care that he never enjoyed his visits, since the Dursleys would have stopped sending him if he had.

In March 1994 Harry saw Dracina Malfoy's face as she watched Cho Chang walk away, perfectly smooth and perfectly still. It put him in mind of one of Mrs Figg's cats sitting on a garden wall, watching a sparrow.

In Harry's dream

In Harry's dream in August 1994 Mrs Figg was sitting on the bench by the bus shelter at the end of the road, in her carpet slippers. She had a cat on her lap, with three more round her feet, and she was knitting something so long that it trailed away along the pavement into the dark. The cats all turned their heads together to watch Harry go by. Without looking up from her knitting she told him: 'You've got the wrong face on, dear. They'll notice.'

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Five: the Dursleys had always left Harry with Mrs Figg, an old woman who lives a few streets away, whenever they went on holiday, so he had never camped anywhere before the World Cup. There Perkins's tent turned out to be done out exactly like her front room, down to the crocheted covers on chairs that did not match, with the same powerful smell of cats.

In their own words

You've got the wrong face on, dear. They'll notice.Mrs Figg (in Harry's dream) · B4 Ch1

pages.title: The television news reporter
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The television news reporter read the news on the Dursleys' kitchen television on the morning of 31 July 1993, Harry Potter's thirteenth birthday. In one bulletin he reported the escape of Sirius Black, the fall of New Delhi to Khan Noonien Singh and an attack on Birmingham.

The bulletin

He warned the public that Black was armed and extremely dangerous. A special hotline had been set up for sightings. He did not say where Black had escaped from, which made Uncle Vernon furious. Khan's forces had ended an eleven-week siege of New Delhi, and the Indian government had withdrawn to Bangalore.

In Birmingham, the afternoon before, a pink creature the size of a double-decker bus had come out of the canal basin near Gas Street and attacked the Bull Ring shopping centre. The city centre was evacuated for six hours. The Californian team in coloured suits came straight over to fight it with their combat vehicle. Nobody was killed, though a number of shoppers were treated for shock.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, Harry watched the bulletin over his toast. Dudley watched the coloured figures with shining eyes.

pages.title: The spokesman at the New York podium
infobox: The joint statement of the Avengers and the Justice League
pages.html:
The spokesman at the New York podium is a man in a very good suit who read out the joint statement of the Avengers and the Justice League on the news in July 1993. He stood at a podium with two flags that Harry Potter did not recognise.

The statement

Khan Noonien Singh had just taken New Delhi, and pressure was mounting on the world's two largest superhuman organisations to step in. Their statement, issued from New York, said that the United Nations accord under which they operate did not allow it. Its terms 'expressly prohibit unilateral action in any ongoing conflict between sovereign states'. The teams would act only 'at the request of the Security Council, and under its authority'. The statement was greeted with anger in Delhi.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Two, Harry saw him on the Dursleys' kitchen television at breakfast on 31 July 1993, his thirteenth birthday.

pages.title: The guardian of the Egyptian tomb
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 4
One of the Amenti, the bandaged guardians of the dead
A stone slab in a tomb in Egypt
Questioning everyone who comes in uninvited
Asking visitors whether they are ready to have their hearts weighed
pages.html:
The guardian of the Egyptian tomb, sometimes called simply the mummy, is a figure wrapped in bandages that lies on a stone slab inside a pyramid in Egypt. It sits up to question anyone who comes in uninvited, and asks whether they are ready to have their heart weighed. In the summer of 1993 it put its questions to Percy Weasley, listened to his answer for about ten minutes and then lay down again.

The weighing of the heart

The guardian is one of the Amenti, the risen dead who serve Ma'at, and its questions are the old Egyptian ones. The Egyptians believed that the dead were led into the Hall of the Two Truths, where the heart was laid in the scales against the feather of Ma'at, the goddess of truth. Anubis watched the balance, while Thoth wrote down the result. A heart that was light with truth went on to Osiris and the fields of the blessed. A heavy one was thrown to Ammit, the Devourer, and its owner went into the dark for ever.

Egyptian wizards filled their tombs with curses and guardians to keep out robbers. Gringotts employs curse-breakers, Bill Weasley among them, to get past them. According to Bill, this guardian questions everyone who goes in uninvited.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, back from their month in Egypt, Fred and George Weasley told Harry Potter at the Leaky Cauldron how they had tried to shut their brother Percy in a pyramid. They had got him through the door when the thing on the slab, all bandages, sat up. It asked Percy whether he had lived with a true heart, what he had done with the years given him and whether he was ready to have his heart weighed.

'And Percy answered,' said George. 'For about ten minutes. With examples.' After that the thing lay back down, and Fred thought it would rather have had the eternal dark. Bill had told them that it did the same to everyone who went in uninvited. They were lucky, he said, that it had only asked questions, since most people came out of there a lot quieter than they went in. Then their mother had arrived.

pages.title: Doomsday
aliases: The grey monster that killed Superman
infobox: The grey monster that killed Superman; The grey monstrous thing
Carried to the end of time, spring 1994
pages.html:
Doomsday is the grey, bone-spurred monster that killed Superman in Metropolis in November 1992, tearing up half the city in the fight. As far as the public knew, it came out of nowhere. To most of the world it is still simply the thing that killed Superman.

Made on Krypton

Doomsday was made on Krypton, long before there was any Kryptonian civilisation, by a scientist named Bertron. Bertron put an infant creature out in the planet's savage wilds and let it die. Then he cloned it from what was left, time after time, so that each new body was proof against whatever had killed the last. What came out of the process was a creature that could not be killed the same way twice, and that felt nothing but the urge to destroy. It killed Bertron and left his world.

After a long rampage across other planets it was bound in restraints at last and buried deep in the Earth, where it lay until 1992. The ruins of Bertron's laboratory, Superman later learnt, were part of the reason Krypton became a culture obsessed with genetic engineering.

Metropolis, 1992

In the autumn of 1992 the creature punched its way out of its prison, still half bound, and began smashing its way across the American Midwest. The Justice League met it and lost badly; Blue Beetle was left in a coma. It went on towards Metropolis, where Superman fought it through the streets for hour after hour. The fight tore up half the city, knocking down building after building. On 18 November 1992 the two struck each other down in front of the Daily Planet, and both of them died.

Its body was taken away and kept. During the confusion of 1993 the Cyborg Superman fired it into space.

Apokolips and the end of time

In the spring of 1994 Doomsday rose again far from Earth and fought its way across Apokolips, the world of Darkseid. Superman went after it and learnt where it had come from. With the help of the time-traveller Waverider he carried it to the end of time, the one place it could not adapt to survive. Superman was brought back. Doomsday was not.

In the saga

In August 1993 Harry Potter remembered that Superman had died while he was at Hogwarts, fighting ‘some grey monstrous thing out of nowhere’ that had torn up half of an American city called Metropolis. On 20 August 1994 a man with a black eye, protesting outside the United Nations, shouted that Doomsday had knocked his building down in 1992. He had rebuilt it, only to see downtown flattened again in May 1994.

pages.title: Frodo Baggins
infobox: Bilbo Baggins, whom he called his uncle
Bearing the One Ring to Orodruin
pages.html:
Frodo Baggins was the hobbit of the Shire who carried the One Ring into Mordor at the end of the Third Age. He had inherited it from Bilbo Baggins, whom he called his uncle. With Samwise Gamgee beside him he went all the way to Orodruin, where the Ring went into the fire on 25 March 3019.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry Potter lay awake at the Leaky Cauldron thinking about the black dog he had seen in Magnolia Crescent. He thought of a boy in a book who had gone out of his front door with a ring in his pocket, knowing perfectly well that something was hunting him. The boy had gone anyway, because the alternative was to sit in the Shire and wait for it to come up the lane. Harry had read that part three times without knowing why. He did not name the hobbit, but it was Frodo.

pages.title: Black Riders
infobox: Unmade when the One Ring was destroyed
pages.html:
The Black Riders were the nine Ringwraiths of Middle-earth, the Nazgûl, the most terrible of Sauron's servants. They had been kings of Men, to whom Sauron gave nine rings of power. The rings bound them to his will until they faded into wraiths. Their chief was the Witch-king of Angmar. They passed away when the One Ring was destroyed at the end of the Third Age.

History

In the last years of the Third Age they rode out of Mordor, cloaked in black, to hunt for the Ring in the Shire. They sat their black horses very still at the edges of fields and sniffed the air for it. On Weathertop their chief wounded Frodo Baggins with a Morgul-knife. At the Ford of Bruinen the river rose against them in a flood.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry Potter read Dudley's copy of The Lord of the Rings properly at last, from the beginning, at the Leaky Cauldron. He read about the Riders at night in bed, with the candle going. Without deciding to, he got up and shut the window. Something about a hooded shape standing very still at the edge of a field, paying attention, had reminded him of the gap between a garage and a fence where he had seen the dog.

In Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express on 1 September 1993, a dementor in the doorway of the compartment drew a long, slow, rattling breath. Harry knew that sound. He had read it a week or so before: a hooded shape on a black horse at the edge of a field, head bent, sniffing the night. He had thought it the most frightening thing in the book. He had been wrong.

pages.title: Rivendell
infobox: A hidden valley below the Misty Mountains, in Eriador
By Elrond, in the Second Age
pages.html:
Rivendell, which the Elves called Imladris, was the house of Elrond Half-elven in a hidden valley at the feet of the Misty Mountains. For thousands of years it was the Last Homely House east of the Sea, a refuge for the wise as well as the weary. The shards of Narsil were kept there. There, too, the Elves reforged them as Andúril, the sword that would one day be called the Sword of Gryffindor.

History

Elrond founded it in the year 1697 of the Second Age, during the war against Sauron. It lay deep in a cleft of the land, reached by narrow paths, with the river Bruinen running below and waterfalls all round. Bilbo Baggins stayed there on his way to the Lonely Mountain, and again on his way home. In the end he went back to live there. In the autumn of the year 3018 of the Third Age the Council of Elrond met in the house. It chose the Fellowship of the Ring, which set out from Rivendell that December.

Elrond's daughter, Arwen, was born in the valley. She married Aragorn. Their line runs down the ages, through Godric Gryffindor, to Harry Potter, who does not know it.

Andúril

Narsil, the sword of Elendil, broke beneath him when he fell fighting Sauron at the end of the Second Age. For three thousand years its shards were kept by Isildur's heirs at Rivendell. Before the Fellowship set out, the Elven smiths reforged the blade for Aragorn and wrote runes down it. It came out of the fire as Andúril, the Flame of the West.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry read The Lord of the Rings properly for the first time, from the beginning and in order. When he got to Rivendell he stopped for a day or two and read it twice. Read like that, a sort of light seemed to come off the place, as though the pages had been left in the sun. It was the first thing he had read since his Hogwarts letter that made him feel there was somewhere, even in a book, where people were simply good. He told nobody.

In Chapter Twenty-One, in June 1994, standing at Professor Flitwick's window with his anger turning cold and steady, Harry thought of Narsil. It had lain broken for three thousand years until the Elves of Rivendell reforged the shards for Aragorn. Harry knew that sword far better than anybody at Hogwarts could have guessed. He had held it in his own two hands.

pages.title: The Shire
infobox: Eriador, in the north-west of Middle-earth
pages.html:
The Shire was the land of the hobbits, in the north-west of Middle-earth: a green country of farms, villages and holes dug snugly into hillsides. It was the home of Bilbo Baggins and of his heir Frodo, who carried the One Ring out of it in the year 3018 of the Third Age. The Lord of the Rings begins there.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry read the book again from the beginning, properly this time. Read in order, it was all new: the Shire, the Road and the Black Riders in the dark. In the same chapter he thought of a boy who had gone out of his front door with a ring in his pocket, knowing perfectly well that something was hunting him, and had gone anyway. The alternative was to sit in the Shire and wait for it to come up the lane.

pages.title: Buckbeak
infobox:
Rubeus Hagrid keeper
Dracina Malfoy injured her, implied rescuer, rescuer
Sirius Black carried to safety
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Condemned in 1994; escaped; in hiding with Sirius Black
pages.html:
Buckbeak is a grey hippogriff with a fierce orange eye. He was one of the dozen hippogriffs Rubeus Hagrid brought to his first Care of Magical Creatures lesson in 1993. He was condemned to death for slashing Dracina Malfoy's arm, and it was Dracina herself who saved him from the executioner's axe. Afterwards he carried Sirius Black away to freedom.

Description

Like every hippogriff, Buckbeak has the forequarters, wings and head of a giant eagle, joined to the body of a horse. His talons are as long as Harry's hand, and his wings are about twelve feet across. Hippogriffs are proud creatures and very easily offended. Anyone who wants to approach one must bow first, then wait for the hippogriff to bow back. Buckbeak eats dead ferrets, and coughs up the bones.

The lesson and the hearing

At Hagrid's first lesson, on 2 September 1993, Buckbeak bowed to Harry and let him pat his beak. Then he carried him round the castle and low over the lake, steadying himself when Harry grabbed at his feathers. Afterwards he bowed to Dracina Malfoy too. When she called him a big ugly lump, he slashed her right arm. Dracina resolved that he would be dead by Easter, and a letter in her handwriting reached her father.

Under the Ministry's ruling Buckbeak was kept tethered on his own. At Christmas Hagrid brought him into the cabin to lie by the fire and eat. Lucius Malfoy had his hearing before the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures moved forward from 20 April to March 1994, and Buckbeak went up to London with Hagrid on the Knight Bus. The Committee condemned him to be beheaded at sundown on 6 June. After that he was chained to a stake beside the pumpkin patch.

Escape

On the day of the execution he kept sniffing towards the Forest, as though he were waiting for somebody, and would not let Harry lead him away. As Walden Macnair's axe came down, a hooded figure threw him a dead ferret. Buckbeak lunged for it, snapped his tether and flew off into the Forbidden Forest with Dracina Malfoy on his back, under the nose of the Minister for Magic. In the Forest he charged the werewolf to defend Harry. He tore at it until it caught him by the wing and flung him into the bracken. He came out again scratched, and deeply offended.

He let Dracina hug him without bowing first. He carried her, Harry and Hermione Granger up to Professor Flitwick's window in the West Tower, then was sent back to hide among the trees. Later that night he answered Dracina's whistle. He hovered at the window, pushed his head into her hands like a cat and accepted Sirius Black's bow. A little before midnight he carried Sirius away, low over the Forest. In the summer of 1994 he went into hiding with Sirius.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: in August 1994 Harry and Ron both guessed that Buckbeak was the 'very good company' Sirius had mentioned in his last letter, since it was hard to think who else would put up with him. In Chapter Five Harry reminded Hermione that it was she who had taken them back in time for Buckbeak the year before.

pages.title: Hippogriff
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A horse behind, a giant eagle in front
Proud, and quick to take offence
pages.html:
The hippogriff is a proud winged beast, a horse behind and an eagle in front, that will carry a witch or wizard on its back if it is treated with proper respect. It will not stand an insult. Anyone who wants to approach one must bow to it first, without blinking, and wait for it to bow back.

Description

A hippogriff has the hindquarters of a horse, with the wings, forelegs and head of a giant eagle. Its beak is the colour of gunmetal, its eyes are a blazing orange, and its talons are as long as a man's hand. Where feather meets hair there is no seam at all; the one simply runs into the other.

Hippogriffs come in many colours. Hagrid's herd of twelve has storm-grey, bronze, strawberry roan and chestnut beasts, with one that is blue-black. In the wild they eat insects, birds and small mammals. A tame one is particularly fond of dead ferrets.

Manners

Hippogriffs are proud, and they take offence at the smallest thing. As Hagrid puts it, ‘Yeh insult a hippogriff, an' it could be the las' thing yeh ever do.’

The approach is always the same. One bows low, keeps one's eyes open, since hippogriffs do not like a blinker, and waits. If the hippogriff bows in return, it may be touched. If it does not, one backs away, quickly.

The standard handbook on the subject holds that hippogriffs attack only when insulted. Its advice for meeting an unfamiliar one is courtesy, distance and a low bow.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, on 2 September 1993, Hagrid brought his dozen hippogriffs to his first Care of Magical Creatures lesson. Buckbeak bowed to Harry Potter and carried him round the castle. Neville Longbottom's hippogriff would not bow to him at all, while Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger tried the chestnut. When Dracina Malfoy called Buckbeak a big ugly lump, he slashed her arm.

In Chapter Eleven, with Buckbeak's case before the Committee, Harry, Ron and Hermione went through two centuries of wizarding law looking for a hippogriff that had been cleared. Hippogriffs had been tried in wizarding courts more than once. A case of 1722 was no use to them, because it had lost.

In Chapter Fifteen Ron took over the appeal, buried in The Handbook of Hippogriff Psychology. Somebody had marked its chapter on the unfamiliar hippogriff with a green ribbon. Soon afterwards Harry saw Dracina in an empty classroom, bowing to a suit of armour without blinking once.

In Chapter Twenty, on the night of 6 June 1994, Dracina flung her arms round Buckbeak's neck without bowing first. To Harry's astonishment, Buckbeak let her.

pages.title: The Grim
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A huge black dog, the size of a bear
Black Shuck, the Barghest, the Gytrash
pages.html:
The Grim is a great phantom hound that walks in churchyards. It is the darkest omen of death in the wizarding world. Most witches and wizards are frankly terrified of it. To see the Grim is to know that somebody is going to die, very often the person who has seen it.

Black dogs

The Grim is one of the black dogs of the British Isles. Black Shuck haunts the Norfolk coast, and the Barghest is found up in Yorkshire. There are the Gytrash and a dozen others besides, under a dozen names. Those who know about such things say that they all come to the same thing in the end. A big black dog that looks at you at midnight is never good news for somebody.

Muggle country people used to say that the first grave in a new churchyard should be a dog's, so that its ghost would guard the ground. The Grim is sometimes said to be that guardian.

Divination takes the Grim very seriously. A black dog the size of a bear stares out from the cover of Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the Worst Is Coming, which is on sale in Flourish and Blotts.

In the saga

In the Interlude of Book Three, on the night in August 1993 when Harry Potter left Privet Drive, John Constantine heard the boy on the Knight Bus describe a big black thing like a dog. John had never met a man in his line of work who liked black dogs. The Grim was one of them, and a big black dog that looked at you at midnight was never good news for somebody.

In Chapter Four, in August 1993, Harry saw the cover of Death Omens in Flourish and Blotts. The manager told him lightly not to read it, but Harry could not put the dog out of his mind.

In Chapter Six, at his first Divination lesson on 2 September 1993, Professor Trelawney looked into Harry's teacup and saw the Grim. Hermione Granger said it looked nothing like a Grim to her. Seamus Finnigan, tilting his head, thought it looked more like a donkey. Ron Weasley was horrified, because his Uncle Bilius had seen a Grim and died the next day.

In Chapter Nine, during the Hufflepuff match in November, Harry saw a great black dog watching him from an empty stand. The old words came back to him: ‘the great phantom hound that walks in churchyards, the darkest portent of them all’.

In Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, Trelawney was still seeing the Grim in Harry's tea leaves, and in her crystal ball. Harry had begun to wonder whether a dog could really be an omen if Crookshanks could see it too.

The dog Harry kept seeing was not the Grim at all. It was Sirius Black.

pages.title: The black dog in Magnolia Crescent
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
A gap between a garage and a fence by number two, Magnolia Crescent, Little Whinging
Sirius Black, in his Animagus form
pages.html:
The black dog in Magnolia Crescent was the huge animal that watched Harry Potter from the dark on the night he left Privet Drive in August 1993. Harry, who was given every reason that year to believe in omens, came to think it was the Grim. It was Sirius Black.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, Harry dragged his trunk out of Privet Drive in a rage and stopped in Magnolia Crescent. In the gap between a garage and a fence by number two stood a black dog the size of a bear. It was all shoulder and skull. Its pale eyes threw back the light of Harry's wand like two discs. It did not growl. It seemed to be paying attention, and Harry had the feeling that it knew exactly who he was.

Harry stepped back and fell over his trunk. When his light swung back to the gap, it was empty. A moment later the Knight Bus came out of nowhere and very nearly ran him over.

In the Interlude of Book Three, John Constantine, riding the Knight Bus that night, heard the boy say there had been a big black thing in the gap, like a dog. John looked for himself. There was nothing in the gap but dustbins, and he told himself firmly that it was not his dog.

In Chapter Six, after Professor Trelawney saw the Grim in his teacup, Harry told Ron Weasley about the dog. Ron went white to the lips.

In Chapter Nineteen Sirius told Harry the truth. He had been in Surrey a few days, working up the nerve to have a look at him, and he had been in that gap, as a dog, when Harry came round the corner with a face like thunder. ‘That was me. You lit your wand at me.’

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994, after glimpsing a shimmering figure across Privet Drive, Harry found himself thinking of the pale eyes that had watched him from the gap beside a garage in Magnolia Crescent the summer before. He thought about Sirius for a while after that.

pages.title: The stuffed creature in McGonagall's office
infobox: A lit glass case above the fire, Professor McGonagall's office
pages.html:
The stuffed creature in McGonagall's office is a Goa'uld symbiote, long dead, kept in a lit glass case above the fire in Professor McGonagall's office at Hogwarts. She killed it herself, a long time ago, with the help of Big Boss.

Description

It is about the length of a forearm, grey-white and segmented like a worm or an eel, with fronds down its back. It has no eyes that can be seen. Its mouth opens four ways at once, in four hinged flaps lined with needle teeth, and it was stuffed with them held wide, as if it were screaming.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the first night of term, Harry Potter noticed the case properly for the first time. He thought the thing in it the most horrible object he had ever seen in a teacher's office, Lockhart's portraits included. McGonagall saw him staring. Her look said yes, Potter, that was alive once, and no, you may not ask.

In Chapter Eight, teaching the limits of Transfiguration, McGonagall described creatures that go in through the flesh, usually at the back of the neck, and speak with their host's mouth. No Transfiguration would separate the two, she told the class. 'I know, because I once tried. It was a long time ago and a very long way from here.' In the end, she said, only a knife had answered, with a good deal of help from a man she would not name. The host died. So did the creature, and she kept it, as a reminder that there are some problems one cannot solve with a wand.

In Chapter Ten, at the Three Broomsticks in December 1993, Cornelius Fudge told McGonagall that at least those parasite creatures would not be bothering them again.

pages.title: Mutants
infobox: An inherited genetic mutation, the X-gene
All dead by 2053 but Wolverine; none born after the Third World War
pages.html:
Mutants are human beings born with a quirk in their genes that gives them powers, which usually show themselves at puberty. Muggles have known about them since 1963 and have been frightened of them ever since. Their answer has been a succession of giant robots, registration laws and hate groups. 'Mutant attack' has become the usual explanation for any destruction nobody can account for, and the Ministry of Magic has found it a useful cover story. By 1994 Muggles had begun to take magic for mutant power, attacking wizards as 'muties'.

Nature

A mutant carries a variation in his or her genes, often called the X-gene, which is inherited rather than caught or acquired. The powers it brings can be of almost any kind: telepathy, flight, command of the weather, of metal or of fire, great strength, quick healing, or changes to the body such as wings, fur or extra limbs. Some mutants can pass for ordinary people. Others cannot hide what they are, however hard they try.

The powers usually arrive at puberty, often suddenly and sometimes destructively, which is a hard thing to happen to anybody at fourteen. Magneto and those who follow him call mutants Homo superior, the species that is meant to replace humanity.

The first of the mutants, Apocalypse, was born in Egypt some five thousand years ago.

Mutants have been born among Muggles in noticeable numbers since the Second World War. Few people minded much until Magneto came along in the 1960s.

A mutant can also be a witch or a wizard, since the X-gene and magic are separate gifts. Wanda Maximoff, the Scarlet Witch, is both: her hexes are her mutant power, while her witchcraft comes from her mother, a Romani witch. Her twin brother, Pietro, is a mutant and a Squib. Muggles take any magic they see for mutant power, which is how the Scarlet Witch and Amanda Sefton have lived in the open for years.

Mutants and the public

The public learnt of mutants in 1963, when Magneto seized the missile base at Cape Citadel and was driven off by Professor Charles Xavier's X-Men. Their history since has been one of fear and reprisal. In 1965 Dr Bolivar Trask unveiled the Sentinels, giant robots built to hunt mutants, on live television. In 1984 Senator Robert Kelly brought in the Mutant Registration Act, which obliged mutants to register with the American government. Mutant rights groups have campaigned against both. In the early 1990s hate groups such as the Friends of Humanity took up arms against mutants and anyone who sympathised with them.

Magneto's blackout of August 1993, which killed patients on life support in hospitals all over the world, is still remembered bitterly a year later. In August 1994 a proposal to revive the Sentinel programme came before the United States Senate, and mutant rights groups called it a licence to hunt.

By 1994 'mutie', short for mutant, had become a Muggle slur for anybody who could do things ordinary people could not. It was generally shouted, as Barty Crouch put it, before somebody was set on fire. That summer it was shouted at the protests outside the United Nations, and in Stockport at a wizard dragged off his ladder. In Britain there was talk of a register of people with powers. Groups such as the Friends of Humanity met in church halls. Stickers reading HUMANS FIRST or KEEP BRITAIN HUMAN appeared on cars.

In August 1996 Onslaught, a being that had begun in the mind of Charles Xavier himself, cost the world the Avengers and the Fantastic Four. Many people blamed mutants for it. That autumn Graydon Creed of the Friends of Humanity ran for President on a promise to lock them away.

The Legacy Virus

Since the end of 1992 mutants have had a plague of their own to fear, the Legacy Virus, which Stryfe left behind him. It has no cure, and nobody is known to have recovered from it. In the summer of 1994 only a handful of people know that it has begun to reach ordinary people too. One of them is Moira MacTaggert, who is fighting it on Muir Island, and has caught it herself.

The end of the mutants

The mutants did not outlive the Third World War. Mutants grow old like anybody else. By 2026, when the war broke out, the first X-Men had died of old age, with most of those who came after them.

The war killed the younger generations. The great powers called up the mutants among their people, as the Weapon programme had once taken Logan. Then they built Sentinels again, to find the mutant soldiers of their enemies. The machines, which detect the mutant gene, could not tell one side's mutants from another's, and by the 2030s the mutants of several countries were in camps.

In the 2040s the Legacy Virus came back as a weapon of the war. The new strain killed anybody who carried the X-gene, whether or not their powers had ever shown, which is why no mutant was born after the war. Colonel Phillip Green's militia, which called mutants genetically unfit, hunted down whoever was left. The nuclear exchange of 2053 burnt the last refuges.

The mutant heroes who were still alive when the war began fell in it, holding back the Sentinels or getting the hunted out. By the end of the war every mutant on Earth was dead but one. Logan, called Wolverine, outlived them all, because his healing power would not let him die. He went into hiding.

In the saga

Book Three, Chapter Three: on the Knight Bus, Stan Shunpike and Ern Prang try to remember how the Ministry explained away the street full of Muggles that was blown up in 1981. Everybody blamed Sirius Black for it. Ern says it was a mutant attack; Stan thinks it was a gas explosion.

Book Three, Chapter Eighteen: in the Shrieking Shack, Harry says sarcastically that the witnesses to Pettigrew's death thought they had seen a mutant attack, 'Bloody Magneto or whoever it is nowadays'.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Three: on the Muggle news of 20 August 1994, a nurse who lost eleven patients at Bellevue Hospital in the blackout of the year before says that it was all the work of one mutant: 'One man, up in a space station, having a tantrum.' Later in the same bulletin, watching film of the Sentinels, Harry wonders what a machine built to hunt down people born different would make of a wizard.

Book Four, Chapter Four: at breakfast on 21 August 1994 Uncle Vernon reads out a piece about the Americans' giant robots, and says the freaks should all be rounded up. At dinner at the Burrow, Arthur Weasley reads out the story of Wilfred Thimble, a retired wizard beaten in Stockport by young Muggles who kept shouting 'Mutie' at him. Harry explains that the word is short for mutant, meaning Muggles born with powers. None of the Weasleys has heard of mutants. Molly tells him kindly that Muggles cannot have powers, since that is what makes them Muggles.

Book Four, Chapter Five: in the scullery Hermione tells Harry of a man in Ohio who could make the lights flicker. Somebody threw a petrol bomb through his window, though he was only an electrician with bad wiring. Her own parents go to Friends of Humanity meetings, though if anybody in their house is a mutant, she says, it is her. At the campsite Mr Roberts, the Muggle manager, is Obliviated just as he starts to call the crowd muties. At lunch Barty Crouch tells Ludo Bagman what the word means. It is what Muggles call people born with powers, generally just before they set fire to them.

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the Top Box Harry tells Cornelius Fudge about mutants. People born with powers have been appearing since the war, he says, but nobody minded much until Magneto seized an American missile base in 1963. Magneto has been at it ever since, with a gang he calls the Brotherhood of Evil Mutants. Now mutie is shouted at anybody who can do things ordinary people cannot. Fudge laughs at the very idea. Harry adds that he is worried the American robots will not be able to tell mutants from wizards.

pages.title: Superhumans
infobox: People of the Muggle world with powers beyond the human
pages.html:
Superhumans are the men and women of the Muggle world who can do what no ordinary person can: fly, climb walls or lift a car over their heads. Superman, the first of them to become famous, was photographed in 1938. By 1993 there were a great many of them. Some work alone, while others belong to organisations such as the Avengers and the Justice League. Almost nobody in the wizarding world knows that any of them exist.

In the Muggle world

Old newspaper photographs from 1938, all grain and grey, show a young man lifting a car above his head. That was Superman, and the Muggle world has never quite got used to such people since. Captain America fought in the Second World War, then spent nearly twenty years frozen in the ice. Spider-Man, a man in a red and blue suit who climbs walls, was in the papers for years. Nobody knows who he is under the mask, which is the whole point, but he was more famous than almost anybody until he gave it up in the summer of 1993.

The two largest superhuman organisations, the Avengers and the Justice League, work under an accord with the United Nations. It forbids them to act on their own in any conflict between sovereign states. Superman died fighting Doomsday in Metropolis in November 1992, and the Muggle world went into mourning for him. He came back in 1993, as young as ever, with long hair. By 1994 the mood had soured. In July of that year the United Nations suspended the Justice League's charter.

The wizarding world

The wizarding world has a wall round it that works both ways. Wizards keep Muggles from knowing about magic, but most of them have no idea what goes on among Muggles either. A few do know. Albus Dumbledore has heard of Superman and Captain America. John Constantine has spent years in the company of people who wear their underpants over their tights and fly. He has shaken hands with Superman, who made the dangerous mistake of owing him a favour.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, when the Weasleys came for him in the flying car in the summer of 1992, Harry said through the bars of his window that he was stuck unless they could get Superman on the phone. 'Who's Superman?' said Fred Weasley, interested. In Chapter Thirteen Dumbledore told Ambrose Greyhame that Harry trusted him as surely as the Americans trust old Superman or Captain America to save them.

In Book Three, Chapter Two, on the morning of 31 July 1993, the Muggle news called the Avengers and the Justice League the world's two largest superhuman organisations. They would act in Khan's war, they said, only at the request of the Security Council. In Chapter Four, in Diagon Alley, Harry asked Lucius Malfoy about Khan. Lucius had never heard of him. Then Harry asked about Spider-Man. If such a man existed, said Lucius, the Wizengamot would have heard of him. 'We have Obliviators for a great deal less than climbing walls.' Harry remembered Fred asking who Superman was, and realised that in two years he had never once heard a wizard say the name. The whole wizarding world, he understood at last, did not know that there were people on the other side of the wall who could fly.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on Saturday 20 August 1994, Harry nearly fell off the Dursleys' sofa when Superman appeared on the news, speaking to the Security Council in New York. He looked just as young as the man in the photographs of 1938, though his hair had grown long. 'People are dying while we wait to be asked,' he said. The Council adjourned without taking a vote.

pages.title: The blood ward
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
Lily Potter, by her death in 1981
The blood of Harry Potter and of Petunia Dursley
While Harry lives where his aunt lives
pages.html:
The blood ward is the protection that keeps Harry Potter safe at number four, Privet Drive. His mother, Lily, left it on him when she died for him in 1981. It lives in his blood, and in the blood of her sister, Petunia Dursley, so it goes on working only while Harry keeps living where his aunt lives. Cornelius Fudge calls it a blood ward. Albus Dumbledore calls it old magic.

How it works

Dumbledore says the protection is older than anything he can do himself: the magic of Elves, and of Númenor. It came down to Lily through her mother, Susan Pevensie, from Aragorn and Arwen. Arwen gave the Elves; Aragorn gave Númenor. Because Petunia shares that blood, her house is the one place where it holds. For that reason Dumbledore insists that Harry go back to Privet Drive every summer, however little he wants to.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, on the castle steps at the end of Harry's second year, with the lake blazing gold behind him, Dumbledore explained why Harry must go back to his aunt. 'When your mother died for you, Harry, she put a protection on you. Old magic. Older than anything I can do. The magic of Elves, Harry. And of Númenor. It lives in your blood, and it lives in hers. And her blood is in one other living person in this world.' Then, after a pause: 'Your aunt.'

In Book Three, Chapter Three, at the Leaky Cauldron in August 1993, Harry told the Minister for Magic that he never wanted to go back to Privet Drive. Fudge said that Dumbledore had described to him how that strange blood ward worked. 'It really is the safest place for you there. I agree with Dumbledore on that much.'

In Chapter Nineteen, in the tunnel beneath the Whomping Willow, Sirius Black offered Harry a home with him. Harry said yes at once, then remembered that he was not allowed. When his mum died, he explained, she left a sort of protection on him. It was in his blood, and in Aunt Petunia's too, so it only kept working as long as he kept living where she lived. Fudge, he added, had called it a blood ward. 'Then Dumbledore knows what he's doing,' said Sirius. 'He generally does.'

In Book Four, Chapter Two, in the summer of 1994, Harry still minded rather a lot being stuck with the Dursleys. But it was the blood that kept him there: his mother's blood, which ran in Aunt Petunia's veins as well as his own.

pages.title: Animagus
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Minerva McGonagall; James Potter, Sirius Black and Peter Pettigrew, all unregistered
pages.html:
An Animagus is a witch or wizard who can turn into an animal at will. The art belongs to Transfiguration. It is difficult enough, and dangerous enough, for the Ministry of Magic to keep a register of everybody who can do it.

The transformation

Each Animagus has a single animal form, which is found rather than chosen, and which carries markings of its own. Professor McGonagall becomes a tabby cat with the marks of spectacles round her eyes. The transformation can go horribly wrong, which is one reason the Ministry keeps a close watch on anybody who attempts it. Its register records what animal each Animagus becomes and what markings it has. Only seven Animagi have been registered this century.

Light magic

Animagus magic is light magic, not Wyrm-touched. It is not as close to God as the Patronus, but it is light magic none the less. That is why Remus Lupin's war form would tolerate his friends in their animal shapes, when it would tolerate almost nothing else.

The Marauders

Three Hogwarts students became Animagi illegally in their fifth year, after the best part of three years' work, so as to keep their friend Remus Lupin company at the full moon. They were James Potter, a stag; Sirius Black, a great black dog; and Peter Pettigrew, a rat. The Ministry never knew.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, on 2 September 1993, Professor McGonagall turned into a tabby cat in front of her third-years. Harry Potter, whose death Professor Trelawney had foretold that morning, was not even looking.

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Hermione Granger said she had looked McGonagall up on the register: only seven Animagi had been registered this century, and Peter Pettigrew was not among them. Lupin explained how James, Sirius and Peter had become Animagi for his sake. ‘Ah, you see, Animagus magic isn’t Wyrm-touched at all. It’s very much light magic.’

pages.title: Witch-hunts
infobox: Chiefly the fourteenth to the seventeenth centuries
Many thousands, almost none of them magical
Witchcraft a felony, a crime against a neighbour
pages.html:
The witch-hunts were the long persecution of supposed witches in Europe, at its worst from the fourteenth century to the seventeenth. Many thousands of people were put to death, nearly all of them with no magic whatever. Real witches seldom came to any harm, since a Flame-Freezing Charm turned the fire into a pleasant warmth. Wizards remember the burnings all the same. They are a large part of the reason the wizarding world went into hiding.

The burnings

A History of Magic records that of the many thousands put to the stake in Europe between 1300 and 1400, the overwhelming majority had no magic at all. On the rare occasions when a real witch or wizard was caught, a simple Flame-Freezing Charm did the rest. The condemned had only to shriek convincingly for the crowd. Wendelin the Weird enjoyed the tickling sensation so much that she had herself burned forty-seven times, under a variety of names.

Felony and heresy

The Church's old rule, the Canon Episcopi, had said that women who believed they rode out by night with a heathen goddess were deluded, dreaming what the Devil put in their heads. The sin was believing in witchcraft, not doing it. The trouble began in the fifteenth century. The Dominican Johannes Nider wrote, in the middle of a fat book about ants, that witches were a secret church with the Devil for its bishop. Then, in 1486, two more Dominicans published the Malleus Maleficarum, the Hammer of Witches. Witchcraft became an organised heresy, a pact with the Devil and treason against Heaven itself. After it the witch-hunts grew.

Britain went its own way. When England, Wales and Scotland came at last to make laws against witchcraft, they made it a felony, a crime against a neighbour like horse-stealing, rather than a heresy. A felony is about what a person has done; a heresy is about what a person is. In England a convicted witch was hanged, not burnt.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, Harry Potter spent the summer of 1993 on a History of Magic essay: Witch Burning in the Fourteenth Century Was Completely Pointless. Discuss.

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Florean Fortescue, who knows a great deal about the medieval witch-burnings, told him over a knickerbocker glory in Diagon Alley that the burners had not been wicked, most of them. 'They were frightened, Mr Potter. That's all.' Harry wrote they were frightened in the margin of his essay, and underlined it.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the Fat Friar told Harry how England had made witchcraft a felony rather than a heresy, and how things went wrong after the Malleus. He had been dead by then. He had watched friends burn who had only ever helped people.

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, Harry wrote his examination essay of June 1994 on the burnings, done properly: the fear behind them, then the long harmony that came before. Nobody, he told Hermione, ever wrote about the wise women in the villages, the priests nodding to them on the way out of church or the Muggle-born boys going into the monasteries.

pages.title: Death of Superman
aliases: the death and return of Superman
infobox: Both killed; Superman returned to life in 1993
pages.html:
The death of Superman was the battle of 18 November 1992 in which Superman and the creature Doomsday killed each other in Metropolis, after a fight that tore up half the city. The world mourned him for months. In 1993 four claimants took up his symbol, one of whom destroyed Coast City, and later that year the real Superman came back to life.

The battle

Doomsday broke out of its ancient prison in the autumn of 1992 and smashed its way across the American Midwest. The Justice League of the time met it first: Blue Beetle, Booster Gold, Guy Gardner, Fire, Ice, Maxima and Bloodwynd among them. It beat them all, and left Blue Beetle in a coma. Superman took up the fight and could not stop it. The creature turned towards Metropolis, and the battle went on through the city for hour after hour, tearing up half of it.

It ended in front of the Daily Planet on 18 November 1992, when each struck the other a final blow. Doomsday fell dead. Superman died in the street a few moments later in Lois Lane's arms, with the cameras watching.

Mourning

The grief was worldwide and very public. Superman's funeral in Metropolis drew his fellow heroes and enormous crowds. He was laid in a memorial tomb in the city. In Britain, as everywhere else, there were retrospectives on every channel. Commemorative mugs and souvenirs were still everywhere well into the summer of 1993. Before long it was discovered that his body had been taken from the tomb.

Four Supermen, and the real one

In 1993 four figures appeared, each wearing Superman's symbol: a young clone calling himself Superboy; the armoured engineer John Henry Irons, called Steel; the cold, visored Kryptonian construct known as the Eradicator; and the Cyborg Superman, who claimed to be Superman himself with his body rebuilt. The Cyborg Superman was the impostor, and a mass murderer. With Mongul's forces he destroyed Coast City in the summer of 1993.

Superman's body had been carried to the Fortress of Solitude and its Kryptonian regeneration matrix. He came back later in 1993, weak at first. At Coast City he fought the Cyborg Superman and Mongul. Hal Jordan and the other claimants fought beside him. Then he went home to Metropolis rejuvenated, with his hair grown long. How he came back has never been explained to the public, who have mostly put it down to his being an alien.

In the saga

Superman died while Harry Potter was at Hogwarts in his second year. Harry came home in June 1993 to find Muggle Britain still half in black, with retrospectives on every channel and a commemorative mug on the Dursleys' shelf. In August he realised that no wizard he knew had heard of Superman at all. A year later, in August 1994, Harry, who had not known of the return, said ‘I thought he was dead,’ and Dudley told him it was ‘on everything’.

pages.title: Sirius Black's street massacre
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
1 November 1981, the day after the Potters died
Black sent to Azkaban without a trial
pages.html:
Sirius Black's street massacre is the name the wizarding world gave to the killing of twelve Muggles in a crowded street on 1 November 1981, the day after Lord Voldemort murdered James and Lily Potter. For twelve years everyone believed that Black had killed thirteen people with a single curse, a wizard and twelve Muggles. He was said to have stood in the crater afterwards, laughing. He was innocent. The curse was Peter Pettigrew's, and the wizard who was supposed to have died was Pettigrew himself.

What the world believed

According to the Ministry, Peter Pettigrew cornered Black in the street, sobbing, 'Lily and James, Sirius! How could you?' He went for his wand, but Black was quicker, and blew him to pieces along with everyone near him. Muggle eyewitnesses had their memories wiped afterwards.

Cornelius Fudge, then Junior Minister in the Department of Magical Catastrophes, was one of the first on the scene. He found a crater so deep that it had broken the sewer underneath, bodies everywhere and Muggles screaming. Black stood in the middle of it, laughing. Twenty members of the Magical Law Enforcement Squad took him away, and he went quietly, still laughing. The biggest piece of Pettigrew ever found was a finger. Pettigrew was awarded the Order of Merlin, First Class, and Black went to Azkaban without a trial.

What really happened

At the last moment Black had persuaded the Potters to make Pettigrew their Secret-Keeper instead of himself, and Pettigrew had betrayed them. When Black tracked him down the next day, Pettigrew shouted for the whole street to hear that Black had betrayed Lily and James. Then he blew the street apart with the wand he had been holding behind his back, killing everyone within twenty feet of himself. He cut off his own finger, turned into a rat and escaped into the sewers. Black, who had been outwitted, stood in the ruins and laughed.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, on the Knight Bus in August 1993, Harry Potter read in the Daily Prophet that twelve years earlier Black had stood in a crowded street and killed thirteen people with a single curse. Stan Shunpike told him what had come next. 'Laughed,' said Stan. 'Jus' stood there an' laughed.'

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, hidden behind the Christmas tree in the Three Broomsticks in December 1993, Harry heard Fudge tell the story to Madam Rosmerta and the teachers. He still dreamt of it, he said.

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Black told Harry what had really happened. Pettigrew, unmasked, was standing in front of them.

pages.title: Grand Prize Galleon Draw
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Arthur Weasley, of the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office
pages.html:
The Grand Prize Galleon Draw is the Daily Prophet's annual draw, with a prize paid in gold. In 1993 it was won by Arthur Weasley, who spent every Knut of the seven hundred Galleons on a month in Egypt for his family. The photograph the Prophet took of them there led, by a very roundabout way, to the escape of Sirius Black from Azkaban.

The 1993 draw

Arthur Weasley, then forty-three, of the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office, told the Prophet that he couldn't quite believe it. He took his wife and children to Egypt to visit his eldest son, Bill, who works for Gringotts as a curse-breaker in the tombs of the pharaohs. Molly Weasley told the paper that they had never been able to afford anything like it. She added that she would know if Fred and George touched anything in the pyramids.

The Prophet printed a photograph of the whole family, all but Charlie, in front of a pyramid. Ron stood at the front in a hat like a fez, grinning, with a hand on the head of his fat grey rat, Scabbers.

What came of it

The photograph did more than anybody could have guessed. On an inspection of Azkaban that summer, Cornelius Fudge gave his copy of the paper to Sirius Black. Black knew the rat at once, by the toe missing from its front paw: it was Peter Pettigrew, the man he had been sent to Azkaban for murdering. Soon afterwards he escaped, the first prisoner ever to do so.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, the cutting reached Privet Drive on Harry Potter's thirteenth birthday, 31 July 1993, in a parcel from Ron. Harry felt glad with his whole chest, since nobody deserved seven hundred Galleons more than the Weasleys. A moment later he was ashamed to find that he minded their going without him.

pages.title: Goblin rebellion of 1612
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The goblin rebellion of 1612 was one of the many risings of the goblins against wizarding rule. According to Sites of Historical Sorcery, its headquarters was an inn at Hogsmeade, the only all-wizard village in Britain.

Background

Goblins have risen against wizards many times, chiefly in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The oldest grievance is the wand. Wizarding law forbids any non-human creature to carry or use one, and wizards have never shared the secrets of wand-making. Of the 1612 rising itself, the date and the inn are most of what is generally remembered.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on the Hogwarts Express on 1 September 1993, Hermione Granger told her friends that Sites of Historical Sorcery gave the inn at Hogsmeade as the headquarters of the 1612 goblin rebellion. It also called the Shrieking Shack the most severely haunted building in Britain. Ron Weasley, who was describing the sweets at Honeydukes, did not hear a word of it.

pages.title: Double-ended newt
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The double-ended newt is a magical newt sold at the Magical Menagerie in Diagon Alley, where the witch behind the counter gives advice on its care.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, on 31 August 1993, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger crossed Diagon Alley to the Magical Menagerie, to see about Ron's ailing rat, Scabbers. The witch behind the counter was already advising a wizard on the care of double-ended newts, so they waited, looking at the cages. When the double-ended newt wizard left, Ron went up to the counter.

pages.title: Green ribbon
infobox: Dracina's green ribbons; Dracina's ribbon; Harry's green ribbon; The green ribbon
A token of favour from a lady
In Harry Potter's copy of The Lord of the Rings
pages.html:
The green ribbon is the thin, silky, Slytherin-green ribbon that tied Dracina Malfoy’s letter to Harry Potter on his thirteenth birthday in July 1993. In the old wizarding families a green ribbon from a lady is a token of favour, and Narcissa Malfoy insisted on it. Harry has kept it ever since, in his copy of The Lord of the Rings, together with a second green ribbon that came his way in 1994.

A token of favour

The custom is very old. When a lady sends a green ribbon with a letter, it means that she regards the recipient with approval, and that he may consider himself under her esteem. A ribbon of favour must never be thrown away, since that is unlucky. Hardly anybody keeps up the custom any more except Narcissa, who keeps up all of them.

So the ribbon was really Narcissa’s doing. She sent her own eagle owl, Ganymede, who knew the way to Surrey; she told Dracina which day Harry’s birthday was; and she insisted on the ribbon. Dracina wanted it understood that the ribbon had not been her idea, and that there was nothing to read into it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, the ribbon arrived tied in a perfect bow. It smelt of something cool and flowery, like the inside of a very expensive shop. It reminded Harry of something, though he could not think what. When he had hidden everything else under the loose floorboard, he wound it round his fingers and put it in his pyjama pocket. He told himself that was only because throwing it away was unlucky.

In Chapter Four, at the Leaky Cauldron in August 1993, he found it crumpled at the bottom of the pillowcase his presents had travelled in, smelling faintly of cold flowers. He used it to keep his place in The Lord of the Rings. Hermione touched the end of it with one finger and said that it was a funny bookmark. ‘It’s the right width,’ said Harry. In Chapter Eleven, by Christmas, it had become a thing wholly his own, not handed down to him by anybody, and he would have fought the whole of Gryffindor to keep it.

Dracina’s own hair ribbons fared worse. In Chapter Six, on 2 September 1993, she screamed at Harry in the hospital wing that somebody had done something to her ribbons at lunch. In Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, she accused Hermione of it. In Chapter Twenty Hermione owned up: she had turned them scarlet and gold.

In the Easter holidays of 1994, the three hippogriff books Ron was sure Dracina had been hoarding came back to Madam Pince’s desk. A thin green ribbon marked the opening of the chapter on the Low Bow in the Handbook, and the corner of that page had been thumbed soft. Ron pulled the ribbon out and dropped it on the floor. Harry picked it up without quite knowing why. That night he tucked it into the back of The Lord of the Rings, next to the first one.

pages.title: Dracina's chocolate violets
infobox: A plain white confectioner's box, tied with brown string
I made them myself. Not from Ginny. D.
pages.html:
Dracina's chocolate violets are the twelve violets, dipped in dark chocolate and each finished by hand, that Dracina Malfoy made for Harry Potter. She gave them to him on the first night of the 1993 term. They took her four days, and no two of them are alike.

The box

They came in two neat rows on a square of white paper, in a thin white box of the plain kind confectioners use, tied with ordinary brown string. Each violet had been dipped in dark chocolate almost to the tips of its sugared petals, so that a little purple showed through. Then each had been finished on its own. One had a single line of silver piped round the rim. The next had a pinhead of white sugar at its heart, and another a tiny H.

The violets were an answer. At the end of his second year Harry had lain in the hospital wing eating a whole box of sugared violets, believing they came from Ginny Weasley. He had never told a soul, and he had worked out the truth for himself months afterwards. The card in the box read: I made them myself. Not from Ginny. D.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Five, on 1 September 1993, Dracina came up out of the rainy dark between the carriages outside the castle, pressed the box into Harry’s hands and was gone. Harry opened it that night behind the hangings of his four-poster, by wandlight, and ate one. He thought it the best thing he had ever put in his mouth.

In Chapter Six, in the hospital wing, she screamed at him that she had spent four days on them, with a brush, and he had never said thank you. In Chapter Fifteen, sitting up in bed with her Easter egg, Harry remembered the thin box pushed into his hands in the rain, with twelve violets inside, no two of them quite the same.

pages.title: Pocket Sneakoscope
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Harry Potter, a present from Ron Weasley
pages.html:
A Pocket Sneakoscope is a small Dark detector shaped like a tiny glass spinning top. When somebody untrustworthy is near, it lights up, spins and whistles. Ron Weasley sent one to Harry Potter for his thirteenth birthday in 1993. It went off time after time that year, and Ron took it for a cheap one that did not work. It did.

Harry's Sneakoscope

Ron bought it on the family's holiday in Egypt in the summer of 1993. His letter warned Harry that Bill thought it rubbish, the sort of thing sold to tourists, and that it had gone off all through dinner the night before. That, Ron admitted, was when Fred and George had put beetles in Bill's soup. Errol carried it to Privet Drive for Harry's thirteenth birthday.

It seemed to go off at all the wrong moments. In fact it was right every time: whenever it went off, Scabbers, Ron's rat, was close by, and Scabbers was really Peter Pettigrew.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, the Sneakoscope stayed dark all through Harry's birthday.

In Chapter Five it stayed dark for Harry on the Hogwarts Express, then began to whistle from inside his trunk. Ron said it had gone haywire before, just as he was tying it to Errol's leg. Hermione asked shrewdly whether he had been doing anything untrustworthy at the time. Ron muffled it in a pair of Uncle Vernon's old socks so that it would not wake Professor Lupin, who was asleep in the corner. They could get it checked in Hogsmeade, he said, at Dervish and Banges.

In Chapter Eleven, on Christmas morning, it spun and whistled inside the socks when Crookshanks went for Scabbers.

pages.title: Broomstick Servicing Kit
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Harry Potter, for his thirteenth birthday
Handle polish, twig clippers, a compass and a handbook
pages.html:
The Broomstick Servicing Kit is the set of polish, clippers and other broom-care tools that Hermione Granger gave Harry Potter for his thirteenth birthday, on 31 July 1993. She bought it in a wizarding shop in Rennes, in Brittany, because she had noticed that he never cleaned his broom.

Contents

It holds a tin of High-Finish Polish for the handle, a pair of clippers for the tail twigs and a little compass with a tiny brass Snitch on its needle, which fixes on to the broom for long journeys. There is also a Handbook of Do-It-Yourself Broomcare, which Hermione fully expected him to ignore.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, Hedwig brought the parcel to Privet Drive from Brittany, where she had turned up on the balcony of the Grangers’ hotel. Hermione’s letter explained that Oliver Wood would shout at Harry if his broom’s tail was bent. It was the nicest thing anybody had ever bought him that was not a broomstick. He cut the string of his next parcel with its clippers.

In Chapter Two, with Aunt Marge in the house, Harry got through three days by thinking about his Handbook of Do-It-Yourself Broomcare whenever she started on him. It gave him such a glazed look that she decided he was mentally subnormal.

In Chapter Eleven, on Christmas Day 1993, he brought the kit down to see to his new Firebolt. There was nothing to do. Not a twig needed clipping, and the handle already shone in a way that put the polish to shame. He was still holding the tin when Professor McGonagall carried the Firebolt away.

pages.title: Handbook of Do-It-Yourself Broomcare
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Hermione Granger to Harry Potter, for his thirteenth birthday
pages.html:
The Handbook of Do-It-Yourself Broomcare is a manual of broomstick maintenance. Harry Potter's copy came in the Broomstick Servicing Kit that Hermione Granger sent him for his thirteenth birthday, in July 1993. That summer he recited it to himself to keep his temper while Aunt Marge was staying.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, the kit arrived with a letter from Hermione saying she had seen it in a wizarding shop in Rennes and thought of his Nimbus, which he never cleaned. There was handle polish, clippers for the twigs, a compass with a tiny brass Snitch on the needle, and a book, which she expected him to ignore.

In Chapter Two Harry got through Aunt Marge's visit on the Handbook. Early on, after she had insulted his mother, he sat on his hands in his bedroom and read page twelve four times without taking in a word. For the next three days he thought about the book whenever she started on him. This worked quite well, though it gave him a glazed look, so that Aunt Marge decided he was mentally subnormal. On her last evening she said he had a mean, runty look about him, and he tried hard to remember page twelve: A Charm to Cure Reluctant Reversers.

pages.title: The Monster Book of Monsters
infobox: Monster Book of Monsters; Monster Books
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Green and hairy, with a gold title
pages.html:
The Monster Book of Monsters is a green, hairy book that bites. Rubeus Hagrid chose it as the textbook for his Care of Magical Creatures classes when he began teaching in September 1993, because he thought it was funny. It opens meekly if stroked down the spine, which nobody thought to tell the class.

The book

It is bound in something green and hairy, with its title stamped in gold. It opens its covers like a mouth. Left to itself it scuttles, gnashes and tears the pages out of its fellows. Its owners keep it shut with belts, rope, Spellotape or bulldog clips.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in the summer of 1993, Hagrid told John Constantine about his new class. 'Got a book fer the class an' all,' he said happily. 'It bites! Took a lump out o' me thumb this mornin'. Lovely thing.' The book was, by every sign, The Monster Book of Monsters.

In Chapter One, Hagrid sent Harry Potter a copy for his thirteenth birthday, with a note telling him to keep his fingers out of it until he had read the other note, which did not exist. The book bit him the moment he had read its title, scuttled under the bed and came out at him like a terrier. Harry fell on it and got his belt round it in the end. 'What,' said Harry, to nobody, 'is he teaching us?'

In Chapter Four, in August 1993, Flourish and Blotts had about a hundred copies in an iron cage in the window, wrestling and tearing one another apart. The manager, who had been bitten five times already that morning, was enormously relieved to hear that Harry had one. He was never stocking them again, he said. He had thought the shop had seen the worst with two hundred copies of the Invisible Book of Invisibility, which they never found.

In Chapter Six, at Hagrid's first lesson, nobody had got theirs open. Harry's was belted. Dracina Malfoy's was tied with rope. Hagrid took Hermione Granger's copy, peeled off the Spellotape and ran one huge finger down its spine. It shuddered, fell open and lay meekly in his palm. 'Oh, of course!' said Malfoy. 'Stroke them! How stupid of us all!'

pages.title: Firebolt
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Superfine ash, under a diamond-hard polish
Birch twigs, hand-honed and finished twig by twig
Nought to 150 miles an hour in ten seconds
Every Irish player at the 1994 World Cup final
pages.html:
The Firebolt is the finest racing broom in the world, a prototype that first went on show in the window of Quality Quidditch Supplies, in Diagon Alley, in August 1993. Harry Potter owns one. It came to him with no card on Christmas Day 1993. The gold that paid for it came out of Sirius Black’s vault.

The broom

Every Firebolt has a superfine ash handle under a diamond-hard polish, with its own registration number burnt into it in gold near the top. The tail is made of birch twigs, honed and finished by hand, twig by twig. It goes from nothing to 150 miles an hour in ten seconds. It has an unbreakable Braking Charm, besides a built-in autobrake. The handle is a little slimmer than a Cleansweep's. It turns at the slightest lean, and when it is let go it hovers on its own at exactly the right height to mount.

Its price is given only on request. The Irish International Side ordered seven, and Which Broomstick predicted that it would be the broom of choice for the national teams at the 1994 World Championship. At the final every Irish player rode one, and little model Firebolts that could really fly were sold to the crowd as souvenirs.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry went back to the window of Quality Quidditch Supplies almost every day of August 1993 to look at it. He wanted it more than anything he had ever wanted. All the same, he would not empty his Gringotts vault for it, when his Nimbus Two Thousand had never lost him a match.

In Chapter Ten, with that Nimbus smashed by the Whomping Willow, Harry came to a full-colour picture of the Firebolt on the last page of Which Broomstick. He looked at it for a long time, then shut the magazine.

In Chapter Eleven, on Christmas morning, a Firebolt lay among his presents with no card. Hermione went straight to Professor McGonagall, who carried it off within hours to be stripped and checked for jinxes. In Chapter Twelve Madam Hooch and Professor Flitwick spent about two months taking it to pieces, while Flitwick suspected a Hurling Hex. At the end of February 1994 McGonagall handed it back, clean and quite unchanged.

In Chapter Thirteen Harry flew it at last. On the Firebolt he pulled off, without even meaning to, the half-roll out of a steep climb that he had never once managed on the Nimbus, and a roll that no other broom could match. In the Ravenclaw match Cho Chang’s Comet could not follow it out of his feint dive.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, after Sirius’s escape, his letter explained everything. Crookshanks had taken the order to the Owl Office for him. He had used Harry’s name, but told them to take the gold from his own vault. Please consider it as thirteen birthdays’ worth of presents from your godfather.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Two, in August 1994, the Firebolt lay in Harry’s trunk at Privet Drive, among his robes and spellbooks.

In Chapter Four Harry packed it on 21 August, among the things he cared about most, with his father's Invisibility Cloak and the Marauder's Map.

In Chapter Five Cedric Diggory asked after it on Stoatshead Hill. Harry told him it had been stuck in his trunk all summer, since his uncle would have had a heart attack if he had flown it. Cedric asked to have a go on it one day, promising to give it back. At lunch, when Ludo Bagman said flying carpets would never replace brooms in Britain, Harry was thinking of his Firebolt. He said he should bloody well hope not. Barty Crouch approved: 'A British broom for a British sky.'

In Chapter Six, through his Omnioculars, Harry read the word Firebolt on every Irish broom. When Aidan Lynch mounted his Firebolt again after Krum's Wronski Feint, the whole Irish team came alight.

pages.title: Hogsmeade permission form
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Hogwarts pupils from the third year on
Written permission from Sirius Black, June 1994
pages.html:
The Hogsmeade permission form is the form a parent or guardian must sign before a Hogwarts pupil may visit the village of Hogsmeade, which third-years and older are allowed to do on certain weekends. Harry Potter's form was never signed. In the end his godfather, Sirius Black, gave him written permission of his own.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter One, the form came with Harry's Hogwarts letter in the summer of 1993.
