In Book Two, Chapter Nineteen, in the small hours of a June morning in 1993, Fawkes led Harry Potter and Ron Weasley to the office after the Chamber of Secrets. The sword was still lying on the desk when Arthur Weasley gave the warning Harry remembered afterwards: 'Never trust anything that can think for itself, if you can't see where it keeps its brain.'

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in a lesson on the limits of Transfiguration, McGonagall described creatures that go in at the back of the neck and wrap themselves round the host's spine. She told the class about the knife that had finally parted one from its host, and the man she would not name who had helped her. Harry realised then what was in the case over her fire. Ron had been in the office that night too, but he had had his mother crying all over him and had never noticed the case.

pages.title: Headmaster's study
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
The Headmaster's study is the room in a top corner of Hogwarts where the head of the school works. It is the same room that is more often called the Headmaster's office, and it has been Albus Dumbledore's for many years.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Fred and George Weasley gave Harry Potter the Marauder's Map in an empty classroom on the third floor. Left alone with it, he watched the tiny labelled dots moving about the parchment. The one called Mrs Norris turned a corner, stopped and went back the way she had come. In a top corner of the castle, in a room marked as the Headmaster's study, the dot labelled Albus Dumbledore was pacing up and down.

pages.title: Madam Hooch's office
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Nine
pages.html:
Madam Hooch, who teaches flying at Hogwarts and referees its Quidditch matches, has an office down by the Quidditch pitch, on the path that runs down from the castle.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in November 1993, Harry Potter was sent to return the tactics slate to Madam Hooch's office, with Dean Thomas for company under Professor McGonagall's rules. On the path down they met the Slytherin team coming up from its own practice. At the back, escorted on either side like visiting royalty, came Dracina Malfoy, with her famous arm in a black silk sling. Harry laughed, and asked her how the arm was.

pages.title: The one-eyed witch passage
aliases: the statue of the hunchbacked witch
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The hump of a statue of a one-eyed witch, third floor, Hogwarts
A trapdoor in the cellar of Honeydukes, Hogsmeade
Fred and George Weasley, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger
pages.html:
The one-eyed witch passage is a secret tunnel from Hogwarts to Hogsmeade. Its entrance is the hump of an old statue of a hunchbacked, one-eyed witch on the third floor of the castle. It comes out under a hidden trapdoor in the cellar of Honeydukes, the sweetshop.

The passage

Tapping the witch's hump with a wand and saying Dissendium opens it. Inside, a smooth stone chute drops into a long earthen tunnel, which ends in more than three hundred steps up to the trapdoor. Coming back, a rap on the inside of the hump with a wand lets you out, and the hump seals itself behind you.

It is one of seven secret passages out of the castle marked on the Marauder's Map. Filch knows four of them. Fred and George Weasley, who had been through this one more times than they had had hot dinners, were fairly sure that nobody else knew about it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, just before Christmas 1993, the Weasley twins popped out from behind the statue and drew Harry into an empty classroom across the corridor, where they gave him the Marauder's Map. Left alone with it, he slipped round behind the witch, read Dissendium off the map, tapped her and watched the hump open.

In Chapter Fourteen, after Sirius Black's second break-in, Filch boarded up everything from cracks in the skirting boards to the smallest mouse holes, but nobody went near the statue. Apart from the twins, the only people in the castle who knew about the passage were Harry, Ron and Hermione. In March 1994 Harry went to Hogsmeade by it under the Invisibility Cloak. Snape had caught him loitering by the statue with Neville that morning, and had run a long pale hand over the witch as though feeling for a seam. She told him nothing, which was exactly what he had expected. Hurrying back that afternoon, Harry stuffed the Cloak into his bag and hid it in a dark corner at the foot of the chute. Afterwards he did not dare go back for it.

In Chapter Sixteen, with Filch going round the dormitories with his sack, Harry dropped the Cloak down the chute to hide it. The next morning Snape was standing in that very corridor, prodding the witch's hump with his wand. After that he seemed to pass along it a dozen times a day, with a sudden passion for statues, and Harry did not dare go near it.

pages.title: Zonko's Joke Shop
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Dungbombs, Stink Pellets, Hiccup Sweets, Frog Spawn Soap, Nose-Biting Teacups
pages.html:
Zonko's Joke Shop is the joke shop in Hogsmeade, which the Weasley twins know very well. It sells Dungbombs, Stink Pellets, Hiccup Sweets, Frog Spawn Soap, Nose-Biting Teacups and a great deal more. On a Hogsmeade weekend it is crammed from wall to wall with Hogwarts students.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, Fred greeted news of the first Hogsmeade weekend with delight, since he was down to his last Stink Pellet. Percy, who thought Hogsmeade overrated, told Harry that Zonko's was frankly a menace.

In Chapter Fourteen, in March 1994, Harry came into the village by the one-eyed witch's passage under the Invisibility Cloak, and went round Zonko's with Ron. The shop was so crowded that Harry had to shuffle round it with his elbows tucked in. He whispered orders into Ron's ear and slipped him Galleons from under the Cloak. They came out with Hiccup Sweets, Dungbombs, Frog Spawn Soap and Nose-Biting Teacups.

Later that day Snape caught Harry with the Zonko's bag and the Marauder's Map. Lupin remarked that the map looked like a Zonko product to him, and at that moment Ron burst in, too out of breath to stand, to say that he had given Harry the stuff, bought in Zonko's ages ago.

pages.title: The Three Broomsticks
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The Three Broomsticks is the inn in Hogsmeade: warm, crowded, smoky and cheerful, with a fire roaring at one end. Madam Rosmerta runs it, and Hogwarts students on their weekends in the village come in out of the cold for her hot Butterbeer. She remembers Sirius Black and James Potter in there as boys, a double act who used to have her in stitches.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, just before Christmas 1993, Harry, Ron and Hermione came in out of the snow. They took a small table at the back, beside a tall Christmas tree with candles burning in it. Then the door opened on Professor McGonagall, with Professor Flitwick, Hagrid and Cornelius Fudge, the Minister for Magic, behind her. Ron and Hermione pushed Harry under the table at once. With a whispered Mobiliarbus, Hermione sent the Christmas tree drifting across in front of it.

Crouched behind its lowest branches, Harry listened while Fudge, Professor McGonagall, Professor Flitwick and Hagrid told Madam Rosmerta the story of Sirius Black. That was how he learnt that Black had been his parents' Secret-Keeper, and his own godfather.

In Chapter Thirteen Harry reminded Hermione of something she had told him there: 'In the Three Broomsticks you said she'd love me the way she'd love a broom she'd set her heart on.' She had meant Dracina Malfoy. Harry had thought Hermione unfair at the time. Now he told her she had only been early.

In Chapter Sixteen he remembered crouching behind the tree while the Minister told Rosmerta and a table full of teachers how worried he was, without doing anything whatever about it. In Chapter Nineteen, once the truth about Black had turned out to be something else again, Harry reflected that he had found out about his godfather from underneath a table. It was not how he would have chosen to find out anything.

pages.title: Hogsmeade post office
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Colour-coded by speed, from Great Greys to Scops owls
pages.html:
The Hogsmeade post office keeps about two hundred owls on its shelves, colour-coded according to how fast a letter needs to go. They run from enormous Great Greys at one end down to tiny Scops owls, which are for local deliveries only.

Description

The owls hoot softly down from their perches. They grow smaller along the shelves, from the Great Greys to middling owls, then to smaller ones still. At the very end is a row of Scops owls under a sign that says Local Deliveries Only. Any one of them would fit in the palm of a hand.

Anybody without an owl of their own may send a letter from here.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, Hermione Granger came back from her first Hogsmeade weekend, at Hallowe'en 1993, still full of it. 'The post office, Harry! There must be two hundred owls, all on shelves, and they're all colour-coded for how fast you want your letter to go...'

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, Harry went in himself on a spring visit to the village, invisible under his Cloak. Ron Weasley spent ages pretending to ask how much it would cost to owl his brother Bill in Egypt, while Harry wandered round looking at the owls.

pages.title: The Hogsmeade quill shop
pages.html:
The Hogsmeade quill shop is a little shop at the end of the village that sells nothing but quills, hundreds of them, eagle, peacock and phoenix. The old wizard who runs it lets customers try every one, and never minds if they buy nothing.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, on Hallowe'en morning in 1993, the day of the first Hogsmeade weekend, Harry Potter had to stay behind at the castle without a signed form. Dracina Malfoy sent Pansy Parkinson and Daphne Greengrass to wait by the door, then stopped to talk to him at the foot of the marble staircase. Uncle Vernon had been going to sign it, Harry told her, until Harry blew up Aunt Marge. Dracina was furious with the Dursleys. Then her face softened, and she told him about the quill shop. 'I thought you'd like that one.' She looked at her gloves. 'I was going to show you. Next time, perhaps.'

Harry answered sourly that next time would be when Sirius Black was caught, in about fifty years, when he would have a beard and need a quill to sign his pension. Dracina giggled before she could stop herself.

pages.title: Tomes and Scrolls
pages.html:
Tomes and Scrolls is a bookshop in Hogsmeade. In 1993 it had in stock a book on Alucard, the dhampir son of Dracula, which Hermione Granger meant to buy there.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Hermione told Harry and Ron about Alucard, the dhampir who hunted his own father. Then she added: 'Tomes and Scrolls have it in, Madam Pince said.' The library's copy had pages missing, and somebody had cut the illustrations out. Hermione meant to buy the book in Hogsmeade instead.

pages.title: The Potters' house
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Godric's Hollow, in the West Country
pages.html:
The Potters' house stood in Godric's Hollow, a village in the West Country, where James and Lily Potter lived in hiding with their baby son, Harry. On 31 October 1981 Lord Voldemort came to it, betrayed to him by their Secret-Keeper. He killed James, then Lily, who begged on her knees for her son, and turned his wand on Harry in his cot. The curse rebounded, and the house was left in ruins.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry thought of Voldemort standing in a bedroom in a village whose name nobody had ever told him, laughing at a girl of twenty-one begging on her knees. Later in the chapter, hidden under a table in the Three Broomsticks, he heard Hagrid tell how he had got Harry out of the ruins, with a great slash across his forehead, while his parents lay dead in the rubble.

pages.title: Galway
infobox: The west coast, on Galway Bay
The birthplace of Angelus, who was sired there in 1753
pages.html:
Galway is a city on the west coast of Ireland, on Galway Bay. Angelus was born there in 1727 as Liam, the son of a linen merchant. He was sired there in 1753.

Liam of Galway

Liam was handsome, idle and nearly always in drink. His father had long since given up hoping for anything better from him. On a night in 1753, after a last quarrel at home, a pale lady from the colonies beckoned him into an alley, and he was never alive again. The lady was Darla.

When Liam came home, he killed the whole household, the servants included, and he saved his father for last. His little sister Kathy had let him in. She had seen her dead brother standing at the window in the moonlight and thought he was an angel, which is where the name Angelus comes from.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter and Ron Weasley the history of Angelus from Blood Nobility: The Great Kindred Lineages. It began in Galway, with the linen merchant's son and the pale lady in the alley.

pages.title: The London convent
infobox: Buffy the Vampire Slayer, 'Lie to Me' (3 November 1997)
The turning of Drusilla by Angelus, about 1860
pages.html:
The London convent is the religious house where, about 1860, Angelus came through the chapel on the day a devout young witch named Drusilla took her holy orders. There he turned her into a vampire. It is one of the places most closely tied to his name.

Drusilla's refuge

Drusilla was a gentle, devout witch with a little of the Sight. Angelus had killed her family one by one, and every door she ran to, he had been through first. The convent was the last of them. She went there to take her holy orders.

On the day she took them he came through the chapel like a wolf through a fold. When nothing of her mind was left but pieces, he turned her, so that she would be mad for ever.

The whole convent

The accounts speak of what Angelus did to the whole convent, not to Drusilla alone. They name it among his worst deeds in London.

In the saga

In September 1992 Hermione Granger began to tell Harry Potter about it and broke off: 'there was a whole convent in-'. In the summer of 1993 Harry remembered reading in her vampire books about what Angelus had done to a whole convent in London.

In October 1993 she sent away for a book on the convent, which came wrapped in brown paper with a Ministry stamp. After reading the story to Ron and Harry, she dreamed about convents all night.

pages.title: Carpathians
infobox: Central and eastern Europe, curving through Romania
The cursing of Angelus by the Kalderash, 1898
pages.html:
The Carpathians are a long range of mountains that curves through central and eastern Europe, much of it through Romania. In 1898 an old Romani clan, the Kalderash, was travelling there when Angelus killed its favourite daughter. The clan's elders cursed him for it.

The curse

The Kalderash were a very old clan, very learned in curse-work. Their elders knew bindings that the Ministry of Magic has never managed to reconstruct. Darla had brought the girl to Angelus as a present, and he killed her. The clan did not hunt him, and they did not stake him. The elders sat down around a fire and cursed him instead.

The curse gave him a soul. It was not his old one, which vampirism had destroyed, but a new one, meant to make him suffer for everything he had done. After a hundred and forty-five years of horrors, Angelus vanished from the world's sight overnight. He was never seen again in his old haunts.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Three, Harry Potter noticed that Hermione Granger's vampire books went on for pages about what Angelus had done in Romania.

In Chapter Nine, on a stormy evening in the autumn of 1993, Hermione read the story to Harry and Ron Weasley from Blood Nobility: The Great Kindred Lineages. She told them how it ended: 'After a century of what he'd done, one girl too many.' The book did not know what the curse had been. Nobody did. Ron's verdict was 'Good for them.'

pages.title: The Siberian village
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 11
Forty miles past the last road, Siberia
Winter of 1966, by Minerva McGonagall and Big Boss
pages.html:
The Siberian village was a settlement of dark wizards that had no business existing, hidden forty miles past the last road in Siberia. For the better part of thirty years the nine men who lived there preyed on the people of the valley below, while the Ministry declined to recognise that the place was there at all. In the winter of 1966 Minerva McGonagall went in after them with a single partner, Big Boss.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, at Christmas dinner in 1993, Professor Flitwick asked McGonagall about a scar on the back of her hand. She answered with Siberia, or with as much of it as she could tell. She had gone with one other, a young man of roughly her own age, whose name she was not permitted to give. There had been nine of them, she said. 'Two is the right number.' The pair waited four days in the snow, and in the end the men came out to them because they were bored.

pages.title: Honeydukes Best
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
About the size of a roof slate
Eight Sickles for the biggest bar
pages.html:
Honeydukes Best is the chocolate sold at Honeydukes, the sweetshop in Hogsmeade. The bars come in several sizes, and the biggest is the size of a roof slate.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, Harry had to stay at the castle at Hallowe'en 1993 while the other third-years went to Hogsmeade. Hermione brought him back the biggest bar of Honeydukes Best the shop had. She had made the man fetch it from the back, Ron reported, because the ones on the front were too small, and it had cost her eight Sickles. Hermione went pink. The chocolate was the size of a roof slate. Harry looked at her; she looked at the fire. 'Thanks, Hermione,' he said.

pages.title: Fizzing Whizbees
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Lift the eater off the floor
pages.html:
Fizzing Whizbees are large sherbet balls sold at Honeydukes in Hogsmeade. Whoever sucks one rises a few inches off the floor while it lasts. The name is sometimes spelt Fizzing Whizzbees.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Fizzing Whizbee was one of the sweets Ambrose Greyhame tried on the gargoyle outside Professor Dumbledore’s office. It was not the password.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry saw them for himself at Honeydukes in December 1993, in a barrel next to one of Every Flavour Beans. Ron had told him about them. ‘Seen the Fizzing Whizbees, Harry?’ he said, taking Harry by the arm to keep him moving round the shop.

pages.title: Toothflossing Stringmints
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Toothflossing Stringmints are splintery mints sold at Honeydukes, the sweetshop in Hogsmeade. They are kept with the odder sweets, on the wall under the sign Special Effects.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, before the Hogsmeade weekend in December 1993, Hermione Granger drew up her Christmas list by the common-room fire. Her parents are dentists. She told her friends: 'I want to get Mum and Dad some of those Toothflossing Stringmints from Honeydukes, they'd be thrilled, they're always saying nobody flosses properly.'

Harry Potter saw them for himself when he reached Honeydukes. The splintery, strange stringmints stood on the Special Effects wall beside Drooble's Best Blowing Gum, Pepper Imps, Ice Mice and exploding bonbons.

pages.title: Cockroach Clusters
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Cockroach Clusters are sweets sold under the Unusual Tastes sign at Honeydukes in Hogsmeade. As far as anybody can tell, they are exactly what they sound like.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Ambrose Greyhame tried the names of sweets on the gargoyle outside Professor Dumbledore’s office. He got as far as Cockroach Cluster before deciding that Albus would never.

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Ron was pushing a jar of them under Hermione’s nose when Harry crept up behind the two of them in Honeydukes. ‘I’m not really into eating clusters of bugs, mate,’ said Harry. Ron very nearly dropped the jar. He clutched his chest with the hand that was not full of cockroaches, apparently in the middle of a heart attack. A little later he wondered aloud whether Fred would eat one if he were told it was a peanut.

pages.title: Acid Pops
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Acid Pops are sweets sold at Honeydukes, the sweetshop in Hogsmeade. They are strong enough to burn straight through a person’s tongue, as Ron Weasley found out at the age of seven.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Ambrose Greyhame stood in front of the stone gargoyle that guards Professor Dumbledore’s office and tried the names of sweets on it, since Albus had a sweet tooth. Acid Pop was one of them. That year the password turned out to be sherbet lemon.

In the Book Three Interlude, in the summer of 1993, John Constantine tried sherbet lemon on the same gargoyle. It did not move. ‘Acid Pop,’ said John. The gargoyle sprang aside.

In Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Ron showed Harry the Acid Pops in Honeydukes. He had good reason to remember them. When he was seven, Fred had given him one and told him it was a Sugar Quill. It went straight through his tongue, and Mrs Weasley went after Fred with her broom. Ron gazed into the Acid Pop box with a brooding look. Then he wondered aloud whether Fred would eat a Cockroach Cluster if he were told it was a peanut.

pages.title: Jelly Slugs
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
In boxes of a hundred and forty-four
pages.html:
Jelly Slugs are sweets sold at Honeydukes, the sweetshop in Hogsmeade. The shop keeps its stock of them down in the cellar, in boxes of a hundred and forty-four.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Harry had just climbed up through the trapdoor into the Honeydukes cellar when a voice at the top of the stairs called down for another box of Jelly Slugs, since the shop was nearly out. Harry hid behind the largest crate. While a large bald man was buried to the shoulders in a box marked SLUGS, JELLY, 144, Harry crept up the stairs into the shop. Upstairs, Ron wanted to know whether he had seen the Jelly Slugs.

pages.title: Peppermint Toads
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Peppermint Toads are peppermint creams in the shape of toads, sold at Honeydukes in Hogsmeade. Once swallowed, they hop about in the stomach, very convincingly.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry saw them at Honeydukes on the shelf of odd sweets: peppermint creams in the shape of toads, which were supposed to hop in the stomach. By the look of the queue for them, they did.

In Chapter Eleven, on the last morning of term, Ron Weasley sat in the emptied common room eating a Peppermint Toad with one hand pressed to his stomach.

In Chapter Thirteen, at the Gryffindor victory party in the common room, George Weasley pelted the crowd with Peppermint Toads. His twin, Fred, was found trying to feed one to the portrait of a sleeping knight.

pages.title: Ice Mice
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Makes the eater's teeth chatter and squeak
pages.html:
Ice Mice are sweets sold at Honeydukes, the sweetshop in Hogsmeade. They make the eater's teeth chatter and squeak.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry saw them in December 1993, on his first visit to Honeydukes. They were on the wall under the sign that said Special Effects, among the odder sweets, near the Pepper Imps that let you breathe fire for your friends. Their label made a simple promise: hear your teeth chatter and squeak.

pages.title: Drooble's Best Blowing Gum
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
On the Hogwarts Express; at Honeydukes
pages.html:
Drooble's Best Blowing Gum is a wizarding bubble gum. Its bubbles are the colour of bluebells. They fill a room and stay up for days.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, it was among the sweets on the Hogwarts Express trolley when Harry bought some of everything. In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, he found it again at Honeydukes, on the wall of special effects, beside Toothflossing Stringmints, Pepper Imps and Ice Mice.

pages.title: Every Flavour Beans
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
Every Flavour Beans is the everyday name for Bertie Bott's Every-Flavour Beans, the jelly beans that come in every flavour there is, the pleasant ones and the dreadful ones alike. Honeydukes in Hogsmeade sells them by the barrel.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, when Harry first saw inside Honeydukes in December 1993, there was a barrel of Every Flavour Beans big enough to bathe in. Beside it stood another, full of Fizzing Whizbees.

pages.title: Blood lollipops
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Blood lollipops are the red lollipops sold under the Unusual Tastes sign at Honeydukes in Hogsmeade. Hermione Granger supposes that they are meant for vampires, and cannot see the point of them.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Harry came up into Honeydukes through the cellar. He found Ron and Hermione in the far corner of the shop, bent over a tray of red lollipops. Hermione was quite sure Harry would not want one. ‘Vampires can only consume real blood anyway,’ she said, as firmly as if she were correcting the shop. Ron pushed a jar of Cockroach Clusters under her nose instead.

pages.title: Stink Pellets
pages.html:
Stink Pellets are small pellets that let off a truly dreadful smell, sold at Zonko's Joke Shop in Hogsmeade. They are a favourite with anybody who wants a corridor cleared in a hurry, and the Weasley twins are among Zonko's most faithful customers.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, when the first Hogsmeade visit was announced for Hallowe'en 1993, Fred Weasley was delighted. 'Zonko's. I'm right down to my last Stink Pellet.'

On the day itself, with the others gone, Harry ran into Filch, who wanted to know why he was not down in the village buying Belch Powder, Stink Pellets and Whizzing Worms. 'I'm a bit skint, Filch. And I'd only get the premium Stink Pellets anyway if I had some Galleons.'

pages.title: Dungbombs
pages.html:
Dungbombs are stink bombs sold at Zonko's Joke Shop in Hogsmeade. One is enough to clear a corridor. Argus Filch, the caretaker, takes every one of them personally.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Fred and George told Harry how they had come by the Marauder’s Map in their first year. Filch had dragged them off to his office over a Dungbomb in a corridor. While he was ranting, they noticed a drawer in his filing cabinet labelled Confiscated and Highly Dangerous. George dropped another Dungbomb as a diversion, and Fred had the drawer open in a second.

In Chapter Eleven, at the end of the autumn term in December 1993, the twins let off half a dozen in the Gryffindor common room in the space of an hour, by way of celebration. First-years hung out of the windows, gulping the winter air.

In Chapter Fourteen Harry, hidden under the Invisibility Cloak, went round Zonko’s whispering orders to Ron and slipping him Galleons. Their pockets came out stuffed with Dungbombs, Hiccup Sweets and a good deal more. In Chapter Sixteen, on the Saturday after the Quidditch final, somebody let off a whole crate of them outside the Slytherin common room.

pages.title: Belch Powder
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Belch Powder is a joke powder that sets whoever swallows it belching. Hogwarts students buy it in Hogsmeade, which is reason enough for Argus Filch, the caretaker, to disapprove of it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, on Halloween 1993, the day of the first Hogsmeade visit, Filch caught Harry wandering the castle on his own. He wanted to know why Harry was not down in the village with the rest of his horrible little friends, buying Belch Powder, Stink Pellets and Whizzing Worms. Harry told him he was a bit skint.

pages.title: Whizzing Worms
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Whizzing Worms are a joke article sold in Hogsmeade. Argus Filch counts them, with Belch Powder and Stink Pellets, among the rubbish that Hogwarts students carry back from the village.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, on Hallowe'en 1993, the day of the third years' first visit to Hogsmeade, Filch found Harry Potter skulking about the castle on his own. He demanded to know why Harry was not down in the village with the rest of his horrible little friends, buying Belch Powder, Stink Pellets and Whizzing Worms. Harry, who had no signed form, told him he was a bit skint. Filch sent him back to his common room.

pages.title: Gillywater
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Gillywater is a wizarding drink served at the Three Broomsticks in Hogsmeade. Professor McGonagall takes hers small.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Professor McGonagall came into the Three Broomsticks with Professor Flitwick, Hagrid and the Minister for Magic, Cornelius Fudge. When Madam Rosmerta brought their drinks over, the first thing on her tray was a small gillywater. ‘That’s mine,’ said Professor McGonagall. Harry heard every word from the floor under his own table, where Ron and Hermione had pushed him, hidden behind the Christmas tree that Hermione had charmed across in front of it.

pages.title: Mulled mead
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Mulled mead is mead, the old honey wine, served hot with spices. Madam Rosmerta serves it by the pint at the Three Broomsticks in Hogsmeade.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Rubeus Hagrid ordered four pints of it at the Three Broomsticks, all of them for himself. He was at the next table to Harry's with Professor McGonagall, Professor Flitwick and Cornelius Fudge, the Minister for Magic. Harry, who had come to Hogsmeade without permission, was crouched on the floor behind a Christmas tree that Hermione had just moved in front of their table with a charm. 'Ta, Rosmerta,' said Hagrid, when the mead came.

pages.title: Cherry syrup and soda
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Cherry syrup and soda is a cold drink served at the Three Broomsticks in Hogsmeade. It comes iced, with a little umbrella in it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Professor Flitwick came into the Three Broomsticks with Professor McGonagall, Hagrid and the Minister for Magic. When Madam Rosmerta brought round her tray, the cherry syrup and soda, iced, with the umbrella, was his. He gave a little smack of the lips over it. Harry, hiding on the floor behind the Christmas tree, could hear it perfectly well.

pages.title: Redcurrant rum
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Redcurrant rum is a drink served at the Three Broomsticks in Hogsmeade, and the one that Cornelius Fudge, the Minister for Magic, takes there.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, on the last weekend of term in December 1993, Madam Rosmerta brought Fudge his redcurrant rum at the Three Broomsticks. It came on the same tray as Professor McGonagall's small gillywater and Hagrid's four pints of mulled mead. Professor Flitwick had a cherry syrup and soda, iced, with the umbrella. Over their drinks the talk turned to Sirius Black, while Harry crouched unseen behind a Christmas tree a few feet away.

pages.title: Boggart-Banishing Spell
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The Boggart-Banishing Spell, cast with the incantation Riddikulus, is the charm against a boggart. A boggart takes the shape of whatever its watcher fears most. The caster must picture that fear made ridiculous while saying the word, and laughter does the rest.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, in September 1993, Professor Lupin took his third-years to the staffroom, where a boggart had settled in the old wardrobe. He had them practise the word without wands first. Neville Longbottom went first. The boggart became Professor Snape. Neville put him into his grandmother's clothes: the vulture hat, the green dress and the great red handbag. Parvati, Seamus and Dean followed him.

For Dracina Malfoy the boggart became her father. He sighed at her, and told her quietly that she was not a real Malfoy, until she began to cry. Then she stopped crying, told it she was sick to death of it and cast the spell with a crack like a shot. The boggart Lucius was suddenly wearing an ancient army greatcoat with string for buttons, a woolly hat with a hole in it and two odd wellingtons. He opened his mouth to say something devastating. What came out was a long, loud hiccup.

Then Ron took the legs off his spider, which went bowling over and over across the floor. When it rolled up to Harry, Lupin stepped in front of him, and Neville finished the boggart off with a second Riddikulus. Only Harry saw its smoke creep back under the wardrobe door. It came out again as a werewolf soaked in blood, and Lupin dealt with it himself, quite quietly. The great grey legs shrank to two furry stumps. The creature toppled on to its chin, and Dean shouted 'Midget wolf!'

In Chapter Twelve, at one of Harry's Patronus lessons, Lupin used Riddikulus to drive the boggart back into its case. In Chapter Sixteen, in his examination in June 1994, Harry used it himself. At the end of Lupin's obstacle course the boggart in the trunk became a dementor. Harry thought of Oliver Wood sobbing into his shoulder after the Quidditch final. 'Riddikulus!' The dementor was suddenly wearing Wood's soaking Quidditch robes, about four sizes too small. It tripped over the hem and fell flat on its hood.

'Excellent, Harry,' Lupin murmured. 'Full marks.'

pages.title: Waddiwasi
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Shoots a small, loose object hard at a target
pages.html:
Waddiwasi shoots a small, loose object, such as a wad of chewing gum, out of wherever it is lodged and sends it flying hard at a target. It is a small, neat piece of magic, and in the right hands a very precise one.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, in September 1993, Remus Lupin was taking his third-years to their first practical lesson when they came upon Peeves. The poltergeist was hanging upside down outside a broom cupboard, stuffing the keyhole with chewing gum. Lupin lifted his wand to the height of his shoulder. 'Waddiwasi!' The wad of gum came out of the keyhole like a cork out of a bottle and went with horrible accuracy straight up Peeves's left nostril.

Peeves spun upright, howling, and shot off down the corridor in a cloud of curses. As he went, he tore a brooch off his bow tie and flung it hard over his shoulder. It was Dracina Malfoy's silver serpent brooch with the emerald eyes, which he had been showing off to her a moment before. It sailed the length of the corridor and landed with a plop in the fire bucket by the far window.

pages.title: Impervius
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Impervius makes whatever it is cast on repel water, so that rain runs straight off it. Among Quidditch players, at least, its most valued use is on a pair of glasses.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Gryffindor played Hufflepuff in November 1993 in what was very nearly a hurricane. Harry Potter could hardly see through his streaming glasses. When Oliver Wood called time out, Harry dropped into the huddle of the team, under Professor Flitwick's umbrella charms, and found Hermione Granger there uninvited, already reaching for his face. She tapped his glasses with her wand. 'Impervius!' The rain still hit the lenses, but now it ran off them like water off a duck.

That night, lying in the hospital wing after the lost match, Harry let the weekend file past him one thing at a time. Hermione's Impervius was one of them.

pages.title: Mobiliarbus
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Lifts a tree and moves it
pages.html:
Mobiliarbus lifts a tree a few inches off the ground and moves it wherever the caster wants it. It is the sort of charm nobody expects to need until the day they suddenly do.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Harry Potter was in the Three Broomsticks in Hogsmeade, where he had no permission to be. Then Cornelius Fudge walked in with Professor McGonagall, Professor Flitwick and Hagrid. Ron and Hermione pushed Harry under the table. 'Mobiliarbus!' Hermione whispered.

The pub's Christmas tree rose a few inches with a creak, drifted across the floorboards like a thing on castors and came down directly in front of their table. From behind its lowest branches, with pine needles in his face, Harry heard everything the grown-ups said about Sirius Black.

pages.title: Dissendium
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The hump of the one-eyed witch, third floor
pages.html:
Dissendium is the word that opens the hump of the statue of the one-eyed witch on the third floor at Hogwarts. Tap the witch with a wand, say the word, and the hump splits open on a secret passage that runs all the way to the cellar of Honeydukes in Hogsmeade.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Harry Potter stood behind the one-eyed witch with the Marauder's Map. He tapped the statue, and nothing happened. Then a tiny speech bubble came out of the mouth of the ink Harry on the map, with a single word in it. 'Dissendium,' Harry read under his breath, and tapped the witch again. The hump split along the top without a sound, the way a mouth opens. It swung wide on a dark hole just big enough to take somebody who had not had much to eat lately.

In Chapter Fourteen, on a Hogsmeade Saturday in 1994, Harry muttered 'Dissendium!' and shoved his bag into the opening hump. Neville Longbottom came round the corner before he could climb in after it.

In Chapter Sixteen, in June 1994, Harry told Hermione the word so that she could fetch his Invisibility Cloak, which he had dropped down the chute under the witch. She was back with it in fifteen minutes.

pages.title: Fidelius Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Hides a secret inside a living person, the Secret-Keeper
Only the Secret-Keeper, by choosing to tell
pages.html:
The Fidelius Charm hides a secret inside a single living person, who is called the Secret-Keeper. From then on nobody can find it, unless the Keeper chooses to give it up. The charm is only as safe as its Keeper. Its most famous use, and its most famous failure, was the hiding of the Potters in 1981.

The Potters

In 1981 one of Albus Dumbledore's spies learnt that Lord Voldemort was hunting the Potters. Dumbledore warned them to go into hiding, and told them their best hope was the Fidelius Charm. He was sure that somebody close to them was passing word to Voldemort, so he offered to be their Secret-Keeper himself. James Potter insisted on Sirius Black instead. Everybody came to believe that Black was the Keeper. In fact, at the last moment, Black had persuaded Lily and James to change to Peter Pettigrew, as a bluff: Voldemort would never dream that they would trust anybody so weak. Pettigrew gave the secret to Voldemort.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Harry Potter was hiding under a table in the Three Broomsticks when Professor Flitwick explained the charm to Madam Rosmerta. It was 'an immensely complex piece of magic', he said. So long as the Keeper held his tongue, Voldemort could have pressed his nose to the Potters' sitting-room window and seen nothing but curtains. In Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Harry learnt from Black himself that Pettigrew had been the Secret-Keeper all along.

pages.title: Fire-Making Charm
infobox: Lights a fire from the wand, with no match needed
Remus Lupin, as a defence against vampires (1993)
pages.html:
The Fire-Making Charm lights a fire from the end of a wand, with no match, flint or tinder needed. It is a homely piece of magic, good for kindling a hearth. Remus Lupin taught it to his third-years for a less homely reason.

Against vampires

Fire is one of the very few things a vampire truly fears. Flame does Kindred flesh far more harm than any blade, and the sight of it close by can throw the Beast inside a vampire into a blind panic.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1993, Lupin gave the second half of his lesson on vampires to practical defences. The first was a Fire-Making Charm that could be done without a match, so that nobody in the class would ever be caught without fire in the dark. The second was a charm for making a patch of sunlight.

pages.title: Sunlight charm
infobox: Makes a weak, brief patch of real sunlight
pages.html:
The sunlight charm makes a patch of real sunlight at the end of a wand. The patch is weak and brief. It is genuine sunlight all the same, enough to make most vampires flinch, and that flinch buys a second. A second is sometimes enough.

Why it works

God's curse on Cain set the sun against him and every vampire descended from him. Even a little sunlight hurts, so the Beast inside a vampire shies away from it by instinct.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1993, Remus Lupin taught it to his third-years in a lesson on vampire defences, along with a Fire-Making Charm. He said that it would make most of them flinch. That bought a second, and a second was sometimes enough. 'Right. Homework. A foot on vampire defences, and I want the sunlight charm practised. Off you go.'

pages.title: Warming Charm
infobox: Warms food, drink or a person
pages.html:
A Warming Charm heats whatever it is cast on, gently and evenly: a drink, a dish, a pair of cold hands. It is the kind of small domestic magic that makes a winter in a draughty castle bearable.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in December 1993, Hermione Granger began coming down to the Quidditch pitch to watch Harry Potter's practices, sitting in the top row of the stand beside Ron in the sleet. On the third night she brought a flask. She held it out to Harry at the top of the stand as he came off: something hot and sweet, with ginger in it, which she had made herself in the common room with a Warming Charm. She watched him drink it with her arms folded. She said nothing about its being for him in particular.

pages.title: Patronus Charm
infobox: Expecto Patronum; Expecto patronum; Patronus; Prongs (Harry's Patronus)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Conjures a guardian that stands between the caster and a dementor
A single, very happy memory, and a good soul
God, the caster's soul and the light of Heaven
pages.html:
The Patronus Charm conjures a guardian, different for every caster, that stands between him and a dementor. It is among the oldest spells there are and the plainest example of light magic. It is also the only spell with no dark version, because the caster does not make its light. He lets it through him: the charm draws on God, Who meets the caster's soul in a happy memory.

What it is

Remus Lupin calls the Patronus 'a sort of anti-dementor', a shield made 'of everything the dementor isn't'. It does not hurt, and it does not hold. It simply stands in front. Whatever it does to the things it faces, it does by being what it is, 'as a lamp doesn't fight the dark'. The incantation is Expecto patronum, and the charm works only if the caster concentrates with all his might on a single, very happy memory.

Most magic draws on what a wizard can do. A few spells draw on what he is, and those run in both directions. An Unforgivable Curse takes something out of the caster's soul and never gives it back. The Patronus runs the other way, on light magic alone: something that comes from God meets something in the caster's own soul. The meeting place is a happy memory, because that is the only thing most people own that both of them have touched. Only a good soul can cast it, one with something in it worth guarding.

The charm has three parts: God, the caster's soul and the light of Heaven itself. Each Patronus is a small, licensed piece of that light, admitted through a soul that consents to carry it. That is why the charm cannot be forced. It will not serve a man with nothing worth guarding, and there is no dark version of it. People have tried to make one, and it simply will not go. Every old account, from every country and every century, says the same thing: the caster 'does not make the light; he agrees to it'.

History

Versions of the charm are carved into things older than the Statute of Secrecy, older even than Hogwarts. It was being cast long before anybody in Britain thought of putting magic into a stick. Wizards still argue about who invented it. Lupin's opinion is that nobody did: 'It was found. The way water is found. By somebody who was thirsty.'

The truth is that it was given. It was among the first spells Gandalf taught the earliest wizards of men, after the ice went back, as a defence against Morgoth. The hands that passed it down from there have long been forgotten. The Fat Friar learnt it as a boy at the young Hogwarts, where it was used against all sorts of nasty things. It is also the only known defence against the Lethifold.

Severus Snape holds that all the really old spells are dark, and Lupin concedes that most of them are. The Patronus, in Lupin's words, is 'the exception so completely that it is nearly the proof of the rule'.

Mist and shape

A weak Patronus is a mist, or a shapeless silver shield. A true one takes a solid shape, usually an animal's, and the shape belongs to the caster alone.

On 1 September 1993 Lupin drove a dementor off the Hogwarts Express with a silver defence. At the Hufflepuff match that November, Albus Dumbledore threw an enormous silver Patronus across the flooded pitch and drove more than a hundred dementors off it. On the night of the lake in June 1994 the teachers cleared the frenzied dementors from the grounds with Patronuses of their own, among them a silver cat and something large with wings. They drove the dementors back. They did not hurt them.

Harry Potter's Patronus

Lupin began teaching Harry the charm in January 1994, at eight o'clock on Thursday evenings in the History of Magic classroom, against a boggart that turned into a dementor. Harry's first memory was of his first flight on a broomstick. He collapsed twice. The first time he heard his mother die. The second time he heard his father as well, which had never happened before. All he could produce was a large, shapeless silver mass, like a lantern in a cloud, which would not move forward. After a dream of revenge on the Dursleys, he was privately doubting whether he was good enough to cast it at all.

At the Ravenclaw match in early March 1994, three hooded figures rose up below him just as he reached for the Snitch. He cast without a moment's hesitation. The Patronus came out of him huge, shining, solid and silver-white, streaking downwards with a sound like a struck bell. The three figures turned out to be four people in a set of rigged robes: Crabbe, Goyle, Marcus Flint and, perched on Goyle's shoulders, Dracina Malfoy. Lupin, who had seen its shape, would say only 'Bright'. On the stairs afterwards he told Harry that what he had shown was not the absence of fear, 'because the absence of fear is not available to anybody'.

By the next Thursday the Patronus was too bright to look at, and the boggart backed away from it. Lupin explained why: 'The first time a thing is done, it is done against the whole weight of never having done it before. After that, you are only remembering.'

In June 1994, by the lake, about a hundred dementors closed in on Harry, Sirius Black and Hermione Granger. Harry's faith failed, and his Patronus failed with it. Sent back three hours by Hermione's Time-Turner, he watched the same scene from the far shore. He understood then that the rescuer he had glimpsed across the water was himself. He held on to the memory of an afternoon in January: throwing stones across the frozen lake with Dracina, then four quiet minutes in which neither of them said anything at all. It was the happiest thing he owned. He said 'Deliver us from evil', and cast.

A shining stag went out over the water as though the lake were a floor. Wherever it struck them, the dementors shrieked and came apart into smoke. No wizard's spell had ever killed a dementor before. The survivors fled, and afterwards they kept well away from him. The stag came back across the water, bowed its antlered head and was gone. 'Prongs,' Harry whispered. It was his father's Animagus shape.

Lupin had always taught that a Patronus never hurts anything. It was the Fat Friar who explained the difference. Harry, he said, had touched God. He had stopped doubting and let Him come through into the spell: 'I don't suppose a Patronus has ever been asked to carry anything like it before'.

pages.title: Umbrella charms
infobox: Raises a hovering canopy that keeps off the rain
pages.html:
An umbrella charm raises a hovering canopy that keeps the rain off whoever is underneath it. It is a weather charm of the plainest and most useful kind. A skilled caster can shelter a whole bench of people with a few of them.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Gryffindor played Hufflepuff in November 1993 in what was very nearly a hurricane. The wind took the umbrellas of the crowd one by one and sent them bowling towards the Forest. When Oliver Wood called time out, Professor Flitwick sent umbrella charms up over both team benches. The Gryffindor team huddled beneath them, which is where Hermione Granger found Harry Potter and charmed his glasses with Impervius.

pages.title: Muggle-Repelling Charms
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Turn Muggles away from a place without their knowing why
Diagon Alley, Hogwarts and every wizarding house in Britain
The Camarilla, under the agreement of 1900
pages.html:
Muggle-Repelling Charms keep Muggles away from places they are not meant to find. A Muggle who comes near one suddenly remembers an urgent appointment, and never wonders why. Together with the other concealment wards, they hide Diagon Alley, Hogwarts and every wizarding house in Britain.

The Camarilla's loan

Since 1900 these charms have served the vampires too. In that year the Camarilla came to an agreement with the wizarding governments of the world, the British Ministry of Magic among them. The wizards would lend their wards, their Muggle-Repelling Charms and their other concealment spells to help keep the Masquerade. In return, no vampire who answers to the Camarilla would ever hunt, harm or feed on a witch or wizard.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, in the autumn of 1993, Remus Lupin explained the arrangement to his third-years in a lesson on vampires. He said it had been made about ninety years before. It was an old agreement, and a fragile one. It had held, more or less, for most of the century, because both sides had more to lose than to gain by breaking it.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, on 22 August 1994, Arthur Weasley told Harry Potter that every inch of the World Cup stadium was protected by Muggle-Repelling Charms. All year, whenever Muggles came anywhere near it, they had suddenly remembered urgent appointments and dashed away again. 'Bless them,' he added fondly.

pages.title: Shrinking Solution
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Shrinks a living creature; a toad becomes a tadpole
Daisy roots, caterpillars, one rat spleen, a dash of leech juice
pages.html:
A Shrinking Solution makes a living creature smaller, so that a few drops will turn a toad back into a tadpole. Made properly, it is a clear, sharp, rather poisonous-looking green. Professor Snape teaches it at Hogwarts, where his second-years write essays on it and his third-years brew it.

Brewing

It takes chopped daisy roots, sliced caterpillars and a single rat spleen, with the leech juice added by the drop. The quantities matter a great deal. One rat spleen too many, with a flood of leech juice where a dash was wanted, will turn it orange. An antidote turns a shrunken creature back to its proper size.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, in the autumn of 1993, Snape set the third-years to brew it. Dracina Malfoy, with her arm in a silk sling, said she could not manage her daisy roots one-handed, and looked meaningfully at Harry. He ended up making two potions at once, slicing her caterpillars as well as his own. She told him afterwards that he had done them beautifully.

Neville Longbottom's potion was not green at all. Snape held up a ladleful for the class to see. 'Orange, Longbottom. Remarkable.' He announced that at the end of the lesson he would give a little to Neville's toad, Trevor. With Hermione Granger whispering to him, Neville put it right, and it turned a sharp, clear green. Snape tipped a few drops down Trevor's throat. There was a small pop, and a fat tadpole lay wriggling in his palm.

Snape turned the tadpole back into Trevor with a drop from a little bottle in his pocket. Then he took five points from Gryffindor, because Hermione had been told not to help. Ron was still boiling about it on the dungeon steps. 'Five points because the potion worked!'

In Chapter Fourteen Snape sat in his office in a filthy temper, working through a pile of second-year essays on Shrinking Solutions. He was writing remarks in the margins that would reduce several of their authors to tears when Dracina burst in without knocking.

pages.title: Wit-Sharpening Potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Crocodile hearts, armadillo bile, ground scarab
pages.html:
The Wit-Sharpening Potion sharpens the mind of whoever drinks it. It uses crocodile hearts, armadillo bile and ground scarab, together with a great deal of stirring. Third-years at Hogwarts brew it with Professor Snape.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in November 1993, Snape put the third-years on to the potion in a dungeon so cold that the cauldrons seemed to steam harder just to keep warm. He never once mentioned the essay on werewolves he had set them, and nobody was fool enough to remind him.

Harry had been at his cauldron for ten minutes when three Slytherins pulled up their hoods and began to drift between the cauldrons, imitating the dementors that had come on to the pitch at the Hufflepuff match. One of them glided down the aisle to Ron, bent over him with a long, rattling breath, then did Harry's fall.

pages.title: Lupin's potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Lupin's potion is the Wolfsbane Potion, which Severus Snape brewed for Remus Lupin through the school year of 1993 to 1994 and brought to him in a smoking goblet. It holds down a Garou's war form. Few wizards can make it, and sugar stops it working.

The potion

Even so, it only just holds the war form down, and never completely. Lupin finds Hogwarts hard even with it, since the castle is steeped in dark magic as well as light, and his kind are very sensitive to such things. To Lupin, Snape's Dark Mark reeks of the Wyrm. Without the potion Snape brews him, he could hardly bear to be in the same room as Snape at all.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, Harry was in Lupin's office when Snape came in carrying a goblet with a thin trail of smoke coming off it. 'Professor Snape has very kindly made up a potion for me,' Lupin said. 'I've never been much of a hand at potions, and this one's particularly fiddly.' He sniffed it. 'Pity you can't put sugar in it,' he added. 'Sugar stops it working.' He took a mouthful and shuddered all over. He had been a bit under the weather, he explained, and this was the only thing that helped: 'I'm very lucky to be working with Professor Snape; there aren't many wizards who could brew it.' As he drank again, Harry had a sudden, mad urge to knock the goblet out of his hand.

In Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Lupin told Harry, Ron and Hermione that before the Wolfsbane Potion was discovered he had been at risk of transforming the moment he sensed anything that smelt of the Wyrm. In Chapter Nineteen Hermione realised with horror that he had not taken it that night. Snape had carried it to his office, and Lupin had not been there. 'It's the only thing that holds it down, he told us himself!'

pages.title: Blood Nobility: The Great Kindred Lineages
infobox: Behind Madam Pince's desk; it must be signed for
pages.html:
Blood Nobility: The Great Kindred Lineages is a serious history of the great vampire bloodlines. The Hogwarts library keeps it behind Madam Pince's desk, and a pupil has to sign for it. It gives Angelus a whole chapter, with a footnote saying that none of his kind was ever crueller.

Contents

Every vampire is descended from Cain, sire by sire. The book follows the great lines of that descent, the Kindred lineages of its title. Its chapter on Angelus, the Scourge of Europe, covers the whole hundred and forty-five years of his career as a vampire. The engraving of him that Hermione Granger keeps folded in her bag comes from this book.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, on a stormy evening in November 1993, Ron Weasley asked Hermione to tell them about Angelus, since she had obviously looked him up. It was not a picture, she said with dignity, it was an engraving, from a serious book. Madam Pince kept it behind the desk, and you had to sign for it. 'And he's not one of the famous ones, Ronald, he's the famous one. There's a whole chapter.'

They had called him the Scourge of Europe, she told them. In a hundred and forty-five years, the book said, nobody of his kind had ever been crueller. It said so in a footnote, as though it were agreed.

pages.title: Which Broomstick
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Which Broomstick is a wizarding magazine about racing brooms, with reviews of the latest makes and an order form at the back. In the winter of 1993 to 1994 it carried the news that the Firebolt would be the broom of choice for the national teams at the 1994 World Championship.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry Potter sat by the common-room fire with a copy he had borrowed from Oliver Wood, reading up on makes. He had been flying an ancient school Shooting Star at practice for a month. It pulled to the left. He read about the cheap Cleansweep Seven and the dearer Comet Two Sixty. The whole Slytherin team rode the Nimbus Two Thousand and One, on Lucius Malfoy's money. On the last page was a full-colour picture of the Firebolt, which he had stood in front of day after day in Diagon Alley.

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Wood told Harry it was time he ordered a new broom. There was an order form at the back of Which Broomstick, he said. Harry could get a Nimbus Two Thousand and One, like Malfoy's. Harry said flatly that he was not buying anything Malfoy thought was good.

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, when Harry flew the Firebolt in the match against Ravenclaw, Lee Jordan's commentary quoted the magazine: the Firebolt was going to be the broom of choice for the national teams at that year's World Championship. Professor McGonagall asked him to tell them what was going on in the match.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, at the World Cup campsite, Perkins from Arthur Weasley's office had left an old copy of Which Broomstick in the tent he lent the Weasleys. Hermione Granger sat very close beside Harry Potter all through the afternoon of 22 August 1994, reading it. Later she stopped turning the pages to watch Ron over the top of it with narrowed eyes.

pages.title: The Belmont chronicles
infobox: The Belmont family and its war with Dracula
That Trevor Belmont was Alucard's son by Sonia Belmont
pages.html:
The Belmont chronicles are writings on the Belmont family, the vampire hunters who have fought Dracula since 1094. Among much else, they hold that Trevor Belmont was the son of Alucard, Dracula's own son, by Sonia Belmont. Hermione Granger had read them by December 1993.

Subject

The chronicles concern the Belmont family, who have hunted Dracula since Leon Belmont swore his oath in 1094. They follow the line from Leon through Sonia, Trevor, Christopher, Simon, Juste and Richter to Julius. Each of them took the Vampire Killer up the mountain when Dracula returned. Who compiled the chronicles, and how they reached the wizarding world, is not recorded.

Trevor's father

The best-known claim in the chronicles concerns Trevor, the son Sonia Belmont bore soon after she destroyed Dracula in 1450. They hold that his father was Alucard, the dhampir son of Dracula, whom Sonia loved. Trevor himself was a mortal man all the same, as every Belmont after him has been.

If the chronicles are right, every Belmont since Trevor descends from Dracula. The family has spent five centuries hunting its own forefather with a whip.

In the saga

In December 1993 Harry Potter reflected that Hermione Granger had read everything there was on the Scourge of Europe, down to the footnotes. She had read the Belmont chronicles too. A year before, in September 1992, she had told him about the family and their whip, from Gilderoy Lockhart's Voyages with Vampires. She put their hunt at about four hundred years. The family's war is longer than that: it has fought Dracula for more than five hundred years under that name, and for nine hundred since Leon.

pages.title: The book on Alucard
infobox: Hogwarts library (damaged); Tomes and Scrolls, Hogsmeade
pages.html:
The book on Alucard is a history of Dracula's dhampir son. Hermione Granger meant to buy a copy at Tomes and Scrolls in Hogsmeade at Christmas 1993, because the one in the Hogwarts library had pages missing and its illustrations cut out.

Description

The book tells the story of Alucard, a dhampir, half vampire and half not, who hunted his own father, Dracula. It is a long story. Alucard loved Sonia Belmont in 1450 and fought beside Trevor Belmont in 1476. In 1797 he destroyed Dracula himself.

The Hogwarts library has a copy, but somebody has cut the illustrations out of it, and pages are missing. Madam Pince told Hermione that Tomes and Scrolls, the bookshop in Hogsmeade, had it in stock. Its title is not recorded.

In the saga

In December 1993 Hermione Granger sat by the Gryffindor fire with Crookshanks on her knee, ticking off her list for the Christmas visit to Hogsmeade. She told Harry Potter and Ron Weasley that she meant to buy Toothflossing Stringmints from Honeydukes for her parents. For herself she wanted the book on Alucard. When Ron said 'The who?', she told him: 'Alucard. He was a dhampir, half one of them, half not. He hunted his own father, which is quite a story, Ron, honestly, if you'd read anything.'

Her eyes went bright when she mentioned the missing illustrations. Ron, once she had paused for breath, announced that he was going to go and be sick with excitement in the dormitory.

pages.title: The book on the London convent
infobox: The London convent where Angelus turned Drusilla
Wrapped in brown paper, with a Ministry stamp
pages.html:
The book on the London convent is a work about the religious house in London where Angelus turned Drusilla, about 1860. Hermione Granger sent away for it in October 1993. It arrived wrapped in brown paper with a Ministry of Magic stamp on it.

Description

The book concerns the convent whose chapel Angelus came through on the day a devout young witch with the Sight took her holy orders, and what he did there. He had already killed her family one by one, for sport, and she had fled to the convent to escape him. Nor was she his only victim that day. The accounts speak of what he did to the whole convent, and count it among his worst deeds in London.

It is not a book to be had in Hogsmeade. Hermione had to send away for it, and it came wrapped in brown paper with a Ministry stamp on it. Its title is not recorded.

In the saga

By December 1993 the book had arrived. Harry Potter counted it among the signs of Hermione's steady, unsmiling hunger to know exactly what the famous vampires had done, in what order and to whom. He thought it had nothing to do with the Angelus engraving she still kept folded in her bag. It had everything to do with something colder: the way a person studies the habits of a thing she has privately decided to go and kill one day.

pages.title: The Defence Against the Dark Arts textbook
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Written for the Ministry, and wrong
pages.html:
The Defence Against the Dark Arts textbook set for Hogwarts third-years in 1993 deals with werewolves in its final chapter, from page 394. Professor Snape, who taught that chapter early, told the class that the book was written for the Ministry, and that nearly all of it was wrong.

What it says

According to the textbook, a werewolf can be told from a true wolf by its snout, its pupils and its tufted tail. A bitten man, it says, turns at the full moon and loses his reason for that one night. For the rest of the month he is a wretch to be pitied, registered and found employment.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Snape took Remus Lupin's class in November 1993 and told the third-years to open their books at the final chapter. Hermione Granger protested that they were due to start hinkypunks. 'I was not aware,' said Snape icily, 'that Miss Granger had been appointed to the staff. Page three hundred and ninety-four.' There was a sullen rustle of pages. He told them: 'The textbook is written for the Ministry, and the Ministry classifies what it can bear to think about.' Then he taught them about the Garou.

pages.title: Gryffindor's badger chant
infobox: One Dean swore all Muggle Britain knew
pages.html:
Gryffindor's badger chant was the song Dean Thomas taught the Gryffindor end for the match against Hufflepuff in November 1993. It was about badgers digging their burrows, to a tune Dean swore blind everybody in Muggle Britain knew. Hufflepuff sang back, louder.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Dean spent the whole of Friday evening drilling the lower years in the common room, conducting with a rolled-up essay. Where he came from, he told a baffled pure-blood audience, this was simply how support was done. Next day the whole scarlet end of the stadium swayed in the storm, roaring it in time: 'Oh the badgers dig their burrows nice and deep...' It went round twice more, with stamping.

Then Hufflepuff, the house that apologised when you trod on it, answered to the same tune, five hundred voices strong: 'We don't care about your lions or your cups...' It finished by calling the Gryffindors a bunch of hairy gits. Fred and George Weasley turned as one man to bow to the Hufflepuff stand, hands on hearts. The whole stadium laughed.

pages.title: Hufflepuff's reply chant
pages.html:
Hufflepuff's reply chant is the answer the Hufflepuff end of the Quidditch stadium sang back at Gryffindor in November 1993, to the very tune Gryffindor had just used on them. It ended by calling the whole of Gryffindor a bunch of hairy gits.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, Dean Thomas had spent a Friday evening drilling the younger Gryffindors in a chant about badgers, to a tune he swore everybody in Muggle Britain knew. They roared it in the rain at the start of the match against Hufflepuff. Then the house that apologised when you trod on it came back with its reply, five hundred voices strong, deeper, louder and in better time. Fred and George Weasley bowed deeply to the Hufflepuff stand, hands on hearts, while the whole stadium laughed.

pages.title: Trelawney's sixteenth of October prediction
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
September 1993, at the first Divination lesson of the year
pages.html:
Trelawney's sixteenth of October prediction was the warning Professor Sybill Trelawney gave Lavender Brown in September 1993: the thing Lavender was dreading would come on the sixteenth of October. By Lavender's reckoning, it did.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, Trelawney asked Lavender to fetch her the big silver teapot, thanked her, then told her in passing that the thing she was dreading would come on the sixteenth of October. Lavender went pale.

In Book Three, Chapter Eight, Lavender was crying outside the classroom with Parvati Patil's arm round her. She had had a letter that morning. A fox had got Binky, and the date was the sixteenth of October. Hermione Granger could not leave it alone. Had Lavender really been dreading Binky's death? Was he an old rabbit? He was only a baby, Lavender sobbed. Then why, asked Hermione, would she have been dreading it? Parvati glared at her, but Hermione went on regardless. Binky had not even died that day, she pointed out; Lavender had only heard about it that day. Ron told Lavender, very loudly, to take no notice.

pages.title: The Ministry notice in Honeydukes
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Inside the door of Honeydukes, Hogsmeade, December 1993
Dementors patrolling Hogsmeade every night after sundown
pages.html:
The Ministry notice in Honeydukes was pasted inside the door of the Hogsmeade sweetshop in December 1993. It warned customers that dementors would patrol the village every night after sundown until Sirius Black was recaptured, and that they should finish their shopping well before nightfall. It ended 'Merry Christmas!'

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Harry Potter, who had no permission to be in Hogsmeade, was in Honeydukes with Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger. Ron nodded significantly at the notice over their shoulders. Harry remarked drily, to nobody in particular, that he had always thought the town needed some abject misery and soul-sucking demon creatures. Then he thanked Fudge for them.

pages.title: Aunt Petunia's letter
pages.html:
Aunt Petunia's letter, the first Harry Potter ever had from his aunt, reached him at Hogwarts in November 1993. It ran to six lines, told him the family would be away at Christmas, and ended up burnt on a candle.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, the letter arrived on a Wednesday, not long after Sirius Black had broken into the castle. In six lines it said that the Dursleys had been contacted by the authorities of your school, that they had been assured the matter is being handled, and that it was no more than they had always expected of that world. Under no circumstances was Harry to think of coming home for Christmas, as they would be away.

He read it twice and burnt it on a candle at the Gryffindor table. He was savagely pleased when it flared. Then he sat looking at the little heap of ash, with no idea what he had wanted it to say instead.

pages.title: The Committee's letter to Hagrid
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Hagrid cleared; Lucius Malfoy's complaint upheld
20 April 1994, before the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures
pages.html:
The Committee's letter to Hagrid is the Ministry letter that reached Rubeus Hagrid at Christmas 1993, after the inquiry into the hippogriff Buckbeak's attack on Dracina Malfoy at Hagrid's lesson of 2 September 1993. It cleared Hagrid of all blame. It also upheld Lucius Malfoy's official complaint, which sent Buckbeak to a hearing in London on 20 April.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eleven, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger found Hagrid sobbing over it in his cabin. It accepted Professor Dumbledore's assurances in full, then ordered Buckbeak kept tethered, in isolation, until the hearing. Lucius Malfoy was no longer a governor, but Harry thought that a man did not have to sit on a thing to lean on it. Four words came off the page at him: the official complaint lodged by Mr Lucius Malfoy. In September Dracina had told him, with her chin up, that she had written four pages to her father and never sent them. Harry had believed her.

pages.title: Dracina's serpent brooch
infobox: A coiled silver serpent with emerald eyes
As a clasp in her plaits
pages.html:
Dracina's serpent brooch is a coiled silver serpent with two emeralds for eyes, which Dracina Malfoy inherited from her grandmother Black. She wears it as a clasp in her plaits. By her own reckoning it is worth more than Gregory Goyle's house.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, it vanished on the day Dracina came back to lessons after Buckbeak’s attack. She had put it in that morning in the hospital wing. Before lunch Hermione’s bag split on the steps up from the dungeons. For half a second something small flashed on the stone, silver-green, before she swept it back in. It was a sweet wrapper, she said.

Later that day Peeves turned up with the brooch pinned to his bow tie, crowing that he had found it on the floor by the dungeon steps. When a wad of chewing gum shot up his nose, he tore it off and flung it over his shoulder into a fire bucket. Dracina ran down the corridor, plunged her good arm in up to the shoulder and came up with the brooch, dripping. ‘I’m so sorry about your brooch, Malfoy. That was awful,’ said Hermione, and put her arm through Harry’s.

In Chapter Ten, in front of Harry, Dracina hinted at what she suspected. ‘Entirely, thank you, Granger. The nerve damage is a thing of the past. I expect you’ll be relieved; I know you were so concerned about it, back when my jewellery kept finding its way into your bag.’ Hermione went white. In Chapter Twenty she owned up: she had taken the brooch from Dracina’s hair in a corridor and left it on the dungeon steps for Peeves.

pages.title: Dracina's black silk sling
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Dracina's black silk sling is the sling Dracina Malfoy wore for about two months in the autumn of 1993, after the hippogriff Buckbeak slashed her arm. It certainly had not come from Madam Pomfrey. Her arm had healed long before she gave it up.

The withdrawal

Slytherin used her supposed injury as their excuse to pull out of the opening match against Gryffindor the moment the forecast promised a storm. Gryffindor had to open the season against Hufflepuff instead, in a hurricane, and lost by a hundred points.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, Dracina came back to lessons with her arm bandaged from wrist to elbow, in a black silk sling, with her hair plaited round her head like a crown. In Chapter Eight, six weeks on, she was still fiddling with its edge.

In Chapter Nine Fred reported watching her pass a full salt shaker the length of the Slytherin table with the injured arm. She caught him watching, winced, then put it back in the sling. Harry met her on the path to the pitch and asked after it. ‘How is the arm, Malfoy? Only Madam Pomfrey says bones knit in a night, and that’s the longest night I’ve ever heard of.’ At the match itself she stood in the front row of the Slytherin stand with both hands on the rail, and no sling anywhere.

In Chapter Ten she visited Harry in the hospital wing with the sling arranged across her robes like an order of chivalry. The next day she gave it up. ‘Two months,’ said George. ‘That sling had a longer run than Lockhart.’

pages.title: Dracina's four-page letter
infobox: Overnight in the hospital wing, September 1993, with her left hand
pages.html:
Dracina's four-page letter was written to her father, Lucius Malfoy, overnight in the hospital wing in September 1993, after the hippogriff Buckbeak slashed her arm. She wrote it with her left hand, the wrong one, and it was meant to make things happen to people. Then she told Harry Potter she had decided not to send it. Pansy Parkinson sent it for her.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, Dracina sat beside Harry in Potions, her arm in a black silk sling, to tell him she was sorry: for what she had said about Hagrid, and for shouting at him in the wing. 'I was going to write to Father. I had written to Father, if you must know, I sat up all night, it was four pages. And then I didn't send it. I'm not going to. I've decided.' Harry found that he was smiling. He believed her, rightly.

She had left the pages on the little table beside her bed. In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Pansy Parkinson stood in the same ward two months later, looking at that bare table as though something were still lying on it. Nobody else in the ward knew that four pages had once lain there, written in the small hours with the wrong hand. Nobody else knew that Pansy herself had taken them to the Owlery, thinking it was what a friend would want. She had found out in Potions what her friend had really wanted. She had gone the colour of the wall, and she had said nothing since.

The letter reached Lucius Malfoy, who used it before the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures to have Buckbeak condemned. From Christmas onwards Harry believed that Dracina had lied to him. In Chapter Twenty-Two, in June 1994, Pansy confessed on the front steps of the castle. Dracina had to be held back from her, but in the end she forgave her.

pages.title: Marauder's Map
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
All of Hogwarts, with every person in it as a labelled moving dot
'I solemnly swear that I am up to no good'
pages.html:
The Marauder's Map is a piece of old parchment that shows the whole of Hogwarts, with every person in the castle marked by a tiny moving dot labelled with their name. It was made by Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot and Prongs. A tap of a wand and the words 'I solemnly swear that I am up to no good' bring it up; 'Mischief managed' wipes it blank again.

The makers

Moony was Remus Lupin, Wormtail Peter Pettigrew, Padfoot Sirius Black and Prongs James Potter. They drew the Map from what they found out on their night-time explorations of the grounds and Hogsmeade. They signed it with their nicknames, so that it is presented by Messrs Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot and Prongs.

It has their manners, too. Ordered by Snape to reveal its secrets, it produced a string of insults signed by Mr Moony, Mr Prongs, Mr Padfoot and Mr Wormtail.

What it shows

The Map never lies. It shows people under Invisibility Cloaks as plainly as anybody else, and it shows everybody under their own true name.

It also shows seven secret passages out of the castle to Hogsmeade. Filch knows four of them. One, behind a mirror on the fourth floor, has fallen in. One begins under the Whomping Willow. The last comes up in the cellar of Honeydukes, the sweetshop. It opens with a tap on the hump of the one-eyed witch and the word 'Dissendium'.

In the saga
