infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
The Imperius Curse, the Cruciatus Curse and the Killing Curse
pages.html:
The Unforgivable Curses are the three darkest curses there are: the Imperius Curse, which controls its victim; the Cruciatus Curse, which tortures; and the Killing Curse. Using any of them on another human being earns a life sentence in Azkaban. They work only when the caster means them with his whole heart.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, early in 1994, Harry Potter asked Remus Lupin, at one of their lessons against the dementors, why the Patronus Charm needed a memory when no other spell did. Most magic draws on what a wizard can do, Lupin told him, but a very small number of spells draw on what he is. 'You cannot cast an Unforgivable Curse by learning it. Everybody knows the words. Say them with your whole heart behind them, meaning them, wanting them, and the curse works; say them without, nothing happens at all, which is the single most merciful fact in our entire body of law. Dark magic of that order asks the caster for something out of his soul, takes it, then does not give it back.'

pages.title: Revealing Charm
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Makes hidden writing, enchantments or curses show themselves
pages.html:
A Revealing Charm makes whatever is hidden on or in an object show itself, whether that is invisible writing or a curse waiting to go off. There are several of them, each looking for something different.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Harry Potter woke on Easter Sunday 1994 to find a chocolate egg the size of a Quaffle on his pillow. Somebody had painted a golden Snitch on one side. On the other, in tiny letters of white icing, it said I made it myself. Truly. D. It was from Dracina Malfoy.

Harry took it down to breakfast, which was a mistake. Hermione Granger went rigid at the sight of it. Things did not just appear on people's beds, she said, not with Sirius Black on the loose; it could be cursed. Harry would not let her take it to Professor McGonagall. So she whipped out her wand and tried three different revealing charms on the egg, one after another, while half the Gryffindor table looked on. Nothing happened. Ron broke off a piece and stuffed it into his mouth. 'If I die,' he said thickly, 'tell Mum it was worth it.' He did not die.

pages.title: Confusing Concoction
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
The Confusing Concoction is a potion for muddling the mind, which turns a deep, smoky blue when it is brewed correctly. Its ingredients include scurvy-grass, which curdles it if overdone, and exactly two sprigs of sneezewort. It is stirred anticlockwise.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, it was the third-years' Potions exam. Dracina Malfoy, working across the gangway from Harry, had hers the right smoky blue already, while his stayed as thin as tea. Without moving her lips she coached him: too much scurvy-grass, two sprigs of sneezewort, not three, then stir it anticlockwise. Snape, standing behind Harry, asked silkily whether she was assisting Potter. Dracina did not even look up. 'I was telling him he's hopeless. He doesn't seem to have heard me.' Snape bent over her cauldron and pronounced it excellent. Against Harry's he wrote something on his clipboard that looked suspiciously like a zero.

pages.title: Sleekeazy's Hair Potion
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
By Pansy Parkinson to Dracina Malfoy, early 1994; refused
pages.html:
Sleekeazy's Hair Potion smooths and tames unruly hair. It was invented by Fleamont Potter, Harry Potter's grandfather, and it made the Potters far richer than they had ever been. It is sold in bottles.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, early in 1994, Dracina Malfoy came running back from Hogsmeade with her silver-blonde hair hanging round her face in thick, dripping ropes of mud. Crabbe had already blundered into the Slytherin common room, dripping green, with a muddled story about ghosts, Potter's head and the Weasleys' bedroom. So Pansy Parkinson came straight along with a towel to wait in the passage outside Snape's office. She also brought a bottle of Sleekeazy's Hair Potion, which she held out like a peace offering the moment Dracina stepped into the passage. Dracina would not have it. 'Leave it.'

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry dreamt of a row of little glass jars labelled Sleekeazy's on a sideboard, behind the gleaming white hair of his grandfather, Fleamont.

In Chapter Five Ron spent two weeks' pocket money on a bottle by owl order, to tame Harry's hair for Plan A. In Chapter Six, on the night of the World Cup final, he brought the small bottle along in his rucksack, then pushed a comb into Harry's hand in the wood.

pages.title: Undetectable Poisons
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 12
pages.html:
Undetectable Poisons are the poisons that leave no trace of themselves in the victim. They are part of the Potions course at Hogwarts, where poisons are taught alongside their antidotes. Early in 1994 Professor Snape set Harry Potter an essay on them.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Harry sat grinding through his essay on Undetectable Poisons for Snape at the table next to Hermione Granger's. She was visible only as a quantity of hair over the top of a tower of books.

pages.title: Fire crab
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
A large tortoise with a jewelled shell
Shoots flames from its rear end
pages.html:
The fire crab looks like a large tortoise with a heavily jewelled shell. When it is attacked it shoots flames from its rear end, which makes it a lively subject for a Care of Magical Creatures class.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, early in 1994, Hermione Granger had her eyebrows singed by fire crabs at the paddock in Care of Magical Creatures. Ron Weasley had heard her talking to Professor Vector about an Arithmancy lesson held at the same time, and he held up the fire crabs as proof that she could not have been there. 'She was with us in Care of Magical Creatures, we were up at the paddock with the fire crabs, she had her eyebrows singed.' Hermione was, in fact, using a Time-Turner to get to all her classes.

pages.title: Kneazle
infobox: Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them (12 March 2001)
Cat-like, with spotted or speckled fur, large ears and a lion's tail
Knows an untrustworthy person on sight
pages.html:
The Kneazle is a small magical cousin of the cat, with spotted or speckled fur, outsize ears and a tail like a lion's. It is clever, independent and sometimes bad-tempered. A Kneazle that takes to a witch or wizard makes an excellent pet. It can tell at once when somebody is not to be trusted, and it will lead its owner safely home when they are lost.

Kneazles and cats

Kneazles can breed with ordinary cats, and a licence is needed to keep a pure one. Hermione Granger's cat Crookshanks is part Kneazle, which explains a good deal about him.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, during the Defence Against the Dark Arts exam in June 1994, Harry Potter put his arm round Hermione Granger, who had gone to pieces in front of the boggart. Dracina Malfoy told Hermione that it meant nothing. ‘He'd do it for a kicked Kneazle,’ she said. ‘Potter's kind to anything pathetic.’

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, at supper at the Burrow on 21 August 1994, Molly Weasley told the table that a witch in Godalming had had her windows put in twice. Her Muggle neighbours had seen her talking to her Kneazle.

pages.title: Fanged Geranium
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
pages.html:
The Fanged Geranium is a magical plant with a mouthful of small, sharp teeth. It is grown in the Hogwarts greenhouses, and handling one without being bitten is part of the Herbology examinations.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, in June 1994, the third years sat their Herbology exam out in the greenhouses, with the sun blazing down through the glass. By the end of it half the class had sunburnt necks. A Fanged Geranium bit Neville Longbottom twice. 'Only twice,' he said, looking at his hand with something like pride. 'I thought it'd be loads more.'

pages.title: Dementor's Kiss
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The soul sucked out and eaten
pages.html:
The Dementor's Kiss is the last and worst weapon of the dementors. A dementor lowers its hood only to use it, clamping its jaws upon the victim's mouth to suck out the soul.

What it does

The Kiss does not kill. The body goes on living while the heart and brain still work. But it is an empty shell, with no sense of self, no memory, nothing. There is no chance of recovery. The soul is not sleeping, nor waiting somewhere to be fetched: the dementor has eaten it, and it will not be given back at the end, when everything else is. Its place is filled by something that is never the victim's own, such as a beast of the kind a vampire carries.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, early in 1994, Remus Lupin explained the Kiss to Harry Potter over butterbeer after a Patronus lesson. Of all the things the Ministry had ever licensed, he said, it was the one he would walk to London to stop. Harry asked why the soul would not be given back. ‘Because the thing has eaten it,’ said Lupin. ‘Ask me a happier question.’ The Daily Prophet had reported that morning that the Ministry had given the dementors permission to perform the Kiss on Sirius Black if they found him. Harry, to his own surprise, was pleased.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, Black had been caught and locked away upstairs. The Kiss had been authorised. Earlier that night it had very nearly been performed on Harry himself, down by the lake.

pages.title: Seventy times seven
pages.html:
Seventy times seven is the answer Jesus gave when Peter asked how often he ought to forgive a brother who sinned against him: not seven times, but seventy times seven. The sum comes to four hundred and ninety. The point is to lose count.

The saying

It is in the Gospel of Matthew, in the eighteenth chapter. Jesus followed it with the parable of a servant whose master forgave him a vast debt, and who then had a fellow servant thrown into prison over a small one.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, after a Patronus lesson early in 1994, Remus Lupin told Harry Potter a story about a man who asked his teacher how many times he ought to forgive somebody, and suggested seven. ‘Seventy times seven, said the teacher.’ Harry worked it out as four hundred and ninety. Lupin replied: ‘I’ve always understood that the idea was to lose count.’ When Harry asked about people like Snape, Lupin admitted that he found it difficult every single day. It was written down, he said, if Harry ever went looking.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the saying moved Harry to forgive Dracina Malfoy on the castle steps. In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, it helped him not to mind too much that Hermione Granger had lied to him twice in one night.

pages.title: Christmas
pages.html:
Christmas is the feast of the birth of Christ, kept on the twenty-fifth of December. Every witch and wizard in Britain keeps it too. They put up trees, pull crackers and sing carols, though hardly any of them have the least idea whose feast it is.

Father Christmas

The old man in red who brings the presents is Father Christmas. In Narnia, where the White Witch had kept it winter for a hundred years with no Christmas at all, he came back in 1940 as her power broke.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in Divination in the spring of 1994, Harry Potter asked Professor Trelawney why wizards kept Christmas. She told him it was a very ancient festival of the turning year, which the Muggles had borrowed from wizards and dressed up in their own little stories. Wizards kept it for the feasting, the giving and the light in the darkest days. Harry pointed out that it had Christ in it, and that it was His birthday. Trelawney waved it away: ‘Names are merely labels, dear. The Inner Eye looks beneath them.’

The Fat Friar told Harry, in the same chapter, that wizards laugh at God all year round, then sing His carols on the twenty-fifth because they like the tunes. He had watched them do it for five hundred years. ‘I’ve come to believe it’s a joke. His joke, I mean.’

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Four, on 21 August 1994, Harry Potter called through the boarded-up fireplace at Privet Drive that the Dursleys had blocked it so that Father Christmas could not turn up without notice. Uncle Vernon, deeply offended, said that he was very fond of Christmas and had believed in Father Christmas until he was eleven. The Dursleys watch the film with the Wicked Witch of the West in it every Christmas, and later that day Mrs Weasley's cackle at the Burrow sounded to Harry exactly like her.

pages.title: Natural magic
infobox: Herbs, physic, reading the stars for sowing
pages.html:
Natural magic was what the medieval Church called the kinds of magic it could live with: herbs, physic and reading the stars to know when to sow. There were monks doing it in every county, and the bishops took the cures like everybody else.

The other sort

What the Church would not abide was the other sort. Calling up spirits was forbidden, and so was bargaining with things in the dark. To sell yourself to a demon in return for power was idolatry, which broke the First Commandment.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the Fat Friar explained the difference to Harry Potter. ‘Like a diary,’ said Harry, before he could stop himself. ‘A diary that writes back.’ The Friar looked at him sharply. ‘Exactly like that,’ he said. ‘Signing yourself over to some creature in the dark, in return for power. That’s idolatry, lad.’

pages.title: Wise women
infobox: Witches who went home to their villages as healers
pages.html:
In the early centuries of Hogwarts, most of the witches who left the school went home to their villages to be the wise woman. She was the healer, the one a family sent for in the night when a baby came wrong or a fever would not break. Half the parishes in England had one.

History

The wise woman sat up with the dying to say the prayers with them when the priest could not come. The priest knew perfectly well what she was, and nodded to her on the way out of Mass. Most witches and wizards of that age believed that God had given them their magic on purpose, as a gift to be used.

It did not last. A clever Dominican called Nider, writing a great fat book about ants, began to argue that witches were not deluded old women at all, but an army: a secret church with the Devil for its bishop. Then came the Malleus Maleficarum of 1486. After it, witchcraft was preached as an organised heresy, a pact with the Devil. People who had done nothing all their lives but help began to burn.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, Harry Potter went to the Fat Friar to ask why the wizards hate the Church. The Friar told him about his youth, when the school was new and half the boys who left it went into the Church. Harry asked about witches. 'Oh, the girls went home,' said the Friar, smiling. They went back to their villages, mostly, to be the wise woman. He told Harry about Nider and his book about ants. He told him about the Malleus Maleficarum too, whose ink he could still remember smelling. 'I watched friends burn, young Potter,' he said. 'People who had never done anything in their lives but help.'

pages.title: O.W.L.s and N.E.W.T.s
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
Ordinary Wizarding Level, sat in the fifth year
Nastily Exhausting Wizarding Test, sat in the seventh year
pages.html:
O.W.L.s, sat in the fifth year, and N.E.W.T.s, sat in the seventh, are the two great examinations of a Hogwarts education. The O.W.L. results decide which subjects a student may carry on with. The N.E.W.T.s decide what careers are open to them afterwards.

The examinations

O.W.L. stands for Ordinary Wizarding Level, N.E.W.T. for Nastily Exhausting Wizarding Test. Examiners from the Wizarding Examinations Authority come up to the castle to set them. Only those who did well enough at O.W.L. may go on to study a subject at N.E.W.T. level.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, Remus Lupin told Harry Potter that the Patronus Charm was highly advanced magic: ‘Well beyond Ordinary Wizarding Level.’ In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, before the exams of June 1994, even Fred and George Weasley were seen doing some work, with their O.W.L.s only weeks away. Their brother Percy's N.E.W.T.s were only days away, and he had become almost impossible to live with.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, Percy came out of his N.E.W.T.s with the highest grades there were. Fred and George scraped through with a few O.W.L.s each. They celebrated as though they had won the Quidditch World Cup.

pages.title: Home Life and Social Habits of British Muggles
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Home Life and Social Habits of British Muggles is an enormous textbook for Muggle Studies at Hogwarts, the size of a paving slab. In March 1994 Hermione Granger, who was not speaking to Harry Potter or Ron Weasley, hid behind it at breakfast, then again at the victory party.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, on the morning of the match in early March 1994, Hermione sat four seats along from Harry behind her barricade of books. When she saw his face change she half rose, reaching out, then remembered that she was not speaking to him. She hoisted the book up in front of her face like a shield.

That evening, at the party in the common room after Gryffindor's win, she had a whole corner to herself by the window, with the book propped open in front of her. She had been on the same page for at least half an hour.

pages.title: The Handbook of Hippogriff Psychology
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Approaching the Unfamiliar Hippogriff: Courtesy, Distance and the Low Bow
pages.html:
The Handbook of Hippogriff Psychology is an enormous, musty library book on hippogriffs. Just before the Easter holidays of 1994 Dracina Malfoy borrowed it, which left Ron Weasley without it for Buckbeak's appeal. When it came back, a thin green ribbon marked a chapter read so often that its corner had gone soft.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Ron had taken over Buckbeak's appeal. On the first Monday of the Easter holidays he found that the Handbook had been out since the week before last, with Fowl or Foul? A Study of Hippogriff Brutality and an old Annotated Guide to the Grounds, all on the same ticket. Ron had no doubt whose. Harry Potter suggested that she might be reading them.

The books came back the following Monday, stacked neatly on the end of Madam Pince's desk. A thin green ribbon in the Handbook marked the opening page of a chapter called Approaching the Unfamiliar Hippogriff: Courtesy, Distance and the Low Bow. Ron decided she had been looking up how to get a hippogriff to attack people. Not long afterwards Harry saw Dracina alone in an empty classroom, bowing long and slow from the waist to a suit of armour, with her eyes fixed on its visor.

pages.title: Fowl or Foul? A Study of Hippogriff Brutality
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Hippogriffs, and how dangerous they are
pages.html:
Fowl or Foul? A Study of Hippogriff Brutality is an enormous, musty library book on the dangers of hippogriffs. Ron Weasley used it in 1994 to prepare Buckbeak's appeal, once Dracina Malfoy had brought it back.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Ron took over the appeal, then found that this book and The Handbook of Hippogriff Psychology were both out of the library on the same ticket as the Annotated Guide to the Grounds. He was sure the borrower was Dracina. The books turned up again the following Monday, stacked neatly on the end of Madam Pince's desk before anybody else was awake. Somebody had left a thin green ribbon in the Handbook, marking a much-thumbed chapter on approaching an unfamiliar hippogriff. Ron tugged it out and dropped it on the floor, sure that she had been looking up how to make a hippogriff attack people. Harry picked the ribbon up and kept it. After that Ron was buried in both books.

pages.title: Annotated Guide to the Grounds
infobox: The old one, with a map of the Forest edge in the back
pages.html:
The Annotated Guide to the Grounds is a guidebook to the Hogwarts grounds, kept in the school library. The old edition has a map of the edge of the Forbidden Forest in the back. Dracina Malfoy had it out over the Easter holidays of 1994, with two books on hippogriffs.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Ron Weasley had taken over Buckbeak's appeal. On the first Monday of the Easter holidays he found that somebody had both the hippogriff books he needed out of the library on one ticket. They had the Annotated Guide too, 'the old one with the map of the Forest edge in the back, Pince says'. Ron was sure it was Dracina, hoarding them so that nobody could argue the appeal. The books turned up again the following Monday, stacked neatly on the end of Madam Pince's desk before anybody else was awake.

pages.title: Numerology and Grammatica
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
pages.html:
Numerology and Grammatica is an Arithmancy book. Hermione Granger's copy went missing just before the exams of June 1994, because Ron Weasley had quietly borrowed it.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, Hermione had written out an exam timetable that plainly meant her to sit two exams at once. Asked how she would manage it, she demanded instead to know whether either of the boys had seen her copy of Numerology and Grammatica. Ron said, very quietly, that he had borrowed it for a bit of bedtime reading. Hermione began shoving piles of parchment about the table in search of it. Then Hedwig swooped in with a note from Hagrid: Buckbeak's appeal had been set for the sixth of June, the day their exams ended. Hermione was still hunting for her Arithmancy book when Harry read out that someone from the Ministry was coming, with an executioner.

pages.title: Advanced Rune Translation
pages.html:
Advanced Rune Translation is a textbook for the harder work of Ancient Runes, in which old runic texts are turned into plain English. Hermione Granger's copy very nearly caught fire a little after two o'clock one morning in June 1994, in the middle of the exams.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, in the middle of exam week, Harry Potter woke thirsty and went down to the Gryffindor common room for a glass of water. He found Hermione at the table by the window, still in her school robes, behind a wall of books, with a single candle at her elbow. She was crying quietly as she wrote. When he spoke she started so violently that her elbow caught the candle. Harry grabbed it before it could set fire to Advanced Rune Translation.

pages.title: Malleus Maleficarum
pages.html:
The Malleus Maleficarum, the Hammer of Witches, is a treatise on witchcraft written in 1486 by two Dominican friars, Heinrich Kramer and Jacob Sprenger. More than any other book, it made witchcraft an organised heresy: a pact with the Devil, Christ abandoned and treason against Heaven itself.

The book

It was printed at Speyer soon after it was written, and ran through edition after edition on the Continent. It told inquisitors how to find witches, question them and try them.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter about it. He was already dead when it was written, and he remembered the smell of the ink. After it, he said, witchcraft was an organised heresy, which was a great deal worse than any sin or crime. Once you have decided your neighbour is a traitor to Heaven, there is nothing you will not do to him, even in God's name. In England, Wales and Scotland, by contrast, the law made witchcraft a felony, like horse-stealing: a crime against your neighbour, not a heresy about what you are.

pages.title: Canon Episcopi
infobox: Regino of Prüm, De synodalibus causis et disciplinis ecclesiasticis (about 906)
That night-flying witches were dreaming; that only God can change one creature into another
pages.html:
The Canon Episcopi is an old rule of Church law about witchcraft, first recorded about 906 by Regino of Prüm. It held that women who believed they flew by night with a heathen goddess were deceived by the Devil. Wizards read it as meaning that their magic was God's, lent to them.

The canon

The canon takes its name from its first word, Episcopi, 'bishops', because it opens by telling bishops to root sorcery out of their dioceses. The heathen goddess it names is Diana. Regino took it to be a decree of the ancient Council of Ancyra, though it was not. It was copied into the great collections of Church law that followed, Burchard of Worms's Decretum among them, and it was already old when the Fat Friar was a novice.

How wizards read it

The canon also said that anybody who believed one creature could be changed into another, except by the God who made it, was next door to a heretic. Since wizards did exactly that, they concluded that the gift must be His, and that a wizard who used it in His service was a steward rather than a heretic.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, in the spring of 1994, Harry Potter told the Fat Friar that A History of Magic said the Church had called magic heresy. The Friar roared with laughter, then asked whether Harry had ever heard of the Canon Episcopi. When he had explained it, Harry concluded that the Church had said magic was not real. The Friar put him right: 'It said that believing in it was the sin.'

pages.title: Formicarius
infobox: About 1437, at the time of the Council of Basel
Moral lessons drawn from ants; witchcraft
pages.html:
The Formicarius is a great fat book about ants by Johannes Nider, a Dominican friar of the fifteenth century. Somewhere in the middle of it Nider began to write that witches were not deluded old women at all. They were an army, he said, a secret church with the Devil for its bishop.

The book

Nider wrote it in the late 1430s, while he was at the Council of Basel. It is a book of moral lessons, each drawn from the life of the ant colony, which he held up as a model for Christian people. Its fifth and last part deals with witchcraft. There he set down the tales he had gathered of a sect of witches sworn to the Devil, who raised storms and killed children.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter how things had gone wrong between wizards and the Church: a little at a time, the way most things go wrong. 'There was a Dominican called Nider, a clever man, who wrote a great fat book about ants, of all things.' 'In a book about ants,' said Harry. The Friar agreed. 'In a book about ants. I did say he was clever. I never said he was sensible.' After Nider, the Friar said, came the Malleus Maleficarum, which was far worse.

pages.title: The Bible
infobox: Holy scripture: the Old and New Testaments
Exodus 20:3; Psalms 23 and 84; Matthew 14 and 18; Ephesians 4:26
A little black Bible, from the vicar of St Michael's, 1994
pages.html:
The Bible is the holy scripture of the Christian faith, the Old Testament and the New. Its history is true history: Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, the Flood and the rest. Most wizards dismiss it as Muggle folk tales. Its words have nonetheless carried Sirius Black through Azkaban, held Remus Lupin back from his war form and helped Harry Potter towards faith.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, Lupin told Harry of a man who asked his teacher how often he ought to forgive, and was told seventy times seven. Lupin's eyes creased at the corners. 'I've always understood that the idea was to lose count.' Harry would find it written down, he said, if he ever went looking. In Chapter Fifteen Harry asked Professor Trelawney whether the prophets, who saw visions without crystal balls, counted as Seers. She called the Muggle scriptures desert folk tales. The Fat Friar quoted the First Commandment to him, thou shalt have no other gods before me, against anybody who sells himself to a demon for power.

In Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, Lupin began to change, and Black caught him by the arm. 'Steady, Moony,' he said, low and fast. 'Steady. Look at me. "Be ye angry, and sin not." Remember? Lily had it written up on the wall of that awful flat. You used to read it out to me when I was in a temper.' Lupin ground out the rest of the verse, and came back to himself. Harry had heard the words before, years ago, in assembly at St Grogory's. Black told Harry, too, how faith had come to him in Azkaban, through the old Bible passages printed in The Quibbler. One verse above all had kept him: I'd rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than dwell in the tents of wickedness. A little later, when part of Harry wanted to watch Pettigrew die, he heard Black's voice saying Be ye angry, and sin not as clearly as if it had been spoken aloud beside him. 'NO!' he shouted, putting himself between Pettigrew and the wands.

In Chapter Nineteen, with the Garou tearing at Harry's shield, Black knelt bleeding in the grass with his wooden cross in his fist. He began the twenty-third psalm: though he walked through the valley of the shadow of death, he would fear no evil. In Chapter Twenty, Lupin's seventy times seven came back to Harry when he found that Hermione had lied to him twice in one night.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, the Fat Friar told Harry how Peter walked on the water towards Christ until he looked down. He quoted Christ's words to him: 'O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?'

In Book Four, Chapter Two, the vicar of St Michael's, Little Whinging, pressed a little black Bible into Harry's hands on his second Sunday at Evensong. Harry began reading it in the evenings, after the Dursleys had gone to bed.

pages.title: The Lord's Prayer
infobox: Christ, in the Sermon on the Mount
In assembly at St Grogory's Primary School
pages.html:
The Lord's Prayer is the prayer Christ taught His disciples, beginning 'Our Father, which art in heaven'. It is the best known of all Christian prayers. Harry Potter learnt it in assembly at St Grogory's, with Dudley Dursley pinching him from the row behind. In 1994 he heard Remus Lupin fail to finish it, and finished it for him.

The prayer

Christ gave it in the Sermon on the Mount, as the pattern of how to pray. In the form said in English churches it asks that God's name be hallowed, that His kingdom come, for daily bread and for forgiveness, as we forgive those who trespass against us. It ends by asking not to be led into temptation, but to be delivered from evil.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in the summer of 1993, John Constantine slipped past the wards of Shacklewell House in New Mexico by walking in backwards, reciting the Lord's Prayer backwards under his breath, from Amen to Father. Wards, he reckoned, were like bouncers: they looked very hard at people coming in, and hardly ever at those they thought were going out. It was not a thing he would have wanted his old parish priest to hear.

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, Professor Snape caught Harry with the Marauder's Map and called Lupin to his office. Standing downwind of Snape, Lupin breathed in and went the grey of cold ashes. His hand went to the cross at his collar, and his lips moved without a sound as he held himself back. Afterwards he rebuked Harry and walked away. Then, at the foot of the marble staircase, he stopped with his head bowed. Harry knew the shape of the words from St Grogory's: as we forgive those who trespass against us.

In Chapter Nineteen, under the full moon on the lawn, Lupin began to pray it as the change took him: 'Our Father... which art in heaven... hallowed be thy name...' He never reached the last word of deliver us from evil. The scream came first.

In Chapter Twenty, at the lake, Harry finished the words for him. 'Deliver us from evil,' he said. Then he cast his Patronus, a stag so bright that he had to screw up his eyes, which went galloping across the water as though the lake were a floor.

pages.title: Trelawney's prophecy of the servant
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
The day of Buckbeak's execution, June 1994
Trelawney's room at the top of her tower, Hogwarts
That night, when Peter Pettigrew escaped
pages.html:
Trelawney's prophecy of the servant was the trance Professor Sybill Trelawney fell into on the day of Buckbeak's execution in June 1994, with only Harry Potter there to hear it. She foretold that the Dark Lord's servant would rejoin him before midnight. It came true that night.

The words

Her first words were ‘It will happen tonight.’ Then she went on in a harsh, deep voice that was nothing like her own: ‘The Dark Lord lies alone and friendless, abandoned by his followers. His servant has been chained these twelve years. Tonight, before midnight... the servant will break free and set out to rejoin his master. The Dark Lord will rise again with his servant's aid, greater and more terrible than ever he was. Tonight... before midnight... the servant... will set out... to rejoin... his master...’ Then her head dropped forward on to her chest.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, Harry had finished his Divination examination and was on his way out, with a parting joke about her shawl, when Trelawney spoke behind him. She was sitting bolt upright in her armchair, with her eyes blank and her mouth slack. For a moment he thought she was having a fit.

When the voice stopped, Harry stood rooted to the spot with the hair prickling on the back of his neck. He had faced Voldemort twice already, and twice Voldemort had very nearly come back. He said aloud, ‘Then I'll have to stop him again, won't I... bloody hell.’ A moment later Trelawney's head came up with a jerk. She apologised dreamily for having drifted off in the heat of the day, and remembered nothing she had said. Going down the stairs, Harry wondered whether it had been a real prophecy or only her notion of a dramatic finish to an exam. The servant, Peter Pettigrew, broke free that night.

pages.title: Dracina Malfoy's letter about Buckbeak
infobox: Overnight in the hospital wing, September 1993
Before the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures
pages.html:
Dracina Malfoy's letter about Buckbeak was the four pages she wrote to her father overnight in September 1993, after the hippogriff Buckbeak slashed her arm. It was about Buckbeak and about Hagrid. She decided not to send it. Somebody took it from beside her bed while she slept, then posted it anyway. Lucius Malfoy used it to have Buckbeak condemned.

The letter

Dracina wrote it in the small hours in the hospital wing, with her left hand, the wrong one. It was meant to make things happen to people. By morning she had changed her mind. She left the pages on the table by her bed, then told Harry Potter to his face that she had dropped the whole thing.

The person who took them to the Owlery was Pansy Parkinson, Dracina's closest friend, who believed it was what a friend would want. She found out in Potions what her friend had really wanted, and she said nothing for the best part of a school year. In June 1994 she confessed on the front steps of the castle. Dracina flew at her, then forgave her.

The hearing

Lucius Malfoy lodged an official complaint about Buckbeak, which was upheld. Then he put Dracina's four pages before the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures. He found them most persuasive, and on the strength of them he had the hearing brought forward from the twentieth of April to a date only days away. He took it that Dracina had sent them herself, and he wrote to thank her.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seven, in September 1993, Dracina told Harry in Potions that she was sorry. 'I was going to write to Father. I had written to Father, if you must know, I sat up all night, it was four pages. And then I didn't send it. I'm not going to. I've decided.' Harry believed her. In Chapter Ten, two months later, Pansy stood in the hospital wing looking at the bare table where the pages had lain. In Chapter Eleven, on the last morning of the autumn term, Harry read the Committee's letter in Hagrid's cabin. It spoke of the official complaint lodged by Mr Lucius Malfoy, and Harry decided that Dracina had lied to him.

In Chapter Fourteen Lucius wrote to thank her. He had put her four pages in front of the Committee; they were most persuasive, he said, and he had had the hearing brought forward on the strength of them. Dracina told Professor Snape that somebody had sent her letter. She had written back begging her father to drop it, but he would not. She was sure the thief was Hermione Granger. Walking back to the Slytherin common room, she told Pansy, of all people, that she would find out who had taken it. 'When I do,' she said softly, 'I am going to make them wish they had never learnt to write.'

In Chapter Twenty Hermione Granger, who had long suspected Dracina of posting it herself, told her that she had never touched it. In Chapter Twenty-Two, the day after Buckbeak's rescue, Pansy broke down on the front steps of the castle and confessed: she had thought Dracina wanted the letter sent. Dracina screamed that she had nearly ruined everything, and Daphne Greengrass had to hold her back. When Ron Weasley spoke up for Pansy, Dracina forgave her.

pages.title: The Ministry letter on Hagrid's table
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
'The official complaint lodged by Mr Lucius Malfoy'
pages.html:
The Ministry letter on Hagrid's table is the letter, under a Ministry seal, that Harry Potter read in Rubeus Hagrid's cabin at Christmas 1993. In the middle of it stood the official complaint lodged by Mr Lucius Malfoy, and those words convinced Harry that Dracina Malfoy had lied to him. It is the same letter that sent Buckbeak to his hearing. In truth Dracina had written to her father but never posted it. Pansy Parkinson had.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in November 1993, Pansy Parkinson stood in the hospital wing looking at the bare table beside the bed Dracina had used in September. Four pages had once lain on it, written in the small hours and meant to make things happen to people. Pansy had taken them to the Owlery, thinking it was what a friend would want. She had found out in Potions what her friend had really wanted, and she had said nothing since. Harry saw her look at the table, but he knew none of this.

In Chapter Eleven, at Christmas, Harry read the letter aloud in Hagrid's cabin. Four words came off the page at him: the official complaint lodged by Mr Lucius Malfoy.

In Chapter Twelve, early in 1994, he was still carrying the letter about in his head. In September a girl had sat at his elbow in a dungeon, with ink on her left hand, telling him she had not sent a thing. As far as Harry could see, only one of the two could be true. He was thirteen, he was not a fool, and he could do that sum.

In Chapter Fifteen, at the foot of the castle steps, Dracina swore to him that she had not sent it. She had written it, she said, four pages of it, on the night he came to the hospital wing to tell her she was horrible. In the morning she could not bring herself to send it. She had left it on the table by her bed, and somebody had taken it while she was asleep.

pages.title: Hagrid's notes about Buckbeak
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Hermione Granger; Harry, Ron and Hermione
pages.html:
Hagrid's notes about Buckbeak were three notes Hagrid sent in 1994 as the hippogriff's case went against him. The first, after the hearing, was so tear-stained that the words had to be guessed at. The second gave the date of the appeal. The third, in a shaking hand, said that the appeal was lost and the execution set for sunset. It told the three friends not to come.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the first note reached Hermione Granger after the hearing in London. Enormous tears had splashed on to it, so that in places the ink had run into blue blots: 'Dear Hermione, We lost. I'm allowed to bring him back to Hogwarts. Execution date to be fixed. Beaky has enjoyed London. I won't forget all the help you gave us. Hagrid'.

In Chapter Sixteen Hedwig brought the second. Buckbeak's appeal was set for the sixth of June, the day they finished their exams. Somebody from the Ministry of Magic was coming up for it, with an executioner. Hermione saw at once what that meant: they had already decided.

On 6 June the third came. This time Hagrid had not cried on it, but the writing wobbled all over the page, as though his hand had been shaking too badly to hold the quill: 'Lost appeal. They're going to execute at sunset. Nothing you can do. Don't come down. I don't want you to see it. Hagrid'. They went down all the same, under the Invisibility Cloak.

pages.title: Percy Weasley's list
infobox: Reforms for when he is Minister for Magic
pages.html:
Percy Weasley's list is the programme of reforms Percy keeps in his trunk for the day he becomes Minister for Magic, which he has been planning since he was about six. Some of it would help families like his own. The rest is frightening.

What it says

Poor families would get help with money for books and robes. The old families would be stopped from buying people jobs at the Ministry; Percy's mother nearly cried at that part. Then come identity papers that everybody must carry, a register of everybody's blood, curfews, and a department to decide what everybody else may read.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, Ron Weasley told Harry Potter about it in the weeks before the exams of 1994. It held ideas, Ron said, that would make Grindelwald tell Percy to steady on. Ron had said so to Percy's face once, and Percy had not spoken to him for a week. Harry thought the first half sounded good. Wizarding Britain, he thought, could do with a good shake.

pages.title: The Gryffindor chant against Slytherin
infobox: Gryffindor supporters, led by Dean Thomas
Gryffindor against Slytherin, the first match of the 1992 to 1993 season
pages.html:
The Gryffindor chant against Slytherin is a crude song mocking the Slytherins as slimy snakes. Dean Thomas wrote it for Gryffindor's first match of the 1992 to 1993 season, against Slytherin. Professor McGonagall stopped it by threatening to take fifty points from Gryffindor. Dean revived it for the final against Slytherin in 1994.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, Dean had been working on the song since the summer holidays, writing it on the backs of envelopes and in the margins of his Potions notes. For three weeks he taught it to the Gryffindors one at a time, under his breath, until nearly every Gryffindor in the castle knew every word. The singing started the moment the brooms went up. By the third chorus the Hufflepuffs and Ravenclaws had joined in. The Slytherin stand went berserk. Professor McGonagall seized Lee Jordan's megaphone and announced that if she heard one more verse, Gryffindor would lose fifty points. Dean sat down with a look of deep disappointment.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the teams had hardly left the ground at the final when Dean was on his feet at the front of the Gryffindor stand, waving his arms like a conductor while the whole stand roared out the song from the year before. He had obviously decided that last year's threat had worn off over the summer. Professor McGonagall's mouth went thin in the commentators' box. Before she could get hold of the megaphone, the Slytherins began their own reply, slow and swaying, as though at a funeral.

pages.title: The Slytherin funeral chant
infobox: Harry Potter's fall and his dead parents
The whole house pretending to faint
pages.html:
The Slytherin funeral chant is the song the Slytherins sang at the Quidditch final of 1994, slowly, swaying from side to side with their hands pressed to their hearts as if at a funeral. It mocked Harry Potter's fall from his broom and his dead parents. At the end every one of them pretended to faint.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the Slytherins sang it in answer to Dean Thomas's chant, and they had clearly practised. When they all flopped sideways on to the benches, the Gryffindor stand exploded. The Hufflepuffs booed, and even the Ravenclaws, who usually stayed out of things, were on their feet shouting. Harry flew on with his face perfectly still. Dracina Malfoy, the Slytherin Seeker, drew level with him, her face a dark, dull red. She opened her mouth as though to speak, then wheeled away without a word.

pages.title: The song about Oliver Wood
pages.html:
The song about Oliver Wood was started in the Gryffindor common room at the party after Gryffindor beat Ravenclaw in March 1994. It had eleven verses, nine of them about Oliver Wood.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, Harry Potter had caught the Snitch on his new Firebolt, and the whole house was celebrating. Wood, told that he was crying on the mantelpiece, insisted it was the smoke, then went off to find another butterbeer. Somebody in the corner started the song. Meanwhile Neville Longbottom, after one and a half butterbeers, gave the room his impression of Marcus Flint trying to get out of a hooded robe. To everybody's astonishment, it was extremely good.

pages.title: Executioners' Union
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Sixteen
pages.html:
The Executioners' Union is the body that speaks for wizarding executioners, among them Walden Macnair of the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures. In June 1994 Macnair threatened to lodge a formal complaint on its behalf, after the hippogriff he had come to behead escaped.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, at sunset on 6 June 1994, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger heard the swish of the axe from up the lawn. A moment later Buckbeak burst up out of Hagrid's garden into the red evening sky, with a hooded rider crouched on his back, and was gone over the Forbidden Forest. Hagrid danced in his pumpkin patch. Macnair's voice rose, high and furious: 'I'm lodging a formal complaint, Hagrid, on behalf of the Executioners' Union! You hear me? Nobody pays a man for a job he never done!'

In Book Three, Chapter Seventeen, Macnair stopped shouting about the Union. He stamped up and down the pumpkin patch with his axe instead, kicking at pumpkins. 'Walden, please,' Fudge kept bleating. 'Walden, think of the Prophet...' As Harry found out in Chapter Twenty, the hooded rider had been Dracina Malfoy.

pages.title: The Marauders
infobox: Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot and Prongs; Mr Moony; Mr Padfoot; Mr Prongs; Mr Wormtail
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Remus Lupin (Moony); Peter Pettigrew (Wormtail); Sirius Black (Padfoot); James Potter (Prongs)
pages.html:
The Marauders were four Gryffindor friends at Hogwarts in the 1970s: Remus Lupin, Peter Pettigrew, Sirius Black and James Potter. Among themselves they were Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot and Prongs. They made the Marauder's Map, and three of them became Animagi so that they could keep Lupin company at the full moon.

At Hogwarts

Lupin is a Garou, made by the bite when Fenrir Greyback attacked him as a very small boy. At the full moon the tide in him rose past holding. His friends found out what he was. Instead of deserting him, they made his transformations the best times of his life.

James and Sirius were the cleverest students in the school. They worked out how to become Animagi, then helped Peter through it. In their fifth year all three managed it: James became a stag, Sirius a great black dog and Peter a rat. They roamed the grounds and Hogsmeade with Lupin at night, unregistered, without Dumbledore ever knowing.

They also drew the Marauder's Map, a chart of the whole castle that shows where everybody in it is, and signed it with their nicknames. Lily Evans, whom James married, was the only Christian in the Marauders' circle through all their years at school.

Afterwards

In 1981 Peter betrayed James and Lily to Voldemort, then let Sirius take the blame. Sirius spent twelve years in Azkaban without a trial. Peter spent them as Scabbers, the Weasleys' rat.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fourteen, the map insulted Professor Snape in the names of all four of its makers. Snape suggested that Harry had got it straight from its rather hairy manufacturers, and Lupin's fingers tightened on his chair. Asked afterwards whether he knew the mapmakers, Lupin said only: 'We've met.'

In Chapter Eighteen Lupin told Harry who the four had been, and how three of them became Animagi in their fifth year. In Chapter Twenty-two Dumbledore told Harry that Sirius had explained it all to him: 'An extraordinary achievement, not least keeping it quiet from me.'

pages.title: Order of Saint Benedict
pages.html:
The Order of Saint Benedict is the oldest monastic order of the Western Church: the monks who live under the Rule that Saint Benedict of Nursia wrote in the sixth century. The Fat Friar, the ghost of Hufflepuff, was one of them, which makes him no friar at all.

History

Benedict wrote his Rule at Monte Cassino about 530. It binds a monk to one community for life, with his day divided between prayer, study and work. Many of the great abbeys and priories of medieval England were Benedictine, until Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries in the 1530s. The Fat Friar haunted his own priory on the Wash for a few hundred years, until King Henry pulled it down to sell the lead off the roof. Then he came home to Hogwarts.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, Harry went to the Fat Friar with his questions about God. Hermione had told him the Friar was fourteenth-century, which made the ghost laugh: he was older than that by a long chalk. He was a monk, strictly, a Benedictine. The friars came along a couple of hundred years after he died, but the name stuck to him like porridge, and he gave up correcting people round about the time of the Armada.

pages.title: Dominican Order
infobox: The Order of Preachers; the Blackfriars
pages.html:
The Dominican Order, properly the Order of Preachers, is a Catholic religious order founded by Saint Dominic in 1216. Dominicans wrote the books that turned witchcraft, in the eyes of the Church, into an organised heresy.

History

Dominic's friars were preachers and scholars, vowed to poverty. From the 1230s the Popes put much of the work of the Inquisition into their hands.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter how the Church had come to burn witches. It had happened a little at a time. He was dead by then, and he had watched. There was a Dominican called Nider, who wrote a great fat book about ants, in which witches became a secret church with the Devil for its bishop. 'I did say he was clever. I never said he was sensible.' Then two more Dominicans wrote the far worse Malleus Maleficarum. 'Fourteen eighty-six, that was, and I remember the smell of the ink.'

pages.title: Take That
infobox: Gary Barlow, Howard Donald, Jason Orange, Mark Owen, Robbie Williams
pages.html:
Take That are a Muggle pop group from Manchester, the most popular boy band in Britain in the early 1990s. Lavender Brown and Parvati Patil follow them devotedly.

The band

The group was put together in 1990: Gary Barlow, who writes most of their songs, with Howard Donald, Jason Orange, Mark Owen and Robbie Williams. In 1993 'Pray' and 'Relight My Fire' both went to number one. More followed in 1994, along with a great many posters on a great many bedroom walls.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, Harry reflected that Hermione Granger followed real vampires the way Lavender and Parvati followed Take That.

pages.title: Synod of Whitby
infobox: The abbey of the Abbess Hilda at Whitby, Northumbria
How to reckon the date of Easter
pages.html:
The Synod of Whitby was the council that King Oswiu of Northumbria called in 664 to settle whether the Church in his kingdom should follow the customs of Rome or those of the Irish monks of Iona. The chief question was how to reckon the date of Easter. Oswiu decided for Rome.

The synod

The trouble had come into the King's own household. Oswiu kept Easter by the Irish reckoning, as he had been taught. His queen, Eanflæd, who had been brought up in Kent, kept it by the Roman one, so that one of them could be feasting while the other was still fasting in Lent.

The synod met at the abbey of the Abbess Hilda at Whitby. Bishop Colmán spoke for the Irish customs, which he said came down from Saint John. Wilfrid spoke for Rome, which had Saint Peter. When Oswiu heard that Christ had given Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, he chose Rome, so as not to find the door shut against him when he came to it. Colmán went home to Iona, and the English Church followed Rome from then on.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter in the spring of 1994 that Hermione Granger had been to see him. He called her a formidable young woman. 'She asked me three questions about the Synod of Whitby and corrected me on two of the answers.'

pages.title: Spanish Armada
infobox: Defeated by the English fleet and by storms
pages.html:
The Spanish Armada was the great fleet that Philip II of Spain sent against England in the summer of 1588, to carry an invading army across the Channel from the Netherlands. The English fleet harried it up the Channel and broke its formation with fireships off Calais. Storms wrecked many of the survivors on the long way home round the north of Scotland and down the coast of Ireland.

The Armada

Philip meant to restore the Catholic faith in England, and to put an end to English raids on his treasure fleets. About a hundred and thirty ships sailed under the Duke of Medina Sidonia, to meet the Duke of Parma's army in Flanders. Lord Howard of Effingham commanded the English fleet, with Sir Francis Drake as his vice-admiral.

After the fireships scattered the Spanish off Calais, the two fleets fought at Gravelines. The wind then drove the Armada into the North Sea, with no way home but the long way round. Barely half of it reached Spain. In England it was remembered as a deliverance.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter in the spring of 1994 that he was really a Benedictine monk, not a friar: the friars reached England a couple of hundred years after he died. The name stuck to him like porridge all the same, and he gave up correcting people round about the time of the Armada.

pages.title: Dissolution of the Monasteries
infobox: Thomas Cromwell and the King's commissioners
Every religious house in England and Wales closed
pages.html:
The Dissolution of the Monasteries was King Henry VIII's closing of every abbey, priory, nunnery and friary in his kingdom, from 1536 to 1541. The Crown took their lands and their treasure. The King's men stripped the lead off their roofs to sell, melted down their bells and left most of the buildings to fall into ruin. One of the houses pulled down was the Fat Friar's own priory on the Wash, which sent the Hufflepuff ghost home to Hogwarts.

The suppression

Henry had broken with Rome so that he could marry Anne Boleyn. In 1534 he made himself Supreme Head of the Church in England. The monasteries were rich, and they owed their first loyalty to the Pope. Thomas Cromwell, the King's chief minister, sent commissioners round them in 1535 to value their wealth and report on their morals.

An Act of 1536 shut the smaller houses. The greater ones were made to surrender one by one over the next four years, and abbots who resisted were tried for treason. At Glastonbury, one of the oldest abbeys in England, the aged abbot, Richard Whiting, was hanged, drawn and quartered on the Tor in November 1539, together with two of his monks.

Wizards in the Church

For centuries the Church had found room for wizards. When the Fat Friar was young, in the early days of Hogwarts, half the boys who left the school went into the Church, most of them Muggle-born. Most monks were ordinary men who got up in the dark to sing. A wizard with a mind to spend his life mending people, though, often took the habit. The Friar was himself a Benedictine monk, and after his death he haunted his own priory on the Wash for a few hundred years.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party on 31 October 1992, Hermione Granger met Brother Aldric, a monk of Glastonbury who had been hanged, drawn and quartered by Henry the Eighth's men. He confirmed that he had hidden the abbey's books from the King's commissioners in a cave on the Tor, where they were never found.

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter that he had haunted his own priory, on the Wash, for a few hundred years, until King Henry pulled it down to sell the lead off the roof. He came home to Hogwarts after that.

pages.title: Goblin rebellions
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Wizarding rule, and the law that bars goblins from carrying wands
pages.html:
The goblin rebellions were the risings of the goblins against wizarding rule, which broke out again and again over the centuries. Their dates are one of the great trials of History of Magic at Hogwarts.

The rebellions

Goblins are a proud, clever people, masters of metalwork and of money, who have long resented the place wizards keep them in. The chief grievance is the wand. Wizarding law forbids any non-human creature to carry or use one, and wizards have always refused to share the secrets of wand-making. Goblins have magic of their own, but they have never accepted the ban.

The quarrels broke out in open rebellion many times, most often in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. In 1612 the rebels made their headquarters at an inn in Hogsmeade. The risings were bloody, and neither side has forgotten them. At Gringotts, where goblins keep the wizards' gold, relations are correct rather than warm.

In the classroom

Professor Binns teaches the rebellions in his usual voice, which is to say no voice at all. Every pupil who wants to pass History of Magic has to learn their dates.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Harry Potter noticed in his first weeks at Hogwarts that Binns gave out the marriages of the old pure-blood houses in exactly the voice he used for goblin rebellions.

In Book One, Chapter Eleven, revising for the examinations of 1992, Harry, Ron and Hermione learnt the dates of the goblin rebellions by heart, along with those of the great magical discoveries.

In Book Three, Chapter Five, Hermione Granger told her friends on the Hogwarts Express that an inn at Hogsmeade had been the headquarters of the 1612 rebellion.

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, outside the History of Magic examination in June 1994, Ron Weasley tested Hermione on the dates of the goblin rebellions. He had made her a set of little cards for it, with the questions on the front and the answers on the back, in his large, messy handwriting. So far as Harry knew, it was the first thing Ron had ever made for anybody, unless you counted trouble.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, in the scullery at the Burrow before dawn on 22 August 1994, Harry Potter asked Hermione Granger why she had never talked about the troubles in the Muggle world. She talked about everything, he said; she had once talked about the goblin rebellions for a whole train journey.

pages.title: 1994 Quidditch World Cup
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Britain, for the first time in thirty years
Ireland against Bulgaria, Monday night, 22 August 1994
pages.html:
The 1994 Quidditch World Cup was the World Championship of Quidditch, played in the summer of 1994. Britain had not hosted the Cup for thirty years, and tickets were extremely hard to come by. The Firebolt, the fastest broom ever made, was expected to be the broom of choice for the national teams. The final, Ireland against Bulgaria, was played on Monday night, 22 August 1994.

The Cup

The World Cup goes back at least to the fifteenth century. One match of 1473 was so violent that every one of the seven hundred possible fouls was committed in it. For more than a thousand years the English and the French argued over the rules, sometimes with wands, until every national team agreed, from 1901, to play by the Austrian rules. The rules on nationality are strict as well: a national side must be made up of its own country's witches and wizards.

The tournament is run through the Department of Magical Games and Sports at the Ministry of Magic. England failed to bring the Cup home in 1994, and Ron Weasley was miffed about it.

The Firebolt

In the summer of 1993 the Firebolt went on show at Quality Quidditch Supplies in Diagon Alley, price on request. The shop's proprietor told the crowd that the Irish International Side had just put in an order for seven of them, and that Ireland were favourites for the Cup. Which Broomstick predicted that it would be the broom of choice for the national teams at the World Championship.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry Potter saw the Firebolt in Quality Quidditch Supplies in August 1993 and heard about the Irish order. In Chapter Thirteen, when Harry flew his own Firebolt in the Ravenclaw match, Lee Jordan's commentary passed on the verdict of Which Broomstick: it was going to be the broom of choice for the national teams at that year's World Championship. Professor McGonagall asked whether he would mind telling them what was going on in the match.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, on the train home in June 1994, Ron asked Harry to come and stay for the World Cup. His father, he said, could usually get tickets from work.

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on Saturday 20 August 1994, Molly Weasley's letter reached the Dursleys. Arthur had got prime tickets for the final through his connections at the Department of Magical Games and Sports. Britain had not hosted the Cup for thirty years, she wrote, and it was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Ron's note came by owl the same morning: 'DAD GOT THE TICKETS. Ireland versus Bulgaria, Monday night.' He was a bit miffed that England had not brought it home. Of Ireland he added: 'They're all Irish at least. Quidditch has strict rules about that sort of thing.'

pages.title: Johannes Nider
pages.html:
Johannes Nider was a German Dominican friar of the fifteenth century, a reformer and a theologian. In the middle of a long book about ants, the Formicarius, he set down the idea that witches were not deluded old women at all, but an organised army: a secret church with the Devil for its bishop.

Life

Nider was born in Swabia about 1380, became a Dominican as a young man and rose to be prior of the Dominican house at Basel. The Formicarius, which he wrote in the mid-1430s, draws moral lessons from the habits of ants. He died at Nuremberg in 1438. Half a century later two more Dominicans wrote a far worse book, the Malleus Maleficarum of 1486.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Fifteen, the Fat Friar told Harry Potter how things had gone wrong between wizards and the Church: a little at a time, the way most things go wrong. 'There was a Dominican called Nider, a clever man, who wrote a great fat book about ants, of all things.' Harry could not quite believe it. 'I did say he was clever. I never said he was sensible.'

pages.title: Ephraim Shacklewell
infobox: Shacklewell House, New Mexico, south of the Cleft
Owning, and losing, the Linking Book to Myst Island
pages.html:
Ephraim Shacklewell is a rich American pure-blood wizard. He lives at Shacklewell House in the New Mexico desert, south of the D'ni dig at the Cleft. He bought the Linking Book to Myst Island from a digger for fifty dollars and kept it in a glass case as a ‘No-Maj picture book’, until John Constantine took it from him in August 1993 for Albus Dumbledore.

Family and fortune

The Shacklewells have been in America since a great-great-grandfather stepped off a ship in Boston with a wand in his pocket and a price on his head. For most of that time they were not rich. Ephraim's father made the family's money in the 1960s, once the old American law forbidding wizards to have dealings with No-Majs had been done away with. He sold a scouring potion to the copper mines of Arizona as a miracle cleaning fluid, through a string of front companies. The Magical Congress never quite managed to prove it.

Ephraim has spent the money on Shacklewell House, a vast pink adobe mansion in the Spanish style, with towers, balconies and a long colonnade. To anyone passing on the road it looks like a derelict filling station, with a sign reading LAST GAS FOR 90 MILES. There is a fountain shaped like a Thunderbird. Because Ephraim once went to a Quidditch World Cup and never got over it, there is also a swimming pool shaped like a Golden Snitch. A six-legged Wampus cat sleeps at the foot of the stairs.

The wards were put up by MACUSA's own security men, who were bribed to do it. They cost more than most wizards earn in a lifetime, and they were built entirely to keep out wizards.

Like most American wizards of his class, Ephraim went to Ilvermorny, the wizarding school of North America, on Mount Greylock in Massachusetts.

The trophy room

Shacklewell collects things. His panelled trophy room on the first floor holds a lump of metal labelled as a fragment of a No-Maj flying saucer from Roswell, 1947, which is in fact half a hubcap off a Ford. There is also a shrunken head that talks from time to time, a stuffed jackalope, a pair of boots that once belonged to a Wild Bill and a jar of something that moves.

In the last case, on a cushion of red velvet, lay a big brown leather book with one word in gold on the cover. Its label read NO-MAJ PICTURE BOOK (NATIVE?), CHARMED PHOTOGRAPH INSIDE, MOVES, FROM THE DIG, $50. He never touched it, which was lucky for him.

The night of the burglary

Shacklewell is a large, pink man with a moustache like a yard brush, and he suffers from insomnia. On the night John Constantine broke in, he was the one person in the house still awake. In a silk dressing gown, a hairnet and monogrammed slippers, he found the burglar in the trophy room. He had his wand in one hand and a glass of warm milk in the other.

Constantine showed him an expired Liverpool library card, which a glamour turned into whatever Shacklewell most feared. He told him, too, that MACUSA would say no more about the copper mines. Shacklewell handed the book over in relief. He offered his visitor coffee, asked for a receipt and waved the thief off from the step. The receipt is signed ‘J. Lennon, MACUSA’. A battered Jackie Collins paperback now lies on his velvet cushion.

Dumbledore's verdict was that Shacklewell had no more right to the book than a magpie has to a wedding ring.

In the saga

Shacklewell's only part in the saga comes in the Interlude of Book 3, on the August night in 1993 when John Constantine burgled Shacklewell House. Constantine and Dumbledore talked him over afterwards at Hogwarts.

pages.title: Susan Pevensie
infobox: Queen Susan; Susan; Queen Susan the Gentle; Susan Evans; Mrs Evans

Lily Potter daughter
Petunia Dursley daughter
Harry Potter grandson
Peter Pevensie brother
Edmund Pevensie brother
Lucy Pevensie sister
The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (16 October 1950)
Queen Susan the Gentle of Narnia
A bow, a quiver of arrows, an ivory horn
October 1981, at the hands of Lord Voldemort
In the true Narnia, with her brothers, her sister and Aslan
pages.html:
Susan Pevensie was a crowned Queen of Narnia, Queen Susan the Gentle, who reigned through a grown-up life there and came back to England a girl. She was the only one of the four Pevensies to survive the railway accident of 1949. Grief, and the memory of Aslan, brought her back to Christ. As Mrs Evans she raised her daughters, Petunia and Lily, in the Anglican faith. She is Harry Potter's grandmother. Through her the blood of Aragorn and Arwen came down to Lily, then to Harry. In October 1981, days before he came for Lily, Lord Voldemort killed her in her own home. She fought him.

The wardrobe

Susan was born in 1928, the second of the four Pevensie children: Peter was older, Edmund and Lucy younger. In 1940 the four were sent out of London, away from the war, to the country house of Professor Digory Kirke. There they went through a wardrobe into Narnia, where the White Witch had held the land in winter for a hundred years.

Susan was the sensible one, and at first she did not believe Lucy about the wardrobe either. The Professor asked her and Peter whether Lucy was in the habit of telling lies.

Father Christmas gave Susan a bow, a quiver of arrows and a little ivory horn. If she blew the horn, help would come to her wherever she was. He told her to use the bow only in great need, since he did not mean her to fight in the battle.

That night Susan and Lucy followed Aslan to the Stone Table. They watched him give himself up to the Witch in Edmund's place. They wept over him through the night. In the morning the Table cracked, and he rose again. Afterwards he carried them on his back to the Witch's castle, where he breathed on the stone statues and brought them back to life.

Queen Susan the Gentle

Aslan crowned the four at Cair Paravel. Susan reigned as Queen Susan the Gentle through the Golden Age of Narnia. She was an archer of great skill, and a queen sought in marriage by princes, Rabadash of Calormen among them. She refused him, and when he meant to keep her in Tashbaan by force, she got away home by sea. Years later, as grown kings and queens, the four went hunting the White Stag. It led them back through the wardrobe, where they found themselves children again, at the very moment they had left.

She grew into a tall and gracious woman, famous throughout Narnia for her kindness. The bards called her the Gentle, and meant it.

Prince Caspian

In 1941 Prince Caspian blew her horn in his need, and it called the four of them back to Narnia. They found Cair Paravel in ruins, and an orchard grown up where the great hall had been. In the old treasure chamber Susan found her bow and quiver again. Her horn was gone, because it was the horn that Caspian had blown.

She beat the dwarf Trumpkin in a shooting match, and she shot a wild bear that came at Lucy. For a while she would not follow Lucy, who said she could see Aslan when the others could not. Afterwards she admitted that, deep down, she had believed Lucy all along.

Afterwards Aslan told Peter and Susan that they were too old to return.

Growing up

In 1942 she went to America with her parents. As she grew up she stopped speaking of Narnia, and the others came to say that she was no longer a friend of Narnia. For a while she cared more for parties, clothes and growing up quickly than for any of it. She called Narnia a game they had played as children.

Grief and faith

In 1949 Peter, Edmund and Lucy were killed in a railway accident, together with their parents. Susan was not on the train. In one morning she lost everybody she could have talked to about Narnia. Broken by grief, and moved above all by the courage of Aslan, who was Christ, she came back to Christ afterwards. Hers was an adult faith, arrived at late.

For a long time she was alone with it. What brought her through was the memory of Aslan: a lion who had walked to the Stone Table for a traitor's sake, and had not been afraid. She understood at last who he was. She believed that the others had gone on to Aslan's own country, the true Narnia, of which the Narnia she had known was only a shadow, and she meant one day to follow them.

From that morning she was the last crowned Pevensie. She was also the last of a line whose full length she may never have known. All four Pevensies descended from Aragorn, the King of the West, and from Arwen, the Evenstar.

Mrs Evans

Susan was an Anglican. She married, and became Mrs Evans. She had two daughters: Petunia, the elder, and Lily, born on 30 January 1960 into the household Susan made. She made sure that both of them were brought up to follow Christ. They were christened, they went to church every Sunday, and they said their prayers at night.

Lily believed from the start, and she never stopped. She took the faith seriously from childhood, and stayed devout after she found out she was a witch. Petunia went through the motions and never really believed.

Sirius Black remembered Susan as 'Lovely woman, made sure her kids were godly'.

Narnia and Lily

All her adult life, nobody believed what Susan said about Narnia. For more than twenty years she told nobody at all. In 1971 her younger daughter got a letter from Hogwarts, and Susan knew at once that here was somebody who would believe her. That summer she began to tell Lily everything: the wardrobe, the Witch, the Stone Table and the lion.

Lily believed every word. She had just found out that magic was real, and she saw nothing strange in a country on the other side of a wardrobe. Her faith and her magic sat side by side in her without any quarrel. Susan's stories of Aslan only strengthened both.

Lily's magic reconciled mother and daughter. In a daughter who was a witch Susan at last had somebody who could not dismiss Narnia, and the two were close for it.

Susan tried to tell Petunia as well. Petunia met it with scorn and derision. She told her mother that she was too old for fairy stories, and Susan did not try again.

It drew Lily closer to her mother than ever. Her elder daughter, Petunia, refused both halves, faith and magic alike. She resented Lily with the bitterness of a sister shut out of two countries at once. One was the country her sister went to every September. The other was the country her mother had once ruled.

The last fight

In the last days of October 1981, Lord Voldemort was hunting for Lily and James Potter, who had gone into hiding under the Fidelius Charm. Before he found them, he came to Susan's house.

He did not know who she was. To him she was a Muggle, a woman of fifty-three in her own front room, who might know where her daughter had gone. He never learnt that she had been a queen of Narnia.

He demanded to know where Lily and James were. Susan did not know, and she would not have told him if she had.

He lost his temper and raised his wand to kill her. It became a real fight. Susan had stood beside Aslan in Narnia's wars, and she had not forgotten how to fight. She was quick, she kept her head, and for a while the most feared wizard in Britain could not finish one Muggle woman. She had never given up the bow, and one of her arrows drew his blood.

But she was fifty-three, and her age betrayed her. Her knees would not do what they had done at Cair Paravel, and at last he caught her. He killed her in her own home. On 31 October he came to Godric's Hollow, and Lily died for Harry.

The true Narnia

Susan went at last to join her brothers, her sister and Aslan in the true Narnia, Aslan's own country, which is Heaven. She had been the one left behind for thirty-two years. Her parents were waiting there too, with the others from the railway.

Legacy

In 1993 Dumbledore told Harry that his mother's blood lived on in only one other person in the world: his aunt. The descent runs from Susan to Lily to Harry, with nobody else in it. It is the line Dumbledore means by 'the magic of Elves, Harry. And of Númenor'. Only Dumbledore and Lord Voldemort know of it. Harry does not.

On the night of the lake in June 1994, Harry's stag Patronus scattered the dementors. Then a horn sounded, far off and high up. It was a clear, bright note, like a hunting horn on a winter morning. An arrow of white light fell out of the stars as straight as a plumb line, and it destroyed the last of them. Harry had the strangest feeling that somebody up there had a very good eye, and knew exactly who he was. He felt, too, that she had been waiting a very long time to do that. Afterwards the arrow seemed to him not merely familiar but familial, the way you can tell across a crowded street that somebody belongs to you.

pages.title: Xenophilius Lovegood
infobox: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (21 July 2007)
pages.html:
Xenophilius Lovegood is the wizard who edits The Quibbler, a wizarding magazine of the odder sort. Sirius Black thought him a smart man who knows his nargles.

The Quibbler

Lovegood runs The Quibbler from his home near Ottery St Catchpole, in Devon, where he lives with his daughter, Luna. Most wizards do not take it seriously. It had at least one faithful reader in Azkaban all the same.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in June 1994, Sirius Black explained how he had spotted Peter Pettigrew in a newspaper that Cornelius Fudge gave him in Azkaban. 'Normally I just have the Quibbler. Lovegood's a smart man who knows his nargles. But I just wanted a good crossword.'

Black told them, too, that it was the Quibbler that had brought him to faith. It printed mad old Bible passages, and among the godless, miserable murderers of Azkaban they were all he had. They did nothing for him until he began truly to believe them. One of them was I'd rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than dwell in the tents of wickedness. Once he believed, the dementors stopped coming.

pages.title: Rita (Hogwarts student)
infobox: Being blamed, wrongly, for Remus Lupin's monthly absences
pages.html:
Rita was a girl at Hogwarts in the early 1970s, in the days of the Marauders. For nearly two months the thirteen-year-old Sirius Black told the whole common room that she was the reason Remus Lupin disappeared once a month. She was not: Lupin was a Garou, and went away at every full moon to change.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack in June 1994, Lupin told Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger how his friends had found him out. "James worked it out," said Sirius. "In the end. I'd have got there first, if I hadn't been so sure it was a girl."

"You did think that," said Lupin. "For nearly two months. You told the entire common room that it was Rita." "I was thirteen," said Sirius. "You were an idiot." "Yes," said Sirius, and the not-quite smile came back. "That too."

pages.title: Dawlish
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
Tough-looking, with very short, wavy grey hair
pages.html:
Dawlish is an Auror of the Ministry of Magic. On the night of 6 June 1994 he was one of the Aurors sent up to Professor Flitwick's office at Hogwarts to bring Sirius Black down to the dementors. He was the one told to get the door open. By the time it opened, Harry Potter, Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy had linked away from the room through a D'ni book.

Career

Dawlish is a tough-looking wizard with very short, wavy grey hair. He did well at Hogwarts: Albus Dumbledore remembers him as a pupil who got Outstanding in every one of his N.E.W.T.s.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, Harry, Hermione and Dracina heard men's voices in the passage outside Flitwick's office.
