pages.title: Lime Street station
pages.html:
Lime Street is the main railway station of Liverpool, a great Victorian terminus in the middle of the city. In August 1993 John Constantine bought a battered Jackie Collins paperback there for one particular purpose: to leave behind in place of the Linking Book to Myst Island when he stole it.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John burgled the house of a wizard collector in New Mexico. In the long room of glass cases he laid the paperback on the red velvet cushion where the book had been, then closed the lid of the case.

When Hagrid met him at Hogwarts afterwards, he told John that he looked terrible, then asked whether he was eating properly. 'I had a butty at Lime Street,' said John. 'Tuesday, I think.'

pages.title: The Soho pub
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Interlude
pages.html:
The Soho pub is little known, even in Soho, and nobody there asks anybody's name. John Constantine chose it for exactly that reason. A man can sit in a corner of its back bar for six hours with one pint and a crossword.

In the saga

In the Interlude of Book Three, at two o'clock on a Tuesday afternoon in the summer of 1993, an owl found John there anyway. It came in through a window that did not open, landed in his pint and looked at him as though the whole thing were his fault. The letter it carried was in green ink, from Albus Dumbledore, asking him to fetch a book from Ephraim Shacklewell in New Mexico. John sat a long time without opening it, then bought a whisky. It was in that pub, too, that he admitted to himself that he was afraid of Dumbledore.

pages.title: New Mexico
infobox: The cavern of D'ni; the Cleft; Shacklewell House
pages.html:
New Mexico is a desert state in the south-west of the United States. Under its desert lies the vast cavern of D'ni, reached from the Cleft, a crack in the ground beside an old volcano. In the 1990s a small, secretive excavation is digging its way into the dead city.

History

In 1540 the Spanish explorer Francisco Vásquez de Coronado led an army north into New Mexico in search of the Seven Cities of Cíbola. They were supposed to be made of solid gold, and they did not exist. A few wizards marched with him unrecognised. In 1541, experimenting with long-distance Apparition across the desert, they arrived by accident in the cavern of D'ni. Its people sent them back to the surface and told them never to return. Two centuries later Anna, a Muggle woman of the New Mexico wilds, found her own way down.

New Mexico became a state of the Union in 1912, with its capital at Santa Fe. In July 1945 the first atomic bomb was exploded at Trinity, in the desert of the Jornada del Muerto, after being built in secret at Los Alamos.

Wizards in New Mexico answer to the Magical Congress of the United States of America. Not all of them are respectable. Ephraim Shacklewell is a pure-blood whose father made his fortune in the 1960s, selling a scouring potion to the copper mines of Arizona. Some miles south of the Cleft he built Shacklewell House, a pink adobe mansion with towers, a Thunderbird fountain and a swimming pool shaped like a Golden Snitch. To any No-Maj driving past, it looks like a derelict filling station with a sign reading LAST GAS FOR 90 MILES. His trophy room holds, among other things, a lump of metal labelled as a fragment of the Roswell flying saucer of 1947.

In 1947 a wounded man from another world came down near Roswell. He was Eubulon, the Advent Master of the Kamen Riders of Ventara, thrown to Earth in battle with the warlord Xaviax. A secret office of the American government, the No-Men, sealed him in a capsule in a frozen sleep. In the summer of 1994 he is sleeping still.

The excavation

In 1987 the artefact hunter John Loftin found D'ni tunnels and machines under the desert. In 1988 Elias Zandi began buying the land round the Cleft. In the 1990s the dig is small and secret. It goes on behind a wire fence, with a hand-painted geological-survey sign. All the same, D'ni artefacts have leaked from it to Muggle and wizard collectors across America. Strangers watch the place: in 1993 a black van with no number plates waited a mile down the road. The D'ni Restoration Council was founded there in 1997.

In the saga

Book 3: John Constantine arrived in New Mexico in the summer of 1993, at a desert crossroads a little after midnight. He walked past the dig at the Cleft and burgled the Myst linking book from Shacklewell House. On Myst Island in June 1994 Hermione Granger told Harry and Dracina that the D'ni had lived in a cavern under the desert in New Mexico.

Book 4: In the summer of 1994 Hermione found Muggles on a newsgroup who could not stop thinking about a desert they had never seen. Some talked about going to New Mexico, and one got as far as a fence where men told him to go home. Nobody, Hermione wrote, should know about New Mexico. In August 1994 Dr Richard Watson spoke to the Muggle news from New Mexico about his friend Daniel Jackson.

Book Four, Chapter Four: by 21 August 1994 eleven Muggles on the newsgroup had described a calling to one particular place in the New Mexico desert. Hermione believed that a few D'ni survivors had come up into that desert in 1788, when New Mexico was still Spanish. She feared that the Muggles digging there might put the story together before anybody else did.

pages.title: The Cleft
infobox: The New Mexico desert, beside an old volcano
Elias Zandi; his son Jeff from 1996
Fenced, with tents, a caravan and a survey sign
pages.html:
The Cleft is a deep crack in the ground at the foot of a long black ridge, beside an old volcano in the New Mexico desert. Anna made her home there after the Fall of D'ni, and Atrus grew up there. Since the 1980s it has been the way down to the excavation of the D'ni cavern.

History

The Cleft is a fissure of volcanic rock above the cavern of D'ni. It lies near the place where Anna first found her way down in the eighteenth century, and where she came up again with her son Gehn after the plague. She made her home in it. There was water, a tree and shelter from the desert sun. Gehn brought his dying wife, Keta, to her there. Anna raised their son Atrus in the Cleft until Gehn came back for him, when the boy was about fourteen.

In 1993 the Muggle game Myst, made from Catherine's journals, began to draw people of D'ni blood towards the Cleft, as Yeesha had meant it to.

In 1987 the artefact hunter John Loftin found D'ni tunnels and machines in the desert. On 19 March 1988 he took Elias Zandi down with him. Zandi bought the land round the Cleft and brought in Dr Richard Watson, after which the small group began to dig. When Zandi died in 1996 the land passed to his son Jeff; the following year the excavators formed the D'ni Restoration Council. In later years the Cleft became the place where the explorers who felt called to the desert first arrived.

In the saga

Book 3: In the summer of 1993 John Constantine walked past the dig at night on his way to Shacklewell House. There was not much to see: a wire fence round a patch of desert at the foot of a long, black, broken ridge, a hand-painted sign about a geological survey, a couple of tents, a caravan in darkness and a deep crack in the ground with a ladder going down into it. In Dumbledore's letter it was the place the people digging there called the Cleft. A mile further on, a black van with no number plates waited by the road. Books and other things dug out of the Cleft were leaking into the hands of whoever would pay. The Myst linking book was one of them. As Constantine walked back at dawn with the book, the sun came up behind the black ridge of the Cleft.

Book 4: In 1994 one poster on a Muggle newsgroup kept dreaming of an old volcano with a crack in the ground beside it. Another got as far as a fence in the middle of nowhere, where men told him to go home. In August 1994 Dr Richard Watson spoke to the Muggle news from New Mexico, with the corner of a caravan behind him.

pages.title: D'ni
infobox: A vast cavern deep beneath the New Mexico desert
1788, to a plague let into the cavern by A'Gaeris and Veovis
The Art: books that link to other worlds
Atrus, Yeesha and a few others
The 1980s, by way of the Cleft
pages.html:
D'ni is the name of an ancient people, and of the city they built in an enormous cavern deep beneath the New Mexico desert. There they lived apart from Muggles and wizards alike for nearly ten thousand years. They were masters of the Art, the writing of books that open on other worlds. In 1788 a plague, let into the cavern by A'Gaeris and Veovis, killed nearly all of them within a few weeks. Their empty city is now being quietly dug out, and things from it have been leaking into the world ever since the work began.

Origins

The D'ni came to Earth nearly ten thousand years ago. Their ancestors were the Ronay of the Age of Garternay. Their founder, Ri'neref, brought them through a linking book into a great cavern far under the desert of what is now New Mexico. They gave one name, D'ni, to the cavern, to the city they raised in it and to themselves.

The city climbed in terraces round a great underground lake, with the island of Ae'gura at its heart. Visitors from the surface wrote of lamps that burnt without fire, and water that ran uphill. The handful of scholars who care about such things still argue over whether the D'ni were a magical race or an offshoot of humanity. To the few outsiders who met them they looked like ordinary people, only very pale, with odd eyes. They lived far longer than any people of the surface. Glowing algae in the lake lit the whole cavern. D'ni machines were far beyond anything known to Muggles or wizards, and they could cut a tunnel through solid rock.

Society and the Art

For most of their history the D'ni were ruled by kings, and afterwards by a council of lords. Daily life, though, was ordered by the great guilds. The Guild of Writers wrote Ages, and the Guild of Maintainers inspected them for safety. Other guilds made inks, made paper, surveyed the rock, healed the sick and kept the law. The D'ni had a language and a script of their own. They counted in twenty-fives.

Their wealth came from the Art. A good enough Writer could describe a world so exactly that a book would link to it. The D'ni wrote thousands of these worlds, which they called Ages, for food, timber, stone and ore. Their priests taught that a Maker had made every world that could possibly be, branching like the leaves of an enormous tree, and that a Writer only described a world that already existed.

Many D'ni behaved as though they owned the worlds they wrote, peoples and all. Some came to believe they had made them, which the priests called heresy. Anna, the one outsider who lived among them for long, thought it was pride that destroyed them. They had thousands of years of rules, they were sure they were right, and they never asked questions about the Art itself.

Contact with the surface

The D'ni kept themselves to themselves. In 1541 the army of Francisco Vásquez de Coronado came north looking for the golden Seven Cities of Cíbola, and a few Spanish wizards were travelling with it, unrecognised. They slipped away to experiment with long-distance Apparition across the desert, and arrived in the cavern by accident. The D'ni talked with them for a few hours through an interpreter. Then they sent them back up to the surface, firmly and rather rudely, telling them never to return. The Spaniards wrote it all down afterwards, which is the only reason anybody knows of the meeting. They did not think the D'ni were magical at all.

In the eighteenth century a Muggle woman named Anna found her own way down through the rock. The D'ni took her prisoner, then took her in. She married Aitrus, a D'ni, and learnt the Art. She took the name Ti'ana and bore a son, Gehn.

The Fall

In 1788, a few years after Anna came to live among them, a plague loosed by the renegade A'Gaeris went through the cavern and its Ages. With his accomplice Veovis he blew a hole in the wall of the cavern with an explosive charge, letting in a gas made on purpose to carry it. Everybody who breathed the gas fell ill. Within a few weeks the plague had killed nearly every D'ni, and even the glowing algae in the lake. Anna escaped to the surface with Gehn, and the Art was lost with the D'ni, more or less. The city stood empty for two hundred years.

A few D'ni survived, scattered across their Ages. Anna's grandson Atrus later gathered some of them together, and wrote the Age of Releeshahn as a new home for them. In the twentieth century the D'ni are all but extinct. Atrus, his daughter Yeesha and a few survivors are all that is left of them. D'ni lives are long enough for that to be possible.

Every wizard who has read Anna's journal believes that the D'ni died out completely, and the Art with them. Some, it seems, escaped to the surface. Muggles who feel a calling to one place in the New Mexico desert have each found, somewhere in the family tree, a strange, clever ancestor who turned up from nowhere and made things nobody else could make. Every one of those ancestors first appears in the records just after 1788.

Rediscovery

In the 1980s a small group of Muggles, among them John Loftin, Elias Zandi and Dr Richard Watson, found a way down from the Cleft, a deep crack beside an old volcano in the New Mexico desert. They began to dig. In the 1990s the excavation is still small and secretive. All the same, a great many artefacts have leaked out of it to Muggle and wizard collectors in America, at least one working linking book among them. Anna's journal, which turned up in America about 1985, is the source of most of what is known about the D'ni.

Yeesha, the daughter of Atrus, gave Catherine's journals to the brothers Rand and Robyn Miller of Cyan, a small American games company. From them the brothers made the computer game Myst, released on 24 September 1993, and the games that followed it. It was all Yeesha's plan, meant to draw people of D'ni blood to the Cleft and the D'ni caverns. After Zandi's death in 1996 the excavators carried on, and in 1997 they formed the D'ni Restoration Council to see the work through.

In the saga

Book Three: John Constantine, carrying the Myst linking book across Britain in 1993, knew as much about the D'ni as anybody who cared to know. They had been a people who lived for ten thousand years in a cavern under New Mexico, cut off from Muggle and magical peoples alike, writing books that were doors. About two hundred years before, a disease had spread and killed them. He passed the dig at the Cleft and judged that it was run by a handful of well-meaning amateurs with clipboards.

In June 1994 Hermione Granger recognised the big brown book in Flitwick's office as D'ni. She had read about linking books in at least three books, starting from a footnote in Lost Civilisations of the Ancient World. On the dock on Myst Island she told Harry and Dracina about the Spanish wizards. She went on to Anna, the Art and the plague. There were rumours too, she said, that Muggles had found the cavern again and had been digging there quietly for years, while odd D'ni things turned up on the black market. Dracina concluded that the D'ni had been very advanced Muggles, and Hermione agreed with her.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Two: in the summer of 1994 Hermione found six people on a Muggle newsgroup, in different countries and unknown to each other, who described a calling towards a desert they had never seen. One of them had got as far as a fence in the middle of nowhere, where men told him to go home. Hermione thought nobody should know about New Mexico. She wondered whether Anna had borne a child among the D'ni, so that people might be walking about with a little D'ni blood in them without knowing it.

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994, in Arthur Weasley's shed at the Burrow, Hermione told Harry and Ron what she had found since. Eleven people on the newsgroup now shared the calling, all Muggles, a couple of them occultists. Each had found a strange, clever ancestor who first appeared in the records just after 1788, the year D'ni fell. Hermione then told them what she had kept back on the island. Anna had married a D'ni, the reformer Aitrus. A'Gaeris, thrown out of the Guild of Writers in disgrace, had forged evidence to turn Veovis against him. The two of them blew a hole in the cavern wall to let in a gas, made on purpose, that carried a plague. A civilisation thousands of years old was gone in a few weeks.

Her hypothesis was that a handful of D'ni had survived, away from the city when the gas came or finding a way up through the rock. They came up into the desert in 1788, when New Mexico was still Spanish. Some stayed. Others went east into the young United States, married settlers and were forgotten within a few generations. A man from a historical society in Pennsylvania had typed out old newspaper reports for her, from the 1790s to the 1830s. They told of strange men going round farms and workshops after contraptions nobody could explain. Hermione thought somebody had been quietly collecting whatever the D'ni left behind. She suspected, too, that Atrus, who wrote Ages in the game long after the fall, was Anna's grandson. Ron, who had followed it all in her letters, marvelled at the lamps that never went out.

Book Four, Chapter Five: the next morning Harry told Hermione he could not have managed without her, since she had worked out all the D'ni stuff while the rest of them sat about eating cake.

pages.title: Shacklewell House
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Interlude
The New Mexico desert, some miles south of the Cleft
Pink adobe, in the Spanish manner
Wards against wand magic; a six-legged Wampus cat
pages.html:
Shacklewell House is the desert home of Ephraim Shacklewell, a pure-blood American wizard, some miles south of the D'ni dig at the Cleft in New Mexico. To No-Majs it looks like a derelict filling station. Behind the illusion stands a vast pink adobe mansion in the Spanish style, built with the fortune his father made selling a scouring potion to the copper mines of Arizona.

The house

From the road there is nothing to see but a single rusted pump on the forecourt and a sign hanging off one hinge. The sign reads LAST GAS FOR 90 MILES, creaking in the hot wind. Any No-Maj who drives past feels a sudden urge to keep going, and remembers an urgent appointment somewhere else.

Inside the illusion are towers, balconies and a long colonnade. There is a fountain shaped like a Thunderbird, with a swimming pool shaped like a Golden Snitch. The wards were built by MACUSA security men whom Shacklewell bribed, and they are made to detect wand magic. A six-legged Wampus cat sleeps across the foot of the stairs.

The trophy room

The panelled trophy room on the first floor holds Shacklewell's collection, every piece in a glass case with a label. A lump of twisted grey metal is labelled as a fragment of a No-Maj flying saucer from Roswell, 1947; it is half a hubcap off a Ford. A shrunken head carries a label saying that it talks, occasionally. There is a stuffed jackalope, a pair of boots that belonged to somebody called Wild Bill, and a jar of something that moves.

Until the summer of 1993 the last case held the Myst book, on a cushion of red velvet. Its label called it a No-Maj picture book with a charmed photograph inside, from the dig, priced at fifty dollars. That was what Shacklewell had paid a digger for it.

In the saga

In the Interlude of Book Three, one night in the summer of 1993, John Constantine let his eyes go soft in front of the filling station until he could see through it. He burgled the house for Albus Dumbledore. In the trophy room he slid the Myst book into a carrier bag, leaving a battered Jackie Collins paperback on the velvet in its place. Shacklewell found him there, in a silk dressing gown, a hairnet and monogrammed slippers. He had a wand in one hand, with a glass of warm milk in the other.

John held up his old Liverpool library card, which carried a very small glamour, and announced himself as MACUSA. He was confiscating the book, he said, and would say no more about the business with the copper mines. Shacklewell's face filled with relief. He offered his visitor a cup of coffee, then asked whether there was some kind of receipt. John wrote him one on the back of an envelope, in large clear capitals, and signed it J. Lennon, MACUSA.

pages.title: Myst Island
infobox: Anna (Ti'ana); its linking book by Atrus
pages.html:
Myst Island is a small Age of grey rock and dark pines in an empty grey sea. It was once the home of Atrus and his family. Its linking book, written by Atrus, carried Sirius Black there from Flitwick's office in June 1994. Harry, Hermione and Dracina followed him.

Description

The island is the whole of its world. From the end of the dock nearly all of it can be seen at once. Beyond it there is only grey water in every direction, meeting a sky of the same colour, with no land on any horizon. A long wooden dock runs out from a rocky cove. Beside it lies a sunken wooden sailing ship with a single leaning mast, and on a post at the shore end stands a small brass switch. Offshore a squat stone tower rises out of the water, with a clock face as big as a cartwheel.

A path climbs from the cove past an enormous stone gear, as tall as a house and half sunk into the hill. It goes on past a little pool with a perfect model ship in it, to a long, low library with stone pillars. There is also a round domed building, a tall silvery thing like a rocket, a brick chimney and, on the summit, a tree so enormous that it makes the pines look like weeds. The library is panelled in dark wood. One wall holds a great map of the island, and at the far end are two small stone stands, rather like lecterns.

History

Anna wrote the Age as a refuge for her family, and Atrus wrote its linking book. When Atrus and Catherine escaped Riven through the Star Fissure, Atrus linked to Myst as he fell. The family lived on the island for years. Atrus kept his books in the library. By the island's machines he joined it to the Ages he wrote: the rocket to Selenitic, the ship to Stoneship, the clock tower to the Mechanical Age, the great tree to Channelwood. Small brass switches on posts about the island marked the places that mattered.

Early in the nineteenth century Atrus's sons, Sirrus and Achenar, turned on their parents. When the Stranger arrived on the dock with nothing in his hands, he found the island empty. Many of the library's books had been burnt. The two brothers were trapped on the stands, one in a red book and one in a blue. The Stranger freed Atrus, who came home and removed his sons' books. After that the island was left to itself.

In the saga

Book 3: Harry, Hermione and Dracina linked to Myst Island from Flitwick's office in June 1994, just as the Aurors opened the door. They found it decaying. The dock was furred with weed and rotten through. The brass switch had gone green, and the clock had stopped at a quarter past two behind cracked glass. Moss had crept up the pillars, ivy had got in at the windows, and the library's books were burnt or burst with damp. Both stands were empty. Harry, not knowing it, stood on the same planks where the Stranger had once arrived. The grey sea made him think of drowned Númenor. He judged that the island was the whole of that world, and tiny.

On the dock Hermione and Dracina quarrelled. Dracina broke down. By the end of it the two girls were friends, and rivals as well. Harry, standing apart, heard none of it. They followed Sirius's footprints up the path to the library, where Sirius sat against the wall beneath the map. A woman had kept him company there; she was Yeesha. The four of them went home one at a time by the small leather book.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Two: in the summer of 1994 Hermione found the island in the Muggle computer game Myst, new, clean and sunlit. Everything was where she had seen it with Harry: the dock, the ship, the gear, the clock tower, even the library with the map. She sent Harry photographs of the screen, with copies to Dracina, who replied that she did not need a Muggle box to remember the island, because she had been there.

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994 Harry puzzled over a line in Sirius's latest letter, saying he had been in very good company lately. Harry supposed he meant Buckbeak. The only other company Sirius had ever mentioned was the woman in the library on Myst, whom he had tried to introduce to them, though nobody but Sirius ever saw her. That same day Yeesha was watching over Harry as a favour to Sirius, glimpsed only as a shimmer in the air. In Arthur Weasley's shed Hermione admitted that on the island she had not told Harry that Anna married a D'ni.

Book Four, Chapter Five: told that a Portkey was an object that carried people off, Harry said he had had enough of that from the bloody Myst book. Before touching the boot on Stoatshead Hill, he muttered that if he ended up on another rainy and dilapidated island he would file a complaint.

Book Four, Chapter Six: meeting Narcissa Malfoy in the Top Box, Harry remembered the library on Myst on the night of Sirius's escape. Hermione had stood at one of his shoulders and Dracina at the other, guarding him like the last slice of a birthday cake. 'Bella and Cissy, all over again,' Sirius had murmured, looking from one girl to the other. Narcissa had just told Harry that she and her twin, Bellatrix, had fought over his father for years.

pages.title: Greta Grindelwald's fortress prison
infobox: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (21 July 2007)
pages.html:
Greta Grindelwald's fortress prison is Nurmengard, a black fortress in the mountains of Austria. She built it to hold her enemies, and she carved her own words over its gate: For the Greater Good. Since Albus Dumbledore defeated her in 1945, she has been its prisoner herself.

History

During her war Greta filled Nurmengard with the witches and wizards who stood in her way. When Dumbledore beat her in their duel of 1945, she was shut up in its topmost cell. She has been there ever since, for nearly fifty years, under her own motto.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in his office in the summer of 1993, Dumbledore told John Constantine that he had asked braver men than John to go to their deaths, and would do it again if he must, 'for the greater...' He stopped dead in the middle of the phrase. John knew the words. He had seen them once, carved over the gate of the black fortress in the mountains of Austria that was now Greta's prison. He had heard whispers in the pubs he drank in that she had once been far more than an enemy to the young Dumbledore, and he had never believed them until then.

pages.title: Hell
infobox: The First of the Fallen, who is the Devil
The Second and the Third of the Fallen
Dukes and Great Earls, Andromalius among them
Runs wrongly: an hour can last a year
pages.html:
Hell is the realm of the Devil, where he rules over the fallen angels and the damned. To its lords he is the First of the Fallen, the eldest and greatest of them all. The Second and the Third of the Fallen rule beneath him. Time does not run properly there: an hour can last a year, and a year can go past in an hour.

Visitors

John Constantine, the Liverpool occultist, has been there more than once. On one visit he was carried down in a lift made of screaming. He has sat across a card table in Soho from a Duke of Hell, who shortly afterwards lost his shirt. In 1991 he sold his soul separately to the Second and the Third of the Fallen, so that the First could not collect it without starting a war in Hell.

In August 1993, to get past the wards of a house in New Mexico, John drew the seal of Andromalius, a Great Earl of Hell whose particular talent is catching thieves and returning stolen property.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, riding the Knight Bus in August 1993, John thought of the places he had been where time did not work properly. There had been Hell, more than once. When the name of Harry Potter rang a faint bell, he remembered the baby of 1981 who had done for Voldemort. Then he remembered that he had been busy with something in Hell for a while afterwards, and had forgotten all about it.

pages.title: The Styx
pages.html:
The Styx is the river that bounds the underworld of the ancient Greeks, the land of the shades. Charon the ferryman takes the dead across it in his boat, for a coin. The gods of Olympus swore their most binding oaths by its water.

In the saga

In the Interlude of Book Three, riding the Knight Bus in the summer of 1993, John Constantine reflected that he had sailed the Styx, been carried down to Hell in a lift made of screaming, and once driven a hearse over the Pennines in a snowstorm, with the corpse sitting up in the back giving him directions. None of it had been as bad as the Knight Bus.

pages.title: The poisoned quarry in mid-Wales
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 19
Above a village in the hills of mid-Wales
Poisoned a whole valley for thirty years
Remus Lupin's pack of Garou, most of them Fianna
pages.html:
The poisoned quarry in mid-Wales stands above a village in the hills. For thirty years it poisoned the whole valley below, and things crawled out of its slag heaps that were no longer animals. The Garou pack Remus Lupin found in those hills put them back where they came from.

The pack

To the Garou, poison of that kind is the Wyrm's work. Lupin's pack were mostly Fianna, one of the thirteen tribes. They still send for him now and then, as they did at Christmas 1993.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Nineteen, in June 1994, Lupin told Harry, Ron and Hermione about the years he had spent where wizards do not go. In the end he had found a pack in the hills of mid-Wales. 'Fianna, most of them, Hermione,' he said. 'It's one of the thirteen tribes. I could see you were about to ask.' They had done good work, and he told them about the quarry quite simply, the way he might have described a school trip. But he had never been one of them: he had been bitten, not born, and he was a wizard besides.

pages.title: MACUSA
aliases: the Magical Congress of the United States of America
Magical Congress of the United States of America
infobox: Magical Congress; Magical Congress of the United States of America
Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them (film, November 2016)
The Woolworth Building, New York (by the 1920s)
pages.html:
MACUSA, the Magical Congress of the United States of America, governs the witches and wizards of America. It was founded in 1693, in the aftermath of the Salem witch trials. From 1790 to 1965 it kept American wizards apart from No-Majs under Rappaport's Law, the strictest separation anywhere in the wizarding world.

Founding

MACUSA was founded in 1693, after the Salem witch trials. In those trials the Scourers, a band of corrupt wizard bounty-hunters, had helped the Puritans hunt down real witches and wizards, along with a great many innocent No-Majs. The new Congress was set up to break the Scourers, and to deal with the wizarding criminals who had fled Europe for the colonies. Its first President was Josiah Jackson.

Some of the Scourers escaped into the No-Maj world, where they married and settled. They passed down to their descendants a hatred of magic, which American wizardry has had to reckon with ever since.

Rappaport's Law

In 1790 Dorcus Twelvetrees, the daughter of a MACUSA official, gave away the secrets of the Congress to a No-Maj called Bartholomew Barebone, who was descended from Scourers. President Emily Rappaport answered with the law that bears her name. It forbade American witches and wizards to befriend or marry No-Majs. It also made every wand in the country subject to permit. It was not repealed until 1965.

For 175 years the law shaped American wizardry. Some families kept to it rigidly, while others broke it quietly. The stage magician Zatara broke it in public every night of his career, doing real magic for No-Maj audiences who took it for illusion. He broke it again by marrying a No-Maj, Sindella. MACUSA pursued him for years without ever convicting him, because no No-Maj who had seen him perform would believe that the magic was real.

In the twentieth century

In 1900 MACUSA was among the wizarding governments of the world that made an agreement with the Camarilla, through the International Confederation of Wizards. Wizards lend their own concealment spells to help keep the Masquerade, while Camarilla vampires never hunt or feed on wizards.

By the 1920s MACUSA sat in the Woolworth Building in New York, under President Seraphina Picquery. Through the age of the costumed heroes it kept the American wizarding world out of sight. It was content to let No-Majs take any magic they happened to see for the powers of metahumans, or for the tricks of the stage. Zatara's half-blood daughter, Zatanna, went on to do much the same thing on stage as her father had. MACUSA has left her alone since 1965.

After the repeal American wizards were free to deal with No-Majs again, and some of them made fortunes at it. One was the father of Ephraim Shacklewell, who sold a scouring potion to the copper mines of Arizona through front companies. The Congress never quite managed to prove that the companies were his.

MACUSA has always let New Salem, a hidden town in Colorado founded by witches who fled the Salem trials, govern itself by its own elders. Its best-known witch, Agatha Harkness, became governess to the son of Reed and Sue Richards of the Fantastic Four in 1969, which Rappaport's Law would not have allowed four years before.

In the saga

In August 1993 John Constantine posed as a MACUSA officer of "Magical Security, Artefacts Division" to take the Linking Book to Myst Island from Ephraim Shacklewell. He signed the receipt "J. Lennon, MACUSA". He reckoned that Dumbledore could have taken the house apart brick by brick, but would have had MACUSA on the doorstep by breakfast and a diplomatic incident by lunch.

pages.title: Delta Green
infobox: Section P4 of the Office of Naval Intelligence, from 1917
1942, after its clearance in the Office of Strategic Services
The Joint Chiefs of Staff, 1947 to 1970
Cells lettered A to Z, run by A Cell, from 1994; agents known by code names
2001, into the Program and the Outlaws
Officially closed in 1970; still at work
In the Third World War, by 2053
Section 31, an idea that its survivors' heirs carried into Starfleet
pages.html:
Delta Green is a secret American organisation that would prefer nobody knew its name. It hunts things that ought not to exist, and it takes the dangerous objects they leave behind into its own keeping. It grew out of the government's raid on Innsmouth in 1928, fought the Second World War in secret and served the Joint Chiefs of Staff until 1970, when it was shut down. It went on without leave. In the summer of 1994 it is a conspiracy of agents inside the government, newly organised in cells after the murder of its informal head. Most of what it has fought, it has burnt.

Innsmouth

Delta Green grew out of the American government's raid on the town of Innsmouth, Massachusetts, in 1928. Its roots go back a little further, to a small section of the Office of Naval Intelligence called P4. The Navy set it up in 1917, the year America went to war with Germany, to look into reports that nobody else would touch.

The raid on Innsmouth was the work of several federal departments at once, with the Navy offshore. For generations the people of the town had been marrying into the Deep Ones, a people of the sea who lived beyond the reef outside the harbour. Hundreds of the townspeople were carried off to military prisons without trial. Whatever could not be carried off was dynamited, which has been Delta Green's way with such places ever since.

What was learnt at Innsmouth went to P4. In the years that followed the section hunted the Deep Ones wherever the Navy could reach them, bombing their haunts off the Philippines in 1930 and off Nicaragua in 1933. Nobody outside the section was told why.

The war

After Pearl Harbor P4 was folded into the new Office of Strategic Services. Its papers carried a clearance of their own, DELTA GREEN, and the men who were allowed to read them came to be called by it.

Its enemy was the Karotechia, a section of the SS that searched the world for occult knowledge with which to win the war. In 1942 Delta Green met its British counterpart, PISCES, for the first time. Together they wrecked a bargain that the Karotechia was striking with the Deep Ones off the coast of France. Its last battle came in the three months after Germany surrendered, against what was left of the Karotechia. In October 1945 it was disbanded with the rest of the OSS.

None of this reached the heroes of the war. Because Hitler held the Spear of Destiny, the strongest of them fought at home or at the edges of occupied land. Captain America and the Invaders fought the Red Skull in plain sight. Delta Green's war was fought by ordinary soldiers in archives, cellars and the holds of ships. It told nobody about it, not even the rest of the OSS. Nor did it ever learn what Greta Grindelwald was. To Delta Green she was one more villain of the war with powers nobody could explain, and the Invaders' business.

Roswell and Majestic

Delta Green was not gone for long. In the summer of 1947 something came down near Roswell, in New Mexico, and veterans of the unit were among the first men sent to look at it. More than one thing came down near Roswell that summer. The No-Men took one of them, and Delta Green never learnt of it.

The veterans persuaded President Truman to bring the unit back. He had the Joint Chiefs of Staff set it up again as a military intelligence unit drawn from every service, answering to them alone. At the same time he set up a second body, Majestic 12, to take charge of what had crashed. Several of its first members were old Delta Green men who wanted to study what they found, not destroy it.

That was the beginning of the oldest quarrel in Delta Green's life. Majestic kept the craft and the bodies. In time it came to an understanding with the beings it calls the Greys. Delta Green was left with everything else, and it has never trusted the bargain.

Everything else was a great deal. From 1948 to 1956 Delta Green hunted what was left of the Karotechia across South America, in an operation called SOUTHERN HOSPITALITY. From 1955 it began to deputise friendlies: officials, police officers, doctors and soldiers who would help on a single matter without ever being told the truth about Delta Green.

Cambodia

The end came out of the war in Vietnam. Delta Green followed the unnatural into Indochina, where it found the Tcho-Tcho. On 23 November 1969 Operation OBSIDIAN sent Marines against a temple complex behind the Cambodian border. More than three hundred of them died there.

Such a disaster could not be explained to anybody without the clearance, and Delta Green's enemies in Washington made the most of it, Majestic among them. On 24 July 1970 the clearance was withdrawn. Officially, Delta Green no longer existed.

It went on all the same, without anybody's leave. Later that year forty men who had held the clearance met quietly in Washington. They agreed to carry on as a conspiracy of agents inside the government, answering its call whenever it came. On Christmas Day 1971, in Operation BINGO, they diverted American bombers on to every village and holy place of the Tcho-Tcho that they knew of.

The conspiracy

For twenty-four years Delta Green was a loose network of old friends. They called on one another when something came up, borrowed what they needed from the agencies they worked for and covered for each other afterwards. Its informal head in the later years was a retired general, Reginald Fairfield.

On 25 February 1994 Fairfield was shot dead at his farm. Delta Green believes that Majestic 12 had him killed, by the hands of its enforcers, NRO DELTA. Outside Delta Green it is far from clear that anything is left of Majestic 12 at all. Delta Green knows better, or believes that it does.

Fairfield's death taught the survivors that a network of friends could be rolled up by anybody who knew one of them. That year an old agent, Joseph Camp, rebuilt Delta Green as a conspiracy of cells. Each cell is known by a letter from A to Z and has three agents at a time. Each agent has a code name beginning with his cell's letter. Camp himself is Alphonse, of A Cell, which runs the rest. An agent knows the others in his own cell, together with the code names of one agent in the cell above and one in the cell below. He does not try to learn anybody else's real name.

The agents keep their ordinary jobs: in the FBI, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the CIA, the armed forces, the Centers for Disease Control and elsewhere. Friendlies may know the truth about a single operation. They are never told the truth about Delta Green.

Rules

Delta Green's rules are short and old. The first is not to get caught. Its agents lie to everybody outside, the government they serve included, and they lie consistently. An operation that feels wrong is called off.

Anything unnatural is to be destroyed, together with the place it came from, so that the public never hears of it. Books and objects are carried off where possible, burnt where not. Nothing is studied that can be destroyed. No agent may use what he finds, however useful it looks. Success is judged by A Cell, never by the agent.

It is the opposite of Majestic's way. It is also the opposite of the SCP Foundation's, which collects such things and keeps them.

What it fights

Delta Green calls what it fights the unnatural. Behind most of it lie the powers that its few scholars call the Great Old Ones and the Outer Gods. None of them is God, nor anything like His equal. They are strong enough all the same to spoil His work, out of spite or for ends of their own that no man understands. Delta Green does not try to understand them. It tries to keep them out.

It has fought the Deep Ones since Innsmouth and the Tcho-Tcho since Indochina. Since 1955 it has burnt every copy it can find of a play called The King in Yellow, which carries the influence of the King in Yellow from mind to mind. Its files call the King the avatar of Hastur, by which they mean no being but a force, the one that men now call entropy. In New York it keeps an eye on the Fate, a ring of sorcerers in the city's underworld.

Its human enemies are more ordinary, and more numerous. Remnants of the Karotechia survive in South America. Abroad it has counterparts, PISCES in Britain and GRU SV-8 in Russia, which it trusts no further than anybody else.

None of this has ever reached the public, nor the heroes, who have never met the things Delta Green fights or have never known what they met. That is Delta Green's doing, and the reason it exists.

In Britain PISCES has a younger rival in Black Air, a secret unit that grew out of the Ministry of Defence to deal with superhumans. The two know of each other, and each trusts the other no further than it trusts anybody else.

What it costs

Those who join are told at the start that the work means the rest of their lives. An agent sees things that the human mind was not made to hold, and he can tell nobody, not his wife, not his doctor, not his priest. Marriages do not last. Many agents drink. Some end their days in hospitals that do not ask what they saw. Others are killed, and their families are told a lie about how.

Those who last learn to live with what they have done as well as what they have seen: false reports, perjury, planted evidence, fires set at night and killings in the dark. The government they serve would put most of them in prison. Delta Green's view is that the government has never been told enough to have an opinion.

The Program and the Outlaws

After the attacks of 11 September 2001 the American government went looking for anybody who knew how to fight an enemy in the dark. Delta Green was brought back into the fold with a budget and official standing, under cover of the war on terror. Majestic 12 was taken over and folded into it. This official Delta Green is called the Program.

Some of the old agents would not go. They held that the Program would study what Delta Green had always destroyed, as Majestic had done. They were not wrong. They carried on as before, without leave, and are known as the Outlaws.

Silent Hill

Delta Green's dealings with Silent Hill, in Maine, are older than its name. In the spring of 1919 P4 sent Navy divers into Toluca Lake after the pleasure boat Little Baroness, lost the November before with fourteen people aboard, a naval officer home from the war among them. The divers found nothing. One of them came up white to the lips, saying that he had seen people standing on the bottom of the lake. He would not go down again.

In the summer of 1983 a narcotics officer of the town died of a failed heart, with no history of heart trouble, not long after its mayor had died the same way. He had been passing what he learnt about the drug PTV to a federal agent, Hollis Tibbetts, who belonged to Delta Green. Tibbetts reached Silent Hill a few days after 13 September 1983. He found a quiet town, a hospital whose director had disappeared and nobody who would say where. In October he burnt the Order's beds of White Claudia, from which the drug was made. They grew again the next summer.

In June 1994 Tibbetts, now Agent Homer of H Cell, came back for Walter Sullivan, the murderer from the Order's orphanage. Sullivan killed himself in his cell before he could be questioned. That night Delta Green and the SCP Foundation met over his body, in the Silent Hill morgue incident. A Foundation officer was killed and Tibbetts was wounded. While they faced each other, the body disappeared. Alphonse closed the file on Silent Hill that summer, and forbade any agent to go back.

Tibbetts went back all the same. In 1997 he read the number cut into a dead schoolboy of South Ashfield, 12121, as the police had not: twelve of twenty-one. He never found out who the rest were to be. In 2003, as an Outlaw, he burnt the beds again a week before the Program's people came to take some away for study.

Delta Green has never known what the Order of Silent Hill worships. Its agents have wondered whether it might be one of the powers they have fought since Innsmouth, or something wishing to be taken for one. It is neither. It is a demon, a lesser spirit of the Devil's following.

The end of Delta Green

The Third World War broke out in 2026. In its chaos the things that Delta Green hunted found it easier than ever to hide, and its agents fought them in secret, as Delta Green had fought the Second World War. It did not survive the end. In 2053 the nuclear exchange destroyed most of the cities where its cells worked. The Program fell with the government it served, and the last Outlaw cells were lost with it. Majestic 12, folded into the Program in 2001, went the same way.

A few of its agents lived through the war, with what they could carry of its files and a copy of the lore of the Aesir, which had come into Delta Green's keeping as the Stargate programme collapsed. They kept the lore classified through the post-atomic horror. From their heirs came Section 31, an idea held in secret by never more than five people inside United Earth's Starfleet, who went on keeping it.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine took the Myst book from Shacklewell House in New Mexico, at Albus Dumbledore's request. In America, he reflected, a thing like that usually drew flies. There was the organisation that would prefer you did not know its name was Delta Green, with their nice suits and their nasty smiles. There was whatever was left of Majestic 12, if anything was, and there was even the SCP Foundation. John had got in and out before any of them had done more than park a van up the road.

pages.title: Majestic 12
infobox: The crash at Roswell, New Mexico
Doubtful to outsiders; alive and at work, by Delta Green's account
The Greys, from the years after Roswell
pages.html:
Majestic 12 is a secret American committee of twelve men, said to have been set up on President Truman's orders in 1947 to deal with the crash at Roswell, New Mexico. By 1994 it was far from clear that anything was left of it. That is how it looks from outside. Delta Green knows better, or believes it does: in its account Majestic 12 is very much alive in 1994, dealing in secret with the Greys and killing to keep them hidden.

Roswell

Something came down near Roswell in July 1947, and the American government has never been entirely frank about what it was. In the trophy room of Shacklewell House, a wizarding house in New Mexico, a lump of twisted grey metal is labelled NO-MAJ FLYING SAUCER (FRAGMENT), ROSWELL, N.M., 1947. John Constantine thought it half a hubcap off a Ford, and he knew a Mi-go who would have had a chuckle about it.

More than one thing came down that summer. By Delta Green's account one of them was a craft carrying small grey beings, all dead but one. Majestic 12 was set up to take charge of the craft, the bodies and the survivor. Another was a wounded stranger, whom the No-Men took into their keeping.

Truman's order

On 24 September 1947 President Truman set up Majestic 12 by a secret order. It was a committee of twelve, answerable to nobody but the President, to take charge of whatever had been found near Roswell and to keep it from the public. Some of its first members had served in Delta Green during the war. At the end of 1947 it set up Project SIGN, the Air Force's study of flying saucer reports, to explain such sightings away.

Each of the twelve heads a project of his own. Majestic 12 has borrowed its methods wherever it could find them, among them those of the CIA's mind-control experiments, MK-ULTRA. It has a recovery unit, BLUE FLY, made up of Air Force paratroops, and a section for killing, NRO DELTA, hidden inside the National Reconnaissance Office.

The Greys

In the years after Roswell, Majestic 12 made contact with the Greys and came to terms with them. It would hide what they did on Earth: the abductions, the examinations and the dead cattle. In return they gave it technology, which its members sold to make themselves rich, with a promise that one day they would bring it into contact with the other peoples of the galaxy. The promise has never been kept.

Delta Green holds that the Greys are the puppets of the Mi-go, who made them to steer the science of the American government, so that Majestic 12 has been the Mi-go's dupe from the start. Majestic 12 believes it is dealing with visitors from another star.

S.H.I.E.L.D., founded in 1965, is not known to have been let into the secret.

Delta Green

Majestic 12 and Delta Green have been rivals since 1947. When Delta Green's operation against the Tcho-Tcho in Cambodia ended in disaster in November 1969, Majestic 12 and Delta Green's other rivals in the government used it to have Delta Green shut down. Delta Green was officially disbanded in 1970, but it went on without leave.

In February 1994, as Delta Green sees it, the rivalry turned to murder. On 25 February Major General Reginald Fairfield, a retired officer who was the informal head of Delta Green, was shot dead at his farm. He had already sent his files on Delta Green's work before 1970 to other members. Delta Green blamed NRO DELTA. Since then it has rebuilt itself as a conspiracy of cells, to fight Majestic 12.

In 1994

To everybody outside it, John Constantine included, it is far from clear in 1994 that anything is left of Majestic 12. Delta Green knows better, or believes it does. In its account Majestic 12 is very much alive, still dealing with the Greys and still killing to keep its secrets.

Afterwards

In the late 1990s the Mi-go fell silent. They cut Majestic 12 off, and it heard no more from the Greys. In 2000 NRO DELTA destroyed SaucerWatch, a society of saucer-watchers that had come too close to the truth.

In 2001, for the only time known, Majestic 12 worked with Delta Green and GRU SV-8, in an operation that broke the Karotechia. After the attacks of 11 September that year it was disgraced, then taken over from within. What remained of it was folded into Delta Green, which the government had taken back with a budget of its own. A company called March Industries took over many of its assets, four members of its committee among them, and keeps an uneasy truce with Delta Green.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine counted whatever was left of Majestic 12, if anything was, among the American groups that a thing like the Myst book usually drew, like flies. The others were Delta Green and the SCP Foundation.

infobox: Delta Green; Majestic 12; the Global Occult Coalition; the Chaos Insurgency
Unknown; its own staff tell several stories
Sites and Areas, each known by a number
Mobile Task Forces, each with a Greek letter, a number and a nickname
Classes A to D; clearances from Level 0 to Level 5
Safe, Euclid, Keter, Thaumiel; Neutralized; Explained
On file since 1939; in the charge of Mobile Task Force Upsilon-6 from 1983
In the Third World War, by 2053
Section 31, an idea that its survivors' heirs carried into Starfleet
pages.html:
The SCP Foundation is a secret organisation that collects dangerous things and locks them away. Its name stands for its motto: Secure, Contain, Protect. It works across the world, outside the law of any country, from hidden facilities known by numbers. It answers to nobody but its own council, the O5, and it writes everything down. It does not know that the wizarding world exists.

The Foundation

Everything it holds gets a number, a cell and a file. Its catalogue runs to dangerous objects, dangerous people and the occasional demon, each graded by how hard it is to hold: Safe, Euclid or Keter. A council known as the O5 runs it. In America it has rivals in the same trade, among them Delta Green and whatever is left of Majestic 12, if anything is.

The Foundation explains itself in three words. To secure is to take a dangerous thing before anybody else can, whether a government, a rival or a fool. To contain is to stop it spreading, by moving it, hiding it or locking it up, and by seeing to it that nobody hears of it. To protect is to keep the world safe from such things, and such things safe from the world, until somebody understands them.

Its people believe that ordinary men and women should be able to live their lives without fear, which means without knowing. The Foundation keeps the dark so that they need not. It does a great deal that would horrify them in the process. Its own Ethics Committee holds, as an article of faith, that the Foundation is not evil.

Beginnings and command

When the Foundation began, it does not say. Its own staff tell several stories of its founding, and none of them believes the others. Its mission was written down by somebody known only as the Administrator. Whether the Administrator is one person, or ever was, nobody below the O5 Council knows.

The O5 Council runs it: thirteen directors known only by numbers, O5-1 to O5-13. Their names are secret even inside the Foundation. None of them may come near anything the Foundation holds, in case it should get at them. Each facility has a Site Director, who answers to the council. Beside them all sits the Ethics Committee, which asks what is being done and why. It can have a researcher reprimanded, demoted or, in the worst cases, put to death.

Sites and task forces

Its facilities are called Sites and Areas, each with a number. They hide behind whatever front will serve: a government laboratory, a private company, a fenced stretch of empty country.

For work outside them it has its Mobile Task Forces, units drawn from across the Foundation for one kind of trouble each. Every task force has a Greek letter, a number and a nickname. Zeta-9, the Mole Rats, goes into caves, tunnels and places whose insides do not agree with their outsides. Beta-7, the Maz Hatters, deals with poisons, plagues and radiation. Alpha-1, the Red Right Hand, answers to the O5 Council alone. The task forces travel as police officers, firemen, soldiers or hospital staff, whichever will be let through the door.

Staff

Its staff are graded twice over. Their clearance runs from Level 0, for the clerks and cleaners who never see anything, to Level 5, which the O5 Council holds with very few others. Even a high clearance gives nobody more than he needs to know. Their class says how close they may come to what the Foundation holds. Class A staff are too valuable to come near it at all. Class D staff are there to be put in front of it.

The D-class are the Foundation's most notorious habit. They are taken from prisons, chiefly from death row, and given the work most likely to kill them. At the end of each month those who are left are given amnestics, drugs that take memory away, or are put to death. The Foundation uses amnestics freely: on its own people, on witnesses, on anybody who has seen too much. It records everything it does to them.

Classes and files

Everything it holds has an object class, which says how hard the thing is to keep, not how dangerous it is. A thing that will stay quiet in a locked box is Safe. A thing that may or may not is Euclid. A thing that will not stay in any box is Keter. A Thaumiel object is itself the box, used to hold something worse, and the Foundation keeps such things very quiet indeed. A thing that has stopped being strange is Neutralized. A thing that was never strange at all is Explained.

Every file takes the same form. First come the item's number and class, then its Special Containment Procedures, then a plain Description. Addenda follow as the years go by: interview logs, incident reports and the logs of expeditions, some into places from which the team never came back. Whatever the reader is not cleared to know is blacked out, or marked as expunged.

Groups of Interest

The Foundation keeps files on its rivals too, and calls them Groups of Interest. The Global Occult Coalition, which claims the backing of the United Nations, destroys what the Foundation would keep. The Chaos Insurgency was founded by former Foundation people, who mean to bring it down. The Serpent's Hand sets free what the Foundation holds. Marshall, Carter and Dark sell such things to the very rich. The Church of the Broken God believes that flesh is a mistake to be put right with machines. Dr Wondertainment makes strange toys.

In America the Foundation keeps a friendly eye on the Unusual Incidents Unit of the FBI, a small, poor office for crimes that nobody can explain. The rest of the Bureau does not take it seriously, which suits the Foundation very well.

Neighbours

In America the Foundation has rivals in its own trade. It thinks Delta Green reckless for burning what ought to be kept. Majestic 12, or whatever is left of it, it leaves well alone. If the Foundation holds anything of the kind that Delta Green fights, it has never said so to Delta Green.

It keeps out of the way of S.H.I.E.L.D., which fights in the open against enemies the whole world can see. It keeps out of the way of the costumed heroes, too. Nothing that has been seen by millions can be contained, and the Foundation has never tried. Its work begins where nobody has noticed anything. The heroes, for their part, have had no reason to notice the Foundation, which is how it likes things. The Patriots, who believed that they ran America, never ran the Foundation. Nothing on record shows that either ever troubled the other.

It knows nothing of the wizarding world, which hides behind the Statute of Secrecy, its charms and its Memory Charms. These work on the Foundation's people exactly as they do on every other No-Maj. What little magic comes to the Foundation's notice goes into a file as one more anomaly, without a name. In August 1993 a black van stood up the road from the Cleft in New Mexico, where the wizard John Constantine walked past it twice. If it was the Foundation's, it saw a man in a coat out for a stroll and wrote down nothing worth reading.

Silent Hill

The Foundation's file on Silent Hill, in Maine, is one of its longer ones. It has a number, which the Foundation has never let out. Inside the file the town is called the Toluca locus.

The file was opened in 1939, after something happened on Toluca Lake that the town will not talk about. The Foundation's agent found the pages that told of it already torn out of the town's history. In the autumn of 1976, after the fire that took six homes, an analyst counted the visitors to Silent Hill who had never gone home. There were far more than any lakeside resort could explain. The Foundation put a listening post on the Brahms road, in a building got up as a highway depot, and classed the town Euclid.

On the night of 12 September 1983 the post logged every line out of the town going dead at once. It logged a car and a police motorcycle going in. Its orders were to observe, and by the time new orders came the town was quiet again. In October a team of Zeta-9 went in by day with three D-class on lines. Of the eight people who walked into the fog, four did not come back. A fifth came back raving of rust, sirens and his own dead. All five had killed somebody. The three who came back unharmed had seen nothing but empty streets. The Foundation classed the town Keter. It formed Mobile Task Force Upsilon-6 for Silent Hill alone, from people who had never harmed anybody.

Upsilon-6 took White Claudia seed into containment in 1984, from beds that somebody else had burnt. On the night of 22 June 1994 it met Delta Green over the body of Walter Sullivan, in the Silent Hill morgue incident. It lost a man there, and the body as well. In the spring of 2002 it surveyed Room 302 of South Ashfield Heights, found nothing and closed the file on the flat. In the summer of 2004 it took Walter Sullivan's body from the coroner at South Ashfield, ten years late.

That year the Foundation reclassed Silent Hill as Euclid. The addendum gives the reason: the town contains itself better than the Foundation can. Its procedures since have been to watch the roads, send nobody in who has ever killed and keep the public record quiet, which the town does very well on its own.

The file does not say what the Order of Silent Hill worships. It records 'an entity reported by the local religious group', and notes that its existence has never been confirmed. It exists. It is a demon, a lesser spirit of the Devil's following.

The end of the Foundation

The Foundation outlasted most governments, but not the Third World War. As the war spread its sites were lost one by one, to the fighting and to the breaches that followed when their power failed. The nuclear exchange of 2053 destroyed the rest, with the O5 Council. Nothing that the world could see marked its passing, which was how it had always worked.

Some of its people lived, with copies of its files and of the lore of the Aesir, which the Foundation had taken into containment as the Stargate programme collapsed. The file that told where the lore had come from was lost with its site. They went on writing things down through the post-atomic horror, and they kept the lore classified. From their heirs came Section 31, an idea held in secret by never more than five people inside United Earth's Starfleet.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, John Constantine reflected that in America a thing like the Myst linking book usually drew flies. The SCP Foundation was one of them: 'those nutters with their cells, their numbers and their filing cabinets', who collected dangerous things the way little boys collected football cards. He was gone from New Mexico with the book before the Foundation or any of its rivals had done more than park a van up the road.

pages.title: The watchers in the black van
infobox: A mile from the Cleft, New Mexico
A black van with no number plates
pages.html:
The watchers in the black van were the unknown people in a black van with no number plates, parked with its lights off beside the road a mile from the Cleft, in August 1993. Nobody knows who they were.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, on his way to Shacklewell House, John Constantine passed the dig at the Cleft. A mile further on stood the van, at the side of the road with its lights off. He walked past it without turning his head, though he could feel somebody watching him through the tinted glass. At sunrise, coming back with the book, he found it still waiting where he had left it. He lit a cigarette and gave it a cheery little wave as he went by. Nobody in it so much as turned a head.

America has several outfits that collect dangerous things, among them Delta Green, whatever is left of Majestic 12 and the SCP Foundation. Constantine was in and out before any of them had done more than park a van up the road.

pages.title: The Cleft dig
aliases: the Muggles who are digging out there
infobox: John Loftin, Elias Zandi, Dr Richard Watson
pages.html:
The Cleft dig is the small, quiet excavation in the New Mexico desert that has been opening up the lost cavern of D'ni since 1988. It is run by a handful of well-meaning amateurs with clipboards, which in John Constantine's experience is the most dangerous combination in the world.

History

In 1987 the artefact hunter John Loftin found tunnels under the desert, with great digging machines standing in them that nobody living had built. On 19 March 1988 he took Elias Zandi down, and the tunnels led them to D'ni. Zandi had the money. He brought in Dr Richard Watson, and the three of them began to explore the cavern.

In 1993 there was not much to see above ground: a wire fence, a hand-painted sign about a geological survey, a couple of tents, a caravan and a ladder going down into a deep crack in the earth. Things were coming up out of the hole all the same, books among them. Most went straight out of the back door to whoever would pay for them. One, the linking book to Myst Island, was sold to Ephraim Shacklewell for fifty dollars. The diggers founded the D'ni Restoration Council in 1997.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, Constantine passed the dig at night on his way to Shacklewell House. Somewhere under it, his reading said, there was a cavern big enough to hold a city, and a city still in it.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Hermione told Harry and Ron that the Muggles with the calling had one half of the D'ni story, while the wizarding world had the other. She feared that the Muggles digging in New Mexico might put the two halves together before anybody else did.

pages.title: Fianna
infobox: The Celtic peoples and their descendants
pages.html:
The Fianna are one of the thirteen tribes of the Garou, the tribe of the Celtic lands. They are bards, poets and warriors. They keep the oldest songs of their people, and they fight the Wyrm with joy. The pack that took in Remus Lupin in the hills of mid-Wales was mostly Fianna.

Totem and ways

The Fianna follow Stag, the spirit of the wild hunt, of pride and of the greenwood. They are passionate in everything: in drink, in love, in grief and in battle. Galliards are especially honoured among them, for their songs and stories carry the history of the Garou from before the coming of writing. The Fianna are generous hosts and terrible enemies, slow to forget an insult but quick to forgive a friend. Their rites are full of music.

The Fianna are close to the Wyld and to the old powers of their islands. They are on easier terms than most Garou with the Fair Folk who once walked there. They share their name with the war-band of Fionn mac Cumhaill in the old Irish tales. Their Kinfolk are the Irish, the Scots and the Welsh, with all their descendants across the world.

Homelands and history

The tribe's heart is in Ireland, Scotland and Wales. Its oldest caerns lie among standing stones, holy wells and hollow hills. Its songs tell of ancient wars in Ireland against the Fomorians, the monstrous servants of the Wyrm. They tell, too, of the long feud with the Get of Fenris, which began with the Viking raids. When the Celtic peoples crossed the sea to America and elsewhere, the Fianna went with them. They are now found wherever the Irish and the Scots have made their homes.

Place in the world

Among the tribes the Fianna are respected for their courage and their lore. They are teased for their tempers and their drinking. Like other Garou they have little love for wizards, who in their view play with the Wyrm's fire. Their sacred places in the hills, the rings of stones and the springs in old woods, are best left untouched by any witch or wizard who comes across them.

In the saga

After the deaths of James and Lily Potter in 1981, Remus Lupin left the wizarding world for years. In the end he found a pack in the hills of mid-Wales, mostly Fianna. They were good people in their way, and did good work. Above one village a quarry had been poisoning a whole valley for thirty years, and things that were no longer animals had crawled out of its slag heaps. The pack put them back where they came from.

The pack still sends for Lupin now and then. It did at Christmas 1993, when Albus Dumbledore told the Hogwarts table that Lupin was unwell. It never let him forget, though, for a single day, that he was biteborn, bitten rather than born, which the tribes hold to be no true Garou. He was a wizard too, which was worse. Lupin told Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger about the pack in June 1994.

pages.title: Shacklewell family
pages.html:
The Shacklewells are an American pure-blood wizarding family. They have been in America since a great-great-grandfather stepped off a ship in Boston with a wand in his pocket and a price on his head. For most of that time they were not rich.

Fortune

The money came in the 1960s, after Rappaport's Law was repealed. Ephraim Shacklewell's father sold a scouring potion to the copper mines of Arizona as a miracle cleaning fluid, through a string of front companies. MACUSA never quite managed to prove it.

Ephraim has spent the money since on Shacklewell House, a vast pink adobe mansion in the Spanish style, hidden in the New Mexico desert behind the look of a derelict filling station. It has a fountain shaped like a Thunderbird, a swimming pool shaped like a Golden Snitch and the most expensive wards that MACUSA's own security men could be bribed into building. In his trophy room he kept the D'ni linking book to Myst Island, which he had bought for fifty dollars from a man who dug it out of the Cleft.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, before he burgled Shacklewell House in August 1993, John Constantine did his reading on the family. They were pure-blood all right, he concluded, but the money was new. Ephraim, who could never sleep, caught him in the trophy room, wearing a silk dressing gown and a hairnet. John passed himself off as an officer of MACUSA. He signed the receipt J. Lennon and left by the front door with the book, while Ephraim waved him off from the step.

pages.title: Sirius Black's wooden cross
infobox: Two splinters of grey bed-frame wood, bound with thread from a blanket
pages.html:
Sirius Black's wooden cross was the cross he made for himself in his cell in Azkaban. It was two splinters of grey wood from his bed-frame, bound together crosswise with a thread pulled from his blanket, and it hung on a dirty string. He clung to it for twelve years. He lost it in June 1994, on the night his godson learnt the truth about him.

Faith in Azkaban

Sirius had never believed in God. That had been Lily, he said, and her mother Susan before her, who made sure her children were godly. Remus went to Him first, after Lily and James were married. Then James started on it too, and so, after a fashion, did Peter Pettigrew.

In Azkaban Sirius had nothing else: not a single happy memory, only the things Lily used to say to him. He made the cross from two splinters of his bed frame and held on to it like a life raft. His thumb rubbed it for years, until the centre was worn smooth and dark.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Seventeen, the cross fell out of Black's robes while Harry fought him in the Shrieking Shack. It lay in the dust by his collar in a blade of moonlight: two splinters of bed frame, bound crosswise with a bit of thread, very small and plain.

In Chapter Eighteen, telling Harry that he had as good as killed Lily and James by persuading them to change their Secret-Keeper, Black fished the cross out from the neck of his robes. He pressed it to his mouth, murmuring into it. My fault... my fault... my most grievous fault... Later, when Hermione asked how he had got out of Azkaban without Dark Magic, he drew the little cross out on its dirty string and held it up in the moonlight. Harry saw it properly for the first time. 'I... I never used to believe in it. God... and all that. That was all Lily.' He had held on to it, he said, like a life raft.

In Chapter Nineteen, the string snapped somewhere in Black's fight with the Garou. By the time he was a man again, crouched at the water's edge, the cross was gone.

In Chapter Twenty-One, Harry found Sirius in the ruined library on Myst Island. As Sirius got up off the floor, his hand went to the place over his heart and closed on nothing. He had lost it down by the lake, he told Harry, when the dementors came. 'Never mind. I don't suppose He needs it to find me.'

pages.title: Remus Lupin's cross
infobox: Plain wood, on a leather cord
pages.html:
Remus Lupin's cross is a little plain wooden cross on a leather cord, which Lupin wore under his shirt from the day James and Lily Potter were married. On the night of the full moon in June 1994 it fell from his neck as he changed, and Harry Potter held it up to the Garou. At the end of that term Lupin gave it to Harry to keep, and Harry has worn it ever since.

The cross

Lupin came to faith through Lily Potter after she married James, the first of the friends to follow her. He has worn a cross ever since their wedding. It has to be wooden, because silver burns him. He keeps a box of them at home, and can easily carve another.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Eighteen, in the Shrieking Shack, with the wolf gnawing at him from the inside, Lupin's hand crept up to his collar. It closed round the cross under his shirt. Harry saw his lips move, and guessed the words. Deliver us from evil.

In Chapter Nineteen, out on the grass under the full moon, the cord snapped as his neck thickened in the change. The cross flew out of his collar and came to rest beside Harry's hand. Harry snatched it up and shoved it into his pocket. When the Garou came for him, he held the cross up between himself and the creature, although he did not even know whether he believed in God. Its nostrils twitched at the scent of it, and for a moment Harry thought he saw Lupin again, far down in its yellow eyes. Whatever it smelt on Harry was stronger than the cross.

In Chapter Twenty, the cross went warm in Harry's inside pocket just before his shield turned white. Afterwards, in the Forest, he found it still faintly warm. He pressed it into Lupin's cold hand, then closed the fingers round it one at a time.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, packing to leave Hogwarts, Lupin drew the mended cord over his head and gave the cross to Harry. 'I think this one would rather go with you. It seems to work rather better in your pocket than it ever did round my neck.'

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry woke from a dream in the summer of 1994 holding the cross so hard that its edges had bitten red marks into his palm. It was warm. In Chapter Two he remembered a night at the end of July when his lamp went out and the moon lit his book until he reached the end of the chapter. The cross had been warm against his chest the whole time.

pages.title: The Myst linking book
aliases: the Linking Book for Myst Island
the book in the Tesco bag
infobox: MYST; Myst; The Myst Island linking book

Atrus writer
John Constantine stole it for Dumbledore
Tall, thick and heavy; cracked brown leather; MYST in tarnished gold
Atrus; Ephraim Shacklewell (as he believed); held for Atrus by Albus Dumbledore
pages.html:
The Myst linking book is the linking book for Myst Island, written by Atrus. It came out of the excavation of the D'ni cavern and was sold for fifty dollars to an American wizard collector. In the summer of 1993 John Constantine stole it back for Albus Dumbledore, carrying it across Britain in a Tesco carrier bag. In June 1994 it carried Sirius Black out of Flitwick's office to Myst Island. Harry, Hermione and Dracina followed.

Description

The book is big, old and heavy, a tall, thick volume bound in brown leather that has cracked with age, its corners rubbed pale. Across the front, in tarnished gold, is the single word MYST. Inside are thick, creamy pages. The left-hand page is blank. On the right is a dark oblong like a little window, and in it a picture moves. It shows a greenish grey sea seen from high above. The view sweeps in towards an island with dark pines, a wooden dock, the mast of a sunken ship, an enormous stone gear half buried on the hill and a squat stone clock tower standing in the water. Through thin plastic the panel shows as a soft greenish flicker, like a television left on in another room. When the book falls open, its picture pulls at the onlooker like a current, inviting him to put out his hand.

History

Atrus wrote the book for Myst Island, the Age his grandmother Anna had written as a home for the family. When he escaped Riven by leaping into the Star Fissure, he linked to Myst as he fell. The book went on falling, out of Riven and down to Earth. He had meant it to be destroyed, and it troubled him to think whose hands might one day hold it. Early in the nineteenth century a traveller from the surface found it. He laid his hand on the picture and arrived on the island's dock with nothing in his hands. The book stayed behind, as such books do.

In the twentieth century it came out of the excavation of the D'ni cavern. Like a great many things from that dig, it went out of the back door. A digger sold it for fifty dollars to Ephraim Shacklewell, a rich pure-blood wizard of Shacklewell House in New Mexico. He put it on a red velvet cushion in the last glass case of his trophy room, next to a piece of hubcap labelled as a Roswell flying saucer. Its card read NO-MAJ PICTURE BOOK (NATIVE?). CHARMED PHOTOGRAPH INSIDE, MOVES. FROM THE DIG. $50. He never touched it.

In the summer of 1993 Dumbledore sent an owl to John Constantine in a Soho pub. The letter, in green ink, asked him to bring the book to Hogwarts before the middle of August, without opening it or looking at it for longer than he must. The job was meant to square an old account between them over a stolen Deluminator. Constantine buried his wand in the desert. He slipped past the wards of Shacklewell House with salt, chalk, his own blood and a Hand of Glory, then took the book. It fell open in his hands and pulled at him; he slammed it shut. He left a Jackie Collins paperback on the cushion in its place. When Shacklewell caught him, he passed himself off as an officer of MACUSA and wrote him a receipt signed J. Lennon.
