The Rolling Stones are a London band, formed in 1962, who made their name playing the blues harder and louder than anybody else in Britain. They were what John Constantine played most often at Hogwarts.

The band

Mick Jagger and Keith Richards had known each other since primary school in Dartford. With Brian Jones, Bill Wyman and Charlie Watts they became the rough answer to the Beatles. Jones died in 1969, but the Stones carried on without him, and in 1994 they are still going.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, John Constantine remembered the old Dansette record player he had kept in an empty classroom on the third floor at Hogwarts in the 1960s. He had charmed it, with a great deal of swearing, to run without electricity. He played the Stones on it, mostly, with some blues, and a few things that would not have a name for another ten years.

pages.title: Jackie Collins
infobox: Bestsellers about the rich and famous of Hollywood
pages.html:
Jackie Collins is an English novelist whose bestsellers about the rich, famous and badly behaved of Hollywood are sold on every railway bookstall in Britain. In 1993 one battered copy took the place of the Myst book on a red velvet cushion, in a glass case in New Mexico.

Life

She was born in London in 1937, the younger sister of Joan Collins. Her first novel, The World Is Full of Married Men, came out in 1968 to a good deal of disapproval, which did its sales no harm at all.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, John Constantine broke into Ephraim Shacklewell's trophy room in New Mexico to steal the Myst book. He had bought a rather battered Jackie Collins at Lime Street station for exactly this purpose. He laid it on the red velvet cushion where the book had been, and closed the lid of the case. Fair swap, he thought. It's a better read, anyway.

pages.title: Wild Bill
infobox: A pair of boots in Ephraim Shacklewell's trophy room
pages.html:
Wild Bill was somebody whose boots, it is said, ended up in Ephraim Shacklewell's trophy room in New Mexico. The most famous man of the American West to go by that name was James Butler Hickok, the scout, lawman and gunfighter.

Hickok

Hickok scouted for the Union army in the Civil War and later kept the peace as marshal of Abilene, in Kansas. In August 1876 he was shot from behind at a card table in Deadwood, holding aces and eights, the dead man's hand.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, in August 1993, John Constantine read the brass labels on Shacklewell's glass cases by the light of a Hand of Glory. A fragment of a flying saucer from Roswell was half a hubcap off a Ford. Further along were a stuffed jackalope, a jar of something that moved and a pair of boots that had belonged to somebody called Wild Bill. Given the hubcap, whether they were ever Hickok's is anybody's guess.

pages.title: Yeesha
aliases: the slim figure in a long hooded robe
the woman Sirius had been talking to
infobox:
Atrus father
Sirius Black companion on Myst
Recovering the small leather linking book, June 1994
pages.html:
Yeesha is the daughter of Atrus and Catherine. She was born in 1815 and is still alive in the twentieth century, because D'ni lives are long. In June 1994 she kept Sirius Black company in the ruined library on Myst Island. After Harry Potter's party had gone, she took back the small leather linking book her father had written long before. In August 1994, as a favour to Sirius, she watched over Harry Potter, who glimpsed her twice in shimmering air without knowing who she was.

Childhood

Yeesha was born in 1815 on Tomahna, the Age where her parents made their home after the Stranger rescued her mother from Riven. She was a baby in 1816, when Saavedro, a man whose world her brothers had ruined, broke into Tomahna and stole the book of Releeshahn, the Age her father had written for the D'ni survivors. The Stranger recovered it.

About ten years later her brothers, released after twenty years in separate prison Ages, struck at the family again. Sirrus kidnapped Yeesha. Achenar, who had come to regret what he had been, died saving her. Sirrus died too. She was a dreamer, like her mother.

Later life

Being of D'ni descent through her father, Yeesha has lived far beyond any ordinary human span. She grew into a strange, solemn woman who speaks in riddles and carries a deep sorrow. She moves between worlds as she pleases. She has given her life to the remnant of D'ni and to the Bahro, the beings the D'ni once enslaved, whom she calls the Least.

The D'ni had bound the Bahro by means of a stone Tablet, and its holder could command them. A prophecy spoke of a Grower who would one day restore D'ni, and Yeesha came to believe that she was that person. She unlocked the Tablet but chose wrongly with it, and could no longer use it. In the end the Tablet was given to the Bahro themselves, and they were freed.

It was Yeesha who gave her mother's journals to the brothers Rand and Robyn Miller of Cyan, in America. From them came the Muggle computer game Myst, released in 1993, and the games that followed it. She meant them to draw people of D'ni blood to the Cleft and the D'ni caverns under New Mexico.

She uses the D'ni word Shorah, which means peace. It also means goodbye, and other things besides.

Relationships

Atrus is her father, and the small leather book she recovered was his. Her mother is Catherine. Her brothers were Sirrus and Achenar. Sirius Black is the only wizard known to have spent time in her company, and he remembers her fondly. In the summer of 1994 he asked her to watch over Harry, and she did so as a favour to him.

In the saga

Book 3: In June 1994 Sirius Black linked to Myst Island from Flitwick's office to escape the dementors. He took refuge in the ruined library and found a woman there. She kept him company. She talked in riddles half the time, and was dreadfully sad about something he never found out. She had a lovely laugh when he could get it out of her. She reminded him of his cousin Bella, before Bella went mad. He never learnt her name.

When Harry arrived she was gone from the corner beside the empty stone stands. Harry privately thought Sirius had imagined her. After the four of them had linked home, the air in the corner shivered like air over a hot road, and she was standing there again. She picked up the little book Harry had dropped and knew it. Her father had written it long ago for a stranger who had done him a very great service, and it had been lost to him for longer than she had been alive. She tucked it into her robe and looked at the place where Sirius had sat. Then she said 'Shorah' softly to nobody at all, so that it sounded rather like a promise, and stepped sideways out of the world.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Two: Hermione Granger searched the whole of the game Myst for the woman Sirius had described, and could not find her. She is not in it: Yeesha was born after the events the game retells.

Book Four, Chapter Four: in the summer of 1994 Sirius asked Yeesha to watch over Harry, and she did so as a favour to him. In the middle of the afternoon of 21 August the air beside the lamp post outside number five, Privet Drive, shimmered like air over a hot road. For a moment somebody seemed to stand in it, perfectly still, looking up at Harry's window. Harry blinked, and there was nothing there but the lamp post. Thinking of Sirius afterwards, he remembered the woman in the library on Myst, whom Sirius had tried to introduce to them all, though nobody but Sirius ever saw her. When Sirius's very good company was mentioned at dinner, Hermione gazed thoughtfully into the dark, and Harry wondered whether she was thinking of Sirius's sad woman in the library.

That night, at the Burrow, Crookshanks sat at the edge of the orchard with his tail lashing, staring at the hill beyond the hedge. On the hilltop, against the stars, a slim figure in a long hooded robe stood in shimmering air, though the night had turned cool. It seemed to be holding a small book. Harry felt that it was looking straight at him, and that it was sad about something. When he blinked, the hilltop was empty.

In their own words

Shorah.Yeesha · B3 Ch21

pages.title: Fleamont Potter
infobox:
James Potter son (in the dream)
Euphemia Potter wife (in the dream)
Harry Potter grandson (in the dream)
Before Harry's birth, of dragon pox
pages.html:
Fleamont Potter was the father of James Potter and the grandfather of Harry Potter. He was a wizard of the ancient Potter line, and he multiplied the family's fortune many times over with Sleekeazy's Hair Potion. Harry had never heard his name until he dreamt it in August 1994.

Life

Fleamont came of the house of Potter, which descends from King Arthur Pendragon. His odd first name was an old family surname, given to him so that it should not die out. His father, Henry Potter, a member of the Wizengamot, caused an uproar during the Great War by publicly condemning the Minister for Magic, Archer Evermonde, who had forbidden wizards to help the Muggles.

Fleamont invented Sleekeazy's Hair Potion, which is still on sale, and it made the Potters far richer than they had ever been. He and his wife Euphemia had their only son, James, late in life, when they had given up hope of children. They loved him dearly. When James's friend Sirius Black ran away from home at sixteen, the Potters took him in and treated him as a second son.

Fleamont and Euphemia died of dragon pox, within days of each other, before their grandson was born. Harry knows nothing about his father's family.

In Harry's dream

In Harry's dream of August 1994 an old man sat at the head of the table in the house on the hill. He was tall and thin, with a long, clever face under a thick mane of white hair, combed straight back so smoothly that it gleamed like metal. On the sideboard behind him stood a row of little glass jars labelled Sleekeazy's. In the dream Harry knew him as his grandfather Fleamont, a name he had never heard before in his life.

The old man's pale eyes rested on Harry for a moment, then slid off him again, as though Harry were a stain on the wallpaper. Then he rose to his feet, very tall and very angry: 'Get out of my house this instant, you filthy little guttersnipe, or I shall call the police!' Harry tortured him with the Cruciatus Curse, then killed him with the Killing Curse.

The man in the dream was not Fleamont. The dream was Lord Voldemort's memory of murdering his Muggle grandfather, Thomas Riddle, in the summer of 1943, with Harry's family put in the places of the Riddles.

In their own words

Get out of my house this instant, you filthy little guttersnipe, or I shall call the police!Fleamont Potter (in Harry's dream) · B4 Ch1

pages.title: Euphemia Potter
infobox:
Fleamont Potter husband (in the dream)
James Potter son (in the dream)
Before Harry's birth, of dragon pox
pages.html:
Euphemia Potter was the wife of Fleamont Potter and the mother of James Potter. She was also the grandmother of Harry Potter, though she did not live to see him.

Life

Euphemia married into the old wizarding family of Potter, whose fortune her husband multiplied many times over with Sleekeazy's Hair Potion. She and Fleamont had their only child, James, late in life, after they had given up hope of a family. They doted on him. Their house was always open to his friends. When Sirius Black ran away from his own family at sixteen, the Potters took him in as a second son.

Both of them died of dragon pox, within days of each other, before Harry was born. Their gold passed to James, and from James to his son.

In Harry's dream

In Harry's dream of August 1994 an old woman sat at the foot of the table in the house on the hill. She wore a grey silk dress with a long rope of pearls round her neck, and her hair was piled up on top of her head. She had a small, tight, disapproving mouth, very like Aunt Petunia's, and she was cutting her meat into tiny pieces. Aunt Marge, squeezed into a maid's black dress with a frilly apron, went on pouring gravy on to her plate until it ran over the edge, across the white cloth. Harry knew that the old woman was his grandmother, and that her name was Euphemia. Without lifting her eyes from her plate, she told James that there was a boy in the doorway, then said it again.

When Harry turned his wand on the family, Euphemia shrieked, then tried to run. She got as far as the curtains before the curse hit her in the back. Her pearls snapped and went rolling away across the carpet. She died in the corner by the fireplace, holding up both thin old hands in front of her face.

The woman was not Euphemia. The dream was Lord Voldemort's memory of murdering his Muggle grandmother, Mary Riddle, and the rest of his father's family in 1943, with Harry's family put in their places.

In their own words

James. There is a boy. In the doorway.Euphemia Potter (in Harry's dream) · B4 Ch1

pages.title: Juniper
pages.html:
Juniper is Dracina Malfoy's owl, a small, brown and thoroughly unremarkable bird. His great virtue is that nobody ever looks at him twice.

Description

Juniper is a small, dull brown male owl. He could hardly be less like Ganymede, the great eagle owl that belongs to Dracina's mother and brings Dracina's parcels from home. Lucius Malfoy reads Vincent Crabbe's post, but he has never once troubled to read Juniper's.

The secret post

On the Hogwarts Express going home in June 1994, Dracina secretly pressed a tiny folded note into Harry Potter's hand. In it she described her owl: 'He's small, brown and dull. Nobody ever looks twice at him.' Harry was to address any letters to Juniper, not to her, since her father never reads Juniper's post. The arrangement let the two of them go on writing to each other in spite of Lucius's ban. On the morning of Harry's fourteenth birthday, 31 July 1994, Juniper brought Dracina's letter to Number Four, Privet Drive.

That letter told Harry to answer the question 'How are you?' properly. It remarked that he had looked thin on the train, and it ended: 'P.S. Burn this. P.P.S. Don't forget me.' It also reported that Lucius kept asking after Harry, that Narcissa was being most helpful in covering for her daughter, and that Pansy Parkinson had developed a sudden passion for the Chudley Cannons.

pages.title: Pigwidgeon
infobox:
Ron Weasley owner
Sirius Black former owner
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (July 1999)
About the size of a tennis ball
A little cage in Ron's attic bedroom at the Burrow
pages.html:
Pigwidgeon, Pig for short, is a tiny, hyperactive grey owl about the size of a tennis ball. Sirius Black sent him to Harry Potter in June 1994, and Ron Weasley adopted him in place of the rat that Sirius had cost him.

Description

Pig is a scops owl, small enough to sit in the palm of a hand, and wildly excitable, never more so than when he has just delivered a letter. To Harry he looks rather like a tennis ball with wings. Ginny Weasley gave him the name Pigwidgeon. Ron thought it a stupid name and shortened it to Pig, although, as Harry noticed, nothing in the world could have looked less like a pig. He is friendly in his own fashion: when he nips somebody's finger, he seems to think it a kindness.

In the saga

Sirius sent the little owl after the Hogwarts Express at the end of term in June 1994. He came struggling along with a letter for Harry that was far too big for so small a bird. The wind of the train kept knocking him head over heels. Each time, he righted himself and came gallantly on. Harry pulled the window down and caught him, which felt like catching a very fluffy Snitch. The owl dropped the letter on Harry's seat, then shot round and round the compartment, hooting shrilly, plainly delighted with himself for having got there at all. Up on the luggage rack, Hedwig clicked her beak at him in dignified disapproval. When Crookshanks's great yellow eyes began to follow his every swoop, Ron grabbed him out of the air.

In the letter Sirius admitted to some doubt about the owl's reliability; still, he was the best Sirius could find, and he had seemed eager for the job. In a postscript, since it was Sirius's fault that Ron no longer had a rat, he offered the owl to Ron. Ron held him out for Crookshanks to sniff and asked the cat whether he was definitely an owl. Crookshanks purred, which was good enough for Ron.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on 20 August 1994, Pig brought Ron's letter to Privet Drive. He bounced off the side of Harry's head, then zoomed round the room like a firework somebody had let off indoors, bursting with pride at having found the right person. While Harry wrote his reply, the owl perched on Hedwig's cage, and she looked up at him coldly, as though daring him to come one inch closer. Tying the note on was hard work, because he would not stop hopping up and down. The moment it was fastened he shot out of the window with Harry's answer, back to the Burrow.

In Chapter Four Harry found Pig bouncing about in a little cage in Ron's attic bedroom, twittering his head off. Ron explained that Ginny had named him Pigwidgeon. He had tried to change it, but it was too late, because the owl would answer to nothing else. Ron kept him upstairs because he annoyed Errol and Hermes. He annoyed Ron too, Ron claimed, though Harry did not believe a word of it.

That night Pig shot out of his cage, bounced twice off the ceiling and twittered with joy. He flew north over the dark orchard with Ron's three-page letter, headed OPERATION GET IT OVER WITH, to Pansy Parkinson.

In Chapter Five the plan reached Pansy at half past eleven, and her answer was back before four in the morning. Reading it, Ron reminded himself how much he owed Harry, who had snatched Pig out of the air for him on the train.

pages.title: The boa constrictor from the zoo
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
At the zoo, June 1991; in Harry Potter's dream, summer 1994
pages.html:
The boa constrictor from the zoo is the great, thick, brown and gold snake that winked at Harry Potter through the glass on Dudley Dursley's birthday, when Harry was ten. In the summer of 1994 it came back to Harry in a dream, dead.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry dreamt that he came through a wood to a shack whose letter box had been nailed shut with planks, the way Uncle Vernon had once nailed up the letter box at Privet Drive. The boa was nailed to the door. It hung upside down by a nail through the end of its tail, longer than Harry was tall, with its head nearly touching the step. It was quite dead. Its eyes were open. As Harry stood looking at it, its mouth moved.

'Thanksss,' it whispered. 'Thanksss, amigo.'

When Harry pushed the door open, the snake swung with it.

In their own words

Thanksss. Thanksss, amigo.The boa constrictor from the zoo (in Harry's dream) · B4 Ch1

pages.title: Williamson
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
pages.html:
Williamson is an Auror of the Ministry of Magic. On the night of 6 June 1994 Cornelius Fudge sent him and Dawlish up to Professor Flitwick's office on the seventh floor at Hogwarts, where Sirius Black had been left locked in to wait for the dementors. The two of them opened the door and found the room empty.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, Fudge wondered aloud to Severus Snape how Black could have vanished from a locked room. Snape named the Aurors Fudge had sent up: 'Dawlish and Williamson. They opened the door a good while before the Headmaster was due back up there. They were the ones who found the room empty.' Harry, listening on the stairs, realised that every word of it was true. All the same it was a lie, because of everything Snape had left out. Snape was covering for Albus Dumbledore, and he hated doing it.

pages.title: The Hufflepuff boy on the frozen lake
infobox: Walked out on the frozen lake, January 1994
pages.html:
The Hufflepuff boy on the frozen lake is the little Hufflepuff who walked out across the frozen lake at Hogwarts in January 1994, as if the ice were a floor, much further than anybody should have gone. Then he looked down, and went straight through.

Peter on the water

The boy's walk mirrored Peter's on the Sea of Galilee. One night in a storm the disciples saw Christ walking towards their boat on the water, and Peter climbed out to go to Him. He walked on the water until he saw the wind and the waves. Then he was afraid, and began to sink. Christ caught him by the hand: "O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?"

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, in January 1994, the boy walked thirty feet out on the ice before he looked down and went through. An enormous sixth-year Hufflepuff pulled him out.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, the day after Harry Potter cast his Patronus by the lake, he went with Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger to see the Fat Friar. The Friar told him it was not his memory that had done it, but the doubt going out of him: he had stopped looking down. Then he told him the story of Peter. Harry described the boy on the lake: somebody had pulled him out, and said, "You were fine till you looked down." He asked whether it had been a sign meant for him. The Friar laughed. "If He went to the trouble of dunking a Hufflepuff in the lake on your account, you must be a very special case indeed." When Harry said that perhaps he was just thick, the Friar grew serious. That, he said, was the doubt: the very thing that had made Peter sink.

pages.title: The first-year who wanted to touch the scar
pages.html:
The first-year who wanted to touch the scar is Mary, a Hufflepuff. In February 1994 she would not believe that a cut through her friend Lizzie's arm had healed until she had put her fingers on the mark, and then she believed. It was the doubt of the apostle Thomas over again: he would not believe that Christ was risen until he had put his finger into the print of the nails.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, in the first week of February 1994, two first-year Hufflepuffs came out from between the library shelves, arguing. Lizzie's forearm had been cut right through, and Madam Pomfrey had healed it in about four seconds. Mary did not believe that a cut could go all the way through somebody's arm on Tuesday and be gone by Friday. "I want to touch it," she said. She took her friend's wrist, quite seriously, like a healer, and pressed two fingers into the thin white line. "Oh," she said. "I'm sorry, Lizzie. All right. I believe you."

Harry Potter watched it all. He had been about to ask Dracina Malfoy about a Ministry letter he had built six weeks of suspicion on, and it struck him that he had never once asked to touch the thing. He told her it would keep.

pages.title: The Ravenclaw girl with the fleece
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 12
A wet fleece on dry stone, then the other way about
pages.html:
The Ravenclaw girl with the fleece is a sixth-year whom Harry Potter found on the front steps of the castle in his third year, testing a fleece that was wet on dry stone. She would not believe it until she had seen it twice, the other way about the second time.

Gideon's fleece

Her test was the one Gideon put to God before he went out against the Midianites. He asked for dew on a fleece only, with the ground dry all round it. Then he asked for the same sign reversed, the fleece dry on wet ground. God gave him both. The girl on the steps wanted exactly the same before she would believe.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, on an evening in late February 1994, Harry came on her outside the oak doors, lying flat on her stomach with a lantern and a notebook. She had had the fleece out for two hours. It was soaked, though there was no dew, while the flagstones round it were bone dry. She meant to do it the other way round the next night, and only then would she believe it.

pages.title: The Peverell brother who received the Cloak
infobox: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (21 July 2007)
pages.html:
The Peverell brother who received the Cloak was Ignotus Peverell, the youngest of the three brothers of the old tale, to whom Death handed over his own Cloak of Invisibility. The Pendragons descend directly from him, and through them the Potters.

The tale

In the tale, Death met the three brothers on a bridge they had made by magic over a dangerous river, and offered each of them a reward. Ignotus, the humblest and the wisest, asked for something that would let him leave without Death following him. He lived to a great age. When he was very old he gave the Cloak to his son, then greeted Death as an old friend.

The line

The Cloak came down his line intact: Peverell, Pendragon, Potter. King Arthur was of it. Harry Potter keeps the Cloak in his trunk, and does not know that he is a Peverell.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, Harry found the Cloak among his Christmas presents in 1991, with an unsigned note: 'Your father left this in my keeping before he died. It's time it came back to you. Use it well.' In Chapter Thirteen Dumbledore told him that James had used it 'mainly for sneaking down to the kitchens for food'.

pages.title: The gardener's little girl
infobox: Dracina Malfoy, when Dracina was six
pages.html:
The gardener's little girl was the daughter of the gardener at Malfoy Manor. When Dracina Malfoy was six, the two of them made friends. By the end of the week the little girl was gone. Dracina never even found out where she had been sent.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, Dracina told Harry Potter and Hermione Granger that she had never had a friend her father did not choose first. Pansy and Daphne had been chosen for her. So had Crabbe and Goyle, because their fathers were useful. The gardener's little girl was the one friend she had made for herself.

pages.title: Dracina's dancing master
infobox: Dancing, for years, at Malfoy Manor
pages.html:
Dracina Malfoy's dancing master is a man from Paris who comes all the way to Malfoy Manor by Floo to teach her to dance. He has taught her for years, because her mother insisted on it. Dracina once described him to Harry Potter simply as a man from Paris.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, during a Quidditch match in the autumn of 1992, Dracina told Harry that she had had lessons for years at the Manor from a man from Paris. Her mother had made her. Harry dropped his shoulder on the turns, she said, which was why he wobbled. She offered to show him, if only he would ask. He did not ask.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, in June 1994, Dracina listed the luxuries of her life for Hermione Granger: forty bedrooms, a wing of her own, a pony, a music room and a man who came by Floo all the way from Paris to teach her to dance. It was, she said, the biggest, most beautiful cage in all Wiltshire.

pages.title: The Malfoy gamekeeper
infobox: Dracina Malfoy a stable boy's whistle
Lucius Malfoy, though not from Narcissa
pages.html:
The Malfoy gamekeeper keeps the game on the Malfoy estate in Wiltshire. At some time in Dracina Malfoy's childhood he taught her a long, shrill, piercing whistle, of the kind a stable boy would use. Her father knows nothing about it. Her mother does.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, Harry Potter had no idea how to get Sirius Black out of the castle, with the dementors circling the walls. Dracina leant out of the tower window, put two fingers in her mouth and whistled. It was the last noise in the world Harry would have expected from her. Hermione asked where she had learnt it. ‘Our gamekeeper,’ said Dracina. ‘Father doesn't know. Mother does.’ Out over the Forest, Buckbeak answered.

pages.title: Dracina's governess
infobox: Handwriting, among other things, for six years
pages.html:
Dracina Malfoy's governess taught her at Malfoy Manor before she went to Hogwarts. She spent six years drilling into her the small, neat, spiky handwriting that Dracina still writes.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, in June 1994, Dracina and Hermione Granger met at the top of the Owlery steps, each with a letter for Molly Weasley. Hermione's ran to eleven numbered pages, with headings and a summary. Dracina's was nine pages long, in green ink on heavy cream parchment, in the hand her governess had drilled into her. It had no headings. It did not need them. Some of the words had gone through the paper.

pages.title: The librarian at Hermione's primary school
pages.html:
The librarian at Hermione's primary school was the only person there who was pleased to see Hermione Granger. Hermione had no friends before Hogwarts, so she ate her lunch in the library.

Hermione before Hogwarts

The other girls at the school hid Hermione's books. They called her Bossy Boots, Swot and Teacher's Pet, along with a good many worse things. She thought that if she learnt absolutely everything, people would have to like her, because they would need her. As she put it: 'People don't leave you if they need you.' It did not work, as she found out on Hallowe'en in her first year at Hogwarts, in the girls' toilets.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, Hermione told Dracina Malfoy about it, while Dracina was crying. 'I used to eat my lunch in the library, because the librarian was the only person who was pleased to see me.'

pages.title: The dinner lady at St Grogory's
infobox: St Grogory's Primary School, Little Whinging
An extra bread roll a day, for a fortnight
pages.html:
The dinner lady at St Grogory's, Harry Potter's primary school in Little Whinging, was kind to Harry for a fortnight. Every day she slipped him an extra bread roll. Then Aunt Petunia came in to complain about the jumper, and after that the dinner lady never looked at him again.

What it taught Harry

Her kindness hurt Harry more, in the end, than all the people who had never been kind to him in the first place. It was one of the ways he learnt the lesson the Dursleys drummed into him for years: kindness is the first half of something. Nobody was nice to you for nothing.

She is not the teacher who held up Harry's jumper in front of the class. That teacher always believed Dudley. The dinner lady was kind for a while, then stopped, and in the end she too believed the Dursleys rather than Harry.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Four, at the Burrow, when Mrs Weasley asked whether what Ron had told her was true, Harry's first thought was to lie. Every grown-up who had ever looked into it had believed the Dursleys in the end: the teachers, the dinner lady and the lady from the council. Mrs Weasley looked at him with such plain, ordinary kindness that the lie would not come.

In Book Three, Chapter Thirteen, trudging up the lawn after the Ravenclaw match, at which Dracina Malfoy and her friends had dressed up as dementors, Harry remembered her among the hurts that had taught him never to hope.

pages.title: The Slytherin fifth-year with the bat theory
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Twenty-Two
Sirius Black turned himself into a bat
pages.html:
The Slytherin fifth-year with the bat theory is a boy who told everybody at the Slytherin table, at breakfast after Sirius Black's escape in June 1994, that Black had turned himself into a bat.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, only five people at Hogwarts knew what had really happened on the night that Black, Buckbeak and Peter Pettigrew disappeared. Everybody else had a theory. At breakfast Harry Potter watched the theories being invented, like somebody blowing up balloons. The Slytherin table, bitter and sulky in defeat, produced them fastest of all. A boy in the fifth year was telling everybody that Black had turned himself into a bat. A girl beside him was quite sure that Black had bribed the dementors. Pansy Parkinson and Daphne Greengrass took up the bat theory, chattering away beside Dracina Malfoy, who never once looked up from her parchment.

pages.title: The Slytherin girl with the bribery theory
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Twenty-Two
pages.html:
The Slytherin girl with the bribery theory was quite sure, at breakfast after Sirius Black's escape in June 1994, that Black had got away by bribing the dementors.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, nobody at the Slytherin table knew how Black had escaped, so the theories came thick and fast. A boy in the fifth year had it that Black had turned himself into a bat. The girl beside him was quite sure he had bribed the dementors. A third Slytherin said loudly that Dumbledore had let Black go on purpose, being soft on Muggles and murderers alike. Dracina Malfoy sat in the middle of all the noise, writing very fast, and joined in with none of it.

pages.title: The Slytherin whose father blamed Dumbledore
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Twenty-Two
Dumbledore let Sirius Black go on purpose
pages.html:
The Slytherin whose father blamed Dumbledore was one of the Slytherins with a theory at breakfast after Sirius Black's escape in June 1994. This one said loudly that Dumbledore had let Black go on purpose.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, the Slytherin table, bitter, sulky and defeated, produced theories about the escape faster than anybody. A fifth-year said that Black had turned himself into a bat; a girl said he had bribed the dementors. A third Slytherin had it from home.

'Dumbledore let him go on purpose,' this one was saying loudly. 'He's soft on Muggles and murderers alike. My father says so.'

In their own words

He's soft on Muggles and murderers alike. My father says so.The Slytherin whose father blamed Dumbledore · B3 Ch22

pages.title: The tawny school owl
infobox: Hermione's and Dracina's letters to Molly Weasley, 1994
pages.html:
The tawny school owl is the large, strong, sensible Hogwarts owl that carried Hermione Granger's and Dracina Malfoy's letters to Molly Weasley at the Burrow in the summer of 1994.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-two, Hermione's letter ran to eleven numbered pages, with underlined headings and a summary at the end in case Mrs Weasley was in a hurry. Dracina's ran to nine, in green ink on heavy cream parchment. They sent them together, which Hermione said was more efficient and Dracina said was harder to trace, if anybody happened to be watching the owls.

The owl took one look at the two thick packets and gave a long-suffering hoot. It reached the Burrow late the following afternoon. Mrs Weasley sat down at the kitchen table and read all twenty pages without saying a single word.

pages.title: The old lady in the back pew
pages.html:
The old lady in the back pew belongs to the small, elderly congregation of St Michael's Church in Little Whinging. When Harry Potter first came in to Evensong, in July 1994, she was the one who turned round. She gave him a kind, short-sighted smile, and he sat down beside her.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, Harry pushed open the church door half expecting to burst into flames. Nothing happened, except that the door creaked. A very old lady in the back pew turned round and gave him a kind, short-sighted smile. Harry slid into the pew beside her. The light from the window over the altar reached all the way down the church to where he sat, though it had no business reaching so far, and lay warm across his hands while the old vicar preached.

pages.title: The woman from number seven
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl of Fire, Chapter 2
Number Seven, Privet Drive, Little Whinging
Telling the street that the Dursleys had rats
pages.html:
The woman from number seven is one of the Dursleys' neighbours in Privet Drive. When something happens in the street she is quick to see it, and quicker still to tell everybody else. Aunt Petunia dreads what she might see.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, on Thursday 18 August 1994, Aunt Petunia opened the fridge to get out Dudley's grapefruit and found every shelf crammed with dead rats. They were all bleeding slowly over the cheese, the margarine and Dudley's yoghurts. Her scream brought the woman from number seven out on to her front step in her dressing gown. By lunchtime she had told everybody in Privet Drive that the Dursleys had rats.

In Chapter Three, two days later, there was more to see at number four. Aunt Petunia wrung her muddy hands and wailed about the neighbours. 'That woman at number seven will have seen the windows…'

In Chapter Four, according to the man at number nine, she was telling the whole of Little Whinging about the Dursleys' drains, with mud coming up through the pipes on top of the rats. Aunt Petunia, scandalised, had not set foot outside the front door since.

pages.title: The Smeltings nurse
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
The Smeltings nurse is the school nurse at Smeltings, Dudley Dursley's school. In the summer of 1994 her remarks on his school report put Dudley on a diet, and Aunt Petunia put the rest of the household on it with him.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Dudley had come home with his school report for the year. His parents found excuses for his marks, as usual, and ignored the parts about bullying. At the very bottom, though, the school nurse had added a few remarks that nobody could explain away. Aunt Petunia could wail all she liked that Dudley was big-boned; the Smeltings outfitters no longer made knickerbockers in his size. The nurse had seen what Aunt Petunia's eyes refused to see.

After weeks of tantrums the nurse's diet sheet went up on the fridge door. Fruit, vegetables and what Uncle Vernon called 'rabbit food' replaced everything Dudley liked. To make him feel better, Aunt Petunia put the whole family on the diet with him.

pages.title: The milkman
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Among them the Dursleys of number four
pages.html:
The milkman does the round in Privet Drive, Little Whinging, where the Dursleys live at number four. Over the years that house has given him rather a lot to put up with.

Number four

In the summer of 1991, while letters from Hogwarts were pouring into number four, he handed Aunt Petunia two dozen eggs through the living-room window. Every one of them had a letter for Harry Potter rolled up inside it. He was very confused.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, in August 1994, the morning news seemed to show the Power Rangers every day. There were six of them now. Dudley Dursley thought the new one, the Green Ranger, with his gold shield across his chest, the most wonderful thing that had ever lived. He went on about him to his parents, to the milkman and once, memorably, to Harry.

pages.title: The man in the corner of the hall
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl of Fire, Chapter One
Harry Potter's dream of the house on the hill, summer 1994
pages.html:
The man in the corner of the hall is a figure in Harry Potter's dream of the house on the hill, in the summer of 1994. He is a tall man in a black dinner jacket who stands with his face to the wall in the corner of the hall, the way Harry was once made to stand in the corner at primary school.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry dreamt that he walked up through Little Whinging to a big white house on a hill. In its long, bright hall, the man stood in the corner without moving. Harry did not look at him. He felt that looking at him would be a bad idea. Finding out who he was would be a worse one.

Later in the dream, after the murders, the man in the hall had turned round. Harry did not look to see his face.

pages.title: The small boy weeding by moonlight
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl of Fire, Chapter One
Harry Potter's dream of the house on the hill, summer 1994
Dudley Dursley's huge old shirt; glasses mended with Sellotape
Weeding a flower bed by moonlight
pages.html:
The small boy weeding by moonlight is a figure in Harry Potter's dream of the house on the hill, in the summer of 1994. He is much too small to be up so late. He kneels in the flower bed beside the drive, pulling up the weeds one by one and laying them on the gravel.

Appearance

He wears a huge old shirt that comes down past his knees, and glasses mended in the middle with Sellotape. His eyes are enormous and green. Harry knew the shirt at once: it had been Dudley's.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter One, the boy sat back on his heels as Harry went past, and looked up at him. ‘They'll say it was me. After. They always say it was me.’

‘I know,’ said Harry. The boy nodded, as though that were all he had needed to know, and went back to his weeding.

In their own words

They'll say it was me. After. They always say it was me.The small boy weeding by moonlight · B4 Ch1

pages.title: The Stranger
infobox: By another road, a rather more alarming one
The small linking book Atrus wrote for him
pages.html:
The Stranger was the traveller who arrived out of nowhere, long ago, on the dock of Myst Island, with nothing in his hands, and wondered where he was. He did Atrus, who wrote the Age of Myst, a very great service. Atrus wrote him a small linking book to take him home, but he never used it.

Myst

The island was empty when he came. In its library he found Atrus's two sons, Sirrus and Achenar. They were trapped in two books, one red, one blue, and each begged him for the missing pages of his own. He believed neither of them, and he set Atrus free instead. Later Atrus sent him to Riven, where in 1806 he freed Atrus's wife, Catherine, and trapped Gehn in a prison book. He went home from Riven by falling through the Star Fissure, which was a rather more alarming road than the one Atrus had written for him.

In 1816 he came to Tomahna at Atrus's invitation, and he recovered the book of Releeshahn after Saavedro stole it. He kept the little linking book all the same. It was handed down for a great many years until at last it came to Albus Dumbledore.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, on the night of 6 June 1994, Harry Potter stood on the dock of Myst Island with Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy. Without knowing it, he was on the very planks where the other traveller had once arrived out of nowhere, and he wondered exactly the same thing: where on earth they were.

After Harry and the others had linked home, Atrus's daughter, Yeesha, picked the little book up off the library floor. She knew it at once. Her father had written it long ago for a stranger who had done him a very great service, and it had been lost to him for longer than she had been alive.

pages.title: Anna
infobox: The eighteenth century, until the Fall about 1788
pages.html:
Anna was the Muggle woman who found the cavern of D'ni in the eighteenth century. She lived among the D'ni for years, survived the plague that destroyed them and went back up to the surface. Her journal is the source of most of what anybody knows about them. Among the D'ni she took the name Ti'ana. She was the mother of Gehn and the grandmother of Atrus.

Finding D'ni

Anna's family lived in the wilds of New Mexico in the eighteenth century. She learnt the rocks from her father, a sort of geologist, and worked beside him in the desert. Exploring the caves there, she found traces of people, then a way down through the rock, and at last the great shaft into the cavern. The D'ni took her prisoner and questioned her. She learnt their language in captivity, and she lived among them for years.

She was given into the keeping of the D'ni lord Kahlis, and she married his son, Aitrus. She took the name Ti'ana and bore him a son, Gehn. Aitrus taught her the Art, which was against D'ni custom and cost him dearly. She had no magic of her own, but she learnt to write, and she recorded everything she saw, the Art above all.

The Fall

Anna saw D'ni's ruin coming. When Lord Veovis was condemned for conspiring with the renegade A'Gaeris, she argued for exile instead of death, and Veovis lived. About 1788, a few years after she went to live in the cavern, the plague of A'Gaeris swept through D'ni. Aitrus died destroying A'Gaeris. Anna took Gehn up through the caves by her husband's maps, and came out on the surface near the place where she had first gone down. She thought it was pride that had destroyed the D'ni, because they never questioned the Art. Gehn never forgave her for sparing Veovis.

Later life

Anna made her home in the Cleft, a fissure beside an old volcano above the cavern. Years later Gehn brought his dying wife, Keta, to her. After Keta's death Anna raised their son, Atrus, and named him after his grandfather.

When Gehn took Atrus away into D'ni, Atrus turned against his father. Anna helped him and Catherine strand Gehn on Riven. She also wrote the Age of Myst as a home for her family, and she lived out her last years with them.

Her journal

Anna's journal turned up in America about 1985, in the hands of a wizard collector, and three or four wizarding books on the D'ni followed. Parts of it had been cut out or blotted before anything was published, leaving holes and gaps in the dates. Some readers believe the missing passages concerned a child she had with one of the D'ni. The journal never mentions anybody called Atrus. It has never been published outside the wizarding world.

In the saga

Book Three: on the dock on Myst Island in June 1994, Hermione Granger told Harry and Dracina Anna's story as the journal tells it. A Muggle out in the desert with her father found a way down through the rock. The D'ni took her prisoner, and she lived among them for years. She survived the plague and got back to the surface. Anna, Hermione said, could not prove that the Art was magic, because she had no magic of her own to compare it with.

Book Four: that summer, in a letter to Harry, Hermione wondered whether Anna had really had a baby among the D'ni. If so, people might be walking about with a little D'ni in their blood without knowing it.

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Hermione told Harry and Ron that Anna had married a D'ni reformer called Aitrus, with whom she proposed many changes that a good many people hated. Anna called the sickness that destroyed D'ni a plague, because that is exactly what it was. Hermione now wondered whether a baby born to Anna down there might be what somebody had cut out of the journal.

pages.title: Anna's father
pages.html:
Anna's father was an eighteenth-century Muggle who studied rocks: a sort of geologist, as Hermione Granger put it. He worked in the desert of New Mexico with his daughter, and it was there that Anna found the way down through the rock into the great cavern of D'ni.

Life

He taught Anna what he knew about rocks, and she worked beside him in the desert. When she found her way down into D'ni, the D'ni took her prisoner. She lived among them for years and married one of them, Aitrus. Through her, Anna's father was the grandfather of Gehn and the great-grandfather of Atrus.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, on the dock at Myst Island in June 1994, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy what she had learnt of the D'ni. 'She was out in the desert with her father, I think he was a sort of geologist, and she found a way down through the rock.'

pages.title: The wizard collector who obtained Anna's journal
pages.html:
The wizard collector who obtained Anna's journal is an American wizard who collects old things. In about 1985 he got hold of the journal Anna kept of her life among the D'ni, though nobody knows how. He let a few scholars read it.

The journal

Anna, whom the D'ni called Ti'ana, was a Muggle who found their cavern under New Mexico in the eighteenth century and wrote down everything she saw there. It is the source of most of what is known of the D'ni and their Art. Once the scholars had read it, three or four of them wrote books, and there was a great fuss in the more obscure journals. Some pages are missing, cut out or blotted before anything was published, and nobody knows by whom. A few people think the missing parts were about a baby, a child Anna had down there by one of the D'ni.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy about the journal, standing in the rain on Myst Island. In Book Four, Chapter Two, she wrote to Harry that the journal never mentions anybody called Atrus, and wondered whether he had been in one of the parts that were cut out.

pages.title: The American wizard collector
infobox: The Linking Book to Myst Island
pages.html:
The American wizard collector who held the Linking Book to Myst Island was Ephraim Shacklewell, a rich pure-blood of New Mexico. The book had leaked out of the secret dig in the D'ni cavern, and he bought it from a digger for fifty dollars.

The book

He kept it in a glass case in his trophy room, labelled as a No-Maj picture book, and never understood what it was. In August 1993 John Constantine burgled it from him for Albus Dumbledore, a long, drawn-out job. The book belonged, as it always had, to Atrus, who wrote it.

In the saga

In the Book Three Interlude, Constantine broke into Shacklewell House by night with a Hand of Glory and lifted the book out of its case. Shacklewell, who could never sleep, caught him in the doorway of the trophy room. Constantine held up a card and passed himself off as a man from MACUSA. Shacklewell, weak with relief, begged him to take the book and asked only for a receipt. In Book Three, Chapter Three, Harry Potter sat across the Knight Bus from Constantine as he carried it north. For a second he saw a soft greenish flicker coming through the thin carrier bag.

pages.title: Achenar
aliases: the brother in the blue book
infobox: The blue book on Myst Island; later the Age of Haven
pages.html:
Achenar was one of the two sons of Atrus and Catherine. With his brother Sirrus he plundered his father's Ages and betrayed both his parents. He ended up trapped in the blue book in the library on Myst Island, claiming that his brother had burnt the library and murdered their father. Years later, sorry for what he had been, he died saving his young sister, Yeesha.

Myst

Achenar grew up on Myst Island and went with his father to his Ages. Where Sirrus loved riches, Achenar loved power over others. The rooms he kept in his father's Ages held weapons, poisons and instruments of torture. The peoples of those Ages suffered for it. Early in the nineteenth century the brothers left their mother a prisoner on Riven and stranded their father in D'ni.

When the Stranger reached Myst, Achenar was caught in the blue prison book. By turns he raged and pleaded for the pages that would free him, blaming his brother for everything. The Stranger freed Atrus instead.

Haven

Atrus held his sons for twenty years in separate Ages, Achenar on the jungle Age of Haven. There, alone, Achenar came to regret what he had been. When Sirrus kidnapped their sister Yeesha, Achenar gave his life to save her.

In the saga

Book Four: in the summer of 1994 Hermione Granger met Achenar in the Muggle game Myst. She wrote to Harry that he is trapped in the blue book, begging for his missing pages. He says it was his brother who burnt the library and murdered their father. Both brothers, it turns out, are lying. In two of the game's four endings, believing one brother means being trapped in his book in his place. She realised, too, that the stands holding the two books in the game were the very stands that she, Harry and Dracina had found empty in the ruined library on Myst Island.

pages.title: Sirrus
aliases: the brother in the red book
infobox: The red book on Myst Island; later the Age of Spire
Died after kidnapping his sister Yeesha
pages.html:
Sirrus is one of the two sons of Atrus and Catherine. With his brother Achenar he plundered his father's Ages and betrayed both his parents. He ended up trapped in the red book in the library on Myst Island. There he begged every visitor for his missing pages, swearing that his brother had burnt the library and murdered their father. Neither claim was true.

Myst

Sirrus grew up on Myst Island and travelled his father's Ages with him. He was clever, polished and greedy. In those Ages he kept rooms of his own, stocked with riches and fine things. With Achenar he stripped the Ages of everything of value, ruining the peoples of some of them. Early in the nineteenth century the brothers took their mother to Riven, where Gehn held her prisoner. They stranded their father in D'ni by tearing a page from his book home.

By the time the Stranger reached Myst, both brothers had been caught in prison books, Sirrus in the red one and Achenar in the blue. Each asked the Stranger to bring him the pages he needed to get out. Each blamed the other. The Stranger believed neither. He freed Atrus instead, and Atrus dealt with his sons.

Spire

Atrus held his sons for twenty years in separate Ages, Sirrus on Spire and Achenar on Haven. Achenar came to regret what he had been. Sirrus did not. Released, he plotted revenge on the family. He kidnapped his young sister, Yeesha, and died in the attempt. His brother died with him.

In the saga

Book 4: Hermione Granger met Sirrus in the Muggle game Myst in the summer of 1994 and wrote to Harry about him. He was trapped in the red book, his face flickering on the page. He begged for his missing pages, blaming his brother for burning the library and murdering their father. She believed neither brother, and the game proved her right. In the game the red book and the blue book sit on two stone stands. She noticed that they were the two empty stands she had seen in the ruined library with Harry and Dracina. Harry, reading the name, wondered whether Sirrus, so near to Sirius, was another of God's jokes at his expense.

pages.title: Catherine
pages.html:
Catherine, the wife of Atrus, was the mother of Sirrus, Achenar and Yeesha. A woman of the Age of Riven, she helped Atrus strand his father, Gehn, there. Later, when her own sons betrayed her, Gehn held her prisoner on Riven until the Stranger freed her in 1806.

Riven and Atrus

Catherine, who was called Katran on Riven, grew up on Gehn's Fifth Age among people who worshipped him as a god. Gehn meant her to be one of his wives. She dreamt of worlds, in dreams so strange and exact that they could be written. When Gehn shut his son Atrus into Riven, she and Atrus fell in love. With Anna's help they stranded Gehn on Riven by destroying the books that led out of it. Catherine went with Atrus through the Star Fissure to Myst Island, where they married and raised two sons.

Betrayal and rescue

Early in the nineteenth century Sirrus and Achenar, who had been plundering their father's Ages, turned on their parents. They took Catherine to Riven and left her there, where Gehn made her his prisoner, while their father sat stranded in D'ni. On Riven she became the leader of the Moiety, the rebels who resisted Gehn. They kept a refuge in the Age of Tay.

When the Stranger freed Atrus, Atrus sent him on to Riven. In 1806 the Stranger released Catherine and tricked Gehn into a prison book. Catherine saw the Rivenese away to safety before she and Atrus left the Age as it began to break apart.

Later life

Catherine and Atrus made their home on Tomahna, where their daughter Yeesha was born in 1815. Guided by her dreams, Catherine wrote Ages of her own, among them Serenia. Some ten years later her sons, released from their long imprisonment, plotted against the family once more, and both of them died. Atrus outlived her, and mourned her in his old age.

Her daughter Yeesha later gave her journals to the brothers Rand and Robyn Miller of Cyan. From them came the Muggle game Myst, with every game that followed it.

In the saga

Book Four: Catherine is known in the saga only through the Muggle game Myst. In the summer of 1994 Hermione Granger wrote to Harry that in the game's good ending Atrus says that his wife, Catherine, is being held prisoner in another world. He has to go and help her.

pages.title: Gehn
infobox: On Riven; in a prison book there in 1806
pages.html:
Gehn is the son of Anna by her D'ni husband Aitrus, and the father of Atrus. A Writer of the Art, he believed that he created the worlds he wrote, and that he owned their peoples. He ruled the Age of Riven as a god until his son stranded him there. In 1806 he was imprisoned on Riven in a prison book.

Early life

Gehn was born in the cavern of D'ni, a sickly child whom the healers did not expect to live. He was still young when the plague of A'Gaeris struck, about 1788. His father, Aitrus, died destroying A'Gaeris, and his mother led him up through the caves to the surface. Gehn never forgave her for having once pleaded for the life of Veovis, the D'ni lord whose plague it had partly been. In the end he left her.

He married Keta, a woman of the surface. When she fell ill carrying their child he brought her to his mother in the Cleft, but Keta died giving birth. Gehn went away, and left the baby, Atrus, to be raised by Anna.

Writer of Riven

Gehn went back down into the dead city and taught himself the Art from the books he found there, without the guild masters who would once have trained him. He wrote Age after Age, numbering them as he went, and his writing was full of flaws. He held the old D'ni heresy that a Writer makes the worlds he writes. He treated their peoples as his own creatures, and on his Fifth Age, Riven, the people worshipped him as a god. When Atrus was about fourteen, Gehn came back to the Cleft for him. He taught his son the Art, then destroyed Atrus's first Age because it did not suit him.

Atrus turned against him. With Catherine and Anna, he stranded Gehn on Riven by destroying every linking book out of it. Gehn ruled Riven for years afterwards from his temple. He fed dissenters to the great sea beasts called wahrk, and slowly rebuilt the means of making books. He kept a private refuge for himself, his Age 233. When his grandsons brought their mother, Catherine, to Riven, he made her his prisoner.

Imprisonment

In 1806 Atrus sent the Stranger to Riven with a prison book disguised as a linking book. The Stranger freed Catherine, found Gehn and offered him the book. Gehn insisted that his visitor go first, so the Stranger let himself be caught. When Gehn followed him in, the Stranger was released and Gehn was held. Riven began to break apart soon afterwards, and the Rivenese were taken to safety.

In the saga

Gehn has not appeared in the saga. Anna's journal, read in the wizarding world since the 1980s, has gaps in its dates where pages were cut out or blotted. Some scholars believe the missing passages concerned a child she had among the D'ni, and Hermione Granger has wondered whether such a child could have left descendants with D'ni blood in them. Anna did bear a child among the D'ni: Gehn, whose son is Atrus.

pages.title: A'Gaeris
infobox: The plague that destroyed D'ni, about 1788
About 1788, trapped in a dying Age by Aitrus
pages.html:
A'Gaeris was the D'ni renegade whose plague destroyed his people about 1788. He had been cast out of the Guild of Writers, and he was bitter against everything D'ni held sacred. He drew the lord Veovis into conspiracy, loosed a plague that killed nearly every D'ni, and died in an Age into which Aitrus had lured him.

The conspiracy

A'Gaeris had once belonged to the Guild of Writers, but he was disgraced and expelled. He came to hate the rule of the guilds and the council of D'ni, working against them in secret.

He fastened on Veovis, a proud young lord of the Guild of Writers who wanted no dealings with outsiders. Veovis loathed his old friend Aitrus for teaching the Art to Anna, a woman of the surface. A'Gaeris set Veovis against D'ni. When Veovis was caught, he was condemned, but Anna pleaded for his life and the council spared him. A'Gaeris later set him free.

The plague

About 1788 A'Gaeris and Veovis loosed a plague on the city. It spread through the cavern and out into the Ages of D'ni, killing nearly all of the people. A'Gaeris then wanted Veovis to write an Age in which the two of them would be worshipped as gods. Veovis refused, and A'Gaeris murdered him. Aitrus, Anna's husband, lured A'Gaeris into an unstable Age, where both of them died.

A'Gaeris's plague ended ten thousand years of D'ni. Anna escaped with her son, Gehn. The Art was lost with the rest, more or less, and the cavern stood empty for two centuries.

In the saga

Through Book Three A'Gaeris goes unnamed. To the wizarding world the end of D'ni is simply a terrible plague, a few years after Anna went to live among them, which killed nearly everybody in the cavern.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Hermione told Harry and Ron what Anna's journal says of A'Gaeris. Thrown out of the Guild of Writers in disgrace, he hated the reforms Aitrus had proposed with Anna, so he forged evidence against Aitrus and used it to turn Veovis against him. In 1788 the two of them blew a hole in the wall of the cavern with an explosive charge, letting in a gas made on purpose to carry the plague that killed nearly all the D'ni.

pages.title: Dr Richard Watson
infobox: Dr Watson; Richard Watson; Richard A. Watson; Red Watson
The excavation of D'ni; founding the D'ni Restoration Council
pages.html:
Dr Richard Watson is an American professor of philosophy and a cave explorer. In the 1980s he was one of the small group, with John Loftin and Elias Zandi, who found the cavern of D'ni. They began to dig it out. In August 1994 he spoke to the Muggle news from New Mexico about his friend Daniel Jackson, who had been declared dead after an accident near Giza. In 1997 he founded the D'ni Restoration Council.

Life and work

Richard Allan Watson was born in 1931. He is a professor of philosophy at Washington University in St Louis, and one of the leading authorities on Descartes. He is also a speleologist of long standing. For decades he has explored the Mammoth Cave system of Kentucky as a member of the Cave Research Foundation, which he led as president from 1965 to 1967. With Roger W. Brucker he wrote The Longest Cave (1976), the account of that exploration. His friends call him Red.

D'ni

Elias Zandi made his first expedition into the tunnels under the New Mexico desert with John Loftin. Afterwards he asked Watson to join the next one, and Watson became one of the few people to see the D'ni cavern in the 1980s.

When Zandi died in 1996, Watson became sole chairman of the restoration. A year later, wanting to share the responsibility, he formed the D'ni Restoration Council with Dr Ikuro Kodama, Victor Laxman and Dr Marie Sutherland.

In the saga

Book Four: in August 1994 the Muggle news carried tributes to the Egyptologist Dr Daniel Jackson, who had been declared dead after the collapse of a shaft beneath the Giza plateau. One of his friends, the American professor and cave explorer Dr Richard Watson, had spoken to the programme the day before from New Mexico, where he was working on an archaeological project he declined to discuss. He appeared with a grey beard and a battered hat, squinting against hard desert sunlight, with the corner of a caravan behind him.

'Daniel could read a wall of hieroglyphs the way you or I read the morning paper,' said Dr Watson. 'Folks laughed at him. I didn't. He thought the world was a whole lot stranger than we've been told. The more I see out here, the more I think he was right.' He looked away from the camera for a moment. 'I'd been meaning to show him something. Now I guess I never will.'

Harry Potter caught the report on the morning news in the Dursleys' living room, on Saturday 20 August 1994.

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow on 21 August 1994, finding that not even Arthur Weasley knew what a mutant was, Harry thought of Dr Watson's startled face on the news the day before.

In their own words

The more I see out here, the more I think he was right.Dr Richard Watson · B4 Ch3

pages.title: John Loftin
infobox: Finding the way down to D'ni, 1987
1991, on an expedition into the cavern
pages.html:
John Loftin, known as Fighting Branch, was the American artefact hunter who found the tunnels leading down to the cavern of D'ni in 1987. With Elias Zandi and Dr Richard Watson, he was one of the small group who began to explore the cavern in the 1980s. Before long they were digging there.

The way down

Loftin made his living in the desert of New Mexico, finding old things and selling them on. One of his customers was the archaeologist Elias Zandi. In 1987, out looking for artefacts, he came upon tunnels beneath the surface with great digging machines standing in them, which nobody living had built. He told Zandi. On 19 March 1988 he led him down, and the tunnels took them to D'ni.

The dig

Loftin stayed with the work while Zandi bought up the land round the Cleft and brought in Dr Richard Watson. He died in 1991, on one of the expeditions into the cavern. It was the year before Zandi told the others that he meant not merely to study D'ni but to restore it, and six years before the excavators formed the D'ni Restoration Council in 1997.

In the saga

Loftin has not been named in the saga. The dig he helped to begin is the one John Constantine walked past at the Cleft in 1993, and it was the source of the Myst linking book.

pages.title: Elias Zandi
pages.html:
Elias Zandi was a wealthy, eccentric American archaeologist, one of the small group of Muggles who found their way down into the cavern of D'ni in the 1980s. He bought the land round the Cleft and paid for the dig. After his death in 1996 the excavators carried on, and in 1997 they formed the D'ni Restoration Council.

Life

Zandi bought ancient artefacts. One of the men who sold them to him was John Loftin, who in 1987 found tunnels under the New Mexico desert, with digging machines in them that nobody on the surface had made. On 19 March 1988 Loftin took Zandi down into them. What they found led to the cavern of D'ni. Zandi began buying up the land round the tunnels and the Cleft. After another expedition he brought in Dr Richard Watson, a philosopher and cave explorer.

From the late 1980s into the early 1990s Zandi's small group explored and dug, quietly, on his money. Loftin died on one of the expeditions in 1991. In 1992 Zandi told the others what he wanted: not merely to study D'ni but to restore it, and one day to see it lived in again.

He died of a massive heart attack in 1996. He left his fortune to the restoration, and his land to his estranged son, Jeff. Watson carried the work on, and a year later he founded the D'ni Restoration Council.

In the saga

Zandi has not been named in the saga. In the summer of 1993 John Constantine passed his dig at the Cleft. He thought it was run by a handful of amateurs who meant well, with clipboards and good intentions, which in his experience was the most dangerous combination in the world. Things were coming up out of the hole, and most of them were going straight out of the back door to whoever would pay.

pages.title: Daniel Jackson
pages.html:
Dr Daniel Jackson is an American Egyptologist and linguist, one of the most gifted translators of ancient Egyptian of his generation. In 1994 he deciphered the Stargate, went through it to Abydos and stayed there. On Earth he was declared dead after 'an accident near Giza', which the Muggle news reported in August 1994.

Early life

Jackson was born in 1965, the son of the archaeologists Melburn and Claire Jackson. His parents died when he was a boy, killed in an accident while they were installing an Egyptian exhibit at a museum in New York. He grew up in foster homes. He took to languages early and never stopped. By his late twenties, a friend said, he could read a wall of hieroglyphs the way other people read the morning paper. He held doctorates in archaeology and linguistics.

He had untidy hair, wore glasses and had a slightly startled look, as though somebody had just asked him a question he found extremely interesting. One colleague called his mind 'brilliant, stubborn and original'.

The lecture

Early in 1994 Jackson gave a lecture arguing that the Great Pyramid had not been built by the pharaohs of the Fourth Dynasty at all. Much of his audience walked out. His funding was withdrawn shortly afterwards. He was, in fact, right: the pyramids were built in the likeness of the landing places of Ra's ships.

As he left the hall, Catherine Langford was waiting for him. She offered him work on a project for the United States Air Force: the translation of two cover stones found at Giza in 1928.

Abydos

In Colorado Jackson saw what the soldiers had missed. The symbols on the ring that the cover stones had guarded were constellations, and the address they gave needed a seventh symbol, the point of origin. The Stargate opened. Jackson went through with Colonel Jack O'Neill's team, having promised that he could read the symbols at the other end and bring them all home.

On Abydos he found a people descended from Egyptians taken by Ra, who were forbidden to write. He was given Sha'uri, daughter of the elder Kasuf, as his wife. In hidden chambers he found the history that the Abydonians had been made to forget. When Ra came, his guards killed Jackson, who was brought back to life in the sarcophagus. With O'Neill he turned the expedition's bomb on Ra, and the Goa'uld died with his ship.

Afterwards Jackson stayed on Abydos with Sha'uri and her people. O'Neill went home. Jackson's own world was told that he had died beneath the Giza plateau.

In 1997 Apophis came to Abydos and took Sha'uri as a host for his queen, Amaunet. Jackson came back to Earth to look for her.

Friends

Among the few who had not laughed at him was Dr Richard Watson, the American professor and cave explorer. In 1994 Watson was working in New Mexico on the D'ni cavern, a project he would not discuss. He had been meaning to show Jackson something. He believed, as Jackson did, that the world was a great deal stranger than people had been told.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: on 20 August 1994 the Muggle news paid tribute to Jackson, declared dead at twenty-nine after a shaft collapsed beneath the Giza plateau, his body not recovered. It mentioned the lecture, the walk-out and the withdrawal of his funding. It added that his parents had died when he was a boy. Dr Watson spoke from New Mexico, beside a caravan: 'Folks laughed at him. I didn't. He thought the world was a whole lot stranger than we've been told. The more I see out here, the more I think he was right.' Harry very nearly missed the item.

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow the next day Bill Weasley mentioned that American soldiers had been all over the plateau at Giza since the spring, and that there had been some Muggle accident down a shaft. It was the accident in which Jackson had been declared dead.

Nobody in the saga yet knows that Jackson is alive; only Jack O'Neill and the men who came home with him know the truth. He returned to Earth in 1997, when the Goa'uld came back through the gate.

pages.title: Myst (game)
aliases: The Surrealistic Adventure That Will Become Your World
infobox: Myst; The Surrealistic Adventure That Will Become Your World; MYST
Riven (1997), Myst III: Exile (2001), Uru: Ages Beyond Myst (2003), Myst IV: Revelation (2004), Myst V: End of Ages (2005)
pages.html:
Myst is a Muggle computer game made by Cyan and released on 24 September 1993, a few weeks after Harry Potter sat across the Knight Bus from the real Myst linking book. It is a fictionalised account of real events two centuries old, made from the journals of Catherine, the wife of Atrus. Their daughter Yeesha gave the journals to the brothers who made the game, meaning it to draw people of D'ni blood to the Cleft and the D'ni caverns.

The game

The player finds a book, touches the moving picture inside it and arrives on the dock of an island, with no idea where he is or why. The island, with its sunken ship, great stone gear, clock tower, rocket and library, is covered in puzzles. Through them the player reaches four other Ages: Selenitic, Stoneship, the Mechanical Age and Channelwood. Atrus's journals lie in the library. There are two books there as well, one red and one blue. In each a man's face flickers on the page, Sirrus in the red book and Achenar in the blue. Each begs for his missing pages. Each swears that the other burnt the library and murdered their father.

Both are lying. Atrus is alive, trapped in D'ni by his sons, because a page is missing from his book home. The game has four endings. In two of them the player believes one of the brothers and is trapped in his book in his place. In the third the player goes to Atrus without the page, and Atrus says 'Welcome to D'ni': the player is stuck there with him for ever. In the last the player brings the page. Atrus returns to deal with his sons, and says that his wife Catherine is held prisoner in another world.

The game was sold on CD-ROM. By 1994 it was being packed in with new computers, because it showed off so well what a CD-ROM could do. Its box shows the island from above, with the words The Surrealistic Adventure That Will Become Your World. It became the best-selling computer game of the 1990s. Sequels followed, some made by Cyan, some by other studios: Riven (1997), Myst III: Exile (2001), Uru: Ages Beyond Myst (2003), Myst IV: Revelation (2004) and Myst V: End of Ages (2005).

How it came to be

Yeesha, the daughter of Atrus, gave her mother Catherine's journals to the brothers Rand and Robyn Miller of Cyan. From those journals came Myst and the games that followed it. It was Yeesha's plan, meant to draw people of D'ni blood to the Cleft and the D'ni caverns under New Mexico. The game was nobody else's idea, and the men digging into the cavern had no hand in it. Because it came from Catherine's own journals, it kept close to the truth. Its island is Myst Island as it looked early in the nineteenth century, new, clean and sunlit. Its story is the history of Atrus and his sons. It leaves out a great deal, all the same. It says nothing of the excavation, nothing of New Mexico and nothing of Anna.

In the saga

Book 4: In the summer of 1994 Hermione Granger's father bought a new computer with a CD-ROM drive for the surgery's accounts, and Myst came with it. He got stuck on the first island and gave up. Hermione did not. She filled two exercise books with notes, sat up until two in the morning over the last puzzle, finished all four endings and went back eleven times. It was their island, she wrote to Harry. The dock, the ship, the gear, the clock tower and the library with the map were all exactly where they had been. The only difference was that in the game they were new and clean. Even the two stands in the library were the two empty stands they had seen. She sent him a photograph of the box and stripy photographs of the screen, taken with her mother's camera, with copies to Dracina.

Hermione thought the story was true. She was nearly certain that Atrus was D'ni, and she reasoned that the two brothers in America who made the game must have been told about it, or else had been there themselves. On the newsgroup comp.sys.ibm.pc.games.adventure, where hundreds of people talked about the game, she found six players who described a calling towards a desert they had never seen.

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Ron wanted to try Myst after hearing about its puzzles and Ages in Hermione's letters, which Harry thought exactly Ron's sort of thing. Hermione still did not know how everything they had seen had ended up in a computer game made by two brothers in America.

pages.title: Cyan
pages.html:
Cyan is the small American computer games company that made Myst, released on 24 September 1993. It was founded by two brothers, Rand and Robyn Miller. They made the game from the journals of Catherine, the wife of Atrus, which her daughter Yeesha had given them.

The early games

Rand and Robyn Miller set up Cyan in 1987, near Spokane in Washington State. They began with gentle exploration games for children: The Manhole (1988), Cosmic Osmo (1989) and Spelunx (1991). Their worlds were made to be wandered through, not won.

Myst

Yeesha, the daughter of Atrus, gave the Miller brothers her mother Catherine's journals. From them the brothers built Myst, the story of Atrus and his sons. Its island is the one the family really lived on. The whole thing was Yeesha's plan, meant to draw people of D'ni blood to the Cleft and the D'ni caverns. Nobody else asked the brothers to make the game. Broderbund published it on CD-ROM on 24 September 1993, and it became the best-selling computer game of the decade. Within a year it was being packed in with new computers, to show off what a CD-ROM drive could do.

Later games

Cyan went on to make the sequel, Riven, released in 1997, then Uru: Ages Beyond Myst in 2003 and Myst V: End of Ages in 2005. Other studios made Myst III: Exile (2001) and Myst IV: Revelation (2004). Each retold, as a story, events that had happened two centuries before, or that were happening under the desert at the time.

In the saga

Book Four: in the summer of 1994 Hermione Granger wrote to Harry that Myst had been made by two brothers in America. Somebody, she reasoned, must have told them all this, or else they had been there themselves. She was right: somebody had.

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Harry asked Hermione how everything they had seen on Myst Island could have ended up in a computer game made by two brothers in America. Hermione admitted that she did not know yet.

pages.title: D'ni Restoration Council
infobox: Dr Richard Watson, Dr Ikuro Kodama, Victor Laxman, Dr Marie Sutherland
The excavation and restoration of D'ni
The Cleft and the D'ni cavern, New Mexico
pages.html:
The D'ni Restoration Council is the body formed in 1997 to carry on the excavation and restoration of the D'ni cavern under New Mexico. Before that year there was no Council. The work was done by the small group of Muggles who had found the cavern in the 1980s.

Before the Council

John Loftin found the way down in 1987, and on 19 March 1988 he took Elias Zandi into the tunnels. Zandi bought the land round the Cleft, brought in Dr Richard Watson and paid for the work. In 1992 he declared that the aim was not just to study D'ni but to restore it.

Through the early 1990s the excavation stayed small and secret. It went on behind a wire fence, with a hand-painted sign about a geological survey. Myst, which came out in 1993, was not the diggers' doing. Yeesha, the daughter of Atrus, had given Catherine's journals to the brothers Rand and Robyn Miller of Cyan, who made the game from them. Many things leaked from the dig in those years to Muggle and wizard collectors in America, among them the Myst linking book.

Foundation

Zandi died of a heart attack in 1996. He left his fortune to the restoration, administered by his D'ni Restoration Foundation, with Watson as sole chairman. A year later, in 1997, Watson founded the D'ni Restoration Council to share the burden, with Dr Ikuro Kodama, Victor Laxman and Dr Marie Sutherland. Michael Engberg joined in 1999.

The Council set about surveying the city, making it safe, restoring its machinery and recording what it found. In time it began to admit outsiders who felt drawn to the desert.

In the saga

In August 1994 the Council does not yet exist. The excavators appear in the saga only as the people digging.
