There was the camp John Constantine passed at the Cleft in 1993, and the men behind a fence in the middle of nowhere who told a Muggle Myst player to go home in 1994. There was also Dr Richard Watson, who spoke to the Muggle news from New Mexico that August about a project he declined to discuss.

pages.title: Riven
infobox: Temple, Jungle, Book Assembly, Survey and Prison Islands
pages.html:
Riven is the Fifth Age of Gehn, a broken archipelago whose people he ruled as a god. Atrus and Catherine stranded Gehn there. In 1806 the Stranger imprisoned him on Riven in a prison book, then went home through the Age's Star Fissure.

The Age

Riven is a group of five islands in a warm sea: Temple Island, Jungle Island, Book Assembly Island, Survey Island and Prison Island. Gehn's writing was full of flaws. The Age was never stable, and it was slowly coming apart at the seams. Its people, the Rivenese, lived in a village on Jungle Island and worshipped Gehn. He kept order from his temple, feeding those who defied him to the wahrk, the great beasts of the sea. A rebel movement, the Moiety, resisted him. Its refuge was in the Age of Tay.

On one island lies the Star Fissure, a crack in the ground that opens not on rock but on a starry sky. Whatever falls into it leaves Riven altogether.

History

Gehn shut his son Atrus into Riven, and there Atrus met Catherine, a woman of the Age. With Anna's help the two of them destroyed every linking book out of Riven, leaving Gehn stranded. Atrus leapt into the Star Fissure, linking to Myst Island as he fell. His Myst linking book went on falling, out of Riven and down to Earth. Gehn ruled on, slowly rebuilding the means of making books. Atrus, from D'ni, went on writing into Riven's descriptive book to hold the Age together.

When Sirrus and Achenar betrayed their parents, they left Catherine on Riven, where Gehn made her his prisoner. In 1806 Atrus sent the Stranger there with a prison book. The Stranger freed Catherine, tricked Gehn into the prison book and signalled Atrus, who came for his wife. The Rivenese were taken to safety. As Riven began to break apart, the Stranger, who had no book home, fell through the Star Fissure. He came out in his own world.

These events were later told, as a story, in Riven, the sequel to Myst, which Cyan released in 1997.

In the saga

Riven has not been named in the saga. In 1993 Dumbledore told John Constantine that the traveller for whom the small leather book was written had never used it. He had found his way home by another road entirely, a rather more alarming one. That road was the Star Fissure.

pages.title: Anna's journal
infobox: The eighteenth century, among the D'ni
pages.html:
Anna's journal is the record kept by Anna, the Muggle woman who lived among the D'ni in the eighteenth century and survived their fall. It turned up in America about 1985. It is the source of most of what the wizarding world knows about the D'ni and the Art.

Contents

Anna wrote down everything she saw in the cavern, above all the Art. The journal tells how she found a way down through the rock, how the D'ni took her prisoner and how she lived among them for years. It records the D'ni insistence that the Art was a science with rules, like mathematics. Anna, who had no magic of her own, could not prove otherwise. It records, too, the teaching of the D'ni priests: that a Maker had made every possible world, and that a Writer only described one. Anna noted how few of the D'ni behaved as though they believed it.

It tells of the plague that killed nearly all of them a few years after she arrived, and of her escape to the surface. It gives her own verdict as well: that pride destroyed the D'ni, who never questioned the Art.

The journal never mentions anybody called Atrus. Her grandson was born after the Fall, in the Cleft.

Rediscovery and the missing pages

About 1985 the journal turned up in America, in the hands of a wizard who collects old things. Nobody knows how he came by it. He let a few scholars read it, and three or four books on the D'ni followed, with a terrific fuss in the more obscure wizarding journals.

The journal had been cut and blotted before anything was published. There are holes where pages should be, and gaps in the dates. Nobody knows who made them. Some readers believe the missing passages concerned a child Anna had with one of the D'ni. Anna did have such a child: her son Gehn, by her D'ni husband Aitrus.

The journal has never been published outside the wizarding world. The Muggles who have pieced the D'ni together from the game Myst have never heard of it.

In the saga

Book Three: Hermione Granger had read everything she could find about the D'ni after a footnote in Lost Civilisations of the Ancient World. On the dock on Myst Island in June 1994 she told Harry and Dracina what the journal says. She guessed that it had got out through the Muggles digging in the cavern.

Book Four: playing Myst that summer, Hermione went through her notes on the journal twice, looking for Atrus, and found nothing. Perhaps, she thought, he was in one of the passages that had been cut out. She also wondered whether, if Anna really had a baby among the D'ni, people might be walking about with D'ni blood in them without knowing it.

Book Four, Chapter Four: every wizard who has read the journal, Hermione explained at the Burrow on 21 August 1994, believes from it that the D'ni died out completely, taking the Art with them. Some days after writing to Harry she had gone back to it to find the name of Anna's husband, Aitrus.

pages.title: comp.sys.ibm.pc.games.adventure
infobox: Adventure games for IBM-compatible personal computers
pages.html:
comp.sys.ibm.pc.games.adventure is a Muggle newsgroup on Usenet, the worldwide system of public noticeboards reached by modem. Players gather there to discuss adventure games for personal computers. In 1994 hundreds of people talked about Myst there. Among them Hermione Granger found a handful who described a calling towards a desert they had never seen.

Description

A newsgroup works like a noticeboard on which anybody in the world can pin things up. It is read by computers talking to each other down the telephone line. Usenet began in 1980, between two universities in North Carolina, and by the 1990s it held thousands of newsgroups. Each is named in dotted parts, from the general to the particular. This one sits under comp, for computers, then sys.ibm.pc, for IBM-compatible machines, then games, then adventure.

In 1994 comp.sys.ibm.pc.games.adventure was crowded with players of Myst, most of them wanting hints for its puzzles.

In the saga

Book 4: In the summer of 1994 Hermione read the newsgroup on her father's new computer, through a modem and a company called Demon Internet, which charged ten pounds a month. Her mother rationed them both because of the telephone bill. Among the hint-seekers she found six posters, in different countries and apparently unknown to each other. They all described the same thing: a calling, and a desert they could not stop thinking about. One kept dreaming of an old volcano with a crack in the ground beside it. Another said it felt like being called home. They were Muggles, clever ones. None of them had heard of Anna's journal, but they were beginning to put things together. A few talked of going to New Mexico. One had got as far as a fence in the middle of nowhere, with men behind it who told him to go home. Hermione wrote to Harry that these people knew nothing, only the feeling.

Book Four, Chapter Four: by 21 August 1994 the posters on the newsgroup describing a calling to New Mexico numbered eleven. All of them were Muggles, though a couple were occultists.

pages.title: Demon Internet
pages.html:
Demon Internet is a British company that connects home computers to the Internet down an ordinary telephone line, for ten pounds a month. Hermione Granger's father is a customer.

The company

Demon was founded in 1992, and it was among the first companies in Britain to offer the Internet to ordinary households at a flat monthly price.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Hermione wrote to Harry Potter in the summer of 1994 that her father had a modem, which let the computer talk to other computers down the telephone line. He paid Demon Internet ten pounds a month for it, though her mother had rationed them both because of the phone bill. Through it Hermione read the newsgroups, which she explained to Harry: 'They're a bit like noticeboards, only anybody in the world can pin things up on them.' On one of them, comp.sys.ibm.pc.games.adventure, hundreds of people talked about Myst.

pages.title: Seven Cities of Cíbola
infobox: North of Mexico, in what is now New Mexico
pages.html:
The Seven Cities of Cíbola were seven cities of solid gold that were supposed to lie somewhere in the deserts north of Mexico. They did not exist. The search for them took the Spanish explorer Francisco Vásquez de Coronado up into New Mexico with a whole army, which had a few wizards in its ranks whom nobody had noticed.

The legend

An old Iberian story told of seven cities founded across the ocean by seven bishops fleeing the Moors. After the conquest of Mexico the story moved north. In 1539 a friar, Marcos de Niza, came back from the northern deserts saying he had seen Cíbola from far off, bigger than Mexico City. Coronado set out the next year. At Hawikuh, the first of the Zuni pueblos, he found villages of stone and mud brick with no gold in them at all. He spent two more years searching further on, as far as the plains of Kansas, and went home with nothing.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, in June 1994, on Myst Island, Hermione Granger told Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy about Coronado. 'They were supposed to be made of solid gold. They weren't, of course. They didn't exist.' But Coronado had a few wizards in his army without knowing it. In 1541 they slipped away on their own to try long-distance Apparition across the desert. One night they Apparated somewhere they had not meant to go, into the great cavern of the D'ni under New Mexico. They were the first wizards ever to meet the D'ni.

pages.title: The house on the hill
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl of Fire, Chapter 1
Harry Potter's dream, the night of 19 to 20 August 1994
Long, white, handsome; every window lit gold
The Riddle House at Little Hangleton
pages.html:
The house on the hill is the big house that Harry Potter dreamt of at Privet Drive on the night of 19 to 20 August 1994. It was long, white and handsome, with every tall window lit gold. In the dream his father, James, was eating his dinner there while Harry's mother died in the orphanage at the bottom of the road. The house in the dream stood for the Riddle House at Little Hangleton, where in 1943 Tom Riddle murdered his father and grandparents.

The house

Red curtains moved at its windows in a breeze that blew nowhere else. Its green front door had a knocker shaped like a stag's head. Inside, the hall had a zigzag tiled floor and a grandfather clock that ran backwards. A gramophone was playing 'Happy Birthday' far too slowly. Beyond lay a golden drawing room, with the dinner table laid for three.

The Riddle House

The real house stands on a hill above the village of Little Hangleton, once the finest building for miles around. Tom Riddle the elder went back to live there with his parents, Thomas and Mary, after he left Merope Gaunt while she was expecting his child. In the summer of 1943 their sixteen-year-old grandson came up the hill. He killed all three of them in their drawing room, and his uncle Morfin was blamed.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry dreamt that he walked past an orphanage that had been number four, Privet Drive, through a leafless wood and up to the big house at the top of the hill. He went in without knocking. In the golden drawing room James sat at dinner with his parents, Fleamont and Euphemia, while Aunt Marge poured the gravy. 'Her name was Lily,' Harry told his father. She had come to that front door in the snow and knocked, he said. James had watched from the window, glass in hand, as she walked back down the hill. Harry tortured all three of them until they said they were sorry. Then he killed them.

Dracina Malfoy came to him there afterwards, in a long dress of deep blue covered in tiny scales. 'You did it,' she said softly. 'Harry. You did it. You made them pay.' She slipped out of his arms, walked away through the red curtains into a circus in the rain and turned into a snake. A flash of green light ended the dream. Harry woke with his scar burning.

pages.title: Harry's dream of the house on the hill
infobox:
Harry Potter dreamer
Lord Voldemort source of the memory
Harry Potter and the Girl of Fire, Chapter 1
Harry woke with his scar burning
pages.html:
Harry's dream of the house on the hill was the nightmare Harry Potter had at Privet Drive on the night of 19 to 20 August 1994. In it he walked to a great house on a hill, where he tortured his father and grandparents, then killed them. He woke with his scar burning. It was Lord Voldemort's memory of murdering the Riddle family, recast with Harry's own family and the people of his life.

What the dream was

The dream was Voldemort's memory of the summer of 1943, when the sixteen-year-old Tom Riddle murdered his Muggle father and grandparents at Little Hangleton. It reached Harry through the fragment of Voldemort's soul that has been lodged in him since 1981.

Its pieces fit Riddle's story. The orphanage is the one where his mother, Merope Gaunt, died just after naming him, on the last night of 1926. The shack is the Gaunt family's hovel, where Riddle took his uncle Morfin's wand with the Gaunt ring; it was Morfin who was blamed for the murders. The pub sign is that of the Hanged Man at Little Hangleton. The small boy weeding by moonlight stands for the Riddles' gardener, who was arrested for the murders before Morfin was. James spoke the elder Tom Riddle's excuse for leaving Merope. The scaled dress, the circus and the open cage recall Nagini, who was once shown in a travelling circus.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter One, Harry dreamt that he walked down the middle of an empty Privet Drive at the bottom of a deep green valley, with the streetlamps humming inside his head. A hosepipe left running on a lawn ran uphill. A cold, heavy stone of anger sat in his chest. Number four was an orphanage, where his mother had come in the snow on the last night of the year, given birth to him, named him and died in an iron bed under the stairs. His father, meanwhile, ate his dinner in the big house on the hill.

In a leafless wood stood a shack built like number four, with the boa constrictor from the zoo nailed dead to its door. Inside, it was the cupboard under the stairs, going back into the dark, full of Dudley's broken toys. A filthy Uncle Vernon hissed at him from a camp bed: 'You're him. Him from up the hill. Him from the big house.' Petunia's sister, he said, had gone running after that man, only to be dropped while she was expecting. She was dead now, he supposed, and it served her right. Harry put him to sleep, then took his wand, with the black-stoned gold ring from his finger, knowing that everybody would think it was Vernon.

He passed the Leaky Cauldron, whose sign showed a man hanging from a tree. He passed a small boy weeding by moonlight. Then he went into the house on the hill without knocking. There James sat at dinner with Fleamont and Euphemia. He claimed that Lily had tricked him, by putting something in his drink. Harry tortured all three with the Cruciatus Curse until they said they were sorry, then killed them with the Killing Curse. Afterwards he felt warm, tall and light.

Dracina Malfoy came to him in a long dress of deep blue, covered in tiny scales. 'You did it,' she said softly. 'Harry. You did it. You made them pay.' She embraced him, then slipped out of his arms and through the curtains into a rainy circus, where an iron cage stood open. There she became a snake of midnight blue, and slid away into the dark. Harry ran after her, screaming that he loved her, begging her not to forget him.

A flash of green light ended it. Harry woke with his scar burning, clutching Lupin's wooden cross, which was warm.

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Harry could remember only pieces of the dream the next morning: a house on a hill, a long golden room full of candles and a hatred for his own father that had felt fair. When he wrote to Sirius Black, he left the dream out on purpose. He did not want Sirius to think he was frightened.

pages.title: Minas Tirith
infobox: Minas Anor, the Tower of the Setting Sun
In seven walled circles, against Mount Mindolluin
pages.html:
Minas Tirith, the Tower of Guard, was the chief city of Gondor, built in seven walled circles against the side of Mount Mindolluin. After the War of the Ring, Gandalf crowned Aragorn there before the whole city as King Elessar.

The city

It was first called Minas Anor, the Tower of the Setting Sun. In the year 3019 of the Third Age it withstood the siege of the armies of Mordor. Aragorn healed the wounded in its Houses of Healing, which was how the people knew him for their king, and on 1 May Gandalf crowned him before its gates.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, in the summer of 1994, Harry Potter finished The Lord of the Rings, near the end of which Gandalf sets the crown on Aragorn's head before the whole city of Minas Tirith. The next evening, at Evensong, the old vicar of St Michael's looked straight at him from the pulpit. Harry suddenly thought of Gandalf lifting the crown above Aragorn's head. Then he told himself not to be so stupid.

pages.title: The Paths of the Dead
infobox: Under the White Mountains of Gondor, from Dunharrow to Erech
Aragorn, in the War of the Ring
pages.html:
The Paths of the Dead were the haunted road under the White Mountains of Gondor, from Dunharrow to the Stone of Erech. Everyone said they led only to death. In the War of the Ring Aragorn took them anyway, and came out at the other end.

History

The Dead who haunted them had once sworn an oath to fight for Isildur against Sauron, and broken it. Isildur cursed them never to rest until the oath was fulfilled. Aragorn, as Isildur's heir, summoned them at the Stone of Erech and led them south to Pelargir, where they routed the Corsairs of Umbar. Then he declared their oath kept and let them go.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, in June 1994, Harry had reached the part where Aragorn decides to take the Paths of the Dead, though everybody tells him they lead only to death. Harry badly wanted to know whether he came out at the other end. In Chapter Twenty-Two, back at Privet Drive that summer, he read the end of the story in bed by the light of the streetlamp. Aragorn did come out, just as Harry had known he would.

pages.title: Narsil
infobox: End of the Second Age, at Orodruin
pages.html:
Narsil was the sword of Elendil. It broke beneath him when he fell before Sauron at the end of the Second Age, and three thousand years later it was forged anew as Andúril, Flame of the West. Long afterwards the wizarding world came to know the reforged blade as the Sword of Gryffindor.

History

Narsil was forged in the First Age by Telchar, the dwarf-smith of Nogrod. It came down to Elendil, who escaped the drowning of Númenor and founded the realms in exile. Its name joins the old words for fire and white light. The one stood for the Sun, the other for the Moon.

In the war of the Last Alliance, Elendil fell fighting Sauron on the slopes of Orodruin, and the sword broke beneath him. His son Isildur took up the hilt-shard and cut the One Ring from Sauron's hand with it. The shards were kept as an heirloom by Isildur's heirs. They lay broken for three thousand years, until the Elves of Rivendell took them to the forge and made the sword new for Aragorn.

As Andúril it went on down Aragorn's line. In time it came to Godric Gryffindor, one of his heirs, and it is by Godric's name that wizards still call it.

In Harry Potter's thoughts

On the night of the lake in June 1994, Harry stood at Professor Flitwick's window with Dracina Malfoy's hand in his. He felt his anger change from a boy's wild, flailing anger into something steadier, colder at the edges and hotter in the middle, that wanted to be used.

He thought of Narsil, broken in two and lying in pieces for three thousand years, until it came out of the fire as Andúril with a blade that burnt. It felt as though something that had lain broken inside him for years had been put back together, still glowing from the forge. He knew that sword better than anybody at Hogwarts could have guessed: he had held it.

pages.title: The palantír
infobox: Seven, by Elendil, out of the ruin of Númenor
Used by Saruman; mastered by Aragorn, March 3019 of the Third Age
pages.html:
The palantír that Aragorn looked into was the stone of Orthanc, one of the seven seeing-stones that Elendil brought to Middle-earth out of the ruin of Númenor. The palantíri are dark globes of crystal, through which one stone can see far off and speak with another. Through this one, in March 3019 of the Third Age, Aragorn wrestled with Sauron himself and decided to be a king.

The stone of Orthanc

Sauron held the stone of Minas Ithil, and through it he ensnared Saruman, who used the stone of Orthanc. After Isengard fell, Gandalf gave the Orthanc stone into the keeping of Aragorn, as Elendil's heir. At the Hornburg Aragorn looked into it in his own name and showed Sauron Andúril, the sword of Elendil reforged. Then he took the Paths of the Dead.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, late on a June night, Harry Potter stood at Professor Flitwick's window. The clouds over the Forest parted, and a single white star shone out low in the west, brighter than any star had a right to be. Without knowing why, Harry thought of Aragorn, looking into the palantír and deciding at last to be a king.

Later that night he badly wanted Dudley's copy of The Lord of the Rings. He had nearly finished it. He had left off where Aragorn looked into the palantír, the dark stone, and wrestled with Sauron himself through it.

pages.title: In Search of Schrödinger's Cat
pages.html:
In Search of Schrödinger's Cat is a Muggle book about quantum physics by the British science writer John Gribbin. Hermione Granger learnt about the Many Worlds interpretation from her father's copy.

Contents

Its title comes from Erwin Schrödinger's famous thought experiment of a cat shut in a box with a bottle of poison. The book also explains the idea the American physicist Hugh Everett put forward in 1957: that whatever can happen more than one way happens every way at once, so that the universe branches with every possibility.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, on the dock of Myst Island in June 1994, Hermione told Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy that the D'ni priests' teaching about worlds was very close to a real Muggle theory. She had read about it in a book of her dad's. She had got as far as the cat in the box when Dracina asked her to get to the point.

pages.title: Many Worlds interpretation
pages.html:
The Many Worlds interpretation is a theory of Muggle quantum physics, put forward by the American physicist Hugh Everett in 1957. It holds that whenever something at the very smallest scale can happen in more than one way, it happens in every way at once. The universe branches, one branch for every possibility, into worlds that are all equally real. The name was given to it later, by somebody else.

The D'ni teaching

The theory comes very close to the teaching of the D'ni priests. They held that a Maker had made every world that could possibly be, and that a Writer created nothing. He only described a world so exactly that his book found one to match.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, on Myst Island, Hermione Granger explained the theory to Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy, having read of it in a book of her father's, In Search of Schrödinger's Cat. She had got as far as the cat when Dracina, freezing, begged her to get to the point.

pages.title: Common Magical Ailments and Afflictions
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Hermione Granger, in Harry Potter's imagination
pages.html:
Common Magical Ailments and Afflictions is a reference book on the illnesses, curses and injuries of the wizarding world. In August 1994 Harry Potter, whose scar had begun to hurt, imagined Hermione Granger looking up curse scars in it.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Harry woke in the small hours at Privet Drive with his scar burning, and wondered what his friends would say if he wrote to tell them. At once Hermione's voice was in his head, high and panicky: 'Your scar hurt? Harry, that's really serious… Write to Professor Dumbledore! And I'll go and check Common Magical Ailments and Afflictions… Maybe there's something in there about curse scars…' That, he thought, was Hermione all over: go straight to the Headmaster, then look it up in a book while you waited.

pages.title: Trelawney's prediction
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
June 1994, at the end of Harry Potter's Divination examination
The return of Lord Voldemort's servant to his master
pages.html:
Trelawney's prediction was the prophecy Professor Sybill Trelawney made in June 1994, in a trance, at the end of Harry Potter's Divination examination. She foretold that Lord Voldemort's servant would set out to return to him before midnight. With the servant's help, she said, the Dark Lord would rise again, ‘greater and more terrible than ever he was’. Afterwards she remembered nothing of it. Albus Dumbledore counted it as only the second real prediction of her career.

Fulfilment

The servant was Peter Pettigrew, who had spent twelve years hiding as the Weasleys' rat. He escaped that same night in the grounds of Hogwarts.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Sixteen, on the day of Buckbeak's execution, Trelawney went rigid in her armchair and spoke in a harsh, deep voice that was nothing like her own.

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two, on the day after Pettigrew's escape, Harry told Dumbledore about it. Her voice had gone all deep, he said, and her eyes had rolled. She had said that Voldemort's servant was going to set out to return to him before midnight, and that the servant would help him come back to power. Dumbledore, faintly impressed, thought she might really have been prophesying. That brought her total of real predictions up to two, he said, and he ought to offer her a pay rise.

Harry was horrified, since it was he who had saved Pettigrew's life. Dumbledore told him that Pettigrew now owed him that life. Voldemort would hardly want a servant in the debt of Harry Potter.

pages.title: Lupin's wooden cross
infobox:
Remus Lupin former owner
Harry Potter owner
Plain wood, on a leather cord
Remus Lupin, from James and Lily Potter's wedding until 1994
pages.html:
Lupin's wooden cross is a small, plain cross on a leather cord. Remus Lupin wore it from the day of James and Lily Potter's wedding until June 1994, when he gave it to Harry Potter. It is made of wood because silver burns him, and it has a habit of growing warm.

Lupin's cross

Lupin came to faith through Lily after the Potters married. He wore the cross under his shirt from their wedding onwards, and years of handling wore it smooth. It has to be wooden, he explained, because silver burns him. He keeps a box of them at home, and can easily carve another.

In his lesson on vampires in 1993 he taught that a cross in a coward's hand is a stick of wood. In the hand of somebody who believes in Jesus Christ, he said, it is a different thing altogether. In moments of strain, when he was holding his war form down, his hand would close round something under his shirt, and his lips would move without a sound.

June 1994

On the Hogwarts lawn the full moon came out. Lupin, who had missed his Wolfsbane, began the Lord's Prayer, and changed. As his neck thickened, the cord snapped. The cross flew out of his collar and landed beside Harry's hand. Harry pocketed it. When the Garou hunted him across the grass, Harry held the cross up between them, feeling more of a coward than he had ever felt in his life. For a moment the creature fixed its eyes on it, and Harry thought he saw Lupin again. Then whatever it smelt on Harry proved stronger.

Later that night, in a clearing in the Forest, the cross went warm in his inside pocket, as though somebody had laid a hand on his chest. A moment afterwards his shield went white and turned the creature back into Lupin. Harry gave the cross back to him there. Lupin woke holding it.

When Lupin resigned at the end of term, he gave it to Harry for good: 'I think this one would rather go with you. It seems to work rather better in your pocket than it ever did round my neck.' Harry wears it under his shirt. It grew warm against his chest when he resolved to use his anger. At his first Evensong at St Michael's he could feel it there.

Since then

One night at the end of July 1994 the bulb in Harry's lamp went halfway through a chapter on Dark creatures. Then the clouds slid off the moon. Its light lay across his desk, exactly where the book was, until he reached the end of the chapter. The cross was warm against his chest the whole time. Harry said 'Thanks' to the window.

In August 1994 he woke from a terrible dream with his scar burning. His right hand was clenched round the cross so hard that its edges had bitten red marks into his palm. It was warm.

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994, packing for the Burrow, Harry left the cross out of his trunk, since it hung round his neck on its cord, where it always hung now.

pages.title: Sirius's cross
infobox: Two bits of wood; a thread from a blanket
By the lake at Hogwarts, June 1994
pages.html:
Sirius's cross was the little cross Sirius Black made from two bits of wood and a thread from a blanket. By his own account it kept him sane through twelve years in Azkaban. He lost it by the lake at Hogwarts in June 1994, when the dementors came.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, Harry found Sirius sitting on the floor of the ruined library on Myst Island, where he had gone through the linking book on Professor Flitwick's desk. As Harry helped him up, Sirius put his hand to the place over his heart and found nothing there. 'Lost my cross,' he said, seeing Harry look. 'Down by the lake, when those things came. Two bits of wood and a bit of thread out of a blanket. It kept me sane for twelve years.' He shrugged his bony shoulders. 'Never mind. I don't suppose He needs it to find me.'

pages.title: The black-stoned gold ring
infobox: Gold ring set with a black stone
A dream of Harry Potter's, August 1994
pages.html:
The black-stoned gold ring is a heavy, ugly gold ring set with a black stone, which Harry Potter saw in a dream in August 1994. In the dream he knew that it had been his mother's.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter One, in Harry's dream, Uncle Vernon wore the ring on his little finger, half buried in the fat. Harry had never seen it before. He was sure all the same that it had been his mother's, and that it belonged to him far more than it had ever belonged to his uncle. He worked it off Vernon's finger and put it on his own. It fitted as though it had been made for his hand, and the black stone was cold against his skin. Harry woke from the dream with his scar burning.

pages.title: Sleekeazy's
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
Sleekeazy's is the name on the jars of Fleamont Potter's hair potion, which tames the most unruly hair. It made the Potters far richer than they had ever been. Fleamont was the grandfather Harry Potter never knew.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter One, in his dream of August 1994, Harry saw a tall, thin old man at the head of a dinner table, with a long, clever face under a thick mane of gleaming white hair. On the sideboard behind him stood a row of little glass jars with Sleekeazy's on the labels. Harry knew that the man was his grandfather, Fleamont, although he had never heard the name before in his life.

Pansy Parkinson had offered Dracina Malfoy a bottle of the same potion earlier that year, in Book Three, Chapter Fourteen.

pages.title: Cruciatus Curse
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
The Cruciatus Curse, cast with the incantation Crucio, is one of the three Unforgivable Curses. It causes pain so great that the victim can think of nothing else. To use it on another human being earns a life sentence in Azkaban.

An Unforgivable

An Unforgivable Curse cannot be cast merely by learning the words. Without the whole heart behind them, nothing happens. Dark magic of that order takes something out of the caster's soul and does not give it back.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, at Harry Potter's first Patronus lesson in January 1994, Professor Lupin told him how the Unforgivable Curses work. 'You cannot cast an Unforgivable Curse by learning it. Everybody knows the words. Say them with your whole heart behind them, meaning them, wanting them, and the curse works; say them without, nothing happens at all, which is the single most merciful fact in our entire body of law.'

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, on the dock of Myst Island in June 1994, Hermione Granger was telling Dracina Malfoy off when she stopped dead at the word 'my'. Harry had no idea what she had been going to say. Dracina knew exactly: Granger had been about to say 'my Harry' out loud. Dracina knew those words very well indeed. She had been saying them to herself, inside her own head, for longer than she would have admitted under the Cruciatus Curse.

In Book Four, Chapter One, in the summer of 1994, Harry dreamt that he came to a long golden room where James Potter sat at dinner with his parents, Fleamont and Euphemia. Harry raised Uncle Vernon's wand. The word was waiting at the back of his throat, the way a sneeze waits. He had never heard it spoken or read it in any book. 'Crucio.' James screamed. He went over backwards, chair and all.

Harry turned the curse on Fleamont, then on Euphemia. He lifted it off them one at a time, only to put it back on again. It was the best feeling he had ever had in his life.

pages.title: Killing Curse
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Curse; one of the three Unforgivable Curses
A flash of green light and a rushing sound
pages.html:
The Killing Curse, Avada Kedavra, kills instantly. It comes as a flash of blinding green light with a rushing sound, like a great wind going past. It is one of the three Unforgivable Curses, and there is no counter-curse.

The curse

Lord Voldemort used it on the Potters at Godric's Hollow on Hallowe'en 1981, then turned it on their son. It left the boy only a scar shaped like a bolt of lightning, and a memory of green light.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Two, on the Hogwarts Express, Ron Weasley asked Harry whether he remembered anything of the night his parents died. 'A lot of green light. That's all.'

In Book Four, Chapter One, in the summer of 1994, Harry dreamt that he walked into a big white house at the top of a hill and killed three people there with it. The first was James Potter. Then he turned on his grandparents, Fleamont and Euphemia. Each time there was a flash of green light and a rushing sound. At the end of the dream the green light filled the whole world and swallowed him. He woke with Lupin's little wooden cross warm in his fist, and his scar was burning.

pages.title: The white star in the west
pages.html:
The white star in the west shone out over the Forbidden Forest on the night of Sirius Black's escape in June 1994, at the moment Harry Potter made up his mind. It was brighter than any star had a right to be, brighter even than the moon had been over the lake, and its light was warm. Dracina Malfoy saw it. Hermione Granger did not.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty-One, Harry stood at Professor Flitwick's window with a hard, hot anger in him that was aimed at the entire wizarding world. Dracina came to stand beside him and slid her cold fingers into his fist. 'You'll make them all pay, Harry,' she said quietly. 'I know it.' 'Yes,' said Harry. He knew then what he would do. The wizarding world must be made to change, whether it liked it or not.

At that moment the clouds over the Forest parted, as if a curtain had been pulled back. Low in the west, a single white star shone out. Its light came straight across the Forest and in through the window, warm on Harry's face, like the hand of somebody who was proud of him. He thought, without knowing why, of Aragorn looking into the palantír and deciding at last to be a king.

'Did you see that?' Dracina whispered. 'Yes,' said Harry. Then the clouds closed again, and the star was gone. Hermione had hold of his sleeve. She had not seen the star. She had been looking at her watch, because they had exactly ten minutes to get back to the hospital wing before Dumbledore locked the door.

pages.title: The white arrow from the stars
infobox: June 1994, over the lake at Hogwarts
Harry Potter, Hermione Granger, Dracina Malfoy
pages.html:
The white arrow came down out of the stars over the lake at Hogwarts on the night of Sirius Black's escape in June 1994, at the end of Harry Potter's Patronus. A clear horn sounded far off, like a hunting horn on a winter morning. Then the arrow struck the last dementor in the chest. To Harry it felt more than familiar. It felt almost familial.

The night at the lake

Harry had gone back in time to the far side of the lake. When nobody came to save him, he cast the Patronus himself, and a shining stag went out across the water. Wherever it touched the dementors they came apart. The last of them, bigger than the rest, did not flee. It came straight across the lake at Harry with its rotting hands stretched out. Then, a long way off and high up, a horn sounded. An arrow of the same white light as the stag came down out of the stars, as straight as a plumb line. It struck the dementor full in the middle of its chest, and the dementor came apart into nothing, taking the cold with it.

Harry stared up at the sky. There was nothing there but stars and the bright moon. All the same, he had the strangest feeling that somebody up there had a very good eye, and knew exactly who he was. For no reason he could name, he thought that she had been waiting a very long time to do it.

'I had help,' he told Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy, pointing at the stars. They had both seen it. Hermione gazed upwards with a sort of uneasy awe, while Dracina pressed her lips together and said nothing at all.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twenty, the horn and the arrow came at the end of Harry's Patronus. In Chapter Twenty-One, lying awake in the hospital wing, Harry kept coming back to the arrow. It had felt more than familiar, almost familial, like seeing somebody across a crowded street and knowing, before you even see their face, that they belong to you. He found that he badly wanted his copy of The Lord of the Rings.

In Chapter Twenty-Two he told the Fat Friar about it. 'It was white, like the stag. It came straight down out of the stars, and it hit the last one right in the chest. And I keep thinking I know it. The arrow, I mean. As if I've seen it somewhere before. I haven't, though. I know I haven't.' The Friar said that never in all his centuries had he heard of a Patronus doing what Harry described. In the same chapter Harry told Professor Lupin too. 'Then there was a horn, a long way off. And an arrow, out of the stars.'

pages.title: Department of Mysteries
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Time, thought, space, death and love
pages.html:
The Department of Mysteries is the most secret department of the Ministry of Magic. The witches and wizards who work there are called Unspeakables, because they may not speak of their work to anybody. Minerva McGonagall, the Deputy Headmistress of Hogwarts, is one of them.

The department

The Unspeakables study the deepest mysteries of magic: time, thought, space, death and love. Nobody outside the department knows much more than that, which is how it likes things.

Professor McGonagall

Minerva McGonagall became an Unspeakable after she left Hogwarts. She began teaching there about 1970, but she never entirely left the department. Through the 1980s she took sabbaticals for its work, and she remains a semi-retired Unspeakable to this day.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Thirteen, Dumbledore sat talking with Ambrose Greyhame, whose old grey staff leant against the arm of his chair. There were not five wizards living, Dumbledore told him, who could do what Ambrose had taught him with a staff. 'Not even the Unspeakables. They've all forgotten. They think it's a quaint old country thing, like Morris dancing.'

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Five, at the World Cup campsite on 22 August 1994, Arthur Weasley pointed out two Unspeakables, Bode and Croaker. They were from the Department of Mysteries, he said, which was top secret. He had no idea what they got up to there.

pages.title: Department of Magical Games and Sports
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Quidditch, Gobstones and the other wizarding games
pages.html:
The Department of Magical Games and Sports is the department of the Ministry of Magic that looks after wizarding sport. In the summer of 1994 its great business is the Quidditch World Cup, which Britain has not hosted for thirty years.

The department

Its head is Ludo Bagman, who was once a Beater for the Wimbourne Wasps and for England. The department houses the headquarters of the Quidditch League, the Official Gobstones Club and the Ludicrous Patents Office.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Mrs Weasley wrote to the Dursleys in August 1994 that her husband had just managed to get prime tickets for the World Cup final 'through his connections at the Department of Magical Games and Sports'. Ron's note to Harry Potter put it more briefly: 'DAD GOT THE TICKETS.'

In Chapter Four Percy complained at dinner that his own department was not getting the support it needed from Magical Games and Sports over the World Cup. He was scornful, too, that its head, Ludo Bagman, had made no effort to find Bertha Jorkins, a member of his department who had gone on holiday to Albania a month before and never come back. In Chapter Five Percy still disapproved of the way Bagman ran things, though he was plainly desperate to impress him.

pages.title: Department of International Magical Cooperation
infobox: Department of International Magical Co-operation; International Magical Co-operation
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
The Department of International Magical Cooperation is the department of the Ministry of Magic that deals with the wizarding governments of other countries. Percy Weasley went to work there in the summer of 1994.

Work

It holds Britain's seats on the International Confederation of Wizards, sets standards for the trade in magical goods across borders and deals with international magical law. Its head in 1994 is Bartemius Crouch.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Ron Weasley wrote to Harry Potter in August 1994 that Percy had started work there. He added a warning: 'Don't mention anything about Abroad while you're here unless you want the pants bored off you.'

In Chapter Four Percy told Harry that the department, under Mr Crouch, was trying to standardise cauldron thickness. At dinner he also hinted that it had a top secret event to organise right after the World Cup. In Chapter Six Cornelius Fudge told Harry that the Portkeys for the World Cup had been, strictly speaking, the work of Crouch's department.

pages.title: Quidditch World Cup (1994)
aliases: the four hundred and twenty-second Quidditch World Cup
infobox: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (8 July 1999)
Britain, for the first time in thirty years
A golden stadium seating a hundred thousand, on a deserted moor
pages.html:
The Quidditch World Cup of 1994 was the four hundred and twenty-second World Championship of the wizarding game, the first to be held in Britain for thirty years. Its final, Ireland against Bulgaria, was played on Monday night, 22 August 1994, in a stadium on a deserted moor before a hundred thousand witches and wizards. Viktor Krum caught the Snitch for Bulgaria, but Ireland won by 170 points to 160. It was exactly the result Fred and George Weasley had bet on, because the twins had quietly fixed the match. Ron Weasley was miffed that England had not brought the Cup home.

The tournament

The World Cup is the greatest prize in Quidditch, and it has been played for at least five hundred years. Since 1901 every national team has played by the Austrian rules. The rules on nationality are strict, so that a national side must be made up of its own country's witches and wizards.

Tickets for the 1994 final were extremely hard to come by. Arthur Weasley got prime ones through his connections at the Department of Magical Games and Sports. The Irish were favourites from the start: in the summer of 1993 the Irish International Side ordered seven Firebolts, the fastest brooms ever made, and Which Broomstick expected the Firebolt to be the broom of choice for the national teams.

In the earlier rounds of 1994 England went out to Transylvania by 390 points to 10, which some people blamed on Dracula. Wales lost to Uganda. Scotland was slaughtered by Luxembourg. Ireland flattened Peru in the semi-finals. The previous final had gone on for five days.

Arrangements

About a hundred thousand witches and wizards came from all over the world, far more than any magical site in Britain could hold. The whole Ministry of Magic worked on the arrangements for months. It found a deserted moor, laid anti-Muggle precautions over it and staggered the arrivals, so that people with cheaper tickets had to come two weeks early. Some visitors Apparated to a wood set aside as the Apparition point. Others came by one of two hundred Portkeys placed around Britain, each timed to the minute. Barty Crouch's Department of International Magical Cooperation organised the Portkeys across five continents.

The crowds camped in fields of tents below a wood, each field with its own Muggle site manager. The Weasleys' manager, Mr Roberts, needed a Memory Charm about ten times a day. Strictly speaking no magic was allowed with so many wizards on Muggle land, but by dusk on the day of the final the Ministry had given up trying to stop it. The Bulgarians asked for their Portkey allowance to be doubled, since Muggle trouble near their western border kept half their supporters from travelling overland. They also demanded twelve more seats in the Top Box.

Beyond the wood a Ministry task force of five hundred spent a year building the stadium. Its great golden walls could have held ten cathedrals, with Muggle-Repelling Charms on every inch of them. Purple-carpeted stairs climb to the Top Box at the summit, exactly halfway between the goalposts, with some twenty purple and gilt chairs. Across the field hangs a giant blackboard showing the score between advertisements.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, Harry Potter heard about the Irish order in Quality Quidditch Supplies in August 1993. In Chapter Thirteen, Lee Jordan's commentary on the Ravenclaw match told the crowd what Which Broomstick thought of the Firebolt. In Chapter Twenty-Two, on the train home in June 1994, Ron asked Harry to come and stay for the World Cup.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on Saturday 20 August 1994, Molly Weasley's letter to the Dursleys arrived, plastered with stamps. The final was on Monday night, she wrote, and Britain had not hosted the Cup for thirty years. Ron's note followed by owl: 'DAD GOT THE TICKETS. Ireland versus Bulgaria, Monday night. I'm a bit miffed England didn't bring it home this time.' The Weasleys meant to fetch Harry at five o'clock on Sunday, whatever the Dursleys said. Harry added a postscript to his letter to Sirius Black, telling him about the tickets.

In Chapter Four, at dinner in the Burrow's garden on 21 August, Arthur Weasley explained that he owed the tickets to Ludo Bagman. He had smoothed over some trouble for Bagman's brother, Otto, involving a lawnmower with unnatural powers. Charlie Weasley backed Ireland, who had seven decent players to Bulgaria's one, Viktor Krum. Molly sent everybody to bed early, since they would be up at the crack of dawn, warning that the last final had gone on for five days.

In Chapter Five, on Monday 22 August, the party left the Burrow before dawn. With Amos and Cedric Diggory they took a Portkey, a mouldy old boot, from the top of Stoatshead Hill, landing on the moor at seven minutes past five. Mr Roberts was Obliviated just as he began to call the crowd 'Muti-'. The Weasleys pitched their tents at the top of their field by the wood, close to an Irish quarter of shamrock-covered tents. In the Bulgarian camp Krum scowled from a poster on every tent. At lunch Ludo Bagman took bets. Arthur put a Galleon on Ireland. The twins staked all their savings, thirty-seven Galleons, fifteen Sickles and three Knuts, with a fake wand thrown in, that Ireland would win but Krum would catch the Snitch. Barty Crouch warned that the Muggles were organised against people with powers.

At dusk the salesmen came out with rosettes, flags, scarves, model Firebolts and Omnioculars. Then a gong sounded beyond the wood, while lanterns of green and red blazed up along the path to the stadium. Unseen, John Constantine followed the party up the path. Albus Dumbledore had sent him to watch over Harry, and he had been trailing the Weasleys since morning.

In Chapter Six the party walked twenty minutes through the wood, then climbed to the Top Box. Barty Crouch's house-elf, Winky, was saving her master a seat there. Cornelius Fudge greeted Harry like an old friend, until Harry unsettled him with talk of mutants, Augments and Sentinels. Lucius Malfoy came as the Minister's guest, with Narcissa and Dracina. Below the box Pansy Parkinson sat in Chudley Cannons orange, in the middle of the Bulgarians. Ludo Bagman opened the final with a Sonorus Charm. A hundred veela danced for Bulgaria, until Harry found himself with one foot on the front wall of the box. Thousands of leprechauns made a comet, a rainbow and a shamrock for Ireland, showering the crowd with gold.

Hassan Mostafa released the balls. The Irish Chasers flew as one, with Troy scoring first, and led thirty to nil within ten minutes. Ivanova scored Bulgaria's first goal. Krum's Wronski Feint then drove Aidan Lynch into the ground, though Krum had never seen the Snitch. With Lynch back on his Firebolt, Ireland scored ten goals in a quarter of an hour to lead 130 to 10. A whistle from the crowd stopped the Bulgarian Chasers in front of an open goal, letting Troy steal the Quaffle to score again.

Zograf, the Bulgarian Keeper, gave away a penalty for cobbing. When the veela danced, Mostafa was so taken with them that a mediwizard had to kick him on the shin. He then awarded Ireland two more penalties after the Bulgarian Beaters argued with him. Troy scored the first while Zograf, fighting his broom, drifted the wrong way. Zograf saved the other two. The leprechauns jeered at the veela in letters of light, then made a gigantic rude hand. The veela turned into beaked, winged creatures hurling fire, and Ministry wizards could not keep the two sides apart.

A Bludger from Quigley broke Krum's nose, but no whistle came, since a veela's fireball had set the referee's broom alight. Moran scored to make it 170 to 10. Lynch dived for the Snitch in earnest, with Krum level beside him, then crashed into the turf a second time. Krum rose bleeding, with the Snitch in his fist. Ireland had won by 170 points to 160, as the stunned commentator announced.

The Bulgarian Minister for Magic, who had let Fudge mime at him all evening, turned out to speak English. The Cup was brought into the Top Box for Fudge to present. Krum came up last of the Bulgarians, with two black eyes, before Troy and Quigley lifted the Cup for Ireland. Bagman paid the twins in full. They had not merely bet on the result. With the help of the leprechauns, broom polish on Zograf's broom and George's fake whistle, they had steered the match to exactly the score they needed. They meant never to tell a living soul.

Then Winky shrieked. A man had stepped back on to her foot from the shadow of the pillar at the top of the stairs: John Constantine. Lucius Malfoy knew him at once and opened fire. The jinxes set the pillar alight, blew off the Bulgarian Minister's hat and bounced off the World Cup. When Constantine fled down the stairs, Lucius chased him through the stands, while leprechauns took Lucius for a Bulgarian and poured down on him like hail. Constantine vanished among the dancing Irish supporters, bowing to them from the last barrier. 'This is better than the match,' said the Bulgarian Minister.

pages.title: Joaquin
aliases: the commander known only as Joaquin
infobox: Augment forces in the Balkans, from July 1994
Kosovo, the Montenegrin coast, most of eastern Bosnia
pages.html:
Joaquin is an Augment commander, known by no other name, who serves Khan Noonien Singh. In July 1994 he led Augment forces into the former Yugoslavia. In five weeks he took more ground than any army in Europe since the Second World War.

Life

Joaquin is one of Khan's inner circle, a big, powerful man of the same engineered stock as his master. He is fiercely loyal to Khan, who trusts him with a command of his own, a very long way from Delhi. Nothing is publicly known of him except his name and what his army has done.

The Balkan campaign

Augment forces appeared in the former Yugoslavia in July 1994, and nobody is sure how they got there. Under Joaquin they took Kosovo, the Montenegrin coast and most of eastern Bosnia within five weeks. Pale, the Bosnian Serb headquarters, fell in a single morning. The Bosnian Serb leadership fled across the Drina into Serbia. The army of the rump Yugoslav state collapsed, and United Nations peacekeepers were withdrawn from Goražde.

By 20 August 1994 his forces were within forty miles of Belgrade. Some three hundred thousand people were on the move, and Nato's ambassadors were meeting in emergency session. Diplomats in Brussels described the mood as close to despair. The alliance had spent the year arguing about how hard to bomb the Bosnian Serbs, and now it faced an enemy that had taken their capital before lunch. Whether Serbia itself could hold out was very much in doubt.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: the Muggle news of 20 August 1994 reported that the Augment forces in the Balkans were led by a commander known only as Joaquin. Harry watched the film of the refugees on the mountain road. An old woman was being pushed along it in a wheelbarrow. A little boy carrying a cockerel was crying the way people cry when they have been crying for days.

pages.title: Augments
infobox: Star Trek, 'Space Seed' (16 February 1967); named Augments in Star Trek: Enterprise, 'Borderland' (3 November 2004)
Findings from Weapon III (Les Enfants Terribles)
Unknown; perhaps as few as a hundred
pages.html:
The Augments are genetically engineered humans, stronger, faster and cleverer than ordinary people. An unacknowledged programme began creating them in 1973, working from the findings of Weapon III. In 1993 Augment rulers seized power in more than forty countries at once. Their leader is Khan Noonien Singh, and the war they wage is the Augment War.

Creation

The Augment programme was built in 1973 on data from Weapon III, Les Enfants Terribles, which had cloned Big Boss the year before. It was never part of the Weapon programme. It was a separate operation, working from findings that had been stolen or passed on, which is the sort of thing that happens to successful research. No government has ever acknowledged it.

Augments were designed to be better than ordinary people in every respect. They are several times as strong, with sharper senses, faster reactions and greater endurance. They heal quickly. Their intelligence is far above the ordinary. They were also made proud, aggressive and certain of their right to rule. Those traits have proved as heritable as all the rest.

1993

In 1993, when the first of them were twenty, genetically engineered rulers seized power in more than forty countries at once. Most of them were overthrown by their own people within a year. The rest swore allegiance to Khan or were destroyed by him. By August 1994 the Augments as a force meant two things: Khan's empire, from the Bay of Bengal to the Persian Gulf, and Joaquin's army in the Balkans.

In battle

Western officials admit that they have no reliable estimate of how many Augments there are. There may be as few as a hundred. The numbers are almost beside the point. Khan's commanders seem to know coalition plans before they are issued. His soldiers fight at night without lights. Nobody has ever taken an Augment alive.

In April 1994 a French television crew filmed an Augment running out of the sugar cane beside a tank. He kept pace with it as easily as a dog beside a bicycle, then leapt on to the turret and tore the hatch off like the lid of a biscuit tin. Two of the crew were killed later that day. One British officer put it this way: 'We were fighting chess grandmasters who could pick up a Land Rover.'

The frozen embryos

The programme made more embryos than it ever brought to life. The rest were kept frozen, and they outlasted the Augment War. In 2154 about eighteen hundred of them were held at Cold Station 12, a secret Starfleet medical station, while nineteen more had been stolen about 2130 by the geneticist Arik Soong. The Augments he raised from those nineteen carried the others off in a Klingon Bird-of-Prey they had seized. When their ship was destroyed above the Klingon colony of Qu'Vat, Klingon scientists recovered some of the embryos. Their attempt to make Augment warriors from them began the Klingon Augment virus.

In the saga

Book Three, Chapter Two: the news of 31 July 1993 described Khan as believed to be one of a group of genetically engineered individuals, created in a programme that has never been officially acknowledged. Harry had no idea what 'genetically augmented' meant.

Book Four, Chapter Three: the Defence Correspondent's report of 20 August 1994 showed the French crew's film, gave the estimate of a hundred and quoted the British officer. Dudley's spoon stopped halfway to his mouth.

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Harry explained the Augments as Khan's genetically engineered people, and Arthur Weasley asked whether they were a Muggle machine. In Chapter Five Hermione told Harry that the Augments in India had moved so many people out of the cities that the coalition could not even count them. In Chapter Six Harry warned Cornelius Fudge that they were not mutants at all but had been made in a laboratory, and that they were nearly at Belgrade.

pages.title: The man in khaki who tore off the tank hatch
aliases: the Augment in the sugar cane
pages.html:
The man in khaki is an unnamed Augment soldier, filmed in April 1994 by a French television crew as he ran beside a tank and tore off its hatch with his bare hands. Two of the crew were killed later the same day.

The film

The film is grainy and jumpy, as though somebody took it while running. A column of enormous sand-coloured tanks grinds along a dusty road between fields of sugar cane. A man in khaki comes out of the cane on foot. He runs alongside the leading tank, keeping up with it as easily as a dog beside a bicycle. Then he jumps on to the turret, takes hold of the hatch with both hands and tears it off its hinges like the lid of a biscuit tin. The picture jerks sideways and goes black.

The film shows the kind of enemy the United Nations coalition met in its spring offensive south of Delhi. American, Russian, British and French troops crossed the front line in March, expecting to reach Delhi within a month. They advanced eleven miles before they were withdrawn in June 1994. Nobody has ever taken an Augment alive. Western officials admit that they have no reliable estimate of how many there are, and there may be as few as a hundred. One British officer put it like this: 'We were fighting chess grandmasters who could pick up a Land Rover.'

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: the film ran in the Defence Correspondent's report on the morning of 20 August 1994. Dudley Dursley, who was eating his half grapefruit in front of the television, stopped with his spoon halfway to his mouth.

pages.title: The British officer
pages.html:
The British officer is a British Army officer who fought in the coalition that tried to retake Delhi from Khan Noonien Singh in the spring of 1994. He asked not to be named.

The spring campaign

In March 1994, under a United Nations mandate, the largest multinational force assembled since the Gulf War crossed the front line south of Delhi. American, Russian, British and French troops fought side by side for the first time since 1945. They were expected to reach Delhi within a month. They were withdrawn in June, having advanced eleven miles.

Khan's commanders seemed to know the coalition's battle plans before they were issued, and his soldiers fought at night without lights.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, the Defence Correspondent quoted him in a report on the Augment War broadcast on 20 August 1994: 'We were fighting chess grandmasters who could pick up a Land Rover.'

In their own words

We were fighting chess grandmasters who could pick up a Land Rover.The British officer · B4 Ch3

pages.title: The little boy with the cockerel
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl of Fire, Chapter 3
A mountain road in the Balkans
pages.html:
The little boy with the cockerel was one of some three hundred thousand refugees on the move in the Balkans in August 1994, after the Augment commander Joaquin overran Kosovo, the Montenegrin coast and most of eastern Bosnia.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on Saturday 20 August 1994, Harry Potter saw him on the news on the Dursleys' television, among a long line of people walking along a mountain road. He was carrying a cockerel under his arm, crying without making any fuss about it, the way people cry when they have been crying for days. An old woman was being pushed in a wheelbarrow.

A few minutes later the weather girl came on, smiling, to promise a lovely weekend, with the football after the weather. Five minutes before, the little boy with the cockerel had been walking out of a country on fire.

In Book Four, Chapter Four, at dinner at the Burrow the next evening, Charlie Weasley spoke of the refugees coming up through the passes, carrying everything they owned. Harry thought of the little boy on the mountain road with the cockerel under his arm.

pages.title: The old woman in the wheelbarrow
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl of Fire, Chapter 3
A mountain road in the Balkans
pages.html:
The old woman in the wheelbarrow was one of the Balkan refugees filmed in August 1994, being pushed along a mountain road in a wheelbarrow. She was among some three hundred thousand people driven from their homes by the Augment advance.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, on Saturday 20 August 1994, Harry Potter saw her on the news on the Dursleys' television. A long line of people was walking along a mountain road with bundles on their backs, and she was being pushed in a wheelbarrow among them. Among them a little boy was carrying a cockerel under his arm.

The correspondent said that Hungary had closed its southern border. Italy had appealed for help with the boats crossing the Adriatic. Greece had put its army on alert.

pages.title: The newsreader
infobox: A neat grey bob; a grave face
pages.html:
The newsreader is a British television newsreader with a neat grey bob and a grave face. On the morning of 20 August 1994 she read a bulletin of very bad news without a flicker.

The bulletin

She began with the Augment War: Khan Noonien Singh's forces were within forty miles of Belgrade. She went on to Superman's appeal to the Security Council, the protest outside the United Nations and a plan in Washington to revive the Sentinels. Last came the news that the American Egyptologist Dr Daniel Jackson, aged twenty-nine, had been declared dead after an accident near Giza. In truth he had stayed behind on Abydos, and the accident was a cover story.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Harry Potter watched the bulletin from the sofa at Privet Drive, beside Dudley. When she reported the Justice League's troubles, Harry waited for her to smile. She did not.

pages.title: The Defence Correspondent
pages.html:
The Defence Correspondent is a British television journalist whose voice, crisp and tired, narrated the report on the Augment War on the morning news of 20 August 1994.

The report

He told of Khan Noonien Singh's empire, which now stretched from Bengal to the Gulf, and of the coalition offensive of the spring, which had advanced eleven miles in three months. He showed film, taken in April by a French television crew, of a man in khaki tearing the hatch off a tank. Two of the crew were killed later the same day. Then he turned to the Balkans, where Augment forces under Joaquin had taken Kosovo, the Montenegrin coast and most of eastern Bosnia in five weeks.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Harry Potter watched it beside Dudley at Privet Drive. When the hatch came off, Dudley's spoon stopped halfway to his mouth. The correspondent quoted a British officer who asked not to be named: 'We were fighting chess grandmasters who could pick up a Land Rover.'

pages.title: The reporter at the United Nations
infobox: The protest outside the United Nations, 20 August 1994
pages.html:
The reporter at the United Nations is a young woman in a raincoat who reported for British television from the protest outside the United Nations in New York. It was just after three o'clock in the morning on 20 August 1994, and she had to shout over the noise.

The report

Police put the crowd at more than twenty thousand. It had begun to gather the afternoon before, as word spread of Superman's appearance before the Security Council. There had been scuffles, and a number of arrests. Similar protests were reported in Los Angeles, in Chicago and in what remained of Metropolis. She told the viewers: 'Many of the people here have come a very long way. Most of them have a story to tell.'

She let them tell those stories one after another. The organisers, she said, meant to keep the protest going until the Security Council met again on the Tuesday. The bulletin cut back to the studio before she could give her name.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Harry Potter watched her report on the Dursleys' television at Privet Drive.

pages.title: The weather girl
infobox: High pressure over the south of England, 20 August 1994
pages.html:
The weather girl presents the weather on British television. On the morning of 20 August 1994 she came on smiling after the news to promise a lovely weekend, under a band of high pressure over the south of England.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, she followed a bulletin of war, protest and grief. Five minutes earlier a woman had been screaming for blood outside the United Nations, and a little boy with a cockerel had been walking out of a country on fire. After the weather came the football, because the new season started that day.

To Harry Potter that was the strangest part of all. The war, the protest and the grief were all happening somewhere else. For most people in Little Whinging they might as well have been happening on the other side of a wall.

pages.title: The red-haired woman at the UN protest
aliases: the woman with his mother's eyes
infobox: Long dark red hair; green eyes; a thin, tired face
pages.html:
The red-haired woman is a Muggle of about forty who spoke at the protest outside the United Nations in New York in August 1994. Ten years earlier, in Central Park, a car thrown by the Hulk had killed her six-year-old son, Mikey, and Danny with him.

Central Park

It was a Saturday in the summer of 1984. She was having a picnic in the park with Danny and Mikey when the Hulk came through the trees. It was fighting somebody, though she never knew who, and it was not even looking at them. It picked up a car and threw it. The car landed right on top of Danny and Mikey.

The protest

She stood at the front of the crowd and told the story into the camera. Then she broke down and sobbed. The people beside her tried to lead her away, but she pulled free, her face blotched and twisted. Now they wanted to send the superhumans to fight Khan, she screamed, and Khan was just the same as all of them: 'They need to be punished, all of them, every last one of them, they need to be punished…'

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Harry Potter saw her on the Dursleys' television on the morning of 20 August 1994. She had long dark red hair scraped back from a thin, tired face, and her eyes were green. To Harry she looked the way his mother might have looked, if she had lived to be forty and had a hard time of it. Of Mikey she said: 'He was six years old. He had his new red shoes on.'

Harry knew the anger in her face. It was the red, roaring, blind thing he had felt twisting his own face, the anger he had spent a whole year learning to put down.

In Book Four, Chapter Four, at the Burrow the next day, Harry saw the same red, roaring, blind look on the face of a Muggle attacker in a photograph in the Daily Prophet. It was the look of somebody who wanted somebody to pay.

In their own words

He was six years old. He had his new red shoes on.The red-haired woman at the UN protest · B4 Ch3

pages.title: Mikey
infobox: The red-haired woman at the UN protest mother
Summer 1984, Central Park, New York, aged six
A car thrown by the Hulk
The red-haired woman at the UN protest
pages.html:
Mikey was a six-year-old boy who was killed in Central Park, New York, on a Saturday in the summer of 1984. He was wearing his new red shoes. Ten years later his mother told his story to the cameras outside the United Nations.

Death

Mikey was at a picnic in the park with his mother and Danny. The Hulk came through the trees, fighting somebody else and not even looking at them. It picked up a car and threw it. The car landed right on top of Mikey and Danny.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, in the small hours of 20 August 1994, his mother spoke of him at the protest outside the United Nations: 'He was six years old. He had his new red shoes on.' Then she broke down and sobbed in front of the camera. Harry Potter watched it on the Dursleys' television at Privet Drive.

pages.title: Danny
infobox: The red-haired woman at the UN protest family
A car thrown by the Hulk
The red-haired woman at the UN protest
pages.html:
Danny was killed in Central Park, New York, on a Saturday in the summer of 1984. He was at a picnic with six-year-old Mikey and Mikey's mother. A car thrown by the Hulk landed on him and the boy. Mikey's mother, the red-haired woman, told their story outside the United Nations ten years later.

Death

The Hulk came through the trees, fighting somebody. Mikey's mother never knew who. It was not even looking at the three of them. It picked up a car and threw it. The car landed right on top of Danny and Mikey.

On camera she gave only Danny's first name, and never said what he had been to her.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Harry Potter saw her tell it on the Dursleys' television on the morning of 20 August 1994: 'We were having a picnic, me, Danny and Mikey.'

pages.title: The Coast City man at the UN protest
infobox: His wife, his two daughters and his parents
pages.html:
The Coast City man is a big man in a baseball cap who spoke at the protest outside the United Nations in August 1994. He held a photograph of his wife and two little girls against his chest. They died with his parents when Coast City was destroyed in 1993.

Coast City

He was in San Diego on the day it happened. He drove back up the coast that night and found no city at all, only a hole with a machine in it, where seven million people had lived. The thing that did it, he said, had worn the S and called itself Superman. It was the Cyborg Superman. Mongul's forces had destroyed the city for him.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, he spoke to the camera in a flat voice: 'So you tell me. You tell me how I'm supposed to know the difference. Because I can't. Nobody can.'

In their own words

So you tell me. You tell me how I'm supposed to know the difference. Because I can't. Nobody can.The Coast City man at the UN protest · B4 Ch3

pages.title: The old man in the cardigan at the UN protest
infobox: Had a heart attack in December 1965
pages.html:
The old man in the cardigan is a small, very upright New Yorker who leans on a stick. At the protest outside the United Nations in August 1994 he told the cameras that he had watched superhumans fight over his head for fifty-four years.

Fifty-four years

He was sixteen in 1940, when the first of them, the Sub-Mariner, came out of the sea and tore up his street. The Sub-Mariner threw a fire engine through the front of the pharmacy. The next year he came back with the water behind him, and the old man's father drowned on the steps going down to the trains.

Just before Christmas 1965 the sky over Manhattan caught fire, because something had come to eat the world. It was Galactus, the devourer of worlds. People said afterwards that the Fantastic Four had talked him out of it. On the second day of the sky fire, the old man's wife had a heart attack.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, he looked straight into the camera with watery old eyes. 'Not one of them ever asked us. Not one. Not once.'

In their own words

Not one of them ever asked us. Not one. Not once.The old man in the cardigan at the UN protest · B4 Ch3

pages.title: The Bellevue nurse at the UN protest
infobox: Eleven patients in the blackout of August 1993
pages.html:
The Bellevue nurse is a young intensive-care nurse from Bellevue Hospital in New York. In August 1994 she spoke at the protest against superhumans outside the United Nations, looking as though she had come straight from a shift.

The blackout

She was on duty in intensive care at Bellevue on the night of the great blackout of August 1993. The lights, the monitors, the ventilators and even the generators all went off at once. She and two other nurses bagged the patients by hand in the dark all night, but they could not go fast enough.

The blackout was the work of one mutant, Magneto, who put out the lights all over the world for a night from his space station, Avalon.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, she told the cameras: 'We lost eleven people on my floor. Eleven. That was one mutant. One man, up in a space station, having a tantrum.' She shook her head. 'And they want us to say thank you to the rest.'

pages.title: The Metropolis man with the black eye
infobox: Knocked down by Doomsday in 1992; rebuilt
pages.html:
The Metropolis man with the black eye is a man in a suit who pushed his way to the microphone at the protest outside the United Nations in August 1994. His part of Metropolis has been flattened twice in two years.

Twice in two years

Doomsday knocked his building down in 1992, in the battle that ended with Superman's death. He rebuilt. Then in May 1994, as he put it, 'some lunatic in a lab coat flattened downtown with torpedoes left over from the alien invasion'. The man in the lab coat was Dr Sydney Happersen, Lex Luthor's chief scientist. Nobody, the man shouted, was even paying for it.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Harry Potter saw him on the news at Privet Drive. 'Every time they fight over Metropolis, we're the ones underneath!' he shouted. Similar protests were reported that night in Los Angeles, in Chicago and in what remained of Metropolis.

In their own words

Every time they fight over Metropolis, we're the ones underneath!The Metropolis man with the black eye · B4 Ch3

pages.title: The woman in the headscarf
pages.html:
The woman in the headscarf was one of the crowd protesting against superhumans outside the United Nations in New York, in the small hours of 20 August 1994. She was crying.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, she was one of the last faces in the report that Harry Potter watched at Privet Drive. Most of the people there, the reporter said, had a story to tell. Hers went untold. Looking at the crowd, Harry thought of what Florean Fortescue had said of the Muggles who burnt witches: they had been hurt, and they had hit back at whatever was nearest.

pages.title: The boy in the Friends of Humanity T-shirt
pages.html:
The boy in the Friends of Humanity T-shirt was a teenager among the crowd protesting against superhumans outside the United Nations in New York, in the small hours of 20 August 1994. He was shouting something that could not be made out, with tears running down his face.

The protest

The Friends of Humanity is an American movement against mutants and other superhumans. Its banner, held up by a dozen people, said FRIENDS OF HUMANITY in neat red letters. More than twenty thousand people had gathered, chanting 'No more capes!', after word spread of Superman's appearance before the Security Council the afternoon before.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, he was among the last faces in the report, which Harry Potter watched on the Dursleys' television. Looking at the crowd, Harry thought of what Florean Fortescue had told him about the Muggles who burnt witches. They had been frightened, as these people were.

pages.title: The fireman with the helmet
pages.html:
The fireman with the helmet was one of the crowd protesting against superhumans outside the United Nations in New York, in the small hours of 20 August 1994. He stood on his own at the edge of the crowd, saying nothing at all, holding up a helmet.

The protest

More than twenty thousand people had gathered there after Superman spoke to the Security Council, watched by mounted police and a line of officers with riot shields. Their placards read HUMANS FIRST, NO MORE CAPES, REMEMBER COAST CITY and WHO PAYS FOR METROPOLIS? Nobody said whose helmet it was.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, he was one of the last faces in the report that Harry Potter watched at Privet Drive that morning.

pages.title: The young man in the loud shirt
pages.html:
The young man in the loud shirt is a shopkeeper in Angel Grove, California. The Power Rangers saved his life from a ten-storey monster, and then their giant robot destroyed his shop. He spoke to the Muggle news in August 1994.

Interview

He was the last face in a report on public anger at superhumans, squinting on a street corner in bright sunshine under the caption ANGEL GROVE, CALIFORNIA. After all the darkness that had gone before, the sunshine looked very strange. He was not against the Rangers, he said.
