In Book Four, Chapter Three, on Saturday 20 August 1994, the news on the Dursleys' television reported the Augment advance in the Balkans. 'Nato's acting Secretary-General, who took over only last weekend after the death of Manfred Wörner, has called the alliance's ambassadors to an emergency meeting.' Diplomats described the mood as close to despair.

pages.title: J. Edgar Hoover
infobox: Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, 1924 to 1972
pages.html:
J. Edgar Hoover ran the Federal Bureau of Investigation for nearly half a century, from 1924 until his death in 1972. He kept files on everybody in America who mattered. The most dangerous of his secrets were kept on a microfilm, which James Bond stole in late 1962.

The Director

Hoover became head of the Bureau of Investigation in 1924, at the age of twenty-nine, and turned it into the FBI. Presidents came and went. Hoover stayed, and it was widely believed that he stayed because of what was in his files.

The microfilm

In late 1962 James Bond, working as John Patrick Mason, a former captain in the SAS, stole the microfilm on which Hoover kept the secrets of the American establishment. He was caught. He refused to say where he had hidden it, and he was locked up on Alcatraz without trial. He has never told anybody where it is.

pages.title: Sirius's tropical birds
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
Sirius's tropical birds are the large, gaudy birds that brought Sirius Black's letters to Harry Potter at Privet Drive in the summer of 1994. Neither letter came by owl. Sirius never said where he was, in case somebody got hold of the letters.

Description

Hedwig thoroughly disapproved of them. She let them drink from her water dish with the worst possible grace before they flew off again. Harry, for his part, liked them. They made him think of palm trees and hot white beaches. He could not imagine dementors lasting long in bright sunshine, which perhaps explained why Sirius had headed south.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, in August 1994, two letters had come from Sirius since Harry got home, both by tropical bird. Harry kept them hidden under the loose floorboard beneath his bed. Both sounded cheerful, and in both Sirius told him to get in touch if ever he needed to. In his reply Harry wrote: 'Thanks for your last letter. That bird was enormous; it could hardly get through my window.'

pages.title: The Chudley Cannons' Keeper
pages.html:
The Chudley Cannons' Keeper guards the goal hoops for the Chudley Cannons, the Quidditch team in bright orange that came bottom of the Prime League. In the summer of 1994 Pansy Parkinson wrote to Dracina Malfoy about the Keeper four times in a single fortnight.

Pansy's Keeper

Pansy had never cared for Quidditch in her life. The Cannons happen to be Ron Weasley's team, and Pansy has a crush on Ron, which he has not noticed.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Dracina Malfoy complained about Pansy in a letter to Harry Potter. Pansy, who used to take a novel to the Slytherin matches, had suddenly taken up the Cannons. She had a poster of them over her bed, in an orange that clashed with everything she owned. Dracina's verdict on the team was short: ‘They came bottom, Harry. Bottom.’ Pansy had also written to her four times that fortnight about their Keeper.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

In Book Four, Chapter Six, at the World Cup final on 22 August 1994, Dracina Malfoy at last put the clues together: the Cannons poster that clashed with everything Pansy owned, the four letters in one fortnight about the Cannons' Keeper and the way Pansy had stared at Ron Weasley on the castle steps in June. Pansy Parkinson was in love with Ron. Dracina, who prided herself on noticing everything, had missed it entirely.

pages.title: Ireland (Quidditch team)
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Green, with each name stitched in silver
pages.html:
Ireland's national Quidditch team won the 1994 Quidditch World Cup in Britain, beating Bulgaria by 170 points to 160 in the final on the night of Monday 22 August 1994. Its Chasers built so great a lead that Bulgaria lost even though Viktor Krum caught the Snitch. Every one of its players is Irish, which Ron Weasley thinks only right.

The team

Known in the Quidditch world as the Irish International Side, the team went into the tournament as favourites, on the seven Firebolts it had ordered in 1993. Its Chasers are Troy, Mullet and Moran. Its Seeker is Aidan Lynch.

Its side in the 1994 final was Connolly, Ryan, Troy, Mullet, Moran, Quigley and Lynch. Ryan keeps goal, while Connolly and Quigley are the Beaters. The players wear green robes, each with the player's name stitched in silver across the back.

The Chasers fly as one, each of them seeming to know where the other two will be. Their moves include the Hawkshead Attacking Formation, an arrowhead with Troy at the point, and the Porskoff Ploy. Lucius Malfoy says the Irish invented the trick of knocking the Quaffle off an opponent's elbow straight back to a team-mate.

Irish supporters cover their tents in shamrocks. Their souvenirs are green, from rosettes that shriek the players' names to hats sprouting dancing shamrocks. The team's mascots are leprechauns.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, Ron Weasley sent Harry Potter word in August 1994 that his father had got tickets for the final. Ron was a bit miffed that England had not brought the Cup home this time. 'But Ireland are all right. They're all Irish at least.'

In Chapter Four Charlie Weasley backed Ireland to win the final. They had flattened Peru in the semi-finals, he said, with seven decent players to Bulgaria's one. Besides, they were more like the British than the Bulgarians were.

In Chapter Five Ludo Bagman thought Ireland's front three the strongest he had seen in years. Arthur Weasley bet him a Galleon on an Irish win, while the twins bet everything they had that Ireland would win but Krum would catch the Snitch. On the campsite Seamus Finnigan's family had a tent so thick with shamrocks that it was hardly a tent at all. Mrs Finnigan made sure that Harry, Ron and Hermione were supporting Ireland.

In Chapter Six the leprechauns opened Ireland's display with a comet of green and gold. The Chasers took Ireland thirty points clear in ten minutes. Lynch was flattened by Krum's Wronski Feint, but his return set the whole team alight, and they scored ten goals in a quarter of an hour. Troy profited from a fake whistle in the crowd. Moran scored the goal that made it 170 to 10. When Lynch dived for the Snitch in earnest, Krum beat him to it, so Ireland won by ten points. The result was exactly the one Fred and George Weasley had bet on, since they had quietly fixed the match.

In the Top Box Moran and Connolly held up the dazed Lynch, whose eyes no longer quite pointed the same way. Troy and Quigley lifted the Cup over their heads. Lynch rode pillion on Connolly's broom for their last lap of honour. Ron decided it was what came of a team whose players were all from one country.

pages.title: Bulgaria (Quidditch team)
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
Bulgaria's national Quidditch team reached the final of the 1994 Quidditch World Cup in Britain, where it lost to Ireland by 160 points to 170 on the night of Monday 22 August 1994. Its Seeker, Viktor Krum, caught the Snitch, but too late to save the match.

The team

Its Seeker is Viktor Krum, who at eighteen is already counted among the finest Seekers in the world.

Its side in the 1994 final was Dimitrov, Ivanova, Zograf, Levski, Vulchanov, Volkov and Krum, all in scarlet. Dimitrov, Ivanova and Levski are the Chasers. Zograf keeps goal. Volkov and Vulchanov are the Beaters, who hit as hard as they can, at Bludgers or at players. The team's mascots are veela.

Bulgarian supporters fly the white, green and red flag of their country. In 1994 every Bulgarian tent at the World Cup carried the same moving poster of Krum, who only blinked and scowled. Their souvenirs ran to red rosettes, scarves with real roaring lions on them and flags that played the national anthem when waved.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Three, a note from Ron Weasley reached Harry Potter at Privet Drive in August 1994: 'DAD GOT THE TICKETS. Ireland versus Bulgaria, Monday night.' Arthur Weasley had got prime seats through his connections at the Department of Magical Games and Sports. As Mrs Weasley told the Dursleys, Britain had not hosted the Cup for thirty years.

In Chapter Four Charlie Weasley called Krum Bulgaria's one decent player. Percy reported that the Bulgarians wanted their Portkey allowance doubled, because of Muggle trouble near their western border. Half their supporters dared not travel overland.

In Chapter Five Harry, Ron and Hermione walked through the Bulgarian camp, where Krum glowered down from every tent. Barty Crouch spent the day sorting out the Bulgarians, who insisted on twelve more seats in the Top Box.

In Chapter Six the Bulgarian Minister for Magic let Cornelius Fudge mime at him all evening, though he spoke English perfectly well. The veela danced so well that Harry nearly jumped out of the Top Box. Ivanova scored Bulgaria's first goal, but the Irish Chasers ran away with the match. Krum's Wronski Feint flattened Aidan Lynch. Zograf, whose broom the Weasley twins had secretly treated with polish, drifted the wrong way for a penalty. Volkov and Vulchanov gave away two more penalties by arguing with the referee. A Bludger broke Krum's nose. With Ireland 160 points ahead, he caught the Snitch, so Bulgaria lost by ten.

The downcast players came up to the Top Box to generous applause, Krum last of all, with two black eyes. 'Vell, ve fought bravely,' said their Minister.

pages.title: Middle-earth
infobox: The First, Second and Third Ages of the elder days
The Ice Age and the Flood, which drowned its memory
The Lord of the Rings, taken for a novel
pages.html:
Middle-earth is the world of the elder days. In it Morgoth made war on Elves and Men, as Sauron did after him, while the Istari walked its roads. Its ages were real. They came before the Hyborian Age and the Flood, which washed away nearly all knowledge of them, so that they reach the present only as a novel somebody wrote.

The ages

In the First Age the Elves and the Fathers of Men fought Morgoth, the being Scripture calls Satan, in the north-west of the world for the Silmarils. The age ended when the Valar overthrew him in the War of Wrath, and the lands of Beleriand went down under the sea. In the Second Age the Men of the West lived on Númenor, and Sauron forged the One Ring. That age ended with the drowning of Númenor and the Last Alliance.

In the Third Age the realms in exile rose, then dwindled, and the Istari came. It closed with the War of the Ring, the destruction of the Ring, the crowning of Aragorn and the departure of the Elves over the Sea. The Fourth Age was the dominion of Men. Through every one of those ages Cain, already cursed, walked the world as a deathless wanderer with no powers at all.

Gandalf belongs to those ages, and remembers them well. He remembers the hobbits who taught him much of the art of not being noticed. He remembers Aragorn, whom he crowned, and a prince of the forest folk with an infuriating habit of keeping score.

How it was forgotten

After the ages of Middle-earth came the Hyborian Age, and after that the Ice Age, whose ending brought the Flood. Nothing came through the water whole. Recorded history has spent the time since forgetting the rest. The great ages survive only as story: Conan as a legend, Arthur as half-history and Middle-earth as a novel. A wizard who goes looking for the origins of his craft finds Egypt, then Stygia, then nothing, because that is where the written record drowns.

So The Lord of the Rings, written by J. R. R. Tolkien and published in the 1950s, is a history book that hardly anybody in either world knows to be one. Tolkien's record of the Blue Wizards goes vague because one of them, Zordon, went off the world entirely, and nobody who could have written it down ever saw him again.

Its inheritance

Two things came down out of the elder days into the present. One is the dark craft of Morgoth. Stygia kept it, the Flood scattered it, and every dark wizard since has inherited some broken piece of it.

The other is a bloodline. Harry Potter descends through his mother from Aragorn and Arwen. That is what Dumbledore means when he speaks of the magic of Elves and of Númenor in Harry's blood. The sword Harry drew from the Sorting Hat in 1993 was Andúril, which Aragorn carried in the War of the Ring.

pages.title: Dracina's Nimbus
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Dracina's Nimbus is the spare racing broom that Dracina Malfoy lent Harry Potter in his third year, while his Firebolt was being taken apart for jinxes. He gave it back the moment the Firebolt returned.

In the saga

The broom is a Nimbus Two Thousand and One, the model the whole Slytherin team has flown since 1992. Dracina has two. In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, at the end of February 1994, she stopped Harry in the Entrance Hall and offered him the spare for the Ravenclaw match, so that he would not have to fly the school’s old Shooting Star. It was not charity, she said. It was entirely selfish, since she meant to beat him in the spring. Harry, who had sworn he would never ride anything with Malfoy money in it, said yes.

It arrived at the Owlery two evenings later, wrapped in brown paper, with a note: Mind the left-hand foot-rest, it goes if you kick it. D. He never took it out of its paper. On the Thursday before the match Professor McGonagall gave him his Firebolt back, and he sent the Nimbus back to Dracina by school owl. His note had taken four drafts: Got my own back off McGonagall, so you’d better have this one. Thanks anyway. It was decent of you. H.

pages.title: Sonic the Hedgehog
infobox: Dudley Dursley, until the summer of 1994
pages.html:
Sonic the Hedgehog is a Muggle computer game, made by Sega for its Megadrive, about a blue hedgehog who runs faster than anything alive. Dudley Dursley owned a copy until the summer of 1994, when he threw his Megadrive out of the window.

The game

Sonic races through hills, caves and factories at tremendous speed, collecting gold rings as he goes. His enemy is the round, moustached Doctor Robotnik, who has shut the island's animals up inside robots. The game came out in June 1991 and sold in enormous numbers.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Harry Potter told Sirius Black in a letter that Dudley had been caught smuggling doughnuts into his room, against his diet. When his parents threatened his pocket money, he threw the Megadrive out of the window. Harry thought it rather stupid, since Dudley now had neither Sonic the Hedgehog nor Shinobi to take his mind off things.

pages.title: Shinobi
infobox: Dudley Dursley, until the summer of 1994
pages.html:
Shinobi is a Muggle computer game, made by Sega, about a ninja called Joe Musashi who fights his way through a gang of criminals with throwing stars and a sword. Dudley Dursley owned one of the Shinobi games until the summer of 1994.

The games

The first Shinobi appeared in the arcades in 1987. Three more followed on the Megadrive: The Revenge of Shinobi in 1989, Shadow Dancer in 1990 and Shinobi III in 1993. Which of them Dudley had is not recorded; Harry Potter called it only 'that Shinobi game'.

In the saga

In Book Four, Chapter Two, Harry wrote to Sirius Black that Dudley, whose diet was not going well, had been caught smuggling doughnuts into his room. Told that his pocket money would be cut, Dudley had thrown his Megadrive out of the window. That left him without Sonic the Hedgehog or Shinobi to take his mind off things.

pages.title: The Ventrue Antediluvian
infobox: About 9300 BC, in Enoch, by one of Cain's three childer
pages.html:
The Ventrue Antediluvian is the founder of Clan Ventrue, and one of the thirteen vampires of the Third Generation from whom every clan descends. What became of him is not known.

The founder

He was Embraced about 9300 BC in Enoch, the First City, by one of Cain's three childer. The Third Generation are called the Antediluvians, although all thirteen were in fact Embraced after the Flood. About 8990 BC he was among those who rose against the Second Generation and slew it. Cain cursed the clans for that slaying about 8980 BC, then departed into Nod. The curse he laid on the Ventrue was a narrowed hunger: each of them can feed on only one kind of mortal.

Afterwards the thirteen built the Second City and ruled it together, the Ventrue among its lords, until it too fell to their wars. No Ventrue will say whether he sleeps somewhere or was destroyed long ago, and it is likely that none of them knows.

The Master's claim

The Master, the fourth-generation Ventrue who founded the Aurelian line, claims that the Antediluvian sired him. If the claim is true, the Master is among the oldest vampires walking. He will never reveal his sire's name. The clan has never been able to prove the claim, or to disprove it.

pages.title: Mr Prentice
pages.html:
Mr Prentice is a Muggle neighbour of the Dursleys in Privet Drive whose cat washes itself on the pavement by the lamp post outside number five.

In Book Four

Between 20 and 21 August 1994 Mr Prentice put a new sticker in the back window of his car reading HUMANS FIRST in neat red capitals. B4 Ch4

pages.title: Mr Prentice's cat
pages.html: Mr Prentice's cat was washing itself on the pavement beneath the lamp post outside number five, Privet Drive, when the shimmering figure vanished on 21 August 1994.

pages.title: The man at number nine
pages.html: The man at number nine, Privet Drive, told Vernon Dursley over the hedge in August 1994 that the woman at number seven was spreading word of the Dursleys' drains.

pages.title: The man who ran the newsagent's
pages.html: Vernon Dursley had used a racial slur about the man who ran the newsagent's.

pages.title: Arthur Weasley's contact at the Floo Regulation Panel
aliases: a useful contact at the Floo Regulation Panel
infobox: Ministry of Magic, Floo Regulation Panel
pages.html: A useful contact of Arthur Weasley's at the Floo Regulation Panel connected the Dursleys' fireplace to the Floo Network for the afternoon of 21 August 1994.

pages.title: Bartemius Crouch
infobox: Bartemius Crouch Senior; Barty; Barty Crouch; Crouch; Mr Crouch

Ludo Bagman Ministry colleague
Percy Weasley admirer
Bartemius Crouch's grandfather grandfather
Winky house-elf
Cornelius Fudge superior
Ministry of Magic, Department of International Magical Cooperation, Crouch family
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Head of the Department of International Magical Cooperation
Head of the Department of Magical Law Enforcement
About a hundred and fifty (Ludo Bagman); over two hundred (Percy Weasley)
pages.html:
Bartemius Crouch is an elderly official of the Ministry of Magic, head in 1994 of the Department of International Magical Cooperation, where Percy Weasley works under him. In the first war against Lord Voldemort he ran the Department of Magical Law Enforcement with an iron hand, and he sent his own son to Azkaban. A stiff British wizarding nationalist, he is one of the very few wizards who read the Muggle newspapers and understand the danger rising against people with powers.

Career

The Crouches are an old pure-blood family. Crouch made his name in the Department of Magical Law Enforcement, and by the height of Lord Voldemort's first rise he was its head. He met the Death Eaters' violence with violence of his own. He gave the Aurors leave to kill rather than capture, he allowed them to use the Unforgivable Curses on suspects, and he sent some prisoners to Azkaban without a trial, as Sirius Black was sent in 1981. Many admired him for it, while others thought him hardly less ruthless than the people he hunted. For a time he was widely expected to become Minister for Magic.

After Voldemort's fall Crouch presided over the hearings of the captured Death Eaters. Igor Karkaroff bought his freedom at one of them by naming others, among them Augustus Rookwood, whose arrest brought Ludo Bagman before the Council of Magical Law. The Council acquitted Bagman amid cheers, to Crouch's fury.

His hardest case was his own son, Barty Crouch the younger. The boy was taken with Bellatrix Lestrange, her husband Rodolphus and his brother Rabastan. All four were charged with torturing two Aurors, the Longbottoms, with the Cruciatus Curse, to learn where their master had gone. The boy begged his father from the dock, while his frail mother wept at Crouch's side. Crouch sentenced all four to life in Azkaban, then disowned his son in front of the court.

In the years after the trial public feeling turned against him, and in 1990 the office of Minister for Magic went instead to Cornelius Fudge. Crouch was moved sideways to head the Department of International Magical Cooperation.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: on Sunday 21 August 1994 Ron Weasley told Harry Potter that Percy could talk of nothing but his boss, Mr Crouch, who even agreed with the scary things Percy wanted. At dinner in the Burrow garden Percy said that Crouch had taken a personal interest in the disappearance of Bertha Jorkins, who had once worked in his department; he was thought to be quite fond of her. When the Bulgarians asked for their Portkey allowance to be doubled because of a Muggle disturbance near their border, Crouch had told them that Muggle disturbances were a matter for the Muggle Liaison Office.

Book Four, Chapter Five: at lunch at the World Cup campsite the next day, Ludo Bagman said that Crouch kept saying somebody should be sent to look for Bertha. Then Crouch Apparated beside the Weasleys' fire, elderly, stiff and very upright, his short grey hair parted unnaturally straight above a narrow toothbrush moustache. In his pressed suit, with shoes that shone like glass, he looked like a bank manager. He told Bagman that the Bulgarians wanted twelve more seats in the Top Box, calling Percy 'Weatherby' as he took his tea. He warned Arthur Weasley that Ali Bashir was on the warpath over the embargo on flying carpets. Give those people an inch, he said, and they would take several miles, claiming they belonged there more than you did. When Harry said that he hoped carpets would never replace brooms in Britain, Crouch looked at him with something like approval. 'A British broom for a British sky.'

He had been busy organising Portkeys across five continents, he said, no mean feat with the Muggles in the state they were in. When Bagman laughed, Crouch told him what the man at the gate had said to one of his people the night before: 'Mutie'. It was the Muggle word for people born with powers, he explained, and it was generally what they shouted before they set fire to them. He read their newspapers, as nobody else in the Ministry troubled to do. The Americans were debating whether to bring back the machines they had built to hunt such people, while in Britain there was already talk of a register. Half the Ministry imagined it could all be tidied away with a few Memory Charms. When Bagman said the Muggles were always getting worked up about something, Crouch's moustache went very straight. 'They are not worked up. They are organised.'

What the Bulgarians' Muggles did on their own border was the Bulgarians' affair, Crouch went on; what Britain's did on British soil was his. He would not have the Statute of Secrecy put at risk on the island because half the world's wizards could not keep their tents plain. British wizards would be left to clear up after them, as always. Harry felt a fierce rush of relief. He was not sure he liked Crouch, but Crouch was the first grown wizard he had met who seemed to see what Harry saw. When Bagman began to let slip that something already agreed and signed was going to happen at Hogwarts, Crouch cut him off sharply. He handed Percy back his tea untouched, then Disapparated with Bagman to meet the Bulgarians.

Book Four, Chapter Six: at the final that night Cornelius Fudge gave Crouch's department the credit for the Portkeys, calling him a splendid fellow. Being no great shakes at languages himself, Fudge admitted, he needed Crouch for dealing with foreigners. Crouch was very busy, so he sent his house-elf, Winky, to save him a seat in the Top Box. When Harry told Fudge that only Mr Crouch seemed to know what the Muggle word meant, the Minister replied with a tight little smile that Barty read a great many Muggle newspapers.

In their own words

They are not worked up. They are organised.Bartemius Crouch · B4 Ch5
A British broom for a British sky.Bartemius Crouch · B4 Ch5
I will not have the Statute put at risk on this islandBartemius Crouch · B4 Ch5

pages.title: Ludo Bagman
infobox: Bagman; Ludo; Ludovic Bagman; Mr Bagman

Otto Bagman brother
Bartemius Crouch Ministry colleague
Wimbourne Wasps former team
Ludo Bagman's Bulgarian opposite number counterpart
Ministry of Magic, Department of Magical Games and Sports, Quidditch, Wimbourne Wasps
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Head of the Department of Magical Games and Sports
Beater for the Wimbourne Wasps and for England
Commentator at the World Cup final
pages.html:
Ludo Bagman is the head of the Department of Magical Games and Sports at the Ministry of Magic. He was once the best Beater the Wimbourne Wasps ever had, and he played for England. Cheerful, careless and fond of a bet, he got the Weasleys their tickets for the 1994 World Cup final. He ran a book on the match, then commentated on it from the Top Box.

Quidditch career

Bagman played Beater for the Wimbourne Wasps, whose robes have broad black stripes on bright yellow, with a giant wasp across the chest. He was the best Beater the club ever had, as well as a favourite with the England crowds.

The trial

After Lord Voldemort's fall in 1981 Bagman was brought before the Council of Magical Law, with Bartemius Crouch presiding. He was accused of passing information to the Dark Lord's supporters through Augustus Rookwood, an old friend of his father's. Bagman said that he had believed Rookwood to be above suspicion. The Council acquitted him to cheers. One witch on it even congratulated him on his game for England against Turkey the Saturday before. Crouch was furious.

At the Ministry

After his playing days Bagman went to work at the Ministry, where he rose to head the Department of Magical Games and Sports. Arthur Weasley calls him the most enthusiastic head the department could wish for, though he has always been lax about security. He loves a bet, a joke or a good game.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: at dinner at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Arthur Weasley said that he liked Ludo, who had got them such good tickets in return for a favour. Arthur had smoothed over the trouble Bagman's brother, Otto, got into with a lawnmower with unnatural powers. Percy thought Bagman likeable enough, but could not see how he had ever become head of a department. Bertha Jorkins of Bagman's department had been missing for over a month, but Bagman only laughed that she had probably misread the map, ending up in Australia instead of Albania.

Book Four, Chapter Five: at the World Cup campsite the next morning a weary Ministry wizard in plus fours complained that Bagman was not helping, trotting about talking of Bludgers and Quaffles at the top of his voice. Arthur admitted that Ludo had always been a bit lax about security. Bagman came to lunch in his old Wasps robes, bouncing as if he had springs in his shoes. With his round blue eyes, short fair hair and pink cheeks, he looked like an overgrown schoolboy. His nose had been flattened, Harry Potter guessed, by a stray Bludger.

Bagman was running a book on the final, with his pockets full of jingling gold. Roddy Pontner had bet him that Bulgaria would score first, while little Agatha Timms had put up half shares in her eel farm on a match lasting a week. Arthur put a Galleon on Ireland. Fred and George Weasley staked everything they had on Ireland to win with Viktor Krum catching the Snitch: thirty-seven Galleons, fifteen Sickles, three Knuts. They threw in a fake wand, which turned into a rubber chicken. Bagman howled with laughter, added five Galleons for it and offered them excellent odds, since he thought their bet had not a chance.

He could not understand a word his Bulgarian opposite number said, and had thought the man wanted to borrow a pair of tweezers. In fact the Bulgarians wanted twelve more seats in the Top Box. Of Bertha Jorkins there was 'not a dicky bird'; she would wander back into the office in October, he said, thinking it was still July. He laughed off Crouch's warning about the Muggles, saying they were always getting worked up about something. Then he nearly let slip that something already agreed and signed was going to happen at Hogwarts, until Crouch cut him off. As he left he reminded the Weasleys that they would be up in the Top Box with him, where he would be commentating.

Book Four, Chapter Six: that night Bagman charged into the Top Box with his round face shining like a large, very excited cheese. He magnified his voice with Sonorus to open the final of the four hundred and twenty-second Quidditch World Cup. He introduced the mascots, both teams and the referee, then commentated on the whole match. He plainly enjoyed the fouls, the fake whistle from the crowd ('naughty, naughty!') and the referee's infatuation with the veela, calling for somebody to slap him. He was as surprised as anyone when Krum caught the Snitch with Ireland still ahead: 'KRUM GETS THE SNITCH, BUT IRELAND WINS!' After the Cup was presented he ended his commentary with Quietus. Then he paid Fred and George their winnings in full. He did not know that the twins had nudged the match their way with the leprechauns, broom polish on the Bulgarian Keeper's broom and a fake whistle.

In their own words

Not a dicky bird. But she'll turn up.Ludo Bagman · B4 Ch5
Glad! Don't know when I've had more fun…Ludo Bagman · B4 Ch5
Somebody in the crowd with a whistle... naughty, naughty! Mostafa is not pleased... but the goal stands!Ludo Bagman · B4 Ch6

pages.html: Otto Bagman, Ludo Bagman's brother, got into trouble over a lawnmower with unnatural powers, which Arthur Weasley smoothed over.

pages.title: Bertha Jorkins
infobox: Ministry of Magic, Department of Magical Games and Sports, missing
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Missing in Albania since the summer of 1994
pages.html:
Bertha Jorkins is a witch of the Ministry of Magic, of Ludo Bagman's Department of Magical Games and Sports. In the summer of 1994 she went on holiday to Albania and never came back. By the World Cup final she had been missing for over a month, with no news of her at all.

Background

Bertha was at Hogwarts a few years ahead of James Potter and Sirius Black. She was very nosy, with little sense but an excellent memory for gossip. At the Ministry she was shunted from department to department for years, gaining a name for being more trouble than she was worth. For a time she worked in the Department of International Magical Cooperation, where Bartemius Crouch is said to have grown quite fond of her. Ludo Bagman says she has a memory like a leaky cauldron, with no sense of direction, and that she has got lost many times before.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: at dinner at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Percy Weasley told his father that Bertha had been missing for over a month. She had gone on holiday to Albania and never come back. Mr Crouch had been taking a personal interest, Percy said, but Bagman only laughed. He was sure she had misread the map, ending up in Australia instead of Albania. Arthur Weasley had asked Ludo about her, only to be told that she had got lost plenty of times before. Arthur said he would be worried if it were someone in his own department.

Book Four, Chapter Five: at the World Cup campsite the next day Arthur asked whether there was any news. 'Not a dicky bird,' said Bagman. 'But she'll turn up.' Poor old Bertha, he said, would wander back into the office sometime in October, thinking it was still July. Crouch kept saying somebody should be sent to look for her, but Bagman said nobody could be spared.

pages.title: Viktor Krum
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Caught the Snitch in the final, which Bulgaria lost 160 to 170
pages.html:
Viktor Krum is the Seeker of the Bulgarian national Quidditch team, and at eighteen he is already counted among the finest Seekers in the world. In the final of the 1994 World Cup he played on with a broken nose. He caught the Snitch when Bulgaria could no longer win, ending the match on his own terms, 160 to 170.

Background

Krum was born in Bulgaria in 1976. He is a pupil at the Durmstrang Institute, the wizarding school of the far north whose headmaster is Igor Karkaroff. Durmstrang admits no Muggle-borns, and it teaches the Dark Arts themselves rather than only the defence against them. Krum was picked to play Seeker for his country while he was still at school. By the summer of 1994 he was famous all over the wizarding world, with posters of his face on Bulgarian tents and toy figures of him for sale.

Appearance and flying

He is thin and sallow, dark-haired, with a great hooked nose under heavy black brows, like a hawk grown too big for its perch. On the ground he is not graceful at all: his feet turn out a little, and his shoulders are round. In the air he barely seems to need a broomstick, moving as though he weighed nothing. His posters show a sullen young man who only blinks and scowls.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Fred Weasley pointed out that Bulgaria had Viktor Krum. Charlie answered that Krum was Bulgaria's one decent player, while Ireland had seven.

Book Four, Chapter Five: at the campsite the next morning his moving poster was stuck to every Bulgarian tent. Ron Weasley said he was only about eighteen, a genius, while Hermione Granger thought he looked really grumpy. At lunch Fred and George bet Ludo Bagman that Ireland would win but that Krum would catch the Snitch. That evening Ron bought a tiny Krum, which marched up and down his palm glaring at his green rosette.

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the final Krum's Wronski Feint drew the Irish Seeker, Aidan Lynch, into the ground, although Krum had never seen the Snitch. While mediwizards poured potions down Lynch's throat, Krum circled high above, hunting for it with nobody in his way. George Weasley sat pale, mouthing, 'Not yet, Viktor.' Later a Bludger from the Irish Beater Quigley broke Krum's nose. No whistle came, because a veela's fireball had set the referee's broom alight, so Krum shook his head, spattering blood, then played on.

When Lynch dived for the Snitch in earnest, Krum drew level with him, streaming blood. Lynch crashed. Krum rose with the Snitch in his fist while Ireland led 170 to 10, so Bulgaria lost by 160 to 170, exactly as the twins had bet. Harry Potter believed that Krum had known the Irish would never be caught, so he chose to end the match on his own terms. Afterwards Krum looked sulkier than ever, refusing to let the mediwizards clean him up. He came last into the Top Box, with two black eyes coming up on his bloodied face, the Snitch still in his fist. Yet the stadium gave him its loudest roar of the night.

pages.title: The Bulgarian Minister for Magic
infobox: Bulgaria, Ministry of Magic, Minister for Magic
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Oblansk or Obalonsk, by Cornelius Fudge's account
Black velvet robes trimmed with gold
pages.html:
The Bulgarian Minister for Magic led his country's party at the 1994 Quidditch World Cup final in Britain. Cornelius Fudge, who called him Oblansk or Obalonsk, believed that he spoke no English, so he mimed to him all day. The Minister let him do it, because he thought it very funny.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: in August 1994 the Bulgarian Minister reported a Muggle disturbance near his country's western border, beyond which Khan's Augments were fighting their way into Yugoslavia. Half of Bulgaria's World Cup supporters were afraid to travel overland, so he asked for the Bulgarian Portkey allowance to be doubled. Bartemius Crouch replied that Muggle disturbances were a matter for the Muggle Liaison Office.

Book Four, Chapter Six: at the final he sat in the Top Box in splendid black velvet robes trimmed with gold. His party had been pressing for twelve more seats in the box all day. Fudge introduced Harry Potter to him in a loud voice, to no effect at all, until the Minister noticed Harry's scar. He jabbed a finger at it, gabbling loudly. Fudge could not manage his name either, presenting him to the Malfoys as 'Mr Oblansk... Obalonsk... Mr...'

After Bulgaria lost, a mournful voice spoke at Harry's back, in English: 'Vell, ve fought bravely.' Fudge was outraged, but the Minister only shrugged, saying it had been very funny. When John Constantine was exposed in the box, Lucius Malfoy's first jinx missed him, blowing the Minister's hat clean off his head instead. He picked up its smoking remains, looking happier than he had all evening. 'This is better than the match.' Arthur Weasley later helped him look for the brim.

In their own words

This is better than the match.The Bulgarian Minister for Magic · B4 Ch6

pages.title: Wilfred Thimble
aliases: the old wizard in the photograph
infobox: wizard, Stockport, Department of Magical Maintenance
pages.html:
Wilfred Thimble is an elderly retired wizard of Stockport who used to work in Magical Maintenance at the Ministry of Magic. In August 1994 a gang of young Muggles dragged him off his ladder and beat him, shouting 'mutie'. It was the third such attack that month.

The attack

One Sunday morning in August 1994 Thimble was mending his guttering with his wand. A gang of young Muggles saw him. They dragged him down off the ladder, beating him while they shouted 'mutie' at him, the Muggle name for people born with powers. Three of them ended up trussed in ropes that seemed to have sprung out of nowhere. The Ministry sent in Obliviators to sort out the memories.

The Daily Prophet reported it under the headline MUGGLE ATTACK BARELY FOILED. Its moving photograph showed Thimble sitting on his doorstep in torn robes, with a split lip, pressing a handkerchief to a black eye. On the ground in front of him writhed the three young Muggle men, shouting soundlessly at the camera. One wore a T-shirt with the words FRIENDS OF HUMANITY across the chest in neat red letters.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994 Harry Potter saw the photograph in the Prophet at the Burrow. He knew the look on the Muggle's face, red, roaring and blind, though he had never seen the man before. At dinner Arthur Weasley told the story of 'that poor old chap up in Stockport'. He asked Harry whether the word the Muggles had shouted meant anything to him. Harry thought of the old wizard on his doorstep, who had not the faintest idea why they had hit him.

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the Top Box at the World Cup final, Harry told Cornelius Fudge what mutie meant. They had shouted it in Stockport, he said, at Mr Thimble from Magical Maintenance, before they dragged him off his ladder.

pages.title: The three Muggle men who attacked Wilfred Thimble
aliases: the young Muggles in the Prophet photograph
pages.html:
In the Daily Prophet photograph of August 1994, three young Muggle men lay trussed in ropes that seemed to spring out of nowhere, writhing and shouting soundlessly at the camera.

In Book Four

One of them twisted his head round to glare out of the picture with the red, blind rage Harry had seen on the red-haired woman at the UN protest; across his T-shirt were the words FRIENDS OF HUMANITY. B4 Ch4

pages.title: Father Christmas
infobox: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (16 October 1950)
1940, as the White Witch's winter broke
The sword Rhindon; a shield with a red lion
A bow, a quiver of arrows, an ivory horn
A cordial of fire-flower juice; a small dagger
pages.html:
Father Christmas is the old man in red who brings presents at Christmas. In England he is mostly a story for children. In Narnia he was real enough to give a queen her bow. He came into Narnia in 1940, when Aslan was on the move and the White Witch's long winter had begun to break. The gifts he gave the Pevensie children went with them through all their reigns.

Always winter

For a hundred years the White Witch had kept Narnia in winter, and Christmas never came. Father Christmas could not get in while her power held.

In 1940, when Aslan came back and her power began to fail, Father Christmas came at last, in a sledge drawn by reindeer with bells on their harness. He was enormous and plainly delighted, in a red robe trimmed with white fur, with a long white beard. Everyone who saw him felt solemn and happy at once.

The gifts

He met Peter, Susan and Lucy on the road with the Beavers. He gave each of them a present. Edmund was not there to be given one, because he had gone over to the Witch.

To Peter he gave a sword, Rhindon, and a shield with a red lion on it. To Susan he gave a bow, a quiver of arrows and a little ivory horn: if she blew it, help would come to her wherever she was. To Lucy he gave a bottle of cordial made from the juice of fire-flowers, a drop of which would heal almost any hurt, and a small dagger.

He told the girls that their gifts were for use in great need, and that he did not mean them to fight in the battle. Lucy, who thought she could be brave enough, was cross about it.

He gave Mrs Beaver a new sewing machine. He told Mr Beaver that his dam had been finished and mended. Then he brought out a tray laid for tea, with the teapot already hot. He wished them all a merry Christmas, cried long life to the true King, and was gone.

What his coming meant

His coming was the first sure sign that the Witch's magic was failing. Christmas could come to Narnia only because Aslan had. Within a day the thaw had begun, and the Witch's sledge stuck fast in the melting snow.

The gifts afterwards

The gifts went with the four through all their reign at Cair Paravel. Peter killed the wolf Maugrim with Rhindon. Lucy's cordial healed the wounded of more than one battle, Edmund among them.

Susan's horn stayed in Narnia when the four went home through the wardrobe. In 1941 Prince Caspian blew it in his need and called them back. Susan never gave up the bow. Forty years later, in her own home, she drew Lord Voldemort's blood with it.

In England

In England Father Christmas is a story for children, and grown-ups know better. The Pevensies knew that he was real, which is more than most grown-ups can say. Many people believe that he grew out of Saint Nicholas of Myra, the bishop who gave presents in secret. Nobody in Narnia ever thought to ask him.

Muggles put fat little Father Christmases with fishing rods on their lawns. Wizards, whose gardens are full of gnomes, find this very funny.

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994 Harry told the Dursleys that Floo powder let wizards come down the chimney like Father Christmas. When the Weasleys found the fireplace boarded up, he called through the boards that the Dursleys had not wanted Father Christmas turning up without notice. Uncle Vernon protested that he had believed in Father Christmas until he was eleven, while Arthur Weasley gently told Harry that Father Christmas is not real.

In Book Four

A'Gaeris forged evidence against Aitrus and used it to turn Veovis against him. B4 Ch4

pages.title: The calling to New Mexico
infobox: Muggles of D'ni descent, who do not know it
One place in the New Mexico desert: the Cleft
Eleven people on a Muggle newsgroup about Myst
pages.html:
The calling to New Mexico is a pull towards one particular place in the New Mexico desert, felt by a scattering of Muggles who have never been there. By August 1994 eleven of them had found each other on a newsgroup about Myst. Every one of them has a strange, clever ancestor who turned up out of nowhere just after 1788, the year D'ni fell.

Those who feel it

They live in different countries, and at first none of them knew any of the others. They are clever people, puzzle people, the kind who notice patterns. They cannot stop thinking about a desert they have never seen. One kept dreaming of an old volcano with a crack in the ground beside it, which is the Cleft. Another said it felt like being called home. A couple of them are occultists. By the summer of 1994 they had begun writing to each other, so that a community was forming. One got as far as a fence in the middle of nowhere, where men told him to go home.

The ancestors

Comparing their families, they all found the same thing. Somewhere in each family tree is an ancestor thought rather strange: odd, but very clever, somebody who appeared out of nowhere, married into a family, then made things nobody else knew how to make. Every one of those ancestors first appears in the records just after 1788. Old newspaper reports from Pennsylvania, running from the 1790s to the 1830s, tell of strange men turning up at farms and workshops to ask after fanciful contraptions that nobody could explain. The papers took the men for natural philosophers collecting experiments.

Hermione Granger believes that a handful of D'ni got out when the plague came, people who were away from the city or found a way up through the rock. Some stayed in the desert, which was still Spanish then. Others went east into the newly formed United States, married settlers and had children, until their families forgot where they came from. She thinks somebody went round afterwards, quietly collecting whatever the D'ni had left behind.

Yeesha, the daughter of Atrus, gave her mother Catherine's journals to the brothers who made Myst, meaning the game to draw people of D'ni blood to the Cleft. Those who feel the calling found one another through that game. In later years the Cleft became the place where explorers who felt called to the desert first arrived.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Two: in the summer of 1994 Hermione wrote to Harry that she had found six such posters on the newsgroup comp.sys.ibm.pc.games.adventure. She wondered whether it was something in the blood.

Book Four, Chapter Four: on the night of 21 August 1994, in Mr Weasley's shed, she told Harry and Ron that there were eleven now, then set out her hypothesis. The Muggles had half the story, she said, while the three of them had the other half, in Anna's journal and the island. Harry asked whether it could wait until after the World Cup.

pages.title: The Pennsylvania historical society member
pages.html: One of the Muggles with the calling belongs to a historical society in Pennsylvania; asked by Hermione about his ancestor, he typed out old newspaper reports for her from the 1790s to the 1830s.

pages.title: The Pennsylvania newspaper reports
pages.html: Old newspaper reports from the 1790s to the 1830s told of strange men turning up at farms and workshops asking after fanciful contraptions that somebody's father or grandfather had made and nobody could explain.

pages.title: The collectors of the strange contraptions
pages.html: Between the 1790s and the 1830s strange men visited farms and workshops in America asking after unexplained machines; the papers took them for natural philosophers collecting experiments, but Hermione thought they were collecting what the D'ni had left behind.

pages.title: Internet
pages.html: Hermione described the internet as a way of joining computers all over the world down the telephone lines, like owls but instant, used by millions; Arthur Weasley explained it to Ron at Easter 1994.

pages.title: Occultists
pages.html: A couple of the Muggles with the calling to New Mexico were occultists; Ron and Hermione both shuddered at the word and would not yet explain it to Harry.

pages.title: Pennsylvania
pages.html: A member of a historical society in Pennsylvania sent Hermione newspaper reports from the 1790s to the 1830s about strange men collecting contraptions.

pages.title: United States
pages.html: The United States had only just been formed in 1788; Hermione believed some D'ni survivors went east into it and married settlers.

pages.title: New York City
pages.html:
The stretchy scientist of the Fantastic Four worked on clean energy in New York in 1994, and twenty thousand people protested outside the United Nations there.

In Book Four

In 1994 protesters in New York shouted 'mutie', and outside the United Nations they demanded that people like Harry be punished. B4 Ch6

pages.title: India
infobox: New Delhi, held by Khan Noonien Singh since July 1993
pages.html:
India is the great republic of South Asia, home to some nine hundred million people in 1994. In the summer of 1993 the Augments of Khan Noonien Singh took New Delhi, and the Indian government withdrew to Bangalore. A year later they had driven so many people out of India's cities that nobody could count them.

History

India won its independence from Britain in 1947, when the subcontinent was divided between India and Pakistan. It became a republic in 1950, with its capital at New Delhi.

The Augment War

In 1993 genetically engineered rulers seized power in more than forty countries at once. In India, Khan's forces laid siege to New Delhi for eleven weeks, taking it in late July 1993. The government withdrew to Bangalore. By the end of the month Khan held the land from the Afghan border to the Bay of Bengal, where he proclaimed a 'new order' for the subcontinent. The Avengers and the Justice League declined to intervene, under their United Nations accord. Delhi greeted their statement with anger.

From India his rule spread west across Pakistan and Iran to the Persian Gulf. In March 1994 a United Nations coalition, the largest multinational force since the Gulf War, crossed the front line south of Delhi. It was expected to reach the city within a month. It was withdrawn in June, having advanced eleven miles. By August 1994 the Augments had moved so many people out of India's cities that the coalition could not even count them. Nobody in Whitehall will say in public what has become of India's nuclear weapons.

In the saga

Book Three, Chapter Two: on 31 July 1993 the Dursleys' breakfast news reported the fall of New Delhi. Harry watched Khan on a balcony above the crowd, looking as if the whole of India were a dog that had finally learnt to sit.

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994 Percy Weasley, at work on a report about cauldron thickness, put his head out of his window at the Burrow to scream at the world in general, and at India in particular, about its shoddy cauldrons. At dinner Harry told the table that Khan's Augments had taken India the year before. Nobody there had heard of them. Arthur Weasley, who loved all things Muggle, had never heard of Khan.

Book Four, Chapter Five: in the scullery before dawn on 22 August, Hermione told Harry that nobody knew how many people the Augments in India had moved out of the cities.

Book Four, Chapter Six: that night in the Top Box Harry told Cornelius Fudge that the Augments, who were made in a laboratory, had taken India the year before. Fudge assured him there were arrangements.

pages.title: Yugoslavia
infobox: 1918, as the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia: Serbia and Montenegro
By Augment forces under Joaquin, July 1994
Kosovo; the Montenegrin coast; most of eastern Bosnia
pages.html:
Yugoslavia, the land of the South Slavs, is a Balkan state with its capital at Belgrade. The old federation broke apart from 1991, leaving only Serbia and Montenegro under the name. In July 1994 Augment forces under Joaquin appeared in the former Yugoslavia. By August, in Harry Potter's words, Khan had half of it.

History

The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was proclaimed on 1 December 1918. It took the name Yugoslavia in 1929. In April 1941 the Axis powers invaded it, then carved it up. Tito's Partisans fought the occupiers throughout the war, after which he ruled a socialist federation of six republics until his death in 1980.

The federation broke apart in 1991. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence that June, Macedonia that autumn, then Bosnia in March 1992. In April 1992 Serbia and Montenegro formed a new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. War followed in Croatia, then in Bosnia, where United Nations peacekeepers were sent in.

The Augment War

In July 1994 Augment forces appeared in the former Yugoslavia, and nobody is sure how they got there. Under Khan's commander Joaquin they took Kosovo, the Montenegrin coast, then most of eastern Bosnia within five weeks. Pale fell in a single morning, sending the Bosnian Serb leadership fleeing across the Drina into Serbia.

By 20 August 1994 the army of the rump Yugoslav state had collapsed. United Nations peacekeepers had been withdrawn from Goražde, while the Augments were within forty miles of Belgrade. Some three hundred thousand people were on the move, some of them up through the mountain passes into Romania. On 19 August Superman told the Security Council that the Justice League could be in Belgrade within the hour. Belgrade had not asked for help, and Russia said it would veto any resolution sending superhumans into Serbia without its consent.

The Bulgarian Ministry of Magic asked for its Portkey allowance for the Quidditch World Cup to be doubled, because a Muggle disturbance near Bulgaria's western border left half its supporters afraid to travel overland. Bartemius Crouch told the Bulgarians to take the matter to their own Muggle Liaison Office.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Three: on 20 August 1994 the news at Privet Drive showed refugees on a mountain road, among them a little boy crying with a cockerel under his arm.

Book Four, Chapter Four: at dinner at the Burrow the next evening, Charlie Weasley spoke of some Muggle war down Serbia way, with refugees coming up through the passes. Harry told the table that it was the Augment War: Khan's people were in Yugoslavia, nearly at Belgrade. Nobody there had heard of them.

Book Four, Chapter Five: before dawn on 22 August Harry asked Hermione whether he should send Khan a card, Congratulations on the Balkans. Khan had half of Yugoslavia, he said, which was more than Uncle Vernon had managed with Grunnings.

Book Four, Chapter Six: that night in the Top Box Harry told Cornelius Fudge that the Augments had half of Yugoslavia, and were nearly at Belgrade.

pages.title: Ton-Tongue Toffee
infobox: Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, joke sweets, Fred Weasley, George Weasley
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
The eater's tongue swells to a great length
An Engorgement Charm, Arthur Weasley thinks
pages.html:
Ton-Tongue Toffees are toffees in shiny, gaudy wrappers, invented by Fred and George Weasley. Whoever eats one finds his tongue swelling into a long, purple, slimy thing. The twins spent six months developing them, then the summer of 1994 looking for somebody to test them on.

Description

The trick is an Engorgement Charm, or so Arthur Weasley believes. The tongue goes on growing until somebody shrinks it. The toffees belong with the fake wands, trick sweets and other joke goods of Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, which the twins meant to sell at Hogwarts. Their mother found the order forms while cleaning their room, then burnt them. Their parents told them to destroy every toffee they had.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994, as the Weasleys were leaving Number Four, Privet Drive, by Floo, a bag of the toffees fell out of Fred's pocket and rolled across the Dursleys' carpet. Fred gathered most of them up again. Dudley, who was on a diet, ate one that was left behind. His tongue grew to four feet, lolling about the carpet like a great slimy python, before his parents would let Mr Weasley shrink it. Back at the Burrow Mr Weasley roared at Fred that he had dropped it on purpose. The twins answered that they had not given it to Dudley because he was a Muggle, but because he was a great bullying git. Later Mr Weasley blamed the toffees for whatever Harry had seen run under the Dursleys' sideboard.

Book Four, Chapter Five: before dawn on 22 August Mrs Weasley caught George trying to smuggle more toffees out of the house. She Summoned them from George's pocket, from the lining of his jacket and from the turn-ups of Fred's jeans, then flung the lot in the bin. 'We spent six months developing those!' Fred bellowed. The twins left for the World Cup without a word to her.

pages.title: Fake wand

pages.title: Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes
pages.html:

pages.title: Arthur Weasley's shed
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
The bottom of the garden at the Burrow
Plugs, batteries and other Muggle things
A car battery labelled EXHIBIT ONE
pages.html:
Arthur Weasley's shed stands at the bottom of the garden at the Burrow, half buried in honeysuckle. It holds Mr Weasley's collection of Muggle things, above all his batteries. Inside, it smells of engine oil and dust.

Description

Shelves run from the floor to the roof, every one of them crammed with Muggle things. There are plugs of every shape and size. There are jars of screws, a dismantled toaster, three telephones and a bicycle pump. Above all there are batteries, hundreds upon hundreds of them, in shoeboxes, in biscuit tins, in careful towers along the workbench. In pride of place, on an old kitchen chair, sits a car battery with a little brass plaque tied to it reading EXHIBIT ONE. Somewhere under the batteries is an old transistor radio.

Here Mr Weasley takes Muggle things apart, puts spells on them, then puts them back together again. His wife calls it all Muggle rubbish. She says that when he wrote the law against bewitching Muggle artefacts, he left a loophole in it on purpose, so that he could carry on tinkering in his shed.

In the saga

Book Two, Chapter Three: in August 1992 Ron told Harry that his father was mad about everything to do with Muggles, so that the shed was full of Muggle stuff.

Book Two, Chapter Four: Mrs Weasley accused her husband of making sure there was a loophole, just so that he could go on tinkering with the Muggle rubbish in his shed.

Book Two, Chapter Nine: George told the Gryffindor team that his father had a picture of a jump-jet in the shed.

Book Three, Chapter Twenty-Two: in June 1994 Mr Weasley came in from the shed with a toaster under his arm, saw the smile on his wife's face as she read the letters about Harry, then went straight back out again.

Book Four, Chapter Four: on the night of 21 August 1994 Hermione hauled Harry and Ron off to the shed while Mrs Weasley was busy shouting at the twins. By candlelight Harry told them about the rats at Privet Drive. Then Hermione told them what she had found out about the D'ni, with the Muggles who felt the calling to New Mexico. Harry offered to buy the Weasleys a computer; Hermione pointed out that it would need mains electricity, which all the batteries in the shed could not supply.

Book Four, Chapter Five: Hermione had been following the Muggle news on the transistor radio. Before dawn on 22 August she told Harry that the crowd outside the United Nations had grown to three hundred thousand.

pages.title: The Bulgarian Ministry of Magic
pages.html: In August 1994 the Bulgarians asked for their Portkey allowance to be doubled, because a Muggle disturbance near their western border kept half their supporters from travelling overland.

pages.title: Portkey
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Anything; usually something Muggles will take for litter
Everyone touching it, at a prearranged time
pages.html:
A Portkey is an object enchanted to carry wizards from one spot to another at a prearranged time. It can take a large group at once, which makes it the usual way to move crowds, families or anybody who cannot Apparate. For the Quidditch World Cup of 1994 two hundred Portkeys were placed around Britain.

Description

Anything can be made into a Portkey. The Ministry of Magic uses unobtrusive things that Muggles will take for litter, so that nobody picks one up to play with it: an old boot, an old newspaper, an empty drinks can or a punctured football. A traveller needs only to touch it, and a single finger will do.

The journey feels like a hook catching just behind the navel, then yanking. The ground drops away, wind roars past and colours stream by in a blur, with the traveller's finger glued to the object as it tows the whole party along. The landing is hard. Experienced travellers keep their feet, but most people end up on the ground.

Regulation

Portkeys are the business of the Ministry. The Portkey Office belongs to the Department of Magical Transportation, which also licenses Apparition, and making a Portkey without the Ministry's authority is against the law. For international events each country is given an allowance of Portkeys. Officials at the arrival point log each party in by its time of departure, then throw the used Portkeys into a box.

The 1994 World Cup

Two hundred Portkeys were placed at strategic points around Britain for the final. Bartemius Crouch, of the Department of International Magical Cooperation, organised Portkeys across five continents. The Bulgarians asked for their allowance to be doubled. Their Minister said the Muggles were having some sort of disturbance near Bulgaria's western border, so that half their supporters dared not travel overland. Mr Crouch told them that Muggle disturbances were a matter for their own Muggle Liaison Office.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: at dinner at the Burrow on 21 August 1994, Percy Weasley complained that the Bulgarians wanted their Portkey allowance doubled.

Book Four, Chapter Five: before dawn the next day Mr Weasley explained Portkeys to Harry, who had had enough of the Myst linking book and called them magic litter. On Stoatshead Hill Amos Diggory held out the Portkey, a mouldy old boot, for nine people to touch. It landed them on the moor at seven minutes past five. Harry fell flat on his back in wet grass, then swore without repeating himself once. 'Who sat down one day and said, I know, let's make a boot that does that?' he asked. 'Wizards,' said Hermione.

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the Top Box that night Harry praised the Portkeys to Cornelius Fudge, all two hundred of them 'to the minute'. Fudge modestly gave the credit to Mr Crouch's department.

pages.title: House gnome
infobox: A thin, hairless garden gnome, with longer fingers and teeth as sharp as pins
pages.html:
The house gnome is a cousin of the garden gnome, thinner, with longer fingers and sharper teeth. If garden gnomes are field mice, house gnomes are house mice. They live inside the walls of houses, where they feed on the bad temper of the people who live there. Molly Weasley calls them a sort of judgement.

Description

A house gnome is small, brown and hairless, rather like a garden gnome, but thinner, with longer fingers. Its teeth are as sharp as pins. It has tiny, knowing black eyes.

Habits

Once house gnomes get into the walls of a house, there is no getting them out again without a proper witch to do it. In Muggle houses they chew the wiring, so that the television goes off just when the programme is getting good. They turn the milk overnight. They take one sock out of every pair, or one shoe if the gnome is a big one. They whisper, too. Muggles never quite see them, only glimpse them out of the corner of an eye, so they think they are imagining things. After a month or two most of them begin to wonder whether they are going a little mad.

House gnomes breed every six weeks or so. What they live on is bad temper and spite. A cross, mean household will keep them fat for years, while a happy one starves them out inside a week. The nastier the people in a house are, the more gnomes it gets, and the longer they stay. They are terribly rare in towns. The Weasleys have never had them at the Burrow. Arthur Weasley thinks the whole arrangement rather fair.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994, while the Dursleys were busy with Dudley's tongue, Arthur Weasley set a house gnome down on their living-room carpet at Number Four, Privet Drive. It ran under the sideboard. That evening, over strawberry ice cream at the Burrow, Harry asked Mrs Weasley whether there were other sorts of gnome besides the garden ones, and she told him all about house gnomes, quite placidly. Hermione went very still, then said it was brilliant. She murmured that 'she' would never believe it; asked who, she said quickly that she meant her mother. When Harry said he thought he had seen one in Mr Weasley's bag, he was told it had been Floo powder, one of Fred's toffees or a trick of the Floo smoke.

Book Four, Chapter Five: before dawn the next morning Mr Weasley murmured over the World Cup tickets, 'Six weeks, Molly. Right on time.' The gnomes at the Dursleys' were breeding on schedule. Mrs Weasley silenced him with his name, and he went pink trying not to laugh.

pages.title: The house gnome at Privet Drive
aliases: the thing from Mr Weasley's bag
infobox: House gnome, Number Four, Privet Drive
Number Four, Privet Drive, Little Whinging
Mr Weasley's drawstring bag of Floo powder
pages.html:
The house gnome at Privet Drive is the house gnome that Arthur Weasley let loose in the Dursleys' living room at Number Four, Privet Drive, on 21 August 1994. It ran under the sideboard. Planting it was entirely Mr Weasley's own idea.

Description

It is small, brown and hairless, rather like the gnomes in the garden at the Burrow, but thinner, with longer fingers. When it bares its teeth they are as sharp as pins. It has tiny, knowing black eyes. Like all house gnomes it lives on bad temper and spite.

Background

The gnome was one more blow in a campaign against the Dursleys. In June 1994 Hermione Granger and Dracina Malfoy wrote to Molly Weasley about Harry's life at Privet Drive, twenty pages between them. That summer pond mud erupted from the Dursleys' kitchen sink, which afterwards gurgled whenever Petunia was about to snap at Harry. Mrs Weasley told Harry it had only been a little nudge. The woman at number seven told the whole of Little Whinging about the Dursleys' drains, on top of the rats.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: on 21 August 1994 Mr Weasley blasted his way into the Dursleys' living room through the boarded-up fireplace to fetch Harry, making as much mess as he possibly could. When he took out his drawstring bag of Floo powder, Harry saw the cloth bulge and wriggle, as though some small animal had got in among the powder; Mr Weasley caught his eye, then pulled the drawstring tight. While the Dursleys were busy with Dudley's swollen tongue, his hand slipped back into the bag. With a mischievous grin at Harry, he bent down as though to tie a shoelace, then set the wriggling thing on the carpet. It looked up at Harry before it scurried under the sideboard.

At dinner at the Burrow Mrs Weasley asked her husband whether he had mended the Dursleys' wall before he left. It had gone clean out of his head, he said: 'They had it coming.' Harry supposed he meant the fireplace. Later Harry asked about other sorts of gnome, and Mrs Weasley described house gnomes at length. When he said he thought he had seen one in Mr Weasley's bag, there was the very slightest pause. Mr Weasley said it had been Floo powder shifting about, or one of Fred's toffees. Mrs Weasley said they were terribly rare in towns. Hermione blamed the Floo smoke, citing chapter three of Floo Travel for the Nervous Witch. Harry let it go.

Book Four, Chapter Five: before dawn on 22 August Mrs Weasley was murmuring to Hermione about trouble twice in one night at the Dursleys' sink, with a second plumber who would not set foot in the kitchen. She told Harry she had been talking about her own sink. Over the tickets Mr Weasley murmured, 'Six weeks, Molly. Right on time,' for the gnomes at Number Four were breeding. 'Arthur,' said his wife.

pages.title: Ron's letter to his pen pal
infobox: OPERATION GET IT OVER WITH; PLAN C
pages.html:
Ron's letter to his pen pal was the three-page plan that Ron Weasley sent by owl to Pansy Parkinson on the night of 21 August 1994. It set out several schemes for getting Harry Potter together with Dracina Malfoy. Ron told Harry it was for a pen pal.

Contents

The first page was headed OPERATION GET IT OVER WITH. The second was headed PLAN C (IF THE BOAT ONE DOESN'T WORK EITHER); Harry's name appeared on it eleven times, Dracina's twelve. Between them the pages offered a boat plan, a Plan A and a Plan C. The address was written in Ron's very worst handwriting, to a girl who had lately bought a Chudley Cannons poster that clashed with everything she owned. Ron thought this showed excellent taste. It had never once crossed his mind to wonder why she was so very keen to help.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: Ron had left the roll of parchment, tied up with string, on his pillow, and nearly forgot to send it. He let Pig out of his cage, said 'Pen pal' very fast when Harry asked, then dashed off downstairs. A minute later a tiny owl shot away north over the dark orchard. Harry had not known Ron would write to anybody if he could possibly help it. He decided it was none of his business, then went to sleep. He might have slept less soundly if he had read the letter.

Book Four, Chapter Five: Pansy's answer reached Ron before dawn. She had received his plan at half past eleven and read all three pages, which she said was more than Professor Binns had ever got out of her. The boat plan was out of the question, since Dracina will not get into a boat. Plan C was worse. They would do Plan A. Later Mrs Weasley asked Ron, with a twitch at the corner of her mouth, whether his letter had been from that pen pal of his.

pages.title: Amos Diggory
infobox:
Cedric Diggory son
Arthur Weasley friend
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Department for the Regulation and Control of Magical Creatures, Ministry of Magic
pages.html:
Amos Diggory is a wizard of the Ministry of Magic who works in the Department for the Regulation and Control of Magical Creatures. He is the father of Cedric Diggory, the Hufflepuff Seeker, of whom he is loudly proud. He travelled to the 1994 World Cup final by Portkey with the Weasley party.

Family

Amos is a cheerful wizard with a scrubby brown beard and a ruddy face. The Diggorys live near Ottery St Catchpole, not far from the Weasleys, and Amos is a friend of Arthur Weasley's. Cedric is his only son. Amos is so proud of him that he boasts on his behalf, which embarrasses the modest Cedric.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Five: before dawn on 22 August 1994 Amos waited with Cedric on top of Stoatshead Hill, holding the Portkey, a mouldy old boot. He called Arthur over. They had had to get up at two, he said, and he would be glad when Cedric had passed his Apparition test. He would not have missed the World Cup for a sackful of Galleons, which was about what the tickets cost.

When Arthur introduced Harry Potter, Amos exclaimed, 'Merlin's beard.' Harry told him his name was Barry Trotter, at which Amos let out a huge belly laugh; Cedric had told him Harry had a wicked sense of humour. Then he boasted that Cedric had beaten Harry Potter, which would be something to tell his grandchildren. Cedric muttered that Harry had fallen off his broom. 'Yes, but you didn't fall off, did you?' Amos boomed, clapping him on the back. Cedric looked embarrassed, while Fred and George scowled.

Amos told Arthur that the Lovegoods had been at the site for a week already, while the Fawcetts had not been able to get tickets. He had had complaints, he said, about the Lovegood girl's small apparatus. At the Portkey arrival point on the moor the official, Basil, sent the Diggorys to the second field, under the site manager, Mr Payne.

In their own words

Ced, that'll be something to tell your grandchildren, that will… You beat Harry Potter!Amos Diggory · B4 Ch5

pages.title: Bartemius Crouch's grandfather
pages.html: Mr Crouch's grandfather owned an Axminster flying carpet that could seat twelve, before carpets were banned in Britain.

pages.title: Basil
infobox: The Portkey official in the tweed suit colleague
Ministry of Magic, Quidditch World Cup (1994)
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
The Portkey arrival point at the World Cup
A kilt, topped with a poncho
pages.html:
Basil is a Ministry of Magic wizard who manned the Portkey arrival point on the moor at the 1994 Quidditch World Cup. His idea of Muggle dress was a kilt, topped with a poncho.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Five: when the Weasley party landed from Stoatshead Hill at seven minutes past five on the morning of 22 August 1994, two weary, grumpy wizards were waiting. One, in a tweed suit with galoshes up to his thighs, held a big gold watch. Basil held a quill with a fat roll of parchment. Arthur Weasley greeted him by name. Basil tossed the party's Portkey, a mouldy old boot, into a box of used ones that held an old newspaper, an empty drinks can and a punctured football.

'Not on duty, eh?' he said wearily to Arthur. 'It's all right for some...' He had been there all night. He told them to get out of the way, because a big party from the Black Forest was due at five fifteen. Running his quill down his list, he sent the Weasleys to the first field, under Mr Roberts, while the Diggorys went to the second, under Mr Payne. Mr Roberts noticed him later as 'a bloke walking round in a kilt and a poncho'.

pages.title: The Portkey official in the tweed suit
infobox: Ministry of Magic, Quidditch World Cup (1994)
pages.html:
This weary, grumpy Ministry wizard worked the Portkey arrival point on the moor with Basil at the 1994 World Cup. He held a big gold watch and wore a tweed suit above galoshes that reached his thighs.

In Book Four

A voice, implied to be his, announced the Weasley party's arrival: 'Seven past five from Stoatshead Hill.' B4 Ch5

pages.title: Mr Roberts
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Manager of the first field at the 1994 World Cup campsite
A little stone cottage by the field gate
pages.html:
Mr Roberts is the Muggle who managed the first field of the campsite at the 1994 Quidditch World Cup, where a hundred thousand wizards camped round him. He was the only genuine Muggle for acres. The Ministry of Magic had to modify his memory about ten times a day to keep him happy.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Five: Mr Roberts lived in a little stone cottage beside the gate of the first field. When the Weasley party arrived on the morning of 22 August 1994 he gave them a space up by the wood for one night. Arthur Weasley struggled with the Muggle banknotes, so Mr Roberts asked whether he was foreign. Harry Potter answered sarcastically that they were from Timbuktu. Ten minutes earlier, Mr Roberts said, two campers had tried to pay him with great gold coins the size of hubcaps.

He was growing suspicious. There had been hundreds of prebookings, when people usually just turned up. There were foreigners everywhere, as well as weirdos, such as a bloke walking round in a kilt and a poncho. They all seemed to know each other, he said, like some sort of rally. 'If I had half a mind, I'd reckon they were Muti-' With a soft pop a wizard in plus fours appeared beside his door to cast a Memory Charm on him. Mr Roberts's frown smoothed away into a dreamy, untroubled look. He serenely handed Arthur a map of the campsite along with his change.

The wizard told Arthur that Mr Roberts needed a Memory Charm ten times a day to keep him happy. Harry was furious that the wizards could think of nothing better than wiping the man's memory, while the whole Muggle world looked for any excuse to batter anybody strange. At lunch Bartemius Crouch revealed that Mr Roberts had used the word 'Mutie' to one of Crouch's people the night before, ahead of another Memory Charm.

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the Top Box that night Harry told Cornelius Fudge about Mr Roberts, who was quite a lot the wiser about wizards. The Obliviators had had to deal with him about ten times a day, Harry said, the last time halfway through the word 'mutie'. Fudge waved it away: the Accidental Magic Reversal Squad had it all in hand.

In their own words

If I had half a mind, I'd reckon they were Muti-Mr Roberts · B4 Ch5

pages.title: The Ministry wizard in plus fours
infobox: Ministry of Magic, Obliviators, Quidditch World Cup (1994)
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Memory Charms on the Muggle site manager at the 1994 World Cup
pages.html:
The Ministry wizard in plus fours was one of the Ministry of Magic's officials at the campsite of the 1994 Quidditch World Cup. His task was to keep the Muggle site manager, Mr Roberts, from noticing too much. That meant casting a Memory Charm on him about ten times a day.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Five: on the morning of 22 August 1994 the Weasley party was paying Mr Roberts for their pitch when he began to say that the campers must be 'Muti-'. With a soft pop the wizard in plus fours appeared beside the door. 'Obliviate!' he snapped, with his wand on Mr Roberts, whose face went soft, blank and untroubled.

Harry Potter glared at him, hissing, 'This is not bloody efficient!' Mr Weasley steered Harry away. The wizard was worn out, badly in need of a shave, with purple smudges under his eyes. Walking with them to the gate, he complained to Arthur that Mr Roberts needed a Memory Charm ten times a day. Ludo Bagman was not helping, he added, trotting round talking about Bludgers and Quaffles at the top of his voice, without a worry about anti-Muggle security. He would be glad when it was all over, he said, then Disapparated with a crack.

To Harry it seemed all that wizards could be bothered to do. A hundred thousand of them were camping round one ordinary Muggle, while the whole normal world looked for any excuse to batter anybody strange. Yet they did no more than wipe his memory, the way you might put a plaster on a werewolf bite. Harry made the sign of the cross, as the vicar did at the end of the service.

Arthur had written to Ali Bashir the week before the World Cup, and Mr Crouch said he could barely understand Bashir's accent. B4 Ch5

In Book Four

The Department of Magical Transportation gave them a heavy fine. Arthur did not think they would try it again in a hurry. B4 Ch5

pages.title: The Muggles who saw the splinched body parts

pages.title: The old woman Charlie Weasley Apparated onto
pages.html: When Charlie Weasley failed his first Apparition test, he landed five miles south of his target, right on top of an old woman doing her shopping.

pages.title: Elizabeth II
