pages.title: Hermione Granger's parents
infobox: Muggle, Granger family, Friends of Humanity
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
pages.html:
Mr and Mrs Granger are the Muggle parents of Hermione Granger. Both are dentists, with a surgery of their own, and both are atheists, like their daughter. By August 1994 both were going to Friends of Humanity meetings.

The family

Nobody in either family has ever had any magic. The Grangers learnt that their only child was a witch when her Hogwarts letter came in 1991, which was a great surprise to all three of them. They write to her every week during term. They have taken her camping in France.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Five, they went with Hermione to Diagon Alley in August 1992. Arthur Weasley was delighted to meet two real Muggles. He insisted on taking them to the Leaky Cauldron for a drink, towing them up the street in a way that looked to the Grangers a good deal more like a kidnapping. Both Grangers were left shaking after Lucius Malfoy insulted them and Arthur fought him in Flourish and Blotts.

In Book Three, Chapter Six, talking with Harry about why Hogwarts has no chapel, Hermione told him plainly: 'I'm an atheist. My parents are.'

In Chapter Twenty-One, on the dock at Myst Island in June 1994, Hermione told Dracina Malfoy what it had been like to find that half the castle thought her dirt because of her parents: 'Because they're dentists who fill people's teeth, and they love me.'

In the saga: 1994 to 1995

Book Four, Chapter Five: on 22 August 1994 Hermione told Harry that her parents went to Friends of Humanity meetings in a church hall on Thursday nights, though not to the marches. They thought magic different from mutation because it came in a book with rules, while their daughter was simply special. Hermione was sure that they loved her, and that they would keep the Statute for her sake if it killed them.

pages.title: Stoatshead Hill
pages.html:
Stoatshead Hill is a great dark hill beyond Ottery St Catchpole, pitted with rabbit holes and thick clumps of grass. In 1994 its top held the nearest World Cup Portkey to the Burrow.

In Book Four

On 22 August 1994 the Weasley party and the Diggorys left the top of Stoatshead Hill by Portkey, an old boot, arriving on the moor at seven minutes past five. B4 Ch5

pages.title: Quidditch World Cup campsite
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
A wide, empty moor in Britain
The Quidditch World Cup final, 22 August 1994
About a hundred thousand witches and wizards
Mr Roberts (first field); Mr Payne (second field)
By Portkey on the moor, or by Apparition into a nearby wood
No magic, strictly speaking, on Muggle land
pages.html:
The Quidditch World Cup campsite was the city of tents on a wide, empty moor where the world's witches and wizards gathered for the final of the 1994 World Cup. Muggle site managers ran its fields, and had never seen a crowd like it. Beyond a wood at the top of the slope stood the stadium.

Arrangements

About a hundred thousand wizards come to a World Cup, and Britain had no magical site big enough to hold them. The Ministry of Magic chose a deserted moor, then spent months on anti-Muggle precautions. Arrivals were staggered: people with cheaper tickets came two weeks early, some Apparated into a nearby wood, while most came by Portkey.

The fields

Behind a little stone cottage, hundreds upon hundreds of tents covered the long slope of a huge field, right up to a black line of trees. The Muggle Mr Roberts managed this first field; Mr Payne had the second. The Ministry had to put a Memory Charm on Mr Roberts about ten times a day.

Most tents could almost have passed for Muggle ones, spoilt only by a chimney, a bell pull or a weather vane. Others were blatantly magical. Halfway up rose the Malfoys' palace of striped silk, with white peacocks tethered at its entrance; Pansy Parkinson's family had a tent with a green silk awning two rows behind it. There was a tent three storeys high with turrets, another with a front garden, birdbath, sundial and fountain, another shaped like a pyramid. The Irish tents were covered in shamrocks. Every Bulgarian tent bore the same moving poster of Viktor Krum. The Weasleys camped at the very top, beside the wood, by a main path busy with Ministry officials.

The day of the final

At lunchtime haggard Ministry wizards dashed past to deal with a magical fire spitting violet sparks above the tents. By dusk the Ministry had given up trying to prevent magic. Salesmen popped up everywhere, selling shrieking rosettes, hats of dancing shamrocks, flags that played anthems, model Firebolts that really flew, Omnioculars. Then a deep gong boomed beyond the wood. At once lanterns of red and green lit a path through the trees to the stadium.

John Constantine was at the campsite all day, keeping out of Lucius Malfoy's sight while he watched over Harry Potter for Albus Dumbledore. The cigarette end smoking by the edge of the wood was his, as was the smoke from the trees behind the Weasleys' tent.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Five: the Weasley party arrived at seven minutes past five on the morning of 22 August 1994. A wizard in plus fours Obliviated Mr Roberts in the middle of a word: 'Muti-'. The tent Mr Weasley had borrowed from Perkins turned out to be a flat inside, done out like Mrs Figg's front room, smelling of cats. Ludo Bagman took the twins' bet beside the Weasleys' fire at lunch.

Book Four, Chapter Six: after the final, Ron led Harry back past the Bulgarian tents, making for the pine with the forked trunk.

pages.title: The clearing by the forked pine
pages.html:
At the top of the Bulgarian end of the World Cup campsite there is a clearing in the wood, past a big pine with a forked trunk, with a stream and a fallen tree to sit on.

In Book Four

Pansy Parkinson found the clearing on Saturday 20 August 1994 and hung it with fairy lanterns for Plan A. On the afternoon of 22 August she met Ron under the forked pine. B4 Ch5

pages.title: The Top Box
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
The summit of the 1994 World Cup stadium, halfway between the goalposts
About twenty purple and gilt chairs, in two rows
The purple-carpeted stairs, as high as they go
Cornelius Fudge; the Bulgarian Minister for Magic; the Malfoys; the Weasleys and their party
pages.html:
The Top Box was the best box at the stadium of the 1994 Quidditch World Cup, perched at the very summit of the stands, exactly halfway between the golden goalposts. The Minister for Magic watched the final from it with his guests, while Ludo Bagman commentated. The Cup was presented there.

Description

It was a small box at the top of the purple-carpeted stairs, holding some twenty chairs of purple picked out in gilt, set in two rows. From the front row the pitch looked as smooth as velvet, with the great scoreboard hanging opposite, almost at eye level. In the back corner, by the top of the stairs, stood a gilded pillar that hid anybody behind it from most of the seats. Just below the box was the block of the most expensive seats in the stadium.

Places in it were much sought after. The Bulgarians demanded twelve more chairs in it. Mr Crouch's house-elf, Winky, sat in the back row saving his seat, though she was terrified of heights. For the presentation of the Cup the box was lit by magic with a blinding white light, so that the whole stadium could see in.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Five: at lunch on 22 August 1994 Mr Crouch told Ludo Bagman that the Bulgarians were insisting on twelve more seats in the Top Box. Bagman had thought their man wanted to borrow a pair of tweezers.

Book Four, Chapter Six: the Weasley party had seats in the front row. Harry charmed Cornelius Fudge there in front of Lucius Malfoy, who then took him behind the gilded pillar to thank him, as one man to another, for saving Dracina from the werewolf. Narcissa Malfoy introduced herself to Harry in the same box, told him how her twin sister Bellatrix had loved his father, then pronounced him just right for her daughter. After the match Krum's team climbed up to it, followed by the Irish with the Cup.

While the twins were collecting their winnings, John Constantine, who had slipped in behind the pillar during the presentation to keep Harry in sight, stepped back on to Winky's foot. Lucius Malfoy knew him at once. His first jinx missed, blew the Bulgarian Minister's hat off and set the pillar alight; Fudge dived behind the World Cup. Constantine fled down the purple stairs with Mr Malfoy after him. Mr Weasley put out the burning pillar with a flick of his wand. A moment later Pansy Parkinson appeared at the top of the stairs to fetch Dracina away, on the pretext of a lost earring.

pages.title: Black Forest
pages.html: A big party of wizards from the Black Forest was due at the World Cup Portkey arrival point at five fifteen on the morning of 22 August 1994.

pages.title: The wizarding school in Brazil
pages.html: There is a wizarding school in Brazil, at which Bill Weasley once had a pen pal.

pages.title: Ohio

Arthur Weasley claimed the French smell of garlic so that you cannot be in the same room as them. B4 Ch5

Winky warned Dobby that his high jinks would land him before the Department for the Regulation and Control of Magical Creatures like a common goblin. B4 Ch6

In Book Four

Arthur Weasley pointed out one of its officials passing the Weasleys' tents at the World Cup. B4 Ch5

pages.title: Goblin Liaison Office
pages.html: Cuthbert Mockridge is Head of the Goblin Liaison Office.

pages.title: Registry of Proscribed Charmable Objects
pages.html: The Registry of Proscribed Charmable Objects defines carpets as a Muggle Artefact, which is the basis of the British ban on flying carpets.

pages.title: Wimbourne Wasps
pages.html: The Wimbourne Wasps play in robes of broad black stripes on bright yellow, with a giant wasp across the chest. Ludo Bagman was the best Beater they ever had.

pages.title: Omnioculars
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Brass binoculars bristling with knobs and dials
Replay; slow motion; a play-by-play breakdown
Ten Galleons a pair, at the World Cup campsite
pages.html:
Omnioculars are magical binoculars for watching Quidditch. They look like brass binoculars bristling with strange little knobs and dials. Besides bringing the action close, they can replay it, slow it down or flash up a play-by-play breakdown.

Description

A knob works the replay. A speed dial slows the action until even players on the fastest brooms in the world can be followed move by move. A breakdown button on the top names each move as it happens, in glittering purple writing that flashes across the lenses: HAWKSHEAD ATTACKING FORMATION, PORSKOFF PLOY, WRONSKI DEFENSIVE FEINT. The drawback is that a watcher busy with the dials can miss what is happening at normal speed.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Five: at dusk on 22 August 1994 a saleswizard at the World Cup campsite was selling Omnioculars at ten Galleons a pair. Ron, who had spent his pocket money on a hat of dancing shamrocks, gazed at them longingly. Harry bought three pairs, for himself, Ron and Hermione, telling Ron he would get nothing for Christmas for about ten years. Hermione held hers against her chest as though he had given her a ring.

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the Top Box Ron tested his on an old man in the far stands, making him pick his nose again and again. Through them he signalled to Pansy Parkinson in the seats below, who was watching the box through Omnioculars of her own. Through hers Dracina worked out that Pansy was in love with Ron, while Cho Chang trained a pair on the Top Box from the stands opposite. Harry slowed the match to read the moves, missed how Troy's first goal was scored, then spotted the Snitch through his lenses by the Irish goalposts, where neither Seeker had seen it. Ron paid him back for his pair with leprechaun gold, which vanishes after a few hours. During the presentation, thousands of Omniocular lenses winked up at the Top Box.

pages.title: Fred and George's fake wand
pages.html: Fred and George's fake wand squawks loudly and turns into a rubber chicken. Percy called it rubbish, but Ludo Bagman howled with laughter and valued it at five Galleons in the twins' bet.

pages.title: Hermione's red notebook
infobox: A list of curses headed For anyone who hurts my Harry
pages.html:
Hermione's red notebook is a small notebook bound in red leather that Hermione Granger keeps in her pocket. In its back pages, under a heading in her neatest handwriting, is a list of curses: For anyone who hurts my Harry. She tells people it is homework.

Contents

The list began at Hogwarts, with a book that Madam Pince keeps on the top shelf behind her desk, then grew all through the summer of 1994. It includes a hex that turns the skin inside out, very slowly, an inch a day; a jinx that fills the lungs with frogspawn; and a very old curse, banned in 1612, that makes the teeth go on growing until the jaw can no longer close round them. Elsewhere in the notebook is a page headed Privet Drive, underlined three times, above a very long list in two columns.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: at the Burrow on 21 August 1994 Hermione asked Harry exactly what the Dursleys had fed him that summer, writing down his answers: a quarter of a grapefruit, cottage cheese, about a stick of celery, grated. She closed her fingers round his wrist, found that her thumb met her forefinger with room to spare, then went back to writing. Asked what it was, she said it was homework. Harry glimpsed the page headed Privet Drive.

Book Four, Chapter Five: in the scullery before dawn the next morning she promised Harry that she would never hurt him, that she was making it all better. Behind her eyes she was going down the list. Later, at the World Cup campsite, Harry said aloud that all he remembered of being small was the cupboard. Hermione went quite white. Her hand slipped into the pocket where she kept the notebook, while her lips moved very slightly, as though she were committing something to memory.

Book Four, Chapter Six: when the veela's dance nearly took Harry over the front of the Top Box, Hermione quietly added every one of them to a list that already had the Dursleys on it.

Quotations

For anyone who hurts my Harry.Hermione Granger · B4 Ch5

pages.title: The curse book on Madam Pince's top shelf
pages.html: Madam Pince keeps a book on the top shelf behind her desk from which Hermione began copying curses for anyone who hurt Harry.

pages.title: The inside-out hex
pages.html: This hex turns the skin inside out very slowly, an inch a day. Hermione copied it into her red notebook in 1994.

pages.title: The frogspawn jinx
pages.html: This jinx fills the victim's lungs with frogspawn. Hermione copied it into her red notebook in 1994.

pages.title: The tooth-growing curse
pages.html: This very old curse makes the teeth go on growing until the jaw can no longer close round them. It was banned in 1612, and Hermione copied it into her red notebook in 1994.

pages.title: Fairy lanterns
pages.html: Fairy lanterns do not blow out. Pansy Parkinson hung them in the clearing by the forked pine for Plan A, and Ron thought them brilliant.

pages.title: Flying carpet
pages.html:
Flying carpets are banned in Britain, being defined as a Muggle Artefact by the Registry of Proscribed Charmable Objects, and Arthur Weasley enforces an embargo on them.

In Book Four

Ali Bashir wants to export flying carpets to Britain as a family vehicle. Mr Crouch's grandfather owned an Axminster that seated twelve before the ban. B4 Ch5

pages.title: Muggle money
pages.html: Arthur Weasley could not tell Muggle banknotes apart. Harry pointed out that the value is printed in the corners and across the middle, and that the Queen is the same on every one.

pages.title: Quidditch World Cup souvenirs
pages.html: At dusk on 22 August 1994 salesmen sold glowing rosettes that shrieked players' names, hats of dancing shamrocks, Bulgarian scarves with roaring lions, flags that played the anthem, flying model Firebolts and finger-high player figures that strutted on the palm.

pages.title: Perkins's tent
pages.html:
Perkins's tent looks like a shabby two-man tent outside, but inside it is an old-fashioned flat with three rooms, a bathroom and a kitchen. Four bunk beds stand in the bedroom.

In Book Four

The tent was done out exactly like Mrs Figg's front room, with crocheted covers on mismatched chairs, and smelt powerfully of cats. The girls' tent beside it was a little smaller and did not smell of cats. B4 Ch5

pages.title: The Malfoys' World Cup tent
pages.html:
Halfway up the World Cup field the Malfoys pitched a towering affair of striped silk, like a little palace, with a row of live white peacocks tethered at its entrance.

In Book Four

Dracina wrote to Hermione that the tent had a fountain inside, which she thought vulgar. B4 Ch5

pages.title: The Parkinsons' tent
pages.html: The Parkinsons' tent at the 1994 World Cup has a green silk awning and stands two rows behind the Malfoys'.

pages.title: Pansy Parkinson's letter to Ron
pages.html:
Pansy Parkinson's letter to Ron was her reply to Ron Weasley's three-page plan for getting Harry Potter together with Dracina Malfoy. It reached him before dawn on 22 August 1994. In it she chose Plan A, then set out exactly how it was to be done.

Contents

It was written in small, neat, very black handwriting, beginning Ronald. Pansy had read all three pages, more than Professor Binns had ever got out of her. The boat plan was out of the question: Dracina will not get into a boat, saying boats are for Muggles and Hufflepuffs. Plan C was worse. 'We're doing PLAN A,' she wrote, 'and we are doing it properly.'

She described the clearing past the pine with the forked trunk, which she had hung with fairy lanterns, then the earring she would pretend to have lost. Ron was to bring Harry looking presentable, doing what he could about the hair, then leave. Afterwards the two of them would have to find something to do for an hour or so. Since her mother said a girl should not walk about a campsite alone after dark, Ron would have to walk her back to her family's tent, the one with the green silk awning two rows behind the Malfoys'. He was to wear the maroon jumper, because it suited him. She signed it Yours, Pansy, with a postscript: Burn this. Dracina reads everything.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Five: Ron read the letter twice, sitting on his bed under his orange posters, and was greatly impressed. Pansy was like Hermione, he thought, only on his side for once. He would never have thought of fairy lanterns. Puzzled by the jumper, which nobody had ever told him suited him, he decided it must be because maroon would hardly show up among the trees. He put it on without a word of complaint. He supposed Yours was just how they signed letters in Slytherin. Then he stuffed the letter deep into his pocket, quite forgetting the postscript.

Harry had seen him come down trying to cram a piece of parchment into his back pocket. He guessed it was from Pansy Parkinson, probably some sort of love letter. When Ron came down at last in the maroon jumper, Mrs Weasley asked whether the letter had been from that pen pal of his. Ron said he was entitled to some privacy.

Quotations

We're doing PLAN A, and we are doing it properly.Pansy Parkinson · B4 Ch5

pages.title: Ron and Pansy's Plan A
infobox: Plan A; Ron and Pansy's plan

Ron Weasley plotter
Pansy Parkinson plotter
To leave Harry Potter alone with Dracina Malfoy
A lantern-lit clearing past the pine with the forked trunk, at the top of the Bulgarian end of the World Cup campsite
After the World Cup final, 22 August 1994
pages.html:
Plan A was the scheme by which Ron Weasley and Pansy Parkinson meant to leave Harry Potter alone with Dracina Malfoy in the wood after the Quidditch World Cup final of 1994. Ron first drew it up in a three-page letter, which also offered a boat plan and a Plan C. Pansy threw out the other two, chose Plan A and filled in the details herself.

The plan

Pansy found the place on Saturday 20 August: a clearing past the big pine with the forked trunk, with a stream and a fallen tree to sit on. She hung it with fairy lanterns, which would not blow out. After the match Ron was to bring Harry, made presentable, while Pansy brought Dracina on the pretext of a lost earring. Then both would leave. On no account was Ron to stay and watch.

Pansy built a second purpose into it. Afterwards she and Ron would need something to do for an hour or so, so as not to blunder back at the wrong moment; then Ron would have to walk her back to her tent. She meant to win him.

Ron's reasons were his own. Harry, he thought, would never get round to it in a hundred years, but would only go on pretending he could not stand Dracina. Ron owed him: Harry had shared everything with him from the very first day, without once making him feel poor.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Four: on the night of 21 August 1994 Ron sent his plan north by Pig, telling Harry it was for a pen pal.

Book Four, Chapter Five: Pansy's answer reached him before dawn. He packed a comb borrowed from Percy, a bottle of Sleekeazy's Hair Potion, a box of Honeydukes chocolates and a list headed THINGS HARRY COULD SAY, on which only 'You look nice' survived. That afternoon Harry saw him under the forked pine with a girl in a green cloak, who pressed something into his hand.

Book Four, Chapter Six: Ron kept the plan on a crumpled sheet of parchment inside his programme. All through the final he signalled its progress to Pansy in the seats below, tapping his nose, pointing at the back of Harry's head, then winking. After the presentation Pansy appeared at the top of the stairs, crying that she had lost a diamond earring in the wood. Dracina looked for a long, thoughtful moment at Ron before agreeing very sweetly to help. Her mother, who seemed to have guessed, told her to take as long as she needed.

Ron sent Hermione back to the tents with Ginny, who he said was feeling sick. He handed Harry Percy's comb, asking him to do something about his hair, then led him off towards the forked pine. Harry decided that Ron was going to meet Pansy with a friend along for moral support.

pages.title: Things Harry Could Say
pages.html: Things Harry Could Say is a sheet of parchment Ron prepared for Plan A, nearly all of it crossed out. The only surviving line was Ron's own: 'You look nice.'

pages.title: Dracina's birthday letter to Harry
pages.html:
Harry carried Dracina's 1994 birthday letter folded very small in the back pocket of his jeans to the World Cup.

In Book Four

Its line that Pansy had 'all of a sudden' got the Chudley Cannons let Harry work out that Pansy was Ron's pen pal. B4 Ch5

Quotations

Now, all of a sudden, she has got the Chudley Cannons.Dracina Malfoy · B4 Ch5

pages.title: Dracina's letters to Molly Weasley
pages.html:
Dracina's letters to Molly Weasley are written on very good parchment in small, spiky writing and green ink. Molly keeps them in a box under her bed and has read every one twice.

In Book Four

The letters led Molly to decide that Miss Malfoy was a delightful young lady who would make Harry a wonderful wife. B4 Ch5

pages.title: Summoning Charm
pages.html: The Summoning Charm, cast with 'Accio!', draws objects to the caster's hand. Mrs Weasley used it to find every Ton-Tongue Toffee Fred and George had hidden.

pages.title: Splinching
pages.html: Splinching is what happens when Apparition goes wrong and the wizard leaves half of themselves behind, stuck and unable to move either way. The Accidental Magic Reversal Squad has to sort it out.

pages.title: Cornelius Fudge's wife
pages.html: Cornelius Fudge is married; Lucius Malfoy predicted that Fudge would go home after the 1994 World Cup final and tell his wife what a charming boy Harry was.

pages.title: Winky
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
A tea towel worn like a toga
pages.html:
Winky is the house-elf of Bartemius Crouch. She is a devoted servant of the old kind, who believes that a house-elf should do as she is told and never ask for wages. At the 1994 World Cup final her shriek exposed John Constantine in the Top Box.

Service

Winky serves the Crouch household, keeping house for Mr Crouch. Like Dobby, she speaks of herself by name. She is tiny, with huge brown eyes above a nose as big and round as a ripe tomato. She wears a tea towel wrapped round her like a toga. Her voice is a teeny, trembling squeak, even higher than Dobby's. She is proud of being a good house-elf, which to her means doing what she is told, even when it frightens her.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Six: on the night of 22 August 1994 Winky was the first to arrive in the Top Box of the World Cup stadium, perched on a chair with her face buried in her hands. Her master had sent her to save him a seat, because he was very busy. She does not like heights at all; she shaded her eyes, peeping at the drop, then covered them altogether in terror. Harry Potter took her at first for Dobby. She knew Dobby too, she told him, and Dobby talked of Harry all the time.

Winky was not sure that Harry had done Dobby a favour by setting him free. Freedom had gone to his head, she said. He had ideas above his station, he could not get another position, and he wanted paying for his work, which appalled her. 'House-elves is not paid, sir!' She had told him to find a nice family to settle down with. She had warned him that if he went on racketing about, he would end up before the Department for the Regulation and Control of Magical Creatures like some common goblin. She wished she were back in her master's tent, she said, but she did as she was told.

Cornelius Fudge noticed her keeping Crouch's seat, which he thought a good job, with the Bulgarians trying to cadge all the best places. After the Cup had been presented, a tall man in a crumpled tan raincoat stepped backwards out of the shadow by a gilded pillar, straight on to Winky's foot. 'Sir is standing on Winky's foot!' Her shriek turned every head in the box. It exposed John Constantine, who had been following Harry all day, to Lucius Malfoy, who chased him out of the stadium with jinxes.

In their own words

Sir is standing on Winky's foot!Winky · B4 Ch6

pages.title: Aidan Lynch
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
pages.html:
Aidan Lynch is the Seeker of the Irish national Quidditch team, which won the 1994 Quidditch World Cup. In the final he crashed into the ground twice, the first time after following Viktor Krum's Wronski Feint, yet Ireland won by 170 points to 160.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Six: Ludo Bagman presented him last of the Irish team on the night of 22 August 1994, flying a Firebolt with his name stitched in silver across his back. Early in the match he and Krum came plunging down through the Chasers together. At the last possible moment Krum pulled up. Lynch did not, hitting the ground with a thud that the whole stadium heard. Krum had never seen the Snitch at all; it was a Wronski Feint, meant to have Lynch ploughed.

During the time out mediwizards poured potions down Lynch's throat, while Krum circled above, hunting for the Snitch unopposed. Ginny Weasley was white with horror, though Charlie told her that Lynch had only been ploughed. When Lynch got to his feet at last, mounting his Firebolt to deafening cheers, his return set the whole Irish team alight. In a quarter of an hour of furious play its Chasers scored ten more goals.

Near the end, with Ireland leading 170 to 10, Lynch went into a dive for the Snitch in earnest. Krum caught up with him. Lynch hit the turf a second time, where a horde of furious veela stampeded straight over him, while Krum rose with the Snitch. Dazed, with eyes that did not quite point the same way, Lynch was held up in the Top Box by his teammates Moran and Connolly. He grinned happily all the same. On the lap of honour he rode pillion on Connolly's broom, hanging on tight round his waist.

pages.title: Troy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Winner; scored the opening goal of the final
pages.html:
Troy is a Chaser of the Irish national Quidditch team, which won the 1994 Quidditch World Cup. With Mullet and Moran he made up what Ludo Bagman called the strongest front three he had seen in years. Troy scored the opening goal of the final.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the final, on the night of 22 August 1994, Troy flew at the point of the Irish Chasers' Hawkshead Attacking Formation, with Mullet and Moran just behind him. In the Porskoff Ploy that followed, he swooped up as if to carry the Quaffle over the top, drawing the Bulgarian Chaser Ivanova after him. Then he let it drop into Moran's arms. Levski seemed to win it, but Moran knocked it off his elbow straight back to Troy, who scored. It was, Dracina Malfoy told Harry Potter, the oldest trick in Irish Quidditch.

Later, when a whistle from the crowd made the Bulgarian Chasers pull up, Troy shot in beneath them. He plucked the Quaffle from under Levski's arm, then scored at the other end before the Keeper, Zograf, had even moved. He scored the first of Ireland's penalties, but a later penalty of his clipped the rim of the hoop. After the match he hoisted the World Cup over his head with Quigley in the Top Box.

pages.title: Mullet
pages.html:
Mullet was an Irish Chaser at the 1994 World Cup final; the Bulgarian Keeper Zograf fouled her for cobbing, winning Ireland a penalty.

In Book Four

Zograf saved Mullet's penalty at full stretch with his fingertips. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Moran
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Winner; scored Ireland's last two goals in the final
pages.html:
Moran is a Chaser of the Irish national Quidditch team, which won the 1994 Quidditch World Cup. She scored Ireland's last two goals in the final, the second after carrying the Quaffle the length of the field through a ball of veela fire.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Six: in the final, on the night of 22 August 1994, Moran flew just behind Troy in the Hawkshead Attacking Formation, with Mullet. In the Porskoff Ploy Troy dropped the Quaffle into her arms. A Bludger from the Bulgarian Beater Volkov made her duck, and the Bulgarian Chaser Levski seemed to win the ball. In fact she had knocked it off his elbow straight back to Troy, who scored the opening goal.

As the match grew more savage, the Bulgarian Chaser Dimitrov flew straight into her while she had the Quaffle, very nearly knocking her off her broom. Ludo Bagman called it skinning, a deliberate collision, and Ireland were given a penalty. Moran then scored twice more. Her second goal came after a run the whole length of the field, past both Bulgarian Beaters, through a ball of veela fire, to bury the Quaffle in the top of the left hoop. That made the score 170 to 10. After the match she helped Connolly hold up the dazed Aidan Lynch in the Top Box.

pages.title: Ryan
pages.html: Ryan was the Irish Keeper at the 1994 World Cup final; Ivanova swerved round him to score Bulgaria's first goal, and he was later caught out of position before the fake whistle.

pages.title: Quigley
pages.html:
Quigley was an Irish Beater at the 1994 World Cup final whose Bludger hit Viktor Krum full in the face and broke his nose.

In Book Four

Quigley and Troy hoisted the World Cup over their heads in the Top Box. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Connolly
pages.html:
Connolly played for Ireland in the 1994 World Cup final; by elimination he is implied to have been the other Irish Beater.

In Book Four

Connolly helped hold up the dazed Aidan Lynch in the Top Box and carried him pillion on his broom for the lap of honour. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Dimitrov
pages.html:
Dimitrov was a Bulgarian Chaser at the 1994 World Cup final, the first Bulgarian player introduced by Bagman.

In Book Four

Dimitrov deliberately flew into Moran while she had the Quaffle, giving away a penalty for skinning. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Ivanova
pages.html: Ivanova was a Bulgarian Chaser at the 1994 World Cup final who broke through the Irish line and swerved round Ryan to score Bulgaria's first goal.

pages.title: Levski
pages.html:
Levski was a Bulgarian Chaser at the 1994 World Cup final who seemed to win the Quaffle in the Porskoff Ploy until Moran knocked it off his elbow.

In Book Four

Bearing down on an open goal, Levski pulled up at George's fake whistle, and Troy took the Quaffle from under his arm. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Zograf
pages.html:
Zograf was the Bulgarian Keeper at the 1994 World Cup final; he was penalised for cobbing Mullet.

In Book Four

Zograf's broom drifted helplessly left as Troy's penalty went in on the right; he saved the next two penalties but kept glaring at his broom handle, implying the twins' broom polish had been at work. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Volkov
pages.html:
Volkov was a Bulgarian Beater at the 1994 World Cup final who smashed a Bludger at Moran during the Porskoff Ploy.

In Book Four

Volkov and Vulchanov argued with the referee over the leprechauns and cost Bulgaria two penalties; neither seemed to mind whether they hit a Bludger or a player. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Vulchanov
pages.html: Vulchanov was a Bulgarian Beater at the 1994 World Cup final; he and Volkov dropped out of the sky to argue with Hassan Mostafa and were penalised twice.

pages.title: Hassan Mostafa
infobox: Quidditch, referee, International Association of Quidditch
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
Chairwizard of the International Association of Quidditch
Referee of the World Cup final
pages.html:
Hassan Mostafa is an Egyptian wizard, the Chairwizard of the International Association of Quidditch. He refereed the final of the 1994 Quidditch World Cup, between Ireland and Bulgaria.

Appearance

Mostafa is small, skinny and completely bald, with a moustache to rival Vernon Dursley's. At the final he wore robes of the same gold as the stadium, with a silver whistle poking out from under the moustache.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Six: on the night of 22 August 1994 Ludo Bagman introduced him to the crowd as the acclaimed Chairwizard, all the way from Egypt. Mostafa strode out with a big wooden crate under one arm, his broomstick under the other. He mounted, kicked the lid off the crate to release the four balls, then started the match with a piercing blast on his whistle.

Later a whistle shrilled from the crowd. The Bulgarian Chasers pulled up, looking for the foul, while Mostafa looked round with his mouth open, his own whistle still dangling on its cord. It was George Weasley's. Ireland scored, and the goal stood. Mostafa gave Ireland a penalty when the Bulgarian Keeper, Zograf, fouled Mullet by cobbing.

When the veela danced again, Mostafa landed in front of them, flexing his arms like a strongman at a fair while he twirled his moustache. Bagman called for somebody to slap the referee. A mediwizard ran across the pitch with his fingers in his ears to kick him on the shin. Mostafa woke up, turned a deep, embarrassed red, then tried to send the veela off. The Bulgarian Beaters, Volkov and Vulchanov, dropped down to argue with him. When they would not get back on their brooms, he awarded Ireland two penalties.

Later still a veela's fireball set the tail of his broom alight. He was too busy with it to see Quigley's Bludger break Viktor Krum's nose, so no whistle came.

pages.title: The mediwizards at the World Cup final
pages.html:
Trained mediwizards treated Aidan Lynch with potions after Krum's feint at the 1994 final, and swarmed to Krum after his catch, though he would not let them clean him up.

In Book Four

One mediwizard ran across the pitch with his fingers in his ears and kicked the entranced referee on the shin to wake him. B4 Ch6

pages.title: The ticket witch at the World Cup stadium
aliases: the witch from the Ministry who checked their tickets
pages.html: A Ministry witch checked the Weasley party's tickets at the stadium entrance on 22 August 1994, hailed them as prime seats, and sent Arthur straight up to the Top Box.

pages.title: The old wizard picking his nose at the World Cup
pages.html: Testing his Omnioculars, Ron replayed an old wizard in the far stand picking his nose again and again.

pages.title: The two wizards who carried the World Cup
pages.html: Two puffing wizards lugged the enormous golden World Cup into the Top Box and handed it to Cornelius Fudge.

pages.title: The Irishman whose hat Constantine took
pages.html: Fleeing Lucius Malfoy, John Constantine snatched a green shamrock hat off a startled Irish supporter's head and crammed it on his own.

pages.title: Chang family
pages.html:
Dracina had heard that the Changs, Cho Chang's family, were an old family of the East with old magics of their own, though she did not know what those magics were.

In Book Four

The Changs sat in the green stands at the 1994 World Cup final. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Mr Thimble
pages.html: Mr Thimble of Magical Maintenance was dragged off his ladder in Stockport in August 1994 by Muggles shouting 'mutie'; the Obliviators had to go in, and the Daily Prophet reported it.

pages.title: Brotherhood of Evil Mutants
pages.html: The Brotherhood of Evil Mutants is Magneto's gang; Harry remarked to Fudge that the name was at least honest of him.

pages.title: The Quidditch World Cup stadium
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
A Ministry of Magic task force of five hundred, over a year
A lantern-lit path through the wood from the campsite
The final of the 422nd Quidditch World Cup, 22 August 1994
pages.html:
The Quidditch World Cup stadium was the vast golden stadium that the Ministry of Magic built for the final of 1994. It seated a hundred thousand people. It stood beyond a wood, twenty minutes' walk from the campsite along a trail of lanterns.

Construction

A Ministry task force of five hundred worked on the stadium all year. Every inch of it was covered with Muggle-Repelling Charms, so that any Muggle who came near suddenly remembered an urgent appointment elsewhere. Its great golden walls could have held ten cathedrals with room to spare.

Inside

Purple carpet ran up the stairs, with doors on either side opening into the stands. Inside, a strange golden glow hung over everything, as though the stadium itself gave off light. Tier upon tier of seats ran round the long oval of the pitch, which looked as smooth as velvet from above. Three hoops fifty feet high stood at each end. Opposite the Top Box hung a gigantic blackboard, where words in gold raced across, then vanished, as though a giant were writing with an invisible finger. Between scores it carried advertisements: the Bluebottle broom, Mrs Skower's All-Purpose Magical Mess Remover, Gladrags Wizardwear, Fizzing Whizzbees.

At the final the Irish supporters filled the green stands, while the Bulgarians made a single scarlet block on the right. The best seats of all were in the Top Box at the summit, with the most expensive block just below it.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Six: on the night of 22 August 1994 the Weasley party came out of the trees into the shadow of the stadium, so huge that Harry's neck ached from staring up at it. Mr Weasley told him about the five hundred builders, adding a fond 'bless them' for the Muggles who kept remembering appointments. Harry wondered whether he would bless the protesters in New York. A Ministry witch sent them straight up to the Top Box. There Harry watched Ireland beat Bulgaria by 170 points to 160, although Viktor Krum caught the Snitch.

After the match Lucius Malfoy chased John Constantine down through the stands, hurdling seats, into a ring of dancing Irish supporters. The leprechauns took Mr Malfoy for a Bulgarian, pouring down on him like hail. Far below, Constantine climbed the barrier of the last stand in a borrowed shamrock hat, bowed to several thousand cheering Irish, then dropped out of sight.

pages.title: The World Cup scoreboard
pages.html:
A gigantic blackboard hung opposite the Top Box at the 1994 World Cup, almost level with it, with gold words racing across it as if written by an invisible giant; it showed advertisements and then the score.

In Book Four

At the end of the final the scoreboard flashed BULGARIA: 160, IRELAND: 170. B4 Ch6

pages.title: The Quidditch World Cup trophy
pages.html:
The Quidditch World Cup is an enormous golden cup, which two wizards carried into the Top Box on 22 August 1994 and gave to Fudge.

In Book Four

Fudge hid behind the Cup during Lucius Malfoy's jinxes, one of which bounced off it with a clang like a church bell; Troy and Quigley lifted it for Ireland. B4 Ch6

pages.title: The World Cup programme
pages.html:
The 1994 World Cup final programme was velvet with tassels; it announced a display from the team mascots before the match, and page eleven covered 'The Irish Chasers and their methods'.

In Book Four

Ron hid his plan in his programme, Fred did his sums on the back of his, Dracina hid her laughter behind hers, and a jinx took the tassel off Hermione's. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Veela
infobox: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
The loveliest of women, with skin like moonlight and white-gold hair
A dance that empties men's heads
Beaked bird heads, long scaly wings; they hurl fire
Bulgaria, at the 1994 World Cup final
pages.html:
Veela are magical beings who look like the loveliest of women. Their skin shines like moonlight, while their white-gold hair streams out behind them in a wind that is not there. They are not human. When they dance, men forget everything else; when they are angry, they become something else entirely.

Nature

The veela's dance empties a man's head of everything, blissfully. Nothing matters but to go on watching, and wild thoughts come with it: the urge to do something tremendous, this minute, something nobody will ever forget. Men under the spell will happily make fools of themselves, or worse. Women watch unharmed. Wise wizards at a match put their fingers in their ears whenever the veela get up to dance.

Their beauty is only half of them. Roused to anger, veela hurl fistfuls of flame. Their faces lengthen into sharp, cruel bird heads with beaks, while long scaly wings sprout from their shoulders. When the fury passes they go back to looking beautiful. As Arthur Weasley told his sons, it is why a man should never go for looks alone.

Muggle folk tales of the Balkans tell of the vila, beautiful women of the mountains who dance in rings by moonlight. Anyone who wrongs them suffers a terrible revenge. They are the veela, as Muggles remember them.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Six: a hundred veela came out as Bulgaria's mascots before the World Cup final on 22 August 1994. 'Veela!' cried Mr Weasley, whipping off his glasses. When they danced, Harry found himself with one foot up on the front wall of the Top Box, about to jump. Hermione had hold of his arm, while Dracina was hauling on the back of his jumper; Ron had frozen like a boy about to dive. The two girls exchanged very sweet words over his head, neither of them letting go. Hermione added every veela to a list that already held the Dursleys.

When Bulgaria scored, the veela danced again, so Hermione clamped her hands over Harry's ears while Dracina covered his eyes. After the leprechauns jeered HA, HA, HA at them, they danced at the referee, Hassan Mostafa, until he was flexing his arms like a strongman at a fair; a mediwizard had to kick him on the shin. Mostafa tried to send them off. When the Bulgarian Beaters argued, he gave Ireland two penalties. When the leprechauns made a rude sign at them, the veela charged across the field hurling flame, beaked and winged. One of their fireballs set the tail of Mostafa's broom alight. As Aidan Lynch crashed at the end, the veela stampeded straight over him. Afterwards they went back to looking beautiful, though very sad and sorry for themselves.

pages.title: Leprechaun gold
pages.html:
Heavy gold coins rained down from the leprechauns' shamrock at the 1994 final, and many spectators scrabbled under their seats for them.

In Book Four

Ron gave Harry a handful of leprechaun gold to pay for his Omnioculars, and Constantine pretended to pick up a leprechaun's Galleon to hide from Lucius. B4 Ch6

pages.title: The Bluebottle
pages.html: The Bluebottle is a broom advertised on the World Cup scoreboard in 1994 as a broom for all the family, safe and reliable, with its own Anti-Burglar Buzzer.

pages.title: Gladrags Wizardwear
pages.html: Gladrags Wizardwear, with shops in London, Paris and Hogsmeade, was advertised on the World Cup scoreboard in 1994.

pages.title: Wronski Feint
pages.html:
The Wronski Feint is a Seeker's dive that tricks the opposing Seeker into following him into the ground; Harry's Omnioculars labelled it a dangerous Seeker diversion when Krum used it on Lynch in 1994.

In Book Four

Dracina and Hermione named the Wronski Feint at precisely the same moment. B4 Ch6

pages.title: Hawkshead Attacking Formation
pages.html: The Hawkshead Attacking Formation is a tight arrowhead of three Chasers; the Irish used it in the 1994 final with Troy at the point and Mullet and Moran behind.

pages.title: Porskoff Ploy
pages.html: In the Porskoff Ploy a Chaser swoops upward as if to carry the Quaffle over the top, then drops it to a teammate below; Troy used it in the 1994 final.

pages.title: Cobbing
pages.html: Cobbing, the excessive use of elbows, is a Quidditch foul; Zograf was penalised for it against Mullet in the 1994 final.

pages.title: Skinning
pages.html: Skinning, deliberately flying to collide with an opponent, is a Quidditch foul; Dimitrov was penalised for skinning Moran in the 1994 final.

pages.title: Sonorus
pages.html: Sonorus, cast with the wand pointed at one's own throat, magnifies the voice; Ludo Bagman used it to commentate on the 1994 final.

pages.title: Quietus
pages.html: Quietus returns a magnified voice to normal; Ludo Bagman muttered it with his wand to his throat after the 1994 final.

pages.title: International Association of Quidditch
pages.html: Hassan Mostafa, referee of the 1994 World Cup final, is acclaimed Chairwizard of the International Association of Quidditch.

pages.title: St Mungo's Hospital for Magical Maladies and Injuries
pages.html: Lucius Malfoy made a very generous contribution to St Mungo's Hospital for Magical Maladies and Injuries shortly before the 1994 World Cup final, and came as Fudge's guest.

pages.title: Fred and George's World Cup bet
aliases: the fixing of the 1994 World Cup final
infobox:
Fred Weasley plotter
George Weasley plotter
Ludo Bagman bookmaker
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (8 July 2000)
37 Galleons, 15 Sickles, 3 Knuts, with a fake wand that Bagman valued at five Galleons
Ireland to win, but Viktor Krum to catch the Snitch
Ireland 170, Bulgaria 160; Krum caught the Snitch
pages.html:
Fred and George's World Cup bet was the wager the Weasley twins made with Ludo Bagman at lunchtime on 22 August 1994: that Ireland would win the World Cup final, but that Viktor Krum would catch the Snitch. They staked every Knut they had. Then they spent the rest of the day making sure they won.

The wager

Catching the Snitch earns a side 150 points, so the bet could only come off if Krum caught it while Ireland led by more than that. Bagman thought it hopeless, so he offered the twins excellent odds. Their stake was thirty-seven Galleons, fifteen Sickles and three Knuts, with a fake wand thrown in; when it turned into a rubber chicken, Bagman added five Galleons for it. Arthur Weasley protested that it was all their savings. Bagman told him not to be a spoilsport.

How it was won

The twins did not so much bet on the World Cup as nudge it, quietly, from several directions at once. They spent the afternoon 'just having a look at the pitch', then came back smelling of broom polish. That night the Bulgarian Keeper, Zograf, kept drifting on his broom, glaring at its handle between saves.

The leprechauns seemed to be in league with them; Fred and a leprechaun swapped a thumbs up. Their jeering goaded the veela into conduct that cost Bulgaria penalties. Their last insult, a gigantic rude hand, was the very sign Fred had made at Percy across the campfire at lunch.

With the Bulgarian Chasers through on an open goal, a whistle shrilled from the crowd. They pulled up to look for the foul, letting Troy snatch the Quaffle away to score, while something small and silver vanished into George's pocket.

Fred did sums all evening. George, pale, willed Krum not to catch the Snitch too soon: 'Not yet, Viktor. Not yet, there's a good lad.' At 160 to 10 Fred mouthed, 'One more and then he can have it.' Moran scored. Krum then caught the Snitch, so that Ireland won by 170 points to 160.

In the saga

Book Four, Chapter Five: the bet was struck over lunch beside the Weasleys' campfire, while Percy hissed at the twins for showing Mr Bagman rubbish. At dusk the twins bought no souvenirs, having given Bagman every last bit of their gold.

Book Four, Chapter Six: when Krum caught the Snitch, the twins collapsed against each other, laughing helplessly. Bagman, as surprised as anybody, paid them in full. They resolved never to tell a living soul how they had won, least of all their mother. When John Constantine fled the Top Box with Lucius Malfoy after him, they leant out over the front of the box to cheer: 'Go on, raincoat!'

pages.title: George Weasley's fake whistle
pages.html: A whistle shrilled from the crowd during the 1994 final, stopping the Bulgarian Chasers; Mostafa's own whistle was nowhere near his lips, and Harry saw something small and silver disappear into George Weasley's pocket.

pages.title: Ron Weasley's rucksack
pages.html: Ron carried his rucksack to the Top Box and clutched it like the Crown Jewels; inside, rolled socks hid a bottle of Sleekeazy's, a box of chocolates and a comb much like Percy's.

pages.title: Pansy Parkinson's diamond earrings
pages.html: Pansy Parkinson claimed to have lost one of her diamond earrings in the wood on the way to the 1994 final, a pretext for taking Dracina into the wood.

pages.title: The pine with the forked trunk
aliases: the big pine with the forked trunk
pages.html: A big pine with a forked trunk stood in the wood past the Bulgarian tents; Harry had seen Ron there that afternoon with a girl in a green cloak, and Ron led him towards it after the final.

pages.title: Lucius Malfoy's cane
pages.html: Lucius Malfoy's cane has a silver head; it caught Harry on the shin when Lucius lunged to the rail, and Lucius carried it in one hand and his wand in the other as he chased Constantine.

pages.title: Harry's shamrock rosette
pages.html: Harry wore a big green shamrock rosette to the 1994 final, which squeaked the Irish Chasers' names over and over.

pages.title: The Bulgarian lion scarf
pages.html: During Lucius Malfoy's chase a Bulgarian lion on a supporter's scarf woke up and roared back at him.

pages.title: Wiltshire
pages.html: Wiltshire is an English county, implied to be where the Malfoys live; Narcissa declared herself the most satisfying wife in it.

pages.title: Downing Street
pages.html: Fudge visited the Muggle Prime Minister at Downing Street four times between the spring and August of 1994, coming back grey in the face, according to Lucius Malfoy.

pages.title: The Dursleys' Christmas present
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Dursleys' Christmas present to Harry Potter in 1991, his first Christmas at Hogwarts, was a fifty-pence piece. They sellotaped it to a note. Harry gave it to Ron Weasley.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Eight, Harry woke on Christmas morning 1991 to a pile of presents, although he had never once been given a Christmas present before. A very small parcel held a note: We received your message and enclose your Christmas present. From Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia. Sellotaped to the note was a fifty-pence piece. 'That's friendly,' said Harry. Ron, though, was fascinated by the coin, and Harry told him to keep it.

pages.title: The hooded stranger in the Hog's Head
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
Never seen; he kept his hood up
pages.html:
The hooded stranger in the Hog's Head was the cloaked man who lost a dragon egg to Rubeus Hagrid at cards in the spring of 1992. Over the game he got out of Hagrid that music would send Fluffy to sleep. He was Quirinus Quirrell, who carried Lord Voldemort on the back of his head.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Ten, Hagrid told Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger how he had come by the egg. 'Las' night. I was down in the village havin' a few, an' got into a game o' cards with a stranger. Think he was glad ter be shot of it, ter be honest.'

In Chapter Twelve Hagrid admitted that he had never seen the man's face, since he had kept his hood up the whole time. The stranger had kept buying him drinks, and Hagrid had told him how to calm Fluffy down: 'Jus' play him a bit o' music an' he goes straight off ter sleep...'

In Chapter Thirteen, face to face with Quirrell, Harry understood at last who had been under the hood. Afterwards Hagrid sobbed that it was all his fault: 'I told the evil git how ter get past Fluffy! I told him!'

pages.title: The man who sold Fluffy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The man who sold Fluffy is the stranger from whom Rubeus Hagrid bought his three-headed dog in 1990, a year before Fluffy went to guard the Philosopher's Stone at Hogwarts. Hagrid met him in a pub. He had a caravan and a funny voice, so Hagrid decided he was Greek. Harry Potter suspected that he was nothing of the kind.

Fluffy

Hagrid named the dog himself, and in 1991 he lent him to Albus Dumbledore. For the next school year Fluffy stood guard over the trapdoor in the forbidden third-floor corridor. Where the man had found a three-headed dog in the first place is not recorded.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Seven, in the autumn of 1991, Hagrid told Harry, Ron and Hermione where the dog had come from: 'Bought him off a Greek chappie I met down the pub las' year. Well, I think he was Greek. He had the caravan and funny voice the greeks have.' Harry had a growing suspicion that Hagrid was not describing a Greek at all. In Chapter Twelve he decided that the man had been a Traveller.

pages.title: The idol from Romania
pages.html:
The idol from Romania was a present that Charlie Weasley sent to his brother Percy from Romania, where Charlie works with dragons. Their mother took it away from Percy. It had too many tentacles for her liking.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Thirteen, lying in the hospital wing in June 1992, Harry Potter remembered hearing the story of the idol, which had happened the year before. Mrs Weasley had had to take it off Percy. Too many tentacles.

pages.title: The seven-bottles riddle
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
A roll of paper beside the bottles
The potions chamber on the way to the Philosopher's Stone
pages.html:
The seven-bottles riddle is the rhyming riddle on a roll of paper beside the seven bottles in the potions chamber, Professor Snape's defence of the Philosopher's Stone. Snape wrote it in verse of his own. Hermione Granger solved it in June 1992.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, Hermione snatched up the roll of paper as soon as the two fires had trapped her with Harry Potter. It began: 'Before you, danger; safety at your back.' Hermione let out a great sigh and smiled. 'Brilliant,' she said. 'This isn't magic. It's logic. It's a puzzle.' She read it through several times, then walked along the row of bottles, pointing at each in turn. Something very bright came into her face as she worked, which Harry could not have named. At last she clapped her hands. The smallest bottle would get them through the black fire, towards the Stone.

pages.title: The Sorting Hat song (1991)
infobox: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (26 June 1997)
pages.html:
The Sorting Hat song of 1991 is the short new song the Sorting Hat sang before the Sorting on 1 September 1991, the year Harry Potter came to Hogwarts.

The song

The Hat admitted it was patched and plain, but boasted that there was no cleverer hat anywhere. Nothing was hidden, it said, in any head it had ever worn, whatever that head had done. It sent the bold to Gryffindor and the fair of heart to Hufflepuff. The quick of wit went to Ravenclaw, while the cunning thrived in Slytherin. It ended by telling the first-years to try it and never fear, since it had never yet been wrong.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Three, a tear near the Hat's brim opened like a mouth, and it burst into song. The Hall applauded, and the Hat bowed to each table in turn. Harry felt neither bold nor quick-witted. If the Hat had mentioned a house for those who felt slightly sick, he would have known exactly where he belonged.

pages.title: Dean Thomas's terrace chants
pages.html:
Dean Thomas's terrace chants are the football songs Dean has been writing for the Gryffindor stand since his first year at Hogwarts. Dean grew up on the terraces at Upton Park, and he holds that a school with a stadium that size ought to have proper chants. His teachers do not agree.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Nine, in early 1992, he wrote chants against Hufflepuff for the match that Professor Snape refereed. One ended 'Loyal to losing, that's all that you do!' When Harry Potter caught the Snitch almost at once, the stand sang 'Five minutes! Five minutes! You lasted five minutes!'

In Book Two, Chapter Eleven, in the autumn of 1992, his chant against Slytherin, to a tune from West Ham, had a chorus that ran 'I'm a slimy snake, I've got no balls'. Two hundred Gryffindors roared it, then the other houses took it up, until Professor McGonagall stopped it. A later verse, about the Malfoys, called Dracina Malfoy Daddy's girl, with Daddy's gold and Daddy's brooms. It made her miss the Snitch.

In Book Three, Chapter Nine, in November 1993, he taught Gryffindor a chant about badgers digging their burrows, to a tune he swore everybody in Muggle Britain knew. Hufflepuff answered it to the same tune, five hundred voices strong.

pages.title: Pottyhead
infobox: Her only insult for him in their first year
pages.html:
Pottyhead was the insult Dracina Malfoy used for Harry Potter, and the only one, through their whole first year at Hogwarts. She coined it on the spot when he rejected her.

The insult

It is not much of an insult, as Harry told her himself. What made it remarkable was what she left unsaid. Harry had handed her a whole stock of insults that would really have hurt, and she never used a single one. She stuck to Pottyhead.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Four, Dracina first called Harry a pottyhead, and Ron Weasley laughed until he had to wipe his eyes. In Book One, Chapter Six, on the Quidditch pitch, Harry asked her whether that was the best she had got. In Book One, Chapter Seven, he noticed that she had never once used the crueller insults he had given her that night.

In Book One, Chapter Ten, dragged off down a dark corridor at night, she screamed it over and over: ‘I hate you, Pottyhead! I hate you!’ Harry was standing under his Invisibility Cloak, closer to her than she ever knew.

pages.title: The fall of Jorvik
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl Who Noticed Him, Chapter 12
The Norse völvas of Jorvik; the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London
pages.html:
The fall of Jorvik in 954 ended the wizarding war between the Norse völvas of Jorvik and the last Hellenic sorcerers out of London. It came when the Anglo-Saxons took Jorvik, the Viking city of York, which brought the last Norse kingdom in England to an end.

The war

Jorvik had been a Viking city since the Danes took York in 866. Its witches were völvas, Norse seeresses who worked their magic with staff and song. In the south, round London and the old Roman towns, the last Hellenic sorcerers still worked magic the classical way. Their incantations were Latin and Greek, with a great deal of geometry thrown in. Neither side thought the other's magic was the real thing.

In Muggle history the end came in 954, when the Northumbrians drove out Jorvik's last king, Eric Bloodaxe. He was killed at Stainmore, and King Eadred of England took his kingdom for his own. The Viking families of the North-East did not leave. They simply stopped saying they were Norse. Thirty-six years later Hogwarts was founded, the first place where all the quarrelling magical peoples of Britain were made to sit down in the same room.

In the saga

In Book One, Chapter Twelve, the last of the first-years' examinations in the summer of 1992 was an hour of History of Magic on this war. Harry Potter was rather proud of having got the date, 954, to stay in his head.

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, explaining the early Middle Ages to Harry in November 1992, Hermione Granger told him that the Viking families of the North-East had not left when the Saxons took Jorvik. They had just stopped saying they were Norse.

pages.title: The Yorkshire lady found in a chimney
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 9
pages.html:
The Yorkshire lady found in a chimney is the ghost of a lady from Yorkshire whose body was found in a chimney in 1812, when it was swept. Her own steward had bricked her up inside it.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, she was one of the famous ghosts Hermione Granger named in October 1992, when Ron Weasley asked her who would be at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party.

pages.title: The quartered monk
infobox: Harry Potter and the Girl with the Diary, Chapter 9
pages.html:
The quartered monk is the ghost of a monk of Glastonbury who was hanged, drawn and quartered by Henry the Eighth's men, so that he comes in four pieces. He is Brother Aldric, who hid Glastonbury Abbey's books from the King's commissioners in a cave on the Tor.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, at Nearly Headless Nick's Deathday Party on 31 October 1992, the quartered monk told Hermione Granger where Glastonbury's books were hidden. She took about thirty seconds to write the answer down, then came running after Harry and Ron, glowing. 'He told me!' she said.

pages.title: The cursed tea set
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A formerly cursed Muggle French nobleman and his peasant wife
A Muggle woman, who died of shock
pages.html:
The cursed tea set was a set of china that came alive in a Muggle house, danced, talked, and frightened a Muggle woman to death. It had belonged to an old witch, who was given it by a formerly cursed Muggle French nobleman and his peasant wife.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, Ron Weasley told Harry Potter the story in the flying car, to explain what his father's office did. The old witch died the year before, and her tea set was sold to an antiques shop. A little old Muggle lady bought it, took it home and tried to serve her friends tea in it. The pieces came alive. They started dancing and speaking to one another. The old lady died of shock, while the other people went mad.

Arthur Weasley worked overtime for weeks. There are only two of them in his office, Arthur and an old warlock called Perkins. They had to use Memory Charms, among other things, to cover it up.

pages.title: Dracina's knight-and-princess picture book
infobox: A knight kneeling to a girl in a tower
pages.html:
Dracina’s knight-and-princess picture book is a big, old, battered picture book of the kind small children are given at Christmas. Dracina Malfoy had it with her at Hogwarts, and did not want it seen.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Ten, Harry passed Dracina at a library table, alone, behind two fat volumes of wizarding genealogy, one with the Malfoy crest on its spine. Open on top of them was the picture book. Its page showed a painted knight in silver armour kneeling before a girl with long pale hair in a tower, holding out his sword to her hilt first. When she saw him looking, Dracina slammed the book shut so hard that Madam Pince shot out from behind her desk. She swept it under the genealogies and glared at him, her face burning.

In Chapter Twelve, watching a little stone knight on a chessboard, Harry thought of it again. In Chapter Eighteen, in the Chamber of Secrets, Dracina looked up at Harry standing over her with the sword, between her and the dark, with the Basilisk dead at his feet. He looked like the knight from the painted book, except that he was not kneeling in a tower.

pages.title: Peeves's song
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
'Oh Potter, the plotter, he's at it again'
pages.html:
Peeves's song is the mocking song Peeves the poltergeist sang about Harry Potter while the Chamber of Secrets was open. It is better known by its first words, 'Oh Potter, the plotter'.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Twelve, in December 1992, Peeves burst into it over the Petrified bodies of Justin Finch-Fletchley and Nearly Headless Nick: 'Oh Potter, the plotter, he's at it again'. Professor McGonagall sent him packing. He went on singing it in crowded corridors through the early months of 1993, and later added a dance with a great deal of high kicking.

pages.title: The wall messages
infobox: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (2 July 1998)
A wall of the second-floor corridor, Hogwarts
The memory in Tom Riddle's diary, through the possessed Dracina Malfoy
pages.html:
The wall messages were the two warnings from the Heir of Slytherin daubed on a wall of the second-floor corridor at Hogwarts in the school year 1992 to 1993. They were the work of the memory in Tom Riddle's diary, which wrote them with the hand of the girl it had possessed, Dracina Malfoy.

The messages

The first appeared on Hallowe'en 1992. It was daubed between two tall windows in letters a foot high, and it glimmered red in the torchlight: ‘THE CHAMBER OF SECRETS HAS BEEN OPENED. ENEMIES OF THE HEIR, BEWARE.’ Filch's cat, Mrs Norris, hung Petrified from a torch bracket beside it.

The second appeared directly under the first when Ginny Weasley was taken into the Chamber in the summer term of 1993: ‘Her skeleton will lie in the Chamber for ever.’

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Nine, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger found the first message on Hallowe'en night. Hermione screamed when she saw Mrs Norris. When the feast ended, students came pouring into the corridor from both ends. Dracina Malfoy pushed her way to the front and shouted, ‘Enemies of the heir, beware! You'll be next, Mudblood!’ Nobody noticed the red stain down the side of the finger she was pointing with, not even Harry. In Book Two, Chapter Ten, the message was still there, with Filch's empty chair against the wall below it.

In Book Two, Chapter Eighteen, Professor McGonagall told the staff that a student had been taken into the Chamber itself. The heir had left a second message, she said, directly under the first. The student was Ginny Weasley.

pages.title: The pyramid mummy
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter Four
Wrapped in bandages, lying on a slab
Whether a visitor has lived with a true heart
pages.html:
The pyramid mummy is a bandaged guardian of the dead that lies on a slab in an Egyptian pyramid. When anybody comes in uninvited, it sits up to question them. Have they lived with a true heart? What have they done with the years given them? Are they ready to have their heart weighed?

The weighing of the heart

In old Egyptian belief, the heart of the dead is weighed against the feather of truth. Only a heart as light as the feather may pass on into the life beyond.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, the Weasley twins told Harry Potter at the Leaky Cauldron how they had tried to shut Percy in a pyramid in Egypt that summer. They got him through the door before their mother spotted them. The mummy sat up on its slab. It asked Percy whether he had lived with a true heart, what he had done with the years given him and whether he was ready to have his heart weighed. ‘And Percy answered,’ said George. ‘For about ten minutes. With examples.’ The mummy lay back down. Fred thought it would rather have had the eternal dark.

Their brother Bill, a curse-breaker for Gringotts, had told them that it did that to everyone who went in uninvited. They were lucky it was only asking questions, he said; most people came out of there a lot quieter than they went in.

pages.title: Lizzie and Mary
pages.html:
Lizzie and Mary are two first-year Hufflepuffs, close friends, who started at Hogwarts in September 1993. In February 1994 a cut that went right through Lizzie's forearm was healed by Madam Pomfrey in four seconds. Mary would not believe it until she had touched the mark.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, in the first week of February 1994, the pair came out from between the library shelves in the middle of an argument, loud enough to bring Madam Pince's head up behind her desk like a vulture's. Mary was not saying Lizzie was lying, she said; she only could not believe in the healed arm until she had touched it. So Lizzie held it out. Mary pressed two fingers into the thin white line, then left them there for a long moment. "I'm sorry, Lizzie. All right. I believe you." The two of them went off between the shelves arm in arm.

Dracina Malfoy had been watching from her table with Harry Potter. "What," she said, "in the name of Merlin was that?" "Hufflepuffs," said Harry. "They're like a sort of weather," said Dracina.

Harry had been about to ask her about a Ministry letter he had built six weeks of suspicion on, without ever once asking to touch the thing. After watching the two Hufflepuffs, he told her it would keep.

pages.title: The boy on the lake ice
pages.html:
The boy on the lake ice is a thin Hufflepuff second-year who walked thirty feet out on the frozen lake at Hogwarts in January 1994, on ice only four inches thick. He was doing perfectly well until he looked down, and then he went through.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, the lake had frozen hard in the second week of January 1994. Harry Potter and Dracina Malfoy were on the bank fifty yards off when a knot of Hufflepuffs began roaring. The boy had gone out past the reeds with his arms straight out from his sides, laughing, white-faced with it. At thirty feet he turned to wave, and looked down. He floundered, took two steps at a run and went through to the chest. An enormous sixth-year Hufflepuff lay flat on the ice to haul him out. Afterwards, as they carried him up to the castle, the sixth-year kept demanding furiously, "Why did you look down?"

pages.title: Dracina's dragon-hide gloves
pages.html:
Dracina's dragon-hide gloves are the pair of black, supple, lined Quidditch gloves that Narcissa Malfoy sent her daughter, and that Dracina passed on to Harry Potter in December 1993. Harry was fairly sure they had cost more than everything he was wearing put together.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, Dracina had taken to watching Gryffindor’s evening practices, moving a little closer each night until she was sitting in the Gryffindor stand itself. One night in the sleet she rose as Harry came past and held out a small flat parcel. ‘Mother sent these. Dragon-hide. They were going spare.’ She would rather he did not lose his fingers before he had to play Slytherin, she said. It would make the victory less satisfying.

Hermione called down from two rows up that his drink was getting cold. Dracina told her it was very loyal of her, like a dog with a Thermos. Harry was left standing between them in the sleet, with the gloves in one hand and the flask in the other.

In Chapter Fourteen Dracina told Professor Snape that her teammates had been saying she was soft on Potter ever since the hospital wing and the gloves.

pages.title: The Buckbeak letter
infobox: Dracina Malfoy, with her left hand
Lucius's complaint against Buckbeak was upheld
pages.html:
The Buckbeak letter was the four-page letter Dracina Malfoy wrote to her father from the hospital wing in September 1993, after the hippogriff Buckbeak slashed her arm. She wrote it with her left hand, then decided not to send it. Pansy Parkinson sent it all the same, believing it was what Dracina wanted, and Lucius Malfoy's complaint against Buckbeak was upheld.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Six, lying awake in the hospital wing with her arm aching, Dracina made up her mind to write to her father first thing in the morning. She would use her left hand and make the injury look worse than it was. She would use the words bone, scar and permanent. Father would do what Father did, which was make things happen to people.

In Chapter Seven, in Potions, she apologised to Harry for what she had said about Hagrid. She had dropped it all, she told him. 'I had written to Father, if you must know, I sat up all night, it was four pages. And then I didn't send it.'

In Chapter Ten, two months later, Pansy stood in the hospital wing, visiting Harry, and looked at the bare table by the bed that had been Dracina's. Nobody else knew that four pages had once lain on it. Nobody else knew who had taken them to the Owlery, thinking it was what a friend would want. Pansy had found out in Potions, two tables away, what her friend had really wanted. She had said nothing about it to anybody.

In Chapter Eleven, a letter to Hagrid told him that the official complaint lodged by Mr Lucius Malfoy had been upheld. Reading it, Harry remembered Dracina at his elbow in the dungeon in September, telling him she had not sent anything. From then on he believed she had lied to him.

In Chapter Fourteen, Lucius wrote to thank his daughter. He had put her four pages in front of the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures, and had the hearing brought forward on the strength of them. Dracina told Professor Snape that she had written back, begging her father to drop it, but that once Father had decided a thing, it happened. Walking back to the Slytherin common room, she told Pansy that somebody had taken the letter off the table by her bed while she slept. 'I'm going to find out who.' Pansy followed her with a towel.

In Chapter Fifteen, Dracina told Harry the whole story. She had written the letter in a rage, on the night he came to the wing to tell her she was horrible, and in the morning she could not send it.

In Chapter Twenty-Two, on the front steps of the castle, Pansy broke down and confessed. 'I thought you wanted the letter sent,' she sobbed. 'I thought… I thought you left it and I was being helpful. I'm so sorry.' Since the spring Dracina had blamed Hermione Granger. Now Daphne Greengrass had to hold her back by both arms. 'You didn't even ASK,' Dracina shouted. 'You nearly RUINED EVERYTHING!'

pages.title: The green bloke on the news
infobox: On the Muggle television news, by 1992
pages.html:
The green bloke on the news is a green superhuman whom Harry Potter had seen on the Muggle television news by the summer of 1992. Harry mentioned him in the same breath as Superman. He never said who he meant.

Candidates

The news in those years had more than one green figure to show. The Hulk, Bruce Banner's huge green other self, had been wrecking parts of America since 1962. J'onn J'onzz, the green-skinned Martian Manhunter, was a founder of the Justice League.

In the saga

In Book Two, Chapter Three, in the summer of 1992, Ron Weasley and the twins came for Harry in the flying car. They found him behind the bars that Uncle Vernon had paid a man to put on his window. Harry told Ron: 'Unless you can get Superman on the phone, or that green bloke I saw on the news, I reckon I'm stuck.' 'Who's Superman?' said Fred, interested.

pages.title: The dwarf and warlock feud
infobox: Harry Potter and the Imprisoned Girl, Chapter 4
A beard-to-gold ritual that only made the dwarfs' beards itch
1,100 years by the dwarfs' count; 950 by the warlocks'
pages.html:
The dwarf and warlock feud, better known as the beard-gold feud, is a quarrel over a ritual that was supposed to turn the beards of the dwarfs' ancestors to gold. It made them itch instead. The dwarfs say the feud has lasted 1,100 years; the warlocks say 950. They cannot agree on that either.

The feud

The quarrel began in the tenth century. Nobody now remembers what the ritual was for, only that it failed. The two sides still carry it on whenever they meet.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Four, in August 1993, a party of warlocks in bearskins and a party of dwarfs breakfasted at neighbouring tables in the Leaky Cauldron, throwing kippers at each other. Tom, the innkeeper, explained the two counts to Harry Potter. Nobody, he said, remembered what the ritual had been for. 'That's the thing about carrying a grudge, Mr Potter. You carry it. Not the other fellow. He's gone home and put his feet up. Heavy things, grudges.'

pages.title: The Prewetts
infobox: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (21 June 2003)
pages.html:
The Prewetts are an old pure-blood wizarding family, the family Molly Weasley was born into. Her brothers, Fabian and Gideon Prewett, were killed fighting Death Eaters in the first war against Voldemort.

The family

It took five Death Eaters to kill Fabian and Gideon. Their sister, Molly, had married Arthur Weasley in 1969, and her sons know of a face she once wore, the morning she came back from the Prewetts'. Bill told the twins about it. They know what it means: somebody's house is about to be taken apart.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Twelve, when Harry was set on going after Sirius Black, Fred and George Weasley told him that he had the face on. It was the one their mother had worn the morning she came back from the Prewetts', the time Bill had told them about. Fred explained what it meant: 'The one that means somebody's getting their house taken apart.'

pages.title: The social worker with the folder
pages.html:
The social worker with the folder visited Number Four, Privet Drive, once, while Harry Potter was growing up there. She looked at Harry in the Dursleys' front room with her head on one side, then went away, and never came back.

Privet Drive

Harry was used to grown-ups believing the Dursleys. His teachers at St Grogory's believed them. So did the dinner lady and the lady from the council. The social worker went away and left things exactly as they were.

In the saga

In Book Three, Chapter Ten, in the hospital wing, Harry dreamt of taking revenge on everyone who had hurt him, with Dracina Malfoy standing very close at his side. When the social worker with the folder came, Dracina said that one, Harry, that one especially. He did, and she laughed her real laugh, with her hand over her mouth.

pages.title: The teachers at St Grogory's
infobox: St Grogory's Primary School, Little Whinging
pages.html:
The teachers at St Grogory's taught Harry Potter at his Muggle primary school in Little Whinging. They believed Dudley Dursley every time.

Harry's teachers

One of them held up Harry's school jumper in front of the class to show them what neglect looked like, then let Dudley off for breaking Harry's glasses. Another shut Harry in the stock cupboard for something Dudley had broken.

At assembly the school said the Lord's Prayer, with Dudley pinching Harry from the row behind or kicking the back of his chair.

In the saga
