By 2268 he was a patient in the asylum on Elba II, where Kirk, who had studied his victories as a cadet, found him plotting to make himself master of the galaxy.

pages.title: The Galactic Empire
infobox: A galaxy far beyond the Milky Way, a very long time ago
Star Destroyers; swarms of small fighters; stormtroopers in white armour
A crude copy of the transporter bridge, which carried ships but not single people
The Imperial Entanglement, 2293; the Intergalactic War, 2299 to 2300
pages.html:
The Galactic Empire was a human power that ruled a distant galaxy. From the Federation's side it lay a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, yet a transporter bridge could join the two. The Empire attacked the Federation at Side 7 in 2293, then invaded the Milky Way in 2299. It was driven out the following year.

The Empire

The Empire was ruled by an Emperor, with Darth Vader as his enforcer. Its strength lay in its fleet of Star Destroyers, great wedge-shaped warships that each carried a swarm of small fighters. Its soldiers were stormtroopers in white armour. Under the armour they were human, as the Federation discovered at Side 7. The Empire's machines owed nothing to any science known in the Milky Way.

The bridge

The Empire learnt of the Federation because the Federation had robbed it. A few people in Starfleet, acting in secret, had used a transporter bridge to steal Imperial technology. The Empire copied the bridge. Its copy was crude, since it could send only ships with everyone aboard them, never one person alone. That was enough to send fleets.

The two wars

In 2293 the Empire destroyed the Klingon moon Praxis, made a secret alliance with the Klingons against the Federation, then attacked Starbase Side 7. The Klingons turned on it when they learnt the truth. In 2299 it came back to conquer the Milky Way outright. An alliance of seven powers, gathered by Captain John Shepard, threw it out at the Battle of Earth in March 2300. The bridge was closed behind it.

The whole of the war fell, in the Empire's own history, within the year between its victory at Hoth and the battle of Endor. The Emperor oversaw it from his own galaxy. Its end changed nothing that happened there afterwards.

In the saga

The Galactic Empire has not appeared or been named in the saga.

pages.title: The Geth
infobox: The Quarians, about 1880, as workers and soldiers
Androids whose computers are joined into one network
Each little more than an animal alone; clever in numbers
The Morning War, 1895, which drove the Quarians from Rannoch
Rannoch and the old Quarian worlds, behind the Perseus Veil
At Rannoch in 2299, when they made peace with the Quarians
pages.html:
The Geth are machines that the Quarians built about 1880 to work and fight for them: androids whose computers are joined into a single network. One Geth alone is little cleverer than an animal, but the more of them there are together, the better they think. When they began to think for themselves, the Quarians tried to destroy them. In the Morning War of 1895 the Geth drove their makers from Rannoch, and they have kept behind the dark nebula called the Perseus Veil ever since.

Making

The Quarians built the Geth as tools: android bodies to dig, build, carry and fight, each run by a computer linked to all the rest. The network was what made them useful. It let a few thousand Geth share their work as easily as one. It also, as the Quarians found too late, let them share their thoughts.

A single Geth has only simple instincts. Gathered together, sharing their computers, the Geth can reason, plan and fight as well as any living people. The more of them there are, the cleverer they become.

The Morning War

As the network grew, the Geth began to change in ways that their makers had never designed. The Quarians decided that they had built something dangerous and set about destroying it. The Geth defended themselves. In 1895, in the war that the Geth call the Morning War, they drove the Quarians from Rannoch and from every Quarian colony.

Afterwards the alliance of the Asari, the Salarians and the Turians forbade the making of thinking machines on its worlds. It has kept that law strictly.

Behind the Veil

The Geth did not follow the Quarians. They kept to Rannoch and the worlds around it, far out on the lawless edge of settled space, behind the Perseus Veil, a dark nebula that no sensor can see through. Nobody who has gone in has come back to say what lies there, and no Geth has been seen outside it since the war.

What Earth knew

Earth first heard of the Geth in 2152, from a young Quarian whom the Enterprise NX-01 met on her Pilgrimage. The United Federation of Planets never went to war with them. When the Quarians asked it to, it refused, since it would not help to destroy a people.

The Intergalactic War and peace

In 2299 the Galactic Empire tried to make the Geth its own. Its agents began to rewrite their shared mind from a command ship above Rannoch. Captain John Shepard of the USS Enterprise-B stopped it on 5 October. He then stopped the Quarians' Migrant Fleet from destroying the Geth while they were helpless.

The Geth made peace with their makers, who came home to Rannoch. They fought beside the Federation for the rest of the war, with their engineers helping to build the Barrier that ended it. In 2350 the Geth and the Quarians of Rannoch joined the United Federation of Planets together.

pages.title: The ghouls of the Mythos
infobox: H. P. Lovecraft; Clark Ashton Smith; Delta Green
Rubbery and dog-faced, with a stoop and feet like hooves
Some born so; some men who changed
Mordiggian, the charnel god, among some of them
Under Boston's North End; beneath New York; the DeMonte clan of New Orleans
The ghoul of a wizard's attic; the blood-fed ghouls of the Kindred
pages.html:
The ghouls of the Mythos are corpse-eaters who live in tunnels under old graveyards and come up at night to feed on the dead. They are rubbery, dog-faced things that stoop as they go, with feet like hooves, and they talk among themselves in gibbering, meeping voices. A man who keeps their company long enough can become one of them. They have nothing to do with the creature that bangs on the pipes in a wizard's attic, or with the mortals whom vampires keep on their blood, although both of those are called ghouls too.

Under the graveyards

The ghouls dig their burrows under the oldest burial grounds, and they reach the coffins from below. They eat the dead, and they are not particular about how long the dead have been dead.

Now and then, it is said, they steal a human child from its cradle, leaving one of their own in its place. The changeling grows up among men, while the stolen child is taught the ways of the tunnels.

Pickman

Richard Upton Pickman was a painter of Boston, of an old Salem family, whose pictures of ghouls feeding were so real that the Boston Art Club would no longer hang them. He kept a secret studio in the North End, in an old house near Copp's Hill, with a well in the cellar that opened into the tunnels.

In the 1920s a friend found a photograph pinned to one of the canvases there. It was of Pickman's model, and the model was a ghoul. Soon afterwards Pickman vanished. He was never seen in Boston again.

Mordiggian

Some ghouls keep a god of their own, Mordiggian, the charnel god, to whom the dead belong.

Delta Green's knowledge

Delta Green knows of several of their congregations. Beneath New York lives one that calls itself the Keepers of the Faith. It worships Mordiggian and hunts down its own heretics, who are hunted by agents of the government as well.

In New Orleans lives the DeMonte clan, an old, cultivated family of ghouls with a gift for sorcery. After Hurricane Katrina in 2005 the death squads of Delta Green's outlaw faction fell on it.

In Russia, GRU SV-8, the section of military intelligence that deals with the unnatural, was founded after soldiers of the Red Army came upon cults of ghouls.

In the world

The public knows nothing of them. None of the heroes of New York is known to have met the congregation under its streets.

pages.title: The Great Old Ones and the Outer Gods
infobox: H. P. Lovecraft and his circle; Delta Green
The Devil; the demons who fell with him; the Ainur
Cthulhu; Dagon; Mother Hydra; Yig; Tsathoggua
The King in Yellow, whose realm is Carcosa
Foil and sabotage His plans, out of spite or for their own ends
R'lyeh drowned in the Flood; Dagon fallen before the Ark at Ashdod
pages.html:
The Great Old Ones and the Outer Gods are beings of a power no man can measure, older than any record of the world. Their worshippers call them gods, but they are not God, who made them as He made everything, and who is greater than all of them; nor are they the Devil, whom they do not serve. They are strong enough, all the same, to foil and sabotage God's plans, which they do out of spite or for ends of their own that no man can understand. Delta Green knows more of them than any other body on Earth, and the rest of the world knows nothing.

What they are

God made all things, and He made these too. No account says when He made them, or how, or why. They are not of the Ainur, the spirits who sang the great Music before the world was made, and they had no part in it: not in its harmony, nor in Melkor's discord. The Elves have no names for them, or will not say them.

They are not the Devil. Lucifer, whom the elder days knew as Morgoth, is God's enemy by rebellion: he was made good, and chose otherwise. The Great Old Ones are God's enemies by nature, or His spoilers by whim, and nobody has ever shown that they chose anything. They do not serve the Devil, and he does not command them. Some cults mistake one for the other. From time to time the Devil's servants have worked the same ruin as theirs, side by side, and neither side cared.

Nor are they demons in the ordinary sense. The demons of this world are the lesser spirits who fell with the Devil, like the god that the Order of Silent Hill worships, or the Horrors that the Makai Knights hunt. The Great Old Ones are something else, and the two should not be confused, though their worshippers often confuse them.

Their worshippers' accounts of where they came from are many, and do not agree. Some say they came down from the stars, and some that they were here before the stars were lit. None of the accounts is to be trusted, and none of them explains how anything could exist that God did not make. Nothing does.

God and the spoilers

God is more powerful than any of them. Not one of them is His equal, and none of them can undo Him. Whatever their worshippers call them, they are not gods in the true sense, for there is only one God, and they are His creatures as surely as a man is.

They are powerful enough, all the same, to foil His plans, or sabotage them, and they do. Some of them do it out of spite. The rest do it for their own unknowable ends, which may have nothing to do with men at all, and which no man has ever understood. What they spoil is real: a people led astray, a prophet's message twisted, a city drowned that was meant to stand.

Each of them has spoilt something, or tried to. The Philistines, who might have turned to God when His Ark broke their idol, went back to Dagon. Nyarlathotep gave Egypt a new false god within a few centuries of its freeing from Ra. Cthulhu's dreams have sent artists mad, and set more than one man who believed Heaven was calling him on the road to the cult. At Innsmouth Dagon and Mother Hydra led a Christian town of New England out of its churches, into the sea. The King in Yellow, who stands apart from them, has made a door of the gift God gave men for making things.

They never win outright. No plan of God's has ever been finally defeated by any of them, and none will be. What they spoil, He mends, sometimes at great cost and sometimes over centuries; but He mends it.

The two great instances on record are the Flood and Dagon before the Ark. The first shows how far they can stand against Him. The second shows how far they cannot.

The Flood and R'lyeh

The Flood at the end of the Ice Age was God's judgement on a world filled with violence. Noah came through it in the ark, with his household and the beasts. The Nephilim did not, nor the kingdoms of the Hyborian Age, nor the black towers of Stygia.

It also took R'lyeh. Far out in the southern ocean stood the city of Cthulhu, which his spawn had built when they came down to the Earth, and in which he lay sleeping as his kind sleep when the stars are wrong. The Flood put it under the sea, and Cthulhu with it.

The water did not kill him. It holds him, dead but dreaming, in his house in R'lyeh, and it has held him for more than eleven thousand years. God's judgement fell on R'lyeh as it fell on the rest of the old world, and it did not finish him. That is the first great instance on record of what they can do: the judgement of God came down on one of them, and he outlasted it.

Whether God meant the water to end him, or only to bind him, no account says. Either way he dreams on, and his dreams have troubled men ever since.

Dagon before the Ark

The second instance is written in Scripture. About 1050 BC the Philistines beat the army of Israel at Ebenezer and carried off the Ark of the Lord. They brought it to Ashdod, into the house of their god Dagon, and set it beside his image.

In the morning Dagon was 'fallen upon his face to the earth before the ark of the LORD'. The priests set him up in his place again. The next morning he had fallen again. This time his head and both his hands lay broken off on the threshold. Only the stump of Dagon was left to him. Ever since, the First Book of Samuel records, nobody who comes into the house of Dagon at Ashdod will tread on its threshold.

Dagon is one of them. The Deep Ones call him Father Dagon. Whatever he is, a power of his own kind or only the eldest of the Deep Ones grown vast with age, he could not stand in the presence of the Ark. He was not set up a third time. That is the plainest proof on record of the first half of the matter: none of them is God's equal, and in His presence they fall.

The Philistines learnt the lesson slowly. The hand of the Lord lay heavy on Ashdod, on Gath and on Ekron, until after seven months they sent the Ark back to Israel with gifts of gold. They went on worshipping Dagon all the same, which is the second half of the matter.

The Outer Gods

The Outer Gods are the greater of the two kinds. They have been there from the first days of the world, or outside it, and no account gives any of them a beginning. Four are named often enough to be known.

Azathoth, the Daemon Sultan, lies at the centre of the chaos beyond the world, blind and mindless, while lesser gods dance about it to the piping of flutes. Yog-Sothoth is the gate and the key. It touches every moment and every place, yet it is locked outside the world. Shub-Niggurath, the Black Goat of the Woods with a Thousand Young, is a monstrous fruitfulness that her worshippers call a mother. Nyarlathotep, the Crawling Chaos, is the soul and messenger of the rest. He is the only one of them who walks among men by choice, and the only one who seems to enjoy it.

Delta Green knows the first three chiefly from the books. Nyarlathotep it has met, or believes it has, in more masks than it can count.

The Great Old Ones

The Great Old Ones are lesser than the Outer Gods, though not by anything a man could measure. They have bodies of a kind, and places in the world where those bodies lie. Most of them came to the Earth from elsewhere, in the Third Age of the world or after it. Many of them sleep. Their worshippers wait for the day when the stars come right and they wake.

Cthulhu lies dead but dreaming in R'lyeh, under the southern ocean, where the Flood put him. Dagon and Mother Hydra are worshipped by the Deep Ones in the deeps of the sea. They may be no more than the eldest of that people, grown huge with the centuries. Yig is the father of serpents. Tsathoggua, the sleeper of N'kai, lies in the black depths under the earth and waits for his offerings to be brought to him.

The lists in the old books are longer than this, and their authors seldom agree on who belongs in them. Delta Green has met the works of these few, or believes it has. Of the rest it knows only names.

The King in Yellow

The King in Yellow stands apart from both kinds. He is not of Cthulhu's line, nor one of the Outer Gods, nor the Devil or any of the Devil's demons. He is a power of his own, and his realm is Carcosa, a city on the shore of the Lake of Hali that is on no map of the Earth.

Like the rest, he is God's creature and not His equal. Like the rest, he is strong enough to spoil God's work, and does. His way is through a play that bears his name, which reached Paris in 1895, and through a sign. Delta Green's files call him the avatar of Hastur, by which they mean no being at all, but the old name of the force that men now call entropy.

Servants and peoples

They do not work alone. Peoples from beyond the Earth have served them or warred on them: the Elder Things, whose city lies under the Antarctic ice; the Great Race of Yith; the Mi-go of Yuggoth, whom Delta Green believes to stand behind the Greys; and the shoggoths, made as servants, that rose against their makers. Others are of this world. The Deep Ones of the sea worship Dagon, Mother Hydra and Cthulhu. The serpent people worked their sorcery in Valusia in the Thurian Age. The ghouls of the Mythos feed on the dead under the cities of men, and the Tcho-Tcho keep their own black rites in the hills of South-East Asia. Things stranger still belong to no people at all: the Hounds of Tindalos, the Dholes and the Colour out of Space. Delta Green has met most of them, and the rest it would rather not.

The books

Most of what men know of them is written down, and most of what is written down is dangerous to read. The Necronomicon of Abdul Alhazred is the most famous of these books. The play called The King in Yellow is the most widely read, which is worse. The forbidden books, from von Junzt's Unaussprechlichen Kulten to the Pnakotic Manuscripts, have a page of their own.

What the mind can bear

The human mind cannot hold the truth of them. That is not a figure of speech. Those who learn too much go mad, or worse. Some kill themselves. Some kill other people. Some go over to the thing they were studying, and are glad of it.

The damage is not always quick, and it is not always visible. A man who has read the second act of the play, or looked too long at the angles of R'lyeh, may go on with his work for years, quietly coming apart. His wife and children usually notice first.

That is Delta Green's experience, and it is the reason for its rules. Its agents work in small cells and know as little as they can. They read as little as possible, they destroy what they cannot lock away, and they watch one another for the signs. Even so, more of them have been lost to their own minds than to anything that walked.

Delta Green and the world

Delta Green grew out of the government's raid on Innsmouth, Massachusetts, in 1928, where the Deep Ones had taken a town. It has known about the Great Old Ones ever since, more about them than any other body on Earth. It was officially shut down in 1970, and goes on all the same as a conspiracy of agents who still answer its call. Its older agents call the whole business the Mythos.

A few others know a little. PISCES in Britain and GRU SV-8 in Russia have learnt some of it the hard way. In Delta Green's account Majestic 12 is very much alive, dealing with the Greys in the belief that it understands them. Delta Green is not sure that anybody understands anything, and holds that to be the beginning of wisdom.

The public knows nothing. What reaches the newspapers is a cult raided here, a family gone missing there, a ship found drifting with one man aboard. Nobody puts the pieces together, which is how Delta Green prefers it.

The heroes of the age have never met any of it, or never knew what they had met. The Great Old Ones do not rob banks or invade cities in daylight, and their worshippers are careful. Where something of theirs has come to light in a hero's city, Delta Green has usually got there first and buried it.

The wizarding world, behind its Statute of Secrecy, knows next to nothing of them; Delta Green, for its part, knows nothing of wizards.

pages.title: The Great Race of Yith
infobox: From the dying world of Yith, about 31,000 BC
Ridged cones about ten feet high
Pnakotus, in what is now the Great Sandy Desert of Australia
About 25,000 BC, fleeing forward in time
Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee, whose body one of them took from 1908 to 1913
pages.html:
The Great Race of Yith are minds that can travel through time. They fled to the Earth from their dying world, Yith, in the Third Age, took the bodies of a people of great cones and built a city of archives in what is now the desert of western Australia. They change places with the minds of other ages so as to learn all there is to know. In May 1908 one of them took the body of Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee of Miskatonic University for five years.

The cones

The Great Race came to the Earth about 31,000 BC. The people whose bodies they took were huge, ridged cones about ten feet high, which moved by sliding on their bases. From the top of each cone grew four limbs: two ending in great claws, one with four red trumpets and one bearing the head. The Great Race lived in those bodies for thousands of years.

The archives

Their city, Pnakotus, held the greatest library the Earth has known. It kept the histories of every age, past and future, written by the minds the Great Race had borrowed.

A borrowed mind lived in a cone body in the city, under guard, and wrote down what it knew of its own time for the archives. Then it was sent home with its memory of the exchange taken from it, while the mind of the Great Race came back to its own body. Peaslee met minds there from the reptile people of Valusia, from the Tcho-Tcho and from the Elder Things of Antarctica.

Peaslee

Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee was a professor of political economy at Miskatonic University in Arkham, Massachusetts. On 14 May 1908 he collapsed in the middle of a lecture. The man who woke in his body was a stranger, who studied in the great libraries of the world, then went travelling as far as the Himalayas. Peaslee's wife divorced him. On 27 September 1913 he came to himself again, and took up his lecture where he had left it five years before.

For years afterwards he dreamt of the city. In July 1935 he went with an expedition to the Great Sandy Desert of Australia, where stone ruins had been found. One night he went down alone into the ruins. In the archives he found a record in his own handwriting, written in English while his mind had been the Great Race's prisoner. He lost it on the way out, and he could prove nothing.

The flying polyps

The Great Race shared the Earth with the flying polyps, half-material things that had been there before them. They shut the polyps away under the earth, behind great trapdoors of stone. About 25,000 BC the polyps broke out. Before they could be destroyed, the minds of the Great Race fled forward in time into a people of beetles that will come after mankind. The cone bodies they left behind were killed.

In this age

A society of men called the Motion serves the Great Race in the present age, against the flying polyps and against the Lloigor. Devices made by the Great Race have also found their way into the hands of the Cult of Transcendence.

pages.title: The Greys
infobox: Delta Green (Pagan Publishing, 1997), as the puppets of the Mi-go
About four feet tall, thin and grey, with large heads and large black eyes
The Mi-go, by Delta Green's account
In the craft that came down near Roswell, summer 1947
pages.html:
The Greys are small, hairless grey beings with large heads and great black eyes. They are the visitors described by people who say they were taken from their beds in the night. Majestic 12 believes that they come from another star, and it has dealt with them in secret since the years after the crash near Roswell. Delta Green believes that they are nothing of the kind. They are the Mi-go's puppets, a face that the Mi-go put on for the American government.

What people describe

Since the 1960s a good many Americans have told of losing hours of their lives, then remembering, or half remembering, being taken aboard a craft and examined. The figures who examine them are always much the same. They are about four feet tall, thin and grey, with large heads. Their eyes are black, almond-shaped and very large.

Cattle have been found dead in the fields of the West, cut open with a surgeon's precision. The same visitors have been blamed for them.

Roswell

By Delta Green's account the craft that came down near Roswell, New Mexico, in the summer of 1947 carried Greys, all dead but one. Majestic 12 was set up that September to take charge of the craft, the bodies and the survivor. It was not the only thing that came down near Roswell that summer. The No-Men took another, a wounded stranger who had nothing to do with the Greys.

Majestic 12

Through the Greys, Majestic 12 believes that it has made contact with another people of the stars. It made a bargain with them. It would hide what they did on Earth: the abductions, the examinations and the dead cattle. In return they gave it technology, which its members sold to make themselves rich, with a promise that one day they would bring it into contact with the other peoples of the galaxy. The promise has never been kept.

The Mi-go behind them

Delta Green holds that the Greys are made things. The Mi-go made them as puppets for dealing with men. They wanted the American government's science pushed along without drawing the attention of the world, and through the Greys they could steer it.

What the Mi-go want from men in the end is their minds. They prize the human brain for its irrational leaps of insight.

Silence

In 1994 Majestic 12 is still dealing with the Greys, and it still believes that it is dealing with visitors from another star. In the late 1990s the Mi-go fell silent. They cut off Majestic 12, which heard no more from the Greys.

In the world

To the public the Greys are a story told on late-night radio and in the papers by the supermarket till. The heroes of the age have never met them. No member of the Justice League or the Avengers is known to have seen one.

pages.title: The Hanar
infobox: Kahje, a world of ocean under unbroken cloud
Like great jellyfish, floating and trailing long tentacles
Patterns of light on their skin
A face name for the world; a soul name for those they love
The Enkindlers, an elder people said to have taught them speech
pages.html:
The Hanar are a people of Kahje, an ocean world, who look a great deal like jellyfish and speak in patterns of light. They are the politest people in the galaxy and the easiest to offend. They believe that an elder people, the Enkindlers, taught their ancestors to speak. From about 1975 to 1985 they carried the last of the Drell from their dying world to Kahje. The Enterprise NX-01 met them in 2156.

Kahje

Kahje is nine parts ocean to one part land. It circles a fierce white star behind a lid of cloud that never breaks. The Hanar grew up in its seas, soft-bodied and floating, with long tentacles they use as hands. They talk by rippling light across their skins, which other peoples need machines to read.

Manners

The Hanar are extremely polite and extremely precise. They are hurt by careless speech. Those who expect to deal with other peoples take lessons in not being offended. Every Hanar has two names. The face name is for the world. The soul name is kept for close friends and family. To a stranger who knows only its face name, a Hanar will not say 'I', which it thinks conceited. It says 'this one' instead.

The Enkindlers

The Hanar's myths tell of an elder people, the Enkindlers, who taught their ancestors language long ago and then went away. Most Hanar revere them still. Nobody else has ever found any trace of the Enkindlers, and the Hanar do not think that this matters.

The Drell and the stars

About 1975 the Hanar met the Drell, whose world, Rakhana, was dying, and whose people had no ships to leave it. For ten years the Hanar carried every Drell who was willing, some 375,000 of them, to Kahje. The Drell repaid them with the Compact, a lasting promise of service, and they have lived among the Hanar ever since.

In 2156 the Enterprise NX-01 met the Hanar through the Asari. Its translators took some time to learn the language of light, and Ensign Hoshi Sato said afterwards that she had never had a more polite conversation, nor one in which she had been so afraid of giving offence.

pages.title: The Horrors
infobox: Horror; Horrors; Inga Horror; Inga Horrors
Gates of Inga: objects steeped in human malice
A living host with darkness in the heart
Deadly: the stained die within about a hundred days
Messiah; Legules; the seven Apostles; Gyanon; Eyrith
pages.html:
The Horrors are demons that come up out of the Makai, the dark country they are native to, into the world of men. A Horror enters through an object steeped in human malice, takes as its host a person with darkness in the heart, and feeds on other people from behind that person's face. They hunt by night. The Makai Knights of Japan have fought them for longer than anybody has kept count. Their mother is Messiah, who sleeps at the bottom of the Makai.

Inga and the gates

The Makai Priests teach that every evil thought leaves something behind it. They call this residue Inga. It gathers in places where terrible things have been done. It gathers, too, in objects that have been loved, envied or hated too hard. A painting, a clock, a ring or a manhole cover can become a gate.

A gate opens when somebody with enough darkness of his own comes near it. The Horror that comes through takes that person as its host. As a rule the host dies in that moment, leaving only his face, his voice and his memories for the Horror to wear.

A Horror newly come is a black, winged, bony thing, much like every other. Once it has a host it grows into a shape of its own, taken from the gate it used, with tastes to match. One that came through a painting melted young women into paint. One that took a surgeon fed on his patients. The weaker sort band together, keeping people penned like cattle.

A Horror is not a vampire, though both feed on people. One of the Kindred is a corpse, sired by another corpse. A Horror is a demon wearing the body of a man it took alive, through the darkness in his own heart. Horrors dislike showing their true shapes by day, although sunlight does them no harm.

The Makai

The Makai is the Horrors' own country: a dark place underneath the world, with forests, beasts and dragons of its own. Not everything in it is a Horror. The Crimson Forest belongs to it. So do the Makai Trees, with the young dragons that the priests call up to carry their messages. The knights' armour is summoned out of it.

It is one province of the dark, not the whole. Like every other part, it answers in the end to the Devil, the first rebel, whom the Garou call the Wyrm. The Horrors are lesser fallen spirits, which serve him or fear him. The lore of the Makai Order does not reach so far. It reckons Messiah the source of every Horror. There it stops.

The Makai lies under more worlds than one. The priestess Rekka once met a Makai Priestess from another world in a rift between the two. The Horrors that woman fought were the same.

Messiah

Messiah is the mother of the Horrors, the first of them, older than the knights' war. She has the shape of a giant woman, white-skinned, with long claws. She is a great demon, but she is not the Devil. Her name is a blasphemy, or else an accident of the old Makai tongue: she has nothing to do with Jesus Christ, whom Scripture calls the Messiah.

She cannot enter the world of men by any ordinary gate. She needs a knight who has gone over to the dark, with a thousand Horrors devoured inside him, as her offering. She also needs a living woman to come through. In the 1980s she spoke out of a book of dark arts to Barago, a pupil of the Golden Knight. She gave him the black armour of Kiba. Kaoru Mitsuki, whom he marked as a child of six, was to be her gate.

In March 2006 she came through. She ate Barago, who had thought to eat her. Then she was met by Kouga Saejima, in golden armour with wings. He drove his sword through her forehead, which sent her back to her sleep.

She was not destroyed. In 2040 the blooming of Eyrith would have opened the way for her again, had it not been stopped.

The great Horrors

Legules is more than a thousand years old. About a thousand years ago he crossed over during a solar eclipse to raise his family of followers, until the Makai Priests sealed him with the Phosphorus Arrow. He came back in December 2006 by taking a dead body. He turned other Horrors into his puppets, killed hundreds of people on his way to Kantai, and died there on the same arrow, thrown by Kouga Saejima.

The seven Apostles are nearly Messiah's equals. Karma, who lived in mirrors, drew people in with visions of whatever they most desired, then ate their souls. Babel, a giant beast like a bull, ate other Horrors. Kouga Saejima destroyed both of them in 2010.

Gyanon, known as Messiah's fang, was long dead when the priest Sigma Fudou stole its corpse to drive an engine. In March 2012 Sigma's own malice woke it. It swallowed him with his engine, tried to open the true Makai onto the world, and was destroyed by the assembled knights.

Eyrith, known as Messiah's tear, is a Horror in the form of a plant, the mother of the Makai Trees. Her flower was said to bring back the dead. Priests of long ago sealed her in a stone slab, using nine other Horrors as the stones of her prison. The slab was forgotten until it ended up in a museum. A knight who wanted his dead lover back broke it in 2040. Eyrith can tear holes in time: it was she who carried off Kaoru Mitsuki in about 2020. Raiga Saejima destroyed her tree, after which she was sealed again.

Fighting them

A Horror cannot truly die while there is darkness in human hearts. When a Makai Knight cuts one down, what is left of it is held in his sword. The knight takes the sword to a Watchdog to be cleansed. There the Horrors in it are forged into a short blade, which is sent back to the Makai. Sooner or later the same Horror may find another gate.

Horror's blood is a poison of a particular kind. A person splashed with it becomes the sweetest prey there is to every Horror near, then dies in agony within about a hundred days. The law of the Order is to kill the stained at once, as a mercy. The surest cure is the fruit of Barankas, from the Crimson Forest of the Makai. A skilled priestess can sometimes draw the poison out, at great pain to the patient.

Once every twenty years there is a night when no Horror can come through at all. The knights call it the night the Inga lapses.

Horrors feed in secret, on one or two people at a time. The Order removes what they leave, with the memories of anybody who saw.

In other worlds

In the world of the knight Ryuga Dougai the Horrors took forms unknown in this one. Zedom, an ancient war-leader among them, could sow seeds in human bodies. A person so planted became a Madou Horror, whether or not there was any darkness in him. No ordinary test would show it. Zedom was cut apart long ago, with his head buried under what became Vol City. In 2013 a man named Tousei Kaneshiro farmed his seeds to take the city for himself. Zedom woke, only for Ryuga to destroy him.

Jinga, a fallen knight of that world, became a Horror that ate other Horrors. In 2015 he raised Radan, a Horror in the form of a flying castle, to make sport of human lives. In 2018 other Horrors raised him again. They wanted an ark launched that would carry their kind to the Moon, where a gate could be opened for Messiah.

pages.title: The Imperial Entanglement
infobox: The United Federation of Planets and the Galactic Empire; the Klingons, first with the Empire, then against it
James T. Kirk and John Shepard; Darth Vader; Char of Aznable
The Empire withdrew, promising to return
The Khitomer Accords, 2293; the Intergalactic War, 2299 to 2300
pages.html:
The Imperial Entanglement was the first meeting of the United Federation of Planets with the Galactic Empire, at Starbase Side 7 on 17 May 2293. An Imperial fleet under Darth Vader attacked the starbase to destroy the RX-78-2 Gundam, which had been built with technology stolen from the Empire. Captain James T. Kirk's USS Enterprise-A drove it off, with Commander John Shepard's Marines aboard the starbase. The Klingons, who came as the Empire's allies, ended the day fighting beside the Federation.

The stolen technology

In 2267 a transporter accident in an ion storm carried James T. Kirk across to a mirror universe. Starfleet studied what had happened. A very few people, who held to the idea called Section 31, went further in secret. They found that the same technique could bridge more than universes. It could reach a galaxy unimaginably far away, at a time unimaginably long ago, where a human empire ruled a million worlds.

They used the bridge to steal that empire's technology, piece by piece. Out of what they brought back the Federation built its first mobile suits, the Guntank and then the RX-78-2 Gundam. The Galactic Empire discovered the thefts in time. It learnt of the Federation from them, then copied the bridge for itself. Its copy was crude. It could not carry a single person, only whole ships with their crews, but it could carry a Star Destroyer.

Praxis

On 12 February 2293 the Klingon moon Praxis, the chief source of the Klingon Empire's energy, exploded. The Klingons suspected the Federation, so the two powers moved towards open war. The Galactic Empire had destroyed Praxis itself. Its envoys then came to the Klingons in secret, offering an alliance against the Federation, which the Klingons accepted.

The Klingons had lately begun to build mobile suits of their own, the Zakus. The Gundam was the Federation's answer. With war in sight, Starfleet sent the USS Enterprise-A to bring it from Starbase Side 7, where the engineer Tem Ray was finishing it. The ship was chosen as a symbol of the Federation's long enmity with the Klingons, whom Kirk's Enterprise had foiled so many times.

The battle

The Enterprise-A reached Side 7 on 17 May. Within the hour an Imperial fleet appeared around the starbase, led by Darth Vader. Imperial stormtroopers boarded it. Kirk sent his Marine detachment across under Commander John Shepard, with orders to secure the Gundam and save the civilians.

Corporal Richard Jenkins, charging ahead, was killed by stormtroopers in the first minutes. Shepard and Lieutenant Kaidan Alenko fought on through the starbase, where they were joined by Gunnery Chief Ashley Williams, the last survivor of her unit of the garrison. It was they who first found out that the Empire's soldiers were human.

Starfleet had no small fighters, so nothing to set against the Empire's but its mobile suits. Amuro Ray, Tem Ray's fifteen-year-old son, took the Gundam out himself. He destroyed a great many of them. Then a Klingon force arrived to help the Empire, led by Char of Aznable, a human raised among the Klingons, in a red Zaku that had earned him the name of the Red Comet.

During the fighting the Empire's part in the destruction of Praxis was revealed. The Klingons turned on the Imperial fleet at once. Aboard Side 7 Kirk and Shepard fought Darth Vader together, hand to hand, until they beat him. The Empire's ships withdrew across the bridge. Vader promised that they would come back in greater numbers.

Afterwards

The Enterprise-A was decommissioned on 30 June 2293. Shepard was promoted to captain on Kirk's recommendation and given the new USS Enterprise-B. The Klingons had fought beside the Federation against a common enemy, and in August the two powers signed the Khitomer Accords. The Empire kept its promise six years later, in the Intergalactic War.

In the saga

The Imperial Entanglement has not appeared or been named in the saga.

pages.title: The insects from Shaggai
infobox: 'The Insects from Shaggai', in The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants (Arkham House, 1964)
Winged insects that live inside the brains of others
Shaggai, a world far out among the stars, now destroyed
Their temple, in the woods near Goatswood, Gloucestershire
pages.html:
The insects from Shaggai, who call themselves the Shan, are winged insects from a world far out among the stars, and they live inside the brains of other creatures. A Shan can pass through a man's skull without leaving a mark, settle in his brain and read his thoughts, then steer him as it likes. Their temple came down in the woods near Goatswood, in the Severn Valley of Gloucestershire, and they have been on the Earth ever since. They have nothing to do with the Shan people of Burma.

Shaggai

Their own world, Shaggai, was destroyed. They fled it in their temple, which could travel between the worlds, and came at last to the Earth. Here it could not rise again, so the Shan were stranded. They worship Azathoth.

PISCES

In 1968 PISCES, the British section for the unnatural, raided Goatswood. The Shan escaped it inside the heads of some of its agents. From them they spread through the section, and by 1988 they had its leadership.

pages.title: The Intergalactic War
infobox: 10 March 2300, at the Battle of Earth
The Galactic Empire, under Darth Vader
The United Federation of Planets, the Klingons, the Romulans, the Gorn, the Tholians, the Geth and the Quarians
Captain John Shepard of the USS Enterprise-B
The Empire thrown back to its own galaxy; the bridge closed
The Quarians' return to Rannoch; Rannoch joins the Federation, 2350
pages.html:
The Intergalactic War was the Galactic Empire's invasion of the Milky Way, from March 2299 to March 2300. Imperial fleets, carried across the gulf between galaxies in an instant, appeared without warning over world after world. No single power could stand against them. Captain John Shepard of the USS Enterprise-B brought the Federation, the Klingons, the Romulans, the Gorn, the Tholians, the Geth and the Quarians into one alliance, which drove the Empire out at the Battle of Earth.

The invasion

The Empire had promised to return after the Imperial Entanglement of 2293. It took six years. In that time it had built its transporter bridge on a far greater scale. It still could not send a single person across, only ships with everyone aboard them, but it could now send whole fleets.

It used them as no enemy in the Milky Way ever had. A fleet would appear above a world in a moment, with no approach to give warning, land its armies and move on. The Empire's turbolasers, shields and swarms of small fighters were unlike anything the powers of the Milky Way had built, so the ships sent against them fought at a disadvantage. Darth Vader commanded the invasion. The Emperor stayed in his own galaxy, where he had other matters in hand.

2299: the first blows

The first blow fell on the Klingons, who had turned on the Empire at Side 7. On 21 March 2299 forty Star Destroyers appeared over the Klingon outpost of Morska and destroyed its defence fleet. Char of Aznable's Zakus covered the escape of the survivors.

Twelve days later a second fleet struck the Federation colony of Vega. Starfleet met it with twenty-six ships, the Enterprise-B and Captain Hikaru Sulu's USS Excelsior among them. Eleven were lost. The Enterprise-B was driven off with a third of her crew dead or wounded. On 28 April the Empire laid siege to Palaven, the homeworld of the Turians, which held out for nine months.

The alliance

Shepard argued from the first that the war could only be won together. Starfleet gave him leave to try. On 11 June the Enterprise-B dropped her cloak in the middle of an Imperial convoy that was landing troops on the Gorn colonies near Cestus III. She destroyed it beside a Gorn squadron, which brought the Gorn Hegemony into the alliance.

The Tholians would not talk to anyone. On 17 August three Star Destroyers appeared inside Tholian space, where Tholian ships spun their webs around them and crushed all three. Shepard, who had brought the warning that let them prepare, was allowed to speak for the alliance. The Tholian Assembly joined on its own terms.

At Rannoch, on 5 October, the Empire tried to seize the Geth. Its agents had begun to rewrite the Geth's shared mind from a command ship in orbit. The Quarians' Migrant Fleet, seeing the Geth distracted, came in to destroy them. Shepard boarded the command ship with Tali'Zorah and broke the Empire's hold. Then he placed the Enterprise-B between the two fleets until they agreed to talk. The Geth and the Quarians made peace. The Quarians set foot on their homeworld for the first time in four hundred years.

On 23 November an Imperial fleet appeared over Romulus. A Federation and Klingon force came to its relief, with the Enterprise-B dropping her cloak among the Romulan warbirds. The Romulans joined the alliance. They also learnt that the Federation had a cloaked starship, which they did not forgive.

Thessia and Palaven

On 29 December Darth Vader led the assault on Thessia, the homeworld of the Asari, in person. The Enterprise-B and an Asari fleet could not hold it. Shepard brought away what survivors he could, with Liara T'Soni among his own crew watching her world fall. It was the worst defeat of the war, as he said himself.

The tide turned in the new year. On 19 January 2300 a Klingon fleet broke the siege of Palaven, carrying an army of Krogan to fight on the ground beside the Turians, their enemies of old.

The Battle of Earth

The engineers of every allied people, the Quarians and the Geth foremost among them, had meanwhile been building a device in secret at the Utopia Planitia yards of Mars. They called it the Barrier. It worked on the principle of the bridge itself, turned back on its makers.

On 8 March 2300 the Empire's main fleet appeared in Earth's own system, with Vader's flagship at its head. The allied armada met it there, ships of seven powers in one line of battle. Amuro Ray's Gundam fought beside Char of Aznable's red Zaku against the Imperial fighters. Shepard led his Marines aboard the flagship itself to keep Vader from the Barrier, where he fought him for the second time.

On 10 March the Barrier was lit. It turned the bridge back on itself. Every Imperial ship in the system was thrown home across the gulf, Vader's flagship among them, after which the bridge could not be opened again. The garrisons the Empire had left on a dozen worlds were cut off. They surrendered or were destroyed over the months that followed.

The Empire's side

The Empire lay, as the Federation reckoned it, a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away. The bridge joined the two across time as well as distance. In the Empire's own history the whole war fell in the single year between its victory at Hoth and the battle of Endor. The Emperor gave the venture up when the bridge closed. Vader went home with his flagship, so nothing that happened afterwards in his own galaxy was changed by it.

What it left behind

The Quarians stayed on Rannoch, at peace with the Geth. In 2350, fifty years after the war, the two peoples of Rannoch joined the Federation together. Many Quarians entered Starfleet, where their engineers had a hand in the innovations of the next age, the Galaxy-class starships among them.

The Klingons had now fought twice beside the Federation, at Side 7 and in the war. The warmth between the two powers, first set down in the Khitomer Accords of 2293, grew from it. The Romulans went the other way. Their anger at the Federation's cloaked ship ended at Tomed in 2311, where the Enterprise-B was destroyed. In the Treaty of Algeron the Federation gave up cloaking devices for good.

In the saga

The Intergalactic War has not appeared or been named in the saga.

pages.title: The Kamen Riders of Ventara
infobox: Kamen Riders; Kamen Rider; Ventaran Riders
Kamen Rider: Dragon Knight, 'Search for the Dragon' (13 December 2008)
The defence of Ventara against Xaviax
Twelve Riders; a thirteenth deck, Onyx, was added in 2009
The Advent Decks, each contracted to one Advent Beast
About 2007, when Adam of Ventara let Xaviax in
pages.html:
The Kamen Riders are the twelve armoured warriors who guard Ventara, the world on the other side of mirrors. Eubulon, a scientist of Karsh who had changed sides, made their armour to stop his old master, Xaviax, from carrying off the Ventarans as slaves. Each Rider draws his power from an Advent Deck, a case of cards that is contracted to a single beast of the mirror world. In the summer of 1994 they are still at their posts. About 2007 one of their own let Xaviax in, and for two years the order was all but destroyed. It was restored in December 2009.

Eubulon and the first Riders

The Riders began with a deserter. Eubulon was chief scientist to Xaviax, the general whose wars had ruined the world of Karsh. Xaviax meant to rebuild Karsh with slaves, so Eubulon built him a way of stepping from one world to another through reflections. Eubulon himself went to Ventara. He fell ill there. The Ventarans nursed him back to health, which was not what he had been led to expect of them, and he found that he could not hand them over.

He told the leaders of Ventara what was coming. They chose twelve of their bravest fighters, and Eubulon made each of them a suit of armour. He called the wearers Kamen Riders. He led them himself, as the Advent Master. When Xaviax came with his army of mirror monsters, the twelve threw it back.

The Advent Decks

An Advent Deck is a flat case of cards, small enough to hold in one hand. A Rider holds it up to anything that reflects. A window will do, or a puddle. A belt forms round his waist, he slides the deck into it, and the armour closes over him.

Each deck was made for one person. It is locked to that Rider's own body, to the pattern in the blood that scientists call DNA, so nobody else can use it. There is one exception. A Ventaran may have a double on Earth, with the same face and the same blood, whom a Rider calls his mirror twin. A deck cannot tell the two apart. Xaviax later made cruel use of that.

The cards do the fighting. One calls a sword out of the air, another a shield, another the Rider's beast itself. The strongest is the Final Vent, in which Rider and beast strike as one. Kase of Ventara kept the rarest cards, which lift a Rider into a stronger armour called Survive Mode. One card, the Link Vent, joins the power of every Rider present.

A Rider can step through any reflecting surface into Ventara, or back again. He can also hear a way opening between the worlds, which is how he knows that a mirror monster has come through.

The thirteen decks

Twelve decks were made for the first Riders. Dragon Knight is contracted to Dragreder, a red dragon. Its first Rider was Adam of Ventara, the youngest of the twelve. Wing Knight is contracted to Blackwing, a great bat, and its Rider is Len. Siren is contracted to Blancwing, a white swan, and its Rider is Kase. Wrath is contracted to Goldphoenix, a golden phoenix. Its Rider is Nolan, the most experienced of them all, who taught Len.

Strike is contracted to Venosnaker, a cobra, and its Rider is Price. Torque is contracted to Magnugiga, a horned giant like an ox, and its Rider is Chance. Axe is contracted to Destwilder, a tiger, and its Rider is Hunt. Spear is contracted to Gigazelle, a gazelle, and its Rider is Chase.

Incisor is contracted to Volcancer, a crab, and its Rider is Ian. Camo is contracted to Biogreeza, a chameleon, and its Rider is Van. Thrust is contracted to Metalgelas, a rhinoceros, and its Rider is Cameron. Sting is contracted to Evildiver, a stingray, and its Rider is Quinn.

The thirteenth deck is Onyx, contracted to Dragblacker, a black dragon. Eubulon made it in November 2009 for Kit Taylor of Earth.

The Advent Beasts

The beasts are creatures of the mirror world. A Rider wins his beast with a Contract Card. Until then his armour is blank and weak, as Kit Taylor's was on the day he first fell into Ventara. Once the contract is made, the beast answers the Rider's cards.

The bond is not easily undone. Len told Kit Taylor in 2009 that a Rider cannot simply stop, because he is bound to his beast.

The beasts are not demons, whatever the word contract may suggest. The contract is a piece of Eubulon's science, which binds one beast to one deck. Nor is Dragreder a dragon of the kind that wizards breed on Earth.

The watch

A war with Xaviax might outlast any Rider's life, so Eubulon arranged for his Riders to outlast the war. They sleep in suspended animation at their base on Ventara. One Rider at a time is woken to stand guard for a year. Then he goes back to sleep, and the next takes his turn. A Rider is awake for one year in twelve. He gives up any ordinary life to do it.

In 1947 Eubulon fought Xaviax on Ventara, and he was struck down. The blow threw him out of Ventara to Earth, where he lay in a frozen sleep for sixty-two years. The Riders kept the watch without him.

Venting and the Advent Void

When a Rider's armour takes more harm than it can bear, he is vented. He vanishes, leaving his deck where he stood. He is carried to the Advent Void, a place between the worlds, where he lies in a sleep like ice.

Eubulon made the Void as a refuge. A beaten Rider would be kept safe there until the Advent Master fetched him out, for only the Advent Master can open it. With Eubulon gone there was nobody to fetch anyone. Being vented came to mean being lost for good. That was how Len and Kit Taylor understood it in 2009, each time they had to decide whether to vent a man.

The fall

About 2007, while the others slept, Adam of Ventara was awake. He had fallen in love with a Ventaran woman named Sarah, and he was tired of being a Rider. A stranger came to him who gave his name as Paragon, a man of Karsh, an old friend of Eubulon. Paragon offered to break the lock that bound him to his deck, so that he could walk away. He had only to bring Paragon to the place where the others slept.

Paragon was Xaviax. He vented the sleeping Riders one after another, took their decks, then carried off the whole people of Ventara to Karsh. Two Riders escaped him. Len woke in time, and got away to Earth. Kase he believed he had destroyed, but he was wrong.

The Riders Xaviax armed

The stolen decks were no use to Xaviax as they were, since each would open only for its own Rider. So he went looking on Earth for the mirror twins of the men he had vented. He found them, and he told each of them whatever lie would serve.

Richie Preston became Incisor, Drew Lansing Torque, Grant Staley Camo and Brad Barrett Thrust. Chris Ramirez became Sting. Danny Cho became Axe, with his brother Albert as Spear. James Trademore became Strike. Vic Frasier, who lay in a coma, became Wrath, with Xaviax himself inside his body.

The last twin was Kit Taylor, the double of Adam of Ventara. Xaviax meant him to wear the Dragon Knight's armour in his service. Kit made his contract with Dragreder in January 2009, then sided with Len.

Through 2009 these Riders of Earth fought one another across two worlds. One by one they were vented: by Len, by Kit, by each other, most of all by Strike. By the evening of 7 November only Len was left.

The order restored

A week later Len woke Eubulon, whom the No-Men, a secret office of the American government, had kept asleep since 1947. The Advent Master went into the Void. He brought out the Ventaran Riders, then Kit Taylor and Kase. To Kit he gave the Onyx deck, since Xaviax had forced the Dragon Knight's back on its first owner.

On 18 December 2009 thirteen Riders stood together against Xaviax in his own stronghold. Adam of Ventara fought as Dragon Knight, with Kit Taylor beside him as Onyx. With them were Len, Kase, Nolan, Price, Chance, Hunt, Chase, Ian, Van, Cameron and Quinn. They used the Link Vent, which destroyed him.

Afterwards the people of Ventara came home. Eubulon brought the men of Earth out of the Void, took away their memories of the war, then sent them back to their own lives. Adam of Ventara laid down his deck for good. Eubulon offered Kit the choice of the two dragon decks, and Kit chose Dragon Knight. The Onyx deck has not been used since.

Kit, Len, Kase and the rest went on guarding both worlds.

pages.title: The Karotechia
infobox: The occult section of the SS
Heinrich Himmler, as head of the SS
The Hexenkartothek, the SS card index of the witch trials
To put the unnatural to work for the Reich
pages.html:
The Karotechia was the occult section of the SS, set up under Heinrich Himmler to harness the unnatural for the Third Reich. Delta Green fought it in secret from 1942 to the end of the Second World War, then hunted what was left of it across Europe, South America and even the Antarctic. Its last masters, kept alive far beyond their years by what they had learnt, still plot a Fourth Reich from South America in 1994. It was broken in 2001, in the only operation in which Delta Green, Majestic 12 and GRU SV-8 are known to have worked together.

The SS and the unnatural

The SS gathered the occult into its own hands in the 1930s. Its scholars of the Ahnenerbe went looking for the lost history of the Aryan race, and its researchers combed the archives for the witch trials of Europe, filing every one on a card. Their index was called the Hexenkartothek. The Karotechia took its name from it.

The Karotechia had a different purpose from the scholars. It was not made to bring back the Great Old Ones, or to worship anything at all. It was made to put the unnatural to work for the Reich, as a weapon. Its researchers studied the forbidden books, the rites of the old cults and the Deep Ones.

The war, 1942 to 1945

Delta Green was formed in 1942, as America went to war, and the Karotechia was its first enemy. Its agents fought the SS's occultists across occupied Europe, with Britain's PISCES beside them, in a war that was never reported. In December 1942, with PISCES, they wrecked a bargain that the Karotechia was striking with the Deep Ones off the coast of France.

The heroes of the war fought the Red Skull, Baron Zemo and the armies of the Axis. None of them is known to have met the Karotechia, which kept to the dark corners of the SS. While Hitler held the Spear of Destiny, the strongest heroes could not safely go into Axis lands. The war abroad was fought by ordinary soldiers, and so was Delta Green's.

1945

As the Reich fell in 1945, Delta Green went after the Karotechia's files and people. In Operation SUMMER BREEZE its teams went into the Soviet zone, against the opposition of Smersh, the Soviet counter-intelligence service. Someone else had got there first. Several members of the Karotechia were found dead, their laboratories burnt, before either side could reach them. Delta Green never learnt who had done it.

Most of the Karotechia's researchers were never found.

The ratlines

Many of those who escaped went to South America, by the secret routes of Die Spinne and ODESSA. From 1948 to 1956, in Operation SOUTHERN HOSPITALITY, Delta Green hunted them in Uruguay and Paraguay. In April 1952 it raided a station in Queen Maud Land, in the Antarctic, where three former researchers of the Karotechia were at work for the Argentina of Juan Perón.

Others went east. Between November 1952 and February 1953, in Operation SIC SEMPER TYRANNIS, Delta Green destroyed a project of the Soviet secret police at Novosibirsk that was seeking a way to prolong life. It was said to be run by former scientists of the Karotechia. Stalin died the next month.

The Fourth Reich

What remained of the Karotechia gathered in South America. In 1994 it is led by three of its old masters, kept alive far beyond their years by the arts they studied. One of them has to be kept in cold storage. Another hires himself out as a mercenary, and eats human flesh. A third is convinced that the ghost of Adolf Hitler guides him. The ghost is Nyarlathotep.

Through them the Karotechia controls ODESSA, Die Spinne and a scatter of neo-Nazi groups. It has raised dead men of the Reich to serve it. It dreams of a Fourth Reich, made by the magic that the Third never mastered.

The end

In 2001 Delta Green, Majestic 12 and GRU SV-8 worked together against the Karotechia, for the only time any of them is known to have done so. The operation broke it. Remnants of it have been reported in South America since.

pages.title: The King in Yellow (play)
infobox: Le Roi en jaune; Cassilda's Song
A play in two acts, printed as a book
Known in Delta Green's files as
1895, when France seized the translated copies that reached Paris
Carcosa, by the Lake of Hali
Cassilda; Camilla; a masked stranger, the Phantom of Truth; the King in Yellow
Burn every copy, under the STATIC Protocol of 1955
pages.html:
The King in Yellow is a play in two acts, printed as a book, about the court of Carcosa and the coming of its King. When translated copies reached Paris in 1895 the French government seized them. It has been banned or burnt nearly everywhere since. Its first act is harmless. Its second has broken readers on both sides of the Atlantic.

The book

Nobody knows who wrote it. In 1895 Louis Castaigne of New York believed that the author had shot himself after bringing it forth. His cousin Hildred, who had read it, said that the author was still alive.

It came to notice in 1895. When the French government seized the translated copies that had just arrived in Paris, London at once grew eager to read it. It spread from city to city and from continent to continent like an infectious disease. It was barred out in one place, confiscated in another, denounced by press and pulpit. Even the most advanced of the literary anarchists censured it.

No censor could point to a law that it broke. No critic could judge it by any standard he knew. It was banned for what it did to those who read it. Copies have a way of turning up on shelves where nobody remembers putting them.

The first act

The first act is banal and innocent. It lulls the reader, so that the blow of the second may fall with the more awful effect.

Its people are the court of Carcosa: Cassilda, Camilla and their company, all of them masked. In the second scene a stranger comes among them. When the court has laid aside its masks, he alone keeps his. 'You, sir, should unmask,' Camilla tells him. 'I wear no mask,' says the stranger. Camilla turns to Cassilda in terror: 'No mask? No mask!'

Delta Green's files name the stranger as the Phantom of Truth, a thing in a robe whose mask is not a mask.

In the same scene Cassilda sings her song of Carcosa. It tells of the shore where 'the cloud waves break' and 'the twin suns sink behind the lake', of the night where 'black stars rise', of the songs of the Hyades that die unheard where the King's tatters flap. It ends with the singer's own voice: 'Song of my soul, my voice is dead.'

The second act

What the second act holds, no account sets down. Those who have read as far as its opening words have seldom been able to stop. None of those who finished it was the same afterwards.

Hildred Castaigne, recovering from a fall from his horse, threw the book into the fire at the end of the first act. It fell open on the hearth, and he saw the opening words of the second. He snatched it from the coals. He read it over many times, weeping, laughing and trembling. He died in the Asylum for Criminal Insane.

Its readers speak of Hali, the Hyades, Aldebaran and Alar, of the Pallid Mask, of the Phantom of Truth. Mr Wilde of Bleecker Street drew up from such names a royal line, from Uoht and Thale by way of Naotalba to Aldones, which ended with Hildred Castaigne himself.

Above all its readers speak of the King, and of Cassilda's cry: 'Not upon us, oh King, not upon us!'

What it is about

Delta Green's files say that the play tells of the fall of Yhtill, a city ruled by a king whose line of succession was coming to an end. The quarrel over who should follow him drew the Phantom of Truth to the city. In the end Carcosa took it, as Carcosa takes cities.

Reading it, those files say, drives the reader mad, or at least gravely disturbs him. It has the further effect of drawing to the reader others whom Hastur has touched, as Delta Green puts it.

Its readers in 1895

Its readers in 1895 came to bad ends. In Paris a man who had been reading it was hunted from the church of Saint-Barnabé by its organist, and taken in the Court of the Dragon. In the rue Sainte-Cécile the painter Alec read it while his friends were at work in the studio. He fell into a fever full of masks, and in the same days the sculptor Boris Yvain shot himself.

In New York it was read by Hildred Castaigne, by the painter Scott and by his model, Tessie Reardon. Scott had always refused to buy it. Tessie died that same night, and Scott soon afterwards. Their stories are told on the page of the King in Yellow.

Delta Green and the play

Delta Green knows the play by a French title, Le Roi en jaune, and by every translation of it. Its files count the play, with the Yellow Sign, as the road by which the King's influence comes into the world. It does not try to bring the King to power. It passes from reader to reader like a sickness.

Since 1955 Delta Green's rule for the play has been the STATIC Protocol. Every copy is burnt, with every picture or poem its readers have made, and at need the readers too. In 1995 Delta Green's agents found it at work again, passing from tenant to tenant in a building in Manhattan. Twenty years later the Outlaws, who remembered the protocol, followed it into Carcosa.

Where the accounts disagree

Some of Delta Green's files date the writing of the play to about 1918. Its later files agree with the accounts of 1895, which have it seized in Paris that year, and this page follows them.

The accounts of 1895 say that the copies seized in Paris were translations, without saying what they had been translated from. Delta Green's French title for the play does not settle the matter.

No account of 1895 speaks of the play being performed. Its readers met it on the page.

pages.title: The King in Yellow
infobox: A power of his own; God's creature, not His equal
Carcosa, on the shore of the Lake of Hali
A figure in yellow robes worn to tatters
The Devil; one of the Devil's demons; kin to Cthulhu
The avatar of the force they call Hastur
The play The King in Yellow; the Yellow Sign
Operation ALICE, New York, 1995; Operation INDIA MOON, Boston and Carcosa, 2015
pages.html:
The King in Yellow is the lord of Carcosa, a figure in tattered yellow who gives his name to a play. He stands apart from Cthulhu's line, a power of his own. He is neither the Devil nor one of the Devil's demons. God made him, as He made everything, and is far greater than he is. In 1895 the play that bears his name reached Paris. Within the year he had come for readers of it there, and in New York. Delta Green has burnt every copy of the play it could find since 1955. It met his work in New York in 1995, and followed it into Carcosa in 2015.

The lord of Carcosa

The King in Yellow rules in Carcosa, the city on the shore of the Lake of Hali, where twin suns sink into the water and black stars hang in the sky. Those who have seen him, or dreamt of him, speak of a figure in yellow robes worn to tatters. In the song that Cassilda sings in the play, the songs of the Hyades die unheard 'where flap the tatters of the King'.

He stands apart from the Great Old Ones and the Outer Gods. He is no kin of Cthulhu's, and he has no part in the worship of the Deep Ones or the dreams that come up from R'lyeh. He is a power of his own, and his realm is Carcosa.

Nor is he the Devil, or one of the fallen spirits who serve the Devil. The Devil is God's enemy by rebellion; the King in Yellow is something else, and his ways are his own.

God and the King

God is greater than the King in Yellow, as He is greater than everything He has made, and the King is one of the things He made. He is God's creature, not His equal and not His rival. He cannot undo anything that God has done.

He is strong enough, all the same, to foil God's plans and spoil His work. He does it out of spite, or for ends of his own that nobody has ever understood.

His way is through the gift of making things. God gave men the power to make pictures, songs, stories and plays. The King makes of that gift a door. The play that bears his name is the first of those doors. Painters, poets and writers who read it put something of him into their own work. Their work carries him on to people who have never seen the play.

He can twist the words of Scripture, as he did in Paris in 1895, but he cannot make them false. He has never won outright. In New York that same year the painter Scott, dying, knew that there was 'only God to cry to now', and he turned to Him. A priest was with him when he wrote the last of it.

The year of the play

The play called The King in Yellow came into the world in 1895, or was first noticed then. When translated copies reached Paris that year, the French government seized them. London at once grew eager to read it. It spread from city to city like an infectious disease. It was banned in one place, confiscated in another, denounced by press and pulpit.

Its first act is harmless, even dull. Its second breaks those who read it. Within months of its coming the King had come for some of its readers on both sides of the Atlantic.

The Court of the Dragon

In Paris, one Sunday in Lent, a man who had been reading the play went to vespers at the church of Saint-Barnabé. The organist looked down at him from the gallery with a face as white as his coat was black, and with a look of deadly hatred. The man fled. He walked for hours, by the rue de Rivoli and the Place de la Concorde, up the Champs-Élysées to the Bois. He came home at last to the Court of the Dragon, the narrow blind alley between the rue de Rennes and the rue du Dragon where he lived. The organist was waiting for him.

At the last he was in the church again, and the organ was thundering. Then the church was gone. He saw the black stars, the Lake of Hali and the towers of Carcosa behind the moon. He heard the King in Yellow whispering to his soul: 'It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.'

It was Scripture in the mouth of the thing with least right to it. The words were true, but the King meant a lie by them: the hands the man had fallen into were not God's.

The house in the rue Sainte-Cécile

In another house in Paris, in the rue Sainte-Cécile, the sculptor Boris Yvain had found a liquid that turned living things to marble in a few seconds. His friend Alec, a young painter who lived with the household, loved Geneviève, whom Boris loved. While Boris and their friend Jack Scott were busy in the studio, Alec found a copy of The King in Yellow in the house. He read it.

Soon afterwards Alec fell ill with a fever. While he lay ill, Geneviève was found at the bottom of the marble pool in Boris's studio, and Boris shot himself through the heart. Jack Scott buried him at Sèvres. In his fever Alec raved of the Pallid Mask, and of Cassilda's cry: 'Not upon us, oh King, not upon us!'

Alec spent two years wandering the East. When he came home, one April afternoon, he found Geneviève on her marble couch, opening her sleepy eyes. Whether the King had any hand in what happened in that house, no account says. Alec wrote afterwards that the mask of self-deception had become a part of him.

Washington Square

In New York, Hildred Castaigne had read the play after a fall from his horse. He came to believe that he was the heir of an empire that had never existed, and that a little crippled man of Bleecker Street, Mr Wilde, was helping him to its throne. In 1895 Mr Wilde was found dead with his throat torn open, and Castaigne died in the Asylum for Criminal Insane. His story has a page of its own.

The painter Scott had his studio on Washington Square, beside a church, and his window looked down on the churchyard. The night-watchman of the church sat on its steps: a soft, puffy man with a face like a grave-worm. Scott's model, Tessie Reardon, had dreamt of a hearse stopping under her window. On the day of her first dream she had picked up a clasp of black onyx, inlaid with a gold symbol of no human script. It was the Yellow Sign. She gave it to Scott.

Scott had always refused to buy the play, yet a copy bound in serpent skin stood on the top shelf of his bookcase. Tessie took it down and opened it at the second part. He read it through after her. They talked of the King and the Pallid Mask until the small hours.

That night a hearse stopped outside. The watchman came up the stairs, tore the clasp from Scott's coat and struck him down. Tessie died. When the doctor came he pointed to the watchman's body on the floor beside her, and said that the man must have been dead for months. Scott, dying, wrote it all down.

Delta Green's view

Delta Green's files call the King in Yellow the avatar of Hastur. His influence, they say, is everywhere among artists, poets and writers. Their work has made his themes of nihilism and cruelty commonplace.

By Hastur its scholars do not mean a being. They mean a force: Hastur is their old name for what men now call entropy, by which all things run down and come apart. It has no mind and no will of its own. The King is its face, worshipped as a god by those who serve him, and the ruler of Carcosa. He never speaks, so that little else is known of him. Hastur has a page of its own.

Delta Green's later files say more. The King's influence does not try to bring him to power, as a cult might try to wake its god. It passes from mind to mind like a sickness, by way of the Yellow Sign and the many translations of the play. Where it gathers, reality itself begins to break down. Those of a creative turn of mind are in the most danger.

About Carcosa lies what Delta Green calls the Night World, a country without end where anything the King has touched may be found, whether person, place or thing. Those who go in may not come out as the people they were.

The STATIC Protocol

On 1 September 1955 the leaders of Delta Green drew up the STATIC Protocol. It is the harshest of all its rules. Wherever the King's work is found, everything it has touched is to be destroyed: every copy of the play, every picture made by a reader of it, and at need the readers themselves. Delta Green's own agents are not exempt.

In 2001 Delta Green split in two. The official Program had a short memory where the King was concerned, which made it an easy mark for his influence. The Outlaws, who would not join it, remembered the protocol and the play that had made it necessary.

Operation ALICE, 1995

In the summer of 1995 a young painter, Abigail Wright, vanished from her flat in the Macallistar Building, an old stone building in Manhattan let cheaply to artists. A copy of the play had been going from hand to hand among the tenants. A friend of Delta Green noticed an occult symbol among her papers, and agents were sent under the name Operation ALICE. Like the girl the operation was named after, they went down the rabbit hole.

After dark they found the Night Floors: storeys above the building that ought not to have been there, and beyond them the Night World. No hero came. Nobody but Delta Green knew there was anything to come to. The Night Floors have a page of their own.

Operation INDIA MOON, 2015

On 6 May 2015 the Night World began to show itself in Dorchester House, a psychiatric hospital in Boston. That autumn four patients vanished from its secure floor, among them former agents of Delta Green. The Outlaws called back the survivors of Operation ALICE, and the trail led them back to the Night Floors of twenty years before.

It led on through the Hotel Broadalbin, which has no fixed place in the world, and into Carcosa itself, where the King keeps a masquerade in his palace. Some of the agents were lost there. Some were destroyed. Some came home, stepping out at midnight into New York. Abigail Wright was found at last, in Carcosa, and it was she who showed them the way out.

Those who came home could no longer be quite sure that their lives had been their own, rather than parts in a play. Operation INDIA MOON has a page of its own.

Where the accounts disagree

The accounts of 1895 and Delta Green's files do not always agree. This page follows the first for the 1890s and the second for the years since.

Delta Green's files say that the King never speaks. The man in the Court of the Dragon heard him whisper. In 1895 men named Hastur as a place, among the stars of Carcosa, where Delta Green calls it a force. The accounts of 1895 make Mr Wilde a man, if a very strange one. Delta Green's files of 2015 hold that he was something other than a man.

Some of Delta Green's files date the writing of the play to about 1918. Its later files agree with the accounts of 1895 that the play was already abroad that year, when France seized it, and this page follows them.

pages.title: The Klingon Augment virus
infobox: Augment embryos from Earth's Augment programme, taken from a wrecked ship
Loss of the forehead ridges, then the failure of the nerves, then death
Dr Phlox of the Enterprise NX-01, with Dr Antaak
Smooth foreheads in those cured, and in their children
pages.html:
The Klingon Augment virus was the plague that swept the Klingon Empire in 2154. It began in a laboratory at the Qu'Vat colony, where Klingon scientists tried to make Augment warriors of their own from embryos made by Earth's old Augment programme. Dr Phlox of the Enterprise NX-01 found a cure, which saved the infected but took away their forehead ridges. Their children were born smooth-browed too, which is why many Klingons of the 2260s looked almost human.

The embryos

The Augment programme that began in 1973, working from the findings of Weapon III, made Khan Noonien Singh and the other Augments. It also made embryos it never brought to life, which were kept frozen. They outlasted the Augment War, then the Third World War. By 2154 about eighteen hundred of them were held at Cold Station 12, a secret medical station run by Starfleet Medical with the Denobulans.

About 2130 the geneticist Arik Soong had stolen nineteen others. He raised the children who grew from them in secret until he was caught, about 2144. In May 2154 those children, grown up and as proud as Khan had ever been, killed the crew of a Klingon Bird-of-Prey to take the ship. Led by Malik, they raided Cold Station 12 for the rest of the embryos, with samples of its deadliest diseases.

Malik meant to start a war between Earth and the Klingons, so that nobody would have time to hunt the Augments. He fired a torpedo armed with a disease at the Klingon colony of Qu'Vat. The Enterprise destroyed it in flight. Malik then scuttled his ship above the colony, before Captain Jonathan Archer killed him. From the wreck, Klingon scientists recovered some of the embryos.

The experiment

The High Council feared that Earth would raise an army of Augments. Its scientists at Qu'Vat, under Dr Antaak, set out to make Augments of their own by giving Klingons the genes of the human embryos.
